title: Astilbe
content: Astilbe is one of those go-to perennials that brings so much to the garden. Its distinctive blooms range from bright and bold to soothing pastels, and they last for weeks—even months when you have the right combination of astilbes. The ferny, pest- and disease-free foliage provides great texture for your shade garden, and deer and rabbits usually give it a pass. Astilbe can even grow in full sun if you have a spot with plenty of moisture.

title: Astilbe
content: Astilbe spp. and hybrids include Chinese astilbe, Japanese astilbe and star astilbe, with blooms in pink, white, red, peach, cream or lavender plumes from late spring to fall. They like moist, well-drained soil and can tolerate full sun to full shade. Keep them watered and they will reward you with long-lasting color in the shade garden.

title: Astilbe
content: Large shade-garden photo showing the astilbe border and the lush planting texture used on the opener spread.

title: Astilbe tip
content: For lots of these pretty plumes, water astilbe regularly or site it where the soil stays consistently moist. Then you can grow other moisture-loving companions, such as queen of the prairie.

title: Astilbe
content: Tall border photo of astilbe with the white caption box describing moisture-loving companions.

title: Grow Gorgeous Astilbe
content: Keeping your border filled with color can be a challenge, but when you grow astilbe it’s a snap. These beautiful blooms last 3 to 4 weeks, and when you grow a mix of astilbe with a range of bloom times, you can keep borders colorful for 2 to 3 months. Start the season in late spring with early bloomers, such as pale pink ‘Europa’ Japanese astilbe or medium pink ‘Flamingo’ star astilbe. After that, mid- to late-summer varieties like hybrid ‘Maggie Daley’ take over. The combination of upright flower stems, tidy mounds and deeply dissected leaves makes astilbe an excellent companion in almost any situation.

title: Grow Gorgeous Astilbe
content: Large astilbe border photo with pink plumes and layered shade plantings.

title: Caring for Astilbe
content: Water, water, water. Astilbe doesn’t do well with dry soil. When the roots dry out, the leaves get brown edges and can even die back to the ground. Grow plants in a spot that gets regular water or site them near a natural water feature. Is deadheading necessary? Some gardeners prefer to cut the blooms off once the color fades and enjoy the foliage as a ground cover for the rest of the season. Get more astilbe by division in spring when new growth is poking through the soil. Each section should have at least three growth points.

title: Brighten Shade
content: When you want to kick your shade garden design up a notch, astilbe is a great solution. ‘Red Sentinel’ and ‘Snowdrift’ both grow to about 2 feet tall and wide — big enough to make a statement but small enough that they still work well near the front of a border. You can see the wonderful contrast in texture between the lacy astilbe foliage and the broad hosta nearby. White flowers like those of ‘Snowdrift’ practically glow in deeper shade under the trees, drawing visitors along the path to explore more of the garden.

title: Brighten Shade
content: Astilbe border photo showing 'Red Sentinel' and 'Snowdrift' brightening a deeper shade planting.

title: More Gorgeous Astilbe
content: Astilbe’s range of flower colors and season-extending help are just the beginning of its versatility and charm. When you want colorful height for a border, you might not think about astilbe, as most grow in the 18- to 30-inch range. But there are a few taller varieties that make great border additions. ‘Superba’ Chinese astilbe can grow up to 4 feet tall and provides beautiful back-of-the-border interest. Looking for even more height? Try Appalachian false goat’s beard, which despite its common name is an astilbe native to North America.

title: More Gorgeous Astilbe
content: Large border photo showing taller astilbe varieties and companion plantings in a moist garden bed.

title: Astilbe bouquet tip
content: Cut a few astilbe blooms to enjoy in your summer bouquets. For the longest vase life, snip the stems when half to two-thirds of the individual flowers are open and get them in water right away.

title: Peppers
author: Niki Jabbour
content: It doesn’t matter if you prefer the sweet crunch of a bell pepper or the fiery heat of a habanero; growing your own peppers is easy and rewarding. Sweet peppers have little to no heat and ripen through a range of colors, while hot peppers can run from the mildly spicy poblano to the five-alarm fire of a Carolina Reaper. Peppers are heat- and sun-loving vegetables that need a long growing season, so they are typically grown from seeds started indoors or purchased as transplants in late spring.

title: Scoville scale
content: The Scoville scale measures the hotness of a pepper in Scoville Heat Units. Capsaicin is the compound in peppers that produces a burning sensation. Knowing where a pepper ranks on the scale, from 0 for sweet bell peppers to 1,500,000+ for Carolina Reaper, helps you choose ones that are best for your heat tolerance.

title: Scoville scale
content: Scoville scale infographic showing heat levels from bell pepper to Carolina Reaper.

title: 4 Tips for Growing Peppers
author: Niki Jabbour
content: Start seeds indoors 8 to 10 weeks before your last frost date, using a heated mat if you have one and giving seedlings at least 16 hours of light each day. Transplant peppers after the last frost into full sun and fertile soil, spacing plants 12 to 18 inches apart and staking them at planting time. Peppers do best in a long growing season and will respond to consistent care.

title: 4 Tips for Growing Peppers
author: Niki Jabbour
content: Seed tray and transplanting photos showing peppers started indoors and moved to the garden.

title: 4 Tips for Growing Peppers
author: Niki Jabbour
content: Water peppers by checking the soil 2 inches down and keep them evenly moist to avoid blossom end rot. Mulch to reduce watering needs and fertilize every 2 to 3 weeks after planting with a liquid organic fish and seaweed fertilizer. Harvest sweet peppers at their mature size and color, clip ripe peppers with garden snips rather than yanking them, and preserve the surplus by dehydrating, pickling, freezing or turning them into hot sauce.

title: Be on the lookout
content: Blossom drop can come from overwatering, cool nights or daytime temperatures over 90 degrees F. Sunscald appears as white to brown papery patches when young fruit is suddenly exposed to the sun. Bacterial leaf spot causes leaf loss and stunted fruits; if it’s been a problem before, use resistant varieties, rotate crops and space plants for good air flow.

title: Meet 6 Types of Peppers
author: Niki Jabbour
content: Sweet peppers have little to no heat and a sweet, fruity flavor. Bell peppers are essential in the kitchen and the garden, while corno di Toro and banana peppers bring long, tapering fruit and plenty of versatility. Specialty cultivars such as ‘Candy Snax Mini Pepper Mixture’, ‘Majestic Red’, ‘Cornito Giallo’, ‘Carmen’, ‘Goddess’ and ‘Sweet Banana’ offer a range of colors, sizes and ripening times.

title: Chili Peppers
author: Niki Jabbour
content: Hot peppers can run from mildly spicy to fire-alarm fiery. Jalapeños are a kitchen staple, cayenne peppers are excellent dried for flakes and habaneros bring scorching heat and citrusy flavor for hot sauce and spicy salsas. Other notable selections include ‘Jedi’, ‘Fiesta Cayenne Blend’, ‘Red Flame’, ‘Red habanero’ and ‘Red Savina’. Hot peppers contain capsaicin, so wear gloves when slicing and dicing and wash your hands carefully when you’re done.

title: 1st Prize Foliage
content: Stacey Toomey’s 60×14-inch windowbox is attached to an east-facing window in part shade. An antique shutter on the front provides interest when the plants are still small. She bought three 12-inch preplanted hanging basket combos that included wing begonia, inch plant and potato vine, then filled in with individual 4-inch pots. Maintenance is simple: water, feed and trim.

title: 2023 Reader Container Challenge
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: This is the time of year that containers are top of mind for every gardener. Half the fun of planting them is trying out new combinations or swapping plants out for new looks each season. The other half is seeing what other gardeners have come up with — a little inspiration can really get the creative juices flowing. Last year we put out a call to readers asking them to send in their best container designs so we can share them with everyone here. The response was amazing — our readers really know how to put together beautiful containers!

title: Containers that Make an Entrance
content: Shirley’s 17-inch-tall and 24-inch-square containers provide a brilliant greeting on either side of the sidewalk that leads to her front door. They’re packed with colorful annuals that bloom from spring to frost. The large-leaved coleus splashed with pink makes an eye-catching thriller, while globe amaranth and lantana are drought tolerant and don’t need deadheading. Shirley’s palette of bright, warm colors could easily be swapped for pastels or a monochromatic theme if that fits better with your garden’s style.

title: Sophisticated Color
content: Sandy’s container combination uses shades of purple to bring a relaxing vibe to her deck. Sunny yellow from the variegated vinca and bright magenta petunia adds some pop. Most of the plants are quite heat and drought tolerant and take summers in stride. To keep this container flowering, Sandy sprinkles Osmocote® on top of the potting mix at planting time, then fertilizes every 3 weeks with a liquid plant food.

title: Taste of the Tropics
content: Joyce put this grouping together with leftovers from other containers she’d planted up earlier, and it turned out great. Its bright and bold blooms from lantana and mandevilla bring warmth, excitement and a tropical feel to the patio. The plants don’t need any deadheading and are quite drought tolerant. Look for mandevilla varieties with a bushy habit, such as Sun Parasol® Original Red.

title: Keep Shade Colorful
content: A shady out-of-the-way corner can be a challenging place to put a container, but Claudia found a group of plants that thrive on neglect, providing color and texture from spring to frost. Snake plant, purple heart, tall sedum, lantana, asparagus fern and dichondra keep this sophisticated container going without much fuss.

title: One Terrific Trough
content: When you have a special planter like this 48×18-inch antique stone trough, you want to give it pride of place. Sophath has done that by incorporating it into the foundation planting so it sits outdoors in this zone 6 garden all year and the contents get swapped out seasonally to keep curb appeal high. Mounds of begonia, iresine and purple Swedish ivy cover the long stems of the row of elephant ears that provide lots of interest and drama.

title: Passionate About Purple
content: Charlene’s planter is really a plastic insert slipped into a decorative wrought-iron plant stand, but you can’t tell by looking at it. The growing conditions on the west side of the house in full sun can be harsh, but this group of plants did just fine. Angelface Blue angelonia makes a great thriller and provides a stately presence and loads of color from late spring to frost.

title: Cottage Garden in a Box
content: Linda has been trying different plants over the years to get a cottage garden look for the 8-foot-long windowbox just outside her dining room window. She finally discovered a combination that provides maximum color with minimal effort. This mix of annuals, from the upright angelonia to the bacopa spilling over the front, doesn’t need deadheading and looks great with just an occasional feeding and watering.

title: Flowers to the Max
author: Leanne James, CT
content: Adding a windowbox is a great way to integrate the storage shed in with the garden. Leanne plants 4 1/2-inch pots in a custom-made 36×10-inch wooden windowbox, adds a slow-release fertilizer at planting time and then starts using a water-soluble plant food every 10 days. Most of the plants are vigorous growers and need maintenance pruning every 3 weeks to keep the look full instead of wild.

title: Sun-Soaked Side Yard
content: Sure, your side yard might be hidden from sight, infrequently traveled or have minimal square footage — but is it sunny? With careful planning, this area can become its own secret garden: an intimate spot that delights all the senses with lovely sights, smells and even tastes. Take advantage of this full-sun situation and grow stunning blooms as well as flavorful edible plants. You just need to employ some tried-and-true small space design hacks to make it happen.

title: Sun-Soaked Side Yard
content: Large design illustration of the side yard plan with layered plantings and a central path.

title: Seeing Diamonds / Double Duty Fig Tree
content: Purchase a customizable kit to make this diamond-patterned trellis of nylon line and train the clematis onto the wires as new growth emerges in spring. The small patio is a place to naturally stop and observe the garden more closely while you’re on your way to the backyard. Large, soft-lobed leaves and deep purple fruit of ‘Fignominal’ fig make an interesting focal point and it also keeps its leaves through winter, which makes it a great indoor houseplant for colder zones.

title: Seeing Diamonds / Double Duty Fig Tree
content: Trellis illustration and patio vignette showing the diamond-patterned clematis support and the fig tree focal point.

title: Minimal Effort, Maximum Benefits
author: Chloe Deike
content: You’ll want to get a start on this garden in late winter. It’s most economical to grow the annual plants from seed, especially the basil and the marigolds. Start a flat of each indoors 4 to 6 weeks before your average last frost date. When the seedlings have three or four sets of true leaves, pinch them back to the next lowest leaf node to encourage more branching and a fuller habit. When nighttime temperatures are consistently in the 50s, harden off the annuals and plant them in the ground.

title: Design Challenge key plants
content: The planting plan uses delphinium, marigold, Greek basil, bearded iris, balloon flower, tomato, blueberry, clematis, dwarf fig and two apple trees to create a sunny, highly productive side-yard planting. The design emphasizes a tall backbone of trellis and fruiting plants with lower annual color to keep the space layered and useful all season.

title: Tips for Growing Healthy Trees in Containers
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Container-grown trees provide height in spots where you can’t plant in the ground and add drama and permanence where you might normally just grow annuals. Use a container at least 20 inches in diameter and height, avoid pots that narrow at the top and root prune every 2 to 3 years to encourage smaller feeder roots and prevent girdling. Many trees can be grown in pots for up to 20 years or more if the roots stay healthy.

title: Tips for Growing Healthy Trees in Containers
content: Large container tree photo showing a red-leaf Japanese maple in a teal pot.

title: Root pruning steps
content: Slice the bottom roots, shear the sides, untangle the roots and then replant the tree. Trim about 2 inches off the bottom of the root ball, shear 1 to 2 inches off the sidewalls, tease out tangled roots with your fingers or a hand rake and repot into the same container or one no more than 2 inches larger in diameter. Water thoroughly and keep the tree planted at the same level as before.

title: Alliums rising to the surface
author: Kristi Boone, MI
content: If you planted alliums several years ago and now they’re poking through the soil, it’s probably the winter freeze-thaw cycle. If the bulbs are completely above soil level, gently tuck them just below the surface. If only these alliums are affected, that is pretty normal. If your bulbs have been planted for years, as clumps multiply, young bulbs often rise to the surface. Alliums are related to onions and can adjust their depth to what they like better.

title: Q&A: Plant sale divisions
content: If you’re getting perennials ready for a plant sale, go big with large, robust divisions that have several growing points. Wash all of the soil from the roots so you don’t pass along weeds, insects or disease, label each plant clearly, be honest about aggressive growers, get newly potted plants established before the sale and check for patents before selling divisions.

title: Horticultural oils and pollinators
author: Hunter Reagan, AR
content: It all depends on time of day and time of year. Horticultural oils are intended to smother or suffocate crawling or stationary insects, so they must be applied directly to the pest. It is best to spray early or late in the growing season, while temperatures are cold and bees and other pollinators are dormant. If you apply oil sprays during the growing season, use a more diluted concentration and spray early in the morning or late in the evening when temperatures are cool but pests are still active.

title: Weed watch: Pilewort
content: Pilewort, Erechtites hieracifolia, is a native annual with tall stems topped by loose panicles that can look like buds that never open. Its tiny tubular flowers are held inside a tight bract, and after pollination the seedhead reveals tiny brown seeds attached to tufts of soft white hairs. It prefers moist soil in full sun to part shade and is easiest to control by pulling or mowing young plants before they set seed.

title: Colorful Shade
content: There are plenty of flowers and loads of gorgeous foliage in this combo to keep shade borders bright from spring until frost. Deadhead the hosta and coral bells by cutting the spent stems off below the foliage. The yellow corydalis and Solomon’s seal may reseed, but it’s easy to pull the ones you don’t want to keep.

title: One Tough Hosta With Long-Lasting Color
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: When it comes to hostas you don’t want to miss, put ‘Wolverine’ at the top of your list. This fast-growing variety with blue-green leaves edged in gold has been tough as nails in shade or sun and looks good even with 4 to 6 hours of sun a day. Lavender flowers top the scapes in late summer, and the plant grows into a broad mounded habit that holds its own in a mixed border.

title: 6 Solutions Every Gardener Needs
content: Taking care of a garden requires many skills, and you might be a master of the basic ones. But for every gardener there are days when you walk outside and find your regular rhythm interrupted by an unexpected need. This bonus feature gathers six tricky situations so you can prepare yourself with the know-how to tackle them and be ready to keep yourself and your garden in tip-top shape.

title: Garden edge solutions
content: Use trenched edging to dig straight down 4 to 5 inches and create a slope that keeps soil in place. Brick or stone edging needs a shallow trench filled with sand, and metal edging can be pounded into place with a rubber mallet and secured with stakes.

title: Garden Solutions
content: Illustrations for trenched, brick or stone and metal edging solutions.

title: A disorganized garden shed is slowing you down
content: Clear and easy access to your tools and supplies can make gardening much easier, and it helps you take better care of your gear. Separate tools and gear by size or purpose, use shelves for stakes and twine, keep a workspace for gloves and rags, and store long-handled tools upright by the door so you can grab them fast.

title: A disorganized garden shed is slowing you down
content: Garden shed photo showing tools, pots and supplies arranged in the workspace.

title: An aggressive plant is taking over
content: If a plant is dominating the border or reseeding where you don’t want it, remove it altogether. Pull out the plants growing in the wrong place, including the roots and stems if it spreads by runners. If it covers a large area, smother it with cardboard and thick mulch. If it’s spreading by seed, remove the flowers before they set seed.

title: The nectar feeder needs cleaning
content: A nectar feeder should be cleaned routinely, otherwise you risk harming the hummers. Drain the nectar, take apart the feeder and soak the pieces in warm water with vinegar. Scrub the basin and feeder holes, rinse thoroughly and let everything dry completely before refilling. Replace the nectar regularly, as often as once a day in hot full sun.

title: The nectar feeder needs cleaning
content: Photo of a hummingbird feeder used in the cleaning instructions.

title: Outdoor furniture is dirty and worn
content: A set of furniture that’s continually exposed to the elements can take a beating. Wicker should be dusted, washed with warm soapy water and protected from sun and moisture. Wood can be cleaned, dried and sanded; plastic can be scrubbed with soapy water and a little baking soda; metal can be wiped down with dish soap and dried completely to prevent rust.

title: Outdoor furniture is dirty and worn

title: Dress for success
content: Wear long sleeves and long pants, even in the heat of summer, to keep yourself protected from rashes and bugs. Hang a long-sleeved button-up shirt near your gardening gloves, keep a light pair of elastic-waist pants by the door and wear tall boots or long socks with your shoes and gloves to protect your ankles and wrists from potential hazards.

title: Your health is at risk
content: Gardening is good exercise and mentally stimulating, but there are also some serious hazards lurking out in the garden. Wearing the right clothes is a great example, and you can keep yourself safe and healthy by dressing in long sleeves, long pants, boots and gloves, then checking for ticks and using repellents when needed.

title: Your health is at risk
content: Photo of a pair of tall garden boots used in the dress-for-success advice.

title: Mosquitoes, soil-borne bacteria and poison ivy
content: Mosquitoes can carry diseases such as West Nile virus, La Crosse virus and Eastern equine encephalitis, so remove standing water and use bug repellent to deter bites. Tetanus bacteria live in soil, dust and manure and can enter through cuts or wounds, so wear gloves and stay up to date on your vaccine. Poison ivy contains urushiol oil that can cause an itchy rash, so cover exposed skin, remove the vine carefully and wash clothing and skin after contact.

title: Reader Tips
author: Joanne Meyer, IA
content: Perfectly poised florals: Level up your home-grown floral arrangements with this simple hack: Re-use plastic drinking straws to support cut flowers with floppy heads. Just rinse the straw and slide it on or slit the straw down the side and wrap it around the stem. It’ll provide extra support for weak spots along the stem and drooping flower heads. Professional florists use a similar product to keep blooms upright, but you can achieve the same look—for free!

title: Reader Tips
author: Eva Woodring, TN
content: Tomato shade: When the weather turned from cool spring to hot summer in a matter of days last year, Eva looked for a way to get her tomato seedlings into the garden as soon as possible without letting the tender plants burn in the hot sun. Some plastic 5-gallon bucket lids saved the day. After she planted the tomatoes, Eva slid a lid into each tomato cage and rested it on the bottom ring, where it provided a little shade while the sun was high and hottest. She removed the lids after a few days once the tomatoes had adapted to the outdoors and were less vulnerable to direct sun. You can purchase bucket lids separately if you don’t have any on hand.

title: Reader Tips
author: Maryanne Weaver, PA
content: Water at the ready: Recycle your empty laundry detergent dispenser (the type you lay on the side with a button to dispense the soap) and use it in the garden! Rinse it well, fill with clean water and then place it wherever you might need to do some rinsing. Maryanne keeps one on the picnic table in the summertime to wash messy hands. You could also place it next to the vegetable patch to clean soil off of produce before bringing it indoors. Or keep the dispenser on the potting bench to rinse pots and tools. It would even work as a backup watering can for containers that are far from a hose spigot.

title: Reader Tips

title: Reader Tips
author: Virginia Ayers, IN
content: Easy feeding station: Looking to add a little more life and color to a corner of your yard? Virginia discovered that an old three-armed clothes rack packed a big punch in a little space. On the arms of the clothes rack, she hung three hummingbird feeders. At the base, she stabilized the clothes rack with three planters filled with colorful annuals. Look for a used three-armed clothes rack at thrift stores and garage sales to save money. You might find that three hummingbird feeders attract more hummingbirds to the spot, or you might have one aggressive hummingbird who defends all three feeders for himself until the hummers to realize there’s enough food for everybody.

title: Reader Tips
author: Valerie Baxter, IL
content: Save a little water and time by keeping your watering can in your bathroom! While you’re waiting for your shower or bath water to warm up, place the can under the faucet to catch the extra. Valerie also keeps her water-soluble fertilizer nearby to add to the can so it can dissolve while she finishes getting ready.

title: Pest Watch
content: Elderberry rust (Puccinia sambuci), Appearance: This fungal disease affects elderberry plants (Sambucus spp. and hybrids) in mostly aesthetic ways, although severe infections can decrease fruit production. You might first notice bright orange lesions, called pustules, followed by unusual galls, typically the pale yellow color in the photo above.

title: Pest Watch
content: Elderberry rust (Puccinia sambuci), Damage and control: The pustules appear in spring and can cause leaves to defoliate and stems to deform. In severe infections, rust-colored dust covers flower stems and disrupts fruit production. The strange galls appear in summer. If you grow both elderberry shrubs and sedge grasses (Carex spp. and hybrids), there’s a higher risk of infection. In late summer, the spores travel from the galls to the sedge leaves to overwinter, creating rusty spots with yellow halos. Eliminating sedge grasses in your yard is the most effective, though sometimes the most difficult, form of control, because it will prevent the disease from surviving the winter. You can keep a small infection at bay by cutting back any leaflets that show signs of infection. A small infection is unlikely to affect the fruit production, so just a little trimming goes a long way in keeping the disease from becoming a problem.

title: Fabulous Summer Flowers
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Fabulous Summer Flowers: There are two ways to keep the color going in your garden through the summer: First, choose a variety of annuals that bloom from the moment you set the seedlings in the ground until frost (the combo at right is a great example of this technique). Second, plant combinations of perennials that bloom at different times. Meet some good candidates for early and late summer on the next pages. Choose one or two of these combos or grow them all in different spots in your garden to guarantee that you (and visiting pollinators) will have plenty of blooms to enjoy from the time the weather warms up until the cold shuts everything down in fall.

title: Fabulous Summer Flowers
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Show-Stopping Annuals: It’s never too late to grab a few annuals at the garden center and pop them in the ground, where they’ll splash color across your garden until frost. Long-blooming, easy-care zinnias, salvias and marigolds offer so many different colors that you can have a lot of fun creating combinations. Plus, the mounding, draping habit of hakonechloa makes a perfect front-of-the-border plant and frames its companions beautifully. Regularly deadheading zinnia, salvia and marigolds encourages new blooms and keeps plants looking tidy.

title: Fabulous Summer Flowers
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Show-Stopping Annuals plant A, Canna (Canna spp. and hybrids): Tender perennial; red, orange, yellow, pink, white or salmon flowers in summer; full sun; 2 to 8 ft. tall, 1 to 4 ft. wide; cold hardy in USDA zones 7 to 11.

title: Fabulous Summer Flowers
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Show-Stopping Annuals plant B, Zinnia (Zinnia elegans State Fair Mix): Annual; red, orange, yellow, pink, purple, white or bicolor flowers from summer to frost; full sun; 36 to 48 in. tall, 12 to 14 in. wide.

title: Fabulous Summer Flowers
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Show-Stopping Annuals plant C, Mealycup sage (Salvia farinacea): Tender perennial; white, purple or blue-purple flower spikes from summer to frost; full sun to part shade; 12 to 36 in. tall, 9 to 16 in. wide; cold hardy in USDA zones 8 to 11.

title: Fabulous Summer Flowers
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Show-Stopping Annuals plant D, French marigold (Tagetes patula): Annual; white, yellow, orange, red or bicolor flowers from early summer to frost; full sun to part shade; 6 to 12 in. tall and wide.

title: Fabulous Summer Flowers
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Show-Stopping Annuals plant E, Hakonechloa (Hakonechloa macra ‘Aureola’): Perennial; variegated foliage with insignificant yellow-green flowers from late summer to fall; full sun to part shade; 12 to 24 in. tall and wide; cold hardy in USDA zones 5 to 9.

title: Fabulous Summer Flowers
content: Show-stopping annual flower combination with red cannas, pink and orange zinnias, purple mealycup sage, orange French marigolds, and variegated hakonechloa.

title: Fabulous Summer Flowers
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Early Summer Beauty: It’s no secret that blue and yellow flowers create striking contrast. Choose one in a spike shape and the other in a daisy shape, and you’ll have the perfect pairing. For a long-lasting show of color, deadhead spent flowers to encourage new ones throughout the summer. Pollinators love both of these perennials, but deer tend to avoid them. When the last of the blooms have faded, cut back flower stems to the foliage to tidy up the plants.

title: Fabulous Summer Flowers
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Early Summer Beauty plant A, Spike speedwell (Veronica Moody Blues® Sky Blue): Perennial; spikes of blue flowers from late spring to frost; full sun; 12 to 14 in. tall and wide; cold hardy in USDA zones 4 to 9.

title: Fabulous Summer Flowers
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Early Summer Beauty plant B, False sunflower (Heliopsis helianthoides ‘Sunstruck’): Perennial; yellow daisylike flowers with golden centers from summer to frost; full sun; 14 to 16 in. tall, 12 to 14 in. wide; cold hardy in USDA zones 4 to 9.

title: Fabulous Summer Flowers
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Late-Summer Show-Off: After the nonvining clematis retires for the season and sends out the fluffy white seedheads above, the purple blooms of ornamental onion and creamy pink and red flowers of sedum make their debut. All are equally loved by bees and butterflies, plus deer and rabbits tend to avoid them. Cut clematis down to 3 to 4 inches from the ground in early spring and give plants extra support by using stakes or cages. Cut spent flowers of allium to keep the plants looking their best.

title: Fabulous Summer Flowers
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Late-Summer Show-Off plant A, Clematis (Clematis ‘Stand by Me’): Perennial; blue bell-shaped flowers followed by fluffy seedheads from late spring to midsummer; full sun to part shade; 34 to 38 in. tall, 24 to 36 in. wide; cold hardy in USDA zones 3 to 7.

title: Fabulous Summer Flowers

title: Help Drought-Proof Your Garden
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Help Drought-Proof Your Garden: If you’re tired of watering to keep your garden going through a hot, dry summer, take a few tips from Denver Botanic Gardens’ Panayoti Kelaidis. He’s had to learn how to create a good-looking garden that thrives through heat and drought and has some advice that can help all of us.

title: Help Drought-Proof Your Garden
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Right plant, right place: For starters, Panayoti suggests doing an inventory of your yard with an eye out for microclimates. Make sure you’re growing drought-tolerant plants in the driest spots and not trying to baby something along that isn’t happy there. You might find dry microclimates at the top of a slope or even in the shade of shallow-rooted trees. Most common are spots near driveways, house foundations or retaining walls, where heat from the sun is often reflected onto the garden. Panayoti likes to say that the north side of his house is like Alaska, and the south side is like Arizona. He grows ferns and woodland plants on the north side, while xeric plants make their home on the hot, dry Arizona side. If a plant is struggling, it’s probably not in the right place. The wall absorbs heat during the day and releases it into the air and soil, even at night.

title: Help Drought-Proof Your Garden
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: How plants tolerate drought: Characteristics that help plants through dry times include large, thick or fleshy root systems and leaves that are slender, succulent, waxy or fuzzy. Prairie plants, such as little bluestem, purple coneflower and cup plant, grow roots deep into the soil to seek out moisture. Fleshy bulbous roots or bulbs of all types, including the foxtail lily at right and the woody rhizomes of bearded iris, store water. Small-leaved herbs, such as lavender, rosemary and fennel, are able to withstand long periods without rain.

title: Help Drought-Proof Your Garden
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Botanical Names: Bearded iris, Iris hybrids; Cup plant, Silphium perfoliatum; Fennel, Foeniculum vulgare; Lavender, Lavandula spp. and hybrids; Little bluestem, Schizachyrium scoparium; Maple, Acer spp. and hybrids; Purple coneflower, Echinacea purpurea; Rosemary, Rosmarinus officinalus.

title: Help Drought-Proof Your Garden
content: Portrait of Panayoti Kelaidis, Director of Horticulture Outreach at Denver Botanic Gardens.

title: Help Drought-Proof Your Garden
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Foxtail lily (Eremurus spp. and hybrids): When Panayoti wants an exclamation point for the border, foxtail lily is what he chooses. Its massive blooms are made up of tiny starlike flowers clustered along the stem. They open from the bottom up, supplying butterflies and hummingbirds with a tasty feast. The foliage withers as the flowers start, so grow this plant with midsized companions to hide the fading leaves. Bulb; Blooms: Yellow, orange, pink or tan in late spring to early summer; Light: Full sun; Soil: Average, well-drained; Size: 36 to 72 in. tall, 18 to 24 in. wide; Cold hardy: USDA zones 5 to 9. What gets it through drought? Swollen roots store water and nutrients that supply plants in lean times.

title: Help Drought-Proof Your Garden
content: Tall yellow foxtail lily flower spikes rising above grassy foliage in a sunny garden.

title: Help Drought-Proof Your Garden
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Peony (Paeonia hybrids): Peonies may have lush, romantic-looking flowers, but this perennial is no shrinking violet. Plants will grow with no care in old cemeteries and on deserted properties for decades. Thick roots keep peonies going through summer with minimal watering, but they do need cold winters to flower well. Besides that, the key to flowering success is to make sure the roots aren’t planted too deeply—just an inch or two below the soil. Perennial; Blooms: Pink, red, white, coral or yellow single, semidouble or petal-packed fully double blooms in early to late spring; Light: Full sun; Soil: Well-drained; Size: 2 to 4 ft. tall and wide; Cold hardy: USDA zones 3 to 8. What gets it through drought? Thick, tuberous roots store plenty of moisture.

title: Help Drought-Proof Your Garden
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Gas plant (Dictamnus albus): This garden stalwart takes more time to reach mature size than other perennials, but the payoff is worth the wait. Its slender stems are filled with white, pink or lilac blooms that pollinators adore, and plants are long-lived. Its clumping root system grows down instead of out so it reaches for water deep in the soil. Because the woody crown is difficult to divide successfully, plants are better left in place. But you can also grow gas plant from seed. Sow them outdoors in fall so the seeds get a winter chill, and you’ll see flowers on this slow grower in 3 to 4 years. Perennial; Blooms: White, pink or lilac flower spikes in late spring to early summer; Light: Full sun; Soil: Well-drained; Size: 24 to 36 in. tall, 18 to 30 in. wide; Cold hardy: USDA zones 3 to 8. What gets it through drought? A fleshy clumping root system goes deep into the soil, and the thick leathery leaves conserve water.

title: Help Drought-Proof Your Garden
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Jupiter’s beard (Centranthus ruber): If you’re looking for a no-brainer plant that’s super drought tolerant, Panayoti recommends Jupiter’s beard. This Mediterranean native can even reseed between cracks in a retaining wall or sidewalk. Deadhead spent blooms if you want to prevent plants from reseeding. Tiny flowers are clustered at the top of stems and come in shades of pink or white. Butterflies love Jupiter’s beard, and it makes a great cut flower. Plants thrive in poor soils but can grow a bit shorter there. Perennial; Blooms: Dark pink, red or white flowers in late spring to early fall; Light: Full sun; Soil: Well-drained; Size: 18 to 36 in. tall, 24 to 30 in. wide; Cold hardy: USDA zones 5 to 8. What gets it through drought? Fleshy gray-green leaves conserve water, and clump-forming roots go deep into the soil.

title: Help Drought-Proof Your Garden
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Bearded iris (Iris hybrids): With a thick rhizome and waxy leaves, bearded iris is well equipped to get through summer without a lot of water. In fact, too much water will cause it to rot. The orchidlike blooms can help create a tropical look next to a hot sunny patio. Panayoti suggests growing older varieties, such as ‘Honorabile’, or a passalong plant that you get from a friend or your grandmother. The flowers and plants may not be quite as large as some of the newer ones, but you’ll know that they have survived the test of time. Perennial; Blooms: Purple, pink, red, orange, yellow or white flowers in spring; Light: Full sun; Soil: Well-drained; Size: 10 to 48 in. tall, 18 to 24 in. wide; Cold hardy: USDA zones 3 to 8. What gets it through drought? Thick rhizomes store water, and waxy leaves conserve moisture.

title: Help Drought-Proof Your Garden
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: English lavender (Lavandula angustifolia): Lavender has pretty flowers like those of ‘Hidcote’ above, and its slender gray-green leaves have a fantastic fragrance. Plants need full sun and well-drained soil to thrive and avoid rot. You can use English lavender flowers and stems in cooking, crafts and dried arrangements. Deadheading will encourage a light rebloom. If you garden in an area with humid summers, French (L. dentata) and Spanish lavender (L. stoechas) are better choices. Perennial; Blooms: Fragrant lavender to dark purple, pink or white flowers in summer; Light: Full sun; Soil: Well-drained; Size: 1 to 4 ft. tall, 1 to 5 ft. wide; Cold hardy: USDA zones 5 to 9. What gets it through drought? Small gray to silver leaves conserve moisture.

title: Help Drought-Proof Your Garden
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: 3 Tips for New Plants, Water deeply: Even if you start with drought-tolerant plants, they will still need some extra attention to help get established. Instead of watering daily, water every other day or even every 2 to 3 days. Frequency depends on your soil type and the weather. The denser the soil and the cooler the temps, the longer you can wait. Let a stream of water run on the soil near your new plant for 20 or 30 seconds. Then wait a few minutes—water a few nearby containers if they need it before returning to the new addition and giving it a second soak. Even repeat the process a third time.

title: Help Drought-Proof Your Garden
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: 3 Tips for New Plants, Mulch matters: Apply a 1- to 2-inch layer of organic mulch to keep soil temperatures even and conserve moisture.

title: Help Drought-Proof Your Garden
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: 3 Tips for New Plants, Look for cues: Watch “signal” plants for cues. Panayoti keeps an eye on plants with large leaves, such as sunflower (Helianthus spp. and hybrids), lettuce (Lactuca sativa) and brunnera (Brunnera macrophylla). They tend to droop at the first sign of dryness. When he sees that, he knows that nearby new transplants are probably in need of a drink too.

title: 11 Easy-to-Dry Flowers
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: 11 Easy-to-Dry Flowers: Drying flowers doesn’t have to be complicated. To get beautiful colors and sturdy blooms, sometimes it’s just a matter of choosing the right ones and using simple techniques. Erin Howell-Conner, manager of Howell’s Greenhouse & Pumpkin Patch in Cumming, Iowa, knows a lot about this process. She’s been designing with flowers she has grown and dried herself all her life.

title: 11 Easy-to-Dry Flowers
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Simple drying: When you want to make a dried-flower wreath, a posy or even a larger arrangement in a container, air drying is the simplest and easiest method. All you have to do is hang a small bunch of stems upside down in a warm, dry spot—at least 60 to 70 degrees F—out of direct sunlight, such as an attic or closet. This will give you the quickest results with colors that won’t fade. Flowers can be ready in as little as two weeks, depending on how dense and water-filled the bloom is. The plants you’ll find here are all great choices for air drying and ones that Erin has found hold their color well, don’t shatter easily and grow tall enough to be able to cut long stems for hanging.

title: 11 Easy-to-Dry Flowers
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: How to harvest: The time to cut flowers is after the dew has dried so mold won’t form later. Try to cut stems that are 18 to 24 inches long so you have enough length to assemble the bundles for drying and to make putting the projects together easier later. You don’t have to remove the foliage—sometimes it looks nice dried too.

title: 11 Easy-to-Dry Flowers
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: How to air dry: Gather a handful of stems to hang and dry—up to 30 of slender-stemmed plants, such as salvia, but only five to seven of thicker stems, such as celosia. If you try to bundle too many together, they may dry unevenly or mold. Erin likes to hang her flowers in odd-numbered groupings (odd numbers look better in designs) so that when she needs a bunch for an arrangement, she can grab and go with just the right number of blooms.

title: 11 Easy-to-Dry Flowers
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: How to air dry: You can use twine, rubber bands or twist ties to hold the stems together. Whatever you use, check them every few days because as the stems dry, they shrink and can fall out of the bundle. Allow a few inches of space between bunches to let air circulate.

title: 11 Easy-to-Dry Flowers
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Dried flower care: You can leave the flowers hanging once they’re dry or just set them in an empty vase until you’re ready to work on a project. An arrangement can last for years if you’re careful. Dust build-up is a common problem on dried flowers. A thorough spray with a dust cleaner, such as Dri Splendor™ Dried Floral Cleaner, will freshen up your arrangement. So if you hate to say goodbye to the beautiful blooms from your garden, take a look at the flowers that this dried-flower pro recommends for long-lasting color, sturdy stems and shatter-proof blooms.

title: 11 Easy-to-Dry Flowers
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Statice (Limonium sinuatum): This classic dried flower is a short-lived perennial that’s grown as an annual in cold-winter areas. It grows best in full sun and dry growing conditions, but high humidity can be hard on plants. A low rosette of foliage produces long, winged, well-branched stems that produce lots of colorful papery bracts. Tiny white flowers emerge from the bracts in summer. Once those turn brown, stems are ready for harvest. Tender perennial; Blooms: Purple, yellow, white, pink or apricot papery bracts from late spring to frost; Light: Full sun; Soil: Well drained to sandy; Size: 24 to 36 in. tall, 18 to 24 in. wide; Cold hardy: USDA zones 8 to 11; Source: Johnny’s Selected Seeds, johnnyseeds.com, 877-564-6697.

title: 11 Easy-to-Dry Flowers
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Ornamental millet (Pennisetum glaucum): In the garden or in an arrangement, the deep purple-brown seedheads of ornamental millet will capture attention. Though it survives winter in USDA zones 9 and warmer, most gardeners grow it as an annual. ‘Purple Majesty’, below, is one easy-to-find variety that grows long stems for cutting. The leaves dry nicely and provide some added shape contrast for designs. Stems and flower heads grow larger as the summer progresses, so those you harvest early in the year are better for smaller-stature arrangements, and those taken later work beautifully in dramatic late-season arrangements. Once the seed starts to develop, save some to sow next year, but get them before the birds do. Tender perennial; Blooms: Deep purple-brown spikes top green, chartreuse or purple foliage from summer to frost; Light: Full sun; Soil: Well drained; Size: 48 to 60 in. tall, 9 to 12 in. wide; Cold hardy: USDA zones 9 to 11; Source: Johnny’s Selected Seeds, johnnyseeds.com, 877-564-6697.

title: 11 Easy-to-Dry Flowers
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: ‘Blue Bedder’ mealycup sage (Salvia farinacea): Growing up to 3 feet tall, ‘Blue Bedder’ has blooms that are a delicious shade of purple-blue. Erin has found that this variety’s color lasts well and the dried flowers don’t shatter easily. Plus the blue gets even deeper when nights start getting cooler at the end of the season. You can hand pick the blooms for drying by following the stem back to its lowest leaf junction and breaking it off. If you find a lot of resistance, give it a few more days. A stem that snaps off is at the right stage for harvest—those that are ready will often have several open blooms near the bottom of the spike. Tender perennial; Blooms: Blue-purple flowers from early summer to frost; Light: Full sun; Soil: Well drained, tolerates clay; Size: 30 to 36 in. tall, 12 to 18 in. wide; Cold hardy: USDA zones 8 to 10; Source: Pine Tree Garden Seeds, superseeds.com.

title: 11 Easy-to-Dry Flowers
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: ‘Parker’s Variety’ fernleaf yarrow (Achillea filipendulina): With domes of gold, ‘Parker’s Variety’ fernleaf yarrow (also called ‘Parker’s Gold’) provides bold color that brightens up arrangements fresh or dried. Its ferny foliage makes a great contrast to companions with broader leaves and has a spicy fragrance that you’ll notice if you run your hands through it. Fernleaf yarrow is easy to grow in infertile, dry soil but can rot in clay. Stems are ready to cut when all the individual flowers are open and yellow. If in doubt, gently push down on the top of the flower. If it’s firm instead of spongy, it’s ready to harvest. Perennial; Blooms: Yellow blooms in late summer; Light: Full sun; Soil: Lean, well drained; Size: 3 to 4 ft. tall and wide; Cold hardy: USDA zones 3 to 8; Source: Digging Dog Nursery, diggingdog.com, 707-937-1130.

title: 11 Easy-to-Dry Flowers
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Spike blazing star (Liatris spicata): The tall, straight spires of fuzzy blooms make spike blazing star a real attention-getter. This showy native provides an easy summer buffet for passing butterflies in moist or clay-soil areas.

title: 11 Easy-to-Dry Flowers
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Spike blazing star harvest: The blooms of spike blazing star open from the top down, which makes it a balancing act when you want to cut some to dry. Erin likes to cut them when as much purple is showing as possible, but the top hasn’t yet turned brown. Then group three or four stems together in a bundle to hang in a warm dry spot out of direct sunlight.

title: 11 Easy-to-Dry Flowers
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Spike blazing star color touch-up: If the color does happen to fade too much, give it a light coat of floral spray paint, such as Design Master®, to boost the intensity. Keep the can 10 to 12 inches away from the flowers and use a steady movement along the stem so paint doesn’t pool in one spot.

title: 11 Easy-to-Dry Flowers
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Spike blazing star plant facts: Perennial. Blooms: Purple-pink bloom spikes in summer. Light: Full sun. Soil: Moist, well drained, tolerates clay. Size: 18 to 48 in. tall, 12 to 24 in. wide. Cold hardy: USDA zones 3 to 8. Source: Local garden centers.

title: 11 Easy-to-Dry Flowers
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Armenian basket flower (Centaurea macrocephala): These long-lasting, 3- to 4-inch yellow blooms will brighten up sunny borders in summer. Plants grow best in well-drained soil and tolerate drought quite well. Armenian basket flower can be an aggressive spreader in some areas if it’s allowed to go to seed. So to keep it under control, be sure to harvest before seeds scatter.

title: 11 Easy-to-Dry Flowers
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Armenian basket flower harvest: Both the papery bract-covered bud and the bloom are great for dried flower projects. Erin suggests harvesting the bloom when it’s not quite open.

title: 11 Easy-to-Dry Flowers
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Armenian basket flower plant facts: Perennial. Blooms: Yellow blooms in midsummer. Light: Full sun. Soil: Well drained. Size: 36 to 48 in. tall, 18 to 24 in. wide. Cold hardy: USDA zones 3 to 8. Source: Digging Dog Nursery, diggingdog.com, 707-937-1130.

title: 11 Easy-to-Dry Flowers
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Cockscomb celosia (Celosia argentea cristata): The vivid colors and dramatic shape of cockscomb celosia blooms make great focal points. Plants grow best in full sun and warm temperatures. Don’t rush to plant them in spring because plants may rot in cool, wet conditions. Erin has tried a lot of different celosia varieties, but not all of them are tall enough or hold their color. She’s had good results with Cramer’s Rose or Burgundy and Kurume™ Rose or New Scarlet.

title: 11 Easy-to-Dry Flowers
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Cockscomb celosia harvest: You’ll know the blooms are ready to harvest when you see the tiny black seeds forming. But they aren’t where you’d expect them to be - look under the bloom on the side of the stem that supports the cockscomb. Tie just a few of the sturdy stems together and be patient because it can take a month for these beauties to dry.

title: 11 Easy-to-Dry Flowers
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Cockscomb celosia plant facts: Annual. Blooms: Rosy pink, red or burgundy blooms from early summer to frost. Light: Full sun. Soil: Moist, well drained. Size: 28 to 47 in. tall, 10 to 12 in. wide. Source: Annie’s Annuals, anniesannuals.com (Kurume New Scarlet); Johnny’s Selected Seeds, johnnyseeds.com, 877-564-6697 (Cramer’s Rose).

title: 11 Easy-to-Dry Flowers
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: ‘Silver King’ artemisia (Artemisia ludoviciana): The silvery white foliage of this perennial is a great border companion for full sun and dry growing conditions. Plus, deer and rabbits leave it alone. Both the dried foliage and flowers make a wonderful filler for arrangements and backing for wreaths.

title: 11 Easy-to-Dry Flowers
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: ‘Silver King’ artemisia harvest: Harvest the foliage any time, and the blooms when the buds are just showing color. Test to see if the stems are ready to dry by hanging a few upside down for a couple of hours. Then turn them right side up in a vase. If they droop, they weren’t ready. Wait a few days and try the process again. When they stay upright, you can harvest more.

title: 11 Easy-to-Dry Flowers
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: ‘Silver King’ artemisia plant facts: Perennial. Blooms: Inconspicuous yellow blooms in late summer, silver leaves from spring to frost. Light: Full sun. Soil: Well drained. Size: 2 to 3 ft. tall and wide. Cold hardy: USDA zones 4 to 9. Source: Sooner Plant Farm, soonerplantfarm.com.

title: 11 Easy-to-Dry Flowers
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: African marigold (Tagetes erecta): Give African marigolds plenty of sun and a bit of extra water in the heat of summer and you’ll have loads of flowers until frost. These old favorites provide long-lasting color with little effort. Harvesting flowers for your arrangements will encourage new ones to form.

title: 11 Easy-to-Dry Flowers
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: African marigold harvest: While it’s true that you can dry any marigold, the long stems of tall varieties are easier to use in dried-flower projects. Hybrid ‘Orange and Yellow Beast’ can grow up to 42 inches tall! Let the flowers open completely to get maximum color in arrangements, but don’t wait too long or the petals will start to fall.

title: 11 Easy-to-Dry Flowers
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: African marigold plant facts: Annual. Blooms: Orange or yellow flowers from summer to frost. Light: Full sun. Soil: Well drained. Size: 10 to 48 in. tall, 12 to 24 in. wide. Source: Local garden centers.

title: 11 Easy-to-Dry Flowers
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: QIS™ globe amaranth (Gomphrena globosa): This globe amaranth series is taller and bushier than the ones that you usually find at the garden center, and plants have lots of branching so there are plenty of blooms to harvest. There are several QIS colors and mixes from which to choose; Erin finds that the orange and red ones mature in midsummer, while the purple and pink ones are ready in early fall.

title: 11 Easy-to-Dry Flowers
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: QIS™ globe amaranth harvest: To see if they’re ready for harvest, check a stem or two to test if they’ll snap off of the plant. Then hang a few to dry for a couple of days and make sure the stems stay straight. If stems curl or arch, they’re more difficult to work into arrangements. Wait a few more days to harvest more, then repeat the process until the stems dry the way you want them to.

title: 11 Easy-to-Dry Flowers
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: QIS™ globe amaranth plant facts: Annual. Blooms: Purple, pink, white, lavender, red or orange papery globe-shaped flowers from early summer to frost. Light: Full sun. Soil: Well drained. Size: 22 to 26 in. tall, 8 to 10 in. wide. Source: Johnny’s Selected Seeds, johnnyseeds.com, 877-564-6697.

title: 11 Easy-to-Dry Flowers
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Sea holly (Eryngium spp. and hybrids): The well-branched stems of sea holly produce lots of those distinctive flowers with stiff starlike bracts. Plants grow in a range of sizes that provide interesting texture and silvery blue flowers for dried arrangements of all types.

title: 11 Easy-to-Dry Flowers
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Sea holly harvest: To harvest, Erin looks for blooms that are showing plenty of blue and lots of bees and flies buzzing around. Small-flowered types, such as ‘Blue Glitter’ or tripartite sea holly (E. tripartitum), can be used as a unique filler while larger-flowered varieties, such as ‘Miss Wilmott’s Ghost’ (E. giganteum), make a great focal point.

title: 11 Easy-to-Dry Flowers
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Sea holly plant facts: Perennial. Blooms: Silver-blue starlike blooms in midsummer to fall. Light: Full sun. Soil: Well drained to lean and sandy. Size: 12 to 36 in. tall, 10 to 24 in. wide. Cold hardy: USDA zones 3 to 9. Source: Local garden centers.

title: This or That: Colocasia vs. Alocasia
content: Colocasia (Colocasia spp. and hybrids): Commonly called elephant ear or taro, colocasia may be a tropical plant, but it is easily grown anywhere. Its enormous leaves can grow up to 3 feet long or larger, ranging from shades of green and chartreuse to black, purple, burgundy and cream, often with striking patterns or mottling.

title: This or That: Colocasia vs. Alocasia
content: Colocasia where it works best: This statement plant grows best in a sunny spot with plenty of water. Colocasia is an eye-catcher in garden borders and container plantings, where it works well alone as a specimen plant or in a combination surrounded by trailing vines and mounded fillers.

title: This or That: Colocasia vs. Alocasia
content: Colocasia how to grow it: Colocasia maintains its foliage color best when grown in full sun, especially the darker-leaved varieties. It prefers wet soil and can be grown in some standing water, as long as the crown is not submerged. Fertilize colocasia once a week throughout the summer with a water-soluble all-purpose plant food to keep it growing strong.

title: This or That: Colocasia vs. Alocasia
content: Colocasia overwintering: In USDA zones 8 and warmer, colocasia can overwinter in the ground. In colder zones, cut back foliage to 6 to 12 inches after a light frost. Dig the corms and store them in a dark, cool, dry location. Or leave it in its pot, cut back all but the top two leaves, reduce watering and set in a sunny window for the winter.

title: This or That: Colocasia vs. Alocasia
content: Colocasia root system: The tuberlike corm is plump and marked with bands. Offsets form along the mature corm or on runners, which can be cut off and planted.

title: This or That: Colocasia vs. Alocasia
content: Colocasia leaves: Arrow- or heart-shaped leaves point downward because the stems attach near the center. Leaves have a matte finish and distinctive veins on the underside.

title: This or That: Colocasia vs. Alocasia
content: Colocasia habit: Leaves emerge on long stems, directly from the corm, in a tight cluster. Plants normally range in height from 3 to 6 feet tall.

title: This or That: Colocasia vs. Alocasia
content: Colocasia blooms: A yellow modified leaf shields a fleshy spike of tiny flowers to form the bloom.

title: This or That: Colocasia vs. Alocasia
content: Colocasia did you know? The colocasia tuber, also known as taro, is a major food source in the world, but must be thoroughly cooked because it is toxic if eaten raw.

content: Colocasia try these: A. ‘Waikiki’ 36 in. tall and wide. B. ‘Coffee Cups’ 3 to 5 ft. tall and 3 to 4 ft. wide. C. ‘Hawaiian Punch’ 24 to 40 in. tall, 24 to 36 in. wide. D. ‘Mojito’ 3 to 5 ft. tall and wide. E. ‘Black Magic’ 3 to 6 ft. tall and wide.

title: This or That: Colocasia vs. Alocasia
content: Alocasia (Alocasia macrorrhiza and hybrids): Alocasia, also known as upright elephant ear or giant taro, is easily confused with colocasia, but its thicker, stiffer leaves are often the giveaway. Leaves can grow from 16 to 20 inches up to 5 feet long. They can be found in shades of green to burgundy with distinctive or colorful veins, sometimes with wavy or scalloped leaf edges.

title: This or That: Colocasia vs. Alocasia
content: Alocasia where it works best: The unique foliage makes alocasia an excellent specimen alone in a pot or planted as a focal point in the ground in shady locations. It has bold texture and structure when planted in combination with other annuals in summer containers. Alocasia is also easily grown as a houseplant in a bright location.

title: This or That: Colocasia vs. Alocasia
content: Alocasia how to grow it: Unlike colocasia, alocasia prefers full or part shade because its foliage can burn in hot sun. It grows best in warm, humid weather but the soil should be well-drained, even dry between waterings. In USDA zones 9 to 11, it can overwinter outdoors with a 2- to 4-inch layer of mulch to protect it if temperatures drop below 50 degrees F. In zones 8 and colder, reduce watering and grow it indoors in a bright east or west window where it gets morning or afternoon sun. Move it outdoors again when temperatures are above 60 degrees F overnight.

title: This or That: Colocasia vs. Alocasia
content: Alocasia leaves: Stiff arrowhead-shaped leaves are waxy or shiny and usually point upward or horizontally, with petioles that attach at the notch.

title: This or That: Colocasia vs. Alocasia
content: Alocasia habit: Leaves emerge from the top of the rhizome, growing upright and often vase-shaped. Plants can grow 2 to 15 feet tall and 2 to 10 feet wide.

title: This or That: Colocasia vs. Alocasia
content: Alocasia root system: Rhizomes look like long, thickened roots. Offshoots may form new plants alongside the main rhizome or at the end of a long stolon.

title: This or That: Colocasia vs. Alocasia
content: Alocasia blooms: Green-white modified flowers followed by red berry-type fruits occasionally form on mature plants.

content: Alocasia try these: A. ‘Stingray’ 1 to 5 ft. tall, 3 to 4 ft. wide. B. ‘Sumo’ 6 to 10 ft. tall and wide. C. ‘Frydek’ 2 to 3 ft. tall, 4 to 5 ft. wide. D. ‘Hilo Beauty’ 2 to 3 ft. tall and wide. E. ‘Golden Dragon’ 4 to 5 ft. tall and wide.

title: Vegetables to Plant Now for a Fall Harvest
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Vegetables to Plant Now for a Fall Harvest: While your baskets are filling with your long-awaited tomatoes, zucchini and peppers, you might not be thinking about the months to come. But the garden season doesn’t have to end when the weather cools off. Midsummer is the perfect time to start plants for a second harvest. Here are five vegetables you can plant right now and enjoy in a couple of months. Happy harvesting!

title: Vegetables to Plant Now for a Fall Harvest
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Sweet basil (Ocimum basilicum): By midsummer, basil is usually sending up flowers and setting seed, causing the flavor to decline. Although basil isn’t a cool-season crop, now is the perfect time to plant another round so you can keep the harvest going until temperatures regularly drop below 50 degrees F, when plants start to decline.

title: Vegetables to Plant Now for a Fall Harvest
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Sweet basil when to plant: If you start seeds, sow them 60 to 90 days before you want to harvest, depending on the variety. If you can keep the seed bed moist, sow directly in the garden. If not, start indoors and move transplants outdoors later. Even easier, just pick up a few packs of seedlings from the garden center and plant them in the garden in summer so you can keep harvesting into fall.

title: Vegetables to Plant Now for a Fall Harvest
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Sweet basil what to choose: Lemon basil (O. basilicum var. citriodorum) and ‘Purple Ruffles’ (Ocimum basilicum var. purpurascens) are two of the best cool-weather performers and can handle temperatures below 50 degrees F.

title: Vegetables to Plant Now for a Fall Harvest
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Sweet basil growing tips: Plant in a warm, sunny spot and apply a 2-inch layer of mulch to the base of the plant to help keep soil and roots warm when air temperatures begin to drop. Or grow basil in pots and bring plants indoors to keep them going longer.

title: Vegetables to Plant Now for a Fall Harvest
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Bush beans (Phaseolus vulgaris): Bush beans are super easy to grow, don’t require trellising like pole beans do, and mature faster. This makes them perfect for a second quick crop before a frost shuts them down.

title: Vegetables to Plant Now for a Fall Harvest
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Bush beans when to plant: Depending on the variety, bush beans take 50 to 60 days to mature, so to give yourself time to harvest, count back at least 75 days from your average first frost date to find the best time to plant seeds. They germinate best between 70 and 80 degrees F. If you’re going through a hot, dry spell when it’s time to plant, you might choose to start seeds indoors and transplant seedlings into the garden when outdoor temps are regularly between 65 and 85 degrees F.

title: Vegetables to Plant Now for a Fall Harvest
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Bush beans what to choose: Look for varieties with shorter maturity times, such as ‘Tenderpod’, which takes 50 to 55 days from germination to maturity. Varieties with the word “early” in the name are usually good choices for a fall crop.

title: Vegetables to Plant Now for a Fall Harvest
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Bush beans growing tips: Expect to harvest bush beans for up to 2 weeks. If you’re expecting a light frost, protect plants by covering them with landscape fabric and mulching the roots.

title: Vegetables to Plant Now for a Fall Harvest
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Lettuce (Lactuca sativa): Lettuce is a great fall crop because of its ability to handle temperatures as low as 28 degrees F before plants succumb to the cold.

title: Vegetables to Plant Now for a Fall Harvest
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Lettuce when to plant: Lettuce grows best between 45 and 65 degrees F, and typically only needs 30 to 70 days from seed to harvest. This means you can wait a little longer to start them than some of the other plants here. Keep in mind that seeds germinate best when soil temperatures are between 70 and 75 degrees F, so as the weather cools off in fall, you might want to start them indoors and set plants in the garden once they’re established.

title: Vegetables to Plant Now for a Fall Harvest
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Lettuce what to choose: All types of lettuce are fast growers and good candidates for fall planting and harvest. Try varieties like ‘Red Incised’, ‘Green Butter’ or ‘Red Sweet Crisp’.

title: Vegetables to Plant Now for a Fall Harvest
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Lettuce growing tips: Add an inch or two of organic mulch, such as straw, after seeds have germinated or after you set transplants out to keep soil temperatures cool and moist. This also helps protect plants from last-minute heat waves. If you’re expecting a light frost (28 to 32 degrees F), cover the lettuce with burlap, landscape fabric or row cover to protect plants from frost damage.

title: Vegetables to Plant Now for a Fall Harvest
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Carrots (Daucus spp. and hybrids): Carrots thrive in cooler temperatures and are tolerant of frost. And while their green tops might take a hit from the cold, the roots will keep growing, and they actually taste sweeter after a light frost. Just make sure to wrap up your harvest before night temperatures are regularly 28 degrees F or below, because after that, the roots become hard and bitter.

title: Vegetables to Plant Now for a Fall Harvest
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Carrots when to plant: Starting in midsummer, sow seeds every week until 6 to 8 weeks before your average first frost date.

title: Vegetables to Plant Now for a Fall Harvest
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Carrots what to choose: Grow fast-maturing varieties that take 45 to 65 days from seed to harvest, such as ‘Napoli’, ‘Royal Chantenay’, ‘Little Finger’ and ‘New Kuroda’.

title: Vegetables to Plant Now for a Fall Harvest
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Carrots growing tips: Plant carrots in loose soil in an area that receives full sun. Keep your soil moist and cool by applying a 6-inch layer of straw after germination so the seedlings don’t dry out.

title: Vegetables to Plant Now for a Fall Harvest
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Snow peas (Pisum sativum): You should be able to continue to harvest snow peas until the first frost, but the harvest will slow down as days grow shorter through fall.

title: Vegetables to Plant Now for a Fall Harvest
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Snow peas when to plant: Seeds germinate best between 45 and 75 degrees F, and plants grow best between 55 and 65 degrees F. Count back 70 days from your first predicted frost date to decide when to plant. Snow peas are heat sensitive: If outdoor temperatures are still warm, provide extra shade using a row cover.

title: Vegetables to Plant Now for a Fall Harvest
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Snow peas what to choose: Snow peas take 50 to 60 days to mature but they can be enjoyed at any stage, which gives you a longer harvesting window. Eat them when they are young and tender or wait until they mature.

title: Vegetables to Plant Now for a Fall Harvest
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Snow peas growing tips: In late fall, protect them from frost damage by covering with burlap or landscape fabric.

title: Hardy Hibiscus
content: Hardy Hibiscus: These impressive blooms bring drama and a touch of the tropics. For big results with little effort, hardy hibiscus is a great perennial for your summer border. The biggest draw is those gorgeous 8- to 12-inch-diameter flowers - they make quite the statement! You’ll find them in shades of pink, red or white with a long pistil and bright yellow anthers that give it some tropical flair. Flowers aren’t the only attraction here - hardy hibiscus has good-looking (and disease-free!) deep to olive green or purple foliage. And leaf shapes vary from round to maplelike. These big, usually 3- to 4-foot-tall perennials take up a large footprint in the border and mimic a shrub in habit.

title: Hardy Hibiscus
content: Hardy Hibiscus meet the family: Most plants that you’ll find at the garden center are hybrids or cultivars of Hibiscus moscheutos. The species and some older varieties tend to be tall and lanky with blooms near the top. But newer breeding efforts are bringing tidier, mounded habits and new flower colors, such as solid white and shades of pink and red with bluer tones. Another big plus to new hybrids is that plants develop buds up and down the stems, and petals overlap instead of having gaps between them. That provides a bigger show of color and helps the flowers stand up to rainy weather better. ‘Holy Grail’ is one example of a newer introduction with stunning red blooms and deep purple foliage.

title: Hardy Hibiscus
content: ‘Holy Grail’ hardy hibiscus has 8- to 9-inch red flowers with a bright green calyx that pops against the near black maplelike foliage. It grows 48 to 54 inches tall and wide in USDA zones 4 to 9.

title: Hardy Hibiscus

title: Meet More Hardy Hibiscus
content: Hardy hibiscus (Hibiscus hybrids) plant facts: Blooms: Red, pink, lavender or white blooms from midsummer to fall. Light: Full sun to part shade. Soil: Moist, well-drained. Pests: Occasional Japanese beetles or hibiscus sawflies. Size: 2 to 8 ft. tall, 2 to 6 ft. wide. Cold hardy: USDA zones 4 to 9.

title: Meet More Hardy Hibiscus
content: Meet More Hardy Hibiscus: Choosing a hardy hibiscus for your garden is quite a challenge - they’re all so pretty! Whichever one you go with, you can count on enjoying those lovely blooms for weeks in summer. Plus they’ll provide a feast for passing hummingbirds.

title: Meet More Hardy Hibiscus
content: A. ‘Cherry Choco Latte’ Hibiscus hybrid: White 8- to 9-in. flowers with deep pink veining and large eye; deep olive-green foliage with splashes of bronze; 4 ft. tall and wide; cold hardy in USDA zones 4 to 9.

title: Meet More Hardy Hibiscus

title: Meet More Hardy Hibiscus

title: Meet More Hardy Hibiscus

title: Meet More Hardy Hibiscus
content: E. ‘Airbrush Effect’ H. hybrid: Pink 8- to 8½-in. blooms with a soft white halo and red eye; dark green foliage; 42 to 48 in. tall, 48 to 54 in. wide; cold hardy in zones 4 to 9.

title: Meet More Hardy Hibiscus

title: Hardy Hibiscus Care
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Hardy Hibiscus Care: The secrets to growing gorgeous hardy hibiscus are plenty of sun and regular moisture. And while well-drained soil is best, this perennial also tolerates clay.

title: Hardy Hibiscus Care
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Grow gorgeous hardy hibiscus plants: If you’ve noticed that your hibiscus leaves turn yellow and drop along with the flower buds, the plant may be drought stressed. Either water more or add a layer of organic mulch to help conserve moisture. Or, think about where you’re growing it: Laura Robles, regional product manager for Walters Gardens, a wholesale grower that’s introduced several new hardy hibiscus in recent years, suggests looking for a naturally damp spot in the garden. In her backyard, she’s found that those planted at the bottom of a slope, where rain settles, don’t need much attention, while the ones at the top of the slope, where it’s drier, need regular watering during summer.

title: Hardy Hibiscus Care
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Hardy hibiscus bloom size: You might think that the size of the bloom is determined by how much water or fertilizer you give the plant, but it’s actually determined by temperature. When nighttime temperatures stay between 50 and 60 degrees F consistently, hibiscus will typically produce the largest flowers.

title: Hardy Hibiscus Care
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Hardy hibiscus blooms and soil: Blooms last just a day, but there are clusters of them up and down the stem so you’ll have plenty of color for a month or so in summer. Hibiscus flowers are nyctinastic - the bottom petals grow faster than the top ones, which forces flowers to close at night. Hibiscus will do just fine in average garden soil without extra feeding. If your soil is on the sandy side, it’s a good idea to amend it with compost to help it hold more moisture.

title: Hardy Hibiscus Care
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Hardy Hibiscus Trouble: Plants aren’t growing well, have crispy foliage or flower buds have dropped and the foliage has turned yellow: They may need more water. Flowers are smaller than they should be: Nighttime temps are higher than 60 degrees F. Plants haven’t started growing in spring: Be patient - it’s a soil temperature thing. Holes in the flowers or foliage: Japanese beetles or hibiscus sawfly larvae have shown up. Seeds haven’t germinated: Try soaking or scarifying the seeds.

title: Hardy Hibiscus Care
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Hardy hibiscus pruning caption: When you see new growth, cut last year’s dead stems back to the ground.

title: Hardy Hibiscus Care
content: Pink hardy hibiscus bloom on dark foliage used as the background for a trouble-shooting care sidebar.

title: Hardy Hibiscus Care
content: Pruners cutting last year’s dead hardy hibiscus stem close to emerging green spring growth.

title: Hardy Hibiscus Care
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Spring cleanup: Though you might be tempted to clean up hardy hibiscus in fall, wait until spring to cut the dead stems back. Laura says that the stems are slow to die back in fall and it takes time for them to send all the energy gathered during the growing season back to the crown. So if you cut the stems back before they’re completely dormant, plants may be more susceptible to winter dieback. Besides, the long stems with spent calyxes can add interest to the winter landscape. Plants take their time emerging in spring because they need soil temperatures that are 60 to 75 degrees F to break dormancy. Just when you think the plant has died, you’ll see green growth starting to emerge. That’s a good time to cut the old growth back. Cut the stems as close to the ground as possible, but if you can only get as far back as the stems in the photo at left, that’s fine too.

title: Hardy Hibiscus Care
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Hardy hibiscus Japanese beetle problems: Hardy hibiscus is usually pretty trouble free. But plants can be susceptible to Japanese beetles. These insects chew big holes in the buds and leaves. Hand pick and drop them in a bucket of soapy water.

title: Hardy Hibiscus Care
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Hibiscus sawfly problems: Hibiscus sawfly is another potential pest. The 3/16-inch-long adults have a black body with a red brown thorax and black wings. Caterpillars are pale green when they’re young and develop a black head with tiny black spines as they mature. Caterpillars feed from the undersides of the leaves, leaving them looking lacy, from May to October. You might notice the small brown cocoons near the base of the plant.

title: Hardy Hibiscus Care
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Hardy hibiscus pest control: For both of these pests, you can use neem oil, an organic pest control that they need to ingest. Spray leaves thoroughly on the top and bottom in the early morning or late evening just before sunset so it has time to dry before pollinators are active.

title: Hardy Hibiscus Care
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Get more hardy hibiscus: Budget-minded gardeners can get more hardy hibiscus plants by taking stem cuttings in spring or starting seeds.

title: Grow Hardy Hibiscus from Seed
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Grow hardy hibiscus from seed: ‘Disco Belle’, Honeymoon™ and ‘Luna’ are three series that can be started from seed. Sow them indoors 6 to 8 weeks before your expected last frost date.

title: Grow Hardy Hibiscus from Seed
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Scarify hardy hibiscus seeds: Hardy hibiscus seeds need scarification and soaking to germinate better. To scarify a seed, just run it across some sandpaper a few times to rough up the outer coating. This helps water penetrate better.

title: Grow Hardy Hibiscus from Seed
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Soak hardy hibiscus seeds: After scarifying the seeds, soak them for a few hours. When the seeds swell, pull them out and plant. Don’t leave them soaking for longer than 24 hours or seeds may get mushy. If seeds sink to the bottom, you know they are well saturated and ready to plant.

title: Grow Hardy Hibiscus from Seed
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Plant hardy hibiscus seeds: Sow hardy hibiscus seeds ½ inches deep in seed-starting mix and keep them where temperatures are between 69 to 75 degrees F. Germination usually takes 3 to 5 days. Keep seedlings in a sunny south-facing window or under lights until they’re ready to go outdoors.

title: Grow Hardy Hibiscus from Seed
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Pinch hardy hibiscus seedlings: Once the seedlings have grown about 6 inches tall, Laura suggests pinching the young plants back so there are four to six leaves on the stem. This encourages the plant to branch low enough to develop a balanced habit - too high and it looks awkward.

title: Grow Hardy Hibiscus from Seed
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Move hardy hibiscus seedlings outdoors: About this time you can start hardening seedlings off by putting them out in a shady spot for an hour or two each day. Gradually move them into more sunlight for increasing amounts of time over the course of a week or two.
