title: How to Feed Anything
author: Robert Balek
content: How to Feed Anything: Have questions about fertilizer? We have answers! Deciding on a fertilizer plan can seem overwhelming. Do you just skip it because you don’t want to make a mistake, or do you just pick one, use it on everything and hope for the best? The fact is, soil conditions, time of year, the type of plant and your particular soil all play a role in choosing the best way to feed plants. Here are some questions you might have and the answers to help you feed almost anything.

title: How to Feed Anything
author: Robert Balek
content: How do I know if my plants need fertilizer? Fertilizer and water go hand in hand, so when your plants are getting enough water and look healthy but are not growing like they should, they probably need fertilizer. Common nutrient-deficiency symptoms include smaller than normal flowers, fruit and leaves; pale or yellow foliage and stunted growth; diseases and insect infestations; shrubs and trees with shorter branches than normal; and fewer leaves.

title: How to Feed Anything
author: Robert Balek
content: What is N-P-K? Before you start feeding your plants, it’s a good idea to get the soil tested. This will tell you if it needs the macronutrients nitrogen (N), phosphorus (P) and potassium (K). Nitrogen supports healthy green foliage, phosphorus supports strong roots and blooms, and potassium supports healthy plant growth.

title: How to Feed Anything
author: Robert Balek
content: Fertilizer N-P-K ratios: All fertilizers list an N-P-K ratio on the packaging. A fertilizer’s N-P-K indicates the percent by weight of nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium in the fertilizer. For example, bone meal usually has a high-phosphorus ratio of 0-12-0 or 3-20-0. For starters, find a slow-acting fertilizer with a N-P-K ratio similar to the one your soil test recommends.

title: How to Feed Anything
author: Robert Balek
content: Annual nutrient boosts: In addition, annual plants can benefit from a boost of specific macronutrients during the growing season to encourage leafy growth, flowering and fruit set, and to remedy deficiencies as they crop up.

title: How to Feed Anything
author: Robert Balek
content: Can I use the same fertilizer for everything? Probably not. Plants have different needs depending on soil fertility, type of plant, weather conditions and time of year. There are two types of fertilizers.

title: How to Feed Anything
author: Robert Balek
content: Quick-release fertilizer: Examples include water-soluble plant food, liquid fertilizers, mined fertilizers such as potassium or phosphorus, and fish emulsion. Best for: One-season plantings like containers, vegetables, annuals. Timing: When planting, during the growing season.

title: How to Feed Anything
author: Robert Balek
content: Slow-acting fertilizer: Examples include compost, manure and organic pellets. Best for: Permanent plantings of perennials, trees and shrubs, lawns. Timing: Before the growing season starts.

title: How to Feed Anything
author: Robert Balek
content: Timed-release fertilizers: Timed-release (also called slow-release) fertilizers are really quick-release fertilizers with coatings that break down over time, releasing the nutrients.

title: How to Feed Anything
author: Robert Balek
content: Can I feed too much? Yes! Add too much fertilizer and the nutrients can burn plant roots and leaves. Ultimately the soil limits how much fertilizer it can hold, so if you overfeed, fertilizer and nutrients can leach out or run off into streams and waterways, causing environmental problems like algae blooms and fish kills. Test your soil to find how much it really needs.

title: How to Feed Anything
author: Robert Balek
content: If I use compost, do I still need to fertilize? In perennial beds, around trees and shrubs and in lawns, probably not. Compost is a slow-acting fertilizer, so unless your soil is deficient in nutrients, compost should be enough. However, vegetables and annuals that you replant every year will still likely need a boost of nutrients during the growing season. That’s when a quick-release targeted nutrient fertilizer can come in handy to supplement slow-acting compost.

title: How to Feed Anything
author: Robert Balek
content: Best time to feed annuals: Early spring or when planting: Before you plant, add quick-release food with high P so new plants can use it right away. Mid- to late spring, when leafing out and rapid growth or flowering begins: Spread a slow-acting fertilizer high in N 4 to 6 weeks after planting. For foliage annuals, add a high-N quick-release fertilizer now. Summer: Water in a balanced quick-release fertilizer according to package directions. Fall: After frost kills plants, spread a layer of compost to improve soil fertility and texture.

title: How to Feed Anything
author: Robert Balek
content: Best time to feed containers: Early spring or when planting: Use potting mix with timed-release fertilizer mixed in. Mid- to late spring, when leafing out and rapid growth or flowering begins: Use quick-release water-soluble fertilizer high in N for foliage plants, but high in P for flowers. Apply according to package directions. Fall: Stop feeding 2 weeks before average last frost date in your area.

title: How to Feed Anything
author: Robert Balek
content: Best time to feed vegetables: Early spring or when planting: Spread a balanced slow-acting fertilizer before planting; add quick-release N to asparagus before growth begins in spring. Mid- to late spring, when leafing out and rapid growth or flowering begins: Apply extra quick-release N, especially for brassicas like cabbage and broccoli 3 weeks after planting, and to onions at bulb formation; tomatoes need an extra shot of quick-release calcium now to avoid blossom end rot. Summer: Apply balanced quick-release fertilizer at blossom time, fruit set and during development of fruits; give tomatoes quick-release N one week before fruit ripens. Fall or winter: Spread compost over garden beds.

title: How to Feed Anything
author: Robert Balek
content: Is it OK to fertilize my plants in a heat wave? Yes, but be careful. Adding fertilizer during heat or drought can burn roots and leaf tips. Always water plants prior to applying fertilizer when it’s hot or dry and be sure your plants aren’t wilted or stressed. In addition, keep water-soluble fertilizer off foliage.

title: How to Feed Anything
author: Robert Balek
content: Perennials: Fertilize perennials with a slow-acting fertilizer with similar amounts of N-P-K once in spring. Late-summer-flowering perennials may need a second application of a slow-acting fertilizer in summer during unusually rainy summers, as excessive water can wash nutrients out of the soil. Don’t feed now. It can decrease hardiness. After a killing frost, top dress with organic mulch or compost to improve soil and protect crowns.

title: How to Feed Anything
author: Robert Balek
content: Trees & shrubs: Use 3-1-1 slow-acting fertilizer on established trees if you didn’t in late fall. Don’t feed after plants have leafed out. To preserve winter hardiness, don’t feed in summer. Use 3-1-1 N-P-K ratio on established trees in late fall as dormancy begins but before ground freezes.

title: How to Feed Anything
author: Robert Balek
content: Lawns: Use a balanced, quick-release lawn starter fertilizer on new seeds, sod or sprigs. Fertilize warm-season lawns with a quick-release, high N lawn food as new growth starts in spring. To encourage heat- and drought-tolerance, avoid fertilizing cool-season lawns in summer. Fertilize cool-season lawns with a slow-acting high N lawn food to build roots over the winter. Avoid fertilizing lawns in winter on frozen soil or when lawn is dormant.

title: How to Feed Anything
author: Robert Balek
content: Do I need to feed every year? For annual plantings of flowers and vegetables, it’s a good idea. Test your soil for nutrient availability every two or three years and keep a feeding regimen based on those recommendations each growing season, until you test again. For permanent plantings of perennials, woody plants and lawns, only feed when your soil test recommends it.

title: The Ever-Changing Garden
content: Stone steps climb through terraced flower beds filled with yellow coreopsis, purple blooms and layered greenery in Joyce and Jon Householder’s Kansas garden.

title: The Ever-Changing Garden
author: Marisa Reyes
content: The Ever-Changing Garden: Learn how one gardener transformed an erosion-prone landscape into a striking flower-filled oasis. When Joyce and Jon Householder moved into their Kansas home in 1988, they didn’t inherit a garden—just an overgrown lawn and a few shrubs. But with a lot of hard work Joyce has transformed this blank slate into the ultimate reprieve from everyday life.

title: The Ever-Changing Garden
author: Marisa Reyes
content: She prefers a laid-back approach to gardening and allows plants to grow where they please, creating beds and borders full of life and color. In the next few pages, you can learn about the challenges she has faced and take a walk through this unique and resilient garden.

title: The Ever-Changing Garden
content: Colorful perennial border along a stone edge with yellow coreopsis, purple salvia-like blooms and mature trees behind the Householder garden.

title: The Ever-Changing Garden
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Fill in the cracks: Joyce loves to incorporate low-growing plants like tasteless sedum and hens and chicks into the cracks of her retaining wall for added color.

title: The Ever-Changing Garden
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Terraced borders: Over the years Joyce has transformed her 1¼ acres into the garden oasis it is today. It all started in the front yard, which sits at the bottom of a steep slope. While this was a fun sledding hill for her kids in the winter, it was a pain to mow. After a few summers of struggling with the lawn, she decided to install terraced flower beds instead, and that was the project that started it all.

title: The Ever-Changing Garden
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Retaining walls are the garden’s foundation: Enlisting the help of neighbors and friends, the couple ripped out the existing junipers and railroad ties and chopped up the original sidewalk leading to the front door. Then they brought in topsoil, leveled out three terraced beds that range from 12 to 20 feet wide and 5 to 12 feet deep, and installed limestone retaining walls to hold the soil in place. These beds hold colorful perennials that bloom throughout spring and summer, such as coreopsis, purple coneflower, salvia and baptisia. Shrubs and small trees, such as panicle hydrangea, Drift roses and Japanese maple, add structure and a backdrop all year. Later they installed a second set of terraces that curve along the driveway in the side yard. They used two sizes of limestone blocks to create two 20-foot-long beds and allow for ground cover sedums to trail over in the spaces between the stones and at the base of the front 6-foot-tall wall. Walk up the steps, and you’ll find yourself in the backyard.

title: The Ever-Changing Garden
content: Wide view of limestone terraced beds and stone steps packed with coreopsis, grasses, potted succulents and layered shrubs.

title: The Ever-Changing Garden

title: The Ever-Changing Garden
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Garden at a Glance: The entire property slopes toward the front, so the Householders installed retaining walls to create level beds in the front and sideyard.

title: The Ever-Changing Garden
author: Marisa Reyes
content: 4 Easy Steps to Overwinter Bananas: Here’s how Joyce protects her banana in winter. This technique could also work for many plants that are usually not cold hardy enough for your garden. 1. After the first frost, cut the banana down to about 1 foot from the soil. 2. Build a 3- to 4-foot-tall chicken wire or hardware cloth fence around the remaining stems. 3. Add a few handfuls of granular high-nitrogen fertilizer to the soil for energy next spring and surround the plant with organic mulch, such as bark or leaves. 4. Remove the mulch after danger of frost has passed and you can see new growth poking through.

title: The Ever-Changing Garden
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Gardening is unpredictable: A few years ago a tornado passed between this property and the next. Although the home was left standing and their family was unharmed, it took out a flowering crabapple and redbud tree near the house, as well as the work shed roof. The aftermath was a yard full of debris and very different growing conditions in the front terraced beds. After the tornado, the perennials near the front entry were suddenly in full sun. Bear’s breeches and daylilies that hadn’t bloomed well for years started thriving again.

title: The Ever-Changing Garden
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Make the most of microclimates: Stone retaining walls store heat from the sun and can create extra warmth for garden beds. The one in the sheltered spot next to the garage is the perfect microclimate to experiment with plants that aren’t normally hardy in this zone 5 garden, such as hardy banana. As a Master Gardener, Joyce loves to try new things and stretch her gardening skills, and she’s found a way to overwinter this not-usually-hardy banana in the ground. It makes quite a statement and is one of the first things people see when they pull into the driveway.

title: The Ever-Changing Garden
author: Marisa Reyes
content: More slope solutions: The steep slope caused Joyce more problems than just mowing and affected her entire lot, which also collected water from neighboring properties. Rainwater used to rush down from all sides of the yard, eroding soil, and collected at the bottom of the driveway.

title: The Ever-Changing Garden
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Erosion solution: The first project Joyce and Jon tackled to address this problem was to make part of their driveway permeable. They removed a portion toward the top of the long drive, installed a layer of sand, laid pavers in a fun design, then filled in with pea gravel. This allows some of the rain to filter into the soil as it runs down the driveway.

title: The Ever-Changing Garden
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Rain garden to the rescue: However, the permeable driveway doesn’t catch all of the water. In addition, Joyce took advantage of a local rain garden grant program and installed a 35×15-foot rain garden in the low spot at the bottom of the driveway. This bed holds water runoff until it’s absorbed back into the ground. Installing a rain garden helps reduce water pollution and prevent flooding, all while providing a beneficial habitat for wildlife. It’s an attractive solution to a not-so-attractive problem.

title: The Ever-Changing Garden
author: Marisa Reyes
content: This spot already sat in a ditch, but to build the bed, they dug down a bit more, then mixed in a layer of heavy clay soil with the existing soil to help prevent further erosion. Finally, starting with a list of recommended native plants from their municipality, they planted the bed with perennials and shrubs that thrive in heavy, wet soil, and also tolerate drying out when rain is scarce.

title: The Ever-Changing Garden
content: Rain garden and driveway edge planted with amsonia, maiden grass, iris-like foliage and shrubs to catch runoff from the sloped property.

title: The Ever-Changing Garden
author: Marisa Reyes

title: The Ever-Changing Garden

content: Filling the rain garden: Use plants that can withstand both flooding and drought to effectively control runoff.

title: The Ever-Changing Garden

content: Perfect perennials for a rain garden: Plants that are good candidates for a rain garden have extensive root systems to help them quickly absorb water, prevent erosion and retain moisture during dry periods.

title: The Ever-Changing Garden
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Perfect perennials for a rain garden: Amsonia, Amsonia tabernaemontana. Pale blue flowers from late spring to early summer; full sun to part shade; 2 to 3 ft. tall and wide; cold hardy in USDA zones 3 to 9.

title: The Ever-Changing Garden
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Perfect perennials for a rain garden: Copper iris, Iris fulva. Copper-colored flowers in early summer; full sun to part shade; 2 to 3 ft. tall, 1 to 2 ft. wide; cold hardy in USDA zones 5 to 9.

title: The Ever-Changing Garden
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Perfect perennials for a rain garden: Gray-headed coneflower, Ratibida pinnata. Tall yellow flowers with prominent center “cones” in summer; full sun; 24 to 48 in. tall, 18 to 24 in. wide; cold hardy in USDA zones 3 to 8.

title: The Ever-Changing Garden
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Perfect perennials for a rain garden: Joe-Pye weed, Eutrochium maculatum. Pink blooms from midsummer to fall; full sun to part shade; 3 to 7 ft. tall, 2 to 4 ft. wide; cold hardy in USDA zones 3 to 9.

title: The Ever-Changing Garden
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Perfect perennials for a rain garden: Maiden grass, Miscanthus sinensis. Silver, bronze, pink, copper, tan or burgundy plumes from late summer to fall; full sun to part shade; 1 to 12 ft. tall, 1 to 6 ft. wide; cold hardy in USDA zones 4 to 9.

title: The Ever-Changing Garden
author: Marisa Reyes
content: A natural approach: Once you’ve reached the backyard, you can meander through a series of beds packed with colorful shrubs, perennials and reseeding flowers like the purple larkspur. If a flower, such as chamomile or forget-me-not, reseeds, Joyce will usually let it complete its life cycle unless it’s overcrowding perennials or popping up in ground covers. She also finds perennials like coreopsis and purple coneflowers emerging in her garden beds because of snacking birds like goldfinches. Every year the garden transforms and looks a little different. One year, there might be more larkspur in the border. The next year, it might show off an assortment of fluffy fennel and purple and pink cosmos.

title: The Ever-Changing Garden
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Vegetable garden: Though most of her garden focuses on ornamental plants, Joyce does grow a few of her favorite vegetables in the six 8×4-foot raised beds. The 2-foot-tall beds are made of rot-resistant Douglas fir—a necessity since the property collects so much moisture. Every spring, she loosens the soil with a spade, then adds a 2-inch layer of her own compost before planting.

title: The Ever-Changing Garden
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Grow reseeding plants: Don’t deadhead your flowers after the blooms are spent if you want them to reseed.

Some of her favorite specimen conifers are unique and airy weeping blue atlas cedar, ‘Green Knight’ oriental spruce and the ‘Lemon Thread’ false cypress.

Here, walk the paths made of limestone steppers and Joyce’s leaf castings, and you’ll see a pond, a charming collection of hypertufa fairy houses and her hosta rescue bed.

title: The Ever-Changing Garden

content: Years ago, Joyce worked for a hosta breeder. For every variety that is selected to bring to market, several more are thrown away. She couldn’t let those poor plants go to waste, so she brought home the ones she liked for her own garden. This is a perfect example of her “no plant left behind” approach to gardening. There’s always room for a few more!

title: Hypertufa How-To
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Hypertufa How-To: Joyce has made thousands of hypertufa projects over the years. This lightweight mixture of cement, peat moss and vermiculite can be used to make garden planters and other projects. She loves the versatility of hypertufa and the satisfaction of creating something with her hands. Here is her recipe and a few tips to help you start your own hypertufa projects.

title: Hypertufa How-To
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Hypertufa ingredients: 1 gallon bucket of sifted sphagnum peat moss (no sticks or bark); 1 gallon bucket of medium-sized vermiculite; 1¼ gallon bucket of Portland cement. These ingredients will make a 6- to 8-inch wide container with walls about an inch thick.

title: Hypertufa How-To
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Mix: This is a messy project, so be sure to wear old clothes and protective gloves to keep your hands from getting dried out. Measure the dry ingredients into a tub then add water a little at a time. Mix until you have a consistency of thick brownie mix or the mix holds together when you squeeze it.

title: Hypertufa How-To
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Form: Depending on the project, pack the mixture onto or inside your form, leaving a thickness of about 1 to 2 inches all the way around. Lining or covering the form with a plastic bag before you start adding the mixture will make the hypertufa easier to remove later.

title: Hypertufa How-To
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Cure: Let your project harden for at least 24 hours before removing the mold. You might have to cut the mold off of the shape once it solidifies, especially in the case of larger projects.

title: Hypertufa How-To
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Joyce uses several custom-made molds with different shapes and surface textures to create mini fairy houses.

title: Hypertufa How-To
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Accent the edge of a shallow pot by firmly pressing small tiles or stained glass into the wet hypertufa.

title: Hypertufa How-To
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Apply hypertufa mix to the inside of a basket to capture its woven texture. While the mix is still wet, use a wooden dowel to make a hole in the bottom for drainage.

title: Attract Butterflies to This Hot Spot
author: Jennifer Howell
content: The challenge: Existing plants have struggled in this south-facing bed, surrounded by heat-absorbing stone. The homeowner wants plants that can disguise utilities and draw butterflies while surviving in the full sun.

title: Attract Butterflies to This Hot Spot
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Located on the south-facing wall of Ruth Powell’s home, this corner garden has no escape from the sun, with extra heat reflecting off the walls. Surrounded by river rock edging and flagstone walkways, it can feel even hotter there in the summer than its New York zone 5 designation might suggest. This garden calls for some tough inhabitants.

title: Attract Butterflies to This Hot Spot
author: Jennifer Howell
content: All the plants in this design thrive in full sun and heat. Sedum, yucca and prairie coneflower are drought-tolerant and can take this hot spot when summer starts to get parched, in fact preferring dry, poor soils. Missouri primrose and swamp milkweed have tap roots that help them survive periods of drought, but extra water during dry spells will keep them hydrated and healthier.

title: Attract Butterflies to This Hot Spot
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Planting for pollinators: Ruth loves to plant different types of zinnias in this bed and watch the butterflies that visit as family and friends gather at the swimming pool across the walkway. Heat-loving zinnias, native to Mexico, are a great source of food for these pollinators and other insects. Single-flowered Profusion zinnias are an easily accessible butterfly buffet. Swamp milkweed is another important pollinator plant: Milkweed species are the host plant for monarch butterfly caterpillars, who feed on the foliage, and this flower provides nectar-rich flowers for many other butterflies too. Native meadow blazing star, prairie coneflower and New York aster also draw butterflies and hummingbirds to this flower-filled bed that peaks from summer to early fall.

title: Attract Butterflies to This Hot Spot
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Hide the AC: Swamp milkweed is tall enough to disguise the air-conditioning unit in the back of the bed, and evergreen false cypress conceals the fireplace vent on the wall year-round. But leave 2 to 3 feet of empty space around the air conditioner and vent for air movement and maintenance.

title: Attract Butterflies to This Hot Spot
content: Before photo of a south-facing corner bed beside a house, air-conditioning unit, river rock edging and flagstone walkway.

title: Attract Butterflies to This Hot Spot
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Hot and cold: Hot colors of zinnia, daylily and prairie coneflower are tempered by cool lavender New York aster and meadow blazing star. This combination hits its peak in the heat of summer, at just the right time to benefit rising pollinator populations.

title: Attract Butterflies to This Hot Spot
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Extra irrigation: Swamp milkweed, New York asters and daylilies can use extra water when summers get hot and dry. A drip irrigation system on a timer can help keep these plants hydrated by applying water directly to the soil around their roots without wasting it.

title: Attract Butterflies to This Hot Spot
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Cover the edges: Plant low-growing sedum and Missouri primrose close to the rock edging, allowing their stems to spill out over the stones and soften the transition between the plant border and the hard flagstone walkway. The thick foliage will also shade the rock, keeping the area cooler while preventing weed seeds from sprouting.

title: Attract Butterflies to This Hot Spot
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Sharp contrast: Variegated yuccas create structure and repetition in the garden. Their stiff, swordlike leaves contrast with the loose, airy forms of their flowery companions. Yuccas are evergreen in zone 5, so the garden will have winter interest along with the Golden Hinoki false cypress.

title: Attract Butterflies to This Hot Spot
content: Watercolor design rendering of a sunny pollinator border with yucca, false cypress, zinnias, asters, sedum and flagstone edging along a house wall.

title: Attract Butterflies to This Hot Spot
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Planting plan note: Scale: 1 square = 1 square ft. Apply a 2-inch layer of organic mulch to conserve moisture.

title: Attract Butterflies to This Hot Spot
author: Jennifer Howell
content: How to Care for This Border: After planting, check water daily and keep these new transplants evenly moist for the first growing season to help get plants established. By the second summer, you can water less, but try to make sure the bed gets the equivalent of an inch of rain per week. After that, many of these plants are tolerant of hot, dry spells and won’t need extra watering. But daylilies, New York aster and swamp milkweed benefit from supplemental water in the heat of summer for more robust foliage and a better show of flowers. If you don’t regularly receive this much rain, consider a drip irrigation system.

title: Attract Butterflies to This Hot Spot
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Summer to-do list: Meadow blazing star grows taller in rich, moist soils and may need to be supported by tomato cages or closely planted companion plants. Cut back swamp milkweed and New York aster by a third in late spring to early summer to encourage branching, compact growth and more flowers.

title: Attract Butterflies to This Hot Spot
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Find multipacks of Profusion zinnias at local garden centers or grow them from seed, either starting indoors 6 to 8 weeks before the frost-free date, or direct sowing outdoors when all danger of frost is past and soil temperatures are warming up. These zinnias don’t typically need deadheading, but snip off spent blooms if you like a more manicured look.

title: Attract Butterflies to This Hot Spot
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Cut back daylily bloom stalks once flowers have dropped to encourage reblooming. Prairie coneflower and meadow blazing star can be deadheaded to prolong their flowering period, but leave a few to set seed for the birds.

title: Attract Butterflies to This Hot Spot
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Some of these perennials are easy to divide or may reseed. Cut off new shoots growing alongside the main yucca plant to transplant the divisions. Let seeds fall from swamp milkweed, meadow blazing star and prairie coneflower to get more plants. However, if you don’t want volunteers sprouting up, deadhead them after the blooms are spent to prevent reseeding.

title: Attract Butterflies to This Hot Spot
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Overwintering and spring care: If you leave stems in place all winter, beneficial insects can overwinter in dried stems and birds can find food on leftover seedheads. Then in early spring as plants begin to sprout, try a chop and drop method of cleanup: Use hedge shears to cut back the dead stems in 6- to 12-inch lengths and let them fall on the ground to act as a mulch and compost naturally. This improves the soil and gives overwintering pollinators time to emerge.

title: 3 Invasive Tree Pests to Watch
author: Jennifer Howell
content: 3 Invasive Tree Pests to Watch: It is devastating when a tree loses the battle with an insect pest, leaving a hole in the landscape that can’t be refilled quickly. Sadly, many trees fall prey to invasive insects—here are three destructive ones to watch. But before you panic and kill an unusual or new-to-you insect you have found, make sure it is correctly identified and not a native harmless or beneficial bug lookalike.

title: 3 Invasive Tree Pests to Watch
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Spotted lanternfly, Lycorma delicatula. Found in 14 Eastern and Midwestern states, spotted lanternfly has more than 70 host species, including tree of heaven (Ailanthus altissima), maples (Acer spp. and hybrids), oaks (Quercus spp. and hybrids), many fruit and nut trees, and grapes. How to identify it: Egg masses look like a smear of mud and are found on tree bark, as well as outdoor furniture or vehicles. Nymphs are black or red with white spots and are mobile from spring to fall. Adults appear in summer and are 1 inch long with gray or brown front wings with black spots and red hind wings with black spots and black and white bands at the edge. Damage: Sap-feeding nymphs excrete sticky honeydew, often causing black sooty mold to grow on foliage. Plants are stressed by the feeding and may not die right away, but will be cosmetically affected, and fruit and nut crops will have lower yields. What to do: Inform your state’s Department of Agriculture if you find spotted lanternfly so they can track its spread. Take a picture and note its location, then destroy the insect. Scrape off egg masses and seal in a plastic bag to destroy. These insects can hitchhike as adults or egg masses to new locations on vehicles and transported items like firewood, so some affected states have enacted quarantines on items likely to host egg masses.

title: 3 Invasive Tree Pests to Watch
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Asian longhorned beetle, Anoplophora glabripennis. Found in New York, Ohio, Massachusetts and South Carolina, this beetle has the potential to spread and devastate trees in backyards, forests and parks. It prefers hardwood trees, including maple (Acer spp. and hybrids), birch (Betula spp. and hybrids) and sycamore (Platanus spp.). How to identify it: Adult beetles are shiny, black with white spots and up to 1½ inches long. The long, segmented antennae and legs have white or pale blue bands. Adults chew oval pits in tree bark to lay eggs. Cream-colored larvae hatch and burrow beneath the bark to feed, eventually tunneling deeper into the tree to pupate into adults that emerge from exit holes in early summer to fall. Damage: Exit holes are visible on the bark. Adult beetles eat leaves and twigs, but larvae tunneling under the bark cause yellow leaves, branch dieback and eventual death of the tree by disrupting the flow of water and nutrients. What to do: Unfortunately, a tree infested with Asian longhorned beetle must be cut down and destroyed by chipping or burning. A certified arborist can treat unaffected trees in the area with a systemic insecticide containing imidocloprid to kill larvae and adults that attempt to feed on the tree.

title: 3 Invasive Tree Pests to Watch
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Spongy moth, Lymantria dispar. Though spongy moth has been in northeastern to midwestern United States and eastern Canada for many years, its population explodes periodically, putting tree-filled landscapes at risk. Spongy moth defoliates many kinds of trees, such as oak (Quercus spp.), birch (Betula spp.), and some evergreens. How to identify it: Tan, fuzzy egg masses are laid in bark crevices but also on furniture, garbage cans and vehicles. The larval stage is a hairy gray caterpillar with five pairs of blue dots and six pairs of red dots down its back. Adult males are brown moths with feathery antennae. Females are beige with brown marks on the wings. Damage: Adult spongy moths do not feed, but the caterpillars are voracious eaters and can swiftly devour all the leaves on a tree. Repeated defoliation will weaken and kill the host plant. Unhealthy trees are especially susceptible. What to do: If you find an egg mass in fall, scrape it off and dispose of it in a sealed plastic bag. Spray tree foliage in late spring with a biological insecticide containing Btk (Bacillus thuringiensis kurstaki) to kill feeding caterpillars.

content: Confirm Before You Crush: If you think you have found an invasive insect, contact one of these resources to get a positive ID: local county extension office; State Department of Agriculture (USDA); State Department of Natural Resources (DNR); USDA Animal Plant and Health Inspection Service (APHIS).

title: Q&A
author: Phyllis Dill, CA
content: Q: My camellia shrub turned black and quickly died back. I cut it down and it’s resprouting at the base. What’s going on? A: Camellia (Camellia japonica) leaves can turn black for several reasons. Sooty mold, a fungus caused by insect droppings, appears black. Over time it will flake off, or you can wipe it away. Another possible culprit is mites, which darken leaves and usually leave behind a metallic sheen. Sunburn is another possibility if the shrub suddenly gets more sun than it used to. But none of these problems is known to cause a rapid dieback of stems. Because branches are dying, with new growth sprouting near the base, your shrub is probably stressed because of a root problem. It could be caused by an excessively wet year. Or maybe you need to redirect your lawn sprinklers or downspout. To help your camellia, pull mulch away from the base of the shrub, then lightly cultivate the soil and let it dry out. Trim away dead branches, and if the roots have not been too severely damaged, the new growth coming from the base can be retrained into a new bush. But if you aren’t able to improve the soil moisture problem, you may need to move the shrub to a better spot.

title: Q&A
author: Marge Hunt, IL
content: Q: I finally got my garden mums to survive winter, but this year they are so much taller than they were last year. Why? A: Garden mums (Chrysanthemum hybrids) grown for sale as potted plants are often treated with plant growth regulators (PGRs). These hormones keep plants compact, making them easier to ship or display. The following year, planted in the garden, mums grow to their normal height. But you can keep them compact by using this pruning technique: In spring, when stems are 6 to 10 inches tall, pinch out the growing tip. A couple weeks later, pinch the tip of each new side branch to make your plants even bushier. By fall you’ll have short, stocky plants covered with blooms. Or if you prefer, wait until your mums are taller and shear off the top third to half of all of the stems at once. The plant will look rough for a week or so, but will quickly fill in with new branches. Stop either technique by midsummer so your mum has time to set buds for the autumn show.

title: Garden Jargon
content: Nyctinasty: If you’ve had a plant close its petals at night and open again in the morning, you’ve seen nyctinasty, the movement of plant parts caused by changes in light and darkness, in action.

title: Q&A
author: Pat Oberlander, PA
content: Q: Any tips on how to fill gaps in my border when early perennials or bulbs go dormant? A: To camouflage a spot, you could set an ornament or plant-filled pot there. But for a more permanent solution, add a few billowing perennials next to those that take a summer break. Here are a few easy-to-grow favorites.

title: Q&A
author: Pat Oberlander, PA
content: Baby’s breath, Gypsophila paniculata. Billows of tiny white flowers in summer; full sun; 2 to 3 ft. tall and wide; cold zones 3 to 9. Baby’s breath leaves plenty of room for spring perennials to shine before it puts on most of its growth in summer.

title: Q&A
author: Pat Oberlander, PA
content: Clematis, Clematis recta ‘Purpurea’. Nonclimbing species with lax stems and small fragrant white flowers in late spring to early summer; full sun to part shade; 2 to 4 ft. tall and wide; cold zones 3 to 9.

title: Q&A
author: Pat Oberlander, PA
content: Bloody cranesbill, Geranium sanguineum striatum. Long-blooming soft pink flowers in early summer; full sun to part shade; 6 to 9 in. tall, 12 to 18 in. wide; cold zones 3 to 8.

title: Q&A
author: Pat Oberlander, PA
content: Catmint, Nepeta racemosa ‘Walker’s Low’. Sprawling stems of lavender-blue flowers in summer; full sun; 18 to 36 in. tall and wide; cold zones 3 to 9.

title: Q&A
author: Carole Nash, TN
content: Q: What’s happening to my rose bushes? A: The deformed growth in the photo, often called a “witch’s broom,” is a main symptom of rose rosette disease. You may also find thickened or excessively thorny stems. Over a few years, the rose weakens and eventually dies. Rose rosette is a virus transmitted by tiny wingless eriophyd mites. Horticultural oil and insecticidal soap help reduce the spread of these mites to healthy plants, but at this time there is no cure once a rose is infected. Always remove an infected plant as soon as you spot symptoms. Cover the entire shrub in a plastic bag to contain the mites before cutting stems close to the ground. Then dig out the roots, put everything in the bag and send it away in the trash or burn. Research and testing are being conducted on a beneficial predatory mite to attack the harmful one. And breeders are hard at work on resistant rose cultivars. Watch for these developments in coming years. Rose rosette causes clumps of small, red-tinted leaves that never grow larger.

title: Weed Watch
content: Redroot pigweed, Amaranthus retroflexus: What it looks like. This summer annual can grow 1 to 6 feet tall. Stout, almost woody, stems are covered with tiny hairs and only lightly branched. Near the base, leaves may grow 4 to 6 inches long, gradually becoming smaller near the top and at stem tips. You’ll see a reddish tint on stems, especially near the root. And as the weather cools, the color becomes even more pronounced. In late summer to early fall, dense bristly panicles of tiny greenish flowers form at the top and tips of branches. Seeds are tiny, dark brown to black and very prolific. One plant can produce up to 100,000 seeds that can remain viable in the soil for 30 years.

title: Weed Watch
content: Redroot pigweed, Amaranthus retroflexus: Where to find it. Pigweed is common across much of North America, found in sunny spots that are occasionally cultivated. But it also likes undisturbed sites.

title: Weed Watch
content: Redroot pigweed, Amaranthus retroflexus: How to get rid of it. Seedlings are easy to hoe out, and older plants have a taproot that make them easy to pull. Repeated mowing helps, but even very short plants produce seeds. Preemergent applied in spring keeps seeds from sprouting.

title: Blast Off With Bright Color!
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Starship™ Scarlet lobelia, Lobelia x speciosa: Perennial. Blooms: Spikes of deep red flowers atop lightly bronzed foliage in midsummer to fall. Light: Full sun to part shade. Soil: Average to wet, well-drained. Pests: None serious. Size: 18 to 24 in. tall, 6 to 12 in. wide. Cold hardy USDA zones 6 to 10.

title: Blast Off With Bright Color!
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Peer at an individual flower from the inflorescence of Starship Scarlet lobelia, and you might be reminded of a hummingbird hovering in flight. Plant these in your garden and you’ll see plenty of the actual bird zipping about, feeding from the stunning red blooms. A cross of several native lobelias, this cultivar is loaded with flower spikes that bloom from midsummer to fall, just when hummingbirds and butterflies are fueling up for their migratory journeys.

title: Blast Off With Bright Color!
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Sunshine and water: Starship Scarlet lobelia is a columnar-growing plant that fits into tight spaces with ease, which also makes it a great candidate as a container thriller. Its dark green leaves are blushed on the edges with bronze or burgundy, turning darker in sunnier spots. It loves full sun, but give it some afternoon shade where summers are hot and dry.

title: Blast Off With Bright Color!
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Grow Starship Scarlet lobelia in rich, consistently moist soil. It is perfect for rain gardens or the edges of a water feature, as in “Along the Water’s Edge” below, where roots stay moist but are not submerged for long periods of time.

title: Blast Off With Bright Color!
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Maintenance tips: This upright-growing lobelia has a better branching habit than others in its family, but to ensure it stays compact and full, you can pinch the growing tips and first two sets of leaves on each stem in late spring before the plant sets flowers. When blossoms fade, cut the spent stalks off at the first leaf node to promote more flowers from side branches and extend the bloom time. Divide plants every two to three years in early spring. Simply split the clump in two and replant to fill the voids of space in your garden with these bright red rockets.

title: Blast Off With Bright Color!
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Along the Water’s Edge: Framed by soft switchgrass, moisture-loving lobelia, coral bells, canna and pitcher plant grow on the shore of a small pond, and don’t mind if the water overflows its banks occasionally. Position pitcher plant closest to the pond’s edge to keep its roots wet.

title: Blast Off With Bright Color!
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Along the Water’s Edge plant A, switchgrass (Panicum virgatum ‘Heavy Metal’): Perennial; blue-gray foliage with maroon fall color topped by pink-tinged seedheads in mid- to late summer; full sun to part shade; 4 to 5 ft. tall, 1 to 2 ft. wide; cold hardy in USDA zones 5 to 9.

title: Blast Off With Bright Color!
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Along the Water’s Edge plant B, canna (Canna x generalis Cannova® Orange Shades): Bulb; bright orange flowers rise above huge green leaves in summer to fall; full sun to part shade; 30 to 48 in. tall, 14 to 20 in. wide; cold hardy in USDA zones 7 to 12. Lift canna rhizomes in fall in zones 6 or colder and replant in spring.

title: Blast Off With Bright Color!
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Along the Water’s Edge plant D, coral bells (Heuchera ‘Paprika’): Perennial; spikes of white flowers in late spring to early summer over red-orange foliage with a silver veil; full sun to full shade; 8 to 12 in. tall, 12 to 16 in. wide; cold hardy in USDA zones 4 to 9.

title: Blast Off With Bright Color!
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Along the Water’s Edge plant E, pitcher plant (Sarracenia ‘Bug Bat’): Perennial; tubular pitchers shading from green at the bottom to cinnamon red near the top with white speckles along the back and a darker red hood; full sun to part shade; 14 to 16 in. tall, 12 in. wide; cold hardy in USDA zones 5 to 9. Simulate bog conditions by planting pitcher plants in a peat-filled tub with drain holes 1 inch above the bottom of the tub.

title: Design Dilemmas
content: Design Dilemmas: Struck by the unexpected beauty of a plant at the garden center, in a flurry of inspiration, we grab other beautiful companions, purchase them all, and head home full of grand plants and visions but no real plan. Sometimes it works out, and many times it doesn’t because designing a garden takes attention to nuts and bolts: the hows, wheres and with-whats. Flip through the following pages of inspiring photos and get practical solutions to your garden woes. Improve your garden’s layout, add function, color it with your personality, and find that perfect fix that boosts your garden from good to better to best.

title: Design Dilemmas: What should I do with an empty entrance?
content: The whole experience of walking into your home can be enhanced by the colors, aroma and appeal of a prolific planting. An entrance is guaranteed to garner attention, and a front door is an automatic focal point, so concentrate your efforts here, and don’t be shy.

title: Design Dilemmas: What should I do with an empty entrance?
content: The goal is to lead attention to the door. When you’re making decisions about color scheme, plant heights and placement, use your door as a determining factor: If it doesn’t enhance the front door, then it doesn’t fit your design.

title: Design Dilemmas: What should I do with an empty entrance?
content: The key is to remember that this is precious real estate—not just a place to make an impression, but a space to garden. So let’s look at how to pack in a variety of plants you love while still making an eye-catching, welcoming and well-considered entrance.

title: Design Dilemmas: What should I do with an empty entrance?
content: Deal with proportions: This two-story home doesn’t sit very far from the street. Tall, lush plantings hide just enough of the house to give the illusion that it sits farther back on the lot. Site tall plants in a spot that softens a harsh line or emphasizes a feature, such as in line with the corners of the front porch here. Then, working outward, make sure each successive layer is shorter than the one before to help frame the home.

title: Design Dilemmas: What should I do with an empty entrance?
content: Emphasize an entrance: Lining the stairs with container gardens is one way to making an entrance pop. But here, all of the interest is jam-packed into the small front yard. The key to a flower-filled front yard is to taper the plant heights down toward the pathway to keep a clear view of the door. More containers here would just add clutter.

title: Design Dilemmas: What should I do with an empty entrance?
content: Add color and liveliness: Here, colorful native plants, such as anise hyssop (Agastache foeniculum), black-eyed Susan (Rudbeckia spp. and hybrids) and coneflower (Echinacea spp. and hybrids), attract native bees — some of the best pollinators around. Bluebirds and goldfinches also love these plants. Feeders filled with nyjer seed feed the goldfinches, shown in inset, through winter and spring. Their cheerful presence is another way to color your entrance.

title: Design Dilemmas: What should I do with an empty entrance?
content: Front-yard entrance garden with layered perennial plantings framing a brick two-story house and red front door.

title: Design Dilemmas: What should I do with an empty entrance?
content: Inset close-up of a bird feeder among colorful front-yard plantings, illustrating added liveliness near an entry.

title: Design Dilemmas: Where do I start with a blank space?
content: Don’t get overwhelmed with big-picture ideas. Instead, divide your garden up into rooms to take it one section at a time. Start by giving each room a purpose. Will you use it to entertain? Or do you simply want a space to grow your favorite plants?

title: Design Dilemmas: Where do I start with a blank space?
content: The garden below and at right is designed for entertaining, so building a multilevel deck with multiple rooms for gathering and dining was the starting point.

title: Design Dilemmas: Where do I start with a blank space?
content: After the why and where, get to work organizing your room with walls, a floor and transitions. Should a fence, trellis or tall plants be added to mark the boundaries? This garden uses both manmade structures, such as the side of the home and deck railings, and trees, bamboo and tall plants to create boundaries. Now, what will you use underfoot? A solid surface is best for seating areas. Lawn or mulch are good choices for making plants the focus. Finally, add transitions to mark the entrances. A showy arbor or winding path are both great options.

title: Design Dilemmas: Where do I start with a blank space?
content: As you think through these questions, explore the garden rooms pictured here. Use our practical tips for working magic in your blank space and finally create that showpiece garden you’ve always wanted.

title: Design Dilemmas: Where do I start with a blank space?
content: Add transitions with levels and stairs: Here stairs take you from the entertaining area of the wooden deck to a terraced walkway that leads down another set of stairs to a lush lawn, signaling a change in atmosphere, aesthetic and function. Find a spot where you might be able to add a set of steps or retaining wall to help define your room.

title: Design Dilemmas: Where do I start with a blank space?
content: Think of the lawn as a floor: The low retaining wall meets the border of tall shade plants to make walls, the lawn makes a floor, and bamboo arches over to provide a rooflike sense of enclosure. Look for spaces in your garden that may already be marked by boundaries and add a fountain or seating to give it some purpose.

title: Design Dilemmas: Where do I start with a blank space?
content: Layered backyard garden room with lawn floor, stone retaining wall, bamboo, stairs and seating areas leading toward a deck.

title: Design Dilemmas: Where do I start with a blank space?
content: Give each element purpose: This level of the deck is for smaller gatherings, so it only needs a bench, chair and small table to provide a place to sit and sip a drink while dinner cooks on the grill (positioned across from the seating area). Containers make great dividers for garden rooms, but make them double-duty: Herbs and edible flowers are perfect for garnishing whatever is cooking on the grill.

title: Design Dilemmas: Where do I start with a blank space?
content: Keep some things hidden: Screen part of the view between garden rooms for a sense of mystery that entices you and gives each space more privacy. Here, a tree grows up between this level and the upper level, which has space for larger gatherings, in order to make the area more intimate.

title: Design Dilemmas: Where do I start with a blank space?
content: Multilevel deck garden room with bench seating, small table, potted plants and stairs partly screened by a small tree.

title: Design Dilemmas: Where do I start with a blank space? Continued
content: If you’re looking for a way to lay out a space for your favorite flowers, here’s a garden room with nothing more than plants and pathways. Unlike an indoor room, not every garden room needs to have a spot to sit.

title: Design Dilemmas: Where do I start with a blank space? Continued
content: So how do you enjoy a garden room that doesn’t have seating? With paths that wander through the beds so you can admire plants up close. Let plants grow right up to the path’s edge, listen to the gravel crunch beneath your feet and you’ve made your garden room a fascinating multisensory experience. Paths also separate the garden into distinct planting beds and organize your space.

title: Design Dilemmas: Where do I start with a blank space? Continued
content: This gardener put the garden immediately next to his home and the lawn further away so that he could step out his back door and into a flower-filled wonderland. How exactly do you organize a garden like this? Let’s take a look at some of the elements.

title: Design Dilemmas: Where do I start with a blank space? Continued
content: Start with a rectangle: Garden rooms can be any shape, but if you’re having trouble deciding, mimic the shape of a room in your home. A rectangle is an obvious choice.

title: Design Dilemmas: Where do I start with a blank space? Continued
content: Create year-round structure: Nestled into the border of plants is a fence that marks the boundary. This structure defines the garden room year-round, though for most of the growing season it takes second place to the plants. If all of your plants primarily bloom in one season, you might need a secondary structure like this. To forego a fence and rely solely on plants to mark your boundaries, make sure to choose some that have multiple seasons of interest for year-round definition.

title: Design Dilemmas: Where do I start with a blank space? Continued
content: Wide view of a flower-filled garden room beside a house, with paths, lawn edge, rope-and-post fencing and an arbor.

title: Design Dilemmas: Where do I start with a blank space? Continued
content: Keep fencing simple: A thick rope connects solid wooden posts for a fence that adds just enough structure. Rope is relatively inexpensive, easy to install and has few maintenance needs. It keeps the room open, lets air flow and doesn’t obstruct any views into the rest of the yard.

title: Design Dilemmas: Where do I start with a blank space? Continued
content: Install arbors as doorways: We’re already accustomed to walking through a doorway to enter a new room, so add a “doorway” by using a garden arbor. Let a fragrant or colorful vining plant climb up an arbor to add to the experience of passing through. It also lifts your eye up to draw your gaze into the garden.

title: Design Dilemmas: Where do I start with a blank space? Continued
author: DESIGN: Andrew Grossman, www.andrewgrossman.com
content: Garden room detail with rope-and-post fence, flowering vine on a post, lush plantings and a wooden arbor as a doorway.

title: Design Dilemmas: How do I add color to my garden?
content: Nailing down the right colors can be an unexpectedly tricky element of garden design. Here are some tips to help you keep a tight, unified color scheme that stuns and pleases.

title: Design Dilemmas: How do I add color to my garden?
content: Make colors pop: Choose one or two bright colors to stand out among the neutral ones. Red seat cushions draw attention to the red door and red flowers speckled about. Bright yellow art hanging on the wall makes the yellow flowers pop even more.

title: Design Dilemmas: How do I add color to my garden?
content: Add an accent wall: You know how painting one wall a different color in an indoor room calls attention to an area? The same applies here. Paint a shed or garage wall a different, deeper color to make a great backdrop. Containers of bright, cheery plants in front of the wall become the center of attention. Or use the accent wall to set the color scheme: Paint the wall a catchy light blue or red and then use blue or red plants in borders for a unified look.

title: Design Dilemmas: How do I add color to my garden?
content: Patio garden with containers, red chair cushions, red-trimmed door, yellow wall art and a blue-gray accent wall used for color coordination.

title: Design Dilemmas: How do I add color to my garden?
content: Go for the gold foliage: A fun way to add a variation of color is with foliage, such as this spiderwort (Tradescantia hybrid) with gold leaves. It stands out in the border and captures the admiration of those who may have never seen one like it before. But use gold foliage sparingly in a bed or border because it works best as an accent. Too much gold foliage can dominate the bed.

title: Design Dilemmas: How do I add color to my garden?
content: Variations of a theme: For a garden bed’s color scheme, use no more than three main colors, and repeat them. Here the color scheme is purple, gold and green. But you don’t have to stick to just one shade of purple. Fuchsia-purple spotted orchid (Dactylorhiza maculata) flowers are echoed by light purple spiderwort blooms and multiple plants with dark purple foliage.

title: Design Dilemmas: 5 Design Dilemmas You Can Fix in a Weekend!
content: Sometimes your design dilemmas might not be all that obvious to you, but they could be disrupting your productivity and your garden’s functionality in a big way. Here are five simple solutions to common design flaws. The good news is that you can do most of them this weekend with few extra materials or tools required. Say hello to simpler gardening!

title: Design Dilemmas: 5 Design Dilemmas You Can Fix in a Weekend!
content: Organize your potting bench: A potting bench becomes an easy spot to dump odds and ends. Adding narrow shelves gives you a spot to put unused pots and garden décor without leaving room for too much clutter. Add hooks to the side to hang small tools, such as trowels, and weather-tight plastic containers are perfect places for seed packets, plant tags, small bags of fertilizer, and other notes and papers that might have useful information. There’s a bottom shelf of this bench that stores 5-gallon buckets, bigger pots, unused stakes and watering supplies. And that pack of plants you still need to plant? Leave it front and center so you don’t forget about it!

title: Design Dilemmas: 5 Design Dilemmas You Can Fix in a Weekend!
content: Outdoor wooden potting bench organized with narrow shelves, pots, garden décor, plastic storage bins, buckets, tools and plants ready to plant.

title: Design Dilemmas: 5 Design Dilemmas You Can Fix in a Weekend!
content: Give yourself a place to rest: Some garden tasks can take a couple of hours and quickly drain your energy. Of course you’ll need a place to sit and give yourself a minute to rest. A chair and even a small table tucked near your higher-maintenance garden areas gives you a spot to take a breather and rehydrate. Don’t let yourself wander all the way back indoors toward the air conditioning and comfy couch — you might lose motivation and never return to your task!

title: Design Dilemmas: 5 Design Dilemmas You Can Fix in a Weekend!
content: Hang your tools: There are a few tools that you might use weekly in your garden. Hang them in a quickly accessible place. This gardener hangs her shovel and some pruning tools by the back door so she always knows where they are, and sometimes even just seeing them as you walk by becomes a gentle reminder of tasks that need to be done.

title: Design Dilemmas: 5 Design Dilemmas You Can Fix in a Weekend!
author: DESIGN: Mary Ellen Asmundson
content: Small chair and table tucked into a lush garden beside stone pavers, providing a resting place near maintenance areas.

title: Design Dilemmas: 5 Design Dilemmas You Can Fix in a Weekend!
content: Back-door garden area with hanging shovel and pruning tools near containers and a small chair for quick access.

title: Design Dilemmas: 5 Design Dilemmas You Can Fix in a Weekend!
content: Add instant interest: Do you have a drab garden bed that dampens your mood every time you look at it? It’s hard to be motivated to take care of an area you aren’t fond of. Give yourself a reason to love the bed by adding a showy accent piece. A periwinkle obelisk rounds out the charm and adds height here. Choose a height that balances out two extremes, such as the peak of the shed and the low planting. For a shady spot, pick a structure with enough visual weight to stand out. Opt for thicker wooden materials over thin metal ones, but keep them in proportion to your bed size. Choose colors that stand out but don’t disrupt the overall look, just like how this obelisk pulls from the color of the dusty blue hosta (Hosta spp. and hybrids).

title: Design Dilemmas: 5 Design Dilemmas You Can Fix in a Weekend!
content: Find a solution with steppers: Maintaining deep garden beds can get overwhelming, unless you give yourself a place to start. Add a few stepping stones that lead deeper into the garden bed. This way you’ll be able to work even if it’s muddy or getting overgrown with weeds.

title: Bad Brussels Juju
author: Jamie Seitz
content: Late-summer heartbreak: In August, I came out to my garden one morning to do a few morning affirmations with my Brussels sprouts. It was then I discovered that squash bugs had descended on my garden with an appetite of Augustus Gloop guzzling from Willy Wonka’s chocolate river and had turned an entire garden bed to ash. In slow motion, I turned to the bed where my Brussels sprouts were growing. One plant was done for, but the other looked like it might survive. I now know I should have harvested everything I could off the healthy plant, but I got greedy. Too many weren’t quite ready and I really wanted a big bowl of roasted Brussels sprouts, so I waited. Two days later, all my precious sprouts were gone, and I was devastated.

title: from the editor
content: There are a whole lot of reasons why we garden. It may start with the practical returns, like growing your own food or improving your property value with attractive landscaping. Eventually you enjoy a sense of accomplishment, and might even get a few compliments from the neighbors. And then there are the physical and mental health benefits...

title: from the editor
content: By the end of summer it’s tempting to just throw in the towel and forget all that. But then I notice a dry plant that I loved so much (and probably spent too much on) last spring, is desperate for water. Or the weeds have become embarrassing. Or maybe I hear buzzing on the coneflowers and want to investigate. Whatever the reason, the garden lures me out and before I know it, I’ve cleaned up the weeds, deadheaded and had a lovely chat with a neighbor. Physically, I may feel it in the morning, but I’m mentally restored, and my garden looks respectable again!

title: Reader Tips
author: Rebecca Sweet, CA
content: If you have a heavy insect pest infestation taking over your garden, you might want to harness all the resources available. Oak tree worms devoured Rebecca’s garden every spring so she worked to bring more insect-eating birds into her garden. The lure: peanuts. Birds who eat oak tree worms, such as nuthatches, woodpeckers and sparrows, also feast on peanuts. When Rebecca placed a peanut feeder under her oak tree, she saw that these birds ate from the feeder and also fed on the oak worms as they hatched from within the oak bark, preventing the worms from reaching the garden.

title: Reader Tips
author: Anna Ellenberger, PA
content: When Anna buys multipacks of plants, the garden center puts them in plastic trays with gridded bottoms. Don’t just throw those useful trays away. Anna keeps them stored until fall. Then when she digs up tender bulbs, such as gladiolus, dahlias or cannas, to overwinter indoors, she shakes the loose soil off the bulbs, and places them on the ventilated trays to dry before storing them for winter. These trays are also useful for drying walnuts after the hulls are removed.

title: Reader Tips
author: John Wachowicz, TN
content: Looking for a smart way to store your seeds? Instead of using a plain envelope, repurpose return envelopes with a glassine window for seed storage. John finds it extra helpful to easily see the seeds inside without having to open a sealed envelope.

title: Reader Tips
author: Lou Dammrich, MO
content: Leaf litter can make a good mulch for your garden beds: After suppressing weeds during the growing season, the leaves break down to nourish the soil and increase drainage. But just raking leaves directly into your beds in the fall might leave a messy look and risk smothering some perennials. Instead, Lou rakes leaves as usual in the fall, but instead of composting or disposing of them, he builds a temporary leaf mulch bin out of a 3x10-foot length of 1/2-inch hardware cloth.

title: Reader Tips
author: Lou Dammrich, MO
content: To make a temporary leaf mulch bin, form the hardware cloth into a cylindrical shape by connecting the two 3-foot ends together with cable ties. Stand it on end and place it somewhere accessible but unnoticeable. Dump leaves into the bin as you rake them up throughout the fall. Turn the leaf mulch with a pitch fork once a month throughout the winter and water once in a while if there is little precipitation. In early spring, disconnect the two ends, scoop out the leaf mulch and spread it around the garden.

title: The Wild Side
content: Fiery searcher beetle (Calosoma scrutator) appearance: If you glimpse these speedy ground beetles, you’ll be amazed by the massive 1 1/4-inch size and the colorful metallic green and violet body with iridescent red margins. These beneficial bugs, also known as caterpillar hunters, hunt grubs, larvae and other insects on the ground and even scale branches and trunks to seek out prey. They aren’t afraid to use their big pinching mandibles to bite you too.

title: The Wild Side
content: Fiery searcher beetle (Calosoma scrutator) life cycle: Females lay small, oblong off-white eggs in the soil in spring. Larvae are 1/4 to 3/4 inches long with black mandibles and white and black bodies. They feed above the soil on other bug larvae, then return to the soil to pupate into adults. The adults live 2 or more years. Adults and larvae feed on insect pests, particularly tent caterpillars, gypsy moth caterpillars, cabbage worms, Colorado potato beetle and even slugs.

title: The Wild Side
content: Fiery searcher beetle (Calosoma scrutator) habitat: These mostly nocturnal beetles live in the United States and southern Canada in gardens and grassy areas. They’re active spring through fall, especially in spring when caterpillars and larvae emerge. Leave spaces for them to find shelter; a patch of tall grasses and some rocks or small logs can provide a haven.

title: Choose the Perfect Tree Shape
content: Round tree shape: Great shade trees because of their wide canopies, single specimens make a statement, grouped round trees create solid backgrounds, and they soften edges of buildings nicely. Examples include Ohio buckeye (Aesculus glabra), 20 to 40 feet tall and wide, USDA zones 3 to 7; river birch (Betula nigra), 40 to 70 feet tall and 40 to 60 feet wide, zones 4 to 9; sugar maple (Acer saccharum), 40 to 80 feet tall and 30 to 60 feet wide, zones 3 to 8; and white oak (Quercus alba), 50 to 80 feet tall and wide, zones 3 to 9.

title: Choose the Perfect Tree Shape
content: Vase tree shape: Few lower branches make these trees useful where you want to set a chair under the canopy, line a street or driveway without blocking visibility, or create a striking single specimen. Examples include American elm ‘Valley Forge’ (Ulmus americana), 60 to 70 feet tall and 50 to 60 feet wide, USDA zones 5 to 9; crape myrtle (Lagerstroemia indica), 6 to 25 feet tall and 6 to 20 feet wide, zones 6 to 9; golden raintree (Koelreuteria paniculata), 30 to 40 feet tall and wide, zones 5 to 9; and hackberry (Celtis occidentalis), 40 to 60 feet tall and wide, zones 2 to 9.

title: Choose the Perfect Tree Shape
content: Weeping tree shape: Weeping trees make interesting focal points, fit tight spaces, work well on retaining walls where branches can cascade to a lower level, and often provide movement or sound when rustled by a breeze. Examples include blue atlas cedar ‘Glauca Pendula’ (Cedrus atlantica), 15 to 25 feet tall and wide, USDA zones 6 to 9; weeping beech ‘Pendula’ (Fagus sylvatica), 20 to 50 feet tall and 15 to 30 feet wide, zones 4 to 7; weeping cherry Snow Fountains (Prunus), 8 to 15 feet tall and 6 to 8 feet wide, zones 5 to 8; and weeping redbud ‘Ruby Falls’ (Cercis canadensis), 6 to 8 feet tall and 5 to 6 feet wide, zones 5 to 9.

title: Choose the Perfect Tree Shape
content: Columnar tree shape: Columnar trees make good hedges, windbreaks or screens, create a focal point when several are clustered together, and one or a pair can create a formal entry accent. Examples include English oak fastigiata (Quercus robur f. fastigiata), 50 to 60 feet tall and 10 to 20 feet wide, USDA zones 5 to 8; European hornbeam ‘Frans Fontaine’ (Carpinus betulus), 20 to 25 feet tall and 6 to 10 feet wide, zones 4 to 8; Irish yew ‘Fastigiata’ (Taxus baccata), 15 to 30 feet tall and 4 to 8 feet wide, zones 6 to 8; and juniper Sky High (Juniperus scopulorum), 12 to 15 feet tall and 4 to 5 feet wide, zones 3 to 8.

title: Choose the Perfect Tree Shape
content: Pyramidal tree shape: Pyramidal trees have a heavy, structural presence that works well for a screen or windbreak, and their strong shape frames the corner of a house nicely. Examples include Colorado spruce (Picea pungens), 30 to 60 feet tall and 10 to 20 feet wide, USDA zones 2 to 7; European larch (Larix decidua), 60 to 100 feet tall and 20 to 30 feet wide, zones 2 to 6; little-leaf linden (Tilia cordata), 50 to 70 feet tall and 35 to 50 feet wide, zones 3 to 7; and pin oak (Quercus palustris), 50 to 70 feet tall and 40 to 60 feet wide, zones 4 to 8.

title: Choose the Perfect Tree Shape
content: Irregular tree shape: Irregular trees can fill a lot of space and provide shade in a casual landscape. Examples include sycamore (Platanus occidentalis), 75 to 100 feet tall and wide, USDA zones 4 to 9; live oak (Quercus virginiana), 40 to 80 feet tall and 60 to 100 feet wide, zones 8 to 10; pagoda dogwood (Cornus alternifolia), 15 to 25 feet tall and 20 to 30 feet wide, zones 3 to 7; and pawpaw (Asimina triloba), 15 to 30 feet tall and wide, zones 5 to 9.

title: Add Quick Fall Color with Containers
author: Kristin Beane Sullivan
content: Even as the rest of your garden starts to slow down in fall, there’s still time to add a splash of color with a couple of high-impact containers. Since plants aren’t as likely to grow as quickly at the end of the growing season, go ahead and pack them together to get a look you love right away. The nice thing about fall containers is that as the weather starts to cool and the sun becomes less intense, they don’t usually require as much water or attention to remain healthy.

title: Window Dressing
author: Kristin Beane Sullivan
content: If there’s anywhere that can benefit from a seasonal refresh, it’s a windowbox by the front door. This high-impact autumn plan uses bright color contrasts and a variety of textures. Let the stipa grass, violas and petunias spill over and soften the front edge of the box, and back it up with the tall spires of bright red celosia. Fill the space between with floss flower, marigolds and ornamental kale. Add long-lasting interest with dried stems or twigs; hydrangea stems were picked green and aged beautifully.

title: Window Dressing
author: Kristin Beane Sullivan
content: Windowbox plant list: A, Aloha Blue floss flower (Ageratum houstonianum); B, ‘Smart Look Red’ crested celosia (Celosia argentea var. cristata); C, ‘Fireball’ French marigold (Tagetes patula); D, viola (Viola hybrid); E, ‘Sirocco’ stipa grass (Anemanthele lessoniana); F, SuperCal Premium Cinnamon petchoa (Petunia x calibrachoa); G, ornamental kale (Brassica oleracea). The windowbox is 36 by 8 inches. Field corn tassels, cattails, maiden grass seedheads and dried hydrangea blooms add height and seasonal interest along the back and center.

title: Crowning Glory
author: Kristin Beane Sullivan
content: For dramatic height in a container, the burgundy leaves of cordyline can’t be beat. Surround it with easy-to-grow lantana, geranium and licorice plant, and your container will make quite an impact. Cordyline is a slow grower, especially in a container, so purchase one that’s the size you need now. A large one can be expensive, but you can overwinter it as a houseplant and put it out again in spring.

title: Crowning Glory
author: Kristin Beane Sullivan
content: Crowning Glory plant list: A, ‘Red Star’ cordyline (Cordyline); B, Patriot Classic Firewagon lantana (Lantana); C, Fantasia Cardinal Red geranium (Pelargonium); D, ‘Silver Queen’ bugleweed (Ajuga reptans); E, licorice plant (Helichrysum petiolare). The container is 14 inches square.

title: Cool Fall Look
author: Kristin Beane Sullivan
content: The ornamental kale and sweet alyssum have been in this container since spring, but by late summer the other spring-planted companions had fizzled out. To refresh it for autumn, a showy dahlia was added in the center and zinnias and Mexican heather were tucked in around the large ornamental kale heads. Mexican heather also works well in summer because it tolerates heat and drought and attracts butterflies and other pollinators. Cold-hardy kale will last long after frost kills everything else in the container.

title: Plants Pollinators Love
content: If you’re trying to make your garden more pollinator friendly, knowing which plants to grow is key. Sam Hoadley, manager of horticultural research at Mt. Cuba Center in Delaware, leads researchers who conduct plant trials on native plant species and their cultivars and hybrids. Each 3- to 5-year trial evaluates plant performance, ornamental value and attractiveness to pollinators. Based on these tests, he has shared some of the best plants you can grow to help birds, bees, butterflies and other pollinating insects.

title: Plants Pollinators Love
content: Native plants often attract lots of pollinators, but two cultivars, ‘Jeana’ garden phlox and ‘Jacob Cline’ bee balm, were head and shoulders above the other plants in their respective trials. These are wild selections, meaning they occurred naturally without typical human intervention, so the blooms are very similar to the species. In Mt. Cuba’s coreopsis study, different bee species had definite favorites among 25 mostly yellow species and cultivars.

title: Plants Pollinators Love
content: Lead photo of a colorful pollinator planting with yellow, orange and pink flowers at Mt. Cuba Center.

title: Plants Pollinators Love
content: Portrait photo of Sam Hoadley, manager of horticultural research at Mt. Cuba Center.

title: Plants Pollinators Love
content: Single coneflowers: Coneflower’s “flower” is botanically an inflorescence made up of individual ray and disc flowers. The fertile disc flowers develop seed once pollinated. Double coneflowers: The extra petals on double flowers may not leave enough room for the floral parts that produce pollen, nectar or seed that pollinators need.

title: Plants Pollinators Love
content: Flower shape matters. Breeding or continued selection that changes the inflorescence, or cluster of individual flowers on a stem, can make it less appealing to pollinators. During Mt. Cuba’s coneflower trial, double varieties had far fewer visits than singles. If you like double blooms and still want to feed pollinators, Sam recommends planting a sweep of singles and tucking in a few clusters of doubles.

title: Plants Pollinators Love
content: Grow a long-lasting buffet by creating borders that bloom from early spring to late fall. Columbine and downy serviceberry can feed just-emerging bumble or mason bees in spring; summer-blooming coreopsis and coneflower provide meals for insects and birds; and late-flowering goldenrod can help wildlife prepare for migration or winter dormancy.

title: Plants Pollinators Love
content: Comparison photos of single and double coneflowers showing accessible pollen-bearing disc flowers versus petal-filled double blooms.

title: Pollinator Plant Picks
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: The trials at Mt. Cuba run for 3 to 5 years and are like a boot camp for plants: nutrition comes from the soil, and supplemental water is only given the first year or in times of drought. Watch team volunteers regularly document which pollinators visit each species or cultivar. At the end of the trial, Sam’s report rates flowering, habit, disease resistance and pollinator visits.

title: Pollinator Plant Picks
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: ‘Jeana’ garden phlox (Phlox paniculata) was popular with butterflies at Mt. Cuba, and lavender-pink ‘Jeana’ was the star of the 2017 trial. It has loads of flowers and excellent powdery mildew resistance, though overhead watering should be avoided and space between plants helps air circulate. Other butterfly-favored garden phlox included pale pink ‘John Farich’ and ‘Thai Pink Jade’. It blooms in large clusters from midsummer to fall, grows in full sun to part shade in moist, well-drained soil, reaches 3 to 5 feet tall and 2 to 3 feet wide, and is cold hardy in USDA zones 4 to 8.

title: Pollinator Plant Picks
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: ‘Jacob Cline’ bee balm (Monarda hybrid) was tops with hummingbirds in the 2016 report, with far more visits to its tubular bright red flowers than other varieties or even the species. Mt. Cuba staff guessed it may be due to large flowers on tall stems, which make it easy for birds to see and access. It is not very powdery mildew resistant; if the plant looks shabby, stems can be cut back to within a few inches of the ground and clean foliage will regrow. Moths and butterflies found ‘Claire Grace’ and ‘Violet Queen’ most appealing. It blooms in summer, grows in full sun to part shade in moist, well-drained soil, reaches 3 to 4 feet tall and 2 to 3 feet wide, and is cold hardy in USDA zones 4 to 9.

title: Pollinator Plant Picks
content: Photo of lavender-pink ‘Jeana’ garden phlox flower clusters used as a pollinator plant pick.

title: Pollinator Plant Picks
content: Photo of red ‘Jacob Cline’ bee balm flowers used as a hummingbird-favored pollinator plant pick.

title: Pollinator Plant Picks
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: ‘Fragrant Angel’ coneflower (Echinacea purpurea) was popular in Mt. Cuba’s coneflower trial. The white-flowered natural selection was even more popular with pollinators than the species: bees, wasps and butterflies were frequent visitors. Its petals stay horizontal when they open instead of reflexing, and it has a light fragrance. Other pollinator picks included magenta ‘Ruby Star’, deep pink ‘Amazing Dream’ and Sombrero Baja Burgundy. It has white summer blooms with a large center cone, grows in full sun to part shade and well-drained soil, reaches 2 to 3 feet tall and 1 to 2 feet wide, and is cold hardy in USDA zones 3 to 8.

title: Pollinator Plant Picks
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Ironweed (Vernonia spp. and hybrids) is a tough, low-maintenance perennial that tolerates heat and humidity well and is great for attracting medium-sized bees and butterflies. Most species grow best with plenty of moisture, while western ironweed (V. baldwinii) also tolerates dry soils better than many others. The hybrid ‘Southern Cross’ is smaller, at 3 feet tall and wide. Ironweed has purple blooms from late summer to fall, grows in full sun in moist, well-drained soil, reaches 2 to 8 feet tall and 2 to 5 feet wide depending on type, and is cold hardy in USDA zones 4 to 9.

title: Pollinator Plant Picks
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Goldenrod (Solidago spp. and hybrids) is an under-appreciated perennial. Pollinators of all kinds flock to its late-season blooms, which can be plumed, flat topped or spike shaped depending on the species or variety. Bees, butterflies, wasps, flies and others feed on the pollen and nectar. Goldenrod grows in a range of soil types, and stiff goldenrod (S. rigida) even tolerates clay. Grow it in plenty of sun to maximize the blooms. It has golden yellow flowers from late summer to fall, grows in full sun to part shade in average to moist, well-drained soil, reaches 1 to 6 feet tall and 2 to 3 feet wide, and is cold hardy in USDA zones 3 to 9.
