title: 16 Problem-Solving Perennials
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Gardening is rewarding, but it comes with challenges. Greedy deer can make a buffet of borders, swarms of Japanese beetles chew up plants, and bad soil or juglone-producing walnut trees can inhibit plant growth. These problem-solving perennials tolerate those problems and still thrive.

title: 16 Problem-Solving Perennials
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Tall sedum (Hylotelephium hybrids) is a good choice when you want all-season interest without Japanese beetle damage. This tough perennial takes heat and drought, is super cold hardy, and only needs dead stems cut back in early spring. Most tall sedums have rust-red blooms that age to brown by late fall and plain green foliage. Autumn Charm has gray-green leaves edged in yellow or cream with pale pink summer blooms that age to rust-red, and grows 14 to 18 inches tall and wide in USDA zones 4 to 9. ‘Chocolate Drop’ has deep chocolate-brown foliage with pink blooms and grows 6 to 12 inches tall and 12 to 14 inches wide. Tall sedum blooms pink, red, white, burgundy, brown or yellow from summer to fall, grows in full sun to part shade and well-drained soil, reaches 9 to 36 inches tall and 12 to 36 inches wide, and is cold hardy in USDA zones 3 to 10.

title: 16 Problem-Solving Perennials

content: Full-page photo of Autumn Charm tall sedum with gray-green variegated foliage and aging pink flower heads, labeled as Japanese beetle-resistant.

title: 16 Problem-Solving Perennials
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Impatiens (Impatiens hybrids) provide nonstop shade color and Japanese beetles pass them by. Give plants regular moisture through the driest part of summer and they will flower without deadheading. Downy mildew has been a problem for bedding impatiens, but resistant varieties such as the Big Bounce series are available. Big Bounce Cherry, Lilac and Lavender grow 20 to 30 inches tall and 20 to 36 inches wide. Impatiens bloom in all colors but blue from late spring to frost, grow in part to full sun in moist, well-drained soil, reach 8 to 36 inches tall and 12 to 36 inches wide, and are cold hardy in USDA zones 9 to 11.

title: 16 Problem-Solving Perennials
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Nasturtium (Tropaeolum majus) has distinctive round foliage and pretty blooms. The large round seeds are easy to handle and do best direct-sown after all danger of frost has passed. Nasturtium prefers lean soil, so too much fertilizer produces foliage with no flowers. Water regularly. If nighttime temperatures stay above 70 degrees F and plants develop pale foliage that drops off, cut plants back by half and wait for regrowth as temperatures cool, or pull them and grow something else for summer. ‘Alaska’ has green foliage splashed with white and is usually sold as a mix of yellow, orange, red and salmon flowers. Nasturtium blooms red, orange, yellow, cream, pink or bicolors from spring to frost, grows in full sun to part shade and well-drained soil, and reaches 6 to 15 inches tall and 12 to 60 inches wide.

title: 16 Problem-Solving Perennials
content: Photo of Big Bounce impatiens in cherry, lilac and lavender shades used as a Japanese beetle-resistant shade plant.

content: Photo of variegated ‘Alaska’ nasturtium foliage and yellow-orange blooms.

title: 16 Problem-Solving Perennials
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Lantana (Lantana camara) has bright dome-shaped blooms that Japanese beetles do not favor, while hummingbirds and butterflies do. This tender shrub’s flowers come in mostly warm hues and can be solid or multicolored. Little Lucky Red grows 10 to 12 inches tall and wide; the Luscious series grows 20 to 30 inches tall and wide. Midsized choices include solid yellow Luscious Citron and pale pink, cream and yellow Luscious Pinkberry Blend at 18 to 24 inches tall. Where lantana is cold hardy it can reseed prolifically, but sterile varieties such as the Bloomify series and ‘New Gold’ will not drop seeds. Lantana blooms white, yellow, orange, red, pink, purple or bicolors from early summer to fall, grows in full sun and well-drained soil, reaches 12 to 48 inches tall and 12 to 36 inches wide, and is cold hardy in USDA zones 9 to 11.

title: 16 Problem-Solving Perennials
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Japanese beetle adults show up in the garden between May and July, depending on where you live. They feed for 30 to 45 days and eat more than 300 plant species. Growing plants they don’t like can reduce the number of Japanese beetles visiting the garden.

title: 16 Problem-Solving Perennials
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Old-fashioned bleeding heart (Lamprocapnos spectabilis) is a shade plant deer usually do not bother. Traditional types have green foliage with pink or red and white flowers or solid white flowers. ‘Gold Heart’ has golden yellow leaves with pink and white blooms and can brighten a shade border; it grows 18 to 24 inches tall and 24 to 36 inches wide. Give old-fashioned bleeding heart regular moisture to keep foliage standing through summer heat. Even if it goes dormant, plants return the following spring. It blooms pink or red with white, or solid white, heart-shaped flowers in late spring to early summer, grows in part to full sun in moist, well-drained soil, reaches 24 to 36 inches tall and 15 to 24 inches wide, and is cold hardy in USDA zones 3 to 8.

title: 16 Problem-Solving Perennials
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Deer tend to avoid some plants because of traits such as pungent aroma, bitter taste, or fuzzy or prickly leaves. No plant is deer proof: if deer populations are high and food is scarce, they can eat almost anything.

title: 16 Problem-Solving Perennials
content: Photo of ‘Gold Heart’ old-fashioned bleeding heart with golden foliage and pink heart-shaped flowers.

title: 16 Problem-Solving Perennials
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Hay-scented fern (Dennstaedtia punctilobula) has soft fronds with a delicate look but is a tough native plant. It can grow in full shade or in full sun with steady moisture. Plants spread by rhizomes to form colonies, making it hard for weeds to take hold, and deer and rabbits usually pass it by. The fronds release a fresh-mown-lawn fragrance when brushed. Water regularly to start; established plants are drought tolerant. Hay-scented fern has soft green fronds from spring to frost, grows in part to full shade in acid, moist, well-drained soil, reaches 18 to 24 inches tall and 24 to 36 inches wide, and is cold hardy in USDA zones 3 to 8.

title: 16 Problem-Solving Perennials
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Pot marigold (Calendula officinalis) blooms in waves from late spring to frost, but deer and rabbits leave it alone. It is easy to direct-sow after all danger of frost has passed. Give this drought-tolerant annual plenty of sun and deadhead to encourage reblooming, but leave a few seedheads because pot marigold will reseed. Lady Godiva Orange produces few seeds, flowers nonstop and does not require deadheading; it grows 10 to 16 inches tall and 12 to 18 inches wide and is a tender perennial in USDA zones 8 to 11. Pot marigold blooms golden yellow, orange, pink, cream or bronze from spring to frost, grows in full sun to part shade and well-drained soil, and reaches 12 to 24 inches tall and wide.

content: Photo of hay-scented fern forming a lush green colony in shade.

title: 16 Problem-Solving Perennials
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Epimedium (Epimedium spp. and hybrids) is a strong dry-shade perennial with delicate early spring blooms on wiry stems in a range of colors. ‘Sulphureum’ (E. x versicolor) has two-tone yellow blooms and grows 8 to 12 inches tall and 12 to 15 inches wide. After flowering, heart-shaped to narrow pointed leaves provide seasonal color changes; foliage is usually green in summer but can turn red or show a red blush in spring or fall depending on species or variety. Epimedium blooms white, cream, yellow, pink, red, burgundy, orange or lavender in spring, grows in part to full sun and well-drained soil, reaches 8 to 12 inches tall and 12 to 15 inches wide, and is cold hardy in USDA zones 5 to 9.

title: 16 Problem-Solving Perennials
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Yellow archangel (Lamium galeobdolon) is a perennial for dry shade that is not picky about soil and is usually passed over by deer. Yellow summer flowers rise above green leaves splashed with silver. If stems get leggy after bloom, cut them back by up to half for a fresher look. This mint-family perennial roots at leaf joints and can reseed, so it can be aggressive in ideal conditions, but dry shade keeps spreading in check. Yellow archangel blooms yellow in early summer, grows in full sun to full shade and well-drained soil, reaches 12 to 18 inches tall and 18 to 24 inches wide, and is cold hardy in USDA zones 4 to 9.

title: 16 Problem-Solving Perennials
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Brunnera (Brunnera macrophylla) brightens dry shade under big trees. Varieties such as ‘Jack Frost’ have a silvery overlay that catches light through the canopy, and ‘Looking Glass’ offers solid silver foliage. Small blue forget-me-not-like flowers arrive in spring before the mound of foliage reaches full size. As flowers fade, stems lean toward the ground; you can cut them off or let foliage grow over them. Water young plants the first year; mature rhizomatous roots help plants get through summer. Brunnera can reseed, but seedlings may not have the same markings as the parent. It blooms small blue flowers in early to late spring, grows in part shade and well-drained soil, reaches 12 to 18 inches tall and 12 to 24 inches wide, and is cold hardy in USDA zones 3 to 9.

title: 16 Problem-Solving Perennials
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: The thirstiest trees can make gardening underneath difficult because their shallow roots compete with border perennials for moisture. Tough trees to garden under include beech (Fagus spp.), birch (Betula spp.), hackberry (Celtis occidentalis), maple (Acer spp.) and spruce (Picea spp.).

title: 16 Problem-Solving Perennials
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Candelabra primrose (Primula bulleyana) offers tiered orange spring blooms on fragrant stems that can reach 2 feet tall. It reseeds well in low spots near ponds where soil stays consistently moist and acid, and it also does well in regions with winter rain. Butterflies and other pollinators visit regularly. For a similar look, plant three to five together to ensure good pollination and plenty of seed. Deadheading stems down to the foliage can tidy the border and prevent reseeding. Semi-evergreen foliage may look tattered by late winter; cut it back so fresh growth can fill in by spring. Candelabra primrose blooms orange in late spring, grows in part shade in moist, acid, well-drained to clay soil, reaches 20 to 24 inches tall and 12 to 15 inches wide, and is cold hardy in USDA zones 5 to 8.

title: 16 Problem-Solving Perennials
content: Photo of candelabra primrose with tiered orange blooms growing in moist soil near a pond.

title: 16 Problem-Solving Perennials
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Bugbane (Actaea racemosa) sends long flower stems topped by fuzzy white blooms above ferny foliage in late summer, lasting up to 3 weeks. It looks good at the woodland edge or in a shade garden and produces the most flowers and healthiest foliage with 2 to 3 hours of morning sun. Native to Eastern North American woodlands, bugbane grows best in rich, humussy, well-drained soil. It may take several years to establish but is worth the wait. Bugbane blooms long white spikes in late summer, grows in part shade and moist, well-drained soil, reaches 4 to 5 feet tall and 2 to 4 feet wide, and is cold hardy in USDA zones 3 to 8.

title: 16 Problem-Solving Perennials
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Sweet Joe Pye weed (Eutrochium purpureum) thrives in soggy or clay soils and is useful in rain gardens where water stands briefly and then dries out. This native perennial grows 5 to 7 feet tall for back-of-border color from summer to fall, and stems rarely need staking. Compact gardens can use Euphoria Ruby, which grows 24 to 32 inches tall. Sweet Joe Pye weed’s 12- to 18-inch dome-shaped flowers have a sweet vanilla scent and attract bees and butterflies. Leave fuzzy seedheads for late-season interest or deadhead to prevent reseeding. It blooms mauve or purple from midsummer to fall, grows in full sun to part shade and moist, well-drained to clay soil, reaches 2 to 7 feet tall and 2 to 4 feet wide, and is cold hardy in USDA zones 4 to 9.

content: Photo of bugbane with tall white flower spikes above woodland foliage.

title: 16 Problem-Solving Perennials
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: New England aster (Symphyotrichum novae-angliae) provides fall color and a late-season food source for pollinators. Each stem carries dozens of yellow-centered blooms surrounded by pink or purple petals. ‘Purple Dome’ grows 12 to 24 inches tall with a neat mound, and pink ‘Andenken an Alma Pötschke’ grows 30 to 48 inches tall and wide. If plants flop, pinch growth tips back in late spring by a couple of inches at a leaf joint, and repeat once or twice before mid-July. Blooming will be slightly later, but plants will be more compact and have more blooms. New England aster blooms pink or purple in late summer through fall, grows in full sun and moist, well-drained soil, reaches 1 to 6 feet tall and 2 to 3 feet wide, and is cold hardy in USDA zones 4 to 8.

title: 16 Problem-Solving Perennials
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Shasta daisy (Leucanthemum x superbum) is long-blooming, easy to grow and tolerant near walnut trees. Give plants plenty of sun for maximum flowers. Blooms are usually white, but ‘Banana Cream’ and ‘Goldfinch’ are pale yellow, and flowers can be single or double. ‘Belgian Lace’ has light yellow buds that open to double white blooms with yellow centers; plants grow 12 to 24 inches tall and 26 inches wide. If flowering declines, divide in spring as foliage emerges, split the clump and replant. Shasta daisy blooms white or pale yellow single to double flowers from early summer to fall, grows in full sun to part shade and well-drained soil, reaches 10 to 48 inches tall and 12 to 36 inches wide, and is cold hardy in USDA zones 4 to 9.

title: 16 Problem-Solving Perennials
content: Photo of pink ‘Andenken an Alma Pötschke’ New England aster flowers used as a juglone-tolerant plant.

title: 16 Problem-Solving Perennials

title: 16 Problem-Solving Perennials
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Spanish bluebells (Hyacinthoides hispanica) can grow under a big walnut tree and brighten spring gardens with lavender-blue flowers. They spread into colonies by offsets or reseeding. Give plants dappled or part shade for best flowering and provide companions because Spanish bluebells go dormant by summer. Plant bulbs in fall 3 to 4 inches deep. Alternatives to lavender-blue blooms include ‘White City’, ‘Queen of the Pinks’ and deep blue ‘Bakkam Blue’. Spanish bluebells bloom lavender, blue, white or pink in spring, grow in part shade and well-drained soil, reach 12 to 18 inches tall and 3 to 6 inches wide, and are cold hardy in USDA zones 3 to 8.

title: 16 Problem-Solving Perennials
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Juglone facts: All parts of a walnut tree carry juglone, which inhibits growth of other plants. Symptoms of juglone toxicity include wilting, yellow foliage and stunted growth. Plants within the drip line of a walnut, usually about 50 feet from the trunk, are most affected. Roots always have high juglone levels, while new leaves are higher in spring and fruit hulls in fall. Rake up the nuts to minimize their effect on nearby plants.

title: Marvelous Marigolds
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Name a plant that is easy to grow, blooms nonstop from summer through fall, is practically maintenance free and is grown worldwide. Marigold fits that description, and this foolproof flower deserves a spot in every garden.

title: Marvelous Marigolds
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Because marigolds grow in almost any kind of soil and seeds are simple to collect, this Mexican and Central American native has become popular around the world. Marigold flowers come in shades of yellow, orange, cream and red; the edible flowers’ flavors range from citrusy to spicy to bitter; and the dried or fresh petals make additions to salad or soup. Harvest the long-lasting flowers when the petals have opened fully but the center is still tight. The blooms make good cut flowers, dry well for everlasting bouquets, and the petals are used in fabric dyes, food coloring and chicken feed to make egg yolks more yellow.

title: Marvelous Marigolds
author: Jennifer Howell
content: The pungent smell of marigolds is thought to deter many insect pests and animals. Deer do tend to ignore them, while some rabbits find them tasty, but marigolds rarely repel insects. Spider mites and Japanese beetles are attracted to marigolds, so the flowers can be used as a trap crop to lure these insects away from vulnerable plants. They also draw beneficial insects, such as lady beetles and parasitic wasps, and other pollinators.

title: Marvelous Marigolds
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Marigold (Tagetes spp. and hybrids) is an annual with yellow, orange, cream, red or bicolor blooms from early summer to frost. It grows in full sun and average, well-drained soil. Pests can include spider mites, Japanese beetles and powdery mildew. Plants range from 6 to 48 inches tall and 10 to 48 inches wide.

title: Marvelous Marigolds
content: Botanical-style illustration of Hot Pak Fire French marigold used with the marigold plant profile.

title: Marvelous Marigolds
content: Full-page photo of Hot Pak French marigolds in orange, yellow, spry and fire colors showing uniform flower shapes and mounded plants.

title: Marvelous Marigolds
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Uniform flower shapes and sizes make it easy to mix and match different colors in a series such as Hot Pak French marigolds. No matter which color you choose, tidy, mounded plants grow 6 to 7 inches tall and 6 to 8 inches wide.

title: Meet the Marigolds
author: Jennifer Howell
content: The biggest differences between the three main types of marigolds at the garden center are the sizes of the plants and flowers. French, American and signet marigolds each fit different garden uses.

title: Meet the Marigolds
author: Jennifer Howell
content: French marigold (Tagetes patula) plants are tidy and mounded, with fine-cut ferny foliage and often multiple colors on one bloom. Flowers are usually 1 to 2 inches across, but Bonanza Bolero Improved has double orange and red-orange flowers up to 3 inches wide on 10- to 12-inch-tall and 6- to 8-inch-wide plants. Petite 10-inch ‘Bambino’ has single lemon-and-orange-striped flowers all summer. Heirloom ‘Harlequin’ grows 2 to 3 feet tall with maroon and yellow carnival-striped flowers. Crested ‘Strawberry Blonde’ has muted red-orange petals with pink undertones and peachy-yellow center tufts that age to pale yellow or salmon on 10-inch-tall plants.

title: Meet the Marigolds
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Marigold seed sources listed in the feature include Annie’s Annuals, Burpee, Johnny’s Selected Seeds, Kitchen Garden Seeds and Select Seeds.

title: Meet the Marigolds
content: Photos of French marigold cultivars including ‘Strawberry Blonde’, Bonanza Bolero Improved and ‘Bambino’.

title: Meet the Marigolds
author: Jennifer Howell
content: American marigold (Tagetes erecta), also called African or Aztec marigold, includes some of the largest marigold plants and flowers. Plants can reach 48 inches tall and 24 inches wide, with double blooms up to 5 inches across. Tall varieties such as ‘Garuda Deep Gold’ may need staking because heavy golden globe-shaped flowers can flop after rain. The Big Duck series has self-supporting 12- to 15-inch stems with 4-inch yellow and orange blooms. ‘French Vanilla’ has white pompon blooms on 18-inch plants with a lighter marigold fragrance. ‘Mission Giant Yellow’ has 3-inch blooms with a looser, shaggier look and grows 24 to 34 inches tall for the back of the border.

title: Meet the Marigolds
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Signet marigold (Tagetes tenuifolia) is derived from a wild Central American native and has finer, lacier foliage than French and American types on mounded 12-inch plants. Flowers are petite, less than 1 inch across, with five petals around a center ray. Their sweet citrusy, tarragonlike flavor is considered the tastiest among marigolds, and even the foliage is more pleasantly aromatic. The Gem series is available in ‘Red Gem’, ‘Tangerine Gem’, yellow, gold and mixes. Plants carry flowers all season, so petals can be used in salad or drinks without losing garden color.

content: Photos of American marigold cultivars including ‘Mission Giant Yellow’ and ‘French Vanilla’.

title: Designing with Marigolds
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Marigolds are excellent fillers, branching out and meshing together to create a sea of flowers. It makes economic sense to use them for large blocks of color because many marigolds can be grown inexpensively from seed. Sprinkle seeds in the perennial border for quick color when other plants are not at their peak, and use them in streetscapes and public spaces because plants tolerate hot, dry weather and neglect while blooming all season.

title: Designing with Marigolds
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Marigolds thrive in harsh container conditions where heat and dryness might hurt less hardy plants. Their vivid colors show up well in pots mixed with other annuals for curb appeal. French marigolds are especially useful for containers because their smaller size and broad range of flower shapes and colors make them easy to design with. Marigolds can also take a light frost and bloom well into fall, so they can replace overgrown or failing annuals in autumn displays.

title: Designing with Marigolds
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Complementary companions for marigolds can start with color: cool purples and blues make yellow marigolds pop; bronze- or burgundy-foliaged plants such as sedum or purple fountain grass set off orange and red cultivars; and lemon-yellow or cream marigolds suit pastel gardens. Marigolds’ mounded shape highlights companions with linear flowers, big bold leaves or fine-textured blossoms, such as spiky salvia, large-leafed cannas or tiny-flowered sweet alyssum.

title: Designing with Marigolds
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Marigold roots contain a chemical that can inhibit growth of legumes, such as peas, so don’t grow them close together. While gardeners often plant marigolds in vegetable gardens to repel pests, they are not very effective in that role. They do add color, are edible and may help deter deer.

title: Designing with Marigolds
content: Photo of ‘Disco Red’ French marigolds flowing through a perennial border as a mass planting.

title: Designing with Marigolds
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Container stars tip: Tip marigold plants slightly forward when planting at the edge if you want them to spill over the edge of the pot a bit. Complementary companion example: Bright Durango Yellow French marigolds make good flower-bed companions with cool-colored purple ‘Kobold’ blazing star and ‘Blue Horizon’ floss flower. Spike blazing star flowers create a striking contrast with the mass of mounded marigolds.

title: How to Make a Marigold Garland
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Marigold garlands are used in celebrations around the world. Leave a 1/4- to 1/2-inch stub below the calyx. String flowers by running a tapestry needle threaded with size 5 crochet thread up through the hollow stem and out the middle of the blossom. After each flower is strung, tuck each stem into the petals of the previous bloom until the garland reaches the length you want.

title: How to Make a Marigold Garland
author: Jennifer Howell
content: An alternate marigold garland method is to pierce the calyx sideways and arrange flowers on the string in a spiral. Flowers dry and shrink slightly in a few days, but the colors stay bright for weeks.

title: Grow Great Marigolds
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Marigold seeds are easy to handle and germinate reliably in just a few days, which makes marigolds a dependable plant for beginners and experienced gardeners. Plant marigolds in full sun to match their bright flowers. They tolerate some morning or late-day shade, but plants flower more heavily and stay sturdier and fuller with sun for most of the day.

title: Grow Great Marigolds
author: Jennifer Howell
content: You can start marigolds indoors, direct-sow seeds outside in the garden or buy seedlings. To start indoors, plant seeds 4 to 6 weeks before the average last frost. Place the long narrow seeds about 1/4 inch deep in premoistened seed-starting mix, water in, and cover with a dome or plastic wrap to keep the mix moist. Check daily and mist if needed. Seeds germinate fastest when the medium is around 70 degrees F.

title: Grow Great Marigolds
author: Jennifer Howell
content: When seedlings have several sets of leaves and daytime temperatures are regularly above 70 degrees F, transplant marigolds outdoors. Harden them off by setting them in shade for a few hours the first day, moving them indoors at night, and gradually increasing outdoor time and sun until they can stay outside day and night. If seedlings are leggy, remove a set or two of lower leaves and plant them deeper because stems root when they contact soil. Cutting flowers off young transplants encourages branching and more flowers later, but it is fine to leave them if you prefer.

title: Grow Great Marigolds
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Marigolds can be direct-sown outdoors after all danger of frost has passed. Seeds languish in cool, wet soil, so wait until daytime temperatures are regularly around 70 degrees F. Expect flowers in about 8 weeks. Crowded plants are more likely to develop fungal problems such as powdery mildew, especially in rainy weather. Space smaller varieties 8 to 12 inches apart and larger ones up to 18 inches apart.

title: Grow Great Marigolds
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Once established, marigolds are drought tolerant, especially American marigolds, but give extra water or mulch during hot midsummer weather. If marigolds struggle in summer heat, use a half-strength general-purpose water-soluble fertilizer for an extra boost. Night temperatures below 50 degrees F may turn some leaves purple; it will not hurt the plant and adds fall color until a hard frost kills the plants.

title: Grow Great Marigolds
content: Step photos showing marigold seeds started in multipacks, thinning seedlings and transplanting compact young plants.

title: Grow Great Marigolds
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Deadhead spent marigold flowers to keep plants tidy by snapping the hollow stems just below the plump green calyx that holds the petals together. Do this in early morning when foliage is fresh and crisp. Larger flowers may be easier to clip with snips or scissors. Deadheading also encourages more blooms. Signet marigolds often benefit from being sheared back by a third to half in summer if stems grow long and gangly.

title: Grow Great Marigolds
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Marigolds reseed easily in the garden, so leave a few dried flowers to drop seed. Plants will not always look exactly like the parent, but that can be a fun surprise. To collect seed, wait until spent blooms are shriveled and brown. Break open the dried calyx, pluck out the seeds and brush off the withered petals. Air-dry seeds for a couple of weeks, then store them in an airtight container in a cool, dark place.

title: Troubleshooting Marigolds
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Spider mites are attracted to marigolds, especially during hot, dry weather. Watch for webbing, stippled foliage and peppery-looking insects on leaf undersides. A strong stream of water every few days usually washes them away. Purple leaves can be caused by cool temperatures or a phosphorus deficiency; a soil test can show whether a fertilizer amendment is recommended.

title: Troubleshooting Marigolds
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Gray mold can develop on marigold flowers during wet, humid weather. Deadhead fading blooms to keep the fungus from spreading. Powdery mildew is favored by warm, humid weather; prevent it by spacing plants so air can move between them. A general-purpose fungicide can help if the problem is severe. Dispose of infested plants so spores do not persist the next year.

title: Which Grass Is Right for You?
content: Maiden grass (Miscanthus sinensis), or Chinese silver grass, is a hardy, low-maintenance perennial that adds structure and texture almost all year. This airy, clump-forming ornamental grass grows 1 to 12 feet tall and 1 to 6 feet wide depending on variety, with plumes in late summer or fall. Its upward-arching stems and linear, serrated leaves with silvery midribs can be 3 to 4 feet long, and foliage turns red, orange and yellow in fall.

title: Which Grass Is Right for You?
content: Maiden grass works well as shorter cultivars such as ‘Little Kitten’ or ‘Adagio’ in containers with annuals and trailing plants. Taller types such as ‘Kaskade’ or variegated ‘Strictus’ provide back-of-border drama. Feathery late-summer plumes are useful fresh or dried as cut flowers; snip stems at the base. In winter, maiden grass can be left standing because its structure and plumes remain showy.

title: Which Grass Is Right for You?
content: Maiden grass grows in USDA zones 4 to 9 in full sun to part shade, but it maintains its upright habit best in full sun and may flop in too much shade. It prefers moist soil but is fairly drought tolerant once established. Maiden grass can reseed and be invasive in some areas; if that is a problem, choose sterile varieties such as ‘Cabaret’, ‘My Fair Maiden’ or ‘Bandwidth’. Mulching around plants helps reduce reseeding. Cut the plant to the ground in late winter before new shoots emerge.

title: Which Grass Is Right for You?
content: Illustration and photo callouts for maiden grass showing silver-to-pink plumes, linear leaves with silvery midribs, upright clump-forming habit and purple-red ‘Oktoberfest’ fall color.

title: Which Grass Is Right for You?
content: Switchgrass (Panicum virgatum) is a native grass with a dense, columnar habit that can be used almost anywhere in the garden. This medium-sized grass grows 3 to 5 feet tall and reaches up to 8 feet in flower depending on variety. Slender, cloudlike plumes emerge above arching linear leaves in mid- to late summer. In fall, leaves turn orange, yellow and red. In winter, plants can be left standing for interest.

title: Which Grass Is Right for You?
content: Switchgrass handles a wide range of growing conditions and soil types. It is happy near ponds, along stream edges, and in prairies or woodland areas. For year-round foliage color, plant ‘Northwind’ for olive to blue-green leaves or red-tinged ‘Hänse Herms’. Switchgrass tolerates roadside and driveway plantings where winter road salt can be hard on plants. Plumes are useful in late-season flower arrangements.

title: Which Grass Is Right for You?
content: Switchgrass grows best in USDA zones 4 to 9 in full sun to part shade. In too much shade, plants lose their tight vertical shape and become weak and floppy. Although the plumes are not as showy as maiden grass in winter, the remaining seeds feed birds, so it is worth leaving plants standing. Cut switchgrass to the ground in late winter before new growth starts.

title: Which Grass Is Right for You?

title: Permaculture
author: Marisa Reyes
content: People, plants, animals and insects all belong to a giant web of life. Permaculture, or “permanent agriculture,” is a way of thinking about how to promote natural interactions among those players. Environmentalist David Holmgren distilled the concepts into 12 principles centered around caring for the earth, caring for people and fair shares, meaning every living being gets a piece of the pie. Gardeners may already practice permaculture by mixing herbs and vegetables with ornamentals, experimenting with vermicomposting or incorporating the principles into plantings and design.

title: Permaculture
content: Illustrated permaculture diagram showing principles such as observe and interact, catch and store energy, obtain a yield, produce no waste, use renewable resources, use edges, value diversity and respond to change.

title: Permaculture
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Collect water in a rain barrel by using a 50- to 80-gallon plastic barrel or garbage can with a lid and a spigot or faucet at the base for a hose. Place the rain barrel underneath a downspout to collect roof water and use it on flower beds and potted plants. Roofs and gutters can accumulate debris and contaminants, such as bird droppings, so sanitize collected rain water before using it on vegetables by adding 1 ounce of chlorine bleach per 55 gallons of water, waiting 24 hours for it to dissipate, and watering only at soil level when possible.

title: Permaculture
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Permaculture gardeners look for plants with multiple uses. Chamomile (Matricaria chamomilla) works as a living mulch; its roots take up potassium, phosphorus and calcium, and chopped plants can be sprinkled around the garden as a soil amendment. Daylily (Hemerocallis spp. and hybrids) is edible, with tasty, nutrient-packed flowers, flower buds, young stalks and roots. False indigo (Baptisia australis) fixes atmospheric nitrogen into soil nitrogen that benefits neighboring plants.

title: Permaculture
author: Marisa Reyes
content: More multipurpose permaculture plants: Ostrich fern (Matteuccia struthiopteris) produces edible young fiddleheads that can be blanched, sauteed and eaten. Strawberry (Fragaria spp.) retains soil moisture and suppresses weeds as a low-growing living mulch. Yarrow (Achillea millefolium) accumulates nutrients; its leaves release phosphorus and potassium in compost, and leaves and flowers can be used dried as a spice or fresh in salads, soups or teas. Yarrow is also known as a first-aid plant for healing cuts and wounds.

title: Permaculture
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Plant for pest protection by using trap crops that lure pests away from susceptible plants and repellent crops that encourage insects to stay away. For best results, plant trap and repellent crops 3 to 8 feet from susceptible plants, around garden borders, intercropped in alternating rows or mixed randomly within beds. Trap crops include nasturtium for aphids, cabbage moths, cucumber beetles, whiteflies and squash bugs; petunia for aphids, asparagus beetles and tomato hornworms; and sunflower for ants, aphids and beetles. Repellent crops include catmint for aphids, cabbage loopers, Colorado potato beetles, flea beetles, Japanese beetles and squash bugs, and garden mum for Japanese beetles, nematodes and spider mites.

title: Permaculture
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Use a rotating compost bin if you lack room for a large compost pile or want an easy start. Compost needs green materials such as food scraps, grass clippings, fresh leaves and stems and coffee grounds, plus brown materials such as paper, straw or hay, wood ash, newspaper, dry leaves and cardboard. Add 3 or 4 parts brown material to 1 part green material, place the bin in a sunny location and turn it weekly. If compost smells bad, add more brown material.

title: Permaculture
content: Page diagram and tables explaining rain barrels, multipurpose plants, trap crops, repellent crops and a rotating compost bin for permaculture gardening.

title: How to Preserve Fresh Garden Herbs
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Instead of letting fresh herbs go to waste, preserve them. Herb preservation is a way to enjoy favorite herbs all year, and the process is easier than it may seem. Four simple preservation methods can be used from spring until the first frost, with different herbs suited to each approach.

title: How to Preserve Fresh Garden Herbs
content: Opener photo of bundled garden sage used with the fresh herb preservation article.

title: How to Preserve Fresh Garden Herbs
author: Marisa Reyes
content: The best time to harvest herbs is in the morning after dew has evaporated but before heat strips away natural essential oils. Woody-stemmed herbs require pruners or scissors. Tender-stemmed herbs can be snapped off. During the growing season, harvest branching herbs such as basil, oregano or mint by cutting up to a third of a stem back to just above a leaf node, which encourages side shoots and continued growth.

title: How to Preserve Fresh Garden Herbs
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Harvest nonbranching herbs such as cilantro, parsley or chives by cutting individual stems at the base, but don’t harvest all of them or they may not regrow. In general, avoid harvesting more than a third of a plant at one time so enough leaves remain to photosynthesize. For the last fall harvest of annual herbs, cut the entire plant to the ground. Perennial herbs such as rosemary, garden sage and thyme can be harvested lightly in fall, but larger harvests are better in spring and summer so heavy fall cutting does not encourage tender growth susceptible to winter damage.

title: How to Preserve Fresh Garden Herbs
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Tender-stemmed herbs have edible stems and leaves. Woody-stemmed herbs have edible leaves but larger stems are not typically eaten; these plants are often shrubby, more cold hardy and grown as perennials. Examples shown include tender herbs such as basil, dill, mint and cilantro, and woody herbs such as thyme, garden sage and rosemary.

title: How to Preserve Fresh Garden Herbs
author: Marisa Reyes
content: After harvesting herbs, shake them to dislodge insects and snip off dead, dried or discolored leaves. Wash stems and leaves thoroughly in cold water, pat the moisture off and set them on the counter or a drying rack, or use a salad spinner. Herbs must be completely dry before preserving so they do not develop mold or surface bacteria. Once stems are dry to the touch, preserve them right away for the best flavor and color.

title: How to Preserve Fresh Garden Herbs
content: Overhead photo diagram comparing woody-stemmed herbs such as thyme, garden sage and rosemary with tender-stemmed herbs such as basil, dill, mint and cilantro.

title: How to Preserve Fresh Garden Herbs
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Air drying preserves more oils and flavors than some faster methods and requires only scissors, rubber bands and twine. Make small bundles of four to six stems for large-leafed herbs such as sage, mint or basil, and bundles of eight to 10 stems for smaller-leafed herbs such as thyme, rosemary or lavender. If unsure, make smaller bundles because crowded herbs won’t dry evenly and could mold. Remove lower leaves, secure stems with a rubber band and hang with twine in a cool, dry, shady spot away from direct sun.

title: How to Preserve Fresh Garden Herbs
author: Marisa Reyes
content: To air-dry herbs with less mess, place each herb bundle in a paper lunch bag and punch or cut holes in the bottom, sides and middle to encourage airflow and prevent mold. This works especially well for tender-stemmed herbs with moist leaves, such as basil or mint, because the bag absorbs some moisture. Air drying takes a few weeks. Dried herbs are ready to store when they crumble easily. Store crushed or whole herbs in labeled, sealed jars or bags for 2 to 3 years.

title: How to Preserve Fresh Garden Herbs
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Dehydrating herbs in a dehydrator is faster than air drying. A dehydrator is better than an oven because ovens are difficult to keep low enough with enough airflow and can reduce oil potency. Preheat the dehydrator to 95 to 115 degrees F, or 125 degrees F on high-humidity days. Remove large leaves from stems and lay them flat; keep smaller leaves attached and lay stems flat with space between them. Drying takes 1 to 4 hours. Check periodically, remove stems and leaves as they dry and crumble easily, and let them cool before storing.

title: How to Preserve Fresh Garden Herbs
author: Marisa Reyes
content: An air fryer can dehydrate herbs if set to dehydrator mode or the lowest temperature possible. Place herb sprigs or leaves in the air fryer for 1 to 3 hours and check them regularly. If leaves do not dehydrate uniformly or edges begin browning, lower the temperature if possible. Once herbs are dried, let them cool before storing.

title: How to Preserve Fresh Garden Herbs
content: Photos of herb bundles, mint, basil and sage used with air-drying and dehydrating methods for preserving herbs.

title: How to Preserve Fresh Garden Herbs
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Freezing preserves herbs for up to a year. For ice cube trays, fill a tray with fresh herb leaves and cover them with water or olive oil, then freeze. Pesto cubes can also be made for later use. Once frozen, transfer cubes to a resealable freezer bag so they can be added easily to recipes. Silicone ice cube trays work best because herbs release easily and the nonporous material does not absorb flavor. Fruit and herbs can also be mixed and added to water, lemonades or cocktails.

title: How to Preserve Fresh Garden Herbs
author: Marisa Reyes
content: To freeze herbs on a baking sheet, lay fresh herb leaves or stems on a baking sheet or parchment paper and freeze overnight. Once completely frozen, place them in a sealable container or freezer bag and return them to the freezer until needed. This method keeps herbs fresh for 2 to 3 months.

title: How to Preserve Fresh Garden Herbs
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Refrigeration is the right preservation method if fresh herbs will be used within a few days to a few weeks. For woody herbs such as rosemary, thyme, oregano or garden sage, wrap cleaned and dried cuttings, stems and all, in a damp paper towel, put them in a resealable plastic bag and refrigerate. This keeps them fresh for 2 to 3 weeks.

title: How to Preserve Fresh Garden Herbs
author: Marisa Reyes
content: For tender-stemmed herbs such as basil, cilantro, parsley, mint, dill and chives, rinse and dry the stems, place them upright in a jar and add 1 or 2 inches of water. Cover with a plastic bag before storing in the refrigerator. Replace the water daily to preserve herbs for 1 to 2 weeks. Once the basic methods are mastered, experiment with herbal blends and vinegar, oil and butter infusions.

title: How to Preserve Fresh Garden Herbs
content: Photos showing herbs frozen in ice cube trays, cilantro and parsley stored in jars, and fresh herbs covered for refrigerator storage.

title: Neighborly Curb Appeal
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: This flower-filled garden supplies a three-season show everyone can enjoy.

title: Neighborly Curb Appeal
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: In this north-facing front yard, the shady foundation planting dresses up the house, a 60-foot-long border runs along the sidewalk and another accompanies guests up the front walk.

title: Neighborly Curb Appeal
content: Full-page front-yard garden photo showing a shady foundation planting, sidewalk border, white picket fence and porch.

title: Neighborly Curb Appeal
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: This living-roof succulent display adds height and color contrast to the front border. Its 14-by-10-inch roof has a 2-inch lip that holds enough potting mix for shallow-rooted succulents. Jan drilled drainage holes in each corner. The weight of the planted box keeps it in place on the 4x4 post, which makes it easier to lift and move indoors every winter. Even with winter protection, Jan finds that after a few years the plants look tired, so he freshens the exterior latex paint and starts over with a new mix of plants.

title: Neighborly Curb Appeal
content: Photo of a cedar living-roof succulent birdhouse-style display mounted on a 4x4 post in the front border.

title: Neighborly Curb Appeal
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: When Jan and Bette Goins started their Michigan garden 17 years ago, the front yard held only a couple of overgrown Hicks yews. Jan, a retired landscape designer, and Bette, who had worked at a local greenhouse, envisioned a colorful front yard with curb appeal from spring to frost. The finished garden generates comments from people passing by, and some neighbors plan routes to see the changing views.

title: Neighborly Curb Appeal
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: The 30-inch-tall picket fence gives the flower garden a backdrop, but the open picket style feels welcoming and does not block views. Dentils below the molding on the post caps add charm and help tie the fence to the house. The fence sits 18 inches from the sidewalk, leaving room for a tidy row of daylilies, coneflowers and gloriosa daisies. On the other side, the curving border reaches 10 feet at its widest point and displays annuals, perennials and shrubs that peak at different times through the growing season.

title: Neighborly Curb Appeal
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: The view from the house is as nice as the view from the street: a bright ribbon of New Guinea impatiens runs along the border and repeats in the foundation planting. The next-door neighbors liked it enough that Jan extended the edging of impatiens into their yard. The asymmetrical bed layout came from a slightly lower grade on the east side of the north-facing yard. Jan added a small border next to the sidewalk so the drop-off would be less obvious and less likely to cause a misstep.

title: Neighborly Curb Appeal
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Repeating the same edging plant, such as pink New Guinea impatiens, keeps the eye moving through the garden and ties the planting together.

title: Neighborly Curb Appeal
content: Photo of the front walk, porch, foundation planting and pink New Guinea impatiens repeated as border edging.

title: Neighborly Curb Appeal
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: With a garden this pretty along the sidewalk, Jan and Bette get many compliments. The late-summer border is attractive enough that art groups have set up easels on the sidewalk to paint. Jan enjoys neighbors telling him they enjoy the view but are glad he does the work.

title: Neighborly Curb Appeal
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Bette and Jan use a seasonal color theme. Early spring starts with yellow daffodils. Late spring brings deep purple bearded iris and allium. Summer bursts with bold blooms including lilies, daylilies, coneflowers, gloriosa daisies and spider flower, with Bette augmenting reseeders with seeds. They leave room for tender Skyscraper salvia because it blooms from spring to frost. In fall, spider flower and salvia continue as yellow mums open.

title: Neighborly Curb Appeal
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Deer are frequent visitors, and lilies are especially tasty to them. Jan and Bette use two strategies: spray a deer repellent such as Liquid Fence regularly, starting in spring and repeating weekly and after even light rain; and plant less palatable choices, such as daffodils, purple coneflower and spider flower, at garden edges to encourage deer to move on.

title: Neighborly Curb Appeal
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Planting, watering, mulching and deadheading keep the couple outdoors most days. Jan does not mind the effort because he enjoys the results and sees the garden as a gift to people who walk or drive by.

title: Neighborly Curb Appeal
content: Photo of ‘Casa Blanca’ Oriental lily and spider flower used with the curb appeal border and deer deterrent sidebar.

title: Neighborly Curb Appeal
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: A parade of color for every season: Early spring plants include ‘Yellow Queen’ Dutch iris, ‘Dutch Master’ daffodil and ‘Ice Follies’ daffodil. Late spring plants include ‘Rosalee Figge’ bearded iris and ‘Globemaster’ allium. Summer plants include ‘Indian Summer’ gloriosa daisy, ‘Pardon Me’ daylily, PowWow Wild Berry coneflower and ‘Star Gazer’ oriental lily. Fall plants include garden mum, Skyscraper Pink salvia and spider flower.

title: Neighborly Curb Appeal
content: Photo of the white picket fence border in bloom with seasonal plant callouts for daffodil, allium, coneflower, daylily, gloriosa daisy and garden mum.

title: Grow a Fantastic Fall Border
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Balance the border with a 15-foot-tall multistemmed blackhaw viburnum in the back corner as a colorful anchor. Three 7-foot-tall panicle hydrangeas smooth the transition to lower-growing perennials in front.

title: Grow a Fantastic Fall Border
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: The perennials and grasses in this fall border are planted in sweeps so you can cut plenty for seasonal vases without stripping the garden bare. A multistemmed dahlia has plenty of blooms to spare.

title: Grow a Fantastic Fall Border
content: Illustrated fall border design showing sweeps of perennials, grasses, dahlias, hydrangeas and a blackhaw viburnum anchor.

title: Grow a Fantastic Fall Border
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Fall is a good time to think about pollinators, especially birds and butterflies that need extra energy to migrate or prepare for winter. Birds will eat viburnum berries and coneflower seeds, and migrating hummingbirds notice tubular salvia blooms. Asters, goldenrod and dahlias are reliable for butterflies and other insects.

title: Grow a Fantastic Fall Border
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Although this collection has spring-blooming plants, you can start the show earlier by tucking grape hyacinth or spring snowflakes near the front of the border around later-to-peak tall sedum. As sedum fills out, its tidy mound covers fading bulb foliage. Add more color with taller daffodils near New England aster, another perennial that fills out later.

title: Grow a Fantastic Fall Border
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: This fall border plan brings autumn color to a backyard but is not limited to autumn. The mix of shrubs and tender and hardy perennials offers something from spring until frost. Bearded iris and blackhaw viburnum start the show in spring; coneflower and airy switchgrass keep early summer colorful; panicle hydrangeas open white and mature to pink; and salvia, dahlia and tall sedum provide fall flowers.

title: Grow a Fantastic Fall Border
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Beyond flowers, the border has autumn foliage interest. Blackhaw viburnum leaves change to vibrant red and orange, and purple-black dahlia foliage pops against tan switchgrass leaves. Interesting leaf shapes, such as swordlike bearded iris and round tall sedum, add texture among the fall colors. Skip deadheading hydrangea flowers at the end of the season because tan, papery dried blooms add winter interest.

title: Grow a Fantastic Fall Border
content: Illustrated fall border detail with pollinator callouts, spring bulb placement, hydrangea winter-interest note and fall foliage color.

title: Grow a Fantastic Fall Border
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: To keep this flower border looking good, start with spring cleanup. In late winter, remove dead perennial foliage and any remaining hydrangea blooms. Cut switchgrass to within a few inches of the ground and prune hydrangea stems back by a third for a fuller, more compact plant. Blackhaw viburnum needs little pruning; wait to shape it until after bloom so next year’s buds are not removed.

title: Grow a Fantastic Fall Border
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: After all chance of frost has passed, plant salvia and dahlias. Dahlias prefer warm soil temperatures, 60 degrees F or higher, about the same time tomatoes are planted. Tubers can be started indoors 6 weeks before the last average frost date for earlier bloom. Whether started in ground or in a pot, water tubers once after planting and wait to see growth before watering again. After planting the border, apply or refresh mulch to suppress weeds and conserve moisture.

title: Grow a Fantastic Fall Border
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Border maintenance is light. Cut spent bearded iris scapes back to the foliage fan and snip salvia stems back to a leaf joint to encourage side stems with more flowers. Coneflower deadheading is optional because seedheads feed birds. Other plants bloom late enough that deadheading is not needed. Gardeners in USDA zones 8 to 11 can leave dahlias in the ground all year; in colder areas, dig tubers after the first frost and store them through winter.

title: Garden Fact... or Fiction?
author: Jennifer Howell
content: While there is usually some truth behind every myth, sometimes an idea captures gardeners’ imaginations and is eventually accepted as fact even though research does not necessarily back it up. The lowdown on common beliefs may change how you garden.

title: Garden Fact... or Fiction?
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Poison ivy is contagious: The itching and blistered rash is an allergic reaction to urushiol oil in poison ivy, poison oak or poison sumac leaves, stems and foliage, and even in smoke from burning these plants. Contact with pet hair, clothing or tools that still have the oil can expose you, but once the oil is washed away with soap containing a degreaser, irritation cannot spread from person to person. It cannot spread by blister liquid. Every exposure makes you more sensitive and more likely to react.

title: Garden Fact... or Fiction?
author: Jennifer Howell
content: A hollow tree or tree with a hole is not automatically rotting and needing removal. The exterior layer of bark and wood is the living part that gives strength and structure. Since trees form wound wood to heal themselves, there is no need to remove or cut away rot. Many trees live decades with hollow sections and provide refuge for creatures. Consult a certified arborist if the hole is large or in a crotch where a limb may be weakened. Do not fill holes with concrete because it causes damage as the tree flexes. Spray foam can keep animals out, but it is usually best to leave the tree alone.

title: Garden Fact... or Fiction?
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Burying banana peels adds only tiny amounts of potassium and phosphorus to soil. Soaking peels in water and using the water on plants is similarly insignificant because nutrients are released during decomposition, not by leaching. A fresh banana peel can use up nitrogen as it decomposes, so it is better to put peels on the compost pile and use the finished compost.

title: Garden Fact... or Fiction?
content: Illustration of common garden myth callouts, including transplant shock, houseplants and banana peels, on a fact-or-fiction department page.

title: Garden Fact... or Fiction?
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Eggshells do not prevent blossom end rot and do not reliably deter slugs. If soil is calcium deficient, which most soils are not, eggshells do not work fast enough to prevent blossom end rot, which is more often caused by irregular watering. Eggshells are useful in compost. Crushed eggshells around hostas do not stop slugs, which can slide over the shells; use a granular slug repellent instead.

title: Garden Fact... or Fiction?
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Epsom salts is not a miracle fertilizer. It contains magnesium and sulfur, which plants use, but most soils already have enough. Excess magnesium and sulfur are water soluble and can leach into waterways. Aged compost or a general-purpose fertilizer is more useful. A foliar spray of Epsom salts can help some yellowing from magnesium or sulfur deficiency but can scorch leaves in heat or direct sun, so apply on cool, cloudy days.

title: Garden Fact... or Fiction?
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Grass clippings do not need to be removed unless they are long enough to mat into rows. Grass clippings are only a small fraction of the deteriorating stems, roots and stolons that form thatch and are easily broken down. Dethatching is generally unnecessary because the organic layer at the soil surface helps retain moisture.

title: Garden Fact... or Fiction?
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Lemon-scented plants can repel mosquitoes, but the protection range is small. Mosquitoes detect attractants such as sweat and carbon dioxide. Having plants nearby may not be enough. Rub leaves of lemon-scented plants, such as lemon thyme or lemon balm, on your skin to release oils for better results, as long as you do not have allergies to the oils.

title: Garden Fact... or Fiction?
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Reusable seed-starting pots do not always need washing to prevent damping off. Unless there is a confirmed soil-borne disease or you are starting cuttings with wounds where pathogens might enter, this extra step is not required. Rinsing soil and debris out does not hurt. Damping off is usually caused by too much moisture and humidity, poor air movement or overcrowding, not leftovers from a dirty pot.

title: Garden Fact... or Fiction?
content: Illustration callouts about tomato sweetness, old seeds and lemon-scented mosquito-repellent plants.

title: Q&A
content: Spring-blooming bulbs such as tulips and daffodils should be fed twice a year: in early fall as the ground begins to cool, about the time spent annuals are pulled, and again in spring as green noses emerge through the soil. Use a granular fertilizer with a higher middle number, such as 10-15-10, or one labeled for bulbs. Spread 1 cup of bone meal per 20 square feet. Lightly scratch everything into the soil and soak the area if the season is dry.

title: Q&A
content: Japanese knotweed (Polygonum cuspidatum) is difficult to remove. Cut the tall stems as close to soil level as possible and remove them. Let them dry, then burn them if allowed; otherwise, let them dry until crisp and completely dead to prevent cut stems from resprouting, then discard in the trash. If mowing, keep new sprouts as short as possible. If not mowing, cut stems again when they reach 3 to 4 feet tall. Keep cutting until winter stops growth, resume in spring as soon as growth appears, and expect 2 to 4 years of work. Broadleaf herbicide such as glyphosate can be used, but plants still need to be cut down and new foliage sprayed.

title: Garden Jargon
content: Pruinose describes a plant covered with a waxy, powdery coating. You might notice it on grapes or succulent foliage. It works like sunblock and helps regulate moisture transfer. Although the film can be wiped off by hand, it resists being washed away by rain or watering.

title: Q&A
content: Deadheading a perennial garden until frost is not always necessary. Deadheading can encourage new growth that is susceptible to winter damage. When deadheading stops, plants can conserve energy, go dormant and possibly improve winter survival. Seedheads also feed birds and add winter interest. If a plant reseeds aggressively, cut the stalks off in fall to save work next year.

title: Q&A
content: Four spring-blooming bulbs that are resistant to squirrels, voles and chipmunks are glory-of-the-snow (Chionodoxa luciliae), with early spring star-shaped flowers in pink, blue or white for full sun to part shade, 4 to 6 inches tall and 3 to 5 inches wide, USDA zones 3 to 9; Siberian squill (Scilla siberica), with blue or white flowers in early to midspring for full sun to part shade, 3 to 6 inches tall and 2 to 3 inches wide, zones 2 to 8; checkered lily (Fritillaria meleagris), with maroon, white, pink or purple checkered blooms in early spring and skunky-smelling bulbs, full sun to part shade, 8 to 12 inches tall and 3 to 6 inches wide, zones 4 to 9; and golden garlic (Allium moly), with yellow summer flowers, onion-scented bulbs and foliage, full sun, 8 to 10 inches tall and 6 to 9 inches wide, zones 3 to 8.

title: Weed Watch
content: Quackgrass (Elymus repens) has narrow, slightly blue-green leaves along 2- to 3-foot stems and 2- to 6-inch seedheads from early summer into fall. The best identifier is the tangle of segmented pale buff to white roots in a clump. It is often confused with crabgrass, but crabgrass is a warm-season annual that is easy to pull and appears in summer heat.

title: Weed Watch
content: Quackgrass prefers well-drained soil but tolerates most situations in full sun to part shade throughout much of North America. It spreads by rhizomes and seed. Keep it cut short to reduce or prevent seed production. Pulling and cultivating are not effective; dig and remove every pale root segment because missed pieces can grow new plants. Monitor cleaned areas and remove young plants quickly. Nonselective herbicides are an option, but no proven selective herbicides are available.

title: Versatile ‘Viridis’ Japanese Maple
author: Kristin Beane Sullivan
content: ‘Viridis’ Japanese maple makes a living sculpture with interesting branch structure and lacy leaves that develop beautiful fall color. It is one of the more cold-hardy Japanese maples, so gardeners in zone 5 can grow it reliably.

title: Versatile ‘Viridis’ Japanese Maple
author: Kristin Beane Sullivan
content: Japanese maples are often grown as understory trees in part shade and can grow well near walnuts. Usually, the more sun green-leafed varieties get, the brighter their fall color. In zones 5 and 6, ‘Viridis’ can grow in full sun all day, but in zones 7 and warmer it should be shaded during the hottest part of the day to avoid foliage scorch. In zones 5 and 6, a protected spot out of wind helps reduce winter branch dieback. Avoid direct southern exposure, where trunks and branches are more susceptible to winter damage.

title: Versatile ‘Viridis’ Japanese Maple
author: Kristin Beane Sullivan
content: If a ‘Viridis’ branch does not leaf out in spring, prune it off just above the branch collar. Cutting too close or leaving a long stub can make the plant susceptible to insects or disease. Beyond removing dead branches, pruning is optional, but careful thinning can reveal the living-sculpture structure and reduce branch weight that might break under heavy snow.

title: Versatile ‘Viridis’ Japanese Maple
author: Kristin Beane Sullivan
content: Prune ‘Viridis’ after it has leafed out so you can see how much foliage each cut removes. Before cutting, lie under the tree to understand its structure. Remove lowest branches touching the ground, then take out branches that rub, cross or stick straight up and spoil the weeping effect. Work lightly and view the tree from several angles after each branch.

title: Versatile ‘Viridis’ Japanese Maple
author: Kristin Beane Sullivan
content: ‘Viridis’ makes a strong specimen in a mixed perennial and shrub border. It can be uplighted in an entry planting to cast shadows against the house, drape over the edge of a pond or retaining wall, or grow in a large container year round in zones 7 and warmer without extra winter protection.

title: Show Off the Shape
author: Kristin Beane Sullivan
content: Use ‘Viridis’ in a prominent position where its unique form can be appreciated year round. Perennial companions with contrasting leaf shapes frame it well. The illustrated combination includes ‘Viridis’ Japanese maple, ‘Burgundy Lace’ Japanese painted fern with burgundy-to-silvery-green foliage for part to full shade, ‘Thriller’ lady’s mantle with chartreuse late spring and early summer flowers for full sun to part shade, and ‘Contrast in Styles’ Siberian iris with wine-purple and blue-purple blooms for full sun to part shade.

It grows in full sun to part shade and well-drained soil, has no serious pests, reaches 6 to 10 feet tall and wide, and is cold hardy in USDA zones 5 to 8.

title: A Hidden Sanctuary
content: Creative energy abounds in this zone 8 Oregon garden. With nature’s beauty, manmade structures and art, it is easy to be inspired by the work that went into making the backyard retreat where Meredith and Donald Hilderbrand designed and built the home and gardens.

title: A Hidden Sanctuary
content: The property is nestled into a forest of Douglas fir (Pseudotsuga menziesii), blurring the line between native and cultivated. Paths lead to cozy nooks as well as open lawn for parties and play. The garden shows ways to make outdoor areas welcoming.

title: A Hidden Sanctuary
content: Opener photo of the Hilderbrands’ shaded Oregon garden sanctuary with trees, layered plantings, stone walls and a patio.

title: A Hidden Sanctuary
content: A wall of windows separates the inside living space from the outside, creating an optical illusion that they are one larger living area rather than two different ones.

title: A Hidden Sanctuary
content: Surrounded by plants and trees, the patio is one of the Hilderbrands’ main outdoor areas. Its closeness to the house makes it convenient for a quick stroll to see what is blooming or a longer sit with coffee and conversation. A patio can increase home value and extend living space beyond the walls. Comfortable chairs create a place to step outside and escape from the day.

title: A Hidden Sanctuary
content: An island raised bed creates a showcase area for favorite plants and adds color to a prominent patio spot. With shrubs and perennials elevated, blooms are easier to see. When seated, the plants are at eye level, enhancing the view and adding screening. Moss on hardscape toppers can give newer hardscaping a sense of permanence; mist daily at first to encourage moss, but do not scrub, scrape or spray chemicals on it.

title: A Hidden Sanctuary
content: Garden sculpture should be placed where it can be enjoyed. In a smaller setting, a less-is-more approach avoids a busy look. Favorite ornaments belong in frequently used areas, where they remain visible even in winter and from inside the house. Designing a patio with elements you love makes you more likely to spend time there.

title: A Hidden Sanctuary
content: Photo of a patio outside a wall of windows with seating, raised beds, stonework, shade plants and garden sculpture.

title: A Hidden Sanctuary
content: Containers and ceramic orbs add movable pops of color that can be shifted around the patio to create the best views.

title: A Hidden Sanctuary
content: Full-page garden patio photo with colorful containers, red ceramic orb, shade foliage and layered beds.

title: A Hidden Sanctuary
content: For a backyard getaway, it helps to have room to sprawl out and multiple places to relax. The Hilderbrands use their expansive yard with several favorite spots connected by paths and hard surfaces.

title: A Hidden Sanctuary
content: This garden includes intimate spots in different parts of the garden for one or two people to sit and enjoy another perspective. Meredith lets each space and its surroundings determine the seating, rather than forcing the landscape. Some nooks are cut into tree clearings and have room only for one or two people, so a couple of comfortable chairs and a small table are better than too much furniture.

title: A Hidden Sanctuary
content: The gong hut is a protected, intimate garden structure that still feels like part of the garden. It works for larger get-togethers, has room for 10 or more people and provides overhead protection so it can be used in less-than-perfect weather. It was built with split-face concrete block and fir, a locally available wood, to match the house and other features.

title: A Hidden Sanctuary
content: A 40-inch brass gong in the gong hut is an Asian-inspired garden ornament. At sunset, collected light creates a glow that continues into evening. The gong gently sings when touched by breeze or raindrops, and striking it can announce speeches and toasts. Bells or wind chimes can add sound to a garden if you choose one you enjoy hearing.

title: A Hidden Sanctuary
content: Photo of the gong hut garden structure with seating and a brass gong, plus a site illustration connecting patio, hammock, bench, gong hut, archway gates and parking.

title: A Hidden Sanctuary
content: A bench nestled beneath tall trees can offer respite from a large party and support private conversation. A 3-foot-wide concrete path accommodates a wheelchair and provides a smooth surface for visitors of all ages. The curved path slows guests down, makes adjacent beds easier to maintain, and contrasts with fine-textured plants and upright trees and gazebo structures.

title: A Hidden Sanctuary
content: Garden tour photos showing a bench beneath tall trees, the gong hut, and a smooth concrete path curving through shade plantings.

title: A Hidden Sanctuary
content: Japanese maples (Acer palmatum) can function as trees-as-art with intricate leaf shapes and splashes of color. The graceful spreading vase shape of the featured tree makes it a strong specimen in open lawn where it can be admired easily.

title: A Hidden Sanctuary
content: Curvy berms add pleasing contours to a landscape by building up soil for beds and borders. By amending the soil in these raised berms, Meredith improved the clay underneath that had been compacted by logging in the 1960s.

content: A large open archway guides guests to different parts of the garden and signals that they are entering a different area.

title: A Hidden Sanctuary
content: The garden’s architecture and style show Asian influence, but careful thought and planning also unify the house with the surrounding landscape. Two open archway-like gates guide visitors to the garden by the gong hut. The tall gate is built from concrete block and fir, matching the house and gong hut, and its hardscape contrasts harmoniously with surrounding foliage. Arbors can serve a similar purpose in other styles and are readily available or easy to build.

title: A Hidden Sanctuary
content: A colorful Japanese maple, shrubs and a border of shade plants soften the hard angles near the house. Circular shapes such as floating glass orbs and lightweight fiberglass bowls also balance hard lines. Single specimen plants in containers offer flexibility because they can be moved and arranged in different configurations. A relaxed, not overly strict style lets more personality into the garden.

title: A Hidden Sanctuary
content: Break up a large concrete slab with an island bed. Creeping Jenny (Lysimachia nummularia), a somewhat aggressive ground cover, will stay confined there and makes a pretty base for a birdbath.

title: A Hidden Sanctuary
content: Choose a site that highlights the special aspects of a garden sculpture. Look for ways to cast an interesting shadow in the right light and build a sturdy base that adds to the beauty without taking focus away from the sculpture.

content: Full-page photo of a tall rusted metal garden sculpture set on a sturdy base in a woodland garden.

title: A Hidden Sanctuary
content: Garden decorations transform a garden into a personal place. Seasonal touches, antique collections and large sculptures all add focal points and make the garden more interesting.

title: A Hidden Sanctuary
content: Meredith created a sculpture by fitting together pieces of mild steel salvaged from reject piles at a local fabrication shop. Mild steel rusts outdoors, and she likes the abstract shapes and rusty color because they blend with muted oranges and burgundy reds in the garden palette. To protect metal from severe rusting, use a weatherproofing sealant with a matte finish, or use rust-inhibiting outdoor paint for a colorful accent.

title: A Hidden Sanctuary
content: A repurposed metal screen placed at the end of a path keeps focus inside the garden instead of wandering off into the trees. Ornaments added to the screen make it more interesting, and a delicate climber could turn a similar screen into a trellis. A bench can also be a strong horizontal element that contrasts with fine texture and vertical lines in a screen behind it.

title: A Hidden Sanctuary
content: A hand-carved concrete planter by Oregon sculptor Joe Rivera holds ‘Crimson Queen’ Japanese maple (Acer palmatum dissectum). The 48-inch-diameter pot and tree can withstand the mild winters typical of the climate. Plan ahead with objects that are nearly impossible to move, because options are limited if you change your mind. For a natural look and relaxed feel, keep the garden simple and choose focal points whose scale fits the space.

title: Tomatoes on Steroids
author: Jamie Seitz
content: Is it just me, or do tomatoes have a secret supernatural ability to notice when you’ve gone on vacation? They seem to sense the moment you are unable to check on them daily and go completely bonkers and take over your entire backyard.

title: Tomatoes on Steroids
author: Jamie Seitz
content: My family takes a two-ish week summer vacation every year. Over the years, we’ve crisscrossed the country, logging hundreds of hours of driving while eating sandwiches out of a cooler. And as soon as our tired tires hit the end of our driveway, we can see that we are in big trouble. Again.

title: Tomatoes on Steroids
author: Jamie Seitz
content: It’s as if a couple of pesky kids snuck into our yard, started a game of Garden Jumanji that quickly spiraled out of control, and now there are man-eating, killer tomatoes as ginormous as Jack’s ridiculous beanstalk living in our garden. Sigh.

title: Tomatoes on Steroids
author: Jamie Seitz
content: Every year I try my best to coax the twisted branches back into their flimsy cages without snapping them off and killing the wee baby tomatoes. But it’s usually too late. The plants are too big. I have to let them do their thing, which means for the rest of the summer, I’ll be forced to dress head to toe in khaki and hack my way through the wild and tangled jungle of tomatoes to hunt for the elusive red fruit.

title: Tomatoes on Steroids
author: Jamie Seitz
content: Last year while we were out of town, one tomato plant tipped over its cage, spilled out of the planter, and proceeded to grow quite happily along the ground for the rest of the season. Coincidentally, we learned at this same time that our dog really enjoys cherry tomatoes. We had a hard time calling her back into the house several times a day because she had found a new, unlimited favorite treat source in the garden that didn’t require a trick.

title: Tomatoes on Steroids
author: Jamie Seitz
content: As often as this has happened, I take great pride in telling you I always have a bumper crop of tomatoes. With a teenage son who routinely eats his body weight in chips and salsa, we never have a shortage of cherry, Roma, or beefsteaks. There was one summer that the zucchini vines and tomato plants went to war, facing off in the middle of two planters like the Jets and the Sharks of West Side Story.

title: Tomatoes on Steroids
author: Jamie Seitz
content: The excitement of seeing what can happen in two weeks when you leave your garden unattended is kind of fun. Perhaps it’s why we’ve never changed our vacation schedule. Maybe we will next year? But probably not.

title: Tomatoes on Steroids
author: Jamie Seitz
content: With all the tomatoes Jamie grows, her favorite meal to make with them is simple bruschetta: crusty French bread, a drizzle of olive oil, fresh basil and a slice of tomato, topped with fresh mozzarella, and baked for 10 minutes.

title: Reader Tips
author: Lucille Sessions, MS
content: In winter, Lucille noticed that raccoons and opossums made a trail directly through her perennial beds, trampling remaining foliage. After pruning shrub roses, she removes the leaves and lets the canes dry. Then she uses one or two dried canes to mark the location of dormant perennials. The critters quickly learned to avoid the thorny canes and no longer wear a winter path through her garden beds.

title: Reader Tips
author: Edwin Flick, IA
content: Hold onto political signs after campaign season. Edwin removed the sign from the metal frame, bent back the sharp metal ends so they wouldn’t puncture leaves, and sunk the legs into a container planted with red banana (Ensete ventricosum ‘Maurelii’). The frame gave the top-heavy plants with large leaves enough support to keep them from whipping in the wind and flopping until sturdy roots formed.

title: Reader Tips
author: Madeline Spurck, IL
content: Madeline makes unique holiday decor from garden plants. In late fall, she cuts dormant vine stems and weaves them in and out of her metal porch railing and fence gate. This creates a base that can be laced with evergreen boughs and painted pinecones. As the holidays approach, she adds berries and ornaments.

title: Reader Tips
author: Betty Hofstetter, OH
content: To protect cold-frame seedlings from a hard freeze in spring, slip an old mattress pad around the top of the frame and pull the elastic bands to the ground. It is easy to assemble and remove, and the extra layer helps seedlings when temperatures drop.

title: The Wild Side
content: Common redpolls (Acanthis flammea) are small songbirds with patterned brown and white feathers and red markings. Males have red crowns and chests, while females and juveniles develop only red crowns. Black markings surround stout, pointy yellow beaks, and short tails have a small fork. Songs combine sharp chirps, trills and whistles.

title: The Wild Side
content: Common redpolls are social birds that breed in Northern Canada and Alaska in summer. In late fall they migrate in large groups to the northern United States and sometimes dip into the Midwest and East Coast when food is scarce. Their diet includes small seeds, especially willow, birch and alder seeds, plus insects. In winter they are often spotted feeding in masses near forest edges, open fields and weedy ditches.

title: The Wild Side
content: To attract common redpolls in their range, offer foods they prefer and provide seed-rich habitat. They may visit feeders during winter irruptions, especially when natural seed supplies are scarce.
