title: Grow a Showy Shade Garden
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Shade gardens are often perfect spots for seating areas or getaways. Under a mature tree or structure, temperatures are cooler and it is easier to create privacy or seclusion for a calming retreat. Shade gardens can require less maintenance because soil holds moisture longer and weeds sprout less readily. A couple inches of organic mulch each year can lighten the workload.

title: Grow a Showy Shade Garden
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Make foliage the star. Shade borders have fewer showy flowers than sunny ones, but a mix of leaf shapes and colors keeps them interesting. Broad green hosta leaves contrast with burgundy coral bells, while a few pansies add color. Repeating coral bells along the edge with more pansies provides a cohesive look. Back-of-border ligularia adds dramatic yellow spikes and heart-shaped, heavily toothed leaves; regular deep watering prevents crispy leaf edges.

title: Grow a Showy Shade Garden
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Delta Premium Pure Orange pansy has 3-inch orange flowers from spring to fall, full sun to part shade, 6 to 8 inches tall and 8 to 10 inches wide, USDA zones 5 to 8. ‘Silver Scrolls’ coral bells has small white flowers and dark purple leaves with a lacy silver overlay, full sun to part shade, 8 to 12 inches tall and 12 to 18 inches wide, zones 4 to 9. ‘Francee’ hosta has lavender blooms and green leaves with white margins, part to full shade, 12 to 24 inches tall and 24 to 36 inches wide, zones 3 to 9. ‘Patriot’ hosta has irregular white margins, part to full shade, 12 to 18 inches tall and 24 to 36 inches wide, zones 3 to 9.

title: Grow a Showy Shade Garden
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: ‘Superba’ clustered bellflower has deep purple tubular blooms in early to midsummer, full sun to part shade, 18 to 30 inches tall and 12 to 24 inches wide, USDA zones 3 to 8. ‘The Rocket’ ligularia has densely packed yellow midsummer flower spikes and large serrated heart-shaped leaves, part to full shade, 3 to 5 feet tall and 2 to 4 feet wide, zones 4 to 9. ‘Golden Queen’ globeflower has yellow-orange blooms from late spring to midsummer, full sun to part shade, 24 to 36 inches tall and 18 to 24 inches wide, zones 3 to 7.

title: Grow a Showy Shade Garden
content: Full-page photo of a lush shade garden border with hostas, coral bells, ligularia, pansies and other foliage plants.

title: Grow a Showy Shade Garden
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Create a Colorful Path with bedding impatiens and pulmonaria. The Beacon impatiens series provides classic shade-garden color and is resistant to downy mildew. Pulmonaria’s silvery foliage catches light near a part-shade pathway and makes the combination pop.

title: Grow a Showy Shade Garden
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: ‘Silver Bouquet’ pulmonaria has blue-to-pink spring flowers before silver leaves, part to full shade, 7 to 10 inches tall and 18 to 20 inches wide, USDA zones 4 to 9. Beacon Bright Red impatiens has red flowers from late spring to frost, part to full shade, 14 to 18 inches tall and 12 to 18 inches wide, zones 9 to 11. Beacon Coral impatiens has coral flowers from late spring to frost, part to full shade, 14 to 18 inches tall and 12 to 18 inches wide, zones 9 to 11.

title: Grow a Showy Shade Garden
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Border Beauties features ‘Beni’ mountain hydrangea, whose red lacecap flowers add texture and perform best in part shade with 4 to 6 hours of light per day. Too much sun causes flower color to fade. All plants in this border grow best with consistent moisture.

title: Grow a Showy Shade Garden
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: ‘Beni’ mountain hydrangea has white lacecap flowers that blush pink then mature to red in summer to fall, full sun to part shade, 4 feet tall and wide, USDA zones 6 to 9. ‘Ursula’s Red’ Japanese painted fern has silver-gray foliage with a red blush along the central stem, part to full shade, 12 to 18 inches tall and wide, zones 5 to 8. ‘Aureola’ hakonechloa has yellow-green flowers in late summer to fall, part to full shade, 1 to 2 feet tall and wide, zones 5 to 9.

title: Grow a Showy Shade Garden

title: How to Start a Garden Journal
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: A garden or nature journal is a way to slow down, reconnect with the natural world and get to know your garden better. Artist and teacher Carrie Carlson brings her journal wherever she goes, making a quick sketch or note when she sees something interesting in her yard or on a favorite walk.

title: How to Start a Garden Journal
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Keeping a journal is about paying attention to the world around you and using images, words or numbers to record what you see. You can include sketches, poems, or simple facts such as bloom counts, dates and weather events. There is no single right way to keep a journal.

title: How to Start a Garden Journal
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: If getting started is intimidating, Carrie suggests focusing on one plant or a small area you enjoy. Look at it from different angles, count plants, petals or leaves, and note how they are positioned and relate to others nearby. Get curious and ask questions. If you find a new plant, insect or bird, resist identifying it immediately; careful looking improves observational skills and gives you journal details.

title: How to Start a Garden Journal
content: Garden journal page illustration with black-eyed Susan sketches, notes, seeds and a portrait of artist Carrie Carlson.

title: How to Start a Garden Journal
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Carrie uses a simple prompt exercise in journaling classes: look at a photo or garden scene and write from “I think...,” “I wonder...” and “This reminds me of...” prompts. The same exercise works with any photo or outdoors in the garden.

title: How to Start a Garden Journal
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Choose tools that make journaling easy. Look for a journal that is easy to hold and fits in a favorite bag. Choose paper that suits your media; high-quality mixed-media paper will not buckle as easily with water-based media, and all-weather paper can work outdoors. You can also make a journal from scraps cut to size and spiral bound at an office supply store. Micron pens are useful for writing and drawing because they come in a range of colors and widths.

title: How to Start a Garden Journal
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: A garden journal can reveal patterns you might otherwise miss: which flowers butterflies prefer versus bees, when a backyard border has the most flowers, or which vegetables harvest best or have fewer pest problems. Carrie keeps a perpetual journal, revisiting the same spots over 10 days several times each year. Reviewing past journals can reveal seasonal timelines or trends that help make a vegetable garden more productive and borders more flowery.

title: How to Start a Garden Journal
content: Garden journal page sketches of obedient plant, trout lily, hawthorn berries and other observations from a perpetual journal.

title: Irresistible Patterned Petals
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Patterned flowers with bicolored petals, veins, stripes, picotees and bicolored throats often point the way to nectar for insects and create strong visual interest for gardeners. To show off a patterned flower, pair it with more subdued plants. Use green foliage around a showy bloomer in a container or use solid-color companions that match or accent the patterned markings.

title: Irresistible Patterned Petals
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Petunia (Petunia hybrids) offers stripes, speckles, picotees, starbursts, veins, streaks and swirls in a wide range of colors. Veined cultivars such as Headliner Blackberry Vein tend to be a lighter petal shade marked with darker veins. Near-black ‘Phantom’ has a contrasting yellow star, Red Carpet Hippy Chick Violet has a picotee that looks like a flower within a flower, and Splash Dance Calypso Cherry is bred to hold its color pattern even in hot temperatures. Petunias grow well in containers, hanging baskets or the ground; keep them evenly moist, fertilize weekly with a liquid general-purpose food and cut leggy summer growth back by a third to promote branching and bloom.

title: Irresistible Patterned Petals
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Petunia is a tender perennial with white, pink, purple, red, yellow, lavender, near-black, magenta and green flowers in many patterns from late spring to frost. Grow in full sun to part shade and moist, well-drained soil. Plants range from 4 to 24 inches tall and 8 to 96 inches wide and are cold hardy in USDA zones 10 to 11.

title: Irresistible Patterned Petals
content: Photo grid of patterned petunias including ‘Phantom’, Headliner Blackberry Vein, Red Carpet Hippy Chick Violet and Splash Dance Calypso Cherry.

title: Irresistible Patterned Petals
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Tulip (Tulipa spp. and hybrids) often has bold stripes or gentle picotee markings. ‘Chopin’ has bright red stripes on yellow petals, and its 6- to 10-inch foliage also has broken burgundy stripes. Some historic tulip streaking came from a virus spread by aphids, but today’s patterned tulips are disease-free and carefully bred. Plant tulips in soil that stays dry in summer so dormant bulbs do not rot, and grow them near dry-tolerant perennials such as salvia or coneflower so their foliage hides fading tulip leaves.

title: Irresistible Patterned Petals
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Tulip is a bulb with yellow, orange, white, purple, red, pink, green and bicolor flowers marked with streaks, picotees and stripes from early to late spring. Grow in full sun to part shade and average, well-drained soil. Plants range from 4 to 36 inches tall and 3 to 5 inches wide and are cold hardy in USDA zones 3 to 8.

title: Irresistible Patterned Petals
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Viola (Viola hybrids) is recognized for cheerful “face” markings created by colored blotches, usually on the three lower petals. Sorbet XP Pink Halo has a violet-to-pink ring and purple whiskers and grows 6 to 8 inches tall and wide. Violas are cool-weather plants and may die back above 80 degrees F. In the North, plant in early spring and again in early fall; in mild zones, plant in fall for blooms through winter until late spring. Deadhead spent flowers to keep plants producing.

title: Irresistible Patterned Petals
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Viola is a perennial with white, yellow, orange, red, blue, lavender and purple flowers marked with blotches, bicolors, veins and throats from fall through spring. Grow in full sun to part shade and moist, well-drained soil. Plants are 4 to 8 inches tall and 8 to 12 inches wide and are cold hardy in USDA zones 5 to 8.

title: Irresistible Patterned Petals
content: Photos of ‘Chopin’ tulip with red-striped yellow petals and Sorbet XP Pink Halo viola with purple face markings.

title: Irresistible Patterned Petals
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Painted tongue (Salpiglossis sinuata) has herringbone-like vein markings in the throats of lily-shaped annual flowers. Petals range from white to near black with contrasting throat patterns. ‘Gloomy Rival’ is pale lavender-gray with a burgundy-marked yellow throat, while mixes such as ‘Stained Glass’ offer red, orange, purple and yellow.

title: Irresistible Patterned Petals
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Painted tongue is easier to find as seed than as plants. Start seed indoors 8 weeks before the last frost, scatter tiny seed on damp seed-starting mix, dust lightly with mix and cover the tray with black paper because seeds need darkness to germinate. After sprouting, remove paper and grow under lights. Transplant delicate seedlings into cell packs when they have two sets of leaves and let potting mix dry slightly between waterings. Harden off when daytime temperatures are above 55 degrees F. Plants may need support, benefit from deadheading and should be fed weekly in summer.

title: Irresistible Patterned Petals
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Painted tongue is an annual with white, lavender, purple, violet, magenta, bronze, red, orange or yellow flowers with contrasting markings from late spring to fall. Grow in full sun to part shade and moist, well-drained soil. Plants reach 12 to 24 inches tall and 12 to 18 inches wide.

title: Irresistible Patterned Petals
content: Large photo of ‘Gloomy Rival’ painted tongue with pale lavender-gray petals and burgundy-yellow throat markings.

title: Irresistible Patterned Petals
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Zinnia (Zinnia spp. and hybrids) has bright annual flowers with bullseyes, picotees, streaks and stripes. Zahara Sunburst has fiery orange-red and gold bullseye flowers that advertise nectar-rich centers to pollinators and grows 12 to 18 inches tall and wide. ‘Peppermint Stick Mix’ has 2- to 4-inch double flowers in white, cream, yellow and orange flecked with crimson on sturdy 24-inch plants. Start zinnias indoors 4 to 6 weeks before last frost or direct-sow when temperatures are above 50 degrees F. Grow in full sun and water thoroughly during dry spells without wetting foliage. Newer cultivars can be less prone to powdery mildew.

title: Irresistible Patterned Petals
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Zinnia is an annual with pink, yellow, orange, red, white, salmon, green, purple, magenta or bicolor flowers with picotees, stripes and streaks from late spring to frost. Grow in full sun to part shade and moist, well-drained soil. Plants range from 6 to 48 inches tall and 6 to 24 inches wide. Single-flowered zinnias offer easier pollen access and landing space for pollinators than double or pom-pom types.

title: Irresistible Patterned Petals
content: Photo of Zahara Sunburst zinnia with fiery orange-red and gold bullseye patterned blooms.

title: Irresistible Patterned Petals
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Verbena (Verbena hybrids) is useful for mass plantings and containers, with solid colors, darkened throats, white eyes and stripes. Superbena Stormburst has periwinkle and white stripes on 6- to 12-inch-tall plants that spread 18 to 30 inches, trailing well from baskets or filling border space. Lanai Candy Cane has bold red-and-white peppermint markings. Heat-tolerant verbenas grow in sun or part shade, do not need deadheading, and can be trimmed to remove dried blooms or cut back by half in midsummer if leggy.

title: Irresistible Patterned Petals
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Verbena is a tender perennial with red, pink, purple, lavender, periwinkle, salmon, yellow or white flowers with stripes, eyes and dark throats in clusters from late spring to frost. Grow in full sun to part shade and moist to dry soil. Plants are 4 to 14 inches tall and 10 to 48 inches wide and are cold hardy in USDA zones 7 to 11.

title: Irresistible Patterned Petals
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Blackberry lily (Iris domestica) has airy orange or yellow late-summer flowers that last only a day, followed by seed pods. The species grows 2 to 3 feet tall with crimson-speckled orange flowers on stalks up to 4 feet tall. ‘Freckle Face’ has similar coloring with rounder petals. Start from plants or sow seeds indoors 6 to 8 weeks before last frost, transplanting in mid- to late spring. Grow in full sun or part shade with moist soil. It naturalizes by seed; deadhead to extend bloom or prevent reseeding.

title: Irresistible Patterned Petals
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Blackberry lily is a perennial with orange or yellow flowers with red speckles from late summer to fall. Grow in full sun to part shade and moist, well-drained soil. Plants reach 24 to 48 inches tall and 9 to 24 inches wide and are cold hardy in USDA zones 5 to 10.

title: Irresistible Patterned Petals
content: Photos of Superbena Stormburst verbena with striped periwinkle-and-white flowers and blackberry lily with orange speckled petals.

title: Irresistible Patterned Petals
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Blanket flower (Gaillardia spp. and hybrids) is a North American native often used in wildflower mixes. Its daisy-like flowers have colorful bands that attract pollinators before petals fall and leave fuzzy seedheads for birds. ‘Sun Devil’ grows 6 to 8 inches tall with fluted tubular ray petals tipped in gold around burgundy centers. Gaillardias are short-lived but can reseed. Give full sun and keep foliage dry to reduce powdery mildew. Deadhead and cut back leggy stems by half in late summer to encourage branching and fall bloom, but leave some spent flowers for seed and birds.

title: Irresistible Patterned Petals
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Blanket flower is a perennial with daisy-shaped red, yellow, peach, orange and bicolor flowers from early summer to frost. Grow in full sun to part shade and dry to medium soil. Plants range from 6 to 36 inches tall and 12 to 24 inches wide and are cold hardy in USDA zones 3 to 11.

title: Irresistible Patterned Petals
content: Photo of ‘Sun Devil’ blanket flower with fluted red petals tipped in gold around burgundy centers.

title: Irresistible Patterned Petals
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Bearded iris (Iris hybrids) comes in countless color and pattern combinations on upright standards and drooping falls. ‘Gnus Flash’ has irregular splashes and streaks that create a batik effect, and ‘Stepping Out’ is a classic white flower with purple picotee edges. When planting rhizomes in fall or potted plants any time, cover only the roots and leave rhizomes exposed so they do not rot. Water in, then let plants dry before the next watering. Apply a low-nitrogen granular fertilizer in early spring and again a month after bloom. Divide every 3 to 5 years to prevent overcrowding and reduced bloom.

title: Irresistible Patterned Petals
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Bearded iris is a perennial with flowers in shades of white, peach, pink, magenta, red, rust, maroon, yellow, orange, purple, lavender, blue and near-black in many patterns on bloom stalks in late spring to early summer. Grow in full sun and moist, well-drained soil. Plants range from 8 to 40 inches tall and 18 to 24 inches wide and are cold hardy in USDA zones 4 to 9.

title: Irresistible Patterned Petals
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Toad lily (Tricyrtis spp. and hybrids) has small orchid-like flowers sprinkled with purple specks. Blooms form alone or in clusters along unbranched stems in the leaf axils and at stem ends. Variegated cultivars such as ‘Gilt Edge’ or ‘Variegata’ add more color to woodland borders. Toad lilies prefer damp soil and shade so foliage does not scorch, and should be planted near a path or bench so the detailed flowers can be seen up close.

title: Irresistible Patterned Petals
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Toad lily is a perennial with white to lavender flowers with purple speckles from late summer to fall. Grow in part to full shade and moist soil. Plants reach 10 to 36 inches tall and 12 to 24 inches wide and are cold hardy in USDA zones 4 to 8.

title: Irresistible Patterned Petals
content: Photos of ‘Gnus Flash’ bearded iris and speckled toad lily flowers.

title: Which Poppy Is Right for You?
content: Oriental poppy (Papaver orientale) blooms for about two weeks in late spring to early summer with eye-catching papery blossoms that bridge spring bulbs and summer perennials. The bristly foliage contains a substance in its sap that deer usually avoid.

title: Which Poppy Is Right for You?
content: Oriental poppies work best tucked near slower-growing perennials that will fill in and cover their fading foliage in summer. Contrast orange or red Oriental poppies with blue-purple Siberian iris or spike speedwell for a vivid late-spring combination.

title: Which Poppy Is Right for You?
content: Grow Oriental poppies in USDA zones 2 to 7 in full sun or part shade and dry soil, especially during summer dormancy. After bloom, cut flower stems at ground level unless you want reseeding. These long-lived plants like to grow undisturbed. Divide every 4 to 5 years in late summer by lifting the dormant plant, cutting the root clump into three or four sections and replanting divisions 1 inch deep.

title: Which Poppy Is Right for You?
content: ‘Forncett Summer’ Oriental poppy has salmon-pink fringed petals around dark centers in early summer on plants 30 to 36 inches tall and 18 to 24 inches wide, USDA zones 3 to 7. ‘Beauty of Livermere’ has scarlet flowers with black centers on 24- to 40-inch-tall plants, zones 3 to 7. ‘Patty’s Plum’ has plum to mauve flowers in mid- to late spring on 24- to 30-inch-tall plants, zones 3 to 7.

title: Which Poppy Is Right for You?
content: Illustrated comparison page for Oriental poppy showing tissue-paper petals, bristly leaves, dormant habit and variety photos.

title: Which Poppy Is Right for You?
content: Breadseed poppy (Papaver somniferum) comes in vibrant colors with single, double or fringed flowers. Its edible seeds are used in baked goods and salad dressings, and dried pods are attractive in floral arrangements. Late-spring breadseed poppy grows about a foot wide, making it a good companion between spring bulbs and emerging perennials that will fill the space after this short-lived annual dies down. If reseeding is unwanted, pull fading plants and replace with summer annuals.

title: Which Poppy Is Right for You?
content: Grow breadseed poppies in full sun and well-drained soil. Seedlings do not transplant well, so direct sow seeds outdoors from late fall to very early spring, even sprinkling them on top of snow. Seeds need light to germinate, so do not cover them. Deadhead spent blooms so secondary flowers open, but let a few pods dry. When pods are brown and rattle when tapped, shake seeds into a tray and air-dry them for a week. Store in an airtight container in a cool, dry, dark spot. Kitchen seed lasts a long time, but seed for the garden should be planted the next year.

title: Which Poppy Is Right for You?
content: ‘Lauren’s Grape’ breadseed poppy has violet-purple flowers on 24- to 36-inch-tall plants. ‘Sissinghurst White’ has solid white blossoms on 24- to 36-inch-tall plants. ‘Lilac Pompom’ has double pink fringed flowers on 24- to 36-inch-tall plants. Breadseed poppies can produce up to a thousand seeds per pod.

title: Which Poppy Is Right for You?

title: Clematis
content: Full-page photo of deep purple ‘Gipsy Queen’ clematis blooming over an arbor and white picket fence.

title: Clematis
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: A striking show of 5- to 7-inch deep purple ‘Gipsy Queen’ clematis blooms at eye level captures attention and draws visitors through an arbor.

title: Clematis
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Clematis adds more color when borders are already packed with perennials. Trellises, arbors and walls can support clematis blooms in a wide range of colors, shapes and sizes. The showiest are large-flowered hybrids, divided into early-flowering types that bloom on old wood and late-flowering types that bloom on new wood. Many rebloom, so a mix of varieties can bloom from late spring to early fall.

title: Clematis
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Large-flowered clematis hybrids range from dwarf types such as 1- to 2-foot-tall Bijou to 15-foot-tall ‘Ernest Markham’. ‘Gipsy Queen’ grows 10 to 12 feet tall with 5- to 7-inch deep-purple blooms and has been a favorite for generations. Large-flowered clematis is a perennial with pink, purple, blue, white or red single or double blooms from late spring to fall, grows in full sun to part shade and moist, well-drained soil, can have clematis wilt, reaches 1 to 15 feet tall and 2 to 10 feet wide, and is cold hardy in USDA zones 3 to 9.

title: Clematis
content: Botanical-style illustration of ‘Nelly Moser’ large-flowered clematis with a profile box.

title: Clematis
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Early large-flowered clematis hybrids have their biggest flush of single, semidouble or double 6- to 10-inch blooms in late spring, then repeat in summer with usually smaller flowers. Some double or semidouble varieties rebloom with single flowers. Fluffy seedheads can extend interest into fall. Plants range from 6 to 10 feet tall and produce their first big show on last year’s growth, with some rebloom on current-season growth. They are often listed as pruning group 2, and clematis wilt can be a problem.

title: Clematis
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: ‘Countess of Lovelace’ early-blooming clematis has pale lavender-blue double flowers from late spring to summer and a light double rebloom in fall, 6 to 8 feet tall, USDA zones 4 to 9. ‘Niobe’ has velvety 5- to 7-inch deep red flowers with ivory stamens in late spring and summer, followed by fluffy seedheads, 8 to 12 feet tall, zones 4 to 9. ‘Lasurstern’ has lavender-blue flowers up to 9 inches across in late spring and a light late-summer rebloom, 8 to 12 feet tall, zones 4 to 8. ‘Henryi’ has 6- to 8-inch single white flowers with purple-brown anthers in early summer and a light early fall rebloom, 10 to 12 feet tall, zones 4 to 9. ‘Piilu’ has 3- to 4-inch double light pink late-spring flowers with dark pink center bars and single summer-to-fall rebloom, 3 to 6 feet tall, zones 4 to 9.

title: Clematis
content: Photo grid of early-blooming large-flowered clematis varieties including lavender-blue, red, lavender, white and pink cultivars.

title: Clematis
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Prune early-blooming clematis by doing light shaping and cleanup in late winter to early spring. These vines bloom on old wood, or buds formed the previous year, so cutting them to the ground will likely remove the year’s flowers. Thin by removing a few long stems, trim or reposition stems going where you do not want them, and remove dead or broken branches.

title: Clematis
content: Illustration showing how to prune early-blooming clematis by thinning, shaping and removing dead or broken branches.

title: Clematis
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Late large-flowered clematis hybrids bloom from early to midsummer into fall. Flowers range from 3 to 8 inches wide and plants grow 6 to 15 feet tall. They bloom on current-season growth and are pruning group 3. How they are pruned affects how they cover a structure.

title: Clematis
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: ‘Comtesse de Bouchaud’ late-blooming clematis produces many soft rose-pink 4- to 6-inch blooms with creamy yellow stamens from summer to fall and grows 8 to 11 feet tall, USDA zones 4 to 9. ‘Madame Edouard Andre’ has 4- to 6-inch deep red blooms with creamy yellow stamens from summer to fall, often with white flecks, and grows 10 to 12 feet tall, zones 4 to 9. ‘Etoile Violette’ has many 3- to 4-inch deep purple flowers with golden stamens in mid- to late summer and grows 10 to 12 feet tall, zones 4 to 9. ‘Jackmanii Superba’ has 5- to 6-inch deep purple flowers from summer to fall and grows 10 to 12 feet tall, zones 4 to 9. ‘Tie Dye’ has 4- to 6-inch lavender-and-white marbled blooms in early to midsummer and grows 8 to 12 feet tall, zones 4 to 9.

title: Clematis
content: Photo grid of late-blooming clematis varieties including pink, red, purple, deep purple and marbled flowers.

title: Clematis
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Prune late-blooming clematis in early spring as soon as leaf buds swell. Because they bloom on new growth, they can be cut to the ground and still bloom later in the year. For tallest vines with flowers from bottom to top on a gazebo or large arbor, leave a few tallest vines and cut others to the ground. For flowers only at the top of vines climbing a tree or shrub, just clean up dead stems. For smaller structures such as a trellis, cut all stems to within a few inches of the ground.

title: Clematis
content: Illustration showing three pruning options for late-blooming clematis on different structures.

title: Clematis
content: Full-page photo of ‘Jackmanii’ clematis covering a large garden structure with purple blooms concentrated near the top.

title: Clematis
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: ‘Jackmanii’ clematis can act as a colorful cover-up on a structure. If it gets little pruning beyond removing winter-damaged stems, most growth and flowers form at the top. Removing a few vines encourages new growth from the base for more blooms along the sides.

title: Clematis
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Start clematis with the right structure. Clematis vines do not attach themselves to a surface; tendrils next to leaves wrap around nearby structures. Choose supports with crosspieces 1/2 inch in diameter or smaller. Shrubs and trees can also act as structures. Match vine size to support size: let a 7- to 10-foot ‘Jackmanii’ cover a large gazebo, but use a naturally shorter vine on a 6-foot trellis or choose a late-flowering type you can cut to the ground annually.

title: Clematis
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Choose the right clematis spot by following the old advice “head in the sun and feet in the shade.” Clematis can bloom with 5 to 6 hours of sun, though more sun is better. Shade roots with mulch or companion plants to keep soil moist. Plants grow best in rich, well-drained soil with organic matter; avoid soggy soil because roots can rot.

title: Clematis
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Plant clematis in a hole about 18 inches deep and wide, amending the excavated soil with several shovelfuls of compost before backfilling. Kieran Avis of Longwood Gardens recommends removing foliage from the bottom one or two leaf nodes and planting so those nodes sit below the soil surface to encourage more roots. Angle the plant toward the structure to help vines grow in the right direction, and add a couple inches of mulch to keep soil evenly moist and weeds down.

title: Clematis
content: Planting diagram showing clematis planted 2 to 3 inches deeper than it grew in the container, angled toward a trellis, with buried leaf nodes and amended soil.

title: Clematis
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Clematis plants need consistent moisture; about an inch of water per week is right. A 2- to 3-inch layer of composted leaf mulch in spring conserves moisture and enriches soil. Kieran Avis waits until a plant’s second year to feed, then applies organic rose food once at pruning time, once before flowering and once after bloom.

title: Clematis
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Pruning clematis is not mandatory, but plants will be more flowery and have more foliage up and down the vine if pruned. By the second or third year, plants can benefit from pruning. How to prune depends on whether the clematis blooms on old wood, new wood or both. If you are unsure, watch the plant for a year or two and prune accordingly; the worst result of a mistake is losing bloom for one season.

title: Clematis
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Clematis troubles include occasional deer and rabbit browsing, especially on young vines, which fencing can prevent until stems mature. Foliage diseases such as powdery mildew can occur, but clematis wilt is most dreaded. It mostly affects large-flowered hybrids, especially early-blooming types. Symptoms start as dark brown to black spots, and a whole stem or group of stems can wilt. Infected plants may recover in a year or two, but avoid spreading disease.

title: Clematis
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: To reduce clematis wilt damage, provide good air circulation and water at soil level. Remove diseased stems as soon as they appear by cutting below the infected area and sending the stems to the trash. Between cuts, wipe tools with a disinfectant wipe or dip pruners in alcohol or ethanol so the disease is not spread.

title: Clematis
content: Photo of clematis wilt symptoms on foliage and stems, used with care and disease prevention advice.

title: Clematis
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Clematis can be grown in containers for color and height with a trellis or obelisk. Choose a compact variety such as 3- to 4-foot ‘Cezanne’ or ‘The Countess of Wessex’, or prune larger varieties such as ‘Niobe’ annually after flowering to keep them shorter. Use a container at least 18 to 24 inches in diameter. In freezing climates, choose wood, fiberglass or plastic pots for outdoor year-round clematis because ceramic and terra-cotta crack easily. Use potting mix for drainage, and expect to water and feed more often than in-ground plants because potting mix dries quickly and watering flushes nutrients.

title: Garden on a Dime
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: To save money gardening, composting, seed saving and dividing perennials are familiar solutions. Readers also shared ways to stretch the garden dollar while still growing a beautiful garden.

title: Garden on a Dime
author: Sharon Moore, IL
content: Sharon and her friends save money with a seedling swap. They pool resources and coordinate who will start which vegetable seeds each year. One person might start beefsteak tomatoes and eggplants, another might start cherry tomatoes and cucumbers. In spring the friends meet to distribute seedlings, and everyone gets what they need.

title: Garden on a Dime
author: Debi Jones, TN
content: Debi and a friend cut costs by looking for large perennials with potential for division at the garden center. They split the cost and plants. Perennial bachelor’s button with multiple crowns in one pot is easy to pull or cut apart. For dense root balls or a single crown, use a soil knife to cut between crowns and get the divisions you want.

title: Garden on a Dime
content: Photos of seedling trays and dividing a perennial bachelor’s button to save money on plants.

title: Garden on a Dime
author: Joy Haff, KS
content: Instead of buying spillers for shade garden urns, Joy uses easy-to-propagate houseplants such as philodendron, inch plant or variegated ivy. When the season winds down, she repots smaller plants and takes cuttings from large ones to grow in a vase of water over winter. In early spring she plants them up to get ready for outdoor containers.

title: Garden on a Dime
content: Photo of a mixed shade container using houseplants such as inch plant and ‘Neon’ philodendron as inexpensive trailing plants.

title: Garden on a Dime
author: Brenda Lantz, OK
content: Brenda combines a broken floor lamp and a broken umbrella to make a temporary shade for new baby plants. After a couple of days, the plants can take Southern sun.

title: Garden on a Dime
author: Jayme Dare, TN
content: During harvest season, Jayme tosses cracked or damaged cherry tomatoes into a 2-foot-square garden area reserved for volunteers. In spring, instead of tilling, she watches for volunteer seedlings. When they are 3 to 5 inches tall, she carefully digs them up and replants them where she usually grows tomatoes.

title: Garden on a Dime
author: Martin Charlesworth, Shropshire, United Kingdom
content: Martin saves on containers by asking local florists if he can buy buckets used to store cut flowers. He drills holes in the bottom for drainage. These long-lasting containers have held greenhouse peppers, contained mint, grown cuttings and held trees started from seed.

title: Garden on a Dime
author: Pat Kerr, Ontario, Canada
content: Pat reuses retired sheer curtains to protect vegetables from pests such as cabbage moths or deer and to keep birds out of fruit on blueberries and pear and cherry trees. The fabric is lightweight so it won’t crush foliage, but sun and water still pass through. She sews scrap ribbons 2 to 3 feet apart around the edge so panels can be tied together for a long row or secured around a tree or shrub.

title: Garden on a Dime
content: Photos and callouts showing volunteer tomato seedlings, floral buckets reused as containers and sheer curtains used as lightweight crop protection.

title: Garden on a Dime
author: Katy Sullivan, NY
content: Katy reuses empty mulch bags for collecting weeds and as kneeling pads. A single bag works, or several folded into fours make a cushier kneeler. Mulch bags can also serve as waterproof seat covers, trunk liners or transport sleeves for plant divisions shared by friends.

title: Garden on a Dime
author: Christine Cox, MA
content: Christine makes garden arbors from sturdy 5- to 6-foot trellises from a discount store, rebar and metal arches from an old row cover set. She pounds 2- or 4-foot rebar stakes into the ground where the trellis feet will go and secures each trellis with cable ties. Metal arches are secured on top with cable ties. One arbor spans a raised-bed vegetable path and carries cucumber vines.

title: Garden on a Dime
author: Sheryl Clifton, VA
content: Sheryl fills a bird feeder with black sunflower seeds and hangs it in the garden’s “wildflower area.” Some seeds fall and sprout. By letting them mature, visiting birds can eat extra seed from the flowers, and the sunflowers fit into the casual border.

title: Garden on a Dime
content: Illustration of a DIY garden arbor built from trellises, rebar, metal row-cover arches and cable ties, plus a sunflower bird-feeder tip photo.

title: Garden on a Dime
author: Vieve Voss, IA
content: Vieve turns a cracked trash can into a composting planter. She cuts out the bottom and places the cut end 4 inches deep in the soil. During winter she adds kitchen scraps, avoiding meat and oils, until the can is half full. In spring she fills the rest with soil and plants tomato ‘Juliet’, though any plant can work. The kitchen scraps break down and feed the plant through the season. In fall she empties the container into the garden to build soil and starts again.

title: Garden on a Dime
author: Marylou Schoep, KS
content: Marylou makes gift vases from cleaned glass bottles from soda, iced coffee or kombucha. She spray paints them matte white or pale gray, then fills them with garden flowers and foliage plants for hostess gifts or get-well bouquets.

title: Garden on a Dime
content: Illustration of a bottomless trash can used as an in-place compost planter, plus a simple bottle vase with garden flowers.

title: Garden on a Dime
author: Ellen Hull, IA
content: Ellen saves water with a Soil Master moisture and pH gauge. Insert the prongs into garden soil or potting mix and the dial shows whether it is time to water. A switch provides pH readings so amendments can be planned if needed.

title: Garden on a Dime
author: Melissa Kitchens, MS
content: Coir hanging basket liners can last for several years, but once they look thin and shaggy, Melissa repurposes the liners as mulch in containers and around strawberry plants.

title: Garden on a Dime
author: Jeanne Pavero, DE
content: Jeanne makes a quick compost blend by running fruit and vegetable scraps through the blender, then pouring the nutrient-packed liquid in different garden areas to feed plants and soil.

title: Garden on a Dime
author: Karen Weir, TX
content: Karen cuts a worn outdoor carpet into strips the width of vegetable garden paths. The strips allow water to pass through, keep weeds down and last a long time.

title: Garden on a Dime
content: Photo of a soil moisture and pH gauge and a container mulched with reused coir hanging basket liner.

title: Asparagus
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Asparagus is one of the first crops to harvest in spring, and because it is a long-lived perennial, it can produce sweet, crisp spears every year for decades. By midsummer, tall feathery foliage adds texture before plants set seed and go dormant after a hard frost. A good asparagus patch requires time, patience and special techniques.

title: Asparagus
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Choose a spot with 6 to 8 hours of full sun for vigorous asparagus growth, though plants can tolerate part shade. Good drainage is essential because roots rot easily in soggy soil. Asparagus is sensitive to soil compaction and root disturbance, so plant in a raised bed or a place where tall foliage will not shade nearby sun-loving companions. Asparagus is cold hardy in USDA zones 3 to 10, but variety choice can vary by climate.

title: Asparagus
author: Marisa Reyes
content: The quickest and most reliable way to start asparagus is with crowns, which are 1-year-old plants. Most available plants are male hybrids, which live longer than female plants, produce no seeds and grow more small, uniform spears. Plant as soon as soil can be worked, about 45 degrees F, in early spring. Store crowns in the refrigerator until planting, then soak them in water for an hour to hydrate them before planting.

title: Asparagus
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Asparagus needs about an inch of water per week from rainfall or irrigation. Deep, infrequent watering encourages deeper roots so plants tolerate dry spells better. Asparagus is a heavy feeder and benefits from annual applications of balanced all-purpose granular fertilizer. Top dress with 2 to 3 inches of compost or manure in early spring before spears emerge.

title: Asparagus
author: Marisa Reyes
content: To start an asparagus patch, dig a trench 12 to 18 inches deep and 6 to 8 inches wide. Spread a layer of balanced all-purpose granular fertilizer, then cover it with 2 inches of soil. Set crowns 12 inches apart, spreading roots over mounded soil in the trench bottom. Cover crowns with soil, topdress with 2 to 3 inches of compost or manure, add 2 inches of straw mulch and water in.

title: Asparagus
content: Step photos and diagram showing how to dig a trench, fertilize, set asparagus crowns 12 inches apart, backfill, compost, mulch and water.

title: Asparagus
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Keep weed competition down as a new asparagus patch establishes. In early spring, apply a 1- to 2-inch layer of straw mulch to prevent weeds and retain moisture. If weeds still appear, carefully hand pull or hoe lightly.

title: Asparagus
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Do not harvest asparagus spears the first year. Wait two or three years so plants can establish and become vigorous. In the second or third year, harvest spears when they are 6 to 8 inches tall and tips are still tight. Check every day or two because spears grow quickly. After 6 or 8 weeks, stop harvesting and let new spears go to seed so ferny foliage can photosynthesize and store energy for next year. When foliage turns yellow or brown in fall, cut it back to within 2 inches of the ground. Add 4 to 6 inches of straw mulch for winter protection, then remove it before spring spear emergence.

title: Asparagus
author: Marisa Reyes
content: White asparagus can be grown by depriving emerging spears of light. Traditionally, spears are covered with soil, but dark plastic tunnels, sheeting, mulch or a pot with no holes can create the same result with less effort.

title: Asparagus
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Asparagus (Asparagus officinalis) is a perennial planted in early spring when soil reaches 45 degrees F. For fresh eating, plant 5 to 10 plants for one person or about 25 plants for a family of four. Grow in full sun, with part shade tolerated, and rich, well-drained soil. Harvest after the second or third year when spears are 6 to 8 inches tall. It is cold hardy in USDA zones 3 to 10.

title: Asparagus
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Varieties for zones 3 to 5 should emerge late to avoid spring frost damage; options include ‘Jersey Giant’, ‘Jersey King’, ‘Jersey Knight’, ‘Millennium’ and ‘Purple Passion’. In zones 6 to 10, choose heat-tolerant varieties such as ‘Apollo’, ‘Atlas’, ‘Erasmus’, ‘Grande’, ‘Spartacus’ and UC 157.

title: Asparagus
content: Photos showing asparagus spear harvest at the base, crowns or spears in soil, and a variety-selection table for cold and warm zones.

title: Grand Garden Experiment
author: Kristin Beane Sullivan
content: When Philip Zhao and Tingshu Hu moved to their suburban home in northern Massachusetts nearly 20 years ago, it took them 2 hours to mow the 1-acre lawn. They wanted less lawn, less water use and fewer lawn treatments, so they set a goal of reducing the lawn by half. Now they tend large vegetable plots, flower and shrub borders, three ponds, two greenhouses and a flock of chickens.

title: Grand Garden Experiment
author: Kristin Beane Sullivan
content: Tingshu, a professor of electrical and computer engineering, and Philip, a computer engineer, have planned and executed every project themselves. They have experimented with new plants, faced challenges and built innovative garden structures, which led to their selection as Garden Gate's 2023 Reader Garden Award winners.

title: Grand Garden Experiment
author: Kristin Beane Sullivan
content: The border along the front path holds a diverse mix of shrubs, perennials and annuals planned for four-season color. Spring brings bulbs and spring-flowering shrubs; summer includes false indigo, geum, salvia and gloriosa daisy; fall adds dahlias and zinnias; and winter interest comes from conifers such as golden falsecypress, green arborvitae and dwarf blue spruce.

title: Grand Garden Experiment
content: Opening photo of the Reader Garden Award-winning front walk with mixed perennials, shrubs and labeled plants such as Totally Tangerine geum and 'Walker's Low' catmint.

title: Grand Garden Experiment
content: Garden photo of the colorful front walk border with geum, false indigo and dense four-season plantings beside the path.

title: Grand Garden Experiment
author: Kristin Beane Sullivan
content: In the backyard, Tingshu wanted a showy centerpiece tree and chose a 'Prairie Fire' flowering crabapple for bright pink spring bloom, yellow fall foliage and red berries that feed birds. Philip wanted a seating area and pond. Their combined design uses companion plants selected for color in every season.

title: Grand Garden Experiment
author: Kristin Beane Sullivan
content: A tapestry of low-growing plants, including variegated wintercreeper, golden creeping Jenny and ground cover sedums, keeps weeds down between other plants. When Tingshu places smaller plants such as coral bells in this area, she sometimes encircles them with edging to keep aggressive ground covers from overtaking them.

title: Grand Garden Experiment
content: Backyard overview with 'Prairie Fire' flowering crabapple, pond, greenhouse, seating area, layered ground covers and spring and fall inset photos.

title: Grand Garden Experiment
author: Kristin Beane Sullivan
content: In the roughly 9-by-12-foot backyard pond, water lilies and other plants filter waste from the goldfish, while the goldfish eat mosquito larvae and other insects. Philip has mostly stopped filtering the water or feeding the fish because the pond nearly takes care of itself; they mainly need to divide the water lilies every couple of years.

title: Grand Garden Experiment
author: Kristin Beane Sullivan
content: Philip first planned a curved backyard path, but when the pavers arrived, a straight path required much less stone cutting. The straight lines now frame the exuberant, always-changing beds and lead from the house toward a small patio and pond.

title: Grand Garden Experiment
author: Kristin Beane Sullivan
content: After losing a tree at the back of the property, the couple installed a 26-by-10-foot greenhouse for seed starting, overwintering tropical plants and growing vegetables year round in zone 5. Because they did not want it to dominate the view and wanted to use geothermal energy, the family hand dug a 6-foot-deep foundation so the greenhouse rises only 5 feet above the soil. In winter they grow leafy greens, sometimes keep cherry tomatoes until Christmas, overwinter myrtle and figs, and start vegetables, cannas and dahlias early.

title: Grand Garden Experiment
content: Photo of the self-sustaining backyard pond with water lilies and surrounding plants.

title: Grand Garden Experiment
content: Portrait of Tingshu Hu and Philip Zhao with their dog Luke, identified as 2023 Reader Garden Award winners.

title: Grand Garden Experiment
author: Kristin Beane Sullivan
content: After filling most of the backyard and sideyards with gardens, the couple enclosed part of the front yard with a 3-foot-tall picket fence so their Havanese dogs, Didi and Luke, would have a place to run. They added 3-foot-wide perennial borders on both sides of the fence so they and their neighbors could enjoy the planting, using divided ornamental grasses, Russian sage, catmint and other perennials moved from elsewhere in the garden.

title: Grand Garden Experiment
author: Kristin Beane Sullivan
content: When grubs killed a section in the middle of the front lawn, Tingshu and Philip planted the area with drought-tolerant perennials such as dianthus, coreopsis and tall sedum instead of reseeding turfgrass. A robotic mower is the newest front-yard addition, and Philip has been installing paver edging beside perennial borders to make mowing smoother.

title: Grand Garden Experiment
author: Kristin Beane Sullivan
content: Low-growing plants along the front-yard path, including Johnny jump-up, dianthus, sweet alyssum, creeping Jenny, ground cover sedums and blue fescue, weave together tightly enough to reduce weeds. Reseeders such as Johnny jump-ups, sweet alyssum and gloriosa daisy make the garden change from year to year, and Tingshu edits seedlings by leaving patches where she wants them and pulling those that would crowd other plants.

title: Grand Garden Experiment
content: Overhead view of the fenced front yard with koi pond, waterfall, raised vegetable beds, drought-tolerant bed, picket fence and front-door path.

title: Grand Garden Experiment
author: Kristin Beane Sullivan
content: Philip and Tingshu built a unique concrete path with a reusable mold from the home improvement center. Nearby, tufts of bright pink dianthus mix with purple Johnny jump-ups, white sweet alyssum, creeping Jenny and pink-flowered spotted deadnettle. The Johnny jump-ups reseeded from the backyard into the front garden on their own.

title: Grand Garden Experiment
content: Photo group showing the concrete path, drought-tolerant garden, robotic mower charging station and low-growing dianthus, Johnny jump-ups, creeping Jenny and spotted deadnettle.

title: Grand Garden Experiment
author: Kristin Beane Sullivan
content: Inspired by shallow koi ponds in Japan and China, and limited by buried fiber-optic cables, Philip built a 1-foot-deep front-yard koi pond. The pond runs water through an aquaponic planter box, where plants use fish waste and filtered water returns to the pond, reducing the frequency of filter cleaning.

title: Grand Garden Experiment
author: Kristin Beane Sullivan
content: Because the outdoor pond is too shallow for winter fish protection in zone 5, the couple built another 250-gallon tank in the indoor sunroom using the same aquaponic planter technique. The patio has the sound of water, a structure overhead, seating, a bridge that gives fish cover from predators, and concrete-block pockets planted around pergola supports.

title: Grand Garden Experiment
content: Front-yard getaway photo with koi pond, bridge, patio seating, pergola frame and aquaponic planter design.

title: Grand Garden Experiment
author: Kristin Beane Sullivan
content: The 250-gallon sunken sunroom tank protects koi in winter and filters water through an aquaponic container garden. Outdoors, concrete-block pockets near the pergola hold small annuals such as Yellow Charm bidens, Laguna Sky Blue lobelia and sweet alyssum, while the blocks also create a raised bed for a climbing rose and clematis trained up the arbor posts.

title: Grand Garden Experiment
content: Photo group showing the sunroom koi tank with aquaponic container, the outdoor aquaponic pond and concrete-block pockets planted with annuals.

title: Grand Garden Experiment
author: Kristin Beane Sullivan
content: The sunny front yard holds five raised vegetable beds where Tingshu and Philip grow crops such as garlic, harvested for both scapes and bulbs, and stem lettuce, an Asian green grown for its stems rather than leaves. Tingshu sautees and quick pickles the stems.

title: Grand Garden Experiment
author: Kristin Beane Sullivan
content: The picket fence keeps the dogs in but not rabbits out, so Tingshu and Philip stapled chicken wire to the fence and buried it 3 to 4 inches into the soil to protect vegetable beds and flower borders. Other garden challenges include voles eating lilies and tulips, squirrels taking fruit, an occasional black bear near sweet corn, slugs chewing perennial leaves after rainy weather, and freeze damage to fruit, rhododendron and rose buds.

title: Grand Garden Experiment
author: Kristin Beane Sullivan
content: The couple approaches garden problems scientifically by researching options and testing different methods. Secure fences help with most four-legged pests, winter trapping has been the best defense against voles, and rain sometimes reduces irrigation needs even when weather causes other losses.

title: Grand Garden Experiment
content: Photo of raised vegetable beds with garlic, stem lettuce and chicken-wire protection along the picket fence.

title: Grand Garden Experiment
author: Kristin Beane Sullivan
content: Ken Vengren and Harrison Kendall in New Hampshire created the Come for the Views runner-up garden, a 3/4-acre garden with multiple pathways, color and varied plant shapes. The main hardscape features are a sunken greenhouse with stained glass windows and a stone sink, plus a patio and pergola used for garden parties. They built the garden around a historic house over 22 years.

title: Grand Garden Experiment
author: Kristin Beane Sullivan
content: Lynn O'Shaughnessy in Michigan created the Pretty for Pollinators runner-up garden, a 100-foot-diameter circle garden with a 12-point geometric design and 14 species of Michigan native plants for pollinators. She hired help to prepare the soil, then built the rest herself and grew many plants from seed in her greenhouse.

title: Grand Garden Experiment
content: Reader Garden Award runner-up photos showing Ken Vengren and Harrison Kendall's New Hampshire paths, pergola and greenhouse.

title: Grand Garden Experiment
content: Reader Garden Award runner-up photos showing Lynn O'Shaughnessy's geometric Michigan pollinator garden and native planting design.

title: Elevating Small Spaces
author: Marisa Reyes
content: In a small space, cultivating a lush garden can seem difficult, especially with heavy rainfall, extreme heat or drought. Four garden design pros share techniques, products and favorite plants for smaller backyards, patios and rooftops.

title: Elevating Small Spaces
content: Opening image of a small-garden design plan with colored planting areas, pavers and drafting tools.

title: Elevating Small Spaces
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Pearce Butcher uses order, repetition, proportion, color and balance to create small gardens where clients can relax. Dividing a garden into symmetrical quadrants with a 45-degree angle can make a small space feel bigger by creating longer pathways and sight lines toward the corners.

title: Elevating Small Spaces
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Pearce recommends planting in large groups and repeating plants to keep a small garden simple and cohesive. Too many different varieties can make a small space feel cluttered and overwhelming, while complementary foliage textures and a simple color palette create balance.

title: Elevating Small Spaces
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Double-duty furniture expands the use and comfort of a small garden. A stool can work as a side table or extra seating, a covered firepit can become a coffee table, and backless benches can face either direction or serve as low tables.

title: Elevating Small Spaces
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Blurring the line between indoors and outdoors can make a garden feel larger. Repeat elements of the home's architecture, interior style or surrounding landscape, such as brick banding along paths for a brick house or natural stones repeated in the hardscape.

title: Elevating Small Spaces
author: Marisa Reyes
content: For small gardens with drainage challenges, Pearce likes moisture-loving plants that tolerate soggy soil. Dwarf fothergilla has fragrant white bottlebrush spikes in spring and grows 18 to 36 inches tall and 12 to 48 inches wide in full sun to part shade, USDA zones 5 to 8. Siberian iris has white, yellow, violet, blue, pink or maroon spring flowers, grows 24 to 48 inches tall and 18 to 36 inches wide in full sun to part shade, zones 3 to 9. Virginia sweetspire has fragrant white late-spring to early-summer flowers and red, orange and gold fall foliage, growing 3 to 5 feet tall and wide in zones 5 to 9.

title: Elevating Small Spaces
content: Photos of a small patio design with angled hardscape, brick banding, seating, firepit and a Siberian iris plant profile.

title: Elevating Small Spaces
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Kristin Monji designs small gardens, rooftops and balconies by planning carefully. She recommends measuring the area and drawing a floor plan, then testing the top five nonplant elements, such as furniture placement, hardscaping and pergolas, before buying or installing anything.

title: Elevating Small Spaces
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Kristin advises against cluttering a small garden with multiple pieces of small furniture. Bigger pieces, such as a large coffee table or sectional, can make a stronger statement, and custom built-ins such as benches and lounges help maximize awkward spaces where standard furniture will not fit.

title: Elevating Small Spaces
author: Marisa Reyes
content: A small tree can add height and become a focal point. Kristin likes Japanese maples because they grow well in containers and many reach just 8 to 10 feet tall. Placing a tree in the farthest corner from the house draws the eye to parts of the garden that might otherwise be overlooked.

title: Elevating Small Spaces
author: Marisa Reyes
content: A multipurpose planter cluster of three to five pots in varied sizes can be replanted for seasonal interest. Cascading annuals such as calibrachoa, creeping Jenny and sweet potato vine can mix with edible plants such as cucumbers, tomatoes, basil and other herbs.

title: Elevating Small Spaces
content: Small patio photo with built-in seating, planters, Japanese maple and panicle hydrangea used to show planning and height in compact spaces.

title: Elevating Small Spaces
author: Marisa Reyes
content: When garden space is limited, plants that offer multiple seasons of interest earn their place. Catmint has fragrant lavender, blue, white, pink or purple flowers from late spring to summer, grows in full sun, reaches 6 to 48 inches tall and 12 to 48 inches wide, and is hardy in USDA zones 3 to 9. Coral bells have white, pink, red or purple blooms, colorful foliage and grow 6 to 24 inches tall and 10 to 36 inches wide in zones 3 to 9.

title: Elevating Small Spaces
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Long-blooming small-space plants include lemon verbena, a tender perennial with fragrant white to pale lilac flowers from midsummer to early fall that grows 2 to 4 feet tall and wide in full sun, USDA zones 8 to 10, and panicle hydrangea, a shrub with white or green flowers aging to pink from summer to fall, growing 3 to 25 feet tall and 3 to 16 feet wide in full sun to part shade, zones 3 to 8.

title: Elevating Small Spaces
content: Photo of a small patio with large sectional seating, layered plants and a long-blooming plant profile for 'Cat's Pajamas' catmint.

title: Elevating Small Spaces
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Sara Meier suggests designing small spaces for the senses. Fragrant herbs such as rosemary, oregano and lavender can be grown in containers and brushed as you walk by to release their scent, while creeping thyme releases fragrance when stepped on.

title: Elevating Small Spaces
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Sara uses repetition by growing plants that repeat the same color in different textures. Variations of silver and blue can tie a composition together and create a calming feel, dark foliage and flowers can create a moody combination, and repeated yellows and oranges can make a space feel happy and uplifting.

title: Elevating Small Spaces
author: Marisa Reyes
content: For four-season planning, Sara draws a chart with spring, summer, fall and winter columns, then lists the plants that peak in each season. Winter interest might come from evergreen foliage, bark and bright berries, while fall can rely on autumn color and seedheads. Hydrangeas and ornamental grasses are useful because they hold color and form from summer to fall.

title: Elevating Small Spaces
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Water-wise plants for dry climates include Mojave sage, a full-sun perennial with purple flowers from mid- to late summer, 18 to 24 inches tall and 24 to 30 inches wide, USDA zones 5 to 10; seven-son flower, a shrub with creamy white late-summer flowers, deep red calyxes and red-purple berries, 15 to 20 feet tall and 8 to 10 feet wide, zones 5 to 9; and silver edged horehound, a full-sun perennial with fuzzy green silver-edged foliage, 6 to 10 inches tall and 18 to 24 inches wide, zones 4 to 9.

title: Elevating Small Spaces
content: Photos of small-space containers and water-wise plantings with repeated silver and blue foliage and a seven-son flower profile.

title: Elevating Small Spaces
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Sara Bendrick recommends using the vertical plane in small gardens. Walls and fences can become trellises, planting-pocket supports, mural surfaces or places for decorative panels, especially in yards that are mostly concrete and have little ground space for planting.

title: Elevating Small Spaces
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Small yards benefit from details because there are fewer places for the eye to go. A mosaic path can be both practical and artistic, and a plug-in fountain or small corner pond can highlight a different area of the landscape.

title: Elevating Small Spaces
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Sara breaks up square or rectangular yards by adding a larger item such as a tree or sculpture in a corner. She also creates depth by layering plants of different heights; low annuals can sit at the front of a border while dwarf conifers provide year-round structure and color.

title: Elevating Small Spaces
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Sun-loving plants for dry, hot, reflected-heat locations include 'Karl Foerster' feather reed grass with pink plumes aging to tan, 3 to 5 feet tall and 2 to 3 feet wide, USDA zones 5 to 9; Desert Museum palo verde tree with yellow spring-to-summer flowers, 25 to 30 feet tall and wide, zones 8 to 9; and Parry's agave with yellow flower spikes above mature plants, 2 to 3 feet tall and 3 to 4 feet wide, zones 8 to 12.

title: Elevating Small Spaces
content: Photos of a mosaic path, living green wall and drought-tolerant Parry's agave used to illustrate small-space vertical planting and detail.

title: Small Garden Mix and Match
author: Stephanie Polsley Bruner
content: In a small bed, every plant counts, so multiseason plants are valuable. This design collection combines hard-working plants in two different small-space scenarios: a mailbox corner pocket and an easy island bed.

title: Small Garden Mix and Match
author: Stephanie Polsley Bruner
content: For the corner pocket, a stepping stone placed in the middle of snow-in-summer makes it easy to step close to the mailbox. Sedum is omitted because it attracts many bees near a spot someone has to step into. Weigela, phlox and a mandevilla vine on the mailbox provide color.

title: Small Garden Mix and Match
author: Stephanie Polsley Bruner
content: For the easy island bed, the planting can block an unwanted view, break up empty lawn or act as a focal point. Blue oat grass encircles an obelisk supporting mandevilla, while weigela and sedum on the outside edge keep the bloom going from spring to fall.

title: Small Garden Mix and Match
content: Illustrated planting plans and diagrams for a mailbox corner pocket and an easy island bed with labeled plant positions.

title: Small Garden Mix and Match
author: Stephanie Polsley Bruner
content: My Monet weigela has green, cream and pink foliage that holds color all summer and pink early-summer flowers that attract hummingbirds and butterflies. It grows 12 to 18 inches tall and wide in full sun to part shade, moist well-drained soil, prefers afternoon shade in hot climates, needs only old or damaged growth snipped out, and is cold hardy in USDA zones 4 to 6.

title: Small Garden Mix and Match
author: Stephanie Polsley Bruner
content: Blue oat grass forms clumps of blue-gray strappy pointed foliage topped with tan seedheads in early to midsummer. It grows 18 to 36 inches tall and 18 to 24 inches wide in full sun and well-drained soil, has its best blue color when soil stays dry, can be semi-evergreen in warmer climates, should be cut back hard in early spring, and is hardy in USDA zones 4 to 8.

title: Small Garden Mix and Match
author: Stephanie Polsley Bruner
content: 'Autumn Joy' tall sedum has gray-green succulent leaves that form a neat mound all summer, flat-topped rosy-pink flowers from late summer to fall, dried seedheads for winter interest and butterfly appeal. It grows 18 to 24 inches tall and wide in full sun and well-drained soil, tolerates light shade but may flop, and is hardy in USDA zones 3 to 9.

title: Small Garden Mix and Match
author: Stephanie Polsley Bruner
content: 'Junior Dream' garden phlox has bright pink-purple flowers from midsummer to early fall, is shorter than most tall phlox, resists mildew and attracts butterflies. It grows 18 to 22 inches tall and 18 inches wide in full sun to part shade and moist well-drained soil. Deadhead for rebloom and avoid overhead watering to reduce powdery mildew; it is hardy in USDA zones 4 to 8.

title: Small Garden Mix and Match
author: Stephanie Polsley Bruner
content: Snow-in-summer has white blooms in early summer and a low mat of silver-gray foliage that serves as a ground cover. It grows 6 to 12 inches tall and spreads in full sun and well-drained soil. Shear after flowering to clean up foliage, which may decline in late summer. It can be overly aggressive in some regions and is hardy in USDA zones 3 to 7.

title: Small Garden Mix and Match
author: Stephanie Polsley Bruner
content: 'Alice du Pont' mandevilla has bright-pink 4-inch blooms from early summer to frost and can grow 3 to 20 feet tall, though it stays smaller in containers or when treated as an annual. Grow it in full sun to part shade and moist well-drained soil, provide a trellis, and bring it inside to overwinter where it is not hardy. It is cold hardy in USDA zones 10 to 11.

title: Small Garden Mix and Match
content: Plant profile grid with photos of My Monet weigela, blue oat grass, 'Autumn Joy' tall sedum, 'Junior Dream' garden phlox, snow-in-summer and 'Alice du Pont' mandevilla.

title: 4 Bird-Feeding Mistakes
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Adding feeders can supplement the berries, seeds and insects already in the garden when natural food sources are scarce. To keep birds well fed and safe, avoid common mistakes involving food choice, feeder design, feeder placement and feeder variety.

title: 4 Bird-Feeding Mistakes
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Different birds prefer different foods. Black-oil or hulled sunflower seeds attract cardinals, chickadees, finches and sparrows, with hulled seed preferred but more prone to spoiling if wet. Cracked corn attracts doves, quails and sparrows, while whole corn attracts ducks and wild turkeys. Oranges and other fruit can attract bluebirds, catbirds, grosbeaks, mockingbirds, orioles, robins, tanagers, thrashers, towhees, waxwings and woodpeckers, but moldy fruit should be removed immediately.

title: 4 Bird-Feeding Mistakes
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Mealworms are a high-protein treat for bluebirds, chickadees, nuthatches, titmice and wrens. Millet is favored by small ground-foraging birds such as juncos, robins, sparrows, starlings and thrushes. Nyjer, also called thistle seed, attracts finches, pine siskins and redpolls and works best in a tube feeder. Unsalted peanuts attract chickadees, jays, nuthatches and titmice. Suet attracts many insect-eating birds, but should not be offered when temperatures exceed 90 degrees F because it can melt or go rancid. Store birdseed in a cool, dry place where rodents cannot reach it.

title: 4 Bird-Feeding Mistakes
content: Illustrations of bird feeders and food-selection table, including tube, mesh tube and hopper feeders.

title: 4 Bird-Feeding Mistakes
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Complicated feeders with small crevices and complex parts can collect food particles that grow bacteria and mold, and birds can get stuck and hurt themselves. Simple feeder designs are easier for birds to access and easier to clean. Ideally, clean feeders twice a month with one part bleach to nine parts water, rinse thoroughly and let them dry before refilling.

title: 4 Bird-Feeding Mistakes
author: Marisa Reyes
content: To reduce window strikes, avoid placing feeders between 3 and 30 feet from a window. Within 3 feet, a bird cannot gain enough speed to injure itself badly if it hits glass. Beyond 30 feet, birds have more space to escape predators and more time to see and avoid the window.

title: 4 Bird-Feeding Mistakes
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Using only one feeder style limits bird diversity because species feed differently. Tube feeders attract chickadees, finches, nuthatches and titmice. Hopper feeders attract cardinals, finches, jays, robins, sparrows, thrushes and wrens. Ground or tray feeders attract cardinals, doves, finches, jays, robins, sparrows, thrushes and wrens. Suet cages attract chickadees, jays, flickers, nuthatches, starlings, titmice, warblers and wrens. Nectar feeders attract hummingbirds and orioles. Platform feeders attract a wide range including chickadees, grosbeaks, orioles, thrashers, towhees, woodpeckers and wrens.

title: 4 Bird-Feeding Mistakes
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Cornell Lab of Ornithology resources for bird lovers include Merlin, a mobile bird-identification app with sound identification, and feederwatch.org, which helps identify birds and match houses, feeders and foods with species.

title: 4 Bird-Feeding Mistakes
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Homemade hummingbird nectar uses one part sugar dissolved in three or four parts hot or boiling water. Cool before filling the feeder. Store extra solution in the refrigerator for up to one week. Refresh the feeder every 2 to 5 days when temperatures are below 80 degrees F and every day when temperatures are above 80 degrees F. Wash the feeder with soap and water at each refill.

title: Q&A
content: The last garden tool to put away for winter should be the garden hose. If soil is not frozen and feels dry, water in fall or winter, but let the soil guide you because too much water contributes to crown or root rot, especially while many plants are dormant. Disconnect and empty the hose after each use when freezing weather is forecast so it does not burst.

title: Q&A
content: A mangave may look poor after blooming, but small new plants at the base, called pups, can be removed any time of year. Twist off pups by hand or cut them free with a sharp knife. Pot rooted pups immediately in premoistened potting mix with the crown above the mix; let unrooted pups callous out of direct sun for a couple days before pressing them into potting mix. Roots should form in 6 to 8 weeks. Keep newly potted mangaves in indirect light and let soil dry before watering again.

title: Q&A
content: Tent caterpillars and fall webworms are different pests. Tent caterpillars eat foliage in spring and should be treated because they eat tender new growth, weakening trees and making them more susceptible to later pest or disease problems. Fall webworms eat foliage after the plant has stored energy and is preparing for dormancy, so they are usually more unsightly than harmful and can often be left alone.

title: Q&A
content: Monocarpic plants flower once, set seed and die. This can happen within one growing season, as with an annual, or after many years of growth followed by one bloom cycle. Many succulents, including agave species and hybrids, have this trait.

title: Q&A
content: To reduce perennial-garden labor, choose plants that rarely need dividing. Peonies have pink, white, red or purple single or double spring blooms and large fleshy roots that resent disturbance; they grow 2 to 4 feet tall and wide in full sun to part shade, USDA zones 3 to 9. Russian sage has airy lavender-blue flowers from mid- to late summer and deep woody roots that tolerate drought; it grows 2 to 5 feet tall and 2 to 4 feet wide in full sun, zones 5 to 9.

title: Q&A
content: Other perennials that rarely need division include globe thistle, with silvery-blue globe flowers from mid- to late summer and a tough taproot, growing 24 to 48 inches tall and 12 to 30 inches wide in full sun, USDA zones 3 to 8; and Carolina lupine, with long yellow early-summer flower spikes and a deep taproot, growing 3 to 5 feet tall and 2 to 3 feet wide in full sun, zones 4 to 9.

title: Weed Watch
content: Bristly greenbrier is a native deciduous vine with lower stems covered in thorns and upper growth with small bristles. Oval to heart-shaped glossy green leaves are 4 to 5 inches wide with three to seven parallel veins, and dark green tendrils at the leaf base help stems climb. It can grow up to 40 feet tall or ramble over the ground into a dense thicket. Small pale yellow late-spring to early-summer flowers are followed by blue to black berries eaten by wildlife.

title: Weed Watch
content: Bristly greenbrier prefers open woods and thickets in the wild but can ramble into shrub borders or perennial beds. It prefers part shade and moist soil but tolerates bright sun and dry soil. Because it spreads by seed and underground rhizomes, wear thick leather gloves and pull young plants, dig mature plants, or repeatedly cut stems to prevent seed ripening and weaken plants that cannot be dug.

title: A Mighty Fine Addition to the Garden
author: Jennifer Howell
content: 'Mighty Chestnut' daylily is a perennial with ruffled dark orange petals, a burgundy eye and a yellow throat in mid- to late summer. It grows in full sun to part shade and average well-drained soil, has no serious pest problems, reaches 24 to 30 inches tall and 18 to 24 inches wide, and is cold hardy in USDA zones 3 to 9.

title: A Mighty Fine Addition to the Garden
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Deep orange 'Mighty Chestnut' blossoms have a rich burgundy eye, sunshine-yellow throat, light fragrance and ruffled flowers more than 5 inches across. The color contrasts well with dark backgrounds such as a wooden fence, evergreen hedge or ceramic urn. Although it blooms only once each summer, the cultivar has a high bud count for several weeks of successive flowers, and individual blooms can last up to 16 hours. Snap off withered flowers daily and cut spent stalks at the base after all buds have opened.

title: A Mighty Fine Addition to the Garden
author: Jennifer Howell
content: 'Mighty Chestnut' forms robust clumps of strappy foliage in full sun to part shade. Apply granular general-purpose fertilizer in early spring, especially in lean soil. It tolerates dry conditions, but mulch and extra water during hot dry spells help prevent leaves from yellowing and dying back. Foliage dies down in late fall and can be raked away in late winter or early spring. Divide every three to five years in fall or early spring, separating roots into clumps with at least three fans and replanting divisions at the same depth 12 to 15 inches apart.

title: A Mighty Fine Addition to the Garden
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Dark & Handsome companion planting pairs 'Mighty Chestnut' daylily with plants that appreciate extra water during hot dry weather. Simply Scentsational sweetshrub has fragrant burgundy late-spring to summer flowers, grows 6 feet tall and 4 to 5 feet wide in full sun to part shade, USDA zones 4 to 9, and should be pruned after flowering only if shaping is needed. 'Blue Skywalker' spike speedwell has blue flower spikes from midsummer to fall, grows 28 to 30 inches tall and 18 to 20 inches wide, and may rebloom with deadheading. 'Brass Lantern' foamy bells has white bottlebrush flowers above coppery foliage, grows 12 to 18 inches tall and 18 to 24 inches wide, zones 4 to 9.

title: We're Birders Now
author: Jamie Seitz
content: During the quiet of COVID, Jamie and her youngest daughter began a morning habit of sitting in the sun room after breakfast to watch backyard birds. The daily rhythm revealed activity she had not noticed before.

title: We're Birders Now
author: Jamie Seitz
content: The morning pecking order starts with small birds such as chickadees, sparrows, cardinals and dark-eyed juncos. They line up along the fence for a turn at the feeders or bird bath, knock down seed while feeding, and other small birds wait underneath to snatch the fallen seed. Robins and nearby woodpeckers visit occasionally during the small birds' time but usually dine later when it is less crowded.

title: We're Birders Now
author: Jamie Seitz
content: Two blue jays act like yard bosses, driving other birds away while they eat. Crows arrive next, staying mostly on the ground and eating what the smaller birds dropped earlier. Finally the small birds return along with rabbits, squirrels and chipmunks. Dogs and cats watch from the picture window, mesmerized by the animals just outside and eager to chase them away.

title: We're Birders Now
author: Jamie Seitz
content: Birdwatching became a good habit from the last few years. The family now gets excited by unfamiliar visiting birds and notices details such as a robin bathing, puffing and fluffing her feathers while they drink coffee. The sun room may eventually become Birdwatching Central with flight-pattern maps, bird family trees and binoculars.

title: Reader Tips
author: Kayla Ropp, OR
content: To avoid damaging seedling roots, Kayla plants seeds in upside-down drinking cups. Cut the bottoms off the cups, fill them with potting mix and place them upside down in a plastic storage tote. At planting or repotting time, hold the cup over the planting hole and squeeze slightly to release the plant, as long as the leaves and stem still fit through the hole.

title: Reader Tips
author: Donna Van Horn, IA

content: Diane makes plant stakes more visible by reusing crackle-glass globes from worn-out solar lights. She twists off the 3-inch globes and places the small neck of each globe over the top of a garden stake, making discreet stakes less hazardous and adding interest to the garden.

title: Reader Tips
author: Michele Roberge, ME
content: When Michele's overwintered lemon tree is dusty and infected with flat scale insects, she scrubs the tops and undersides of leaves with a damp mesh-covered sponge, rinsing every few leaves. The mesh is abrasive enough to peel off scale and remove dust without harming the leaf.
