title: Native Bees Find Winter Shelter in Surprising Places
author: Nancy Lawson
content: As autumn garden blooms fade, bumblebee stragglers, sweat bees and dwarf carpenter bees disappear, but the bees have not really left. Many North American native bee species build nests on or below the soil surface, where their progeny spend winter before emerging as adults in time for spring bloom. Cavity nesters spend winter in logs, broken wildflower stalks and twigs of shrubs such as elderberry and roses.

title: Native Bees Find Winter Shelter in Surprising Places
author: Nancy Lawson
content: Native bees are not like managed honeybees. Most wild bees are solitary, building nests alone and laying a small number of eggs. They do not have hives to defend and are unlikely to sting. Mother solitary bees usually die after provisioning nests, where larvae develop and overwinter.

title: Native Bees Find Winter Shelter in Surprising Places
author: Nancy Lawson
content: Bumblebee colonies work differently because males, workers and old queens die in fall, leaving newly mated queens to overwinter and start new colonies in spring. Protecting these queens matters because colony survival rests on them, and more than a quarter of North America's bumblebee species face extinction risks tied partly to habitat loss.

title: Native Bees Find Winter Shelter in Surprising Places
author: Nancy Lawson
content: To help native bees, leave insulating leaves under shrubs and trees, line pathways with logs, and trim spent perennial stems to about a foot tall in early spring so cavity-nesting mothers can use them. Let stems stand until the following year so hatching bees can emerge. Avoid tilling and unnecessary digging as weather warms, coexist with vole and small-rodent burrows used by bumblebees, and grow native plants for specialist bees.

title: The Right Light = Happy Houseplants
content: Direct light means spots in south- or west-facing windows without curtains or blinds that get 6 to 8 hours of unobstructed bright sunlight per day. Houseplants suited to direct light include jade plant, string of hearts, bird of paradise and fiddleleaf fig.

title: The Right Light = Happy Houseplants
content: Indirect light includes east-facing windows with bright morning sun and indirect midday light, or south- or west-facing windows filtered by sheer curtains, outdoor trees or tall shrubs. Plants matched to indirect light include heartleaf philodendron, hoya, English ivy and pothos.

title: The Right Light = Happy Houseplants
content: Low light includes north-facing windows, or spots 5 to 8 feet from unobstructed east-facing windows or obstructed south- or west-facing windows. Low-light houseplants include ZZ plant and Chinese evergreen.

title: The Right Light = Happy Houseplants
content: Signs a houseplant gets too much light include leaf burn, brown patches and crispy or droopy leaves. Signs of too little light include leggy new growth, leaning toward a light source and small new leaves.

title: Dreaming of Summer
author: Jennifer Howell
content: When winter drags on and the garden seems awash in dreary browns and grays, it is time to dream of summer color, vibrant foliage, blooming flowers and active pollinators. The article offers three colorful, low-maintenance combinations that also attract wildlife.

title: Dreaming of Summer
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Rooting for Butterflies combines heat-tolerant 'Blue Butterfly' Siberian larkspur, 'Cheyenne Spirit' coneflower, 'Karl Foerster' feather reed grass and 'Blue Boy' bachelor's button. Cut finished larkspur stalks to the ground, deadhead coneflower and bachelor's button to extend bloom, and leave a few seedheads for next year. Dried feather reed grass seedheads provide winter interest and bird cover.

title: Dreaming of Summer
author: Jennifer Howell
content: 'Blue Butterfly' Siberian larkspur has royal blue flower spikes from early to late summer, grows 12 to 15 inches tall and wide in full sun, and is hardy in USDA zones 3 to 7. 'Cheyenne Spirit' coneflower has orange, cream, yellow, red or purple daisylike flowers from summer through fall, grows 22 to 30 inches tall and 12 to 24 inches wide in full sun to part shade, zones 4 to 9. 'Karl Foerster' feather reed grass has wheat-colored summer flowers and fall seedheads, grows 3 to 5 feet tall and 2 to 3 feet wide in full sun, zones 5 to 9. 'Blue Boy' bachelor's button has blue flowers on long stems from early to late summer, grows 24 to 30 inches tall and 9 to 12 inches wide in full sun.

title: Dreaming of Summer
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Welcome for Wildlife uses butterfly weed as an essential host for monarch butterfly larvae, with penstemon and yarrow providing nectar for adult butterflies. Deadhead faded flowers to extend bloom, and leave spent spike blazing star flowers for seeds that goldfinches and other seed-loving birds will eat.

title: Dreaming of Summer
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Welcome for Wildlife plants include butterfly weed with orange flower clusters from early to late summer, full sun, 12 to 36 inches tall, zones 3 to 9; 'Husker Red' penstemon with white flowers blushed pink above burgundy to dark green foliage, 24 to 36 inches tall, zones 3 to 9; 'Firefly Peach Sky' yarrow with peachy-orange clusters aging to yellow, 32 to 36 inches tall, zones 3 to 8; and spike blazing star with purple, pink or white spikes from early to midsummer, 18 to 48 inches tall, zones 3 to 8.

title: Dreaming of Summer
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Simplicity in the Shade is a tightly packed border of shade-loving perennials that leaves little room for weeds. Deer-resistant lady's mantle and coral bells need little care beyond shearing or raking out dead foliage in early spring. Deadheading coral bells, lady's mantle and dalmatian bellflower keeps plants tidy, while shears can keep creeping sedum from spreading over the path.

title: 6 Pro Garden Design Secrets
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Starting a garden can feel overwhelming, and it can be hard to know whether you will like something until after spending time, work and money. Landscape designer Rochelle Greayer shares strategies to help gardeners move more quickly toward enjoying a cohesive garden.

title: 6 Pro Garden Design Secrets
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Work from the center out, not the edges in. Instead of beginning with property-line beds, decide what matters most, such as a vegetable garden or shady getaway, then build traffic patterns, hardscaping and views from that central priority.

title: 6 Pro Garden Design Secrets
content: Garden design feature opener showing a central garden bed, path and pot used to illustrate working from the center outward.

title: 6 Pro Garden Design Secrets
author: Marisa Reyes
content: For privacy, bringing screens and layered plants closer to the area you want to conceal can be more effective than only planting a property-line hedge, wall or fence. A tree placed near a patio corner provides a privacy layer and an overhead canopy that shields views from second-story neighbors.

title: 6 Pro Garden Design Secrets
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Install plants last. Choose the location, put in hardscaping, amend soil and plant trees and shrubs first, then add perennials and annuals. Planting before patios, steps and other structures risks trampling plants and makes soil improvement harder.

title: 6 Pro Garden Design Secrets
content: Photos showing a patio privacy tree, hardscape steps and layered plantings used to demonstrate design sequencing.

title: 6 Pro Garden Design Secrets
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Find a signature plant instead of being discouraged by plants that die or struggle. Choose a plant that speaks to you and that you grow well, then repeat it through the garden. Rochelle repeats ornamental grasses such as fountain grass, sedges and maiden grass because they are easy, and purple fountain grass adds color, texture and movement.

title: 6 Pro Garden Design Secrets
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Add more evergreens, especially in small gardens that need hard-working four-season plants. Clipped boxwoods may recede in summer but take center stage in winter after deciduous plants drop foliage, and dwarf varieties can hide fences, structures or foundation areas.

title: 6 Pro Garden Design Secrets
content: Garden photos showing purple fountain grass, clipped evergreens, arborvitae and boxwood structure.

title: 6 Pro Garden Design Secrets
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Cut spacing recommendations in half for a dense garden that looks full sooner. Closer planting of bulbs, annuals and perennials shades soil, reduces weed germination and minimizes moisture evaporation. Closely planted bulbs such as Siberian squill, daffodils and hyacinths create quick sweeps of color, and annuals such as cosmos can fill in while perennials mature.

title: 6 Pro Garden Design Secrets
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Avoid close spacing for perennials that spread quickly, such as bearded iris or bee balm, because they will need division sooner. title: 2024's Best New Plants
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: The 2024 new-plant standouts include vibrant new color choices, double-flowering varieties of old favorites, interesting foliage variations and compact plant sizes. The feature highlights introductions for sun, shade, fruits, vegetables, perennials, trees and shrubs.

author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Eclipse bigleaf hydrangea (Hydrangea macrophylla) has deep purple, almost black leaves that hold dark color all summer in sun and part shade. Raspberry-pink blooms appear in summer and repeat until frost, fading to green and then brown papery flowerheads for winter interest. This shrub works as a focal point or as a hedge with three-season drama, grows 3 to 5 feet tall and wide in full sun to part shade and well-drained soil, and is hardy in USDA zones 5 to 9.

title: 2024's Best New Plants
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Cappuccino calibrachoa (Calibrachoa hybrid) in the Calitastic series has creamy white and yellow single flowers streaked rusty red from spring to frost. In the test garden, plants stayed covered in bloom all summer, remained compact and did not get very leggy. Grow in full sun to part shade and well-drained soil; plants reach 6 to 12 inches tall and 8 to 12 inches wide and are hardy in USDA zones 9 to 11.

title: 2024's Best New Plants
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Double Vintage Coral calibrachoa (Calibrachoa hybrid) in the Superbells series has double bronze-orange blooms with darker veining from spring to frost. It flowered heavily from spring to fall and handled a hot, dry summer without slowing down. Grow in full sun to part shade and well-drained soil; plants reach 6 to 12 inches tall and 12 to 24 inches wide and are hardy in USDA zones 9 to 11.

title: 2024's Best New Plants
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Blazing Star bidens (Bidens ferulifolia) has larger red-and-yellow striped blooms than many other bidens, giving the bold colors more impact. The mounded plants work well in hanging baskets. Grow in full sun to part shade and well-drained soil; plants reach 12 to 14 inches tall and wide and are hardy in USDA zones 9 to 11.

title: 2024's Best New Plants
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: 'Scentsation White' verbena (Glandularia hybrid) brings fragrance back to verbena. Compact upright plants make useful fillers in containers or patio edging, where the sweet scent is especially noticeable on humid summer evenings. Grow in full sun and well-drained soil; plants reach 9 to 12 inches tall and wide and are hardy in USDA zones 7 to 11.

title: 2024's Best New Plants
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Flamenco Salsa Red vinca (Catharanthus hybrid) is part of the Soiree Flamenco series, known for fringed and ruffled petals. This new selection has deep red ruffled petals edged with white from spring to frost. Grow in full sun and well-drained soil; plants reach 8 to 12 inches tall and 12 to 16 inches wide and are hardy in USDA zones 9 to 11.

title: 2024's Best New Plants
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Moondust coleus (Plectranthus scutellarioides) has rusty red leaves speckled with yellow for all-season color. Plants grow up to 3 feet tall, hold their own in mixed borders and bloom so late that deadheading is rarely needed. Grow in full sun to part shade and well-drained soil; plants reach 14 to 36 inches tall and 12 to 18 inches wide and are hardy in USDA zones 10 to 11.

title: 2024's Best New Plants
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Elderberry Cream nemesia (Nemesia hybrid) has the fragrance of the Escential series with a purple-and-white bicolor bloom and yellow eye from spring to fall. It has good heat tolerance, so bloom is strongest in spring and fall while plants remain colorful in summer. Grow in full sun to part shade and well-drained soil; plants reach 8 to 12 inches tall and wide and are hardy in USDA zones 9 to 10.

title: 2024's Best New Plants
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Hula Red and White Mix begonia (Begonia hybrid) is a new color mix in the Hula series. Plants grow outward more than upward, so fewer are needed to fill a border or container, and they can grow in full sun or full shade. Red and white blooms appear from spring to frost. Grow in well-drained soil; plants reach 6 to 10 inches tall and 20 to 27 inches wide and are hardy in USDA zones 9 to 11.

title: 2024's Best New Plants
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Gourmansun Sunrise and Gourmandia Red beefsteak tomatoes (Lycopersicon hybrids) produced lots of distinctive, sweet, meaty, heart-shaped 10-ounce fruits in the test garden. Both indeterminate varieties take about 85 days to harvest, grow 60 to 72 inches tall and can be used similarly to paste tomatoes. Grow in full sun and well-drained soil.

title: 2024's Best New Plants
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Fruit Snacks apple (Malus hybrid) is a compact columnar apple series for small yards and sunny borders. Tangy Green has pink-to-white spring blooms and tart Granny Smith-like flavor; Tasty Red has pink spring flowers and sweet juicy apples. Other series varieties include All Red, Blushing Delight, Golden Treat and Sweet Tart. Trees grow 10 to 14 feet tall and 3 to 5 feet wide in full sun and well-drained soil, USDA zones 5 to 8.

title: 2024's Best New Plants
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: 'Pastel Duo' baby turnip (Brassica rapa) yields small pink or white turnips with a mild, sweet flavor and radish-like look. Harvest for salads, crisp snacks or sauteed green tops. Sow seeds 1 inch apart in spring or late summer, then thin to 3 inches. Grow in full sun and well-drained soil.

title: 2024's Best New Plants
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: 'Blazing Glory' daylily (Hemerocallis hybrid) has 6-inch golden-yellow summer flowers with a burgundy eye and matching picotee edge, and it reblooms. Plants produced many handsome blooms in the test garden. Grow in full sun and well-drained soil; plants reach 32 inches tall and 18 to 24 inches wide, USDA zones 3 to 9.

title: 2024's Best New Plants
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Frilly Knickers anemone (Anemone hybrid) has double white blooms with lavender backs on dark stems from late summer into fall. Vigorous plants with leathery olive-green foliage make a backdrop for earlier-blooming companions. Grow in full sun to part shade and well-drained soil; plants reach 18 to 24 inches tall and 18 inches wide, USDA zones 5 to 9.

title: 2024's Best New Plants
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: 'Angelic Burgundy' peony (Paeonia hybrid) gives spring borders deep burgundy single to semi-double blooms, among the darkest peony colors. Each sturdy stem holds a single bloom and does not need staking. Grow in full sun and well-drained soil; plants reach 32 inches tall and 44 inches wide, USDA zones 3 to 8.

title: 2024's Best New Plants
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Sugar Shake echibeckia (x Rudbeckia) in the Summerina Glow series produces double blooms in peachy pink to yellow from summer to frost and makes good cut flowers. Plants may return in colder zones but are most reliable in USDA zone 7 and warmer. Grow in full sun and well-drained soil; plants reach 20 to 24 inches tall and 16 to 20 inches wide, USDA zones 7 to 9.

title: 2024's Best New Plants
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: 'Silver Swirl' snowflake dusty miller (Centaurea ragusina) has bright silver leaves with ruffled edges for border edging or container fronts. Grow in full sun and dry, well-drained soil; plants reach 8 to 11 inches tall and 11 to 14 inches wide, USDA zones 6 to 9.

title: 2024's Best New Plants
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Burgundy Stripe gazania (Gazania rigens) in the Sterling Silver series suits hot, dry gardens. Its yellow-and-red striped blooms open from late spring to fall and stay open on cloudy days, unlike more tender types. Grow in full sun and well-drained soil; plants reach 6 inches tall and 24 inches wide, USDA zones 5 to 9.

title: 2024's Best New Plants
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: 'Pink Pearl' agastache (Agastache hybrid) has long spikes packed with pink blooms from spring to frost, attracting pollinators and working well in containers. Grow in full sun and well-drained soil; plants reach 8 to 16 inches tall and 16 inches wide, USDA zones 6 to 10.

title: 2024's Best New Plants
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: 'Strawberries and Cream' moss phlox (Phlox hybrid) is a colorful ground cover covered with mid- to late-spring blooms. Flowers open white with a pink eye and mature to shades of pink, creating a mixed-color effect. Grow in full sun and well-drained soil; plants reach 2 to 4 inches tall and 18 inches wide, USDA zones 5 to 9.

title: 2024's Best New Plants
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: 'Wild Romance' peony tulip (Tulipa hybrid) has lush double white spring blooms edged in striking pink that gradually spreads through the petals for a soft pastel look. Grow in full sun and well-drained soil; bulbs reach 16 inches tall and 5 to 6 inches wide, USDA zones 3 to 9.

title: 2024's Best New Plants
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: 'Little Red Fox' little bluestem (Schizachyrium scoparium) is smaller and less prone to flopping than many little bluestems. Gray-green spring foliage changes to silvery blue with red streaks by mid- to late summer and deepens in fall. Tan summer flowers add texture. Grow in full sun and well-drained soil; plants reach 24 to 30 inches tall and 18 inches wide, USDA zones 3 to 9.

title: 2024's Best New Plants
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Stegosaurus holly fern (Cyrtomium fortunei) has bold, glossy evergreen hollylike fronds for shade gardens, containers and garden beds. Grow in full to part shade and moist, well-drained soil; plants reach 18 to 24 inches tall and 18 inches wide, USDA zones 6 to 9.

title: 2024's Best New Plants
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: 'Table Mountain' hellebore (Helleborus hybrid) has green leaves with gold accents that mature to solid gold with purple petioles. Rosy-purple early-spring flowers fade to dusty rose and last for weeks. Grow in part to full shade and well-drained soil; plants reach 8 to 10 inches tall and 12 to 14 inches wide, USDA zones 6 to 9.

title: 2024's Best New Plants
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: 'Snowtime' bergenia (Bergenia cordifolia) has clear white flowers on 18-inch stems in early spring and again in fall. Glossy cabbagelike leaves contrast with finer-textured border plants. Grow in full sun to part shade and moist, well-drained soil; plants reach 18 inches tall, USDA zones 3 to 8.

title: 2024's Best New Plants
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: 'Goatee' goat's beard (Aruncus hybrid) creates a bright shade-garden spot with abundant creamy white early-summer flowers. Plants can grow in full sun but need more frequent watering there. Grow in full sun to full shade and moist, well-drained soil; plants reach 24 to 26 inches tall and 26 to 28 inches wide, USDA zones 3 to 7.

title: 2024's Best New Plants
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: 'Mr. Mister' hosta (Hosta hybrid) has green leaves with light streaks and speckles, with each leaf showing a slightly different pattern. White tubular flowers rise on scapes up to 48 inches tall in summer. Grow in part shade, protected from afternoon sun for best foliage color, and moist, well-drained soil; plants reach 28 inches tall and 42 inches wide, USDA zones 3 to 9.

title: 2024's Best New Plants
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Itsy Bitsy Peach miniature rose (Rosa hybrid) has peachy-pink blooms from spring to frost on a disease-resistant small shrub. Grow in full sun and well-drained soil; plants reach 18 inches tall and 24 inches wide, USDA zones 5 to 9.

title: 2024's Best New Plants
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: El Nino desert orchid (Chitalpa hybrid) has fragrant orchidlike blooms with a big late-spring flush and sporadic rebloom through summer. It is heat-tolerant, has disease-resistant foliage, develops a mounded habit and needs little pruning. Grow in full sun to part shade and well-drained soil; plants reach 5 to 8 feet tall and 4 to 6 feet wide, USDA zones 6 to 9.

title: 2024's Best New Plants
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Autumn Moonstruck azalea (Rhododendron hybrid) in the Encore series has 2 1/2-inch white flowers in spring and again in summer and fall, plus deep green and chartreuse variegated evergreen foliage for year-round interest. Grow in full sun to part shade and well-drained soil; plants reach 5 feet tall and 4 feet wide, USDA zones 7 to 10.

title: 2024's Best New Plants
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Symphony Pink snowberry (Symphoricarpos doornsbosii) is a tidier, more compact selection of native snowberry with many pink berries for late-summer and fall color. The berries can be used in cut or dried arrangements and also feed birds. Grow in full sun to part shade and moist, well-drained soil; plants reach 3 to 4 feet tall and wide, USDA zones 4 to 8.

title: 2024's Best New Plants
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Hearts A'fire redbud (Cercis canadensis) has dark pink early-spring blooms, but the foliage is the standout. Heart-shaped leaves emerge burgundy, red, tangerine and gold, then mature to red-green by summer. Grow in full sun to part shade and well-drained soil; trees reach 10 to 15 feet tall and wide, USDA zones 5 to 9.

title: Bee Balm
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Bee balm's vibrant blooms and aromatic foliage add color and scent to perennial gardens from early summer to fall. Deer and rabbits usually avoid it, while butterflies, hummingbirds and bees love its flowers. This North American native adapts to various soil and climate conditions.

title: Bee Balm
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Bee balm has unique whorls of shaggy-headed flowers, typically 2 to 3 inches wide, that bloom for up to 6 weeks in red, purple, pink or white. The foliage blends scents of mint and basil.

title: Bee Balm
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Bee balm also offers edible and medicinal uses. Native Americans recognized its antiseptic properties and used it for digestive issues, headaches and infections. Leaves can be used fresh or dried for teas, and flowers have a spicy, minty, oregano-like flavor for salads, garnishes or baked goods.

title: Bee Balm
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Bee balm (Monarda spp. and hybrids) is a perennial with red, purple, pink or white flowers from midsummer to early fall. Grow in full sun to part shade and moist, well-drained soil. Powdery mildew can be a pest issue. Plants range from 8 to 48 inches tall and 8 to 36 inches wide and are hardy in USDA zones 3 to 9.

title: Bee Balm
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Although North America has several native bee balm species, many garden-center varieties are cultivars of common bee balm (Monarda didyma), which has scarlet-red flowers, or hybrids between common bee balm and wild bergamot (M. fistulosa), which has light lavender to pale pink blooms. Breeders have developed red, purple and pink flower colors, varied plant sizes and better powdery mildew resistance.

title: Bee Balm
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Powdery mildew-resistant bee balm choices include 'Leading Lady Plum', 10 to 14 inches tall and 22 to 28 inches wide with early- to midsummer pink-purple flowers, USDA zones 4 to 8; 'Purple Rooster', 30 to 36 inches tall and 26 to 30 inches wide with dark true-purple mid- to late-summer blooms, zones 4 to 9; and 'Petite Delight', 12 to 18 inches tall and 12 to 24 inches wide with lavender-rose mid- to late-summer flowers, zones 4 to 8.

title: Bee Balm
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Additional bee balm choices include 'Red Velvet', 32 inches tall and 36 inches wide with mid- to late-summer blooms and shiny bronze-cast spring foliage, USDA zones 4 to 8; Balmy Pink, 10 to 12 inches tall and 8 to 10 inches wide, one of the earliest bloomers, zones 4 to 9; and spotted bee balm (Monarda punctata), 18 to 24 inches tall and 9 to 12 inches wide with pale yellow flowers marked purple to maroon and white or light purple bracts, zones 3 to 8.

title: Bee Balm
author: Marisa Reyes
content: 'Lilac Lollipop' grows 14 to 24 inches tall and 16 to 32 inches wide with mid- to late-summer flowers and dark green foliage, USDA zones 4 to 8. Grand Parade has lavender-purple flowers from mid- to late summer and shiny dark green leaves, growing 15 to 20 inches tall and 18 to 24 inches wide, zones 3 to 9. 'Peter's Purple' grows 3 to 5 feet tall and 2 to 3 feet wide with lavender-purple mid- to late-summer flowers and more dry-soil tolerance than many cultivars, zones 6 to 9.

title: Bee Balm
content: Bee balm cultivar reference page with spotted bee balm and mildew-resistant varieties such as 'Leading Lady Plum', 'Purple Rooster', 'Red Velvet', Balmy Pink and 'Peter's Purple'.

title: Bee Balm
author: Marisa Reyes
content: For the most flowers and healthiest bee balm plants, grow them in full sun. Plants can grow in part shade but may form fewer flowers; in the Southeast or Southwest, afternoon shade can improve performance.

title: Bee Balm
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Older bee balm varieties such as 'Jacob Cline' or 'Blue Stocking' can spread rapidly, so set crowns as far apart as their expected mature width to avoid overcrowding. Newer hybrid series such as Leading Lady tend to clump rather than spread. Most bee balms need consistently moist soil, but spotted bee balm, wild bergamot and some hybrids such as 'Peter's Purple' need less moisture.

title: Bee Balm
author: Marisa Reyes
content: After bee balm flowers are spent in mid- to late summer, deadhead stems just above a healthy set of leaves. Stems die back in fall; you can cut dead foliage in spring, but if powdery mildew was a summer problem, cut plants back in fall and discard diseased foliage in the trash rather than compost.

title: Bee Balm
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Many bee balms spread by rhizomes and may die out in the center if crowded. Divide in spring or fall every few years to rejuvenate clumps and keep spreaders in check. Dig the patch and break it into chunks with a few healthy stems each, or slice edges off an expanding clump. Fertilize once a year in early spring with general-purpose granular or liquid slow-release fertilizer, compost or manure.

title: Bee Balm
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Powdery mildew may not kill bee balm, but it causes white spots, distorted leaves, premature leaf drop and fewer flowers. Prevent or control it by limiting drought stress, watering at ground level, avoiding overcrowding, dividing clumps when centers die out, and removing infected stems and leaves as soon as symptoms appear.

title: Bee Balm
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Bee balm is easy to design with because of its vibrant flowers and range of sizes. Taller varieties such as 32-inch 'Red Velvet' or 3- to 4-foot 'Jacob Cline' work as backdrops and middle-of-the-bed companions, while dwarf varieties such as 'Leading Lady Plum', 'Petite Delight' and 'Pardon My Purple' can lead the eye along a border front or path.

title: Bee Balm
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Pair bee balm with perennials that contrast in color, shape and texture. Spiky salvia, flat-topped yarrow and round globe thistles create summer combinations beside bee balm's unusual blooms.

title: Bee Balm
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Bee balm is a magnet for bees, butterflies and hummingbirds. Hummingbirds tend to pollinate hybrids with larger flowers, such as 'Gardenview Scarlet' or 'Red Velvet', while bees and other insects favor smaller-flowered species such as wild bergamot or spotted bee balm. Pair bee balms with native plants such as purple coneflower, yarrow, switchgrass and black-eyed Susan.

title: Bee Balm
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Because deer and rabbits usually do not eat bee balm, it is useful in sunny beds with other deer-resistant plants such as lavender or salvia. The right conditions let bee balm keep giving bold blooms, fragrance and pollinator activity.

title: Which Berry Plant is Right for You?
content: Northern highbush blueberry (Vaccinium corymbosum) provides delicious fruit and brilliant fall foliage in red, orange, yellow or purple. It can be grown as an informal hedge, a backdrop for perennials and annuals, in an edible garden, in a mixed border or in a container.

title: Which Berry Plant is Right for You?
content: Highbush blueberry grows best in full sun with well-drained acid soil at pH 4.5 to 5.0 in USDA zones 3 to 8. Apply finely ground elemental sulfur or peat moss in fall to adjust pH if needed, and avoid compost or manure because of their alkalinity. Blueberries produce better yields and larger fruit with another cultivar blooming at the same time. Prune off flower buds for the first two years to encourage foliage and roots, then remove dead or damaged stems in late winter.

title: Which Berry Plant is Right for You?
content: Northern highbush blueberry has clusters of urn-shaped white to pale pink early-spring flowers, dense upright or mounded plants 2 to 12 feet tall and 3 to 10 feet wide, sweet round blue, pink or lavender-purple fruit from mid- to late summer, and 3-inch dark green leaves that turn red, orange, yellow or purple in fall. Compatible varieties include early 'Earliblue', 'Bluetta' and 'Blueray'; midseason 'Blue Jay', 'Northland' and 'Chippewa'; and late 'Aurora', 'Elliot' and 'Jersey'.

title: Which Berry Plant is Right for You?
content: Honeyberry (Lonicera caerulea) is a lesser-known fruit for gardeners in USDA zones 2 to 7 who wish they could grow blueberries but do not have acid soil. Compact plants fit mixed borders, vegetable gardens, containers and patio gardens.

title: Which Berry Plant is Right for You?
content: Honeyberry grows best in full sun and moist, well-drained soil with a pH of 6.5 to 6.8. It needs more than one compatible cultivar for cross-pollination, and netting can keep birds from taking the crop. After harvest in summer, prune old or weak stems to encourage vigorous growth and more fruit the next year. Mulch shallow roots with 1 to 2 inches in spring and 4 inches in winter, and fertilize once in early spring with balanced slow-release fertilizer or organic manure.

title: Which Berry Plant is Right for You?
content: Honeyberry has fragrant tubular white to pale yellow early-spring flowers that can withstand temperatures as low as 20 degrees F and still produce fruit. Teardrop-shaped sweet or tart deep blue fruits ripen from early spring to early summer, oval deep green leaves turn golden brown in fall, and vigorous compact upright plants grow 3 to 5 feet tall and wide. Compatible varieties include early 'Tundra', 'Indigo Gem' and 'Honey Joy'; midseason 'Borealis', 'Honeybee' and 'Aurora'; and late 'Blue Moon', 'Blue Velvet' and Berry Blue.

title: Power in the Garden
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Small lithium-battery garden tools can make tedious hand tasks faster and easier. Battery-powered hand tools can help gardeners with arthritis or limited hand strength and can reduce injury from gripping and repetitive motion.

title: Power in the Garden
author: Jennifer Howell
content: A hand-held trimmer is useful for perennial cleanup, deadheading, pruning shrubs and hedges, trimming grass and shaping topiary. A grass shear blade works for deadheading perennials such as garden phlox or dianthus with an upward clipper motion, and a hedge shear blade cuts both directions for smooth flat or rounded shaping of evergreens and spirea.

title: Power in the Garden
author: Jennifer Howell
content: A bulb auger on a cordless drill can make planting holes in seconds, even in hard ground. It is useful for spring-flowering bulbs, annuals, small perennials and gallon-size shrubs when several holes are augered together. Brace the drill to prevent wrist torque if the auger hits a rock or hard soil, and consider a drill with an auxiliary handle.

title: Power in the Garden
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Battery-powered hand pruners cut branches up to about 1 1/4 inches in diameter and help with repetitive pruning projects such as vineyards or rose gardens. They are especially helpful in tight spots where manual pruner handles cannot open fully or where extra hand strength is needed.

title: Power in the Garden
author: Jennifer Howell
content: A mini chainsaw with a 4-inch blade can cut a 6-inch branch or log and fits into tight spots between branches where a hand saw is hard to maneuver. It is lighter than a regular chainsaw but still needs careful handling, including a free hand on the gripping surface above the trigger handle to prevent kickback.

title: Power in the Garden
author: Jennifer Howell
content: A battery-powered lawn sprayer pressurizes with a button and the compressor restarts automatically when pressure drops, eliminating manual pumping. Clean sprayers thoroughly between uses or keep a separate labeled herbicide sprayer to avoid residue damage. Battery sprayers can apply cleaners, sanitizers, antitranspirants, water-based sealants and pesticides for weeds, insects or fungal diseases.

title: Destination Gardens
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Public gardens generate design inspiration, produce horticultural research and educate visitors about the natural world. The article highlights four North American destination gardens worth visiting for practical ideas and plant inspiration.

title: Destination Gardens
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Idaho Botanical Garden in Boise is useful for water-wise garden ideas. Founded in 1984 on the historic Idaho State Penitentiary site, the 32-acre garden includes an English border, native and drought-tolerant displays, a rose garden, children's garden, vegetable beds, a shady meditation garden with a koi pond and an adjacent Firewise Demonstration Garden.

title: Destination Gardens
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: The Idaho Botanical Garden's Dry Garden showcases drought-tolerant plants for Intermountain West gardeners who want good-looking borders with little water. The Native Plant Garden includes Munro's globemallow, Oregon sunshine, sulphur-flower buckwheat and other regional plants. The garden also works with Boise to increase and reintroduce rare native Boise sand verbena.

title: Destination Gardens
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: The Children's Adventure Garden at Idaho Botanical Garden offers family visits, field trips, a splash fountain, hollow logs, a tree house and a sensory garden. Summer STEAM camps teach soil, plant and insect identification and pollinators.

title: Destination Gardens
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Sarah P. Duke Gardens in Durham, North Carolina is a 52-acre display garden on the Duke University campus. About 5 miles of pathways lead through woods, an Asiatic arboretum with moss garden and Japanese tea house, a rose garden, a white garden and more.

title: Destination Gardens
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: The Terrace Gardens, designed by Ellen Biddle Shipman and opened in 1939, are the oldest and among the most popular areas at Sarah P. Duke Gardens. Locally quarried stone terraced walls hold eye-catching seasonal plantings.

title: Destination Gardens
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: The Charlotte Brody Discovery Garden teaches organic vegetable gardening and shows fruits and vegetables suited to North Carolina. It includes an orchard, bee hives, a chicken coop and the Burpee Learning Center, reconstructed from two historic tobacco barns.

title: Destination Gardens
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: The Piedmont Prairie at Sarah P. Duke Gardens was installed in 2015 to preserve and introduce a native landscape of rolling prairie and open woodland. It displays plants propagated from local seed and peaks from late summer to fall.

title: Destination Gardens
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Plants of the Piedmont Prairie include Appalachian sunflower with golden-yellow late-summer to fall flowers, full sun to part shade, 3 to 4 feet tall, USDA zones 6 to 8; boneset with white late-summer to fall flowers, 1 to 4 feet tall, zones 4 to 8; broomsedge with green leaves turning orange-red then purple by fall, 2 to 4 feet tall, zones 3 to 9; Indian grass with blue-green foliage turning orange-yellow in fall, 5 to 7 feet tall, zones 4 to 9; and smooth coneflower with slender reflexed lavender petals in summer to fall, 36 to 60 inches tall, zones 3 to 8.

title: Destination Gardens
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Longwood Gardens in Kennett Square, Pennsylvania is an 1,100-acre public garden with flower-filled borders, woodland retreats, tree houses, a meadow and illuminated fountain shows. The estate was once the country home of Pierre DuPont and became a foundation-run public garden after his death in 1954.

title: Destination Gardens
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Longwood's Flower Garden Walk, first installed in 1907, is a 600-foot brick walkway with plant combinations that change for maximum color. Spring brings bulbs, summer brings annuals, tropicals and tender perennials, fall swaps in late-season bloomers, and winter offers holiday lights.

title: Destination Gardens
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Longwood's conservatory offers year-round color, including the refurbished Orchid House and East Conservatory plantings in hanging orbs with familiar and exotic tender perennials. In early spring, Peirce's Woods has ground covers and native spring ephemerals such as trillium and rue anemone, plus Carolina allspice and azaleas.

title: Destination Gardens
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Greater Des Moines Botanical Garden began with a geodesic dome and has expanded its outdoor gardens dramatically in the past decade. The 12-acre urban garden includes the Dorothy and Max Rutledge Conifer Garden, Koehn Garden, Lauridsen Savanna and Wells Fargo Rose Garden.

title: Destination Gardens
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: The Dorothy and Max Rutledge Conifer Garden is inspired by Beth Chatto's The Gravel Garden. Plants grow in a 5- to 6-inch gravel layer that discourages weeds and provides sharp drainage. Dry-loving perennials such as moon carrot, Texas plume and sea kale grow with conifers including 'Green Arrow' Alaskan cedar and 'Gold Drift' Norway spruce.

title: Destination Gardens
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: At Greater Des Moines Botanical Garden, roses are grown organically in a mixed perennial border outside the main garden. To protect roses in winter, crowns are covered with compost 4 inches deep and 10 to 12 inches wide. Grafted roses are planted with the graft 4 inches below soil level for better winter survival.

title: Destination Gardens
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Roses that perform well at Greater Des Moines Botanical Garden include Susan Williams-Ellis shrub rose with fragrant small white double blooms from late spring to frost, 54 inches tall and 42 inches wide, USDA zones 4 to 11; 'Pearlie Mae' shrub rose with apricot blooms, 3 to 4 feet tall and wide, zones 4 to 9; Darlow's Enigma hybrid musk with fragrant white clusters and part-shade tolerance, 8 to 12 feet tall and up to 10 feet wide, zones 4 to 9; and 'Emily Carr' shrub rose with 3-inch semi-double red repeat blooms, often 8 feet tall at the garden, zones 3 to 9.

title: Plant a Garden Deer Pass By
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: A tall fence is the surest way to keep deer out, but cost or local rules can make that unrealistic. This border plan uses plants deer usually do not find appealing. Deer prefer broadleaf herbaceous and woody plants, so more ornamental grasses, strong scents, rough textures and bad-tasting plants can reduce damage, though no garden is completely deer-proof.

title: Plant a Garden Deer Pass By
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: The deer-resistant border relies on texture and year-round color. Tall, narrow juniper and big bluestem create vertical accents among mounded shapes. The garden peaks in early summer, while salvia and zinnias bloom until frost, globe thistle dries in place, big bluestem plumes age from purple to tan, juniper supplies winter blue and dogwood adds red winter stems.

title: Plant a Garden Deer Pass By
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Young plants and fresh growth are deer favorites, so protect a new deer-resistant border with temporary fencing or repellents for the first year. Once plants are established, those measures should not be needed.

title: Plant a Garden Deer Pass By
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: This border grows best in full sun and well-drained soil. Add compost yearly or slow-release fertilizer in spring, and use a couple inches of organic mulch to suppress weeds and conserve moisture. In late winter to early spring, cut big bluestem foliage to a few inches, remove dead perennial leaves and prune 'Ivory Halo' dogwood if bright red stems are desired.

title: Plant a Garden Deer Pass By
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: To keep flowers going, deadhead zinnias and salvia by cutting out the center stem to encourage side stems. Shear coreopsis after bloom, remove spent flowers of lady's mantle and coral bells below the foliage, leave globe thistle to dry for fall and winter interest, and either pluck faded sundrops blooms or cut all stems back after bloom. Do not prune dogwood for the first two to three years so it can establish.

title: Plant a Garden Deer Pass By
content: Deer-resistant border care page with plan diagram, dogwood pruning note and salvia care callout.

title: Plant a Garden Deer Pass By
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Plant 3 'Ivory Halo' Tatarian dogwoods with variegated foliage and red winter stems, 4 to 6 feet tall and wide, USDA zones 3 to 7; plant 7 'Blackhawks' big bluestem with purple late-summer plumes and darkening foliage, 5 to 8 feet tall, zones 3 to 9; plant 1 'Moonglow' juniper with silvery blue evergreen foliage, 15 to 20 feet tall and 4 to 8 feet wide, zones 3 to 7; direct sow 'Queen Lime Orange' zinnia and thin to 8 to 12 inches.

title: Plant a Garden Deer Pass By
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Plant 3 'Wendy's Wish' salvia with magenta late-spring-to-frost blooms, 2 to 4 feet tall and wide, USDA zones 9 to 11; plant 12 'Veitch's Blue' globe thistle with deep lavender-blue summer globes, 24 to 36 inches tall, zones 3 to 9; plant 5 'Moonbeam' coreopsis with pale yellow summer blooms, 18 to 24 inches tall and wide, zones 3 to 9; plant 5 lady's mantle with chartreuse late-spring to early-summer blooms, zones 4 to 8; plant 6 Primo 'Black Pearl' coral bells with deep purple foliage, zones 4 to 9; and plant 5 'Sunset Boulevard' sundrops with orange flowers that mature to red by evening, zones 4 to 9.

title: 5 Ways to Stake Tomatoes
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Staking tomatoes keeps fruit off soil, reducing insect and disease damage, makes ripe fruit easier to see and harvest, frees growing space, increases sunlight exposure and air circulation, and helps prevent foliar fungal diseases such as early blight.

title: 5 Ways to Stake Tomatoes
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Match tomato support to plant type. Determinate tomatoes are compact bush plants that stop at a certain height and ripen fruit in one harvest; 3- to 4-foot cages or stakes are usually enough. Indeterminate tomatoes keep growing and ripen fruits over time, so they need sturdy support 5 to 7 feet tall or higher.

title: 5 Ways to Stake Tomatoes
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Pruning side shoots can benefit indeterminate tomatoes but is not usually necessary for determinate types. Pruning encourages bigger fruit, reduces vegetative growth, improves air circulation and makes plants easier to work with. Pinch suckers at the base of the plant or in the leaf axils along the main stem.

title: 5 Ways to Stake Tomatoes
content: Tomato staking opener with photo of tomato vines and diagram showing suckers to pinch in leaf axils.

title: 5 Ways to Stake Tomatoes
author: Jennifer Howell
content: A single stake is the simplest tomato support and works well for determinate tomatoes and containers. Install the stake at planting time, about 4 inches from the tomato base and up to 12 inches deep. Tie the stem every 6 to 12 inches with soft stretchy fabric or nylon stockings. Metal T-posts, plastic-coated metal stakes, bamboo, spiral stakes and wooden posts can all work.

title: 5 Ways to Stake Tomatoes
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Tomato cages work best for determinate tomatoes, while indeterminate tomatoes need tall, sturdy cages. Push cage legs several inches into the ground right after planting and redirect branches into the frame as the plant grows. Strong square cages that fold flat store well. Homemade cages can be made from woven wire fencing formed into a cylinder and anchored with a stake or bottom wire prongs.

title: 5 Ways to Stake Tomatoes
content: Illustrations showing a single tomato stake, tomato cage and tips for tying stems and supporting heavy plants.

title: 5 Ways to Stake Tomatoes
author: Jennifer Howell
content: A vertical tomato trellis saves space and helps tall, vining indeterminate tomatoes. Plant tomatoes a few inches from the trellis, tie the main stem when plants are about 1 foot tall, then add ties every 6 to 12 inches. Trellises can be arbors, fence panels, wooden lattice, netting on posts or A-frame panels with tomatoes growing up each side.

title: 5 Ways to Stake Tomatoes
content: Illustrations showing a tomato trellis, plant clips and a tomato vine trained up a vertical support.

title: 5 Ways to Stake Tomatoes
author: Jennifer Howell
content: A hanging string trellis, often used by commercial greenhouse growers, can be adapted for indeterminate tomatoes in small spaces. Use posts and a horizontal galvanized conduit support, tie twine every 12 to 18 inches, plant tomatoes in line with the strings, anchor each string to the ground with a landscaping pin and wind the string around the main stem about weekly as plants grow.

title: 5 Ways to Stake Tomatoes
author: Jennifer Howell
content: The Florida weave supports rows of determinate or indeterminate tomatoes efficiently. Drive sturdy 8-foot T-posts at row ends and after every third plant, then weave twine between plants and around posts starting 6 inches above the ground. Add another row of twine about every week, 6 inches above the last. Extra angled end posts add anchoring strength for heavy fruiting rows.

title: Q&A
content: River birch suckers at the soil line are a reaction to transplant stress. Remove suckers as they appear: young tender suckers can often be pulled, while older ones should be cut close to the trunk or root with a sharp knife, pruning shears or a small saw. Stubs will regrow. As the tree establishes, suckering should stop. Although river birches bleed sap if pruned in spring, removing suckers promptly will not harm the tree.

title: Q&A
content: Stokes' aster seeds should be gathered as seedheads dry, about 2 to 3 weeks after flowers fade and begin to crack open. Peel off the prickly brown outer bract, dry the heads on paper, separate plump viable seeds from shriveled nonviable seeds and debris, then store dry seed in a small jar in the refrigerator. Four weeks before planting, roll seeds in a moist paper towel, return them to the jar and chill. Start outdoors when soil is at least 60 degrees F, barely covering seeds; they should sprout in 2 or 3 weeks. Many named Stokes' aster varieties are sterile.

title: Q&A
content: Viability is a seed's ability to germinate and grow into a healthy plant. Nonviable seeds may be sterile, lacking the genetic material for germination, or may have been exposed to environmental conditions that prevent germination.

title: Q&A
content: Q&A page with Stokes' aster seedheads, viable versus nonviable seed comparison and river birch sucker advice.

title: Q&A
content: To reduce lily of the valley without lots of digging or chemicals, dig out what you can, loosen soil with a spade or garden fork and tug out runners. Cut a bed edge to slow movement into the lawn. Then starve remaining plants by cutting off growth whenever it appears and mowing shorter than usual in the lawn. Without leaves, plants cannot make food, but the process takes years and may never fully eradicate roots knitted into other perennials and shrubs.

title: Q&A
content: A water-wise curb-strip turf mix can be mostly turf-type tall fescue and perennial rye with some drought-tolerant Kentucky bluegrass or creeping red fescue to knit the turf together. One example mix is 30 to 50 percent fine-bladed tall fescue, 30 to 40 percent perennial ryegrass, 15 to 25 percent Kentucky bluegrass and 5 to 10 percent creeping red fescue.

title: Weed Watch
content: Pineapple weed (Matricaria discoidea) is an annual with a sweet pineapple-like scent when crushed. It forms a low rosette that quickly grows into a bushy plant up to 18 inches tall, with finely divided chamomile-like foliage. Petalless cone-shaped flowers, 1/2 to 1/4 inch tall, appear at branch tips from summer into fall and ripen brown before releasing tiny seeds.

title: Weed Watch
content: Pineapple weed grows across much of North America, especially northern regions, and prefers full sun in dry, poor, gravelly soil. It can appear in lawns, edges and scuffed thin-turf areas but rarely competes in shade or dense plantings. Pull or hoe it from garden beds by its branched taproot. Pre-emergent herbicides work on seedlings, and mowing reduces seed formation in lawns.

title: Garden Essentials
content: A 20-row seed flat helps start many seeds in limited space under lights or on a germination mat. It lets you sow 20 different plants in individual 10-by-1-inch rows and move one row of seedlings without disturbing others.

title: Garden Essentials
content: A mini hand wand seeder helps with tiny seeds that are hard to see, pick up or separate. Squeezing and releasing the bulb creates a vacuum to pick up a seed, and squeezing again drops it. Interchangeable color-coded tips match different seed sizes, and the tool includes a magnifying attachment and small seed jar.

title: Garden Essentials
content: A stainless-steel widger helps transplant tiny seedlings once they have a couple sets of leaves. It scoops up clusters of seedlings and separates them without damaging roots, with a different size on each end.

title: Garden Essentials
content: A 1-pint indoor watering can with a narrow spout delivers a small stream of water that will not smash new transplants. Its detachable rose applies a soft sprinkle over newly sown seeds or germinating sprouts.

ProducePedia offers printable information sheets to send with harvests so recipients know how to use them.

title: An Early Spring Spectacle
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Cowslip (Primula veris) is a perennial with fragrant yellow bell-shaped flower clusters from early to midspring. Grow in part shade and moist, well-drained soil. It has no serious pest issues, reaches 6 to 12 inches tall and 12 to 16 inches wide, and is hardy in USDA zones 3 to 8.

title: An Early Spring Spectacle
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Cowslip's lemon-yellow flowers bloom from April to May and attract bees and butterflies for early spring nectar. It naturally grows in meadows and open woodland and performs best in part shade under taller trees and shrubs, protected from harsh afternoon sun.

title: An Early Spring Spectacle
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Plant cowslip in moist, well-drained soil with the crown slightly above the soil line to avoid rot. A 1- to 2-inch mulch layer keeps soil moist and suppresses weeds. Grow it along a garden path or near a stream in semishaded pockets where flowers can be admired up close.

title: An Early Spring Spectacle
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Cowslip requires little maintenance, but flowers are frost-sensitive, so cover blooming plants if early spring temperatures drop below 32 degrees F. After flowering, cut stalks back to encourage a smaller rebloom. Fertilize in spring with balanced slow-release fertilizer. Cowslip self-seeds, so thin crowded clusters for airflow, especially in shade where powdery mildew is more likely, and divide every 3 to 4 years in spring.

title: An Early Spring Spectacle
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Springtime Magic pairs cowslip with deep purple 'Shanghai' coral bells, old-fashioned bleeding heart and ostrich fern. Coral bells' purple foliage contrasts with cowslip's yellow flowers and bleeding heart's delicate early-spring flowers; later, ostrich fern provides green texture as cowslip and bleeding heart fade.

title: An Early Spring Spectacle
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Springtime Magic plant companions include old-fashioned bleeding heart with pink heart-shaped early- to midspring flowers, full to part shade, 24 to 36 inches tall, USDA zones 3 to 9; 'Shanghai' coral bells with white flowers above silvery purple foliage from late spring to fall, full sun to part shade, 10 to 18 inches tall, zones 4 to 9; and ostrich fern with fiddleheads that unfurl into green fronds, part to full shade, 2 to 3 feet tall, zones 3 to 7.

title: Birds & The Bees (and Bunnies)
author: Jamie Seitz
content: Jamie Seitz's raised beds are not romantic, but neighborhood rabbits use them in spring for bunny rendezvous and nests. The first year, she found baby rabbits by accident while loosening soil and preparing a bed for planting. After the fuzzy layer under dried leaves began to move, she replaced the leaves and left the bed alone for another month.

title: Birds & The Bees (and Bunnies)
author: Jamie Seitz
content: The next year she expected rabbits, noticed the nest, left it alone and planted lettuce elsewhere. That spring, raccoons devastated the neighborhood and killed both the rabbits and baby chickadees in a backyard birdhouse, leaving very few rabbits in the yard for the next two years.

title: Birds & The Bees (and Bunnies)
author: Jamie Seitz
content: A later spring nest seemed empty, but when Jamie pulled away the last of the dried grass, large young rabbits began leaping around the garden bed. Her husband tried to put one back while another escaped and the dogs chased it. Two rabbits ultimately escaped beyond the backyard fence and the rest waited a few more days before leaving. Jamie vowed not to touch a bunny nest until at least June.

title: from the editor
author: Kristin Beane Sullivan
content: As much as I look forward to getting back into my garden every spring, sometimes the to-do list, even if self imposed, can be overwhelming. I used to plant, divide, prune, weed and edge from sunup to sundown. These days I just don't have that kind of time or energy. Can you relate?

title: from the editor
author: Kristin Beane Sullivan
content: Even though I enjoy the activity and how I feel after I do it, sometimes it's hard to make myself start garden cleanup. I worry about getting dirty before heading to another activity or I don't want to drag all the tools out of the garage.

title: from the editor
author: Kristin Beane Sullivan
content: Although I try to keep as much garden debris as possible on site, in spring, the volume is too much to handle. So a few years ago we joined our city's yard waste program. We have a large trash bin dedicated to green waste that's collected and taken to the city compost facility every week.

title: from the editor
author: Kristin Beane Sullivan
content: Now I tell myself I just need to get the bin filled up and to the curb every Sunday night. It gives me a deadline, and also a limit to how much I have to do, although once I'm in the groove, I usually find plenty to keep me working. Spring cleanup goes on for several weeks, but I don't put it off, and I do it in manageable chunks.

title: from the editor
author: Kristin Beane Sullivan
content: Here's my permission for you to be gentle on yourself as you dig into your spring garden. It doesn't all have to happen at once.

title: Reader Tips
author: Kathleen Durkee, MA
content: To remedy the splaying stems of a geranium plant, Kathleen popped some dried agapanthus, Agapanthus africanus, flower stems into her containers for support. The small prongs of the seedheads prop up floppy flowers for a tidier container.

title: Reader Tips
author: Sheryl Fullner, WA
content: Arthritis makes gardening in low beds or at ground level difficult for Sheryl. When she saw used industrial liquid containers, called IBC tanks, for sale on Craigslist, she cut one container in half to make two raised beds. A reciprocating saw or circular saw works well for cutting the metal bars and plastic container, but even most handsaws can do the trick.

title: Reader Tips
author: Sheryl Fullner, WA
content: Most IBC tanks are about 48 by 40 by 40 inches. Cut in half, they're about 20 inches high. Some already have a large drainage hole in the bottom, but it is likely that you will have to drill five or six holes across the base. Used IBC tanks may have some remaining residue, so scrub them with soapy water, put the containers in place, fill them with potting mix and plant away.

title: Reader Tips
author: Sheryl Fullner, WA
content: You should be able to find IBC tanks online on secondhand sites, such as Craigslist or Facebook. Search for 'IBC tank' or 'IBC tote.' Most are sold in the $50 to $100 range, a fine deal for a tall, accessible garden bed.

title: Reader Tips
author: Sylvia Street, IA
content: Birds can leave a big mess under feeders hung on shepherd's hooks. Sylvia tucked a small plastic kiddie pool underneath to catch fallen hulls and excess seeds and prevent unwanted plants from sprouting in the garden. When the pool starts to fill up, she dumps the contents into the compost pile and camouflages the pool with taller perennials planted along the front of the bed.

title: Reader Tips
content: Native photos showing a geranium supported by dried agapanthus seedheads and an accessible raised bed made from an IBC tank set on plastic pallets.

title: Reader Tips
author: Joan Pierro, MA
content: A bunny's munching habits can ruin a garden in no time. Joan protects emerging lilies by cutting the bottom out of a paper grocery bag, fitting it over the plant and driving four plant stakes into the corners inside the bag to keep it in place. Mound an inch or two of soil around the bag edges for extra security.

title: Reader Tips
author: Joan Pierro, MA
content: Leave the paper bag in place for about a week, or until the lily has grown enough that the leaves and stems are no longer tender and new. This might mean the plant has grown several inches or a significant number of leaves have unfurled and matured.

title: Reader Tips
author: Jennifer Butler, NC
content: Jennifer transformed an old metal wine rack into a planter by sliding a coco liner between the sides and securing it with zip ties. She filled the liner with potting mix and plants it with either a vining annual such as mandevilla or foliage-focused plants. Four lengths of chain can turn the wine rack into a hanging basket.

title: Wild Side
content: White M hairstreak, Parrhasius m-album, may flash iridescent blue wings in flight, but usually shows the gray blue underside marked by a skinny M-shaped band and a bright orange-red spot near the tail. These markings create a false face that confuses predators. It is most common in the southern United States but also occurs north to Michigan and into the Southeast.

title: Wild Side
content: White M hairstreak caterpillars are green with long stripes and fine brown hairs. They hatch from round, bumpy white eggs in spring, feed on oak leaves, turn deep red before pupating and form stout, dark brown chrysalises.

title: Wild Side
content: In gardens, the white M hairstreak often flies high in oak canopies and feeds on flowering trees and shrubs such as viburnum. It sometimes flies closer to the ground and feeds on goldenrod and milkweed. If you see one outside its usual range, photograph it and report the sighting to your local extension office.

title: Fast Garden Facts
content: For a skinny deck space with too many exits, create a destination getaway outside the traffic flow created by several exits. Leave at least 4 feet of clearance for a comfortable walkway.

title: Fast Garden Facts
content: For a square deck space, create one large lounging area with a wide path through the middle when exits split up the space. Keep chairs and the love seat within 10 feet of each other for easy conversation, and choose end tables and an ottoman that offer storage.

title: Fast Garden Facts
content: For a small deck with many needs, choose double-duty seating and a table that is easy to move around. A 35-inch-diameter coffee table can double as a dining table, and the fourth dining chair can be used in the lounge area until it is needed at the table.

title: Fast Garden Facts
content: Leave 30 to 36 inches between a table's edge and the wall or deck railing so chairs can scoot out comfortably and people can walk behind seated guests.

title: Fast Garden Facts

title: Welcome Spring With Cool-Weather Containers
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Winter is fading away and spring annual and perennial flowers are starting to pop up in garden centers in full bloom. Even if the ground is still frozen in your beds and borders, you can start planting containers to scratch that gardening itch you have had all winter. Cool temperatures and spring rains mean you should not have to water much.

title: Welcome Spring With Cool-Weather Containers
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Once cool-weather container plants are done blooming, the rest of the garden will be in full swing and you can transplant any perennials into your borders to grow and flower next year.

title: Welcome Spring With Cool-Weather Containers
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Many early spring bloomers are petite plants, but they can make a big statement when grouped together in a wide, shallow planter. These plants love full sun when the weather is cool. Keep the soil evenly moist and they will be happy.

title: Welcome Spring With Cool-Weather Containers
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Purchase bog rosemary when its pale pink flower buds are just popping for the longest show. Its blue-green foliage creates repetition with the ornamental kale even when out of bloom. Deadhead primrose and lewisia to keep them flowering into summer.

title: Welcome Spring With Cool-Weather Containers
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Sink the daffodils, pot and all, into the potting mix in the container, so when blooms are done and foliage turns yellow, it is easy to pull them out without disturbing the rest of the arrangement. Replant the bulbs in your garden or toss them in the compost pile. Pansies and nemesia will eventually succumb to summer heat, so swap them for annuals as temperatures rise in early to midsummer.

title: Welcome Spring With Cool-Weather Containers
author: Jennifer Howell
content: The Small but Mighty container uses Nemesia Nesia Sunshine, Nemesia Nesia Denim, daffodil, bog rosemary 'Blue Ice', pansy, lewisia Elise Ruby Red, ornamental kale 'Pigeon Red' and primrose Danessa Pink with Rose Eye. The container is 20 inches in diameter.

title: Welcome Spring With Cool-Weather Containers
author: Jennifer Howell
content: If a hard freeze is predicted, move pots full of early bloomers to a protected spot in a shed or garage to prevent damage to flowers and foliage.

title: Welcome Spring With Cool-Weather Containers
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Native full-page photo of a cool-weather spring container planted with ornamental kale, pansies, nemesia, primrose, daffodils, bog rosemary and lewisia.

title: Welcome Spring With Cool-Weather Containers
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Though traditionally a winter-blooming indoor plant, the cyclamen you find in a florist shop also makes a nice outdoor container plant in early spring. It prefers dappled shade and cool temperatures, but move it inside if a frost is expected.

title: Welcome Spring With Cool-Weather Containers
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Plant cyclamen in a well-draining potting mix and let it dry on the surface before you water to prevent tubers from rotting. When petals fall, twist and tug the flower stem at the base to deadhead and encourage more blooms. In summer, warm temperatures cause flowering to slow or stop, so leave plants in the container for the foliage or pot them up as houseplants.

title: Welcome Spring With Cool-Weather Containers
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Lobelia makes a great cool-weather shade companion, with tiny blue flowers cascading over the lip of the pot. Spiky 'Blue Dart' rush adds height in the back of the container. It tolerates light shade in early spring but prefers more sun, so move it to another planter for summer.

title: Welcome Spring With Cool-Weather Containers
author: Jennifer Howell
content: The Calming Colors container uses 'Blue Dart' rush, cyclamen and Magadi Dark Blue lobelia. The container is 18 inches in diameter. Cyclamen grows from a corm-shaped tuber that should be planted right at the soil surface, not covered with soil, potting mix or mulch.

title: Welcome Spring With Cool-Weather Containers
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Photo of a cool-weather shade container with cyclamen, blue lobelia and upright 'Blue Dart' rush in a blue pot.

title: Welcome Spring With Cool-Weather Containers
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Deep pink Persian buttercup is the star in this cobalt-blue ceramic pot, sending papery roselike flowers up for weeks as long as you keep deadheading. Buy Persian buttercups in bloom or as tubers you can grow yourself. Start tubers indoors in winter, 12 to 16 weeks before setting them outside when temperatures are between 50 and 60 degrees F during the day.

title: Welcome Spring With Cool-Weather Containers
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Let this planting dry between waterings to prevent the Persian buttercup and dianthus crowns from getting too wet and rotting. As daily temperatures rise, Persian buttercup foliage will get leggy, turn yellow and die as the plant goes dormant. Pull the plant out, pluck off dead foliage, brush soil from the tuber and store it in a paper bag in a cool, dark, dry location until next winter.

title: Welcome Spring With Cool-Weather Containers
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Replace the cool-weather-loving dianthus and pansies with summer annuals, but leave the skirt of sweet alyssum. It will bloom lightly all summer, then flower more robustly when cool weather returns again in fall.

title: Welcome Spring With Cool-Weather Containers
author: Jennifer Howell
content: The Cool in Cobalt container uses Persian buttercup, dianthus, pansy and sweet alyssum. The container is 9 inches square. Persian buttercups, pansies and dianthus are tasty treats for deer, so apply a repellent spray every few days.

title: Welcome Spring With Cool-Weather Containers
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Photo of a cobalt-blue square container planted with pink Persian buttercup, dianthus, pansies and sweet alyssum.

title: These 8 Shrubs Create a Show in Every Season
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Flowers are usually the first thing someone notices about a plant. But once those flowers fade, some of the best plants to invest in are multiseason shrubs. They provide structure for borders filled with annuals and perennials and grow happily in the garden for years.

title: These 8 Shrubs Create a Show in Every Season
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Foliage is one way shrubs provide nonstop border color. Some have variegated leaves or foliage that changes color seasonally. Flowering shrubs often produce berries or seedheads that are interesting to gardeners and provide food for birds. Others, such as oakleaf hydrangea, have flowers that dry in place and peeling bark that brings interest to late-season gardens.

title: These 8 Shrubs Create a Show in Every Season
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Gatsby Gal oakleaf hydrangea, Hydrangea quercifolia, is native to the southeastern United States and can handle heat and humidity, but needs shelter from cold winter winds in USDA zone 5 and colder. Gatsby Gal grows 5 to 6 feet tall, with white early summer flowers that age to pink, fade to tan in autumn and hold through winter.

title: These 8 Shrubs Create a Show in Every Season
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Gatsby Gal oakleaf hydrangea has green leaves in spring and summer that age to wine-red in fall. After the leaves drop, peeling bark takes center stage. Multiseason appeal includes pyramidal white flowers aging to pale pink and brown, mahogany-red fall foliage and cinnamon-colored exfoliating bark. It grows in full sun to part shade in moist, well-drained soil, 5 to 6 feet tall and wide, in USDA zones 5 to 9.

title: These 8 Shrubs Create a Show in Every Season
author: Sherri Ribbey

title: These 8 Shrubs Create a Show in Every Season
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Oakleaf hydrangea does not usually need any pruning to look great. Just remove dead stems in early spring.
