title: These 8 Shrubs Create a Show in Every Season
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Black Lace elderberry, Sambucus nigra f. porphyrophylla, has finely cut inky foliage that looks like Japanese maple, but the plant tolerates cold and full sun better. Large pink flower clusters can grow 6 inches or more in diameter and have a light lemony scent. Bees and butterflies visit the blooms, and birds eat the small purple-black late-summer berries.

title: These 8 Shrubs Create a Show in Every Season
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Black Lace elderberry has the best foliage color in full sun, where the purple-black hue holds from spring to frost. It makes a focal point in mixed borders or can screen a view from the patio. New growth is green but darkens with age, though extra-hot temperatures can cause mature foliage to green up a bit.

title: These 8 Shrubs Create a Show in Every Season
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Pruning Black Lace elderberry is easy but not needed often. Remove dead stems in early spring or shape plants after flowers fade. You can cut up to a third of the biggest stems to the ground in early spring to encourage vigorous new stems.

title: These 8 Shrubs Create a Show in Every Season
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Black Lace elderberry's multiseason appeal includes dome-shaped pink early summer flowers, small late summer purple-black berries and new green foliage that matures to purple-black. It grows in full sun in moist, well-drained soil, 6 to 8 feet tall and wide, in USDA zones 5 to 7. For more berries, plant another cultivar nearby, such as Black Beauty, Instant Karma or Laced Up.

title: These 8 Shrubs Create a Show in Every Season
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Native images of Black Lace elderberry showing pink flower clusters, late-summer berries and dark finely cut foliage.

title: These 8 Shrubs Create a Show in Every Season
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Cranberry cotoneaster, Cotoneaster apiculatus, has stiff arching stems and a low spreading habit that works near the front of the border. It is a tough, salt-tolerant shrub for a parking strip or driveway, and it is deer and rabbit resistant.

title: These 8 Shrubs Create a Show in Every Season
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Small pink cranberry cotoneaster flowers open in late spring among glossy dark green leaves. Bright red berries follow in late summer and feed birds, not people. In fall, foliage turns bright red before falling, and in winter the arching stems and remaining berries provide interest and structure.

title: These 8 Shrubs Create a Show in Every Season
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Cranberry cotoneaster plants are slow growing but form a dense habit and root where stems touch the ground, so they can be used for erosion control or as a ground cover. The plant may struggle in hot, humid regions and parts of USDA zone 7 and warmer. The species grows about 3 feet tall and 3 to 6 feet wide; the hybrid 'Tom Thumb' is smaller.

title: These 8 Shrubs Create a Show in Every Season
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Native images of cranberry cotoneaster showing spring flowers, late-summer red berries, red fall color and the low arching shrub habit.

title: These 8 Shrubs Create a Show in Every Season
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: 'Arnold Promise' witch hazel, Hamamelis x intermedia, blooms in late winter with clusters of large, ribbonlike yellow flowers that are longer lasting than many other witch hazels. The blooms appear before foliage and have a light, sweet fragrance.

title: These 8 Shrubs Create a Show in Every Season
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: 'Arnold Promise' witch hazel has green summer leaves that change to red, yellow and orange in autumn. Once leaves fall, its vase-shaped habit provides winter structure. Grow it near a deck or along a path so the small flowers and fragrance can be enjoyed up close.

title: These 8 Shrubs Create a Show in Every Season
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Some witch hazels are grafted, but 'Arnold Promise' grows on its own roots. If suckers sprout from the base, their flower and leaf colors will match the rest of the plant. Let suckers grow for a denser habit or remove them at the base for a more treelike form. It grows in full sun to part shade in moist, acid, well-drained soil, 12 to 15 feet tall and wide, in USDA zones 5 to 8.

title: These 8 Shrubs Create a Show in Every Season
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Native photos of 'Arnold Promise' witch hazel showing yellow late-winter flowers and orange-red fall foliage.

title: These 8 Shrubs Create a Show in Every Season
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Variegated Japanese pieris, Pieris japonica 'Variegata', has cascading white urn-shaped spring flowers that last for several weeks and showy evergreen foliage. Green leaves are edged with creamy white tinted pink when new growth emerges. Beadlike muted red flower buds form in late summer and wait until the following spring to open, and they are a mason bee favorite.

title: These 8 Shrubs Create a Show in Every Season
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Variegated Japanese pieris is a slow-growing shrub with an upright spreading habit for the middle to back of the border or a hedge. It does best in organically rich, slightly acid soil and grows in full sun or part shade, 5 to 8 feet tall and wide, in USDA zones 6 to 9. Pruning is not usually needed, and removing spent blooms simply tidies the look.

title: These 8 Shrubs Create a Show in Every Season
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Native images of variegated Japanese pieris showing red late-summer flower buds, cascading white spring flowers and pink-tinted new growth.

title: These 8 Shrubs Create a Show in Every Season
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: 'Kaleidoscope' glossy abelia, Abelia x grandiflora, has ever-changing foliage. Pink buds open to fragrant white flowers in late spring with light repeats into fall. At peak bloom, red stems are lined with lime-green foliage edged in bright yellow. By summer, the yellow becomes more golden, and in fall it develops a red flush that hangs on through winter in most areas.

title: These 8 Shrubs Create a Show in Every Season
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Full sun gives 'Kaleidoscope' glossy abelia the most colorful foliage without burning. This dwarf shrub has a mounding habit that works near the front of a border and pairs well with a deep green conifer. It is evergreen in USDA zone 7 and warmer, grows 2 to 3 feet tall and 3 to 4 feet wide, and is cold hardy in USDA zones 6 to 9. In zone 6, plant it out of cold winter winds.

title: These 8 Shrubs Create a Show in Every Season
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Native images of 'Kaleidoscope' glossy abelia showing variegated yellow-green foliage, red stems and white flowers.

title: These 8 Shrubs Create a Show in Every Season
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Amber Jubilee ninebark, Physocarpus opulifolius, is a tough native shrub with good resistance to powdery mildew. Pink buds open to white flowers in spring and attract bees, moths and other pollinators. New growth is orange, red and gold with green veins, maturing to solid green in summer.

title: These 8 Shrubs Create a Show in Every Season
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: In autumn, Amber Jubilee ninebark leaves turn shades of red and purple, and once they fall, the exfoliating bark of mature stems adds winter interest. Grow it in mixed borders with spring bulbs, annuals and ornamental grasses for a colorful show.

title: These 8 Shrubs Create a Show in Every Season
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Amber Jubilee ninebark has an upright habit and is not as likely to sucker as the species. Thin established plants every few years by cutting a third of the oldest stems to the ground to maintain a full habit, colorful new growth and flowers. It grows in full sun in average, well-drained soil, 5 to 7 feet tall and 4 to 6 feet wide, in USDA zones 2 to 7.

title: These 8 Shrubs Create a Show in Every Season
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Native images of Amber Jubilee ninebark showing fall foliage, spring flower buds, colorful new growth and white spring flowers.

title: These 8 Shrubs Create a Show in Every Season
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Koreanspice viburnum, Viburnum carlesii, is worth growing for its clove fragrance. Deep pink buds open to white 3-inch clusters in early spring as leaves emerge, adding height to spring borders. Later, small egg-shaped purple-black berries develop and feed birds. Serrated leaves are dark gray-green through summer and change to dull red, copper or wine-red in fall.

title: These 8 Shrubs Create a Show in Every Season
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Koreanspice viburnum flowers on old wood, so prune for shape soon after flowers fade in late spring. To prevent or minimize powdery mildew, space plants a little farther than mature width to allow air circulation, water at ground level and rake up fallen leaves in autumn so spores do not overwinter.

title: These 8 Shrubs Create a Show in Every Season
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Koreanspice viburnum tolerates juglone from walnut trees. Its multiseason appeal includes pink spring buds, fragrant white blooms, purple-black berries and red-orange fall leaves. It grows in full sun to part shade in moist, well-drained soil, 4 to 6 feet tall and wide, in USDA zones 4 to 8.

title: These 8 Shrubs Create a Show in Every Season
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Native images of Koreanspice viburnum showing spring buds, fragrant spring flowers and the shrub habit.

title: Speedwell
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: It is easy to give ho-hum plantings an exciting new look when you add speedwell to the mix. Long spikes of purple, lavender, blue, pink or white last for several weeks starting in late spring or early summer.

title: Speedwell
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Bees and butterflies are frequent visitors to the dozens of tiny individual flowers on each speedwell stem. Groups of five or more speedwell make it easier for pollinators to spot and provide a splashy focal point for borders.

title: Speedwell
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: 'Red Fox' speedwell is an old favorite known for 15-inch-long deep pink to rosy-red spikes and compact size. There are many more speedwells worth growing, with different colors, sizes and habits available at garden centers.

title: Speedwell
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Speedwell, Veronica species and hybrids, is a perennial with spike-shaped flowers in purple, lavender, blue, pink or white from late spring to early fall. It grows in full sun to part shade in well-drained soil, has no serious pest problems, reaches 6 to 48 inches tall and 6 to 24 inches wide, and is cold hardy in USDA zones 3 to 8.

title: Speedwell
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Botanical illustration of speedwell with upright flower spikes, narrow leaves and the plant profile for Veronica species and hybrids.

title: Speedwell
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Full-page native garden photo of rose-pink 'Red Fox' speedwell combined with cool lavender Russian sage flowers for pollinators.

title: Speedwell
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: There are 250 species of speedwell, ranging from low-growing ground covers to upright border plants. Many have long bloom spikes packed with tiny funnel-shaped flowers, while a few are saucer-shaped. Flower colors include white, bright pink, deep purple and shades of blue. Speedwell is quite cold hardy and is not usually bothered by pests or disease.

title: Speedwell
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Most speedwells sold in garden centers are hybrids or cultivars, but long leaf speedwell, Veronica longifolia, is useful when you want added border height. It grows up to 4 feet tall and has extra-long flower spikes.

title: Speedwell
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: 'Blue Skywalker' speedwell, Veronica hybrid, grows 28 to 30 inches tall and adds midborder color. Long blue-purple flowers arrive in mid- to late summer on plants cold hardy in USDA zones 4 to 8.

title: Speedwell
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: 'Pink Marshmallow' spike speedwell, Veronica spicata, has plump pink spires in early to late summer. Plants grow 12 to 18 inches tall and 18 to 24 inches wide and are cold hardy in USDA zones 4 to 8.

title: Speedwell
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: 'White Wands' speedwell, Veronica hybrid, is part of the Magic Show series. It blooms mid- to late summer, is one of the longest blooming varieties and is an excellent rebloomer. Plants grow 14 to 16 inches tall and 16 to 20 inches wide in USDA zones 4 to 8.

title: Speedwell
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: 'Fairytale' speedwell, Veronica hybrid, is a long leaf speedwell hybrid with 16-inch pale pink blooms in midsummer. The plants are compact, growing 12 to 16 inches tall and 14 to 16 inches wide, and are cold hardy in USDA zones 3 to 8.

title: Speedwell
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: 'Perfectly Picasso' speedwell, Veronica hybrid, has white buds that open to intense pink flowers in mid- to late summer for a bicolor look. Plants grow 22 to 26 inches tall and 22 to 24 inches wide in USDA zones 4 to 8.

title: Speedwell
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Moody Blues Sky Blue speedwell, Veronica hybrid, has pale blue-purple blooms from late spring until frost if deadheaded regularly. Plants grow 12 to 14 inches tall and wide, are very heat and drought tolerant, and are cold hardy in USDA zones 4 to 9.

title: Speedwell
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: 'Pallida' gentian speedwell, Veronica gentianoides, forms a 12-inch-tall rosette of foliage with stems rising to 18 inches in late spring to early summer. White saucer-shaped blooms have blue-purple streaks in the center. Plants are cold hardy in USDA zones 4 to 7.

title: Speedwell
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: 'Crater Lake Blue' Hungarian speedwell, Veronica austriaca subsp. teucrium, has gentian-blue saucer-shaped blooms in spring. Deadheading encourages a light rebloom. It grows 12 to 18 inches tall and 9 to 12 inches wide in USDA zones 4 to 8.

title: Speedwell
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Native photo collage of speedwell cultivars showing flower spikes and colors including blue, white, pink, lavender, purple and yellow garden companions.

title: Speedwell
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Garden design photo with 'Purpleicious' speedwell, yarrow, globe thistle, Shasta daisy and blue fescue, showing a deer- and rabbit-resistant planting combination.

title: Speedwell
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Speedwell makes every border better, with distinctive blooms and a range of sizes for sunny spots. Low-growing speedwells such as 'Crater Lake Blue' or 'Giles van Hees' reach 6 to 15 inches tall near the front of a border. 'Lavender Lightsaber' and 'High Five' work in the middle at 2 to 2.5 feet tall, while long leaf speedwell can reach 4 feet at the back of the border.

title: Speedwell
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Flower shape is one of speedwell's strengths. From long slender wands to plump darts, it adds excitement and interest. 'Purpleicious' contrasts with Shasta daisy, globe thistle and yarrow blooms, and its upright habit varies the mounded foliage at the front of the border.

title: Speedwell
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Use attention-getting speedwell blooms to point toward an ornament or draw visitors along a path. Because speedwell is naturally compact and slender, groups of three to five plants usually have more impact than single specimens.

title: Speedwell
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Speedwell's color range sets the mood for garden rooms and borders. Although the flower spikes create visual energy, cool blues, purples and pinks give a laid-back feeling to a seating area. White-flowered speedwells near a patio glow in evening light.

title: Speedwell
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: 'Blue Sprite' speedwell works well in containers. Position it near the front of the pot and its 18-inch-wide spreading habit will grow over the edge like a spiller. When it stops blooming in mid- or late summer, remove the plant from the container or cut off spent blooms and leave foliage in place.

title: Speedwell
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Container photo of 'Blue Sprite' speedwell with snapdragon, ragged robin, penstemon and dianthus, showing speedwell used as a spiller.

title: Speedwell
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Plant speedwell in full sun and well-drained soil and it will grow with little care. It is not susceptible to many pests or diseases, deer and rabbits usually pass it by, and flowers look good for weeks without fertilizer, though top-dressing with compost in fall never hurts.

title: Speedwell
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Speedwell is not super drought tolerant, but it is fine if plants dry out a bit between waterings. During extra-dry summers, water occasionally to avoid crispy-looking foliage and wilted flowers. Gentian speedwell is the exception; it needs consistent moisture in a spot that is easy to water or a low area that stays moist but not boggy.

title: Speedwell
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Technique photo showing where to cut faded speedwell flowers back to a leaf joint for deadheading.

title: Speedwell
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Most speedwell plants are sold at garden centers, but budget-conscious gardeners can start them from seed. Sow tiny seeds indoors 6 to 8 weeks before the last frost. They need light to germinate, so press them into the seed-starting mix surface. At 65 to 70 degrees F, growth should appear in 12 to 14 days.

title: Speedwell
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: When young speedwell seedlings have three to four sets of true leaves, they are ready to go outdoors.

title: Speedwell
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Hungarian and gentian speedwell bloom once, while spike and long leaf speedwells and their hybrids have side stems that keep blooming after the first flush fades. Individual flowers open from the bottom of the spike upward. Deadhead the central flower when it is partially spent and side stems are nearly open to tidy the plant and encourage more flowers.

title: Speedwell
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Older speedwells such as 'Sunny Border Blue' typically put on a big first show with a light rebloom. Newer varieties often have a larger rebloom, while varieties such as 'White Wands' and 'Ever After' hold their initial flush of blooms all summer and seem constantly in flower.

title: Speedwell
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Speedwells tend to drop lower leaves in summer, especially when it has been hot and dry. If that happens, cutting the plant to the ground may improve its appearance. In a week or so new growth will take off, and you might get a later summer rebloom.

title: Speedwell
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Taller speedwell varieties may need staking if stems start to lean. Coated wire hoop stakes work well, and it is easier to place the stake early before new growth takes off than to wrestle floppy stems into a hoop later.

title: Speedwell
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: The easiest way to get more speedwell is by division, which also revitalizes spindly plants that are not flowering well. In spring or fall, dig the whole plant and split it into pieces with several stems each. If the plant does not need full division, slice a chunk from the main plant, replant divisions at the same level and water well.

author: Sherri Ribbey

title: Which Cottage Garden Spike is Right for You?
content: Delphinium, Delphinium elatum, offers bright blue, purple, pink, red or white late-spring flower spikes with attractive centers called bees. The flowers bring butterflies and hummingbirds, and the plants are not usually attractive to deer or rabbits.

title: Which Cottage Garden Spike is Right for You?
content: Plant delphinium in the back of beds and borders, where its bold spikes can make a statement. It is also a long-lasting cut flower; snip the long stems when at least one bud has opened at the bottom.

title: Which Cottage Garden Spike is Right for You?
content: Delphinium grows best in full sun in fertile, moist, well-drained soil in USDA zones 3 to 8. Hollow stems can topple in wind, so stake plants early with bamboo canes and continue to add ties as plants grow. Fertilize in spring when plants emerge and again when they are blooming. Deadhead for a second flush of smaller blooms in late summer or fall, and divide plants in spring every 3 to 4 years to rejuvenate them.

title: Which Cottage Garden Spike is Right for You?
content: Delphinium forms an 18- to 36-inch-wide basal clump with 36- to 72-inch-tall flowering spikes. Each main stem forms additional branches with smaller spikes. Deeply lobed palmate dark green leaves alternate on the stem.

title: Which Cottage Garden Spike is Right for You?
content: Aurora Blue delphinium has blue semidouble florets with white bees from early to midsummer on 3- to 4-foot-tall and 2- to 3-foot-wide plants. It is useful as a cut flower because of its uniform blooms, small leaves and sturdy stems.

title: Which Cottage Garden Spike is Right for You?
content: 'Pink Punch' delphinium is especially tolerant to heat and humidity and has some of the deepest pink flowers of any delphinium. The white, brown or pink striped bee appears on blooms from early summer to early fall on compact 3- to 5-foot-tall plants.

title: Which Cottage Garden Spike is Right for You?
content: 'Black Eyed Angels' delphinium has white flowers with black bees from early summer to early fall on compact 3- to 6-foot-tall plants. Plants are more tolerant of heat and humidity than many other varieties.

title: Which Cottage Garden Spike is Right for You?
content: Illustrated comparison page showing delphinium flower spikes, plant habit, leaf shape and cultivar photos for Aurora Blue, 'Pink Punch' and 'Black Eyed Angels'.

title: Which Cottage Garden Spike is Right for You?
content: Giant larkspur, Consolida ajacis, is a colorful annual loved by pollinators, deer resistant and likely to self-sow into sweeps of color. Its spiky blue, pink or white flowers tolerate hot summers better than delphinium.

title: Which Cottage Garden Spike is Right for You?
content: Giant larkspur grows 24 to 48 inches tall and adds vertical interest to the midsummer garden. Grow it in groups as a backdrop for lower-growing plants or use it to fill empty pockets in mixed borders where blooms can be enjoyed from spring to frost. Flowers last well cut for fresh and dried arrangements.

title: Which Cottage Garden Spike is Right for You?
content: Giant larkspur prefers full sun and consistently moist, well-drained soil. Direct sow seeds in late fall or early summer, start them indoors 8 to 10 weeks before the last expected frost date or buy seedlings. Fertilize in early spring every 2 to 3 weeks with slow-release granular fertilizer. Deadhead spent flowers for more blooms and to prevent self seeding, or let them seed for next year's plants.

title: Which Cottage Garden Spike is Right for You?
content: Giant larkspur's leaves, flowers and seeds are toxic if ingested.

title: Which Cottage Garden Spike is Right for You?
content: 'Frosted Skies' giant larkspur has flowers with white-tinged centers and lavender-blue edges from spring to summer. Plants grow 34 to 48 inches tall and 12 to 18 inches wide and are light and airy for bouquets.

title: Which Cottage Garden Spike is Right for You?
content: QIS Carmine giant larkspur has double pink blooms on sturdy stems from spring to summer on 30- to 48-inch-tall and 10- to 20-inch-wide plants.

title: Which Cottage Garden Spike is Right for You?
content: 'Fancy Smokey Eyes' giant larkspur has double silvery lavender blooms from spring to summer on 34- to 48-inch-tall and 12- to 18-inch-wide plants, and it makes a good cut flower for fresh or dried arrangements.

title: Which Cottage Garden Spike is Right for You?
content: Illustrated comparison page showing giant larkspur flower spikes, deeply cut leaves and cultivar photos for 'Frosted Skies', QIS Carmine and 'Fancy Smokey Eyes'.

title: Plants on the Move
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Whether you are moving a plant across the yard, across town or across the country, relocating trees, shrubs and perennials can be stressful for them. When the plant is a treasured heirloom peony or an expensive hellebore, you want to do your best to see it transplanted successfully and thriving in its new home.

title: Plants on the Move
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Before moving, ask whether the plant is worth the effort. If it is, make the transition smoother by preparing ahead, taking care during the move and planting thoughtfully afterward.

title: Plants on the Move
author: Jennifer Howell
content: It is best to move most plants when they are dormant. Match the season to the plant if you can. If you cannot move at the optimal stage, minimize transplanting shock by making the move in as short a time frame as possible.

title: Plants on the Move
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Before moving a plant from your garden, prune dead branches and foliage that might harbor pathogens. If moving a perennial when it is dormant or going dormant, cut it back to the ground. Avoid trimming much actively growing foliage because it can stress the plant as it tries to grow both new roots and foliage.

title: Plants on the Move
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Water the plant a day or two before digging to hydrate the foliage and soften the soil. Dig with as much of the root ball as possible, then wrap roots in burlap or slide them into a pot and fill around them with soil. Water thoroughly and store the plant in a shady spot until you are ready to move.

title: Plants on the Move
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Ideally, dig up, move and plant in the same day. If you are not moving right away, water the burlapped or potted plant every couple of days so roots do not dry out. If transporting plants in an open truck, cover foliage with a tarp to protect it from drying winds.

title: Plants on the Move
author: Jennifer Howell
content: After arrival, unpack the plant as soon as possible. Water the root ball thoroughly and set it in a shady spot until you are ready to plant.

title: Plants on the Move
author: Jennifer Howell
content: If possible, choose the new planting spot ahead of time so you can plant right away. Prepare the soil and add amendments such as compost. Work in morning or evening when temperatures are cooler. Set the plant into the ground with the crown at the same level as before, water and add an inch or two of mulch.

title: Plants on the Move
author: Jennifer Howell
content: When transplanting in hot weather, check daily for two to three weeks and water if soil appears dry or the plant looks wilted.

title: Plants on the Move
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Deciduous trees and shrubs move best when dormant with no leaves. Evergreen trees and shrubs move best before new buds sprout or after new growth has hardened off. Perennials move best in cool weather when not actively growing. Spring-blooming bulbs move best after foliage turns yellow and bulbs are dormant.

title: Plants on the Move
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Before moving a plant, ask if it is sentimental, rare or costly; if it will survive a move; if it will thrive in the new environment; whether it is allowed or invasive; and whether you have permission to take it if the garden belongs to a property you sold.

title: Plants on the Move
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Timing chart and decision box for moving plants, with seasons for moving deciduous trees and shrubs, evergreens, perennials and spring-blooming bulbs.

title: Rhubarb
author: Marisa Reyes
content: A rhubarb patch gives the vegetable garden a perennial crop for pies, jams, sauces and syrups. As a bonus, the plants are beautiful, with vibrant red stems and enormous green leaves.

title: Rhubarb
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Rhubarb thrives in full sun with fertile, moist, well-drained soil. Grow plants in an isolated spot where the roots will not be disturbed by foot traffic or at the front of a border where they have room to spread. In zones 7 and warmer, plant rhubarb in part shade to prevent foliage scorch; in zones 9 and warmer, treat rhubarb like a winter annual and harvest in March or April.

title: Rhubarb
author: Marisa Reyes
content: You can start a rhubarb patch from seed, but the easiest method is to buy 1-year-old crowns or get divisions from a friend. Plant crowns 3 feet apart and 4 inches deep. Crowding may encourage crown rot or powdery mildew.

title: Rhubarb
author: Marisa Reyes
content: To divide rhubarb, dig the entire plant in early spring as plants start to emerge or when dormant in late fall. Use a spade or soil knife to split each plant into sections with two to three leaves. Replant divisions with the largest root systems at the same depth and water them in.

title: Rhubarb
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Native photo of red rhubarb stalks and large green leaves used with the homegrown rhubarb article.

title: Rhubarb
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Rhubarb, Rheum x hybridum, is a perennial planted in early spring when soil reaches 50 degrees F or in late fall when crowns are dormant. One plant is enough for fresh eating and preserving for a family of four. Grow it in full sun to part shade in fertile, moist, well-draining soil. Harvest stalks after the second or third year when they are 12 to 18 inches long. Rhubarb is cold hardy in USDA zones 3 to 8.

title: Rhubarb
author: Marisa Reyes
content: For thick rhubarb stems and big leaves, sprinkle a balanced granular fertilizer or spread 1 to 2 inches of aged manure around plants in early spring. Avoid the crown so fertilizer does not burn emerging growth.

title: Rhubarb
author: Marisa Reyes
content: If rhubarb plants are grown from crowns, begin harvesting in the second year; if started from seed, wait until the third year. In late spring, when a stalk is 12 to 18 inches long, hold it firmly at the base, twist and pull to harvest. Cutting stems increases disease risk, and leftover stubs can admit pests.

title: Rhubarb
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Harvest just a few rhubarb stems at a time to avoid exhausting the plant. Remove leaves immediately to prevent stalks from wilting, wrap stems in a damp paper towel inside a plastic bag and store them in the refrigerator. Stop harvesting in early summer when plants no longer send up new stalks, or next year's yield and quality will be reduced.

title: Rhubarb
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Mature rhubarb plants that are three years or older will start to bolt or flower in summer. Cut off blooms so energy returns to the crown for next year's growth.

title: Rhubarb
author: Marisa Reyes
content: 'Chipman's Canada Red' rhubarb is heat tolerant and produces long, thick, deep red stalks that stay red when cooked. 'Crimson Red' has stringless brilliant crimson stalks with sweet-tart flavor. Hardy Tarty has thick nonstringy red stalks with exceptionally tart flavor. KangaRhu has dark red stalks that keep color and flavor when cooked. 'MacDonald' has tender red stalks and high resistance to root rot and wilt. 'Victoria' is an heirloom with tender thick crimson and green stalks and mild sweet flavor.

title: Rhubarb
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Rhubarb stems are never toxic, but the leaves are poisonous in every season and should not be eaten.

title: Love Affair with Texture, Stone and Water
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Downsizing for Ruby and Frank Andrews meant moving from a 30-acre ranch with a 3-acre garden to a 1-acre property in Granite Bay, California. When they arrived 13 years ago, there was little in the yard, and Ruby relished the challenge of bringing life to the mostly empty space.

title: Love Affair with Texture, Stone and Water
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Drawing on her passion for textural plantings, Japanese maples and water features, Ruby created a peaceful retreat that the couple enjoys daily and shares when they open their garden for tours.

title: Love Affair with Texture, Stone and Water
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Initially Ruby thought it would take a year to figure out the garden because it was much smaller than the 3 rocky acres she had gardened on for 32 years. After 12 years, she is still learning about the yard and is in no hurry.

title: Love Affair with Texture, Stone and Water
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: In a climate where the average summer temperature is 92 degrees F, trees are a big help. Ruby and Frank added many trees to the original dogwoods, oleanders and scrub oaks in their northwest-facing yard.

title: Love Affair with Texture, Stone and Water
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Native full-page garden photo showing layered chartreuse and green foliage, mature trees and the start of Ruby and Frank Andrews' texture-focused California garden.

title: Love Affair with Texture, Stone and Water
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Adding a border by the street created curb appeal and screening. Once the plants were established, Frank says the biggest job is editing, or pruning, to make the stone more visible and keep the garden tidy.

title: Love Affair with Texture, Stone and Water
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Trees and turf on the slope near the street used to struggle in poor, dry soil. Ruby and Frank brought in planter's mix, a combination of compost and other amendments, to improve growing conditions. They replaced dying plants with Cousin Itt acacia, 'Breeze' dwarf mat rush, Texas ranger and other drought-tolerant plants.

title: Love Affair with Texture, Stone and Water
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Evergreens such as 'Fat Albert' Colorado spruce, dwarf white pine and 'Wheeler's Dwarf' Japanese pittosporum provide year-round curb appeal. Ruby also adds stones as accents and sets large ones so the best-looking feature faces outward.

title: Love Affair with Texture, Stone and Water
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Native images of the front slope with Colorado spruce, dwarf white pine, Japanese pittosporum, Cousin Itt acacia, dwarf mat rush, Texas ranger, black bark mulch and stone accents.

title: Love Affair with Texture, Stone and Water
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Two privet topiaries stand sentry on either side of the front steps. Trimming new growth three times a year requires a ladder but helps the shrubs keep their distinct form.

title: Love Affair with Texture, Stone and Water
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: At the front walk, evergreens in varied shapes, sizes and colors create a tapestry of texture. Ruby has replaced many littleleaf boxwoods with boxleaf euonymus, which has similar evergreen structure but tolerates hot California summers better.

title: Love Affair with Texture, Stone and Water
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: A dramatic circular arbor was originally installed to look out on the street, but Ruby later moved it after realizing it paired perfectly with a newly installed fountain. Together they became the front yard focal point.

title: Love Affair with Texture, Stone and Water
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Although Ruby replaced at least half of the original lawn, she does not want to eliminate it all because lawn provides a visual resting place and contrast to the borders.

title: Love Affair with Texture, Stone and Water
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Native images of the front walkway, privet topiaries, layered evergreen texture and garden plan map for the Andrews garden.

title: Love Affair with Texture, Stone and Water
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: The northeast-facing side yard gets morning sun, so Ruby grows a mix of sun and shade plants there. In shadier spots she uses 'Moon Bay' heavenly bamboo and hakonechloa; where the sun is more intense, weeping Norway spruce and 'Feeling Blue' deodar cedar thrive.

title: Love Affair with Texture, Stone and Water
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Native garden photo of the shady side yard with weeping Norway spruce, 'Moon Bay' heavenly bamboo, 'Feeling Blue' deodar cedar and hakonechloa.

title: Love Affair with Texture, Stone and Water
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Along Frog Lane, a casual path of stepping stones passes through a layered border of perennials, shrubs and trees. The planting creates a shady secluded feel and sets the stage for a reveal when you step through the arbor into the backyard.

title: Love Affair with Texture, Stone and Water
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Frog Lane is home to Ruby's collection of ornamental frogs. The original frog has pride of place on a pedestal in the border, while others are tucked among foliage waiting to be discovered.

title: Love Affair with Texture, Stone and Water
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Native garden images of Frog Lane, including the shaded path, hakonechloa and ornamental frog figures tucked among foliage.

title: Love Affair with Texture, Stone and Water
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Step through the arbor at the end of Frog Lane and three patios run along the back of the house. Colorful borders around each patio provide close-up seasonal interest and a cozy feel while sitting there.

title: Love Affair with Texture, Stone and Water
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: A curving brick-lined sidewalk edges the patio gardens and leads into the rest of the backyard. To travel between the living room and dining patio, visitors traverse steppers through a colorful path planted with roses.

title: Love Affair with Texture, Stone and Water
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Native images of the backyard patio paths, brick-edged walkway, steppers, Knock Out rose, polyantha rose and colorful patio borders.

title: Love Affair with Texture, Stone and Water
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Rocky soil was a major challenge as Ruby revamped the yard. She ordered 170 yards of topsoil from a local landscaper and worked it into the rocky soil around the yard to make it more hospitable for plants and easier for her to work in.

title: Love Affair with Texture, Stone and Water
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: The builder had pushed stones uncovered during construction into a pile at the back of the property. Ruby and bonsai master Hiro Matsuda redistributed some of the stones to create large planting pockets, arranging many around the base of the natural outcropping to tie stone and garden together.

title: Love Affair with Texture, Stone and Water
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Ruby designed the garden with winding paths, nooks and crannies so visitors do not see everything at once. Among the foliage, a birdbath, bench or special stone creates small discoveries and views.

title: Love Affair with Texture, Stone and Water
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Native images of the backyard boulder, rock planting pockets, subtle stone vignette and hakonechloa framing a garden stone.

title: Love Affair with Texture, Stone and Water
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Ruby's childhood trips to Yosemite National Park may have inspired her love of water features. A blue recirculating fountain, a gift from Frank, is positioned above the patio where the couple often sits and relaxes in the evening.

title: Love Affair with Texture, Stone and Water
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: The fountains can run all year because the garden does not freeze, but Ruby turns off out-of-the-way water features when no visitors are expected to save energy and water.

title: Love Affair with Texture, Stone and Water
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: At the back of the yard, among scrub oaks and redwoods, a patio with a bench sits next to a small waterfall. Farther along the shady path is a tiered fountain that Ruby moved from the front yard after realizing its size and rustic style fit the casual backyard setting.

title: Love Affair with Texture, Stone and Water
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Native garden photo of cobalt blue fountain, chartreuse hakonechloa and shady planted slope in the Andrews garden.

title: Love Affair with Texture, Stone and Water
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Ruby says she likes the sound of water because it makes the garden come alive.

title: Love Affair with Texture, Stone and Water
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Because the tiered fountain is in a shady part of the yard, Ruby watches for falling leaves and skims them out regularly so the pump does not get clogged.

title: Love Affair with Texture, Stone and Water
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Native images of Ruby and Frank Andrews with their dogs, plus the tiered fountain and shaded garden seating area.

title: Love Affair with Texture, Stone and Water
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Ruby has found that the key to texture is growing a variety of plant forms, foliage colors and shapes. A border along the driveway shows how good a mostly foliage garden can look, with bright gold dwarf false cypress, pyramidal arborvitae and other leaf shapes and sizes in shades of green.

title: Love Affair with Texture, Stone and Water
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Ruby experiments freely, moving plants around and trying combinations until the mix feels right. Each year she plans a new bed or renovation.

title: Love Affair with Texture, Stone and Water
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Ruby has more than 100 Japanese maples in the yard and loves the variety they provide. She once accepted a 15-foot-tall Japanese maple from a friend's courtyard, a difficult move that taught the couple to be more careful about accepting free plants.

title: Love Affair with Texture, Stone and Water
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Native garden photo of a foliage-focused border with arborvitae, camellia, bigleaf hydrangea, dwarf false cypress, dwarf mat rush and Japanese anemone.

title: Love Affair with Texture, Stone and Water
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Japanese maples grow well in this zone 8 garden. Working organically rich topsoil into the site before planting has contributed to their success, and regular watering is needed for them to thrive. Ruby uses a mix of drip irrigation and traditional sprinkler heads.

title: Love Affair with Texture, Stone and Water
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Ruby's secrets for Japanese maples are to start with organically rich, well-drained soil; provide regular water, especially when temperatures are over 90 degrees F; and give newly planted trees extra shade with shade cloth or an umbrella for a week or two until acclimated.

title: Sparkling Spring Shade Garden
author: Chloe Deike
content: This spring shade garden has shapes and textures, sharp and soft colors and unusual plants that attract attention. With dainty flowers and delicate details, the spring-focused garden invites close inspection and lingering.

title: Sparkling Spring Shade Garden
author: Chloe Deike
content: For the best experience, situate this zone 5 shade garden along the edge of a treeline, where it can mark the beginning of a woodland stroll. If that is not possible, the space under any large shade tree can also work.

title: Sparkling Spring Shade Garden
author: Chloe Deike
content: Straight rows are too formal for this setting. Curves of mixed perennials, like the hosta and brunnera, can follow the base of the tree and shrub and create a relaxed structure.

title: Sparkling Spring Shade Garden
author: Chloe Deike
content: The planting is denser in the center of the bed, with more space between plants near the edge, imitating how plants naturally disperse on a forest floor.

title: Sparkling Spring Shade Garden
author: Chloe Deike
content: Native illustration of a spring shade garden under a tree with a natural woodland feel, winding rows and mixed hosta, brunnera, hellebore, ferns and spring flowers.

title: Sparkling Spring Shade Garden
author: Chloe Deike
content: To separate a tree from a treeline or spacious yard, add a slightly smaller second focal point. Here, an azalea draws attention, marks a general side boundary opposite the tree and bridges the gap between the tall tree and small spring perennials.

title: Sparkling Spring Shade Garden
author: Chloe Deike
content: Arrange plants around two focal points by placing the tallest perennials around the base of the tallest focal point, then flanking the shorter focal point with the second-tallest set of perennials. Alternate layers back and forth and edge both sides with the same short ground covers so each focal point feels proportionate.

title: Sparkling Spring Shade Garden
author: Chloe Deike
content: This garden comes alive as soon as temperatures warm in early spring and continues into summer with hardworking perennials. Hellebores bloom first and hold attractive sepals for about 6 weeks, then fern fronds unfurl, columbines nod and brunnera flowers sparkle.

title: Sparkling Spring Shade Garden
author: Chloe Deike
content: This low-maintenance planting lets gardeners ease into spring chores. In fall, focus on building soil by scratching compost around plant crowns. Azaleas like acid soil, so test the soil every few years and apply acid fertilizer as needed.

title: Sparkling Spring Shade Garden
author: Chloe Deike
content: Do not be quick to cut plants back in fall. Ferns, coral bells and hellebores provide peeks of green through winter. In early spring, gently pull out or cut back matted or unsightly remaining foliage; even if you do not, new growth will find its way through.

title: Sparkling Spring Shade Garden
author: Chloe Deike
content: Once established, these plants tolerate dry conditions, especially with mulch. Add bark mulch or leaf litter mulch each fall to retain water and suppress weeds. If you would rather not install steppers, add a 3- to 4-inch layer of mulch to create a path.

title: Sparkling Spring Shade Garden
author: Chloe Deike
content: As spring flowers fade, cut back spent stems for a tidy look. Many, like lungwort, will fall on their own or be overtaken by growing foliage. Space along the bed edge is left for long-blooming annuals in summer, while the perennial textures and patterned foliage continue to provide interest.

title: Sparkling Spring Shade Garden
author: Chloe Deike
content: Deer usually avoid eating lungwort and brunnera foliage. 'Hermann's Pride' yellow archangel is compact, so it does not have the same takeover risk as some other yellow archangels.

title: Sparkling Spring Shade Garden
author: Chloe Deike
content: Planting-plan diagram for the spring shade garden showing an existing tree, azalea, curving plant masses, path and plant-letter layout.

title: Sparkling Spring Shade Garden
author: Chloe Deike
content: Coral bells, Heuchera 'Caramel', has pink early-summer flowers and rusty yellow foliage that matures to chartreuse. It grows in full sun to part shade, 9 to 18 inches tall and 12 to 24 inches wide, in USDA zones 4 to 9. Plant 8.

title: Sparkling Spring Shade Garden
author: Chloe Deike
content: Lungwort, Pulmonaria 'Pink-a-Blue', has clusters of pink buds that open and change to blue in late spring, with unusual white-spotted foliage that lasts into winter. It grows in part to full shade, 16 to 18 inches tall and 22 to 24 inches wide, in USDA zones 3 to 9. Plant 4.

title: Sparkling Spring Shade Garden
author: Chloe Deike
content: Amsonia, Amsonia tabernaemontana 'Storm Cloud', has star-shaped sky-blue flowers in late spring. It grows in full sun to part shade, 24 to 30 inches tall and 38 to 42 inches wide, in USDA zones 4 to 9. Plant 1.

title: Sparkling Spring Shade Garden
author: Chloe Deike
content: Autumn fern, Dryopteris erythrosora 'Brilliance', has copper-colored leaves in spring that mature to green in summer and orange in fall. It grows in part to full shade, 18 to 30 inches tall and wide, in USDA zones 4 to 8. Plant 3.

title: Sparkling Spring Shade Garden
author: Chloe Deike
content: Hosta 'Autumn Frost' has purple midsummer flowers and frosty green leaves with thick yellow margins. It grows in part to full shade, 12 to 16 inches tall and 20 to 24 inches wide, in USDA zones 3 to 8. Plant 3.

title: Sparkling Spring Shade Garden
author: Chloe Deike
content: Hellebore, Helleborus 'First Dance', has large double yellow flowers with maroon picotee edges in early to late spring. It grows in part to full shade, 18 to 24 inches tall and wide, in USDA zones 4 to 9. Plant 4.

title: Sparkling Spring Shade Garden
author: Chloe Deike
content: Yellow archangel, Lamium galeobdolon 'Hermann's Pride', has yellow early-summer flowers and small leaves with silver markings. It grows in full sun to full shade, 6 to 12 inches tall and 12 to 18 inches wide, in USDA zones 4 to 9. Plant 6.

title: Sparkling Spring Shade Garden
author: Chloe Deike
content: Brunnera, Brunnera macrophylla 'Alexander's Great', has small sky-blue flowers in late spring. It grows in part to full shade, 12 to 18 inches tall and 24 to 30 inches wide, in USDA zones 3 to 8. Plant 4.

title: Sparkling Spring Shade Garden
author: Chloe Deike
content: Golden columbine, Aquilegia chrysantha, has extra-large yellow flowers in late spring. It grows in full sun to part shade, 30 to 36 inches tall and 16 to 20 inches wide, in USDA zones 4 to 9. Plant 4.

title: Sparkling Spring Shade Garden
author: Chloe Deike
content: Azalea, Rhododendron x 'Cannon's Double', is a shrub with creamy peach and pink flowers in late spring. It grows in full sun to part shade, 5 to 6 feet tall and 3 to 4 feet wide, in USDA zones 5 to 8. Plant 1.

title: Sparkling Spring Shade Garden
author: Chloe Deike

title: 7 Plants I Always Start From Seed
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Seeds can be started outdoors directly in the ground, indoors under lights or in a greenhouse, and even in the refrigerator in a paper towel. The needs of the plant and how it germinates best determine the method, but reasons to grow from seed vary, including finding particular varieties.

title: 7 Plants I Always Start From Seed
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Jennifer grows petunias from seed because she uses them in mass plantings and it can be expensive to fill large beds with flats of plants from the garden center. Fancy colors or double cultivars may not be available, but seeds of many great landscaping petunias, such as the Shock Wave series, are available.

title: 7 Plants I Always Start From Seed
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Start petunias indoors about 10 weeks before the last expected frost so they are blooming and ready for the garden once weather stays above 60 degrees F. Tiny seeds are often pelleted, which makes them easier to handle. Petunias need light to germinate, so pat seeds onto the potting mix surface and use a germination mat until they sprout.

title: 7 Plants I Always Start From Seed
author: Jennifer Howell
content: When petunia seedlings have two sets of true leaves, transplant them into a peat pot or multi-pack. If they get tall and leggy, pinch back a half inch to encourage branching and fuller plants. Similar seed-starting candidates include vinca, wax begonia and zinnia.

title: 7 Plants I Always Start From Seed
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Native images showing a seedling illustration and a mass planting of Shock Wave Deep Purple, Ivory and Pink Vein petunias.

title: 7 Plants I Always Start From Seed
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Jennifer grows gloriosa daisy from seed to save money because she often finds it sold in premium 1-gallon pots, and it is not always winter hardy in her zone 5 garden. Seeds are less expensive, and small seed-grown plants are easier to work into containers.

title: 7 Plants I Always Start From Seed
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Start gloriosa daisy seeds indoors about two months before the expected last frost if growing them as annuals. The seeds need light to germinate, so sow them on the potting mix surface, pat them down and cover with plastic wrap or a dome. Once seedlings have their first leaves, remove the humidity dome because the hairy foliage can damp off or mold easily.

title: 7 Plants I Always Start From Seed
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Jennifer grows annual phlox from seed because unusual plants in catalogs may be hard to find at the garden center. Annual phlox, including the Popstars series, works well in containers with unique star-shaped flowers and light fragrance.

title: 7 Plants I Always Start From Seed
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Annual phlox can be direct-sown, but starting it indoors gives earlier flowers. Sow two or three seeds in a small biodegradable peat or newspaper pot that can be transplanted without disturbing delicate roots. Cover seed with 1/4 inch of potting mix, keep it moist, thin to one seedling per pot and pinch leggy plants at about 6 inches tall for fuller foliage and more blooms.

title: 7 Plants I Always Start From Seed
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Native photos of 'Cherry Brandy' gloriosa daisy and Popstars Purple with Eye annual phlox used with seed-starting reasons.

title: 7 Plants I Always Start From Seed
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Cool-season vegetables are among the first plants at the garden center in spring, but seed catalogs carry unique varieties such as purple 'Bonarda' broccoli. In fall, when plants can be hard to find for another cool-season crop, Jennifer starts seeds in late summer.

title: 7 Plants I Always Start From Seed
author: Jennifer Howell
content: For a spring broccoli crop, start seeds indoors 4 to 6 weeks before the last expected frost and transplant outdoors once temperatures stay above 50 degrees F. For a fall crop, count back the seed packet's days to maturity from the expected first frost date. Jennifer starts fall broccoli indoors in multi-packs under lights so seedlings are easier to keep moist, then moves them outside as summer cools.

title: 7 Plants I Always Start From Seed
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Cosmos has large, easy-to-handle seeds and good germination rates, so Jennifer direct-sows it outdoors after frost. She spaces seeds at the recommended planting distance instead of overseeding and thinning, and her direct-sown cosmos often fill in as quickly as transplants.

title: 7 Plants I Always Start From Seed
author: Jennifer Howell
content: To sow cosmos, rough up the soil where plants should grow, sprinkle seed and rake the soil surface to cover, or scuff a small hole, drop in a seed or two and cover with soil. Cosmos sometimes self-sows and returns as volunteers the next year, though seedlings may not look like the parent plant.

title: 7 Plants I Always Start From Seed
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Native photos of 'Bonarda' broccoli and 'Xanthos' cosmos used with early-start and direct-sowing seed tips.

title: 7 Plants I Always Start From Seed
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Common milkweed grows a long taproot and does best when planted directly where it should stay. To direct sow in fall, scatter seed over loosened soil, rake lightly and water in.

title: 7 Plants I Always Start From Seed
author: Jennifer Howell
content: If common milkweed seeds collected in fall were not planted, soak them in water overnight in early spring, spread them on a damp paper towel, roll it up and place it in a plastic bag. Refrigerate for at least 30 days at 33 to 38 degrees F for cold stratification, then sow directly in a prepared bed.

title: 7 Plants I Always Start From Seed
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Jennifer saves breadseed poppy seedheads every fall and replants them in early spring because the original seeds came from a good friend. Heirloom plants such as breadseed poppy produce abundant seed and are often easy to grow by direct sowing.

title: 7 Plants I Always Start From Seed
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Collect breadseed poppy seed after pods dry and the seed rattles inside. As soon as the ground is workable in spring, rake the area and scratch up the soil. Breadseed poppies need light to germinate, so shake seed from the pod onto the soil surface. Mixing tiny seeds with sand helps distribute them evenly. In snowy climates, seed can be sown on late winter snow so melting snow hydrates and settles it.

title: 7 Plants I Always Start From Seed
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Native photos of 'Lauren's Grape' breadseed poppy, common milkweed and a monarch caterpillar context image used with direct-sowing and transplanting guidance.

title: Q&A
content: To prune an overwintered Spanish lavender topiary, remove dead sections first. Then snip off growth along the main stem and base that distracts from the formal shape. Snip branch ends to encourage dense growth, but do not remove more than a third of the branching and avoid cutting back to woody stems that may not regrow foliage.

title: Q&A
content: Replace topiary ties if they are starting to strangle the main stem. During summer, pinch off spent flowers to encourage more side branches and help keep the head dense and blooming.

title: Q&A
content: To clean a rusty spade without strong chemicals, start by removing loose dirt and rust with a wire brush. Wrap the blade snugly in an old towel, soak it with white vinegar, slip it into a plastic bag and tie it shut for up to 24 hours. Remove the tool and scour with a stiff brush or coarse steel wool, repeating if necessary.

title: Q&A
content: After cleaning rust from a spade with vinegar, pour the vinegar down a drain and prevent future rust by rubbing the blade with vegetable oil.

title: Q&A
content: Native Q&A visuals showing a Spanish lavender topiary pruning diagram and step photos for cleaning rust from a spade with vinegar.

title: Q&A
content: Old-fashioned French lilacs, Syringa vulgaris, grow best in USDA zones 3 to 7 and need roughly 2,000 chill hours below 45 degrees F to bloom well. For zone 8 gardens, use low-chill early flowering lilac hybrids, Syringa x hyacinthiflora, with classic scent, such as 'Angel White', 'California Rose', 'Lavender Lady' or Scentara Double Blue.

title: Q&A
content: Western red cedar mulch will not repel bees and most other pollinators. Many high-quality beehive boxes are made from cedar. High concentrations of fragrant oils can repel some pests such as ants and wood-boring insects, but weathered cedar mulch has not been shown to deter pollinators from visiting flowers.

title: Q&A
content: Cedar wood breaks down slowly, so it makes a durable, long-lasting garden path and works well in shrub borders. In frequently tilled places such as vegetable gardens or annual flower beds, cedar mulch may not be the best choice. Western red cedar is actually an arborvitae, Thuja plicata, and Eastern red cedar is a juniper, Juniperus virginiana; true cedars are not used much for mulch.

title: Q&A
content: Virginia waterleaf, Hydrophyllum virginianum, is a native woodland perennial with flowers popular with many bees. It is not invasive, but it can be aggressive, spreading by seeds and rhizomes to form dense colonies in shrub and perennial beds. Early leaves have white or silvery splotches; later leaves are plain green. Pink, white or pale lavender flower clusters open in late spring to early summer.

title: Q&A
content: Virginia waterleaf is native to much of North America, mainly east of the Rocky Mountains and into Canada. It prefers part sun to light shade in moist, loamy soil but tolerates many soil and light conditions.

title: Q&A
content: To remove Virginia waterleaf, dig up dense roots and remove every piece of rhizome or it can regrow. For a large colony, repeatedly mow to reduce seed production and remove foliage to gradually starve the plant.

title: Garden Essentials
content: A sturdy Ups-A-Daisy planter insert creates a false bottom inside a large pot so shallow-rooted annuals need only 6 to 8 inches of potting mix. The insert makes containers lighter, saves potting mix and has drainage holes. Measure the container where the insert should sit and choose a size that fits the inside pot diameter at least 8 to 12 inches from the lip, or more for large pots and plants.

title: Garden Essentials
content: The Drain Away Drain Tray prevents water puddles from staining a deck or patio. The pot sits on the elevated center pedestal while excess water flows from a drain spout off the deck. PVC pipe fittings can direct water farther away or link several trays together and collect water for reuse.

title: Garden Essentials
content: The Dramm 170PL Water Breaker is a small 1.25-inch-wide watering head for containers and hanging baskets. It delivers water in a concentrated, direct stream, and the threaded end fits any standard hose or water wand. Holes in the aluminum screen break up and soften the water flow to prevent damage to delicate plants.

title: Garden Essentials
content: The DeWit Potting Trowel is part soil scoop and part trowel, with a heart-shaped blade for filling containers and carving planting holes. Its sharpened edge cuts through roots when taking apart containers at the end of the season, and the solid build also handles hard packed soil in the garden.

title: Garden Essentials
content: Containers Made Easy! Volume 6 includes container garden trends, plant-care advice and design ideas for windowboxes, entry pots and multiseason arrangements, with 70 planting plans.

title: Garden Essentials
content: Mulberry Farm & Food in Des Moines, Iowa, is operated by Central Iowa Shelter and Services and combines job training with food production. Staff and clients grow vegetables such as lettuce, cherry tomatoes and snap peas in the greenhouse for the kitchen, share surplus with food pantries or sell to local restaurants and businesses. Proceeds are reinvested in operations and client services.

title: Garden Essentials
content: Mulberry Farm & Food is expanding in 2024 with facilities to raise tilapia and an outdoor Agrihood where seasonal fruits and vegetables are available to people who are food insecure. Shelter clients can apply for paid positions in the greenhouse and raised beds.

title: Garden Essentials
content: Caliburst Yellow petchoa, Petunia x calibrachoa, is the first petchoa available from seed, though plants are also sold at garden centers. This petunia and calibrachoa cross blooms prolifically as temperatures rise, grows 6 to 10 inches tall and 20 to 28 inches wide, and works in sun to part-shade containers.

title: Garden Essentials
content: Jurassic Snowfall rex begonia, Begonia rex-cultorum, lightens shade containers with silvery-green leaves marked by burgundy veins. It grows 16 to 20 inches tall and 18 to 20 inches wide outdoors in shade or indoors in a bright winter window.

title: Garden Essentials
content: Estrella Lobsterfest verbena has two-tone coral blooms that cover 8- to 12-inch-tall and 12- to 18-inch-wide trailing plants all summer. Grow it in full sun in hanging baskets, containers or massed as a ground cover.

title: Jump Start Your Spring
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Senetti Magenta Bicolor cineraria, Pericallis hybrid, is a cool-weather-loving tender perennial with bright 3-inch magenta blooms and a white eye from early spring to early summer. It grows in full sun to part shade in moist, well-drained soil, reaches 12 to 24 inches tall and 12 to 18 inches wide, has no serious pest problems and is cold hardy in USDA zones 9 to 12.

title: Jump Start Your Spring
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Cineraria flowers may be familiar from the houseplant aisle, but the Senetti series is tougher and meant for outdoor growing. Magenta Bicolor is one of several colors in the series, which includes purple, blue, pink and white.

title: Jump Start Your Spring
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Energize a spring border by growing Magenta Bicolor cineraria alongside pansies and hellebores. It can also brighten an entry or patio in containers with jewel-toned blooms.

title: Jump Start Your Spring
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Magenta Bicolor cineraria grows best in full sun and well-drained soil or potting mix. Plants thrive when temperatures are in the 35 to 40 degrees F range. If a freeze is forecast, move the pot indoors or cover plants with an old sheet, because damage to foliage and flowers can set the plant back for the rest of the season.

title: Jump Start Your Spring
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Consistent moisture is important for good cineraria, but let the potting mix dry out between waterings to prevent fungal disease or rot. Check by inserting a finger to the first knuckle; if the mix feels dry, water.

title: Jump Start Your Spring
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: When temperatures reach 80 degrees F and higher, cineraria stems start getting leggy and flowers fade, so replace them with heat-tolerant plants for the rest of the season.

title: Jump Start Your Spring
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: The Cool Weather Color container uses Senetti Magenta Bicolor cineraria, Nesia Sunshine nemesia, 'Harmony Double Blue' windflower and 'Snow Crystals' sweet alyssum. Grow the 9-inch container in full sun and water when the potting mix is dry. No fertilizer or deadheading is needed as cineraria, sweet alyssum and nemesia bloom until summer heat.

title: What's Your Gardening Style?
author: Chloe Deike
content: The gardening style quiz helps define plant and design preferences, quirks and motivations by connecting answers with four global garden styles. The quiz reminds gardeners that no matter where their preferences fall, the element no other garden can contain is their own personal touch.

title: What's Your Gardening Style?
author: Chloe Deike
content: The quiz asks gardeners to choose favorite plant genres, preferred living environments, indoor decor cues, color palettes, foliage colors, entertaining habits, dream garden additions, preferred maintenance level, hardscaping materials and edible plants they are most likely to grow.

title: What's Your Gardening Style?
author: Chloe Deike
content: A mostly A result points to a Mediterranean garden style. The gardener is most comfortable eating and socializing outdoors, has an elegant artistic eye drawn to natural materials and earth tones, and grows plants that are sun loving and easygoing.

title: What's Your Gardening Style?
author: Chloe Deike
content: A Mediterranean garden is framed by tall, slender evergreen conifers and low stone walls. Gravel paths and patios connect contained plantings of fine-textured, drought-tolerant perennials. Groupings of clay pots filled with herbs, citrus trees and large-leaved tropical plants collect in the corners.

title: What's Your Gardening Style?
author: Chloe Deike
content: Bougainvillea, Bougainvillea hybrids, has papery pink, purple, white or tangerine flowers from spring to fall. In USDA zones 9 to 12 it can cover up to 40 feet; elsewhere it can be grown in a container and overwintered indoors, staying around 4 to 6 feet long. Grow it in full sun.

title: What's Your Gardening Style?
author: Chloe Deike
content: Lavender, Lavandula species and hybrids, has fragrant purple, pink or white flowers above drought-tolerant foliage in full sun. It grows as a perennial in USDA zones 5 to 11 or as a potted annual in colder zones, reaching 1 to 4 feet tall and wide.

title: What's Your Gardening Style?
author: Chloe Deike
content: Geranium, Pelargonium species and hybrids, is a sun-loving annual in many areas but a hardy perennial on the Mediterranean coast and in USDA zones 10 to 11. In the ground it can grow up to 2 feet tall and wide in many flower colors except blue.

title: What's Your Gardening Style?
author: Chloe Deike
content: Native style images for the Mediterranean garden result, including a sunlit gravel garden, clipped evergreens, a fountain, lavender, bougainvillea and geranium plant palette examples.

title: What's Your Gardening Style?
author: Chloe Deike
content: A mostly B result points to an English cottage garden style. Flowers exuberantly spill out of beds and borders, echoing a passion for bold beauty. Vegetables and edible plants weave within dense plantings, and the gardener often starts and ends the day with gloves and pruners ready.

title: What's Your Gardening Style?
author: Chloe Deike
content: The cottage garden wastes nothing. Blooms are pollinator magnets that support bumper crops, and flowers may be harvested for herbal teas or tinctures. Beds and borders follow a simple format of short plants in front and large in back. Brick or flagstone paths connect the beds.

title: What's Your Gardening Style?
author: Chloe Deike
content: Foxglove, Digitalis species and hybrids, offers large charming patterned flower spikes in pink, purple and white for full sun to part shade. These biennials grow 2 to 6 feet tall and 1 to 2 feet wide and bloom in spring to early summer. Let plants reseed.

title: What's Your Gardening Style?
author: Chloe Deike
content: Nasturtium, Tropaeolum majus, flowers nonstop until a hard frost in fall. Orange, pink, cream, red or patterned flowers and round flat leaves are edible and useful as salad garnishes. Mounded or spreading plants grow 8 to 120 inches tall in full sun to part shade.

title: What's Your Gardening Style?
author: Chloe Deike
content: Yarrow, Achillea species and hybrids, handles dry weather in USDA zones 3 to 10. Flat dense clusters of yellow, white, pink, red, lavender, peach or violet flowers sit above ferny foliage and add contrast in shape. Plants grow 6 to 60 inches tall and 12 to 36 inches wide in full sun.

title: What's Your Gardening Style?
author: Chloe Deike
content: Native style images for the English cottage result, including a cottage border, weathered watering-can planter, foxglove, nasturtium and yarrow plant palette examples.

title: What's Your Gardening Style?
author: Chloe Deike
content: A mostly C result points to a Japanese garden style. The gardener is captivated by the natural world and seeks balance between drama and tranquility. Each object, from a mounded shrub to a small collection of spaced perennials, is thoughtfully placed.

title: What's Your Gardening Style?
author: Chloe Deike
content: In a Japanese-inspired garden, grandeur meets simplicity through attention to spatial balance. Bridge plantings with moss or boulders, build a stone or wood pathway to intentional vistas, and include a raised platform deck or arbor of natural materials to emphasize passage between garden areas.

title: What's Your Gardening Style?
author: Chloe Deike
content: Azalea, Rhododendron species and hybrids, is an Asian garden hallmark in spring, with shrubs covered in red, pink, purple, white, yellow or orange flowers. They grow 2 to 15 feet tall and wide in USDA zones 4 to 8 in full sun to part shade.

title: What's Your Gardening Style?
author: Chloe Deike
content: Hakonechloa, Hakonechloa macra, has strappy draping chartreuse foliage for a lush shade-garden look. It is hardy in USDA zones 5 to 9 and grows 1 to 2 feet tall and wide in part sun to full shade.

title: What's Your Gardening Style?
author: Chloe Deike
content: Japanese iris, Iris ensata, has patterned purple, white, violet or pink petals above slender foliage. Plant it along the edge of a pond or keep soil consistently moist. It grows 2 to 4 feet tall and 1 to 2 feet wide in USDA zones 4 to 9.

title: What's Your Gardening Style?
author: Chloe Deike
content: For Japanese garden style, prune trees and shrubs to reveal their natural architectural form. If it is not obvious afterward that you pruned, you did well.

title: What's Your Gardening Style?
author: Chloe Deike
content: Native style images for the Japanese garden result, including a tranquil garden scene, Japanese maple, azalea, hakonechloa and Japanese iris plant palette examples.

title: What's Your Gardening Style?
author: Chloe Deike
content: A mostly D result points to a modern meadow garden style. The gardener aims to mimic nature with little intervention, using plants that boost biodiversity, feed and host wildlife, and thrive in the climate with ease.

title: What's Your Gardening Style?
author: Chloe Deike
content: A modern meadow has a hands-off appearance, but intentionality and effort are integral. Control the initial structure by planting a large base of grasses or sedges, weaving in clumps of flowering perennials and adding tall architectural plants with attractive seedheads. Clean up once a year in early spring.

title: What's Your Gardening Style?
author: Chloe Deike
content: Switchgrass, Panicum virgatum, bears airy tan and pink seedheads from midsummer through fall. Use it selectively for height and texture in full sun to part shade in USDA zones 4 to 9. It grows 3 to 7 feet tall and 1 to 6 feet wide.

title: What's Your Gardening Style?
author: Chloe Deike
content: Penstemon digitalis has tubular white, pink or purple flowers on erect racemes in spring and early summer. It is a hummingbird favorite for full sun to part shade in USDA zones 3 to 8 and grows 2 to 3 feet tall and 1 to 3 feet wide.

title: What's Your Gardening Style?
author: Chloe Deike
content: New England aster, Symphyotrichum novae-angliae, blooms in late summer and fall in shades of purple or pink. Plants can reach 1 to 6 feet tall and 2 to 3 feet wide in USDA zones 3 to 8 in full sun.

title: What's Your Gardening Style?
author: Chloe Deike

title: The Ole Rhubarb Switcheroo!
author: Jamie Seitz
content: One of Jamie's earliest memories is following her Grandma Jo to the yard at five or six years old to cut fresh rhubarb stalks for a snack. She and her cousins each had a small Tupperware cup with sugar at the bottom for dipping rhubarb. The sour-and-sweet snack represented the beginning of summer, warm weather and barefoot Sunday afternoons at Grandma's.

title: The Ole Rhubarb Switcheroo!
author: Jamie Seitz
content: Rhubarb is still a favorite for Jamie. She does not get as excited about eating it raw as she did at six, but she makes a mean crisp. When an acquaintance from the gym offered several big bags of rhubarb because neither he nor his mother enjoyed it, Jamie accepted immediately and talked about eating it as a kid.

title: The Ole Rhubarb Switcheroo!
author: Jamie Seitz
content: At home, Jamie pulled out favorite recipes and planned how much rhubarb to use immediately and how much to freeze. Ben arrived with four stuffed grocery bags and was happy to get rid of it. He said they hated it and had even tried it in sugar. Jamie offered to bake a rhubarb crisp, but he refused and left.

title: The Ole Rhubarb Switcheroo!
author: Jamie Seitz
content: When Jamie emptied the first bag into the sink, the produce seemed oddly fuzzy. It did not smell like rhubarb, but like hands after weeding. She broke off a piece, touched it to her tongue and realized it was not rhubarb.

title: The Ole Rhubarb Switcheroo!
author: Jamie Seitz
content: After washing her mouth out several times, Jamie checked the other bags and found the same fuzzy rhubarb imposter plants. A quick online search identified the plant as common burdock, Arctium minus, not rhubarb and not an ingredient for crisp.

title: The Ole Rhubarb Switcheroo!
author: Jamie Seitz

title: from the editor
author: Kristin Beane Sullivan
content: Early on, Kristin and her husband struck a deal: he would handle snow removal and she would mow the lawn. In May she discovered that using a push mower on a lumpy lawn was not as easy as riding over the yard on the mower she used growing up.

title: from the editor
author: Kristin Beane Sullivan
content: Kristin's goal is to have almost no lawn by the time she no longer has kids at home to mow it. She prefers the variety of caring for a garden to the monotony of lawn care.

title: from the editor
author: Kristin Beane Sullivan
content: James Wolfin's bee lawn concept appeals because the mix of flowers and turfgrass feeds hungry pollinating insects through the growing season while requiring less water, fertilizer and mowing than a traditional lawn.

title: from the editor
author: Kristin Beane Sullivan
content: Learning that white clover and violets host butterflies and bees made Kristin feel justified letting them grow in the lawn. A garden can become a hub of butterfly activity by including host plants where butterflies lay eggs, caterpillars feed and chrysalises shelter.

title: from the editor
author: Kristin Beane Sullivan
content: Whether it is staking dahlias early or counting bees diving into clematis flowers, Kristin hopes readers spend spring on garden work that excites them while minimizing monotonous chores.

title: Reader Tips
author: Katie Meyer, IA
content: Filler flowers can make the difference between a wimpy bouquet and an outstanding one. When Katie cut a bouquet of zinnias, she noticed her lime basil and oregano had started to bloom, so she tucked sprigs in with the zinnias. They made pretty, fragrant, long-lasting filler flowers.

title: Reader Tips
author: Katie Meyer, IA
content: When growing basil and oregano for eating, pinch the tips to prevent flowers and encourage fresh growth with the best flavor. If you let flowers grow, expect the harvest to decrease in flavor and amount. Katie plants extra basil so some can be used for bouquets.

title: Reader Tips
author: Katie Meyer, IA
content: Cinnamon, Thai and African blue basil have some of the largest, showiest flowers. For the most blooms, avoid basil varieties bred for bolt resistance. Harvest flowering stems when racemes are just beginning to bloom with lots of buds, and use three fillers for every one focal flower for the most impactful bouquet.

title: Reader Tips
author: Dianna Salsbury, WA
content: When getting up and down in the garden became challenging, Dianna discovered that a sturdy metal garden fork stuck into the ground nearby makes a helpful ergonomic support. If she feels unsteady while weeding or needs help standing, she grabs the fork handle.

title: Reader Tips
author: Irene Fullenkamp, IN
content: To deter cutworms from chewing tomato stems, poke a 2- or 3-inch nail into the soil and nestle it against a tomato stem. For more insurance, add a nail on either side of the plant. The nail prevents the pest from girdling the stem and killing the plant.

title: Reader Tips
content: Native photos showing basil and oregano flowering as bouquet fillers, a zinnia bouquet, and a garden fork used as a support for standing while gardening.

title: Reader Tips
author: Renée Real, CO
content: Rabbits dislike the flavor or scent of garlic. Renée shook garlic powder around the base of vulnerable plants and the rabbits began leaving them alone. Reapply weekly, after heavy rain or more frequently in spring when plants are emerging and most appetizing.

title: Reader Tips
author: Elaine Rourke, OH
content: Elaine uses a sharp old chef's knife to create clean lawn edges along the sidewalk and driveway without getting out the string trimmer. Cut along the concrete to remove grass and soil, then sweep up the cuts with an outdoor broom.

title: Pest Watch
content: Rose curculio, Merhynchites bicolor, is a beetle about 1/4 inch long with a red or black body, black head and long snout. Adults puncture rose buds and flowers, leaving holey marred petals and drooping buds. Creamy white larvae feed on buds and hips before dropping to the ground and pupating.

title: Pest Watch
content: To control rose curculio, act quickly because the beetles can ruin a rose bush in one season. Hand-pick adults and drop them into soapy water, or shake canes over the bowl. Because larvae drop to the ground, parasitic nematodes released into the soil can help. If a cultivar is repeatedly infested, consider replacing it with a darker-flowered rose.
