title: Sensational Summer Containers
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Container gardens transform balconies and patio corners into lush getaways. Tropical-themed containers with palms and vivid underplantings, coleus with trailing fanflower or succulent displays can provide months of vibrant blooms and foliage texture.

title: Sensational Summer Containers
author: Marisa Reyes
content: The Bold Textures container uses elephant ear, El Brighto coleus and Whirlwind Blue fanflower in an 18-inch-diameter container. Elephant ear's cup-shaped coffee-colored leaves create a dramatic backdrop, coleus adds crimson, green and yellow patterns, and blue fanflower forms a delicate fringe around the pot.

title: Sensational Summer Containers
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Bold Textures grows best in full sun to part shade. Too much shade makes coleus foliage fade. Keep the soil moist in hot weather, but avoid waterlogging by using potting mix and a container with drainage holes. Snip coleus stems when plants are 6 inches tall to encourage bushiness and pinch off buds as they form.

title: Sensational Summer Containers
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Native full-page photo of a summer container in an urn with elephant ear, colorful coleus, trailing fanflower and purple-white blooms.

title: Sensational Summer Containers
author: Marisa Reyes
content: El Brighto is part of the ColorBlaze coleus series bred to bloom later and therefore less, so the leaves can take center stage.

title: Sensational Summer Containers
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Succulents are a low-maintenance, resilient option and good candidates for overwintering indoors as houseplants. The Succulent Symphony container uses kalanchoe, blue chalksticks, jade plant, Graptopetalum paraguayense, echeveria, 'Tokyo Sun' sedum, watch chain, stonecrop and Aeonium lindleyi var. viscatum 'Irish Bouquet' in an 18-inch-diameter container.

title: Sensational Summer Containers
author: Marisa Reyes
content: In Succulent Symphony, kalanchoe's large light-green-and-pink tinted leaves and blue chalksticks' blue-green foliage provide strong forms. Smaller compact plants add varied leaf shapes and shades, while stonecrop's delicate light-green foliage brightens the arrangement and fills gaps.

title: Sensational Summer Containers
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Grow succulent containers in bright indirect light to maintain vibrant colors and prevent etiolation. Use a well-drained cactus and succulent soil mix, water sparingly after the soil dries completely, and feed during active growth in spring and summer with diluted balanced fertilizer for succulents.

title: Sensational Summer Containers
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Do not worry if you knock off a succulent leaf or two. Many succulents' leaves will sprout if you leave them lying on the soil.

title: Sensational Summer Containers
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Native photo of a succulent container with kalanchoe, blue chalksticks, jade plant, echeveria, sedum, watch chain, stonecrop and aeonium in a broad bowl.

title: Sensational Summer Containers
author: Marisa Reyes
content: The Tropical Elegance container uses Chinese fan palm, Dragon Wing Red begonia and variegated Swedish ivy in a container 44 inches tall with a 24-inch diameter opening. Chinese fan palm provides a broad-leaved vertical accent, red begonia flowers attract hummingbirds and trailing Swedish ivy softens the edge with variegated texture.

title: Sensational Summer Containers
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Put the Tropical Elegance container in full sun to part shade. Avoid overwatering because the palm can be prone to root rot. During the growing season, a balanced slow-release fertilizer supports lush foliage, and variegated Swedish ivy may need regular trimming for shape and fullness.

title: The Buzz About Bee Lawns
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Bees, butterflies and other pollinating insects need help, and gardeners have been planting pollinator gardens and weaving native plants into landscapes. A bee-friendly lawn is another way to support pollinators.

title: The Buzz About Bee Lawns
author: Marisa Reyes
content: James Wolfin says a bee lawn still functions as a traditional lawn space but is designed to be more beneficial to pollinators. Instead of only turfgrass, a bee lawn adds pollinator-friendly flowers that bloom at different times and overlap, so there is always something flowering in the yard.

title: The Buzz About Bee Lawns
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Letting lawn weeds such as dandelion and creeping charlie bloom does not necessarily make a bee lawn because those plants can be invasive. White clover is non-native but not aggressive enough to be considered invasive, and pollinators love it. The best bee lawn mix includes slow-growing turfgrasses and low-growing flowering plants.

title: The Buzz About Bee Lawns
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Native images of a white clover bee lawn, white clover flowers and conservation specialist James Wolfin.

title: The Buzz About Bee Lawns
author: Marisa Reyes
content: A bee lawn's goal is to keep pollinators fed and flourishing from early spring until frost, especially when their usual buffet is scarce. Bee lawns also require less mowing, water and fertilizer than conventional lawns.

title: The Buzz About Bee Lawns
author: Marisa Reyes
content: You do not have to transform an entire yard into a bee lawn. If you want space for kids and pets, convert a little-used spot such as a front or side yard while keeping the backyard for play and gatherings.

title: The Buzz About Bee Lawns
author: Marisa Reyes
content: No-Mow May lets lawn and flowering plants grow in spring for early pollinator forage, but mowing afterward can shock turfgrass and remove habitat overnight. James Wolfin advocates slow-mow summer instead: let turfgrass grow up to 6 inches, then cut off one-third. This lets flowering plants in the lawn bloom and feed pollinators throughout the year.

title: The Buzz About Bee Lawns
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Selfheal has high nectar content and attracts syrphid flies and bees. In a University of Minnesota study, 95 percent of bees visiting selfheal blooms were native.

title: The Buzz About Bee Lawns
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Native photos showing a front-yard bee lawn and a syrphid fly or bee visiting selfheal flowers.

title: The Buzz About Bee Lawns
author: Marisa Reyes
content: To start a bee lawn, choose a location and select flowers and grasses. Installing can be as simple as sowing flower seeds into existing turfgrass, but some lawns require removing everything and replanting.

title: The Buzz About Bee Lawns
author: Marisa Reyes
content: James Wolfin prefers seeding in fall right before the first frost in Minnesota, because seeds stay dormant through winter and are kept moist by melting snow and spring rains. In areas without reliable snow cover, start seeds in spring or late fall.

title: The Buzz About Bee Lawns
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Bee lawn seedlings may need extra attention in the first year. Water new plants enough that developing roots do not dry out and pull weeds that might overcrowd the growing plants. By year three, the bee lawn should be in full swing.

title: The Buzz About Bee Lawns
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Maintain an established bee lawn much like turfgrass. When the lawn is 5 to 6 inches tall, trim it without cutting more than one-third. When bee-loving blooms are in full swing, let the mower rest longer so pollinators can feed.

title: The Buzz About Bee Lawns
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Established bee lawns require little fertilizer, if any. One light application of lawn fertilizer in spring or fall is enough, and lawn clippings left to decompose act as natural fertilizer.

title: The Buzz About Bee Lawns
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Remove the lawn and plant new turfgrass and flowers if the existing lawn is filled with aggressive turfgrasses such as perennial ryegrass or tall fescue, or if it contains many invasive weeds such as creeping charlie, dandelions, crabgrass or crownvetch. Remove turfgrass, lightly till, rake smooth and rake seed lightly into bare soil.

title: The Buzz About Bee Lawns
author: Marisa Reyes
content: You can overseed a lawn with flowers if turfgrass is primarily slow-growing Kentucky bluegrass or fine fescues and weeds are sparse. Mow to about 1 inch, rake away clippings and aerate if possible, especially in compacted soil, to improve oxygen, water, nutrient flow and germination.

title: The Buzz About Bee Lawns
author: Marisa Reyes
content: A successful bee lawn seed mix is about 92 percent turfgrass and 8 percent flowering plants.

title: The Buzz About Bee Lawns
author: Marisa Reyes
content: The best grasses for a bee lawn require little water or fertilizer and grow slowly so they do not outcompete companions. Good options include hard fescue, other fine fescues, Kentucky bluegrass, bermudagrass, buffalo grass and blue grama grass.

title: The Buzz About Bee Lawns
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Low-growing flowers for a bee lawn should tolerate mowing and foot traffic and continue blooming. Recommended flowers include white clover, creeping thyme, lanceleaf selfheal, Yaak yarrow, tufted poppy and wild petunia.

title: The Buzz About Bee Lawns
author: Marisa Reyes
content: White clover, Trifolium repens, blooms white from spring to fall, fixes nitrogen and has high pollen and nectar content. It is a honeybee favorite, adapts to different soil types, grows 3 to 6 inches tall and 12 to 18 inches wide, and is cold hardy in USDA zones 3 to 10.

title: The Buzz About Bee Lawns
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Lanceleaf selfheal, Prunella vulgaris subsp. lanceolata, has tube-shaped purple flowers from midsummer to early fall, high nectar content and native value. It grows in a wide range of soil types, reaches 6 to 12 inches tall and 12 to 24 inches wide, and is cold hardy in USDA zones 4 to 9.

title: Butterfly Host Plants
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Butterfly populations have been declining partly because of habitat loss, but gardeners can help by growing host plants. Host plants are where butterflies lay eggs, caterpillars feed, chrysalises form and metamorphosis happens.

title: Butterfly Host Plants
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Female butterflies have special taste organs on their forelegs and feet that help determine whether a plant is suitable for eggs. Some species lay single eggs; others lay clusters, usually on the underside or top of a leaf.

title: Butterfly Host Plants
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Newly hatched caterpillars are little eating machines that usually have four to five growth stages, or instars, over several weeks before forming a chrysalis.

title: Butterfly Host Plants
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Foliage is the most common caterpillar food, though some caterpillars eat flowers. Some species are very specific, such as monarchs that only eat milkweeds, while painted lady larvae have been found feeding on 100 different plants including thistles, hollyhock and members of the pea family.

title: Butterfly Host Plants
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Besides growing butterfly host plants, avoid pesticides and herbicides, even organic solutions such as neem oil or pyrethroids, because they are as deadly to butterflies and young caterpillars as they are to insect pests.

title: Butterfly Host Plants
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Black-eyed Susan, Rudbeckia fulgida, is a drought-tolerant, deer-resistant native wildflower that tolerates clay soil. It hosts silvery checkerspot and malachite butterflies; both caterpillars eat the leaves. The malachite's prickly black-and-red larva may rest on the underside of a leaf.

title: Butterfly Host Plants
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Black-eyed Susan flowers best in full sun, and deadheading encourages additional blooms. Cultivars such as 'Goldsturm' are more likely than the species at garden centers. The perennial has single golden-yellow summer-to-fall blooms with brown centers and grows 2 to 3 feet tall and 1 to 2 feet wide in USDA zones 3 to 9.

title: Butterfly Host Plants
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Illustrations of a malachite butterfly and caterpillar used with the black-eyed Susan host plant profile.

title: Butterfly Host Plants
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Native full-page photo of black-eyed Susan flowers with red companion blooms and a note about checking county extension or butterfliesandmoths.org for local butterfly checklists.

title: Butterfly Host Plants
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Purple prairie clover, Dalea purpurea, is an easy-care native perennial found across much of North America. It grows best in full sun and well-drained soil but also tolerates sandy and clay soil. New plants are slow because they form a taproot that can grow up to 6 feet deep, making established plants drought and heat tolerant but hard to move.

title: Butterfly Host Plants
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Purple prairie clover has small thimblelike cones covered with tiny flowers from summer to early fall. Bees and butterflies visit the flowers, while southern and California dogface butterflies eat the foliage. Striped, Reakirt's and Mexican blue caterpillars eat the leaves and nibble flowers.

title: Butterfly Host Plants
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Purple prairie clover can be planted from plants or seeds. Direct sow or start seeds indoors 4 to 6 weeks before the last frost. Seedlings should emerge in 10 to 12 days and can go outdoors when nighttime temperatures stay above 50 degrees F.

title: Butterfly Host Plants
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Reakirt's blue caterpillars on purple prairie clover may attract ants. The caterpillars release a pheromone to attract ants, then secrete a sweet solution that keeps ants nearby and helps protect against parasitic wasps and flies.

title: Butterfly Host Plants
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Native photo of purple prairie clover with rose-purple flower cones and a caterpillar good-to-know callout.

title: Butterfly Host Plants
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Hollyhock, Alcea rosea, adds tall upright stems with saucer-shaped blooms in almost every color but blue. It hosts painted lady and common checkered skipper butterflies. A silky covering on top of a hollyhock leaf with a spiny dark caterpillar inside indicates painted lady; common checkered skipper caterpillars are green with brown heads and fold leaves around themselves as they feed.

title: Butterfly Host Plants
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Hollyhocks are technically biennial, growing foliage the first year and flowering the second, but many newer series such as Spotlight or Halo bloom the first year from seed. Start seeds indoors 6 to 8 weeks before the last frost. Seedlings can go outdoors when they are 3 to 4 inches tall.

title: Butterfly Host Plants
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Hollyhock grows in full sun to part shade in well-drained soil, reaches 3 to 8 feet tall and 1 to 2 feet wide, and is cold hardy in USDA zones 2 to 10. Painted lady butterflies live on every continent except Australia and Antarctica, so hollyhock growers may find their caterpillars.

title: Butterfly Host Plants
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Native photo of 'Halo Cerise' hollyhock flowers plus painted lady butterfly and caterpillar illustrations.

title: Butterfly Host Plants
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Butterfly weed, Asclepias tuberosa, tastes bad to most animals, but monarchs lay eggs on it. Monarch caterpillars eat the leaves and sometimes the flowers, storing the plant's toxins in their bodies to deter predators.

title: Butterfly Host Plants
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Butterfly weed has bright orange blooms, does not spread as aggressively as some milkweeds and lacks milky white sap when stems break. Buy plants or direct sow seed in fall, because seeds germinate best after cold stratification. You can mimic this by refrigerating seed packets for 2 to 3 months before planting.

title: Butterfly Host Plants
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Butterfly weed grows in full sun and dry, well-drained soil. It has clusters of bright orange flowers from early summer to fall, reaches 12 to 30 inches tall and 12 to 18 inches wide, and is cold hardy in USDA zones 3 to 9.

title: Butterfly Host Plants
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Native photo of bright orange butterfly weed blooms with monarch butterfly and caterpillar illustrations.

title: Butterfly Host Plants
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Snapdragon, Antirrhinum majus, supports common buckeye caterpillars. Common buckeyes migrate north in late spring to summer and are year-round residents in the southern United States and along the California coast, so cool-weather snapdragons provide leaves for caterpillars.

title: Butterfly Host Plants
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Snapdragons have blooms in a wide range of colors and sizes for bouquets and borders. Use 6-inch-tall Candy Showers at the edge, 3-foot-tall 'Rocket Orchid' in midborders and the Potomac series, which can reach 5 feet, at the back.

title: Butterfly Host Plants
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Snapdragons are best in cool weather. When nights regularly reach 70 degrees F, plants slow down and may look ragged. Cut them back and keep watering for fall blooms, or pull them and replace with warm-weather plants. They grow in full sun in moist, well-drained soil and are cold hardy in USDA zones 7 to 10.

title: Butterfly Host Plants
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Native photo of 'Rocket Orchid' snapdragon with common buckeye butterfly and caterpillar illustrations.

title: Butterfly Host Plants
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Parsley, Petroselinum crispum, can be stripped by swallowtail caterpillars. Common black swallowtails are mostly black with yellow spots, and Eastern tiger swallowtails are mostly yellow with black markings. Eastern swallowtail larvae often spin a silk mat on top of a parsley leaf to feed from.

title: Butterfly Host Plants
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Curly-leaf and flat-leaf parsley are biennials often grown as annuals. Plants produce lush foliage the first year and yellow flowers the next. Leaves are less flavorful after flowering, but if blooms dry in place, parsley reseeds for more plants the following year.

title: Butterfly Host Plants
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Parsley grows in full sun to part shade in moist, well-drained soil, reaches 12 to 18 inches tall and 9 to 12 inches wide, and is cold hardy in USDA zones 4 to 11. Mature swallowtail caterpillars stop feeding late in the season, search for a dry stem or leaf on which to form chrysalises, and the last generation hibernates through winter.

title: Butterfly Host Plants
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Trees often appeal to multiple butterfly species and provide plenty of foliage for caterpillars. Hackberry hosts tawny emperor, hackberry emperor, question mark, mourning cloak and American snout. Oaks host hairstreak, Horace's duskywing and red spotted purple. Pussy willow hosts swallowtails and green comma.

title: Butterfly Host Plants
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Native photo of curly parsley with a swallowtail caterpillar, plus tree host notes for hackberry, oak and pussy willow.

title: Butterfly Host Plants
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Sundial lupine, Lupinus perennis, has elegant lavender-to-blue, white or occasionally pink spires from late spring to early summer. Stems grow up to 2 feet tall, and after blooming they form 2-inch fuzzy beanlike seedpods. Plants reseed and spread by rhizomes where happy.

title: Butterfly Host Plants
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Sundial lupine is the only larval host for the endangered Karner blue butterfly, found in scattered locations from eastern Minnesota to New Hampshire and New York. Caterpillars hatch from overwintered eggs in April to early May, eat leaves and flowers, and form chrysalises in 3 to 4 weeks. The second generation lays eggs in July in seedpods or on stems near the ground, where they overwinter.

title: Butterfly Host Plants
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Sundial lupine grows in full sun to part shade in dry, sandy, well-drained soil. Too much clay can cause rot. It reaches 12 to 24 inches tall and 12 to 18 inches wide and is cold hardy in USDA zones 3 to 8.

title: Butterfly Host Plants
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Native photo of sundial lupine with lavender-blue flower spikes used with the Karner blue butterfly host profile.

title: Butterfly Host Plants
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Blue grama grass, Bouteloua gracilis, is a host plant for Unca's skipper, Rhesus skipper, Garita skipperling and Ridings' satyr butterflies. Their caterpillars eat the leaves, and Unca's skipper makes a small foliage nest so it can feed out of predators' sight.

title: Butterfly Host Plants
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Blue grama grass is native to the Great Plains and southwestern United States but works across much of North America and has been used as a lawn replacement. Its slender blue-green foliage and tan horizontal flowers work near the front of a border, and plants mature to golden brown by fall and stand for much of winter.

title: Butterfly Host Plants
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: 'Blonde Ambition' blue grama grass resembles the species but has chartreuse flowers aging to lighter tan and grows larger, 2 to 3 feet tall and wide. Blue grama tolerates a wide range of soils except poorly drained soil, where it may rot, and self-seeds where happy.

title: Butterfly Host Plants
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Ridings' satyr is a small butterfly found in western North America. Caterpillars hibernate underground in small tunnels, which protects them from grazing animals such as deer.

title: Butterfly Host Plants
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Native photo of 'Blonde Ambition' blue grama grass with horizontal seedheads and a note about Ridings' satyr caterpillars.

title: Butterfly Host Plants
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Purple passionflower, Passiflora incarnata, has ornamental 2.5-inch blooms and is easier to grow than it looks. This native vine flowers best in full sun to part shade in well-drained soil and is drought tolerant once established. Organic mulch helps conserve water and keep roots cool.

title: Butterfly Host Plants
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Purple passionflower is the hardiest passionflower, but it is not always reliable in USDA zone 5. In cold areas, provide a protected garden spot or grow it in a container and move it into a garage after freezing temperatures kill the foliage.

title: Butterfly Host Plants
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Purple passionflower hosts gulf and variegated fritillary caterpillars on its slender stems, leaves and flowers. Zebra heliconian larvae also eat the foliage, often feeding at night. The vine has fragrant white flowers with ornate purple crowns in summer, grows 6 to 8 feet tall and 3 to 6 feet wide, and is cold hardy in USDA zones 5 to 9.

title: Butterfly Host Plants
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Weeds can host butterflies too. Broadleaf plantain is a host for common buckeye. Green shrimp plant is invasive in Florida but hosts malachite butterflies. Stinging nettle spreads by rhizomes in moist soil and is a favorite of red admiral butterflies.

title: Butterfly Host Plants
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Native photo of purple passionflower with zebra heliconian butterfly and caterpillar illustrations plus broadleaf plantain weed-host reference.

title: Small Backyard Makeover
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Mary Ann Fordyce's small Seattle garden had a newly built three-story condo looming over the backyard. Places where she used to relax or gather with friends were exposed to upper-story windows, so she hired landscape designer Lisa Bauer to create a backyard retreat with privacy, comfortable seating and room to garden.

title: Small Backyard Makeover
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Before the makeover, the small urban backyard had two large decks that were oversized for the space and left little room for gardening. After the neighboring condo was built, Mary Ann felt like she was living in a fish bowl.

title: Small Backyard Makeover
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Before-and-after native photos showing Mary Ann Fordyce's small Seattle backyard with large decks, exposed neighboring condo views and the updated garden retreat.

title: Small Backyard Makeover
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Native full-page after photo of a small Seattle backyard with seating, deck, gravel patio, containers and screening plantings.

title: Small Backyard Makeover
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Mary Ann's backyard wish list was to get more privacy, add more room for the garden and create outdoor living spaces.

title: Small Backyard Makeover
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: At 1,200 square feet, the backyard is not large, but the makeover created a beautiful garden, room to entertain around the firepit and other spots for reading. Lisa Bauer used strategic screening on several levels so the neighboring condo fades into the background and main seating areas feel comfortable again.

title: Small Backyard Makeover
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Fast-growing Leyland cypress trees along the back property line are evergreen and can reach 70 feet tall, screening the whole yard, softening the fence's horizontal lines and forming a backdrop for the 23-by-17-foot patio border.

title: Small Backyard Makeover
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: A 9-foot-tall arbor covered with evergreen 'Apple Blossom' clematis obscures the view of the firepit seating area from above. Several 4-foot-tall decorative metal panels and a patio umbrella make the deck feel private while letting in light and air.

title: Small Backyard Makeover
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Native image of the reimagined small garden with Leyland cypress screening, 'Apple Blossom' clematis, Tiger Eyes cutleaf staghorn sumac, hakonechloa, tassel fern and deck privacy panels.

title: Small Backyard Makeover
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Removing the large rectangular lower deck and building a smaller square gravel patio provided room for windmill palms around the firepit. These evergreen trees can grow up to 30 feet tall and provide screening from above.

title: Small Backyard Makeover
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: The south-facing backyard is shaded by the tall condo and garage, so tassel ferns and hakonechloa add color and soft texture. Gold from Tiger Eyes cutleaf staghorn sumac and hakonechloa moves the eye through the border and brightens the part-shade area.

title: Small Backyard Makeover
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: With more open space and a gravel surface, Mary Ann could add the firepit she had always wanted. Lightweight fiberglass containers filled with annuals and olive trees bring garden planting onto the deck, soften railing and panels, and the darker earthy palette helps hardscaping recede.

title: Small Backyard Makeover
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Native images of the small backyard's firepit patio, windmill palms, deck containers with olive trees and annuals, and screening plants.

title: Which Colorful Annual is Right for You?
content: Petunias, Petunia species and hybrids, have grown in gardens for nearly 200 years. They now bloom in almost any color on mounded, trailing or spreading forms. Their minimal care and ability to bloom from spring until frost make them versatile in containers and borders.

title: Which Colorful Annual is Right for You?
content: Petunias are cold hardy only in USDA zones 10 to 11, so most gardeners grow them as annuals. They thrive in full sun with consistent moisture. Incorporate slow-release granular fertilizer at planting and apply liquid general-purpose fertilizer every 1 to 2 weeks.

title: Which Colorful Annual is Right for You?
content: Petunia flowering slows when temperatures rise above 85 degrees F. When plants look leggy, cut branches back by one-third to encourage new growth and more blooms. Spent petals may cling to sticky foliage, so deadhead fallen flowers for a cleaner look.

title: Which Colorful Annual is Right for You?
content: Supertunia Vista Bubblegum petunia grows 12 to 24 inches tall and spreads 24 to 36 inches wide with bubblegum-pink flowers that keep blooming in summer heat. Crazytunia Sugar Beet has lemon-yellow flowers with deep burgundy starbursts and red-pink streaks on 6- to 12-inch-tall mounded plants. Supertunia Latte has silvery white flowers with purple-brown veining on 4- to 12-inch-tall plants.

title: Which Colorful Annual is Right for You?
content: Illustrated petunia comparison page showing bloom shape, sticky leaves, plant habit and cultivar photos for Supertunia Vista Bubblegum, Crazytunia Sugar Beet and Supertunia Latte.

title: Which Colorful Annual is Right for You?
content: Calibrachoas are mini petunia lookalikes introduced to garden centers in the late 1980s. Their vibrant colors and patterns made them go-to container plants. They do not always perform well in the ground but grow vigorously in light, well-draining potting mixes.

title: Which Colorful Annual is Right for You?
content: Trailing calibrachoas are spillers for hanging baskets and windowboxes, while smaller mounding types are flowery fillers for tabletop pots. Calibrachoas are cold hardy in USDA zones 9 to 11, prefer temperatures above 55 degrees F and need 6 to 8 hours of sun daily for best bloom.

title: Which Colorful Annual is Right for You?
content: Let calibrachoas dry between waterings but not to wilting, or flowering will slow. Add slow-release fertilizer to potting mix and use a general-purpose liquid feed every two weeks during the growing season. Spent flowers drop off without deadheading; trim plants back by one-third if branches get long and spindly.

title: Which Colorful Annual is Right for You?
content: Eyeconic Compact Sunset calibrachoa has bright orange flowers with a dark orange-red eye on plants 12 to 14 inches tall and 12 to 16 inches wide. Superbells Lemon Slice grows 6 to 12 inches tall and 12 to 24 inches wide with yellow-and-white blooms. MiniFamous Uno Double PinkTastic has pale pink picotee-edged double flowers around deep pink centers on 8- to 10-inch-tall plants.

title: Which Colorful Annual is Right for You?
content: A petchoa, x Petchoa, is a hybrid cross between petunia and calibrachoa. It combines medium-sized flowers, non-sticky foliage and better heat tolerance.

title: Which Colorful Annual is Right for You?
content: Illustrated calibrachoa comparison page showing small blooms, medium-green leaves, mounded or trailing habit and cultivar photos for Eyeconic Compact Sunset, Superbells Lemon Slice and MiniFamous Uno Double PinkTastic.

title: Weigela
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Weigela is considered one of the easiest shrubs to grow. It can grow in clay soil, is deer resistant and attracts hummingbirds with bright tubular flowers.

title: Weigela
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Older weigelas can grow up to 8 feet tall, but many newer small cultivars are available. Cultivars over 5 feet tall, such as 'Java Red', make informal screens or hedges. Sonic Bloom cultivars grow 4 to 5 feet tall for the middle of the border, while low spreading varieties such as Spilled Wine fill front edges.

title: Weigela
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Pair weigela's white, pink or rose-red flowers with spring companions such as bearded iris and peony. After spring, weigela backs up summer annuals and perennials. Many cultivars have a light rebloom from summer through fall.

title: Weigela
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Weigela foliage can warm a border even when the shrub is not blooming. Varieties with wine or copper leaves add richness, and variegated My Monet Purple Effect can work as a pretty filler in a pot.

title: Weigela
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Weigela florida is a shrub with clusters of tubular red, pink or white flowers in late spring to early summer and light rebloom from summer to fall. It grows in full sun in moist, well-drained soil, has no serious pests, reaches 1 to 8 feet tall and wide and is cold hardy in USDA zones 4 to 8.

title: Weigela
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Spilled Wine weigela flows along the front of the border, growing 3 to 4 feet wide with deep red to purple foliage and dark pink spring flowers. Its low habit creates a smooth transition from lawn to bed.

title: Weigela
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Native image of Spilled Wine weigela used at the front of a border with dark foliage and pink flowers, plus a botanical illustration and plant profile.

title: Weigela
author: Jennifer Howell
content: 'Java Red' weigela's dark leaves deepen to maroon as summer progresses. An underplanting of burgundy-leaved coral bells unifies the planting.

title: Weigela
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Native garden photo of 'Java Red' weigela with pink spring flowers, dark maroon foliage and coral bells underplanting.

title: Weigela
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Weigela usually thrives in full sun, but variegated cultivars in the South can use afternoon shade so foliage does not scorch. It grows best in moist, well-drained soil and only needs granular slow-release fertilizer in spring every two to three years.

title: Weigela
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Established weigela can tolerate some summer dryness, but an inch of rain each week gives the best flowering. A 2- to 3-inch mulch layer helps maintain even soil moisture.

title: Weigela
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Weigela does not need deadheading after bloom. Compact cultivars rarely need pruning other than removing dead or damaged branches at any time. Because weigela blooms on the previous year's growth, prune to shape or reduce size right after the first flush of flowers slows in early summer.

title: Weigela
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Larger weigelas such as 'Red Prince' can throw long unruly branches. Every three years, do partial rejuvenation pruning by cutting one-third of the largest branches to the ground to refresh appearance and stimulate new growth from the base, which blooms the following year.

title: Weigela
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Czechmark Trilogy weigela has pink, white and rose-red flowers at once on apple-green foliage in late spring to early summer. It grows 36 to 42 inches tall and wide in USDA zones 4 to 8.

title: Weigela
author: Jennifer Howell
content: 'Red Prince' weigela has red mid- to late-spring flowers that do not fade as they age, with a secondary bloom in late summer to early fall. It grows 6 to 9 feet tall and wide in USDA zones 4 to 8.

title: Weigela
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Sonic Bloom Pearl weigela has white flowers aging to pink from early summer to frost on new and previous year's growth. It grows 4 to 5 feet tall and wide in USDA zones 4 to 8.

title: Weigela
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Wine and Spirits weigela has wine to deep purple foliage in full sun, topped with creamy white late-spring to early-summer flowers. It grows 3 to 5 feet tall and wide in USDA zones 4 to 8.

title: Weigela
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Rainbow Sensation weigela has soft pink early-summer flowers over yellow-and-green variegated leaves. It grows 3 to 4 feet tall and wide in full sun to part shade in USDA zones 4 to 8.

title: Weigela
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Midnight Sun weigela has light pink spring bloom but is grown mainly for coppery orange foliage that turns red to purple in fall. It grows 12 to 18 inches tall and wide for the front of the border in USDA zones 4 to 8.

title: Weigela
author: Jennifer Howell
content: My Monet Purple Effect weigela has light pink late-spring flowers and variegated light green, cream and purple foliage. It grows 18 to 30 inches tall and wide and works in containers or near the front of the border in full sun to part shade in USDA zones 4 to 6.

title: Weigela
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Vinho Verde weigela is grown for striking lime-green foliage with black edges, which attracts more attention than its light red-pink late-spring bloom. It reaches 3 to 5 feet tall and wide in full sun in USDA zones 5 to 8.

title: Weigela
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Native cultivar collage showing weigela flowers and foliage, including red, white and pink blooms, variegated leaves, dark wine foliage and lime-green leaves with black edges.

title: Staking Solutions
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Full-page native photo of false indigo supported by a grow-through hoop with a grid that provides interior support and even spacing for multistemmed plants.

title: Staking Solutions
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: When flowers flop and stems lean, stakes come to the rescue. Garden stakes range from commercial products to DIY projects made from garage leftovers. The best results come from installing supports early and matching the stake to the plant's habit.

title: Staking Solutions
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Grow-through hoops help bushy multistemmed plants stay upright. Open hoops work for slender stems with single flowers such as Shasta daisies, while gridded hoops help plants with heavy blooms such as peonies or tall stems such as false indigo. Choose a hoop two-thirds the plant's mature height when pushed 6 to 12 inches into the ground.

title: Staking Solutions
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: DIY hoops help statuesque plants such as Jerusalem sage. Set three or four tall bamboo or plastic-coated metal stakes around the plant, pushing about one-third of each stake into the soil. Encircle the posts with green twine starting a few inches from the ground, and add more hoops every foot as the plant grows.

title: Staking Solutions
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Metal garden fencing formed into a cylinder supports perennials that grow a mound of foliage. The openings support stems at all levels and are wide enough for thick tall sedum stems to grow through. Overlap the fencing ends a few inches to hold the cylinder together.

title: Staking Solutions
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Native technique photos showing a twine-and-stake hoop for Jerusalem sage and a metal fencing cylinder for tall sedum.

title: Staking Solutions
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Single-loop heavy-wire stakes are useful for single-stemmed plants such as lilies. They protect against strong winds while holding stems loosely enough to move naturally. Use one loop stake per stem, choosing a stake about two-thirds the mature plant height when pushed at least 6 inches into the ground.

title: Staking Solutions
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Bamboo stakes are inexpensive and useful for many plants, including large-flowered gladiolas that flop. Add the stake when planting the corm, keeping it close so foliage can be secured later. Tie stems with twine or garden tape in a figure eight and add ties every 6 to 12 inches as needed.

title: Staking Solutions
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Flexible shrub cuttings tied together can support climbing plants. Yellow-twig dogwood or willow stems can help sweet pea blooms climb to eye and nose level, and the colorful stems are ornamental rather than hidden.

title: Staking Solutions
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Native photos showing loop stakes supporting lilies and cut dogwood stems tied together for climbing sweet peas.

title: Staking Solutions
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Nylon netting is useful for cut flowers that need straight stems, such as a mass row of Sweet William dianthus. Attach netting to stakes at both ends of the row, pull it snug and secure the fence two-thirds the mature plant height above the ground with zip ties. Guide wayward stems into the grid as plants grow.

title: Staking Solutions
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Native technique images showing gladiola tied to a bamboo stake with a figure-eight tie and Sweet William stems guided through nylon netting.

title: Mint
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Mint, Mentha species and hybrids, is a perennial cocktail garden herb used for mojitos, simple syrups and other beverages. It is easy to care for, and deer and rabbits tend to avoid it.

title: Mint
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Mint grows best in full sun to part shade in moist, well-draining soil and is planted in spring. One mint plant is enough for a family of four, and plants are harvested from spring to frost. Mint is cold hardy in USDA zones 3 to 11.

title: Mint
author: Marisa Reyes
content: If growing multiple mint varieties, give each its own garden space or container to prevent mingling and cross-pollination that can blur flavors and aromas. Sterile varieties such as peppermint and pineapple mint avoid cross-pollination.

title: Mint
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Spearmint has sweet, subtle flavor and slightly fuzzy leaves. Cuban mint has mild flavor with hints of citrus and hairy, aromatic leaves. Pineapple mint has variegated foliage, round soft hairy leaves and a slightly sweet apple-like taste. Peppermint has pungent almost spicy flavor with a cooling aftertaste, red-purple stems and dark green leaves.

title: Mint
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Illustrated mint profile with mint sprig, plus photos and descriptions of spearmint, Cuban mint, pineapple mint and peppermint for cocktail uses.

title: Mint
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Mint does not need much attention, and too much fertilizer can reduce flavor intensity. The biggest growing challenge is its vigorous spread. Underground rhizomes move quickly, and stems root where they touch soil, so containers are best unless you want to turn an area over to mint.

title: Mint
author: Marisa Reyes
content: When summer heat causes mint to flower and look untidy, cut it back by one-third or even to the ground to encourage new growth and fresh leaves.

title: Mint
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Divide mint in spring or fall when weather is cooler and plants are dormant, or divide during the growing season if you are controlling it. Let unwanted divisions dry in the sun before composting them, or they may start another mint patch.

title: Mint
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Harvest mint as soon as it emerges in spring. For best flavor, harvest in the morning before plants flower and before afternoon heat. Snip young leaves or sprigs just above a leaf node, harvesting no more than two-thirds of the plant.

title: Mint
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Use fresh mint immediately or wrap sprigs in a damp paper towel inside a plastic bag and store them in the refrigerator. This keeps sprigs usable for up to two weeks.

title: Mint
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Three ways to use mint in drinks are as garnish, muddled leaves and simple syrup. To make mint simple syrup, heat 1/2 cup granulated sugar or honey, 1/2 cup water and 1 to 2 mint sprigs until the sugar dissolves, cool to room temperature and discard herb sprigs. It makes about 2/3 cup.

title: Mint
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Native photo and illustration showing mint used in a cocktail or mocktail, with steps for garnish, muddling and making mint simple syrup.

title: Focus on Flowers
author: Kristin Beane Sullivan
content: Native opener photo of Heather Thomas's New Jersey perennial border with an entry arbor, roses, clematis and layered colorful plantings.

title: Focus on Flowers
author: Kristin Beane Sullivan
content: A couple years after Heather Thomas's family moved into their New Jersey home, she wanted to transform a sideyard once used as kids' play space into a garden destination with perennial borders that remained colorful from spring through fall.

title: Focus on Flowers
author: Kristin Beane Sullivan
content: When a tree growing too close to the house was removed, the spot near the kitchen window became the perfect garden entrance. Heather installed an arbor and began digging out Japanese pachysandra, leaving the area fallow for a few weeks to catch new sprouts before planting peonies, daylilies and roses.

title: Focus on Flowers
author: Kristin Beane Sullivan
content: Heather augmented three original forsythia shrubs with more dug from other spots on the property to create a backdrop hedge for the sideyard flower borders. Careful planning and observation led to her design philosophy called the 4 C's, which keeps borders colorful through the growing season.

title: Focus on Flowers
author: Kristin Beane Sullivan
content: Climbing roses and clematis make a strong pairing on the entry arbor: when the clematis finishes blooming, the roses take center stage.

title: Focus on Flowers
author: Kristin Beane Sullivan
content: Native garden photo of Heather Thomas's entry arbor with climbing roses, clematis and stone path through a colorful flower border.

title: Focus on Flowers
author: Kristin Beane Sullivan
content: Heather's four considerations for flowery borders are cultivars, containers, companion plantings and carryover plants. Together they keep something blooming from the earliest spring bulbs through the last garden mums of autumn.

title: Focus on Flowers
author: Kristin Beane Sullivan
content: Heather grows about 30 varieties of early, midseason and late-blooming tulips to stretch tulip flowers from about 10 days to 4 or 5 weeks. Her allium season starts with 'Purple Sensation' and 'Mount Everest', continues with 'Gladiator' and 'Globemaster', and ends with 'Ambassador'.

title: Focus on Flowers
author: Kristin Beane Sullivan
content: Heather also grows several cultivars of salvia and catmint to create continuity in her borders. Plant names can help clue in succession; for example, 'Spring King' salvia is one of the earliest to bloom.

title: Focus on Flowers
author: Kristin Beane Sullivan
content: Containers provide instant border color. Heather slips in a container of showy annuals until nearby shrubs fill out, then moves the vessel and changes the drop-in planting seasonally. Large containers are easier to move when left empty and filled with preplanted nursery liners, sometimes raised on overturned nursery pots.

title: Focus on Flowers
author: Kristin Beane Sullivan
content: Heather plans companion plantings by leaving space next to each spring-blooming plant for a summer bloomer and a fall bloomer. Bearded irises and peonies carry the border through spring, daylilies and garden phlox take over in summer, and turtlehead and bluebeard close the colorful garden year.

title: Focus on Flowers
author: Kristin Beane Sullivan
content: Heather uses long-blooming carryover plants to bridge slow times. 'Rolly's Favorite' silene takes her from tulips through spring to peonies and roses. She keeps pansies blooming into midsummer by deadheading, fertilizing and shading them with floating row cover on hot sunny days above 90 degrees F.

title: Focus on Flowers
author: Kristin Beane Sullivan
content: Floating row cover is one of Heather's favorite garden tools because it helps protect hydrangea blooms from late frosts and cool-loving plants from heat.

title: Focus on Flowers

content: Heather has noticed fewer Japanese beetles on her roses since she started spreading milky spore powder on her lawn in summer and fall every year. This biological control attacks Japanese beetles at the larval stage before they pupate into beetles.

title: Focus on Flowers
author: Kristin Beane Sullivan
content: Heather gardens largely by herself while running her own business full time, and her lush plantings still face familiar challenges such as clay soil, rabbits and weather stresses.

title: Focus on Flowers
author: Kristin Beane Sullivan
content: Heather discovered heavy clay soil when digging out pachysandra in the front yard. To start new beds, she uses compost from three large compost piles and outside sources. At the back of a border, she lays cardboard on turfgrass and tops it with compost; near the front of a new bed, she removes sod before mixing in compost to make bulb planting easier.

title: Focus on Flowers
author: Kristin Beane Sullivan
content: Heather hides a 9-foot-wide workspace between the hedge and wooden privacy fence behind a flower border. It leaves room to turn a wheelbarrow, holds strawberries in drip-irrigated pots, starts dahlias in grow bags for late-summer garden use and keeps new purchases until she finds spots for them.

title: Focus on Flowers
author: Kristin Beane Sullivan
content: As Heather expands the garden, she populates new spaces with seedlings, cuttings and divisions from her own garden. Salvias, bearded irises and daylilies divide easily and rejuvenate the original plants. The original forsythia hedge supplies cuttings for other hedges around the property.

title: Focus on Flowers
author: Kristin Beane Sullivan
content: Heather saves 30 tender geraniums from year to year, many as houseplants in her office. She lets some go dormant and hangs them bare root in a dark, cool spot until restarting them in spring.

title: Focus on Flowers

content: To filter sun along a path to the vegetable garden, Heather planted five 'Pink Diamond' panicle hydrangea standards in large containers on either side. Morning dappled light becomes blazing afternoon sun, and the hydrangeas will shade astilbes, foxgloves and pansies as they mature.

Ordinary garden center plants become a lush harmonious grouping, with pussy willow stems adding height and fuzzy catkins for texture.

author: Sherri Ribbey

title: 2024 Reader Container Challenge

title: 2024 Reader Container Challenge

title: Create Curb Appeal in Challenging Clay Soil
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Foundation planting can be difficult in clay because foundation excavation brings clay subsoil to the surface and equipment can compact soil. Heavy clay can stay wet, then become rock hard when dry.

title: Create Curb Appeal in Challenging Clay Soil
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Clay soil expands when wet, putting pressure on foundation walls and causing cracks or leaks. When dry, it contracts and pulls away, leaving voids where the foundation may bow or settle. Plantings can worsen the wet-dry cycle if they need extra water or thirsty roots absorb soil moisture.

title: Create Curb Appeal in Challenging Clay Soil
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Slope beds down 6 inches for every 10 feet away from the foundation so water diverts into the planting or lawn. If water collects or will not dry out, get a professional to install drainage.

title: Create Curb Appeal in Challenging Clay Soil
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Native illustration of a foundation planting design in clay soil with colorful curb-appeal plants and flow/drainage guidance.

title: Create Curb Appeal in Challenging Clay Soil
author: Jennifer Howell
content: To avoid foundation problems, maintain consistent soil moisture by watering the whole bed rather than only plant pockets, using soaker hoses or drip irrigation to water slowly and evenly, and applying 2 to 3 inches of mulch so the soil does not dry out quickly.

title: Create Curb Appeal in Challenging Clay Soil
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Plant shrubs and perennials at least 5 feet away from the foundation to allow access and keep roots from entering cracks. Leave at least 6 inches of exposed foundation above soil or mulch, and use a 6- to 12-inch gravel strip beside the foundation to keep the area drier and deter insects.

title: Create Curb Appeal in Challenging Clay Soil
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Choose small trees with less aggressive roots, such as red buckeye, and plant them at least as many feet from the house as the tree will grow tall. Avoid maples and willows close to the house because their roots are invasive and vigorous.

title: Create Curb Appeal in Challenging Clay Soil
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Native illustration of a clay-soil foundation border with labels for breathing room, buffer zone and plant placement away from the house.

title: Create Curb Appeal in Challenging Clay Soil
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Tilling clay soil can make it hard and clumpy, and smooth planting hole walls can cause roots to circle. Use smaller 4-inch perennial specimens to minimize digging, carve grooves into the planting-hole sides with a shovel or soil knife to redirect roots, and backfill with native clay soil rather than compost so plants acclimate.

title: Create Curb Appeal in Challenging Clay Soil
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Plant choice is critical in clay soil. The plan uses plants that tolerate or thrive in clay, and dense soil can inhibit some plants that might otherwise spread aggressively, such as obedient plant.

title: Create Curb Appeal in Challenging Clay Soil
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Arborvitae and deutzia need little pruning except dead branch removal in early spring. Shape deutzia only after it blooms so you do not remove buds that form in summer for next year. Encourage new growth on Berry Heavy Gold winterberry by cutting two to three oldest branches to the ground in early spring every year or two.

title: Create Curb Appeal in Challenging Clay Soil
author: Jennifer Howell
content: To get berries on Berry Heavy Gold winterberry, plant a Mr. Poppins winterberry within 50 feet for pollination.

title: Create Curb Appeal in Challenging Clay Soil
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Most deer ignore the plants in this plan, but other wildlife will visit. Compact Euphoria Ruby Joe Pye weed has vanilla-scented flowers that attract butterflies for months if fading clusters are deadheaded. Coneflower seedheads feed birds in fall and early winter, and hummingbirds visit obedient plant and bee balm.

title: Create Curb Appeal in Challenging Clay Soil
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Planting-plan diagram for a clay-soil foundation garden with switchgrass, deutzia, Joe Pye weed, bugleweed, coneflower, arborvitae, obedient plant, bee balm, winterberry and red buckeye.

title: Create Curb Appeal in Challenging Clay Soil
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Switchgrass 'Hot Rod' has purple panicles from late summer to fall over blue-green grassy foliage that ages red to burgundy. It grows in full sun to part shade, 36 to 40 inches tall and 24 to 36 inches wide, in USDA zones 4 to 9. Plant 6.

title: Create Curb Appeal in Challenging Clay Soil
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Deutzia 'Nikko' is a shrub with white spring flowers and burgundy fall foliage. It grows in full sun to part shade, 1 to 2 feet tall and 2 to 5 feet wide, in USDA zones 5 to 8. Plant 5.

title: Create Curb Appeal in Challenging Clay Soil
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Joe Pye weed Euphoria Ruby has ruby-red flower clusters from summer to fall. It grows in full sun, 24 to 32 inches tall and 24 to 28 inches wide, in USDA zones 4 to 9. Plant 8.

title: Create Curb Appeal in Challenging Clay Soil
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Bugleweed 'Pleasant Pheasant' has blue spring flowers over spreading chartreuse, gold and copper foliage. It grows in part to full shade, 4 to 6 inches tall and 9 to 18 inches wide, in USDA zones 4 to 9. Plant 31.

title: Create Curb Appeal in Challenging Clay Soil
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Baja Burgundy coneflower has burgundy flowers from summer to fall. It grows in full sun to part shade, 18 to 22 inches tall and 22 to 24 inches wide, in USDA zones 4 to 9. Plant 16.

title: Create Curb Appeal in Challenging Clay Soil
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Fire Chief arborvitae has globe-shaped golden foliage in spring that ages to orange in summer and red in fall. It grows in full sun to part shade, 2 to 4 feet tall and wide, in USDA zones 5 to 8. Plant 4.

title: Create Curb Appeal in Challenging Clay Soil
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Obedient plant 'Vivid' has pink flower spikes from midsummer to fall. It grows in full sun, 12 to 24 inches tall and 12 to 18 inches wide, in USDA zones 3 to 9. Plant 14.

title: Create Curb Appeal in Challenging Clay Soil
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Bee balm 'Fireball' has scarlet flower clusters from summer to fall. It grows in full sun to part shade, 12 to 18 inches tall and wide, in USDA zones 4 to 8. Plant 10.

title: Create Curb Appeal in Challenging Clay Soil
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Berry Heavy Gold winterberry has small white flowers in early spring followed by gold berries that persist into winter. It grows in full sun to part shade, 6 to 8 feet tall and wide, in USDA zones 3 to 9. Plant 4 plus a Mr. Poppins winterberry pollinator within 50 feet.

title: Create Curb Appeal in Challenging Clay Soil
author: Jennifer Howell

title: 5 Ways to Use a Fallen Tree in Your Garden
author: Jennifer Howell
content: When a tree is lost, stumps and bulky logs can be hard and expensive to remove. Instead of grinding or hauling away remains, fallen tree parts can add charm to the garden through stumpers, pedestals, seating, planters or fairy-garden features.

title: 5 Ways to Use a Fallen Tree in Your Garden
author: Jennifer Howell
content: A stumpery uses exposed roots, trunks, logs, branches and roots to create an organic forest-floor garden. Plant ferns, hostas, hellebores and epimediums among the remains. Logs and stumps eventually deteriorate, so the garden scene changes over time.

title: 5 Ways to Use a Fallen Tree in Your Garden
author: Jennifer Howell
content: For a sculptural element, pull a stump from the ground, trim small roots, then bury the top until stable, leaving the large roots exposed above ground.

title: 5 Ways to Use a Fallen Tree in Your Garden
author: Jennifer Howell
content: A stump still anchored in the ground or a cut log can become a pedestal for a container, birdbath, bird feeder or statue. Arrange cut logs in groups on a patio or tuck them between perennials for height. Multi-trunked stumps cut at different lengths can become a bird-feeding station.

title: 5 Ways to Use a Fallen Tree in Your Garden
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Native photos of garden uses for fallen tree parts, including a stumpery, a stump pedestal with container and woodland-style log features.

title: 5 Ways to Use a Fallen Tree in Your Garden
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Stumps make unique garden seats. Cut the stump about 18 inches high for most adults, angling slightly to prevent water collecting. If skilled with a chainsaw, carve a back into the wood, or use a stump as a table with a woodburned or painted checkerboard top.

title: 5 Ways to Use a Fallen Tree in Your Garden
author: Jennifer Howell
content: To prolong the life of a stump seat or table, let the wood dry for a couple of months after cutting. Smooth rough surfaces with high-grit sandpaper and apply two to three coats of polyurethane outdoor sealant.

title: 5 Ways to Use a Fallen Tree in Your Garden
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Hollow stumps or logs can become planters. Annuals or perennials need a planting hole at least 6 inches deep for roots. Hollow branches laid on their sides can hold succulents for a table centerpiece, needing only a couple inches of soil.

title: 5 Ways to Use a Fallen Tree in Your Garden
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Filling a log with potting mix and watering plants encourages wood to deteriorate. After several years, if the stump gets weak and crumbly, toss it on the compost pile.

title: 5 Ways to Use a Fallen Tree in Your Garden
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Tree parts can become whimsical gnome homes or fairy gardens. A hollow stump can be a house, branch holes become windows or doors, bark can form a shingled roof, twigs make a ladder and bugleweed can become a lawn.

title: 5 Ways to Use a Fallen Tree in Your Garden

title: Q&A
content: Fasciation causes crowded leaves or flowers and flattened distorted stems, such as on perennial geranium. It is a random genetic mutation, is not fatal, is rarely transmitted by insects or cuttings and seldom repeats the next year.

title: Q&A
content: Most autumn sage, Salvia greggii, cultivars grow 2 to 4 feet tall and can become gangly. To reduce height and encourage a dense compact shape, cut all stems back by one-third to one-half in spring. If plants die back extensively each winter, prune stems as low as 4 to 6 inches when new growth starts.

title: Q&A
content: To prevent autumn sage reseeding, deadhead spent blooms. While deadheading, shorten some stems here and there to keep the shape tidy.

title: Q&A
content: Honeybees flying early in the neighborhood are often doing spring cleaning, called a cleansing flight. Bees are moving away from the nest for a bathroom break and are also ready for fresh food as temperatures start reaching 55 degrees F in early spring.

title: Q&A
content: Early-blooming maple and ash trees provide pollen for honeybees, and weeds such as dandelions can help supply pollen after winter. If feeding bees before garden bloom, check with any nearby beekeeper first. Make nectar with one part white sugar and one part water, boiling the water before adding sugar, then use a hummingbird feeder without a bee guard.

title: Q&A
content: Do not feed honeybees with honey because it can carry pathogens and may encourage aggression. Stop putting out sugar nectar once many flowers open, because too much sugar affects honey quality. In a dry spring, provide water with a birdbath or shallow saucer.

title: Q&A
content: Native Q&A images showing honeybee context and a fasciated perennial geranium stem with flattened distorted growth.

title: Q&A
content: Multiflora rose, Rosa multiflora, is a woody shrub imported to North America in the late 1800s as a rootstock for ornamental roses before escaping cultivation. It has clusters of small fragrant pale pink to white flowers in early summer on thorny 10- to 15-foot arching stems. Canes arch and root, forming dense thickets.

title: Q&A
content: Multiflora rose prefers full sun but tolerates dense shade. It establishes quickly in rich to poor soil in minimally cultivated or rarely mowed areas. It does not tolerate wet soil or winter temperatures below -28 degrees F.

title: Q&A
content: Multiflora rose can host rose rosette disease, so remove all plants within 300 feet of cultivated roses, about how far the disease-transmitting mite can travel. Pull or dig seedlings. Cut mature plants to the ground or dig them, and keep mowing new growth several times per year until sprouting stops. Use leather gloves for thorn protection.

title: Q&A
content: Crape myrtle bark scale, Acanthococcus lagerstroemiae, has spread wherever crape myrtles grow. It is rarely fatal to healthy crape myrtles, but it is unsightly and can reduce vigor and flowering. Severe cases can cause stunted growth or dead branches.

title: Q&A
content: Crape myrtle bark scale has small feltlike white or pale gray egg sacs along branches that release up to 300 pink nymphs. Nymphs crawl and attach to bark to feed, while adults excrete sticky honeydew that turns into sooty black mold on leaves, bark and surfaces underneath.

title: Q&A
content: Horticultural oils suffocate crape myrtle bark scale at any life stage. Before spraying, scrub off severe infestation with soapy water and a stiff brush. Multiple sprays during the growing season are likely because several generations can occur each year.

title: Q&A
content: Native Q&A images of multiflora rose flowers and crape myrtle bark scale feeding on a crape myrtle trunk.

title: Add a Touch of the Tropics
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Chinese ground orchid, Bletilla striata, is an exotic-looking but easy-going garden orchid for gardeners without mild winters. Plants grow from pseudobulbs that store nutrients for overwintering, each producing three to five sword-shaped pale green leaves that last until frost.

title: Add a Touch of the Tropics
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Chinese ground orchid has 1.5-inch pink-purple orchidlike blooms. Each stem has 12 blooms from mid- to late spring, followed by green seedheads that age brown as they mature.

title: Add a Touch of the Tropics
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Grow Chinese ground orchid in clusters or drifts under a canopy of trees or along a border edge where flowers can be enjoyed up close. In the right conditions, plants naturalize by underground rhizomes and seeds, creating a carpet of color from mid- to late spring.

title: Add a Touch of the Tropics
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Plant Chinese ground orchid bulbs in early spring after frost danger passes, 2 to 3 inches deep and 8 to 12 inches apart. Apply 1 to 2 inches of compost at planting and avoid fertilizing for the first year or two.

title: Add a Touch of the Tropics
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Divide Chinese ground orchid in fall if you have enough plants, carefully digging pseudobulbs and separating them into sections before replanting at the original depth. In zone 5, protect plants before first frost with 3 to 4 inches of mulch or straw. In colder zones, overwinter pseudobulbs indoors in a cool dark place like tender bulbs.

title: Add a Touch of the Tropics
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Chinese ground orchid grows in part shade in moist, well-drained soil, has no serious pests, reaches 12 to 18 inches tall and 6 to 12 inches wide, and is cold hardy in USDA zones 5 to 9.

title: Add a Touch of the Tropics
author: Marisa Reyes
content: The Shade Garden Trio pairs Chinese ground orchid with 'Maggie Daley' astilbe and 'Emerald Mist' brunnera. Orchid blooms and brunnera's blue flowers and silvery foliage bring early excitement, while astilbe's pink-lavender plumes sustain color in midsummer.

title: Shade Dazzlers!
content: Hosta 'Blue Vision' has white summer flowers and cup-shaped blue-green leaves. It grows in part to full shade in moist, well-drained soil, 16 to 20 inches tall or 24 inches in bloom and 24 to 36 inches wide, in USDA zones 3 to 9.

title: Shade Dazzlers!
content: Siberian squill, Scilla siberica, is a bulb with blue early-spring flowers that naturalize easily. It grows in full sun to part shade in well-drained soil, 3 to 6 inches tall and 2 to 3 inches wide, in USDA zones 2 to 8.

title: Shade Dazzlers!
content: Red monkey flower, Mimulus puniceus, is a tender shrub with red summer flowers loved by hummingbirds and butterflies. It grows in part shade in dry, well-drained soil, 2 to 3 feet tall and wide, in USDA zones 9 to 11.

title: Shade Dazzlers!
content: Browallia, Browallia speciosa, is a tender perennial with blue-purple flowers from summer to frost. It grows in full sun to part shade in well-drained soil, 12 to 18 inches tall and 9 to 12 inches wide, in USDA zones 9 to 11.

title: Shade Dazzlers!
content: Solomon's seal 'Double Stuff', Polygonatum odoratum pluriflorum, has white late-spring flowers and variegated white leaf edges. It grows in part to full shade in well-drained soil, 24 to 26 inches tall and 12 to 16 inches wide, in USDA zones 3 to 8.

title: Shade Dazzlers!
content: Common bear's breeches, Acanthus mollis, has white and burgundy blooms from late spring to midsummer. It grows in part shade in moist, well-drained soil, 3 to 5 feet tall and 2 to 3 feet wide, in USDA zones 7 to 11.

title: Shade Dazzlers!
content: Serbian bellflower, Campanula poscharskyana, has purple or blue flowers in late spring. It grows in full sun to part shade in moist, well-drained soil, 6 to 10 inches tall and 18 to 24 inches wide, in USDA zones 3 to 8.

title: Shade Dazzlers!
content: Queen of the prairie, Filipendula rubra, has fluffy pink summer blooms. It grows in full sun to part shade in moist, well-drained soil, 4 to 8 feet tall and 2 to 4 feet wide, in USDA zones 3 to 9.

title: New & Improved Lawn Mower
author: Jamie Seitz
content: For the first two and a half decades that Jamie and her husband owned homes, they only had two hand-me-down lawn mowers. Their first inherited mower technically worked but required tinkering, regular spark plugs, a fight with the pull cord and wheels that threatened to roll away midtrim.

title: New & Improved Lawn Mower
author: Jamie Seitz
content: At their second home, Jamie wanted a new mower, while her husband researched ways to reattach a wheel and get more years from the existing mower. The second mower was newer but sounded like a jet engine and released black smoke for the first few passes.

title: New & Improved Lawn Mower
author: Jamie Seitz
content: Jamie and her family noticed neighbors using electric mowers and liked the idea of no gas or oil. Their small yard was well suited to electric, but her husband resisted buying something new while they had a mower in the garage.

title: New & Improved Lawn Mower
author: Jamie Seitz
content: For Father's Day, Jamie and the kids surprised her husband with a new electric mower. It has a bag that reduces fall raking, starts with a button instead of a rip cord, runs quietly, cuts the lawn on one charge, collects clippings for compost and folds in half in the shed.

title: from the editor
author: Kristin Beane Sullivan
content: This summer, Kristin is aiming for a good enough garden. With a construction project, a busy summer of travel and other responsibilities, the garden is not getting much attention. Instead of pulling every weed, deadheading every flower, fussing with containers and sweeping mulch off steppers, she is hitting the high points, such as deadheading daylilies along the sidewalk and letting front-yard plantings look good from a distance.

content: With less time and a two-year drought, Kristin is taking a hard look at plants' drought tolerance before buying. title: from the editor

content: Kristin suggests foregoing garden guilt and celebrating good enough gardens, where flowers still bloom among weeds and roots grow deeper without frequent water.

title: Reader Tips
author: Nolynne Lewis, ON Canada
content: Nolynne keeps a small square of nonslip cupboard liner in her garden caddy and one next to her hose spigot. When it is time to undo wet hose connections, the rubberlike material provides the extra grip needed to disconnect the hose.

title: Reader Tips
author: Mary Dickinson, IL
content: Mary saves nursery pots instead of sending them to the landfill. When she prepared to mulch a newly planted garden bed, she inverted one pot over each new plant so she could spread mulch quickly and evenly without burying the plants.

title: Reader Tips
author: Tammy Troglin, GA
content: To water hanging baskets without creating a puddle underneath, Tammy puts a disposable shower cap on the outside of the basket to cover the holes and collect the water. The elastic holds it in place and stretches to fit a variety of basket sizes.

title: Reader Tips
author: Kathleen Ryan, NY
content: Kathy recommends using two kneeling pads to move along a garden bed with less up-and-down effort. Stay kneeling on one cushion while grabbing the other and placing them end to end, then shuffle a little to the side on your knees.

title: Reader Tips
author: Jean Gensemer, PA
content: Jean makes watering more efficient by attaching a hose splitter to the spigot in early summer and running a hose through the garden border on each side of the yard. She nestles the hoses into the backs of the borders so they are out of sight but easy to access, reducing dragging, straining and kinking.

title: Reader Tips
content: Snake flies, Raphidioptera raphidiidae, are long, slender beneficial insects that prey on aphids, mites and springtails. Adults have a long necklike prothorax, translucent double wings, dark brown or green bodies, large eyes and long antennae; females have a needlelike extension from the thorax.

title: Reader Tips
content: Snake fly females lay eggs under tree bark in fall. Larvae hatch a few weeks later and remain under bark, rocks or shrubs, where they eat eggs and larvae of other insects, sometimes for several years before pupating into adults that live one to three months.

title: Reader Tips
content: Snake flies are most commonly found in orchards and woodlands in the western United States. If you have aphids or other preferred prey and live near their habitat, avoiding pesticides helps attract snake flies and other beneficial insects.

title: How to Spot a Drought-Tolerant Plant
content: All plants transpire, taking in moisture from the soil and losing it through their foliage. Some leaves naturally do this slowly, allowing plants to be more drought tolerant. Five common leaf characteristics help plants survive dry conditions.

title: How to Spot a Drought-Tolerant Plant
content: Small or narrow leaves have a small surface area, which means less evaporation. Examples include thyme, Thymus vulgaris, a perennial for zones 5 to 9; switchgrass, Panicum virgatum, a perennial for zones 3 to 9; and rosemary, Salvia rosmarinus, a tender perennial for zones 8 to 10.

title: How to Spot a Drought-Tolerant Plant
content: Succulent leaves are fat leaves that help store moisture. Examples include tall sedum, Hylotelephium hybrids, a perennial for zones 3 to 10; hen and chicks, Sempervivum spp. and hybrids, a perennial for zones 4 to 9; and ice plant, Delosperma hybrids, a perennial for zones 6 to 10.

title: How to Spot a Drought-Tolerant Plant
content: Gray or silver leaves reflect heat and light. Examples include dichondra, Dichondra argentea, a tender perennial for zones 9 to 11; artemisia, Artemisia stelleriana, a perennial for zones 3 to 10; and curry plant, Helichrysum italicum, a tender perennial for zones 8 to 11.

title: How to Spot a Drought-Tolerant Plant
content: Waxy leaves have an extra coating that holds in moisture. Examples include wax begonia, Begonia semperflorens, a tender perennial for zones 10 to 11; holly, Ilex x meserveae, a shrub for zones 5 to 9; and century plant, Agave americanum, a tender perennial for zones 6 to 10.

title: How to Spot a Drought-Tolerant Plant
content: Woolly or hairy leaves shade the tops of leaves and raise humidity on the undersides. Examples include lamb's ear, Stachys byzantina, a perennial for zones 4 to 8; mullein, Verbascum spp. and hybrids, a perennial for zones 5 to 8; and pulmonaria, Pulmonaria spp. and hybrids, a perennial for zones 3 to 9.

title: Dynamic Duos
author: Marisa Reyes
content: The right plant pairings can transform an outdoor space into a living masterpiece. Four summer-to-fall combinations promise beautiful plant partnerships and plenty of pollinators.

title: Dynamic Duos
author: Marisa Reyes
content: ProCut White Nite sunflower's large creamy white blooms with dark centers tower above the delicate white flowers of 'Cupcakes White' cosmos. The bold sunflowers make a strong statement, and the cosmos foliage adds a soft, feathery texture around the sturdy sunflower stems.

title: Dynamic Duos
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Sunflowers and cosmos both thrive in full sun in average, well-drained soil. Sunflowers prefer deep, infrequent watering and fertilizer after planting and every four to six weeks. Cosmos are drought tolerant once established, need less feeding and benefit from deadheading spent blooms.

title: Dynamic Duos
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Sunflower, Helianthus annuus ProCut White Nite, is an annual with 4- to 6-inch pale yellow flowers with dark centers from summer to fall. It grows in full sun, 5 to 6 feet tall and 1 to 2 feet wide.

title: Dynamic Duos
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Cosmos, Cosmos bipinnatus 'Cupcakes White', is an annual with cup-shaped white flowers with yellow centers from summer to fall. It grows in full sun, 3 to 4 feet tall and 1 to 2 feet wide.

title: Dynamic Duos
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Native vertical photo of ProCut White Nite sunflowers and white cosmos blooming together in a full-sun pairing.

title: Dynamic Duos
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Feverfew's citrus-scented foliage naturally repels pests while attracting predatory beneficial insects, such as hoverflies.

title: Dynamic Duos
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Fragrant white-and-yellow feverfew flowers brighten full-sun gardens with bold blue statice. The pair adds complexity to a border and works well for fresh or dried cut-flower bouquets.

title: Dynamic Duos
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Feverfew spreads by rhizomes and self-seeding, so deadhead spent blooms and divide every few years in spring or fall. Cut plants back after the first hard frost. Statice can act as a perennial in zones 8 and warmer and has a two-week vase life; cut stems once blooms are fully open.

title: Dynamic Duos
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Feverfew, Tanacetum parthenium, is a perennial with white flowers with yellow centers from summer to fall. It grows in full sun to part shade, 1 to 3 feet tall and 1 to 2 feet wide, and is cold hardy in USDA zones 5 to 8.

title: Dynamic Duos
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Statice, Limonium sinuatum 'Seeker Blue', is a tender perennial with funnel-shaped, papery blue flowers in summer. It grows in full sun, 24 to 40 inches tall and 12 inches wide, and is cold hardy in USDA zones 8 to 11.

title: Dynamic Duos
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Gloriosa daisy's sunny yellow petals and dark brown central cones provide a classic feel, while Lilliput Mix zinnia's pink pompon blooms add contrast. The full-sun duo is low maintenance, deer resistant and benefits from slow-release fertilizer or compost in spring.

title: Dynamic Duos
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Gloriosa daisy, Rudbeckia hirta, is a perennial with yellow flowers with dark centers from summer to fall. It grows in full sun, 1 to 3 feet tall and wide, and is cold hardy in USDA zones 3 to 9.

title: Dynamic Duos
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Zinnia, Zinnia elegans Lilliput Mix, is an annual with pink, red, purple, orange, white or yellow double flowers with yellow centers from summer to fall. It grows in full sun, 18 to 24 inches tall and 24 to 36 inches wide.

title: Dynamic Duos
author: Marisa Reyes
content: 'Fireworks' globe amaranth has hot-pink flower heads tipped with bright yellow, while 'Buenos Aires' verbena has airy lavender-purple clusters on tall slender stems. Plant them in full sun and well-drained soil; in the South, give afternoon shade and deadhead verbena to prevent unwanted reseeding.

title: Dynamic Duos
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Verbena, Verbena bonariensis 'Buenos Aires', is a perennial with clusters of lavender-purple flowers from summer to frost. It grows in full sun, 36 to 48 inches tall and 18 to 24 inches wide, and is cold hardy in USDA zones 7 to 9.

title: Dynamic Duos
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Globe amaranth, Gomphrena globosa 'Fireworks', is an annual with hot-pink flower heads tipped with bright yellow from early summer to fall. It grows in full sun, 3 to 4 feet tall and 1 to 2 feet wide.
