title: Creating Gardens for Conversation
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Landscape architect Lynn Kuhn explains that a comfortable garden can nurture meaningful personal connections. Her five components turn a collection of plants into a conversation garden: a grabber, spatial definition, thoughtful furnishings, mitigation of Mother Nature and green plants.

title: Creating Gardens for Conversation
author: Jennifer Howell
content: A grabber draws you to a space and makes you want to linger, such as a colorful plant, inviting bench, ornate arbor or sentimental sculpture. Spatial definition uses solid walls and ceilings or implied boundaries to create a sense of safety and enclosure where conversations can flow.

title: Creating Gardens for Conversation
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Thoughtful furnishings such as comfortable seating encourage visitors to stay and chat, while tables, games or firepits define the activity in a space. Shelter from sun, wind, rain, noise and insects makes the garden more usable and pleasant, and plants provide a healing connection to nature.

title: Creating Gardens for Conversation
author: Jennifer Howell
content: A wooden gazebo forms a roof with implied walls in an outdoor room. A brick floor completes the space, and its size defines the kind of gathering there, limiting the number of people to a small, cozy group.

title: Creating Gardens for Conversation
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Native garden photo of a wooden gazebo framed by lush foliage, illustrating spatial definition in a conversation garden.

title: Creating Gardens for Conversation
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Mature trees provide a shady canopy around the gazebo, while ferns and woodland plants create a cool, serene feeling. Potted ferns echo in-ground ferns to create unity, and vines climbing trellis pillars soften the transition between hardscaping and garden.

title: Creating Gardens for Conversation
author: Jennifer Howell
content: A colorful tablecloth in a sea of tranquil green draws visitors into the gazebo space. A succulent centerpiece and colorful hanging basket serve as conversation starters.

title: Creating Gardens for Conversation
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Native full-page garden photo of a shaded gazebo dining area surrounded by ferns and woodland foliage.

title: Creating Gardens for Conversation
author: Jennifer Howell
content: A home's partially concealed entry uses the patio's open space at the end of a curved path as the grabber. Orange pillows then draw attention to the large cozy seating area where guests can pause and chat as they arrive.

title: Creating Gardens for Conversation
author: Jennifer Howell
content: A curved wall creates privacy around a couch that fits into the shape for comfortable interactions. A circular arrangement gives a sense of equality, and for a group of six or fewer, seats should be within 7 to 9 feet so conversation is easy.

title: Creating Gardens for Conversation
author: Jennifer Howell
content: A sunken floor gives an actual feeling of enclosure in an open room. The half wall provides seating for many guests, and when more than six people are in a space, pillows, seats or tables should be arranged in clusters so smaller groups can gather for personal conversation.

title: Creating Gardens for Conversation
author: Jennifer Howell
content: A canopy of trees provides shade while open walls allow a cool breeze. The sunken floor brings seating below the planted berm for wind protection, and the firepit adds warmth and light on chilly nights.

title: Creating Gardens for Conversation
author: Jennifer Howell
content: An evergreen windbreak and slatted wooden screen offer privacy, noise reduction and wind protection. Placed within a few feet of the seating area, they work better than if they were across the yard. A sun sail hung at least 8 feet over the patio can cool the space like a ceiling.

title: Creating Gardens for Conversation
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Lush containers give a patio color and a tropical vibe. Pots can be moved apart for larger groups or closer together for privacy, and fragrant flowers or foliage can set a mood.

title: Grow a Colorful Shade Garden
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Shade gardens have fewer weeds to pull and can feel 10 to 15 degrees cooler because the sun is not hitting your skin. The challenge is creating colorful borders to accent those laid-back retreats.

title: Grow a Colorful Shade Garden
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Shade gardens are often filled with green texture, but plenty of shade-loving plants make a splash with bright flowers and bold foliage. The plant icons in the story identify part shade, full shade, drought tolerance and deer resistance.

title: Grow a Colorful Shade Garden
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Hosta, Hosta spp. and hybrids, grows best with regular moisture in part to full shade. Gold-foliaged hostas are brightest near the edge of shade, blue hostas stay blue in deeper shade, and variegated types tolerate a range of light conditions.

title: Grow a Colorful Shade Garden
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Hosta has white, purple or lavender blooms in late spring to early fall and variegated or solid leaves in green, blue, white, gold or chartreuse. It grows in moist, well-drained soil, 3 to 72 inches tall and 6 to 72 inches wide, and is cold hardy in USDA zones 3 to 9.

title: Grow a Colorful Shade Garden
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Hosta scapes, or flowering stems, vary in height. Some just top the foliage while others, such as those of 'Miss America', tower over it. Once the blooms finish, cut the scapes off below the foliage for a tidier look.

title: Grow a Colorful Shade Garden
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Native plant portrait photo of 'Miss America' hosta in a shade garden with variegated foliage and tall bloom scapes.

title: Grow a Colorful Shade Garden
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Hardy cyclamen species such as purple cyclamen, round-leaved cyclamen and ivy-leaved cyclamen make excellent shade garden plants. They need regular moisture in spring but well-drained soil so corms do not rot, and they prefer to stay dry during summer dormancy.

title: Grow a Colorful Shade Garden
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Plant corms of spring-flowering cyclamen in fall a couple inches below the soil surface and cover them with 1 to 2 inches of bark mulch in zones 6 and colder. Move the mulch away in late winter so small plants have room to take off.

title: Grow a Colorful Shade Garden
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Cyclamen, Cyclamen spp. and hybrids, has pink, magenta, white or bicolor blooms in early spring or fall and blue-green leaves with silvery patterns. It grows in full sun to part shade, average or moist well-drained soil, 2 to 16 inches tall and wide, and is cold hardy in USDA zones 5 to 8.

title: Grow a Colorful Shade Garden
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Cyclamen goes dormant in summer, so grow it with drought-tolerant ferns or ground covers to fill the bare space it leaves behind.

title: Grow a Colorful Shade Garden
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Native plant portrait photo of ivy-leaved cyclamen blooming at the base of a tree in shade.

title: Grow a Colorful Shade Garden
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Ligularia has big leathery leaves that are showstopping in a shady border. Foliage may be round or deeply lobed, green or burgundy, and yellow daisy-shaped blooms appear in clusters or spikes. Consistent moisture and plenty of shade are the keys to foliage that does not burn or die back.

title: Grow a Colorful Shade Garden
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Ligularia, Ligularia spp. and hybrids, has yellow daisy-shaped blooms in summer and green or burgundy foliage. It grows in part to full shade, moist well-drained soil, 1 to 6 feet tall and 1 to 4 feet wide, and is cold hardy in USDA zones 3 to 9.

title: Grow a Colorful Shade Garden
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Foamflower thrives in heavy shade and is usually passed by deer. In humus-rich, well-drained soil, it spreads by stolons to form small clumps, with pink or white bottlebrush blooms lasting up to six weeks in spring and burgundy markings on the leaves.

title: Grow a Colorful Shade Garden
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Foamflower, Tiarella spp. and hybrids, has pink or white bottlebrush flowers in spring and maple-leaf-shaped to deeply lobed foliage in green or green with burgundy markings. It grows in part to full shade, moist well-drained soil, 2 to 28 inches tall and 6 to 36 inches wide, and is cold hardy in USDA zones 3 to 9.

title: Grow a Colorful Shade Garden
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Native plant portrait photo of 'Bottle Rocket' ligularia with yellow flower spikes and broad leaves.

title: Grow a Colorful Shade Garden
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Native plant portrait photo of Stargazer Mercury foamflower with white bottlebrush blooms and marked foliage.

title: Grow a Colorful Shade Garden
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Bugleweed is a vigorous drought-tolerant ground cover that spreads by stolons between plants or pavers along a shady path. Foliage hybrids include glossy purple 'Black Scallop', tricolor 'Burgundy Glow' and bright-yellow 'Tropical Toucan'.

title: Grow a Colorful Shade Garden
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Bugleweed, Ajuga reptans, has purple, blue, white or pink spikes in spring and green, burgundy, gold, purple or tricolor foliage. It grows in full sun to part shade, average or moist well-drained soil, 4 to 10 inches tall and 10 to 24 inches wide, and is cold hardy in USDA zones 3 to 9.

title: Grow a Colorful Shade Garden
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Pulmonaria's early spring flowers and gorgeous foliage look good all season, even in dry soil. Most varieties have green leaves with silver spots, while 'Silver Bouquet' has solid silver leaves and blooms that change from pink to purple to blue.

title: Grow a Colorful Shade Garden
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Pulmonaria, Pulmonaria spp. and hybrids, has blue, pink, white or purple spring blooms and narrow or broad leaves that are spotted, streaked or solid silver. It grows in part to full shade, average well-drained soil, 6 to 18 inches tall and 10 to 40 inches wide, and is cold hardy in USDA zones 3 to 9.

title: Grow a Colorful Shade Garden
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Native plant portrait photo of 'Black Scallop' bugleweed with glossy dark foliage.

title: Grow a Colorful Shade Garden
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Native plant portrait photo of pulmonaria spring flowers and spotted foliage.

title: Grow a Colorful Shade Garden
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Native plant portrait photo of 'Silver Bouquet' pulmonaria with silver foliage.

title: Grow a Colorful Shade Garden
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: 'Sun King' aralia has golden yellow leaves that add bright color in part shade and turn chartreuse in heavy shade. Tiny white midsummer flowers feed bees, and birds eat purple-black berries in late summer.

title: Grow a Colorful Shade Garden
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Aralia, Aralia cordata, has insignificant white summer flowers and green or gold foliage. It grows in part to full shade, average or moist well-drained soil, 3 to 4 feet tall and wide, and is cold hardy in USDA zones 3 to 9.

title: Grow a Colorful Shade Garden
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: In Asia, aralia is grown for edible young shoots, which taste like asparagus and can be blanched, stir-fried or used in tempura.

title: Grow a Colorful Shade Garden
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Native plant portrait photo of 'Sun King' aralia with bright golden foliage in shade.

title: Grow a Colorful Shade Garden
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Wax begonias bloom from late spring to frost in shade with no need for deadheading or extra watering. Series range from the 6- to 8-inch Ambassador series to the bronze-leaved Cocktail series and 18-inch Double Up series with fancy flowers.

title: Grow a Colorful Shade Garden
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Wax begonia, Begonia semperflorens, has pink, red, orange, white or bicolor blooms from spring to frost and glossy round green or burgundy leaves. It grows in full sun to full shade, average or moist well-drained soil, 6 to 34 inches tall and 6 to 12 inches wide, and is cold hardy in USDA zones 10 to 11.

title: Grow a Colorful Shade Garden
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Caladium provides nonstop foliage color for containers or shady borders with arrowhead leaves in red, white, green, pink or combinations. Plant tubers only after soil reaches at least 65 degrees F; in cold regions, start them indoors six to eight weeks before planting outside.

title: Grow a Colorful Shade Garden
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Caladiums are heavy feeders and like regular moisture. Apply mulch at planting and feed monthly with low-nitrogen liquid plant food, because too much nitrogen or soil over 85 degrees F causes leaves to produce more green than bright color.

title: Grow a Colorful Shade Garden
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Caladium, Caladium hybrids, rarely produces a white to pink summer bloom and has arrowhead leaves mottled, splashed or speckled with red, white or pink. It grows in part to full shade, average or moist well-drained soil, 8 to 24 inches tall and 6 to 24 inches wide, and is cold hardy in USDA zones 9 to 11.

author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Native plant portrait photo of Double Up Pink wax begonia with pink blooms.

author: Sherri Ribbey

title: Grow a Colorful Shade Garden
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Coleus comes in many leaf shapes and colors. Kong Jr. Scarlet has broad heart-shaped leaves splashed with burgundy and grows 18 to 24 inches tall and 20 to 35 inches wide. Coleus needs regular water, and some varieties need deadheading if you dislike spiky blooms.

title: Grow a Colorful Shade Garden
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Coleus, Plectranthus hybrids, has lavender spikes in late summer and a wide range of leaf shapes, colors and patterns. It grows in full sun to full shade, moist well-drained soil, 6 to 48 inches tall and 10 to 40 inches wide, and is cold hardy in USDA zones 10 to 12.

title: Grow a Colorful Shade Garden
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Wishbone flower offers spring-to-frost container color on a shady patio or shepherd's hook. Mounded series such as Kauai and Hi-Lite fill gaps in pots, while trailing series such as Catalina and Summer Wave soften container and hanging-basket edges.

title: Grow a Colorful Shade Garden
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Wishbone flower, Torenia hybrids, has white, rose, purple, yellow or blue blooms, often with a contrasting throat, from spring to frost. It grows in part to full shade, average well-drained soil, 2 to 16 inches tall and 8 to 12 inches wide, and is cold hardy in USDA zones 10 to 11.

title: Which Annual Vine Is Right for You?
content: Morning glory vines can cover a 6-foot-tall trellis in six weeks, giving fast color. Lush foliage is loaded with flowers that open early in the morning and wither by midday, lasting longer in afternoon shade or on cloudy days.

title: Which Annual Vine Is Right for You?
content: Morning glory works well in the ground on fences, trellises and arbors, and it can grow in containers with a climbing structure. Supports should be less than 1/2 inch in diameter so tendrils can twine around them easily.

title: Which Annual Vine Is Right for You?
content: Morning glory is commonly grown as an annual but may overwinter in USDA zones 10 to 12. Direct-sow seeds outdoors when soil is above 60 degrees F, or start indoors in biodegradable pots because roots dislike disturbance. Plants bloom best in full sun with consistent moisture and may reseed heavily.

title: Which Annual Vine Is Right for You?
content: Morning glory, Ipomoea spp. and hybrids, has delicate funnel-shaped flowers 2 to 6 inches across in blue, red, purple, pink, magenta or white, with each flower lasting one day. Medium green heart-shaped leaves grow on twining vines 6 to 15 feet tall.

title: Which Annual Vine Is Right for You?
content: 'Heavenly Blue' morning glory has azure-blue 4-inch flowers and grows 8 to 12 feet tall. 'Flying Saucers' has white petals streaked with sky blue on 10- to 12-foot vines. 'Split Second' has twisty, frilled pink double flowers on 6- to 10-foot vines.

title: Which Annual Vine Is Right for You?
content: Moonflower, Ipomoea alba, differs from other morning glories because it blooms at night with fragrant white flowers that attract nocturnal moths for pollination.

title: Which Annual Vine Is Right for You?
content: Black-eyed Susan vine has a vining habit like morning glory but smaller flowers in warm bright colors. It is not related to North American native perennial black-eyed Susan, but it attracts butterflies, bees and hummingbirds.

title: Which Annual Vine Is Right for You?
content: Black-eyed Susan vine works well vining up a trellis in containers or cascading from hanging baskets. It can also grow in the ground along a fence, arbor or obelisk.

title: Which Annual Vine Is Right for You?
content: To improve germination, soak black-eyed Susan vine seeds overnight, then direct-sow after daytime temperatures are consistently above 60 degrees F. It loves full sun, moist soil and general-purpose fertilizer every four weeks. Hose foliage daily or every other day if spider mites or whiteflies become a problem.

title: Which Annual Vine Is Right for You?
content: Black-eyed Susan vine, Thunbergia alata, has 1 1/2-inch trumpet-shaped flowers in orange, yellow, white or pink, usually with a dark throat, from midsummer to frost. Hairy dark green triangular or arrowhead leaves grow on twining vines 3 to 8 feet tall.

title: Which Annual Vine Is Right for You?
content: Tangerine Slice A-Peel black-eyed Susan vine has red-orange flowers with yellow pinwheel markings on 5- to 8-foot vines. Sunny Susy 'Rose Sensation' flowers vary in shades of pink as they age. Coconut A-Peel has creamy white flowers with deep purple to black eyes on 5- to 8-foot vines.

title: Daylily
content: Daylilies offer big, small, single, double, plain and patterned flowers for gardens in full sun to part shade. Some varieties bloom once in summer, while others rebloom into early fall, and cultivar names such as 'Hurricane Bob', 'Octopus Tangles', 'Atomic Inferno', 'Going Bananas' and 'El Desperado' add whimsy.

content: Native opener photo of yellow daylily flowers in a summer garden.

title: Daylily
content: Daylily season varies by region. Late-season-blooming 'El Desperado' flowers in mid- to late July in a USDA zone 5 test garden, while farther south in zone 7 it peaks in late June to early July.

title: Daylily
content: Daylilies are grown for flowers, and single trumpet-shaped blooms are most common, with many colors, patterns and sizes. Miniature 'Little Grapette' has 2-inch purple blooms for small gardens, while 'Webster's Pink Wonder' has 13-inch flowers.

title: Daylily
content: Most daylilies open in the morning and last one day, but each stem produces clusters of buds that open on consecutive days. Grow early, midseason and late-blooming varieties to prolong the show, or choose extended-bloom cultivars such as 'Big Time Happy' and 'Always Afternoon'.

title: Daylily
content: Nocturnal daylilies such as 'Misty Isle' and 'Hazel's Stitchery' open late in the afternoon, continue through the night and into the following day.

title: Daylily
content: For the most impact, plant daylilies in groups of three or more. If growing many varieties, plant similar colors near each other to avoid a hodgepodge effect.

title: Daylily
content: Because daylily flowers are not present forever, pair them with border companions that bloom in spring, late summer and fall. Daylily foliage disguises fading spring-bulb foliage, and contrasting flower shapes and foliage textures, such as queen of the prairie plumes and swamp milkweed's flat-topped blooms, add interest.

title: Daylily
content: Daylily, Hemerocallis spp. and hybrids, is a perennial with a wide range of colors and markings from early summer to fall. It grows in full sun to part shade, moist well-drained soil, 12 to 72 inches tall and 9 to 40 inches wide, with no serious pests, and is cold hardy in USDA zones 3 to 11.

title: Daylily
content: Nearly 89,000 daylily cultivars are registered with the American Daylily Society. Daylilies can have dormant, evergreen or semi-evergreen foliage. Dormant types need cold temperatures and die to the ground in winter, while evergreen and semi-evergreen types keep leaves in zones 8 and warmer.

title: Daylily
content: Daylily shopping labels use specialized terms. A bloom that is all one color is called a self, and a bloom with different petal and sepal colors is a bicolor. Flower-part labels include petal, midrib, throat, scape and sepal.

title: Daylily
content: 'El Desperado' daylily is dormant and late season, with 5-inch yellow blooms, a deep purple eye and matching picotee edge notched at the midrib. It is tetraploid, grows 28 to 30 inches tall and 18 to 24 inches wide, and is cold hardy in USDA zones 3 to 9.

title: Daylily
content: 'Caballero' daylily is evergreen and early to midseason, with fragrant 4 1/2- to 5-inch bicolor blooms and extended bloom time. This diploid heirloom introduced in 1941 grows 36 to 42 inches tall and 24 to 36 inches wide and is cold hardy in USDA zones 4 to 8.

title: Daylily
content: 'Joan Senior' daylily is evergreen and early to midseason, with 6-inch near-white blooms, a soft green eye, slightly ruffled petals and reblooming habit. It is diploid, grows 20 to 26 inches tall and 18 to 24 inches wide, and is cold hardy in USDA zones 3 to 9.

title: Daylily
content: 'Strawberry Candy' daylily is semi-evergreen and early to midseason, with 4 1/2-inch pink self blooms, a raspberry pink eye and a notched midrib. It reblooms, has extended bloom time, is tetraploid, grows 24 to 30 inches tall and 18 to 24 inches wide, and is cold hardy in USDA zones 3 to 10.

title: Daylily
content: 'Dominic' daylily is semi-evergreen and early to midseason, with 5 1/2-inch deep red-black self blooms, a faint midrib and reblooming habit. It is tetraploid, grows 30 inches tall and 18 to 24 inches wide, and is cold hardy in USDA zones 3 to 9.

title: Daylily
content: 'Primal Scream' daylily is dormant and early to midseason, with tangerine-orange 7 1/2- to 8 1/2-inch self blooms, narrow twisted recurved petals and sepals, and gold-dusted flowers. It is tetraploid, grows 34 inches tall and 18 to 24 inches wide, and is cold hardy in USDA zones 3 to 9.

title: Daylily
content: 'Daring Deception' daylily is semi-evergreen and early to midseason, with 5 1/2-inch dusty-pink self blooms, a dark purple eye, overlapping ruffled petals and smooth sepals. It reblooms, is tetraploid, grows 24 inches tall and 18 to 24 inches wide, and is cold hardy in USDA zones 3 to 8.

title: Daylily
content: Lemon lily, Hemerocallis lilioasphodelus, is dormant and early season, with 3- to 4-inch lemon-yellow flowers, strong sweet fragrance and extended bloom time. It is diploid, grows 24 to 36 inches tall and 18 to 24 inches wide, and is cold hardy in USDA zones 4 to 10.

title: Daylily
content: Out-of-the-ordinary daylilies include blue or almost-blue petals, broken patterns, stripes, spots, ruffles and toothed edges. Oakes Daylilies owner Ken Oakes looks for interesting colors or patterns and vigorous growth, and once a variety is selected it can take 10 years to grow enough plants to sell.

title: Daylily
content: Hybridization uses chromosomes as building blocks. Most daylilies are diploids with 22 chromosomes, but breeders can use colchicine treatment to create tetraploids with 44 chromosomes. Tetraploids tend to grow vigorously, with stronger scapes, larger flowers, more intense colors and heavier petals and sepals.

title: Daylily
content: 'Big Kiss' daylily is dormant and midseason, with 5 1/2-inch double light peach blooms, a rose eye, fragrance and reblooming habit. It is diploid, grows 28 inches tall and 18 to 24 inches wide, and is cold hardy in USDA zones 3 to 10.

title: Daylily
content: 'It's Miller Time' daylily is dormant and mid- to late season, with 9-inch self blooms and a toothed edge. It reblooms, is tetraploid, grows 37 inches tall and 24 to 30 inches wide, and is cold hardy in USDA zones 3 to 9.

title: Daylily
content: 'Kaleidoscope King' daylily is semi-evergreen and midseason, with 5 1/2-inch beige-pink petals and sepals, a yellow appliqued throat and a heavily ruffled double edge. It reblooms, is tetraploid, grows 27 inches tall and 18 to 24 inches wide, and is cold hardy in USDA zones 3 to 9.

title: Daylily
content: 'Forbidden Territory' daylily is dormant and early to midseason, with 5-inch maroon-purple fragrant flowers and a white toothed edge. It reblooms, is tetraploid, grows 27 inches tall and 18 to 24 inches wide, and is cold hardy in USDA zones 3 to 9.

title: Daylily
content: 'Hazel's Stitchery' daylily is dormant and midseason, with 2 1/4-inch purple blooms and a dark rose halo above a purple eye. It is diploid and nocturnal, grows 22 inches tall and 18 to 24 inches wide, and is cold hardy in USDA zones 2 to 8.

title: Daylily
content: 'Bali Watercolor' daylily is evergreen and midseason, with 9-inch lavender spider blooms, a silvery watermark and light fragrance. It reblooms, is tetraploid, grows 36 inches tall and 24 to 30 inches wide, and is cold hardy in USDA zones 3 to 9.

title: Daylily
content: 'Malarky' daylily is semi-evergreen and midseason, with 5 3/4-inch blooms and a triangular eye. It reblooms, is tetraploid, grows 22 inches tall and 18 to 24 inches wide, and is cold hardy in USDA zones 3 to 9.

title: Daylily
content: 'Rose F. Kennedy' daylily is dormant and midseason, with 7 1/2-inch chartreuse-green blooms and a wide red-purple picotee edge. It is diploid, grows 29 inches tall and 18 to 24 inches wide, and is cold hardy in USDA zones 3 to 9.

title: Daylily
content: Daylilies prefer rich, well-drained soil and plenty of moisture, but they adapt to less-than-ideal conditions. Hybridizer Jim Bochner grows daylilies in heavy soil and rarely waters, yet they still thrive.

title: Daylily
content: Bare-root daylilies should have plump, firm roots and can go in a nursery pot of moistened potting mix or directly into the ground. Position the white band where roots and foliage meet at soil level. Potted plants go in the ground at the same level they grew in the pot.

title: Daylily
content: Water newly planted daylilies thoroughly for the first few weeks. Apply 1 to 2 inches of organic mulch around plants in spring to conserve water and suppress weeds, but pull mulch back a few inches from the crown to prevent rot.

title: Daylily
content: Daylilies do not need feeding to flower, but an annual spring application helps foliage stay green and healthy and encourages buds. Deadhead spent blooms to tidy plants and help rebloomers put energy into the next flower show; remove a spent bloom by grabbing it near the base and bending until it snaps off.

title: Daylily
content: Once all flowers on a scape have finished, follow the scape beneath the foliage and snip it off close to the base. If leaves look ratty in summer, cut daylilies back with pruners or a string trimmer after flowering so fresh leaves grow from the crown in a few weeks.

title: Daylily
content: Divide daylilies every five to six years to keep plants vigorous. Signs include reblooming varieties losing their usual multiple flushes or a big foliage clump producing only a few flowers.

title: Daylily
content: Divide in spring by digging up the plant. Some roots can be pulled apart by hand, while dense rootballs may need a spade or a tool such as Don's Daylily Divider. Each division should have at least one fan; more fans make same-season bloom more likely. Replant divisions right away so roots do not dry out.

title: Daylily
content: Daylilies are mostly trouble free. Thrips or aphids may appear early in the season, but ladybugs often control them. If distorted and discolored leaves become intolerable, spray with insecticidal soap or knock pests off with a strong stream of water.

title: Daylily
content: Daylily rust looks like rusty orange patches on leaves and is mostly a problem in the South, where winters are mild. Freezing temperatures kill the fungus. Rust will not kill a plant, but it can disfigure foliage.

title: No-Spray Bug Solutions
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Even healthy plants can be invaded by insect pests such as cabbage loopers, Japanese beetles and aphids. Seven eco-friendly methods can help protect plants without reaching for a pesticide spray.

title: No-Spray Bug Solutions
author: Jennifer Howell
content: A strong stream of water knocks soft-bodied insects off plants and often kills them. Green aphids on tropical hibiscus can be blasted from buds, tender growth and petals with a fine sprayer or hose nozzle.

title: No-Spray Bug Solutions
author: Jennifer Howell
content: For extra aphid control, add 2 teaspoons of Dawn dish soap per pint of water and spray plants with a pump sprayer. The soapy film adheres to aphids, removes their protective coating and dries them out, while also cleaning sticky honeydew. Rinse plants afterward so soap residue does not clog pores.

title: No-Spray Bug Solutions
author: Jennifer Howell
content: A stream of water can also be used on oleander aphids, twospotted spider mites and whiteflies.

title: No-Spray Bug Solutions
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Native close-up photo of green aphids clustered on a tropical hibiscus bud.

title: No-Spray Bug Solutions
author: Jennifer Howell
content: For large, easy-to-spot pests, hand pick and squash them or drop them in a bucket of soapy water. Remove smaller, harder-to-pick insects by trimming off infested branches, leaves or flowers. Tobacco budworms damage petunia flowers by chewing holes through petals in the bud stage; check plants daily in late afternoon or evening and destroy the camouflaged worms.

title: No-Spray Bug Solutions
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Hand plucking works for bagworms and Japanese beetles. Cutting off infested portions of a plant helps when you have mealybugs or scale.

title: No-Spray Bug Solutions
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Predatory insects can devour or parasitize specific pests. Encourage natural enemies by providing overwintering sites and food sources such as pollen or nectar, or buy live predators to release. This is not quick, but it is ecologically friendly.

title: No-Spray Bug Solutions
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Tomato hornworms covered with tiny white ricelike objects are carrying braconid wasp larval cocoons. Leave the infested hornworm in the garden so emerging wasps can seek out more hornworms to parasitize and kill.

title: No-Spray Bug Solutions
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Green lacewing larvae feed on twospotted spider mites and aphids. Lady beetles eat aphids, leafhoppers and mealybugs. Spiders are predators of many insects.

title: No-Spray Bug Solutions
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Native insect photo of a tobacco budworm caterpillar on petunia foliage.

title: No-Spray Bug Solutions
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Native insect photo of a tomato hornworm covered with white braconid wasp cocoons.

title: No-Spray Bug Solutions
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Biological pathogens such as bacteria, fungi, beneficial nematodes and viruses can kill pests. These controls are usually specific to one insect, are introduced with sprays, granules or powders, and work slowly to reduce populations.

title: No-Spray Bug Solutions
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Japanese beetle grubs live underground and can be reduced by the beneficial nematode Heterorhabditis bacteriophora. After ingestion, the nematode emits a bacterium that kills the grub, then reproduces and seeks more grubs. Apply nematodes mixed with water to damp soil at dusk or on a cloudy day.

title: No-Spray Bug Solutions
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Bt, Bacillus thuringiensis israelensis, controls fungus gnats in houseplants and mosquitoes in ponds. The fungus Beauveria bassiana kills Colorado potato beetle larvae and adults.

title: No-Spray Bug Solutions
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Sticky traps use adhesive on colored cards, tape, ribbon or fruit-shaped decoys to attract pests. The insect becomes stuck and dies, but traps can also catch beneficial insects and small birds, so use them carefully.

title: No-Spray Bug Solutions
author: Jennifer Howell

title: No-Spray Bug Solutions
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Native insect photo of codling moth caterpillar damage on an apple.

title: No-Spray Bug Solutions
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Yellow sticky traps catch adult fungus gnats emerging from houseplant soil before they lay more eggs, though they do not kill larvae in the soil. Leave traps for several weeks and change them when full.

title: No-Spray Bug Solutions
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Pheromone traps combine sticky adhesive with an artificial pheromone specific to a pest. They lure adults, usually males, into disposable traps. In a home garden they may reduce the population enough that damage is not significant.

title: No-Spray Bug Solutions
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Trap crops are plants so tasty to insects that pests pass by other food sources to feed on them. Plant the trap crop close to or around the perimeter of the plants you want to protect, then pick pests off, remove infested plants or dunk potted trap plants in soapy water.

title: No-Spray Bug Solutions
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Blue Hubbard squash is especially attractive to cucumber beetles and squash vine borers that damage winter squash and zucchini. Plant Blue Hubbard like a fence around desired plants and start it earlier so the plants are larger and more likely to lure insects away.

title: No-Spray Bug Solutions
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Trap-cropping companions include collards around cabbage to keep diamondback moths away, dill near tomatoes to lure tomato hornworms, and nasturtium to lure aphids and flea beetles away from vegetable crops.

title: No-Spray Bug Solutions
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Yellow sticky traps attract whiteflies and aphids, blue traps catch leafminers and thrips, and red apple-shaped traps attract and kill apple maggot flies.

title: No-Spray Bug Solutions
author: Jennifer Howell
content: For codling moths in orchard fruits such as apples, hang one pheromone-infused sticky trap in a dwarf fruit tree and two in a full-sized standard tree. Avoid pheromone traps for Japanese beetles because studies show they attract more pests than they deter.

title: No-Spray Bug Solutions
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Pheromone traps can lower populations of spotted lanternfly and squash vine borer.

title: Harvest Helper
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Marisa learned that harvesting vegetables too early or too late can lead to less flavorful produce or waste. Once gardeners recognize each crop's subtle cues, they can pick at the perfect time to capture peak flavor and nutrition.

title: Harvest Helper
author: Marisa Reyes
content: The perfect harvest window varies by plant. Root vegetables such as carrots can remain in place without going past peak ripeness longer than green beans, which may need checking every day or two. Zucchini can seemingly grow a foot overnight.

title: Harvest Helper
author: Marisa Reyes
content: The harvest guide lists days to maturity from seed, signs of ripeness, signs of overripeness and harvesting tips so both beginners and experienced gardeners can pick vegetables at their best.

title: Harvest Helper
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Beans mature in 50 to 70 days; pick when pods are young and tender and seeds are not visible, before pods bulge and turn pale. Beets mature in 50 to 70 days; pull one or two to check for 1- to 3-inch smooth, firm, rounded roots when foliage turns yellow and withers. Broccoli matures in 60 to 80 days; harvest the dark green, firm central head before yellow flowers appear to encourage side shoots.

title: Harvest Helper
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Cabbage matures in 65 to 80 days; cut firm heads at the base before leaves open or crack. Carrots mature in 50 to 80 days; look for bright color, firm roots and 1- to 3-inch shoulders before roots crack or turn woody. Celery matures in 85 to 120 days; harvest firm green stalks from the outside first and water deeply to prevent bitterness before stalks become stringy and tough.

title: Harvest Helper
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Corn matures in 60 to 100 days; harvest in the morning when silks are brown and kernels plump, before kernels become tightly packed, starchy and dented. Cucumbers mature in 50 to 70 days; pick bright green, firm fruit early in the day and check daily before skin turns yellow, soft or wrinkled. Head lettuce matures in 45 to 60 days; harvest full-sized firm heads in the morning before bolting or bitterness.

title: Harvest Helper
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Watermelons mature in 70 to 100 days; ripe fruit has a dry tendril where it connects to the vine, fragrance at the blossom end, a yellow field spot and a deep hollow sound when thumped. Onions mature in 100 to 120 days; cure bulbs for two weeks after tops fall over and begin to brown. Peas mature in 60 to 70 days; pick plump peas in firm glossy pods while young, before pods dull and peas turn starchy.

title: Harvest Helper
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Peppers mature in 60 to 90 days; pick sweet peppers full sized and ripen off the plant, while hot peppers should stay until uniformly colored, before wrinkles or soft spots appear. Potatoes mature in 90 to 120 days; gently harvest new potatoes two weeks after flowering or wait until foliage dies back and tubers are firm. Spinach matures in 40 to 60 days; harvest outer leaves at any tender stage before yellowing or bolting.

title: Harvest Helper
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Summer squash matures in 50 to 70 days; harvest zucchini and other squash when small, firm, bright and tender, before fruit becomes dull, hard-skinned and oversized. Tomatoes mature in 60 to 80 days; pick rich, uniformly colored fruit, and at season's end pick full-sized fruit to ripen indoors before soft spots, wrinkling or splitting develop.

title: A Garden for Exploring
author: Marisa Reyes
content: In 1998, Bonnie Duma and her husband John purchased a 3/4-acre lot in Lenexa, Kansas. After the house was built, Bonnie turned a blank-slate yard into a garden inspired by her farm childhood, designed to share a love of plants with grandchildren, welcome her dog Boomer and evoke a rustic farm aesthetic.

title: A Garden for Exploring
author: Marisa Reyes
content: A magical oasis wraps around the property with upcycled projects, curated containers and paths around every bend. The Johnson County Master Gardener's garden includes a house, deck, patio, arbors, kitchen garden, lawn, stone wall, bed-frame planter and dog path.

title: A Garden for Exploring
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Native garden-tour photo of Bonnie Duma's raised deck and surrounding shade garden, the central point connecting garden paths.

title: A Garden for Exploring
author: Marisa Reyes
content: The main entrance to Bonnie's garden lies to the right of the garage, marked by an arbor. Along the side-yard path, daylily, iris, coneflower, spirea and panicle hydrangea provide all-season color. Bonnie repeats 'Limelight' panicle hydrangea because it grows well there and she loves its green and white blooms.

title: A Garden for Exploring
author: Marisa Reyes
content: The sunny side-yard kitchen garden holds the vegetable garden and a windowbox full of herbs. Bonnie also keeps a potting bench in this easy-to-access spot.

title: A Garden for Exploring

title: Drought-Defying Curb Appeal
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Hot, dry summers plus reflected heat from a driveway create a tough garden spot. When rain is scarce, daily watering may not keep unsuitable plants looking good; drought-stressed plants stop blooming, wilt, yellow, dry up and drop leaves.

title: Drought-Defying Curb Appeal
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: This design uses plants that thrive in summer heat and prefer dry soil, making it suitable for a west-facing spot next to a driveway. Flowering peaks in summer, foliage looks good all season and compost at planting adds nutrients and moisture-holding organic matter.

title: Drought-Defying Curb Appeal
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Warm colors in soft shades give the border a relaxing summer vibe. Penstemon and allium provide pale pinks and lavenders that tone down the orange, red and yellow of torch lily, blanket flower and sedum.

title: Drought-Defying Curb Appeal
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Native color illustration of a drought-tolerant curbside border with boulders, flowering perennials and a driveway edge.

title: Drought-Defying Curb Appeal
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: The plants are arranged from tall to small, with 4-foot-tall-and-wide 'Lilla' smokebush in the back corner to anchor the planting and screen the sideyard without blocking the driveway view. Lower plants along the driveway provide color, tolerate occasional stepping and will not rub parked cars.

title: Drought-Defying Curb Appeal
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: If snow shoveling or plowing is part of winter maintenance, the path provides extra space for piling snow where it will not smother perennials. Broken smokebush stems can be cut off the following spring and will regrow.

title: Drought-Defying Curb Appeal
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Foliage keeps the garden attractive before flowers take off. Wine-red smokebush leaves attract attention, deep-purple penstemon echoes that color, prairie dropseed creates grassy mounds and silvery lamb's ear forms a steppable carpet beside the drive.

title: Drought-Defying Curb Appeal
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Native color illustration detail of the drought-tolerant border showing layers of shrubs, grasses, perennials and low edging plants.

title: Drought-Defying Curb Appeal
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Even drought-tolerant plants need help establishing. Water regularly the first year so they build robust roots; after that, they should do fine with occasional deep watering during the hottest part of summer and especially dry periods.

title: Drought-Defying Curb Appeal
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Late winter or early spring is cleanup time. Cut prairie dropseed and torch lily to within a few inches of the ground, cut back remaining allium blooms and trim lamb's ear if it grows into the driveway. This compact smokebush does not need size pruning.

title: Drought-Defying Curb Appeal
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: In spring, sprinkle slow-release fertilizer according to label directions and add 1 to 2 inches of organic mulch to reduce weeding, conserve moisture and even soil temperature. Avoid gravel mulch because it adds reflected heat.

title: Drought-Defying Curb Appeal
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: In summer, deadhead torch lily, blanket flower and penstemon to tidy them and encourage more bloom. Kudos Mandarin agastache lasts a long time and should not need frequent cutting back.

title: Drought-Defying Curb Appeal
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: In fall, prairie dropseed foliage turns golden yellow and keeps its mounded shape through winter with dried allium blooms. Smokebush foliage changes from deep purple to orange, red, coral and yellow.

title: Drought-Defying Curb Appeal
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Creeping thyme can be stepped on without damage. The foliage is fragrant, but it is not a good choice for cooking.

title: Drought-Defying Curb Appeal
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Where winter is wet or snowy, pull torch lily leaves up over the crown and tie them together to keep water from collecting and causing rot.

title: Drought-Defying Curb Appeal
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Smokebush, Cotinus coggygria 'Lilla', is a shrub with fluffy pink plumes and wine-red foliage in summer, with leaves maturing to orange, coral and red in fall. It grows in full sun to part shade, 4 feet tall and wide, is cold hardy in USDA zones 4 to 8, and the plan uses one plant.

title: Drought-Defying Curb Appeal
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Prairie dropseed, Sporobolus heterolepis, is a perennial with airy pink to tan panicles above narrow green foliage in summer. It grows in full sun, 2 to 3 feet tall and wide, is cold hardy in USDA zones 3 to 8, and the plan uses five plants.

title: Drought-Defying Curb Appeal
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Torch lily, Kniphofia 'Hot and Cold', is a perennial with bicolor tangerine and creamy white spikes in early to late summer. It grows in full sun, 30 to 36 inches tall and 24 to 30 inches wide, is cold hardy in USDA zones 5 to 9, and the plan uses five plants.

title: Drought-Defying Curb Appeal
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Penstemon, Penstemon 'Blackbeard', is a perennial with tubular lavender blooms in early to midsummer and deep purple foliage. It grows in full sun, 28 to 34 inches tall and 24 inches wide, is cold hardy in USDA zones 3 to 8, and the plan uses five plants.

title: Drought-Defying Curb Appeal
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Allium, Allium 'Bubble Bath', is a perennial with globe-shaped lavender blooms in late summer to early fall. It grows in full sun to part shade, 26 to 28 inches tall and 24 to 26 inches wide, is cold hardy in USDA zones 4 to 8, and the plan uses four plants.

title: Drought-Defying Curb Appeal
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Blanket flower, Gaillardia x grandiflora Mesa Red, is a perennial with 3-inch daisy-shaped red flowers that do not fade from early to late summer. It grows in full sun, 14 to 16 inches tall and 20 to 22 inches wide, is cold hardy in USDA zones 5 to 10, and the plan uses seven plants.

title: Drought-Defying Curb Appeal
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Agastache, Agastache Kudos Mandarin, is a perennial with bright orange flowers from early summer to fall. It grows in full sun, 17 to 20 inches tall and 14 to 16 inches wide, is cold hardy in USDA zones 5 to 10, and the plan uses five plants.

title: Drought-Defying Curb Appeal
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Sedum, Sedum 'Bright Idea', is a perennial with clusters of bright-yellow star-shaped blooms on red stems in early to midsummer. It grows in full sun, 10 to 12 inches tall and 16 to 20 inches wide, is cold hardy in USDA zones 3 to 9, and the plan uses eight plants.

title: Drought-Defying Curb Appeal
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Lamb's ear, Stachys byzantina 'Big Ears', is a perennial with occasional lavender blooms on silver-white stems in summer and fuzzy silver leaves. It grows in full sun, 8 to 12 inches tall and 12 to 18 inches wide, is cold hardy in USDA zones 4 to 8, and the plan uses six plants.

title: Drought-Defying Curb Appeal
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Creeping thyme, Thymus serpyllum, is a perennial with pink flowers in early to midsummer and small mildly fragrant green leaves. It grows in full sun, 2 to 3 inches tall and 6 to 12 inches wide, is cold hardy in USDA zones 4 to 9, and the plan uses 15 plants.

title: 4 Garden Goofs
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Small garden decisions can have effects that linger for years. Jennifer shares four garden mistakes and fixes so readers can avoid the same problems.

title: 4 Garden Goofs
author: Jennifer Howell
content: A friend gave Jennifer six flowering tobacco seedlings with huge leaves and 6- to 8-foot flower stalks covered in fragrant white flowers. Because she failed to deadhead, the plants reseeded everywhere, with tiny seeds clinging to clothes and hair and sprouting unchecked.

title: 4 Garden Goofs
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Prolific reseeders such as flowering tobacco need deadheading before they become weeds. Jennifer also trims breadseed poppies, columbine, fennel and lettuce before seedpods dry. If pods have ripened, carefully cut spent bloom stalks into a garbage bag and send debris to the trash, not compost.

title: 4 Garden Goofs
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Native close-up photo of a flowering tobacco seedpod containing many tiny seeds.

title: 4 Garden Goofs

title: 4 Garden Goofs
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Stringy sedum had established itself in the Garden Gate test garden and hitchhiked home in a division of Serbian bellflower. It creeps through plantings in a low chartreuse mat with yellow spring flowers and can establish from tiny pieces.

title: 4 Garden Goofs
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Before bringing home a plant from another garden, inspect the soil for bonus plants or root pieces. Washing soil from divisions before planting helps stop stowaways. Research purchases too; 'Oriental Limelight' artemisia also spread through Jennifer's garden with divided perennials.

title: 4 Garden Goofs
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Stringy sedum and 'Oriental Limelight' artemisia pull easily. Dry the foliage and roots completely to kill them before composting or throwing them away.

title: 4 Garden Goofs
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Planting an entire seed packet causes overcrowding. Vegetables such as radishes and beets may not form edible roots when crowded, poor air movement can cause fungal or disease problems such as powdery mildew on zinnias, and too much produce may mature at once.

title: 4 Garden Goofs
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Thin overcrowded seedlings by pulling or snipping extras before plants compete with each other. Follow seed-packet spacing, sow only what you need and save seed for succession planting or a fall crop. Most seeds last two to three years in a cool, dry spot.

title: 4 Garden Goofs
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Native technique photo showing overcrowded radish seedlings being thinned.

title: 4 Garden Goofs
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Timid pruning cuts on shrubs can create unnatural growth. Jennifer's red-osier dogwood produced new growth from clipped branch tips and little at the base, losing its natural habit and signature bright red stems.

title: 4 Garden Goofs
author: Jennifer Howell
content: A red-osier dogwood needs renewal pruning by cutting back one-third of the oldest stems every year or two to encourage new growth, more flowers and brighter red winter stems.

title: 4 Garden Goofs
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Prune spring bloomers such as forsythia and common lilac after they flower so you do not remove buds formed the previous year. Prune summer- and fall-blooming shrubs such as summersweet and potentilla in early spring before leaves appear so they still have time to grow flowering branches.

title: 4 Garden Goofs
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Most deciduous shrubs are forgiving. A poorly shaped weigela cut back to the ground in March produced rejuvenated growth that summer and better flowering the next year.

title: Q&A
content: Dehiscence is the process of a seedpod splitting along a built-in line of weakness so seeds can be released. Common dehiscent plants include milkweeds, poppies and impatiens.

title: Q&A
content: Putting copper in a birdbath can help reduce algae because copper releases ions that reduce algae formation in water. Use seven to 12 pennies minted before 1982, because later pennies are mostly zinc, or clean scraps of copper pipe.

title: Q&A
content: Drop copper into a clean birdbath filled with fresh water to reduce algae for a week or two. Algae grows fastest in full sun and when air temperatures reach 90 degrees F or higher. Clean a birdbath with a 1:9 solution of bleach or distilled vinegar and water.

title: Q&A
content: To reduce heat dormancy stress in a bluegrass lawn, sharpen the mower blade and raise the mowing height to 3 or 3 1/2 inches so taller grass shades soil and conserves moisture. In fall, lower the blade to 2 or 2 1/2 inches to make leaf raking easier.

title: Q&A
content: Mow bluegrass early in the morning or late in the day so grass can recover before the hottest part of the day. During hot, dry weather, limit foot traffic because it can crush stressed grass.

title: Q&A
content: Late-season webs on shrubs or lawns are often made by beneficial funnel weaver spiders. The nonsticky webs have a funnel-shaped hole where the spider waits, then pops out to capture insects and drag them beneath the web.

title: Q&A
content: More than 400 funnel weaver spider species live in North America. They are shy and fast moving, and while they may bite if provoked, swelling, itching or redness is rarely serious.

title: Q&A
content: Yellow nutsedge, Cyperus esculentus, has shiny yellow-green leaves 12 to 32 inches tall and golden yellow to brown spikelets arranged in clusters of small bottlebrushes from early to late summer. Pulled plants have triangular stems with red-purple tint at the base and segmented white rhizomes with tubers at the tips.

title: Q&A
content: Yellow nutsedge appears in lawns and beds that are rarely cultivated and spreads quickly in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to part shade.

title: Q&A
content: Control yellow nutsedge by allowing turf to grow tall enough to shade soil and reduce sprouting. In beds and borders, hoe or pull before plants have four to six leaves and have formed tubers, repeating every three to four weeks. Dig established clumps and collect as many roots and tubers as possible.

title: Q&A
content: When choosing large containers, heavy materials such as glazed ceramic, cast iron, wood or concrete work well in windy sites. Wood, glazed ceramic and terra-cotta protect roots from overheating in full sun. Plastic is often most economical, and plastic, foam or fiberglass are light enough for decks or balconies.

title: Q&A
content: Glazed ceramic, metal and plastic containers keep soil moist longer for erratic waterers. Metal and synthetic materials are less likely to crack in cold climates. Unglazed terra-cotta breathes best and lets soil dry out for gardeners who tend to overwater.

title: Bring the Warmth of the Sahara to Your Garden
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Sahara gloriosa daisy has variable flower color: velvety chocolate-brown centers surrounded by copper, rusty red, caramel or gold petals that fade to muted rose, peach or yellow tones with age.

title: Bring the Warmth of the Sahara to Your Garden
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Sahara's changing colors and 20- to 24-inch height make it easy to use in the middle of a border or in containers. It is especially pretty against dark foliage, and cut stems last a week or more in a vase.

title: Bring the Warmth of the Sahara to Your Garden
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Sahara gloriosa daisy is shade and drought tolerant, but it flowers more in full sun with regular watering. Pinch stem ends in early summer for branching and a fuller habit, and deadhead faded or tattered blooms to keep flowers coming. Goldfinches may eat seedheads if left in place.

title: Bring the Warmth of the Sahara to Your Garden
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Start Sahara gloriosa daisy seed indoors eight to 12 weeks before the last frost. It is a perennial but not reliably long-lived or cold-hardy; in zone 5 it may overwinter in a sheltered spot with mulch, and colder gardens can grow it as an annual.

title: Bring the Warmth of the Sahara to Your Garden
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Sahara gloriosa daisy, Rudbeckia hirta, has double or semidouble daisy-shaped flowers in yellow to rusty red with brown centers from midsummer to fall. It grows in full sun to part shade, average well-drained soil, 20 to 24 inches tall and 12 to 18 inches wide, with no serious pests, and is cold hardy in USDA zones 5 to 9.

title: Bring the Warmth of the Sahara to Your Garden
author: Jennifer Howell
content: The Desert Tones in Colder Zones planting peaks in summer with Sahara as the star. Deadhead sea holly and gloriosa daisy for more bloom, and shear oregano by half in midsummer only if it gets leggy.

title: Bring the Warmth of the Sahara to Your Garden
author: Jennifer Howell
content: The Desert Tones combo pairs Sahara gloriosa daisy with oregano 'Drops of Jupiter', a perennial with mauve-purple flowers in early to late summer, full sun, 24 inches tall and 36 inches wide, cold hardy in USDA zones 4 to 9.

title: Bring the Warmth of the Sahara to Your Garden
author: Jennifer Howell
content: The Desert Tones combo pairs Sahara gloriosa daisy with Sweet Cherry Tea ninebark, Physocarpus opulifolius, a shrub with pink spring flowers, a lighter summer rebloom and deep purple foliage. It grows in full sun, 3 to 4 feet tall and wide, and is cold hardy in USDA zones 3 to 7.

title: Bring the Warmth of the Sahara to Your Garden
author: Jennifer Howell
content: The Desert Tones combo pairs Sahara gloriosa daisy with 'Blue Hobbit' sea holly, Eryngium planum, a perennial with thistlelike periwinkle-blue flowers from summer to fall. It grows in full sun, 8 to 12 inches tall and wide, and is cold hardy in USDA zones 4 to 8.

title: Lessons from an Art Teacher
content: Karen Watson-Newlin taught K-12 art for 34 years and applies those lessons to the 1 1/2-acre Wisconsin garden she started 16 years ago with her husband Rob.

title: Lessons from an Art Teacher
content: Karen says the principles of good design apply to the garden. Texture, color, form and contrast are necessary elements, and repetition of those elements provides continuity and balance.

title: Lessons from an Art Teacher
content: Karen's daylily affinity began when a friend shared 'Picasso' daylily because of her artistic sensibilities and then 'A Chorus Line' because her brother was in the original European tour of the Broadway show. She now grows more than 575 different daylily hybrids.

title: Lessons from an Art Teacher
content: The garden is an official American Hemerocallis Society Display Garden and is always evolving. Karen is learning to relax as weather forces change and trees and shrubs grow, focusing more on visual flow and less maintenance so the garden brings joy rather than drudgery.

title: Lessons from an Art Teacher
content: Native landscape photo of Karen Watson-Newlin's Windswept Garden with daylilies, paths and layered plantings.

title: Lessons from an Art Teacher
content: Because the gardens are large, Karen uses sweeps of repeated color to create harmony. Different garden areas have distinct color palettes, usually soft pastels or hot colors, and hot colors look dynamic when punctuated with bright blues, blue-violets or red-violets.

title: Lessons from an Art Teacher
content: Texture is an important repeated element in Karen's garden. The repeated shape and texture of threadleaf coreopsis signals entrances to pathways, and ornamental grasses add repeated texture too.

title: Lessons from an Art Teacher
content: Repeating plants of the same color, such as hot-colored red and orange daylilies flanking a grassy path, ties garden areas together and lends unity. Repeating the same color plant creates a ribbon of color through the garden.

title: Lessons from an Art Teacher
content: Native garden photo of hot-colored red and orange daylilies repeated along a grassy pathway.

title: Lessons from an Art Teacher
content: Mounds of 'Zagreb' threadleaf coreopsis unify a garden area by repeating the same shape and texture. Other repeated rounded shapes can come from begonias, impatiens and boxwoods, while vertical shapes can come from foxgloves, lilies and hollyhocks.

title: Lessons from an Art Teacher
content: Native garden photo of repeated rounded mounds of 'Zagreb' threadleaf coreopsis and surrounding plantings.

title: Lessons from an Art Teacher
content: Focal points draw the eye and force the viewer's perspective to a specific location. A garden design needs highs and lows; same-size plantings may look fine, but unusual trees, conifers, shrubs or contrast plants add visual spark and intrigue.

title: Lessons from an Art Teacher
content: A focal point does not have to be large, but it should be placed in the right spot. Avoid putting it in the center of a space. Garden art, pottery, pathways, seating areas, rose arbors, pergolas and water features can all serve as focal points.

title: Lessons from an Art Teacher
content: Rob designed and built the 5,000-gallon pond, which is home to koi, hardy water lilies and other aquatic plants. A pair of conifers flanking the pond become more prominent focal points in winter.

title: Lessons from an Art Teacher
content: Native garden photo of a pond with koi, water lilies and surrounding plantings used as a focal point.

title: Lessons from an Art Teacher
content: A well-placed container can make a humdrum border settle into perfection, give a pathway a destination and turn lawn into a stage for a botanical display. A container of 'Red Star' cordyline, 'Diamond Frost' euphorbia and mandevilla becomes a focal point in a daylily bed.

title: Lessons from an Art Teacher
content: Columns on decks and porches can elevate garden impact. A violet-purple 'Jackmanii' clematis can cover a column within a few years and take the spotlight for several weeks.

title: Lessons from an Art Teacher
content: Native photo of a focal-point container with 'Red Star' cordyline, 'Diamond Frost' euphorbia and mandevilla in a daylily bed.

title: Lessons from an Art Teacher
content: Native photo of violet-purple 'Jackmanii' clematis covering a porch column.

title: Lessons from an Art Teacher
content: Avoid a disjointed jumble by planting fewer varieties in larger sweeps for impact. Woody plants, long-lived perennials and ornamental grasses in masses seem to float in clouds of colors and textures.

title: Lessons from an Art Teacher
content: Karen plants daylilies in groupings of similar hues rather than multiples of each cultivar. With other plants, such as Knock Out roses and 'David' garden phlox, she plants odd numbers of three, five or seven depending on the size of the space.

title: Lessons from an Art Teacher
content: Scale matters because smaller spaces and narrow borders can use smaller groups of plants without looking timid, while larger spaces can handle bolder groups.

title: Lessons from an Art Teacher
content: Pale pink 'Venusta' queen of the prairie, lavender-pink spider flower and 'All American Chief' daylily form a mass of color.

title: Lessons from an Art Teacher
content: Native garden photo of a large wave of color with 'Venusta' queen of the prairie, spider flower and 'All American Chief' daylily.

title: Lessons from an Art Teacher
content: A garden with all-season interest is planned so that when one plant finishes its show, another takes over. Karen's spring begins with bulbs and flows into salvias, baptisias, amsonias, irises, peonies and roses.

title: Lessons from an Art Teacher
content: Karen's peak summer is the daylily glory season. Late summer features black-eyed Susans, sedums, turtlehead, goldenrod and asters, while winter interest comes from grasses, evergreens and conifers.

title: Lessons from an Art Teacher
content: Permanent structure and plants with multiple seasons of interest create an ever-changing landscape for all 12 months. In Karen's garden, 'Pendula' weeping spruce and drifts of 'Overdam' feather reed grass add winter presence, movement and sound.

title: Salad with a Side of Slug
author: Jamie Seitz
content: Jamie knows intellectually that gardening comes with bugs, pests and creepy crawlies, but knowing this and encountering such creatures in lunch are different things.

title: Salad with a Side of Slug
author: Jamie Seitz
content: The first spring Jamie grew lettuce and spinach in raised beds, unlimited fresh greens seemed like a way to save money and feed her family healthy sides. Leaf lettuce can be sown early, grows quickly and can provide salad greens all spring if cut and not allowed to go to seed.

title: Salad with a Side of Slug
author: Jamie Seitz
content: The first few salad bowls made Jamie feel like a fantastic gardener, but within weeks the novelty wore off for the kids and for her. As quickly as she harvested lettuce, it grew back fuller and thicker.

title: Salad with a Side of Slug
author: Jamie Seitz
content: Jamie cut, washed and spun lettuce for lunch, then added cucumber, cherry tomatoes, cheese, carrots and croutons. A few bites in, she noticed something on her fork that looked like a juicy garden slug.

title: Salad with a Side of Slug
author: Jamie Seitz
content: The slug experience put Jamie off garden lettuce for the rest of the season, but she eventually came back to loving garden greens. Now she washes much more thoroughly and checks every single bite.

content: At Kristin's first house, rabbits started eating green beans in the sunny vegetable bed beside the garage. A small wire edging fence from the home improvement store was not enough; the next morning she watched a rabbit hop through the fence from inside the bed, where it had apparently been eating too.

title: from the editor

content: A fence is usually a big commitment of effort and cash, so it is especially important to match the construction to the fence's purpose before tackling the project.

title: Reader Tips
author: Cathy Costa, ME
content: Cathy plants corn and bush beans in a large container in spring for a dramatic fall display. The corn acts as a thriller and the beans as a productive spiller, and she adds fall-blooming annuals to the pot when the season changes.

title: Reader Tips
author: Cathy Costa, ME
content: Corn grown in a container may not have time or room to make full ears, so Cathy plants several seeds in the center of the pot for a full look. A metal ring support or twine tied around the stems helps hold the corn upright.

title: Reader Tips
author: Jim Childs, IA
content: Jim keeps a piece of plastic in the back of the car and lays an old flannel sheet on top when hauling plants. The plastic protects the trunk and the sheet absorbs excess water; he hangs the sheet to dry afterward so it will not mildew.

title: Reader Tips
author: Gloria Bonde, SD
content: Gloria nestles medium empty clay pots in borders and along pathways so she has a quick place to drop weeds as she pulls them.

title: Reader Tips
author: Mike Northrup, OH
content: Mike repurposes a screen door grille into a compost sifter that fits over a wheelbarrow. The mesh catches undecomposed debris and improves the texture of compost or seed-starting mix; he places small mounds on the screen and shakes or spreads them by hand.

title: Reader Tips
author: Kathleen Faulkner, CT
content: Kathleen lines a garden cart with a fitted sheet face down, stretching the elastic over the cart edges. After filling the cart with debris, she lifts the sheet corners to dump the load into the compost pile and reduces scratches in the cart.

title: Reader Tips
content: Sunflower spittlebug, Clastoptera xanthocephala, appears as white foamy spittle about an inch across on stems and leaves. The insects are about 1/8 inch long with blunt round heads and wings; males are almost black, while females are lighter brown.

title: Reader Tips
content: Sunflower spittlebug nymphs pierce stems and suck sap while hiding in spittle. Larvae feed on sunflower, goldenrod and asters, and adults lay eggs in leaf litter at the base of plants. They rarely cause serious harm, though they may deform leaves.

title: Reader Tips
content: Control sunflower spittlebugs by handpicking them into soapy water or washing nymphs and spittle from stems with a hose. Pesticides are usually ineffective because the spittle protects larvae; cleaning up leaf litter in fall and keeping weeds down reduces overwintering sites.

title: What Makes Fall Color Fabulous?
content: Regular rain during the growing season followed by warm sunny fall days and cool fall nights above 32 degrees F produces the brightest fall leaf color.

title: What Makes Fall Color Fabulous?
content: As days shorten and temperatures cool, chlorophyll decreases and trees withdraw nitrogen and phosphorus from leaves into twigs and branches. As green fades, other pigments take center stage.

title: What Makes Fall Color Fabulous?
content: Abscission is the biochemical process that causes cells at the leaf petiole to break down, allowing trees to drop foliage.

title: What Makes Fall Color Fabulous?
content: Several pigments create fall color. Chlorophyll gives leaves green color, carotenoids produce yellow and orange, anthocyanins create red and purple, and tannins contribute brown.

title: What Makes Fall Color Fabulous?
content: Soil pH can affect color. Acid soil makes red leaves redder, while alkaline soil makes purple leaves more purple.

title: What Makes Fall Color Fabulous?
content: Larch and bald cypress are unusual conifers that turn color in fall and then drop their needles.

title: What Makes Fall Color Fabulous?
content: To choose colorful trees, shop in fall when you can see the foliage or select cultivars known for autumn color.

title: What Makes Fall Color Fabulous?
content: Trees known for yellow fall color include ginkgo, hackberry, quaking aspen, City Slicker river birch and shagbark hickory.

title: What Makes Fall Color Fabulous?
content: Trees known for red fall color include Native Flame American hornbeam, northern red oak, 'October Glory' red maple, staghorn sumac and sweet gum.

title: What Makes Fall Color Fabulous?
content: Trees that can mix orange, red and yellow in fall include 'Autumn Brilliance' downy serviceberry, Early Glow Ohio buckeye, Persian ironwood and sugar maple.

title: A Softer Fall Palette
content: As the season winds down, annuals and late-blooming shrubs and perennials can extend color until frost. Many also provide fall foliage, berries or seedheads that last into winter if they are left standing.

title: A Softer Fall Palette
content: A softer fall palette trades the usual jewel tones for peach, lavender, cream and silvery gray-green. The combinations are meant to keep borders colorful without looking too heavy late in the season.

title: A Softer Fall Palette
content: The Peaches & Cream combination tolerates hot, dry summer weather. Zinnia and St. John's wort benefit from extra water during the hottest part of summer but are drought tolerant once established, while deadheading zinnia and salvia keeps blooms coming.

title: A Softer Fall Palette
content: Zinnia, Zinnia 'Eldorado', is an annual with double salmon to apricot blooms from summer to frost. Grow it in full sun; plants reach 30 to 36 inches tall and 18 to 24 inches wide.

title: A Softer Fall Palette
content: Salvia, Salvia guaranitica 'Purple & Bloom', is a tender perennial with large deep purple blooms and black bracts from late spring to fall. Grow it in full sun to part shade; plants reach 40 to 48 inches tall and 36 to 48 inches wide and are cold hardy in USDA zones 8 to 11.

title: A Softer Fall Palette
content: Artemisia, Artemisia 'Powis Castle', is a perennial with insignificant yellow late-summer flowers and silver-white foliage. Grow it in full sun; plants reach 2 to 3 feet tall and 1 to 2 feet wide and are cold hardy in USDA zones 5 to 9.

title: A Softer Fall Palette
content: St. John's wort, Hypericum x inodorum, is a shrub with bright yellow summer-to-fall flowers followed by red, pink, cream or coral berries. Grow it in full sun to part shade; plants reach 3 to 4 feet tall and 2 to 5 feet wide and are cold hardy in USDA zones 5 to 9.

title: A Softer Fall Palette
content: Lamb's ear, Stachys byzantina, is a perennial with lavender early-summer blooms and fuzzy silver leaves. Grow it in full sun; plants reach 4 to 18 inches tall and 12 to 18 inches wide and are cold hardy in USDA zones 4 to 8.

title: A Softer Fall Palette
content: Native garden photo of the Peaches & Cream fall combination with peach zinnias, purple salvia, silvery artemisia, St. John's wort berries and lamb's ear.

title: A Softer Fall Palette
content: To spend less time deadheading lamb's ear, grow the variety 'Big Ears'. It rarely blooms, so its fuzzy silver foliage carries the planting without many spent flower stems to remove.

title: A Softer Fall Palette
content: Native plant-combination photo showing soft fall flowers and foliage in peach, lavender, cream and silver tones.

title: A Softer Fall Palette
content: The Super Seedheads combination uses 'Millenium' allium seedheads for fall and winter interest, 'Honorine Jobert' Japanese anemone for tall white flowers and Kickin 'Carmine Red' aster for sturdy late-season color.

title: A Softer Fall Palette
content: Aster, Symphyotrichum Kickin 'Carmine Red', is a perennial with red-purple flowers from late summer to midfall. Grow it in full sun; plants reach 2 to 3 feet tall and wide and are cold hardy in USDA zones 5 to 9.

title: A Softer Fall Palette
content: Allium, Allium 'Millenium', is a perennial with rosy-purple globes from early to late summer and dried seedheads that last into winter. Grow it in full sun to part shade; plants reach 12 to 18 inches tall and wide and are cold hardy in USDA zones 4 to 8.

title: A Softer Fall Palette
content: Japanese anemone, Anemone x hybrida 'Honorine Jobert', is a perennial with white flowers from late summer to fall. Grow it in full sun to part shade; plants reach 36 to 48 inches tall and 18 to 24 inches wide and are cold hardy in USDA zones 4 to 9.

title: A Softer Fall Palette
content: The Late-Season Beauty combination uses aromatic aster for late butterflies, juniper for blue-gray evergreen texture and soapweed yucca for sharp architectural foliage.

title: A Softer Fall Palette
content: Aromatic aster, Symphyotrichum oblongifolium 'Dream of Beauty', is a perennial with light pink flowers and orange centers from late summer to fall. Grow it in sun to part shade; plants reach 12 to 15 inches tall and 22 to 24 inches wide and are cold hardy in USDA zones 4 to 8.

title: A Softer Fall Palette
content: Juniper, Juniperus squamata 'Blue Star', is a shrub with prickly evergreen blue-gray foliage. Grow it in full sun; plants reach 12 to 36 inches tall and 12 to 48 inches wide and are cold hardy in USDA zones 4 to 8.

title: A Softer Fall Palette
content: Soapweed yucca, Yucca glauca, is a perennial with bell-shaped green-white summer blooms. Grow it in full sun; plants reach 3 to 4 feet tall and 2 to 3 feet wide and are cold hardy in USDA zones 4 to 8.
