title: 9 Tough Perennials for Clay Soil
content: Clay soil can be difficult because tiny particles hold tightly together, slowing drainage and reducing oxygen around roots. In heavy clay, many plants become anemic or rot.

title: 9 Tough Perennials for Clay Soil
content: Adding organic matter helps in small areas, but amending a large clay garden is hard work. Sand can make clay harder and denser if the proportions are wrong, and a rich compost-filled planting hole may keep roots from moving into the surrounding soil.

title: 9 Tough Perennials for Clay Soil
content: Rough goldenrod, Solidago rugosa, covers itself in yellow blooms from late summer to frost and is a hub for pollinators. 'Fireworks' has larger, 18-inch sprays of blooms that resemble an explosion of sparks.

title: 9 Tough Perennials for Clay Soil
content: Rough goldenrod spreads slowly by rhizomes, and clay soil helps keep it in check. Deer usually leave it alone, and it should not be fertilized because lean soil produces sturdier growth.

title: 9 Tough Perennials for Clay Soil
content: Rough goldenrod is a perennial with upright to arching plumes of tiny yellow blooms from late summer to fall. Grow it in full sun to part shade; plants reach 18 to 36 inches tall and wide and are cold hardy in USDA zones 4 to 9.

title: 9 Tough Perennials for Clay Soil
content: In a five-year Chicago Botanic Garden trial, 'Fireworks' rough goldenrod was a top performer for heavy blooming and disease resistance.

title: 9 Tough Perennials for Clay Soil
content: Native plant portrait photo of 'Fireworks' rough goldenrod blooming with arching yellow sprays in a mixed border.

title: 9 Tough Perennials for Clay Soil
content: Ostrich fern, Matteuccia struthiopteris, brings elegant texture to deep shade and is generally deer and rabbit resistant. It can grow in full sun if watered well, and it spreads by rhizomes; dense or dry clay slows the spread.

title: 9 Tough Perennials for Clay Soil
content: Ostrich fern is a perennial with finely dissected, upright to arching medium-green fronds. Grow it in part to full shade; plants reach 3 to 6 feet tall and 5 to 8 feet wide and are cold hardy in USDA zones 3 to 7.

title: 9 Tough Perennials for Clay Soil
content: Russian sage, Perovskia atriplicifolia, has billowy stems, velvety gray foliage and tiny lavender-blue flowers from summer to fall. Its colorful calyx lasts for months, and shorter cultivars such as 'Sage Advice' and 'Lacy Blue' fit smaller borders.

title: 9 Tough Perennials for Clay Soil
content: Russian sage is drought tolerant and long-lived once established. It grows best in full sun, tolerates clay, is usually passed by deer and rabbits, and attracts pollinators.

title: 9 Tough Perennials for Clay Soil
content: Russian sage is a perennial with tiny lavender-blue spikes from midsummer to fall. Grow it in full sun; plants reach 2 to 5 feet tall and 2 to 4 feet wide and are cold hardy in USDA zones 5 to 9.

title: 9 Tough Perennials for Clay Soil
content: Native plant portrait photo of Russian sage with lavender-blue flower spikes and gray foliage.

title: 9 Tough Perennials for Clay Soil
content: Native plant portrait photo of ostrich fern with fresh green upright fronds.

title: 9 Tough Perennials for Clay Soil
content: False sunflower, Heliopsis helianthoides, produces sunny yellow daisies that feed pollinators and later provide seeds for birds. This short-lived perennial reseeds, though hybrid seedlings may not look like the parent.

title: 9 Tough Perennials for Clay Soil
content: False sunflower grows in bushy upright clumps. 'Prairie Sunset' has purple stems and veins with maroon rings around the flower centers, while variegated forms such as 'Loraine Sunshine' and compact types such as 'Sunstruck' add foliage interest.

title: 9 Tough Perennials for Clay Soil
content: False sunflower is a perennial with yellow daisylike blooms from midsummer to fall. Grow it in full sun to part shade; plants reach 1 to 6 feet tall and 1 to 4 feet wide and are cold hardy in USDA zones 3 to 9.

title: 9 Tough Perennials for Clay Soil
content: Variegated false sunflower sometimes produces vigorous solid-green stems. Cut those stems off at the crown so they do not overtake the variegated growth.

title: 9 Tough Perennials for Clay Soil
content: Native plant portrait photo of false sunflower blooming with yellow daisylike flowers.

title: 9 Tough Perennials for Clay Soil
content: Foxglove penstemon, Penstemon digitalis, is more tolerant of humid weather and denser soil than many western penstemons that need sharp drainage. It is cold hardy, deer resistant and blooms for about a month from late spring to early summer.

title: 9 Tough Perennials for Clay Soil
content: Foxglove penstemon species plants can reach 5 feet tall with green foliage, while hybrids are often smaller and have burgundy foliage. 'Husker Red' has white flowers on 2- to 3-foot plants, and 'Dark Towers' has pink blooms and dark leaves.

title: 9 Tough Perennials for Clay Soil
content: Foxglove penstemon is a perennial with lavender, pink or white tubular blooms from late spring to early summer. Grow it in full sun; plants reach 2 to 5 feet tall and 1 to 3 feet wide and are cold hardy in USDA zones 3 to 8.

title: 9 Tough Perennials for Clay Soil
content: Foxglove penstemon's nectar-rich tubular blooms are favorites of bees, hummingbirds and other pollinators.

title: 9 Tough Perennials for Clay Soil
content: Native plant portrait photo of foxglove penstemon with pale tubular blooms above burgundy-tinged foliage.

title: 9 Tough Perennials for Clay Soil
content: Siberian iris, Iris sibirica, blooms in violet, white, yellow, pink and maroon, with solid or patterned petals. Plant in spring so roots establish before winter, and give plants sun for the best bloom.

title: 9 Tough Perennials for Clay Soil
content: Siberian iris grows in humus-rich soil but also flourishes in clay and even boggy conditions with consistent moisture. Divide every few years in spring, keeping at least three leaves on each division and replanting at the same level.

title: 9 Tough Perennials for Clay Soil
content: Siberian iris is a perennial with white, yellow, violet, blue, pink or maroon spring blooms. Grow it in full sun to part shade; plants reach 24 to 48 inches tall and 18 to 36 inches wide and are cold hardy in USDA zones 3 to 9.

title: 9 Tough Perennials for Clay Soil
content: Goat's beard, Aruncus dioicus, is slow to mature but eventually sends up 4- to 6-foot stems topped with fluffy white plumes. It prefers consistent moisture and blooms more heavily with more light, though it tolerates shade.

title: 9 Tough Perennials for Clay Soil
content: Goat's beard thrives in humus-rich, well-drained soil and tolerates a clay-loam mix, but it does not like dense clay or hot, dry conditions.

title: 9 Tough Perennials for Clay Soil
content: Goat's beard is a perennial with fluffy white plumes from midspring to early summer. Grow it in part to full shade; plants reach 3 to 6 feet tall and 2 to 4 feet wide and are cold hardy in USDA zones 4 to 9.

title: 9 Tough Perennials for Clay Soil
content: Native plant portrait photo of Siberian iris with pale violet flowers.

title: 9 Tough Perennials for Clay Soil
content: Native plant portrait photo of goat's beard with creamy white flower plumes.

title: 9 Tough Perennials for Clay Soil
content: False indigo, Baptisia australis, is an easy-care native that produces pealike blooms for years. If flowers are not deadheaded, they develop deep purple seedpods; species and hybrids may flower in violet, white, yellow, pink or burgundy.

title: 9 Tough Perennials for Clay Soil
content: False indigo sends a large taproot into dense clay, which helps make it drought tolerant once established. It is slow to settle in and hard to divide, so choose the planting site carefully.

title: 9 Tough Perennials for Clay Soil
content: False indigo is a perennial with purple, blue, yellow, white, pink, burgundy or bicolor pealike blooms from late spring to early summer. Grow it in full sun to part shade; plants reach 2 to 4 feet tall and wide and are cold hardy in USDA zones 3 to 9.

title: 9 Tough Perennials for Clay Soil
content: Native plant portrait photo of false indigo with pale yellow pealike flowers.

title: 9 Tough Perennials for Clay Soil
content: Woodland phlox, Phlox divaricata, also called wild sweet William, brightens shady clay borders with lavender-blue spring blooms. Loose clusters of fragrant five-petaled tubular flowers provide nectar for butterflies and hummingbirds.

title: 9 Tough Perennials for Clay Soil
content: Woodland phlox stems root at nodes and self-seed, and the green leaves act as a ground cover after bloom. Varieties include blue-violet 'Blue Moon', white 'May Breeze' and fragrant 'Cloud of Perfume'.

title: 9 Tough Perennials for Clay Soil
content: Woodland phlox is a perennial with lavender-blue or white spring blooms. Grow it in part to full shade; plants reach 8 to 16 inches tall and 8 to 12 inches wide and are cold hardy in USDA zones 3 to 9.

title: Which Native Perennial Is Right for You?
content: Black-eyed Susan, Rudbeckia fulgida, has vibrant yellow daisylike flowers from midsummer to late fall. Leave its brown-purple seedheads standing for birds, and evergreen basal leaves provide winter ground cover.

title: Which Native Perennial Is Right for You?
content: Black-eyed Susan works well at the front or middle of a perennial bed or pollinator border, reaching 2 to 3 feet tall. It also makes a cut flower with a vase life of 8 to 10 days.

title: Which Native Perennial Is Right for You?
content: Grow black-eyed Susan in full sun and dry to medium well-drained soil in USDA zones 3 to 9. It spreads by rhizomes and self-seeding; deadhead for continuous bloom and fewer seedlings, and divide every three to four years in spring.

title: Which Native Perennial Is Right for You?
content: Black-eyed Susan has 2- to 3-inch golden flowers with a brown-purple central disk, oblong serrated dark-green leaves and upright clumps 2 to 3 feet tall and 1 to 2 feet wide.

title: Which Native Perennial Is Right for You?
content: Purple coneflower, Echinacea purpurea, blooms from early summer to midfall with drooping pink-purple petals around spiky dark-orange centers. Hybrids expand the color range to red, orange, green, white and yellow.

title: Which Native Perennial Is Right for You?
content: Purple coneflower works in the front, middle or back of a border depending on variety height, from about 1 to 5 feet tall. Bees and butterflies visit the flowers, and birds eat the seeds if late flowers are left standing.

title: Which Native Perennial Is Right for You?
content: Grow purple coneflower in full sun in USDA zones 3 to 8. Part shade is tolerated but produces fewer flowers and taller plants. It prefers well-drained soil and tolerates dry or rocky conditions once established.

title: Which Native Perennial Is Right for You?
content: Purple coneflower has purple-pink daisylike flowers up to 5 inches across, spiny dark cones with disk flowers, coarse serrated dark-green leaves and multistemmed upright clumps 12 to 60 inches tall and 18 to 24 inches wide.

title: Switchgrass
content: Switchgrass, Panicum virgatum, was once a major native tallgrass prairie grass east of the Rockies from Canada to Mexico. It adapts to sandy soil, dry slopes, open woodlands, salty marshes and even sites under walnuts.

title: Switchgrass
content: Switchgrass is a warm-season grass that blooms in summer as days lengthen. Its panicles develop yellow, pink or purple seedheads, and fall blades turn gold, red or burgundy.

title: Switchgrass
content: Switchgrass offers a native alternative to non-native ornamental grasses. Songbirds, ducks and gamebirds eat its seed, dried foliage provides cover and nesting material, and massed plantings protect small mammals.

title: Switchgrass
content: Switchgrass is a perennial with panicle inflorescences tinted yellow, purple or pink followed by lacy seedheads from late summer to fall. Grow it in full sun and well-drained to dry soil; plants reach 36 to 96 inches tall and 18 to 36 inches wide and are cold hardy in USDA zones 4 to 10.

title: Switchgrass
content: Butterflies that use switchgrass include Arogos skipper, Delaware skipper, Hobomok skipper and northern broken-dash.

title: Switchgrass

title: Switchgrass
content: Switchgrass provides strong vertical lines, airy seedheads, swaying movement and a calming swishy sound. Its upright form stands for most of the year and can structure a border.

title: Switchgrass
content: Switchgrass changes color through the seasons. Blue-green spring blades develop red or burgundy tips, summer flowers add yellow, pink or purple tints, fall foliage turns red, burgundy or gold, and winter stems dry tan or copper.

title: Switchgrass
content: A row of switchgrass can act as a living screen from late summer through winter. For a screen taller than 4 feet, choose cultivars such as 'Heavy Metal' and space plants close for density or farther apart for visible gaps.

title: Switchgrass
content: Switchgrass works well in naturalistic and prairie plantings, in drifts with shrubs and perennials, or in hard-to-maintain spots with companions such as cup plant and gray-headed coneflower.

title: Switchgrass
content: Switchgrass clumping rhizomes can grow 5 to 6 feet deep, helping anchor slopes, slow water, absorb nitrogen and phosphorus, sequester carbon and reduce flooding. It is a useful rain-garden plant because it tolerates wet and dry periods.

title: Switchgrass
content: Switchgrass brings height and verticality to a border while its soft texture rests the eye. Because outer stems may bend into a walkway, choose strongly upright cultivars such as 'Northwind' for high-traffic edges.

title: Switchgrass
content: Colorful companions for switchgrass include annual sunflower, dahlia, Joe-Pye weed, New England aster, ninebark and tall sedum.

title: Switchgrass
content: Annual sunflower, Helianthus annuus and hybrids, has yellow, gold, red, brown, white, burgundy, bicolor, apricot or peach flowers from midsummer to frost. Grow it in full sun; plants reach 1 to 16 feet tall and 2 to 3 feet wide.

title: Switchgrass
content: Dahlia hybrids are tubers with single or double red, orange, pink, white or cream flowers from midsummer to fall. Grow them in full sun; plants reach 1 to 6 feet tall and 1 to 3 feet wide and are cold hardy in USDA zones 8 to 12.

title: Switchgrass
content: Joe-Pye weed, Eutrochium species and hybrids, is a perennial with purple, dusty rose or white flower clusters from midsummer to fall. Grow it in sun to part shade; plants reach 3 to 8 feet tall and 2 to 5 feet wide and are cold hardy in USDA zones 3 to 9.

title: Switchgrass
content: New England aster is a perennial with pink or purple daisylike flowers from late summer to fall. Grow it in full sun; plants reach 1 to 6 feet tall and 2 to 3 feet wide and are cold hardy in USDA zones 3 to 8.

title: Switchgrass
content: Ninebark is a shrub with white or pink flower clusters in late spring to early summer and green, chartreuse, burgundy or near-black foliage. Grow it in sun to part shade; plants reach 1 to 8 feet tall and 2 to 8 feet wide and are cold hardy in USDA zones 2 to 7.

title: Switchgrass
content: Tall sedum is a perennial with pink, red, white, burgundy or green flower clusters from summer to fall. Grow it in full sun; plants reach 8 to 36 inches tall and 12 to 24 inches wide and are cold hardy in USDA zones 3 to 10.

title: Switchgrass
content: Switchgrass tolerates some shade but grows best in full sun. Lean soil is best because excess nitrogen can make stems floppy, so do not fertilize established plants.

title: Switchgrass
content: Switchgrass is slow to emerge in spring and begins growing when the soil warms above 50 degrees F. Leave stems standing through winter, trimming only if snow or ice causes them to block a walkway.

title: Switchgrass
content: For spring cleanup, tie twine or a bungee around the loose clump, cut stems a couple inches above the ground and compost the bundle or cut stems and blades into mulch.

title: Switchgrass
content: Switchgrass can be divided every three years if you want more plants or if the center dies out. Divide in early spring before new growth is about 1 foot tall, cutting pieces from the outer edges with a sharp spade and replanting at the same depth.

title: Why Bulb Depth Matters
content: Spring-blooming bulb depth examples include glory-of-the-snow, hyacinth, wild hyacinth, kaufmanniana tulip, tulip, crown imperial fritillary, giant allium and daffodil. Gardeners in zones 8 and warmer should buy most tulips prechilled and grow them as annuals.

title: Why Bulb Depth Matters
content: If crown imperial fritillary bulbs rot, try planting them tipped slightly on their side so water does not collect in the center.

title: Why Bulb Depth Matters
content: Native bulb-depth diagram showing spring-blooming bulbs at recommended planting depths, including glory-of-the-snow, hyacinth, tulip, crown imperial fritillary, giant allium and daffodil.

title: Why Bulb Depth Matters
content: Each bulb flowers best at a different depth. The general rule is to plant bulbs two to three times as deep as the bulb is tall, measuring from the bottom of the bulb.

title: Why Bulb Depth Matters
content: Proper bulb depth protects bulbs from temperature fluctuations and helps roots anchor the plant for stability. Shallow-planted bulbs may topple.

title: Why Bulb Depth Matters
content: In heavy clay or poorly drained soil, plant bulbs at the shallower end of the recommended range to prevent rot. In dry sandy soil, plant bulbs deeper so they can reach more consistent moisture.

title: Why Bulb Depth Matters
content: Some bulbs are exceptions to the general depth rule. Amaryllis and Guernsey lilies prefer to have the tops of the bulbs near the soil surface.

title: Why Bulb Depth Matters
content: Summer- and fall-blooming bulb depth examples include pineapple lily, Asiatic lily, autumn daffodil, Dutch iris, rain lily, Guernsey lily and autumn crocus.

title: Why Bulb Depth Matters

title: Spinach
content: Spinach, Spinacia oleracea, is a shoulder-season crop with savoy, semi-savoy and flat-leaved types, as well as dark green, light green and red-veined varieties.

title: Spinach
content: Direct-sow spinach seed 1/2 inch deep and 2 inches apart. When seedlings are 2 inches tall, thin plants to 4 to 6 inches apart with scissors.

title: Spinach
content: Spinach germinates best when soil is 45 to 68 degrees F and grows best when air temperatures are 50 to 60 degrees F. Sow spring spinach 4 to 6 weeks before the last frost, using a cold frame or plastic hoop to warm the soil if needed.

title: Spinach
content: As temperatures approach 70 degrees F in early summer, shade cloth can cool the soil and delay bolting. Slow-to-bolt varieties help extend the harvest.

title: Spinach
content: For fall spinach, sow 6 to 8 weeks before the first fall frost. Use shade cloth and consistent moisture while soil is warm, then remove the shade cloth once temperatures stay below 70 degrees F.

title: Spinach

title: Spinach

title: Spinach
content: Grow spinach in full sun with compost, manure or a slow-release vegetable fertilizer applied at planting and every 4 to 6 weeks. A 1- to 2-inch straw mulch helps retain moisture and control weeds.

title: Spinach
content: Spring spinach bolts and turns bitter as days lengthen and temperatures rise near 80 degrees F. Fall crops last longer, often producing until about 20 degrees F, and may overwinter or resume growth in spring in many areas.

title: Spinach
content: Harvest spinach by pinching or cutting outer leaves at the base while leaving the inner leaves to keep growing. Wash grit thoroughly, especially from savoy leaves, spin or pat dry, and store in the refrigerator in a plastic bag or container lined with dry paper towels for about a week.

title: Spinach
content: Spinach is an annual grown 4 to 6 weeks before the last spring frost or 6 to 8 weeks before the first fall frost. A family of four needs about 16 to 32 plants for fresh eating and preserving; grow plants in fertile, moist, well-drained soil in full sun to part shade.

title: Spinach
content: Seasonal spinach solutions include using plastic covers to warm soil for the earliest spring start and shade cloth to cool soil in late spring or late summer. In fall, plastic covers can extend harvest as temperatures drop.

title: Spinach
content: Recommended spinach varieties include 'Bloomsdale Longstanding', 'Equinox', 'Indian Summer', 'Kolibri', 'Red Tabby', 'Regiment' and 'Space', ranging from 25 to 40 days to harvest and offering savoyed, semi-savoyed or smooth leaves with slow bolting tendencies.

author: Sherri Ribbey
content: As trees grow, gardens change. The area near the Lights' back door used to be in full sun, but a pecan canopy now creates the right conditions for hostas, ferns, coral bells and other shade-loving perennials.

title: A Garden of Stories
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Jim and Rachel Light have gardened at their Ohio home for all 49 years of their marriage. Rachel tends weeds and seasonal displays near the back door while Jim works on construction projects.

title: A Garden of Stories
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: The 4 1/2-acre property is Rachel's childhood home. Her parents grew vegetables and a few flowers, and Rachel and Jim transformed the yard around the house into a shady oasis.

title: A Garden of Stories
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Jim built a new home after the couple discovered serious termite damage in the original house, and since then they have continued adding gardens and structures every year.

title: A Garden of Stories

title: A Garden of Stories
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: The first garden bed was a Mother's Day present for Rachel in 1982. Jim and their boys laid out a 6-foot-diameter island bed with a garden hose, and Rachel asked to make it larger year after year until it became a 22-foot-long kidney-shaped bed.

title: A Garden of Stories
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Rachel and Jim built the garden gradually, starting with small beds and adding as time and money allowed. They often bartered: Rachel worked for a hosta grower who paid in plants, and Jim traded labor and cuttings for large deciduous trees.

title: A Garden of Stories
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: The low walls at the front of the house are made of discarded stone from the nearby farm where Jim grew up. They stairstep from 3 feet tall to 4 feet near the entry arch.

title: A Garden of Stories

title: A Garden of Stories
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Each time a new bed goes in, Jim digs out 4 to 6 inches of heavy clay soil by hand and replaces it with equal parts topsoil and compost. The loose mix helps new plants establish and makes weeds easier to pull.

title: A Garden of Stories
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: The most difficult soil-improvement project was a 200-foot-long, 4- to 5-foot-wide border along the driveway. It is now filled with panicle hydrangeas, dahlias and a dwarf hinoki cypress.

title: A Garden of Stories
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Jim and Rachel's borders have color and interest in every season, and containers are key. Ceramic pots, urns, windowboxes and upcycled treasures are filled with annuals, seasonal displays or overwintering perennials such as coral bells and hostas.

title: A Garden of Stories
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Rachel's favorite season is fall. As summer fades, she decorates indoors and out with pumpkins and garden mums, sometimes buying a whole pickup load of pumpkins.

title: A Garden of Stories
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: For fall displays, Rachel saves money by planting in flea-market and yard finds such as iron kettles, wash tubs, an old hog feeder and a hollow log. An old wheelbarrow overflowing with wing begonias is a favorite.

title: A Garden of Stories
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Rachel gives garden mums pride of place by elevating them in containers. A concrete pedestal that once supported a birdbath now holds an elegant planter filled with red-flowering mums.

title: A Garden of Stories
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: When a planting has a hole but is otherwise still going strong, Rachel tucks in a pumpkin.

title: A Garden of Stories
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: To make a pumpkin topiary, Rachel tests which pumpkins stack best. She does not use rods because puncturing the pumpkins would cause rot; instead they sit on a 20-inch pizza pan covered with artificial leaves.

title: A Garden of Stories
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Rachel saw a potting bench in a magazine and asked a neighbor to build one. She also wires handfuls of hydrangea blooms together to create an 8-foot garland that lasts well into winter.

title: A Garden of Stories
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Rachel and Jim use the back door most often because it is closer to the shady sidewalk that leads to the driveway. Beds along the path are filled with shade plants, including hostas and ferns.

title: A Garden of Stories
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: To grow big, healthy hostas, Rachel sprinkles high-nitrogen fertilizer around plants when they are dormant in February so fertilizer will not burn the leaves.

title: A Garden of Stories
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: The garden includes hardy Japanese painted ferns, tassel fern and maidenhair fern in borders, plus Boston ferns in containers that Rachel overwinters indoors.

title: A Garden of Stories
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: The property has nearly 170 trees. Two pecans began from nuts Rachel's mother overwintered in a coffee can of soil in the freezer, and one is now 100 feet tall with a trunk 3 feet in diameter.

title: A Garden of Stories
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Every few years the pecans produce a bumper crop. One recent year Rachel and Jim saved 42 quarts of shelled nuts and gave away gallons of unshelled ones.

title: A Garden of Stories
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Planting near trees with shallow roots is the biggest challenge in Rachel's shade garden. Pine and red maple form dense mats, so replacement trees are chosen for deeper roots, such as black gum, or as smaller understory trees, such as redbuds.

title: A Garden of Stories
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: The old Eastern hemlock behind the house has roots near the soil surface, but epimedium handles the tough competition and even spreads there.

title: A Garden of Stories
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Brunnera, Brunnera macrophylla, has airy pale blue spring flowers over bristly green or variegated foliage. Plants grow 12 to 18 inches tall and 18 to 24 inches wide in USDA zones 3 to 9.

title: A Garden of Stories
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Dutchman's breeches, Dicentra cucullaria, has ferny foliage and winged blooms that look like upside-down pants. Plants grow 6 to 12 inches tall and wide in USDA zones 3 to 7.

title: A Garden of Stories
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: European wild ginger, Asarum europaeum, has mounds of glossy dark green leaves and hidden flowers. Plants grow 4 to 8 inches tall and 9 to 12 inches wide in USDA zones 4 to 8.

title: A Garden of Stories
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Hakonechloa, Hakonechloa macra 'Aureola', forms graceful yellow-and-green-striped arching mounds 12 to 18 inches tall and 6 to 12 inches wide. Plants are cold hardy in USDA zones 3 to 9.

title: A Garden of Stories
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Jack-in-the-pulpit, Arisaema triphyllum, has a spathe and hooded spadix on long stems. Plants grow 12 to 36 inches tall and 12 to 28 inches wide in USDA zones 4 to 9.

title: A Garden of Stories
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Trillium, Trillium sessile, has three variegated leaves and three erect maroon to brown petals in the center. Plants grow 6 to 12 inches tall and wide in USDA zones 4 to 8 and can reseed.

title: A Garden of Stories
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Outbuildings add charm and structure to the Lights' garden. A stone path leads from the back door to Rachel's 9-by-14-foot sewing shed, where she creates quilts and stores seasonal decor.

title: A Garden of Stories
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Jim built a gazebo over an old stone-lined well, and the couple uses the hand pump in the center to draw water for garden plants.

title: A Garden of Stories
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Jim built a 10-by-20-foot greenhouse from scrap lumber and patio doors that had lost their seals. The greenhouse helps the couple save money by starting seeds and overwintering tender plants.

title: A Garden of Stories

title: Garden Fences
content: Brick and wrought iron are elegant, long-lasting fence choices that require minimal care. Wrought iron can be painted or left to age with a rust patina.

title: Garden Fences
content: Native photo of a brick-and-wrought-iron garden fence with roses, illustrating an elegant low-maintenance boundary.

title: Garden Fences
content: A fence can keep animals in or out, declare ownership, separate property and do more than act as a barrier. In a garden it can function as an enclosure, provide security and privacy, guide visitors and set the style of the space.

title: Garden Fences
content: A brick-and-wrought-iron fence planted with soft peachy-yellow roses provides a welcoming look, directs visitors along the walkway and ties the house, garden and structure together.

title: Garden Fences
content: Combining materials, such as wrought iron panels between brick posts, makes a fence more interesting. Rusty iron can coordinate with warm brick, while black paint would create stronger formal contrast.

title: Garden Fences
content: Native vertical photo of wrought iron panels set between brick posts with roses growing through the balusters.

title: Garden Fences
content: The most common reason to build a fence is to mark property edges. A fence can be a physical barrier or an implied boundary that stops the eye and defines spaces such as garden rooms, play areas or pet enclosures.

title: Garden Fences
content: A boundary fence can be almost any size, style or material. Open rail fences mark a boundary while keeping the view open, while closely spaced boards, brick, stone or metal panels make a boundary harder to cross.

title: Garden Fences
content: Fence panels do not have to be continuous to work. Gaps of up to 12 inches can let the gardener slip through during maintenance while discouraging people and pets from the sidewalk.

title: Garden Fences
content: Pet fencing depends on an animal's size, shape, temperament and agility. Chain link is affordable and durable, but jumpy dogs may need a solid wood or vinyl fence with no gaps and vertical boards that are harder to climb.

title: Garden Fences
content: Most dogs will not be able to jump a 5- to 6-foot-tall fence.

title: Garden Fences
content: A cedar or pressure-treated post-and-rail fence left to age naturally can last up to 30 years; untreated pine or spruce may last about half that long. Sealant or paint can extend the life of untreated wood and should be reapplied every three to five years.

title: Garden Fences
content: Native photo of a classic wood post-and-rail fence marking an open boundary.

title: Garden Fences
content: A wood-framed livestock-panel fence can give the illusion of a continuous boundary while leaving gaps between sections for a more open, welcoming feel.

title: Garden Fences
content: A sturdy fence starts with posts buried at least one-third of the total height deep. For a 3-foot fence, use a 4-foot post with 1 foot buried underground, and pressure-treated lumber slows deterioration in moist soil.

title: Garden Fences
content: Native photo of contemporary wood-framed livestock-panel fence sections with black river rock at the base.

title: Garden Fences
content: Privacy fences do not have to follow the property line. They can wrap a patio or be placed strategically after identifying which views need to be blocked, such as a sidewalk or a neighbor's second-floor window.

title: Garden Fences
content: A privacy fence should be 6 feet tall to be effective. Solid fences with no gaps screen views, dampen sound and can hide unattractive features such as air-conditioning units.

title: Garden Fences
content: Solid privacy fences provide seclusion but block light and air movement, which can affect plant growth and comfort. Strong wind can create a downdraft that dries plants or piles snow on one side.

title: Garden Fences
content: Use a wood stain with water repellent and UV stabilizer to protect fences from rotting and fading. Oil-based stain works well on cedar, while pressure-treated lumber must be thoroughly dry before water-based products are applied.

title: Garden Fences
content: A shadowbox fence fastens boards on both sides of a central rail in an alternating pattern, so the fence looks good from either side and appears solid straight on but can be seen through at an angle.

title: Garden Fences
content: Native photo of a shadowbox privacy fence with alternating boards beside a planted border.

title: Garden Fences
content: To reduce fence downdraft, leave gaps at least 1/4 inch wide between boards. Gaps of 2 to 3 inches slow strong wind more effectively but sacrifice some privacy.

title: Garden Fences
content: A lattice extension on top of a solid fence lets light in while most of the fence still provides privacy. Vines grown on the lattice can help block views.

title: Garden Fences
content: A fence placed closer to a seating area provides more privacy than one farther away. Plantings beside a screen soften harsh lines, absorb conversation noise and can add sounds of their own, such as ornamental grass rustling.

title: Garden Fences
content: Trees or large shrubs outside a fence that grow tall or drape over the top provide extra privacy and help incorporate the fence into the garden.

title: Garden Fences
content: Horizontal boards make it easier to step a fence down as the grade changes. Weathered wood can echo patio pavers and furniture lines.

title: Garden Fences
content: Native photo of a contemporary horizontal-board fence stepping down with the slope beside grasses and a patio.

title: Garden Fences
content: Wrought iron and aluminum both make formal fences. Wrought iron is stronger and less likely to bend or dent than aluminum, but it is prone to rust.

title: Garden Fences
content: Painted wrought iron needs maintenance every two to three years if paint chips and rust appear. Remove damaged finish and rust with a wire brush or sander, then repaint with enamel paint.

title: Garden Fences
content: Aluminum does not rust and is available in finishes that do not need repainting.

title: Garden Fences
content: Native photo of a formal wrought-iron or aluminum garden fence in a planted border.

title: Garden Fences
content: Native photo of a short wrought-iron security fence with spiked finials protecting a side-yard planting.

title: Garden Fences
content: A fence can guide visitors and protect plantings. A wrought iron fence can keep plants in a side yard from being trampled, and even a knee-high fence can lead people along a sidewalk and discourage shortcuts through a garden.

title: Garden Fences
content: A fence enhances a garden by acting as a backdrop and contrasting with organic plant shapes. Repetition in posts, rails and balusters pulls the eye along the border and can bring order to casual plantings.

title: Garden Fences
content: Choose a fence that fits the style of the house and garden. A picket fence suits a casual perennial garden, while wrought iron often fits formal, structured plantings.

title: Garden Fences
content: Dark fence colors recede and call less attention to themselves, while bright or light colors attract attention and can pull visitors toward the front door.

title: Garden Fences
content: A white wood picket fence needs repainting every five to seven years. High-quality PVC or vinyl can last 20 to 30 years with occasional scrubbing to remove dirt or mold.

title: Garden Fences
content: Before installing a fence, call 811 or 888-258-0808 in the United States to have utility companies mark underground electric, gas, communications, water and sewer lines. In Canada, use the provincial one-call number.

title: Garden Fences
content: Check local planning and zoning rules before building a fence. Ordinances may control fence materials and height, and a permit may be required.

title: Garden Fences
content: Fence holes are usually needed every 6 to 10 feet. A clam shell post hole digger grabs soil from narrow spaces but is difficult in rocky soil or hard clay.

title: Garden Fences
content: A power auger uses a gas engine and earth-moving bit to dig quickly, but it still requires strength. One-person, two-person and tow-behind sizes are available; a two-person auger is safer than working alone.

title: Garden Fences
content: In general, fence post holes should be 2 to 4 feet deep, and deeper is better. Where the ground freezes, set posts 6 inches below the frost line to prevent winter heaving.

title: Garden Fences
content: In loose, dry or sandy soil, remove sod where the hole will go, wet the soil and let it sit for a few hours or overnight so it holds together and is easier to remove.

title: Garden Fences
content: Fences collect snow in drifts and piles. Avoid placing a fence so the downwind side is on a path, sidewalk or driveway that must be cleared.

title: Garden Fences
content: To deter deer, build a fence at least 8 feet tall if local rules allow it. A solid fence can work shorter because deer will not jump when they cannot see the landing area.

title: Garden Fences
content: Two fences spaced 3 to 4 feet apart can deter deer because of their poor depth perception. Even a row of clothesline can serve as a second obstacle.

title: Garden Fences
content: Eight-foot polypropylene netting stretched between posts or trees can redirect deer. Tie ribbon or cloth strips to the netting so deer see it and do not bolt through.

title: Garden Fences
content: A rabbit fence should be 3 to 4 feet high and buried 1 foot deep. Hardware cloth, chicken wire or woven wire livestock fencing with 1-inch openings keeps rabbits from squeezing through.

title: Garden Fences
content: For groundhogs, raccoons and skunks, use a 4-foot-tall row of chicken wire left loose at the top and attach it to a 4-foot-wide strip of chicken wire laid flat on the ground in an L shape to stop digging.

title: Garden Fences
content: For squirrels, chipmunks and gophers, use fencing with holes smaller than 1/2 inch. Curve lightweight mesh outward into a C-shape at the top and bury the bottom at least 6 inches deep in an outward L shape.

title: Garden Fences
content: Stepped fence framing works best on steep slopes or rolling terrain, with each section level at a different elevation. Sloped framing mirrors gradual slopes.

title: Create a Backyard Border for Birds

content: The birdbox in this plan is designed for the northern flicker, a species that is declining but still commonly found across North America in towns, woodlands and grasslands.

title: Create a Backyard Border for Birds
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Mount a northern flicker birdhouse on a post 6 to 12 feet high at the back of a border with a clear flight path. Fill the house with white pine wood chips, and clean and refresh the chips each year in fall after breeding season or in early spring before it begins.

title: Create a Backyard Border for Birds

content: Offering plenty of food and shelter all season attracts birds and encourages them to consider the garden a nesting site.

title: Create a Backyard Border for Birds
author: Marisa Reyes
content: This garden design uses a mix of native North American species, their cultivars and other plants birds love. Near a woodland with mature trees, it can serve as a transition between woodland and lawn.

title: Create a Backyard Border for Birds
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Site the bird garden where it is easy to view from a window, especially in fall when it has strong autumn color. Avoid placing it next to a patio or driveway so bird messes are less of a problem.

title: Create a Backyard Border for Birds
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Birdhouses offer nesting nooks and safe spots away from predators and weather, while supplemental feeders provide reliable food when natural sources are scarce.

title: Create a Backyard Border for Birds
author: Marisa Reyes
content: To make a nesting basket, shape a 12-by-12-inch piece of hardware cloth and place it 6 to 10 feet high on a forked branch with overhead branches. Secure it with wire; do not put more than one basket in a tree.

title: Create a Backyard Border for Birds
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Elderberry, crabapple and beautyberry provide fall and winter fruit for migrating birds. The perennials in the plan provide seeds after flowers fade, and nectar-rich Joe-Pye weed, threadleaf coreopsis, blazing star and yarrow attract hummingbirds during the growing season.

title: Create a Backyard Border for Birds
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Plant this bird garden in full sun to part shade in moist, well-drained soil. Leave perennials and grasses standing through winter for visual interest and bird food.

title: Create a Backyard Border for Birds
author: Marisa Reyes
content: In late winter, prune crabapple by removing dead, diseased or crossing branches. Prune elderberry by removing unwanted root suckers and dead or diseased branches to improve flower and fruit production.

title: Create a Backyard Border for Birds

title: Create a Backyard Border for Birds

title: Create a Backyard Border for Birds
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Yarrow can spread aggressively by self-seeding and rhizomes. Divide it in early spring or late fall, or cut back spent blooms before seed sets; birds may eat the seed before it germinates.

title: Create a Backyard Border for Birds
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Clean birdfeeders at least once every two weeks, and more often during heavy use or rain, to prevent mold and bacteria that can cause disease among birds.

title: Create a Backyard Border for Birds
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Once a year in late fall or early winter, remove old nests from birdhouses. For birdhouses and feeders, scrub with a solution of 9 parts water to 1 part bleach, rinse well and let them dry completely before reuse.

title: Establish a Monarch Waystation
content: A single monarch butterfly can migrate up to 3,000 miles. Adults that hatch in late summer or early fall do not mate or lay eggs; their job is to migrate south to overwintering grounds.

title: Establish a Monarch Waystation
content: Southbound monarchs stop to feed along the way, storing fat in their abdomens to sustain the flight and winter. In spring, the same monarchs begin moving north and lay eggs on milkweed plants in the southern United States before dying.

title: Establish a Monarch Waystation
content: Newly hatched monarch caterpillars feed on milkweed, then successive generations continue the journey north, feeding and laying eggs until the third or fourth generation reaches the ancestral home range from the previous year.

title: Establish a Monarch Waystation
content: Loss of wildlife habitat has reduced both nectar plants for adult monarch butterflies and milkweed host plants for caterpillars.

title: Establish a Monarch Waystation
content: Monarch Waystations are gardens that feed and house monarchs along migration routes. Many home gardens may already have most of the features needed for a successful waystation.

title: Establish a Monarch Waystation
content: Most monarch butterflies migrate south to central Mexico; those west of the Rocky Mountains overwinter along the southwestern California coast. Short days and cool temperatures trigger the southbound trip, which can take up to two months.

title: Establish a Monarch Waystation
content: A Monarch Waystation should dedicate at least 100 square feet to plants for monarch feeding and egg laying. The area can be continuous or split into patches; groups of three or more like flowers are easier for butterflies to spot.

title: Establish a Monarch Waystation
content: A Monarch Waystation needs at least 6 hours of sun per day so plants produce more flowers and butterflies can warm their bodies for flight.

title: Establish a Monarch Waystation
content: Many monarch-friendly plants, including milkweed, tolerate poor soil and drought but appreciate extra water during summer heat.

title: Establish a Monarch Waystation
content: Space plants close enough for adult butterflies and caterpillars to move from plant to plant, but avoid overcrowding that encourages fungal disease.

title: Establish a Monarch Waystation
content: Choose plants that thrive in your region and can be maintained without herbicides or insecticides that would harm monarch caterpillars or adults.

title: Establish a Monarch Waystation
content: Adult monarch butterflies need nectar plants that bloom sequentially all summer, with a strong emphasis on fall-blooming flowers for migrating monarchs to refuel.

title: Establish a Monarch Waystation
content: Annual nectar plants favored by monarchs include cosmos, lantana, marigold, Mexican sunflower, sweet alyssum, verbena and zinnia.

title: Establish a Monarch Waystation
content: Perennial nectar plants favored by monarchs include blazing star, coreopsis, false sunflower, mealycup sage, New England aster and wild bergamot.

title: Establish a Monarch Waystation
content: Milkweed is the essential host plant for monarch butterfly caterpillars. Grow at least 10 milkweed plants of one species, or at least five each of two or more species native to your region.

title: Establish a Monarch Waystation
content: Different milkweed species may mature at different times. Monarch caterpillars can nearly defoliate milkweed plants, but milkweed is resilient and recovers.

title: Establish a Monarch Waystation
content: Antelope-horn milkweed, Asclepias asperula, has green-yellow flowers from midspring to late fall tinged with maroon, curvy seedpods resembling antelope horns, and a preference for sandy soil. It grows 1 to 2 feet tall and 2 to 3 feet wide in USDA zones 5 to 10.

title: Establish a Monarch Waystation
content: Butterfly milkweed, Asclepias tuberosa, has bright orange flower clusters from early summer to fall above rough, thin-textured leaves. It is drought tolerant and grows 12 to 30 inches tall and 12 to 18 inches wide in USDA zones 3 to 9.

title: Establish a Monarch Waystation
content: Common milkweed, Asclepias syriaca, has fragrant pink flower clusters from early summer through early fall and prefers moist, well-drained soil. It grows 24 to 48 inches tall and 9 to 12 inches wide in USDA zones 3 to 9.

title: Establish a Monarch Waystation
content: Green milkweed, Asclepias viridis, has white to green flower clusters from late spring to early fall and tolerates moist to dry soil. It grows 18 to 24 inches tall and 12 to 24 inches wide in USDA zones 5 to 9.

title: Establish a Monarch Waystation
content: Showy milkweed, Asclepias speciosa, has pink flowers at the top of stems and in leaf axils from late spring to midfall and prefers moist, well-drained soil. It grows 2 to 4 feet tall and 1 to 2 feet wide in USDA zones 3 to 9.

title: Establish a Monarch Waystation
content: Swamp milkweed, Asclepias incarnata, has deep rose-pink flowers from early summer to late fall on branching stems with narrow leaves. It prefers moist to wet soil and grows 3 to 5 feet tall and 2 to 3 feet wide in USDA zones 3 to 6.

title: Q&A
content: Fish emulsion is usually made from cooked fish byproducts. Hydrolyzed fish fertilizer can be made from whole fish or byproducts and is cold pressed, retaining more nutrients and beneficial oils.

title: Q&A
content: Fish emulsion often has a strong lingering fishy smell. Hydrolyzed fish fertilizer still smells like fish, but the odor is less strong and does not last as long. Wild animals and pets may dig where any fish fertilizer has been applied.

title: Q&A
content: Witch hazel cone gall aphid, Hormaphis hamamelidis, causes odd hornlike growths on fall-blooming witch hazel leaves. In spring a female injects a substance into the leaf, a protective gall forms, and she feeds and produces young inside it.

title: Q&A
content: Some witch hazel cone gall aphids stay on witch hazel while others fly to feed on birch trees. In fall, eggs are laid on witch hazel twigs and hatch in spring. The galls are unsightly but the aphids are relatively harmless.

title: Q&A
content: An insect gall is an abnormal growth on a plant caused by a feeding or egg-laying insect. These swellings, lumps or bumps rarely harm the host plant.

title: Q&A
content: Some leaf drop is inevitable when potted plants move indoors to overwinter. Bring plants in before night temperatures drop to 50 degrees F, and wait until spring to prune, repot or fertilize so plants are not stressed further.

title: Q&A
content: Before bringing potted plants indoors, check stems and leaves for insects and treat as needed. Soaking the pot in a tub of water can force pillbugs and other unwanted critters out of the potting mix.

title: Q&A
content: Keep outdoor plants separate from other houseplants for a few weeks after bringing them indoors so any insects do not spread.

title: Q&A
content: Water overwintered potted plants regularly but keep soil barely moist, not wet, because wet roots can rot. Indoor growth slows in lower light, and that change can also cause some leaves to drop.

content: Native photo of hornlike witch hazel cone galls on leaves caused by aphids.

title: Q&A
content: Native technique photo of a potted plant submerged in a bucket of water before being brought indoors to force pests out of the potting mix.

title: Q&A
content: In annual flowerbeds and vegetable gardens, fall leaves can be left in place and worked into the soil or added to the compost pile in spring. Decaying leaves improve soil texture, add nutrients and provide insulation and insect cover.

title: Q&A
content: A heavy wet layer of leaves can smother grass and cause perennial crowns to rot over winter, so those leaves may need to be raked up. In neighborhoods, rake leaves that may blow into neighboring yards.

title: Q&A
content: Hardneck garlic is the best type for Minnesota and other cold-winter areas. Softneck garlic is better suited to warmer zones and is usually the type found at grocery stores.

title: Q&A
content: Do not plant store-bought garlic cloves because they may have been treated to prevent sprouting. Buy cloves for planting from a garden center, mail-order source or local grower.

title: Q&A
content: Plant hardneck garlic in fall in full sun and well-drained soil. Break heads into individual cloves just before planting, leave the papery covering on, and set cloves pointed end up about 5 inches apart and 2 to 4 inches deep.

title: Q&A
content: Garlic does not tolerate competition, so keep the area weed-free. Apply 1 to 2 inches of straw mulch, provide about 1 inch of water per week during the growing season, snap off edible curly scapes and harvest when foliage begins to brown in summer.

title: Q&A
content: White mulberry, Morus alba, is a non-native invasive tree that grows 20 to 60 feet tall and seeds rampantly, crowding out native species.

title: Q&A
content: White mulberry leaves on young plants are heart shaped with toothed margins, while mature leaves can be deeply lobed or mitten shaped. Unlike native red mulberry, white mulberry leaves have a soft gloss on top and smooth undersides.

title: Q&A
content: White mulberry has pale green spring catkins followed by red to dark purple blackberry-shaped fruit in early summer. Its shallow roots are bright yellow to orange, twigs ooze milky sap when broken, and older bark is furrowed and slightly orange-gray.

title: Q&A
content: White mulberry seedlings sprout almost anywhere in North America, in sun or shade and good or poor soil. Remove plants before they set fruit, pull or hoe seedlings, dig saplings and repeatedly cut or cover larger stumps to exhaust regrowth.

title: Attract Wildlife With This Fall-Blooming Perennial
author: Jennifer Howell
content: 'Southern Cross' ironweed has masses of fringed bright purple flower clusters from early to late fall. Bees and butterflies swarm the blooms for nectar, while deer and rabbits tend to pass it by.

title: Attract Wildlife With This Fall-Blooming Perennial
author: Jennifer Howell
content: After ironweed flowers fade, the spent blooms look attractive through winter and birds eat the seeds. Deadheading can prevent possible reseeding, though 'Southern Cross' is less likely to produce viable seed than the species.

title: Attract Wildlife With This Fall-Blooming Perennial
author: Jennifer Howell
content: 'Southern Cross' is a naturally occurring native ironweed hybrid. At about 3 feet tall with slightly wider leaves and a more compact habit than other ironweeds, it fits cottage gardens and mini meadows without looking weedy.

title: Attract Wildlife With This Fall-Blooming Perennial
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Grow 'Southern Cross' ironweed in full sun for best flowering and the sturdiest plants. It tolerates clay, adapts to drought once established and prefers lean soil, so it does not need fertilizer.

title: Attract Wildlife With This Fall-Blooming Perennial
author: Jennifer Howell
content: To reduce powdery mildew and rust on ironweed, do not overcrowd plants. Air movement between plants helps keep fungal diseases from getting established.

title: Attract Wildlife With This Fall-Blooming Perennial
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Combine 'Southern Cross' ironweed with summer- to fall-blooming partners in warm reds, oranges and yellows. Wildlife-friendly companions that attract bees, beneficial wasps, butterflies and birds bring the border alive with color and movement.

title: Attract Wildlife With This Fall-Blooming Perennial
author: Jennifer Howell
content: 'Southern Cross' ironweed, Vernonia hybrid, is a perennial with purple flowers in late summer to early fall. Grow it in full sun to part shade and moist, well-drained but adaptable soil; plants reach 30 to 36 inches tall and wide and are cold hardy in USDA zones 4 to 9.

title: Attract Wildlife With This Fall-Blooming Perennial
author: Jennifer Howell
content: A Fall Feast combination pairs 'Southern Cross' ironweed with 'Purple Emperor' tall sedum, a perennial with pink flower clusters from midsummer to fall and purple-black foliage by summer, and Zahara Yellow zinnia, an annual with yellow flowers from late spring to frost.

title: Timeless Trees
content: In a part-shade container, oxalis skirts the edges with seasonal color, shifting from copper-pink emerging stems in spring to chartreuse summer foliage and golden-bronze fall color.

title: Timeless Trees
content: A topiary mugo pine is hardy in USDA zones 2 to 8 and can stay outdoors all winter. Spray it with an antitranspirant to protect needles from harsh winds, then tuck in evergreen boughs and pine cones after tender coleus and oxalis finish.

title: Timeless Trees
content: The mugo pine container uses one mugo pine, one Sedona Sunset coleus and five Molten Lava oxalis in a 30-inch-diameter container.

title: Timeless Trees
content: Japanese maples are ideal container trees because their size is limited by the pot and they come in many colors and forms, including weeping forms. They overwinter outdoors in containers in USDA zones 6 and warmer and thrive in part shade.

title: Timeless Trees
content: Japanese maples have nonaggressive roots that allow annual underplanting and rarely become pot-bound. Every seven or eight years in early spring, slide the tree from the pot, shear off one-quarter of the roots and replant in fresh potting mix.

title: Timeless Trees

title: Timeless Trees
content: A red coleus provides bright color in a ceramic container, while bacopa and flowering maple contribute more bloom and fullness as they grow. The combination works in full sun to part shade.

title: Timeless Trees
content: David viburnum has glossy leathery evergreen leaves in USDA zones 7 to 9. Plant a female David viburnum in the container and a male nearby in the landscape to pollinate its white spring flowers, producing metallic blue berries in fall that last into winter.

title: Timeless Trees
content: The David viburnum container uses one David viburnum, one Rediculous coleus, one flowering maple, one 'Silver Falls' dichondra, one orange sedge and one Superbells White calibrachoa in a 20-inch-diameter container.

title: Timeless Trees
content: A panicle hydrangea trained into tree form makes a strong container statement. Heavy blooms may need support in rain or wind, so a stake along the trunk can be utilitarian or decorative.

title: Timeless Trees
content: Sun-loving annuals under a tree-form panicle hydrangea accent the evolving display. Hydrangea panicles form in spring, open chartreuse to white in early summer, blush pink as they age and dry papery brown by fall, clinging through winter.

title: Timeless Trees
content: The panicle hydrangea container uses one panicle hydrangea, two petunias, two 'Victoria Blue' mealycup sages, eight floss flowers and eight bacopas in a 24-inch-diameter container.

title: Timeless Trees
content: Camouflage Japanese aralia can grow in a container year round in part shade in USDA zones 7 to 10. In colder zones, bring it indoors as a houseplant when night temperatures drop below 50 degrees F.

title: Timeless Trees
content: For easier overwintering, plant Japanese aralia in a nursery pot and sink that pot into the outdoor container in spring, planting annuals around it. Before freezing weather, lift the nursery pot out and bring the aralia indoors.

title: Timeless Trees
content: The Japanese aralia container uses one Camouflage Japanese aralia, one Angel Wings senecio, one 'Margarita' sweet potato vine, one Vermillion Red Rieger begonia, six Americana White geraniums and one silver nettle in a 32-inch-diameter container.

title: Timeless Trees
content: Native container-garden photo of Camouflage Japanese aralia with senecio, sweet potato vine, begonia, white geraniums and silver nettle.

title: Timeless Trees
content: Purple heart contrasts with downy Japanese maple, while white salvia repeats the color of the container. Downy Japanese maple can spend winter in place, but purple heart needs to come indoors or be propagated from cuttings.

title: Timeless Trees
content: To overwinter purple heart from cuttings, snip 4- to 6-inch stems, remove the bottom two sets of leaves and place stems in water for several weeks until roots form, then pot them up for next year.

title: Timeless Trees
content: The downy Japanese maple container uses one 'Fairy Lights' downy Japanese maple, one 'Purpurea' purple heart and three 'Salsa White' salvias in a 24-inch-diameter container.

title: Timeless Trees
content: Container-grown trees and shrubs that remain outdoors should be hardy in at least one zone colder than your garden zone. Concrete, metal, wood and plastic pots can stay outdoors all winter.

title: Timeless Trees
content: Protect marginally hardy container trees and shrubs by moving pots close to a building in a shady spot, such as under a north or east overhang, out of harsh winds.

title: Timeless Trees
content: Terra-cotta clay and glazed ceramic pots absorb water and may crack or flake during freeze-thaw cycles. Move those containers into a garage or shed where temperatures stay just above freezing so plants stay dormant and pots are protected.

title: Timeless Trees
content: Elevate winter containers on pot feet, bricks or stones so drainage holes stay open and thawing potting mix can drain. Freezing water in saturated mix can crack some pots.

title: Timeless Trees
content: Spray needled and broadleaf evergreens with an antitranspirant to reduce drying from bitter winds, and water container trees and shrubs lightly during warm spells if the potting mix becomes dry.

title: Saving Seeds
content: Saving flower seeds is an easy way to get more plants with little investment. Let blooms fade without deadheading so seeds can ripen; young seeds are usually green and turn hard and dark brown or black when ready.

title: Saving Seeds
content: Harvest seeds with your hands or tap them into a plastic container or paper bag. Remove as much debris as possible, dry seeds on a paper towel for about a week, then pour them into an envelope labeled with the plant name and date gathered.

title: Saving Seeds
content: Store seeds out of direct sunlight and away from heat and humidity. A cool, dark place around 50 degrees F works well, and properly dried and packed seeds can last for years.

title: Saving Seeds
content: Spider flower seed pods are ripe when the long slender pods start to split open.

title: Saving Seeds
content: Native flower photo of spider flower with ripening slender seed pods ready to split open.

title: Saving Seeds
content: A germination test can show whether old seed is worth planting. Scatter 10 seeds on a wet paper towel, roll it up, seal it in a plastic bag and set it in a warm place.

title: Saving Seeds
content: After three to five days, count sprouted seeds and multiply by 10 to find the germination percentage. If 7 of 10 seeds sprout, the germination rate is 70 percent, so sow a little more thickly.

title: Saving Seeds
content: If germination is 30 to 40 percent, sow twice as thickly as the recommended rate. Below that, the seed is probably not worth the trouble.

title: Saving Seeds
content: To presprout larger seeds, soak them in water for at least 4 hours but no more than 12, drain them, wrap them in a wet paper towel and wait a few days for rootlets before carefully planting.

title: Saving Seeds
content: Good annuals and tender perennials for seed saving include calendula, cosmos, flowering tobacco, four o'clock, mallow, spider flower and zinnia. Many hybrids will not come true from seed, and some newer spider flower hybrids are sterile.

title: In the Weeds
author: Jamie Seitz
content: Jamie tried growing cucumbers on a trellis to save space in raised beds and make the garden look tidy. At first the vines climbed, crawled and wound tendrils up the trellis quickly.

title: In the Weeds
author: Jamie Seitz
content: When the cucumber trellis leaned under the weight of baby cucumbers, Jamie reinforced it and expected the fruit to lengthen. Instead, the cucumbers stayed small and started looking like teardrops.

title: In the Weeds
author: Jamie Seitz
content: The seed packet revealed that the plants were pickling cucumbers meant to stay small, but the fruit still became round. The baby cucumbers seemed to go from too tiny to pick to orange-shaped overnight.

title: In the Weeds
author: Jamie Seitz
content: The round yellow cucumbers tasted bitter and seedy rather than crisp. The problem may have been drought, a fluke or grower error, but the first cucumber trellis attempt was not a social-media-worthy success.

title: In the Weeds
author: Jamie Seitz
content: Jamie was not deterred from growing trellised cucumbers again. Next time she planned to choose the cucumber type more carefully and secure the trellis better.

title: Reader Tips
author: Kristen McWilliams, MN
content: After sowing seeds, Kristen covers rows with 12-by-12-inch squares of hardware cloth secured with landscape pins to stop squirrels from digging. After seedlings sprout, she bends the squares into arches over the growing plants, then later moves them between rows to cover exposed soil.

title: Reader Tips
author: Kristen McWilliams, MN
content: Hardware-cloth squares can be flattened, stored and reused each year. The same protection also works for young bulb and perennial foliage that rabbits might browse in spring.

title: Reader Tips
author: Vicky Youmans, PA
content: To make a 5-gallon bucket easier to carry, loosen the hooked end of the wire handle and slide a short piece of old garden hose onto the handle for extra cushioning.

title: Reader Tips
author: Rae Coletti, FL
content: In temperate or tropical climates where unexpected frost can damage tender plants, Rae wraps old-style warm-toned C7 holiday lights around vulnerable plants as insurance. The older bulbs produce enough heat to help protect rubber trees, staghorn ferns and avocado seedlings during cold snaps.

title: Reader Tips
author: Joyce Austin, SC
content: Many Lowe's, Home Depot and local garden centers accept empty nursery pots and trays for reuse or recycling, though participation varies by store. Check first, then take pots to the garden center drop-off or ask an associate where they belong.

title: Reader Tips
author: Alice Frasher, GA
content: Before gardening, run fingernails across a bar of soap until the nails are filled with hard soap. Dirt cannot pack under the nails as easily, and washing afterward removes the soap.

title: Reader Tips
content: Common yellowthroat, Geothlypis trichas, is a small gray-green warbler with yellow from the throat down the belly. Males have brighter yellow coloring and a black mask around the eyes.

title: Reader Tips
content: Common yellowthroats are found across much of the United States in spring and summer, especially around wetlands, marshes and bodies of water. They nest low in reeds and tall grasses and have a distinctive witchety-witchety-witchety song.

title: Reader Tips
content: Because common yellowthroats eat insects, they usually will not visit seed feeders. Gardeners near water, brushy areas or tall grasses may see them, and they may visit a dish or hopper feeder with mealworms.

title: Feed These 5 Birds From Your Garden Every Winter
content: One of the best ways to help birds in winter is to offer some of their favorite foods. Bill shape is a good clue to what each bird eats, and garden plantings can supply seeds, berries, fruit, nuts and overwintering insects.

title: Feed These 5 Birds From Your Garden Every Winter
content: The black-capped chickadee is a small acrobatic bird that can perch on slender stems to feed. Winter foods include sunflower seeds, pinecones, winterberry, elderberry, viburnum, hawthorn, sumac, hemlock berries, insect eggs or hibernating pupae; feeder foods include black-oil sunflower, safflower, peanuts, suet and mealworms.

title: Feed These 5 Birds From Your Garden Every Winter
content: The downy woodpecker quickly hops up and down trunks, using a strong pointed beak to bore into wood and hunt insects. Winter foods include sunflower seeds, pinecones, oak nuts, beech nuts, insect eggs and hibernating pupae; feeder foods include peanuts, sunflower seeds and suet.

title: Feed These 5 Birds From Your Garden Every Winter
content: The northern cardinal hops on the ground and from branch to branch to find food. Winter foods include ornamental grass seed, sunflowers, sumac, hackberry, dogwood and bayberry; feeder foods include black-oil sunflower, safflower and corn.

title: Feed These 5 Birds From Your Garden Every Winter
content: The cedar waxwing hops and flutters through trees, plucking fruit with a short wide beak. Winter foods include cedar, juniper, holly, mistletoe, crabapple and hackberry fruit; feeder foods include dried cranberries or raisins, fresh grapes, oranges, raspberries and jam.

title: Feed These 5 Birds From Your Garden Every Winter
content: The American goldfinch balances on seedheads to feed. Winter foods include thistle, aster, goldenrod, burdock, coreopsis, coneflower, sunflower, ornamental grass and pinecone seed; feeder foods include black-oil sunflower and nyjer seed.

title: Your Garden Can Be Beautiful All Year
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Beds and borders do not need to stop being interesting when the weather turns cold. For inspiring fall and winter views, look for plants with distinctive seedheads, foliage that changes to gold, red or orange, and evergreens that can step into the spotlight.

title: Your Garden Can Be Beautiful All Year
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: In the Fall Foliage Extravaganza combination, common witch hazel becomes a golden autumn showstopper with spidery yellow blooms, while porcupine grass and tall sedum keep structure and interest into winter.

title: Your Garden Can Be Beautiful All Year
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Common witch hazel, Hamamelis virginiana, is a shrub with cream to yellow blooms in mid- to late fall; full sun to part shade; 15 to 20 feet tall and wide; USDA zones 3 to 8.

title: Your Garden Can Be Beautiful All Year
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Porcupine grass, Miscanthus sinensis 'Strictus', is a perennial with copper-tan fall plumes and green foliage with gold stripes; full sun to part shade; 5 to 9 feet tall and 2 to 6 feet wide; USDA zones 5 to 9.

title: Your Garden Can Be Beautiful All Year
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Orienpet lily, Lilium 'Scheherazade', is a bulb with fragrant deep red recurved petals edged gold to white in mid- to late summer; full sun to part shade; 4 to 7 feet tall and 1 to 2 feet wide; USDA zones 4 to 8.

title: Your Garden Can Be Beautiful All Year
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Bluebeard, Caryopteris x clandonensis 'Worcester Gold', is a shrub with fragrant lavender-blue summer flowers and gold spring-to-summer foliage; full sun; 2 to 3 feet tall and wide; USDA zones 5 to 9.

title: Your Garden Can Be Beautiful All Year
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Tall sedum, Hylotelephium telephium 'Matrona', is a perennial with pink summer flowers aging rust-red by fall and blue-gray foliage with purple stems and veins; full sun; 18 to 24 inches tall and wide; USDA zones 3 to 9.

title: Your Garden Can Be Beautiful All Year
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Common witch hazel is slow growing and only needs occasional pruning to shape plants or remove dead stems.

title: Your Garden Can Be Beautiful All Year
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Native garden photo of common witch hazel glowing yellow in a fall foliage combination with ornamental grass and sedum.

title: Your Garden Can Be Beautiful All Year
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: For late-winter interest, shrubs with evergreen foliage make gray days more bearable. Variegated wintercreeper brightens the border, and cold winter temperatures intensify heather's red foliage.

title: Your Garden Can Be Beautiful All Year
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Cotoneaster, Cotoneaster spp., is a shrub with small pink or white spring flowers, winter-persistent red berries and small evergreen leaves; full sun to part shade; 2 to 3 feet tall and 3 to 8 feet wide; USDA zones 4 to 7.

title: Your Garden Can Be Beautiful All Year
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Heather, Calluna vulgaris 'Wickwar Flame', is a shrub with lavender-pink summer bells and golden-yellow to orange summer foliage that turns vibrant red in winter; full sun; 15 to 20 inches tall and 26 to 30 inches wide; USDA zones 4 to 8.

title: Your Garden Can Be Beautiful All Year
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Variegated wintercreeper, Euonymus fortunei 'Emerald 'n' Gold', is a shrub with inconspicuous spring flowers and evergreen variegated foliage; full sun; 18 to 24 inches tall and 12 to 48 inches wide; USDA zones 5 to 9.

title: Your Garden Can Be Beautiful All Year
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: For a quiet winter palette, skip fall cleanup and let faded grasses and seedheads stand. Mixing plant habits and textures makes the winter differences easier to see, especially with a dusting of snow.

title: Your Garden Can Be Beautiful All Year
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Switchgrass, Panicum virgatum 'Dallas Blues', is a perennial with large pink-tinted panicles and blue-green foliage fading to tan; 5 to 6 feet tall and 2 to 5 feet wide; USDA zones 4 to 9.

title: Your Garden Can Be Beautiful All Year
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Purple coneflower, Echinacea purpurea, is a perennial with purple-pink blooms from early summer to fall and seedheads birds eat; full sun to part shade; 1 to 4 feet tall and 1 to 3 feet wide; USDA zones 3 to 9.

title: Your Garden Can Be Beautiful All Year
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Fountain grass, Pennisetum alopecuroides 'Cassian', is a perennial with pink-tinted bottlebrush flowers from summer to fall and golden fall foliage; full sun to part shade; 24 to 40 inches tall and wide; USDA zones 5 to 9.

title: Your Garden Can Be Beautiful All Year
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Spike blazing star, Liatris spicata, is a perennial with fluffy purple summer flower spikes; full sun to part shade; 18 to 48 inches tall and 12 to 24 inches wide; USDA zones 3 to 8.

title: The Art of Flower Pounding
author: Marisa Reyes and Carrie Topp
content: Flower pounding creates botanical prints from fresh flowers, a hammer and natural-fiber fabric such as cotton, linen, bamboo or hemp. The technique can decorate gift bags, towels, tablecloths, shirts and socks.

title: The Art of Flower Pounding
author: Marisa Reyes and Carrie Topp
content: Use an item made of 100 percent natural fibers, pH-neutral detergent, washing soda, alum, fresh flowers and foliage, plus a bucket, tweezers, hammer, cutting board, barrier cloth, cardboard, iron and paper.

title: The Art of Flower Pounding
author: Marisa Reyes and Carrie Topp
content: Scour fabric first so it absorbs flower pigments. Soak it in 1 teaspoon pH-neutral detergent and 2 tablespoons washing soda in 1 gallon of warm water, then hand wash and rinse until the water runs clean.

title: The Art of Flower Pounding
author: Marisa Reyes and Carrie Topp
content: After scouring, mordant the fabric so dye binds to it. Mix 1 gallon hot water with 2 teaspoons alum, soak fabric 2 hours, then add 1 teaspoon washing soda dissolved in 1/2 cup hot water and soak at least 8 more hours before wringing, drying and ironing.

title: The Art of Flower Pounding
author: Marisa Reyes and Carrie Topp
content: To create the design, place fabric on a hard surface and insert cardboard between gift-bag layers so dye does not bleed through to the back.

title: The Art of Flower Pounding
author: Marisa Reyes and Carrie Topp
content: Native project photo of botanical flower-pounded cotton gift bags.

title: The Art of Flower Pounding
author: Marisa Reyes and Carrie Topp
content: Arrange flowers face down on the fabric and cover them with a barrier cloth such as an old pillowcase, scrap fabric or paper towel.

title: The Art of Flower Pounding
author: Marisa Reyes and Carrie Topp
content: Delicate flowers such as Johnny jump-ups transfer color easily. Dense-centered flowers such as marigolds and coreopsis can look muddy if pounded whole, so remove petals and arrange them in a cleaner pattern.

title: The Art of Flower Pounding
author: Marisa Reyes and Carrie Topp
content: Hammer stems and flowers separately if you want to mix and match elements. Place leaves face up so veins and textures imprint clearly on the fabric.

title: The Art of Flower Pounding
author: Marisa Reyes and Carrie Topp
content: Pound softly with a hammer from the outer edges toward the center so dye spreads evenly and details transfer. Pull back the barrier cloth as needed to check progress and adjust shifted flowers or leaves.

title: The Art of Flower Pounding
author: Marisa Reyes and Carrie Topp
content: Let the print dry a few minutes before gently removing plant material with tweezers. Heat set the print by laying paper over the design and ironing on a low setting.

title: The Art of Flower Pounding
author: Marisa Reyes and Carrie Topp
content: Flowers that worked well for pounding include balloon flower, blanket flower, coreopsis, cosmos, garden phlox, gloriosa daisy, hibiscus, Johnny jump-up, mandevilla, marigold and pot marigold.

title: Multiseason Containers Made Easy
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Heather Thomas creates year-round container displays by starting in fall with spring-blooming bulbs, then swapping seasonal layers so the same pot flows from winter to spring, summer and fall.

title: Multiseason Containers Made Easy
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Choose a container that withstands the coldest winter temperatures in your zone. Composite, plastic, wood and metal pots are less likely than porous pots to crack if frozen soil expands.

title: Multiseason Containers Made Easy
author: Jennifer Howell
content: In fall, fill the pot with slightly moistened potting mix and plant bulbs close together; Heather fits 48 tulip bulbs in a 20-by-20-inch square pot.

title: Multiseason Containers Made Easy
author: Jennifer Howell
content: After planting bulbs, set a snug 2-inch-thick piece of craft foam on top and insert evergreen boughs, Southern magnolia branches, pine cones and winter accents into the foam. The foam can be reused for several years.

title: Multiseason Containers Made Easy
author: Jennifer Howell
content: As winter ends, check under the foam for emerging bulb foliage. When foliage appears, remove the foam and winter arrangement, begin watering and add spring accents such as corkscrew willow branches if desired.

title: Multiseason Containers Made Easy
author: Jennifer Howell
content: After bulbs finish blooming, pull them out and bury an empty nursery pot in the mix. Drop in a potted focal plant such as vining mandevilla, which keeps vigorous roots contained and makes overwintering easier.

title: Multiseason Containers Made Easy
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Plant summer annuals around the nested focal plant for color through fall, then remove the focal plant and swap in a garden mum for autumn.

title: Which Annual Is Right for You?
content: Snapdragon, Antirrhinum majus, is valued for tall stature and long-lasting blooms in bold colors, pastels and bicolors. Cut stems can last 7 to 10 days in a vase.

title: Which Annual Is Right for You?
content: Snapdragons vary in size and habit. Use trailing types in containers and hanging baskets, bedding types in mixed plantings and taller types for cut flowers.

title: Which Annual Is Right for You?
content: Grow snapdragons in full sun and moist, well-drained soil. They bloom best in cool weather with daytime temperatures between 40 and 70 degrees F, and are cold hardy in USDA zones 7 to 10.

title: Which Annual Is Right for You?
content: Pinch young snapdragons to promote bushiness and reduce legginess. Fertilize every 2 to 4 weeks once flower stalks appear, and deadhead spent blooms for another flush.

title: Which Annual Is Right for You?
content: Snapdragon varieties include trailing Candy Showers Rose, 14- to 16-inch Snaptastic Yellow and 24- to 30-inch Overture II Orange.

title: Which Annual Is Right for You?
