title: Perennials That Thrive in Extra-Cold Gardens
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Frigid temperatures, early or late frosts, lack of insulating snow, drying winds and a short growing season can damage plants in northern gardens, especially USDA zones 2 to 4.

title: Perennials That Thrive in Extra-Cold Gardens
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Many extra-hardy perennials have cell structures that prevent ice from forming inside; roots store sugars and move moisture out of cells so they do not freeze and burst.

title: Perennials That Thrive in Extra-Cold Gardens
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Some cold-hardy perennials are evergreen in zones 5 and warmer but die back to the ground in colder zones, protecting roots and conserving energy.

title: Perennials That Thrive in Extra-Cold Gardens
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Plants native to cold zones and those grown in local nurseries are often better suited to cold-region conditions than plants shipped from warmer areas.

title: Perennials That Thrive in Extra-Cold Gardens
author: Jennifer Howell
content: For winter survival in zones 2 to 4, mulch as plants go dormant with 2 to 3 inches of straw, wood chips, pine needles or chopped leaves, then pull mulch away from crowns as spring warms.

title: Perennials That Thrive in Extra-Cold Gardens
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Leave dried stems standing in winter to insulate crowns unless foliage shows disease or harmful insects, in which case remove debris to prevent reinfection.

title: Perennials That Thrive in Extra-Cold Gardens
author: Jennifer Howell
content: In zones 2 and 3, plant perennials in early spring so roots establish before winter. In zones 4 to 6, fall planting can also work six to eight weeks before the first frost.

title: Perennials That Thrive in Extra-Cold Gardens
author: Jennifer Howell
content: If fall has been dry, water deeply after the first hard frost around 25 degrees F so roots do not desiccate. In snowless winters, water if several days are above 40 degrees F and the soil is dry.

title: Perennials That Thrive in Extra-Cold Gardens
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Herbaceous peony, Paeonia lactiflora. In northern gardens, cool temperatures and a short season can produce glorious midsummer peony blooms. Plant tubers no more than 2 inches deep or they may not bloom well. In zones 3 and 4, add 4 inches of mulch in late fall, then pull it back as new growth emerges. Grow in full sun with good air circulation and remove powdery mildew-infected foliage at season's end. Profile: fragrant single or double pink, white, red or magenta flowers in late spring to summer; full sun; average well-drained soil; 2 to 4 feet tall and wide; USDA zones 3 to 8.

title: Perennials That Thrive in Extra-Cold Gardens
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Native plant portrait photo of herbaceous peony for extra-cold gardens.

title: Perennials That Thrive in Extra-Cold Gardens
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Peonies need at least 500 hours below 40 degrees F each year to bloom.

title: Perennials That Thrive in Extra-Cold Gardens
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Virginia bluebells, Mertensia virginica. Virginia bluebells emerge with purple foliage that changes to green or blue-green. Pink buds open sky blue in early to midspring, then plants go dormant after bloom. They thrive in moist, compost-rich, shady sites and can reseed into colonies. Profile: pink buds opening to blue flowers in early to midspring; part to full shade; moist well-drained soil; 12 to 18 inches tall and 6 to 12 inches wide; USDA zones 3 to 9.

title: Perennials That Thrive in Extra-Cold Gardens
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Native plant portrait photo of virginia bluebells for extra-cold gardens.

title: Perennials That Thrive in Extra-Cold Gardens
author: Jennifer Howell
content: If you plan to divide Virginia bluebells, mark clumps in spring while they bloom so you can find the roots after plants go dormant.

title: Perennials That Thrive in Extra-Cold Gardens
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Showy lady's slipper, Cypripedium reginae. Showy lady's slipper is a long-lived native orchid for moist, organic woodland soil. It is slow from purchased seedlings and illegal to collect from the wild, so buy only seed-grown plants from reputable sources. Mulch with leaf litter in late fall. Profile: white flowers with a pink pouch in early to midsummer; part shade; moist but not wet soil; 10 to 36 inches tall and 12 to 14 inches wide; USDA zones 2 to 7.

title: Perennials That Thrive in Extra-Cold Gardens
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Native plant portrait photo of showy lady's slipper for extra-cold gardens.

title: Perennials That Thrive in Extra-Cold Gardens
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Candytuft, Iberis sempervirens. Candytuft suits rock gardens, retaining walls and border edges, with white flower clusters covering mounded plants in mid- to late spring. Shear stems back by one-third after bloom. In zones 3 and 4, it may die back and benefits from snow cover or evergreen bough insulation. Profile: clusters of white flowers in mid- to late spring; full sun; average well-drained soil; 6 to 12 inches tall and 6 to 25 inches wide; USDA zones 3 to 9.

title: Perennials That Thrive in Extra-Cold Gardens
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Native plant portrait photo of candytuft for extra-cold gardens.

title: Perennials That Thrive in Extra-Cold Gardens
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Gas plant, Dictamnus albus. Gas plant is long-lived, slow-growing and often takes several years to flower. Its deep taproot protects it in cold winters but makes transplanting and division difficult. Direct-sow seed in fall for winter stratification, and wear gloves because leaf oils can cause a rash. Profile: fragrant pink-purple or white flower spikes in late spring to early summer; full sun; evenly moist well-drained soil; 2 to 3 feet tall and wide; USDA zones 3 to 8.

title: Perennials That Thrive in Extra-Cold Gardens
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Native plant portrait photo of gas plant for extra-cold gardens.

title: Perennials That Thrive in Extra-Cold Gardens
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Gas plant blooms release oils that briefly ignite if a match is held close to a flower spike on a windless evening.

title: Perennials That Thrive in Extra-Cold Gardens
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Lupine, Lupinus hybrids. Lupines thrive in cool summers and attract butterflies, bees and other pollinators. Soak seeds 24 hours or sow outdoors in fall for natural scarification. Plants are often short-lived but can be renewed by sowing seed annually; remove seedheads where reseeding is unwanted. Profile: red, purple, yellow, pink, salmon, white or bicolor spikes in late spring to midsummer; full sun to part shade; average well-drained soil; 12 to 48 inches tall and 6 to 18 inches wide; USDA zones 4 to 8.

title: Perennials That Thrive in Extra-Cold Gardens
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Native plant portrait photo of lupine for extra-cold gardens.

title: Perennials That Thrive in Extra-Cold Gardens
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Balloon flower, Platycodon grandiflorus. Balloon flower has puffy buds that open into star-shaped blossoms. Plant it where it can remain undisturbed because the long taproot handles drought and cold but resents transplanting. Cut stems back by one-third in late spring for branching and more blooms. Profile: puffy purple-blue, white or pink buds opening into star-shaped bells from early to late summer; full sun to part shade; average well-drained soil; 12 to 48 inches tall and 12 to 18 inches wide; USDA zones 3 to 9.

title: Perennials That Thrive in Extra-Cold Gardens
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Native plant portrait photo of balloon flower for extra-cold gardens.

title: Perennials That Thrive in Extra-Cold Gardens
author: Jennifer Howell
content: False sunflower, Heliopsis helianthoides. False sunflower anchors borders, provides summer-to-fall color, feeds pollinators and hummingbirds and produces seed for birds. The native species is especially cold hardy to zone 3 and may need staking; compact and colorful cultivars fit smaller spaces. Profile: 2-inch yellow daisylike flowers from midsummer to fall; full sun to part shade; average to dry well-drained soil; 1 to 6 feet tall and 1 to 4 feet wide; USDA zones 3 to 9.

title: Perennials That Thrive in Extra-Cold Gardens
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Native plant portrait photo of false sunflower for extra-cold gardens.

title: Perennials That Thrive in Extra-Cold Gardens
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Yarrow, Achillea millefolium. Yarrow is a tough filler for butterfly gardens and naturalized plantings. It prefers lean, dry soil and flops in rich soil. Deadhead cultivars to reduce reseeding and divide every two or three years to prevent overcrowded mats. Profile: pink, peach, yellow, red, orange, white or apricot flat-topped flower clusters in mid- to late summer; full sun; average to dry well-drained soil; 18 to 24 inches tall and wide; USDA zones 3 to 10.

title: Perennials That Thrive in Extra-Cold Gardens
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Native plant portrait photo of yarrow for extra-cold gardens.

title: Perennials That Thrive in Extra-Cold Gardens
author: Jennifer Howell
content: To dry yarrow flowers for arrangements, hang them upside down in a cool, dark place for about two weeks.

title: Perennials That Thrive in Extra-Cold Gardens
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Gray-headed coneflower, Ratibida pinnata. Gray-headed coneflower is native to the eastern and midwestern United States and provides food for bees, wasps, butterflies, songbirds and moths. It thrives in lean, dry conditions and looks best massed or mixed with prairie perennials. Profile: drooping yellow petals around gray to brown cones from early summer to early fall; full sun; average well-drained soil; 24 to 48 inches tall and 18 to 24 inches wide; USDA zones 3 to 8.

title: Perennials That Thrive in Extra-Cold Gardens
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Native plant portrait photo of gray-headed coneflower for extra-cold gardens.

title: Perennials That Thrive in Extra-Cold Gardens
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Stiff goldenrod, Solidago rigida. Stiff goldenrod draws bees and butterflies in late fall. Plant it in masses at the back of the border or through a meadow. It reseeds heavily; deadhead to reduce spread or leave seed for songbirds and overwintering goldenrod gall fly larvae. Profile: yellow flower clusters atop tall stems in late summer to fall; full sun; average well-drained soil; 36 to 60 inches tall and 18 to 24 inches wide; USDA zones 3 to 9.

title: Perennials That Thrive in Extra-Cold Gardens
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Native plant portrait photo of stiff goldenrod for extra-cold gardens.

title: Perennials That Thrive in Extra-Cold Gardens
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Turtlehead, Chelone lyonii. Turtlehead has paired flowers on sturdy spikes above glossy dark foliage, offering nectar for bumblebees, butterflies and hummingbirds. It prefers moist, rich soil near water or in rain gardens, and should be divided every two to three years. Profile: pink or white flowers from midsummer to fall; full sun to part shade; moist rich soil; 24 to 48 inches tall and 12 to 24 inches wide; USDA zones 3 to 8.

title: Perennials That Thrive in Extra-Cold Gardens
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Native plant portrait photo of turtlehead for extra-cold gardens.

title: Perennials That Thrive in Extra-Cold Gardens
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Goldenrod pollen is sticky and cannot become airborne, so it will not cause allergies to flare up.

title: Perennial Geranium
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: 'Karmina' cranesbill is a sterile hybrid, so it produces lots of flowers, blooms longer than many types and does not reseed.

title: Perennial Geranium
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Perennial geraniums are low-maintenance plants for full sun or part shade, with many flowers, disease-free foliage and many species and varieties for different garden situations.

title: Perennial Geranium
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Many perennial geraniums grow about 1 foot tall and 2 feet wide, making useful loose ground covers that shade out some weeds. One or two inches of organic mulch beneath new plants helps keep weeds down while they establish.

title: Perennial Geranium
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Low-growing 'Karmina' cranesbill has deep rose blooms in late spring, bridging the gap between earlier moss rose and later sedum. For a softer color with a similar habit, try 'Lohfelden' bigroot geranium.

title: Perennial Geranium
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Bloody cranesbill provides magenta flowers in late spring to early summer and red fall foliage after frost. It reseeds where happy, but seedlings are easy to pull.

title: Perennial Geranium
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: 'Biokovo' cranesbill forms a low mat with dainty white blooms and spreads by underground runners, making edge pieces easy to dig and move.

title: Perennial Geranium
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: 'Tiny Monster' perennial geranium can spread 3 feet wide with magenta late-spring blooms. For dense coverage, space plants less than half their mature width apart so they overlap and knit together.

title: Perennial Geranium
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Perennial geraniums, Geranium species and hybrids, bloom purple, blue, violet, magenta, white or pink from midspring to fall. Grow them in full sun to part shade and well-drained soil; plants reach 6 to 36 inches tall and wide and are cold hardy in USDA zones 3 to 9.

title: Perennial Geranium
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Mixed borders work well with upright perennial geraniums around 2 feet tall and wide because they can compete with neighboring plants. 'Boom Chocolatta' meadow cranesbill adds bronze foliage depth and interest.

title: Perennial Geranium
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Dusky cranesbill, also called mourning widow, is a choice for shadier borders, with green foliage and long stems topped by clusters of small maroon flowers.

title: Perennial Geranium
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Perennial geranium blooms are often single and about an inch across, but 'Orion' has 2 1/2-inch blue-purple flowers, 'Summer Skies' has double late-spring to early-summer blooms, and 'Delft Blue' has white flowers splashed lavender-blue.

title: Perennial Geranium
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: For drought or hot, humid summers, choose bigroot geranium and hybrids such as white-flowered 'Ingwersen's Variety'. Their thick rhizomes store water and help plants tolerate dry summers.

title: Perennial Geranium
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Dwarf geranium and Dalmatian geranium thrive in rock gardens with sharp drainage, though they appreciate extra moisture if rain has not been regular.

title: Perennial Geranium
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: 'Blue Sunrise' perennial geranium has chartreuse foliage and deep purple late-spring flowers; foliage matures yellow-green in summer; 18 inches tall; USDA zones 5 to 9.

title: Perennial Geranium
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: 'Hocus Pocus' meadow cranesbill has bronze-purple leaves topped by lavender flowers in spring to early summer; 14 to 16 inches tall and 17 to 20 inches wide; USDA zones 5 to 8.

title: Perennial Geranium
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: 'Samobor' dusky cranesbill has deep purple spring flowers on stems to 24 inches and maplelike green leaves with a purple ring near the center; USDA zones 4 to 9.

title: Perennial Geranium
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: 'Springtime' dusky cranesbill has spring foliage emerging creamy white with a green edge and maturing green with maroon splotches; dusky purple spring blooms; USDA zones 4 to 8.

title: Perennial Geranium
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Rozanne perennial geranium keeps blooming into fall and tolerates heat, making it reliable for front-of-border color even near reflected sidewalk heat.

title: Perennial Geranium
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: 'Dreamland' has pale pink late-spring to summer blooms that spill over patio or container edges and attract bees and butterflies. 'Brookside' combines long-lasting flowers with red and orange fall foliage.

title: Perennial Geranium
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: If a perennial geranium stays upright after bloom, deadhead instead of shearing. Snip each spent stem back to a leaf joint to leave a clean mound of foliage.

title: Perennial Geranium
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: If a perennial geranium flops open after bloom, grab a handful of fading foliage and cut it off a few inches above the ground, avoiding any new growth near the crown.

title: Perennial Geranium
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Perennial geraniums thrive in full sun or part shade, with afternoon shade helpful in the South. Well-drained soil prevents rot, and plants grow better in alkaline than acidic soil.

title: Perennial Geranium
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Established perennial geraniums are drought tolerant but benefit from watering during dry periods. Organic mulch conserves moisture, while gravel is better around rock-garden species to keep crowns from rotting.

title: Perennial Geranium
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Perennial geraniums in rich soil or too much shade can grow long, lanky stems. Hoop stakes, twigs or small branches can prop them up without looking stiff.

title: Perennial Geranium
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Division can reinvigorate perennial geraniums if plants flop often or bloom poorly. Divide after bloom or in early spring by tugging crowns apart or slicing a piece from the outer edge.

title: Sea Holly
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Sea holly has prickly starburst flowers in blue to gray, is drought and salt tolerant, provides flowers for fresh or dried bouquets and attracts insect pollinators.

title: Sea Holly
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Sea holly flowers have tiny true flowers tucked into thistlelike cones surrounded by stiff bracts that can be long, short, deeply cut or broad. Leaves may be maplelike, rounded or oval with leathery, water-conserving texture.

title: Sea Holly
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Sea holly, Eryngium species and hybrids, is a perennial with spiky silver-blue flowers from summer to fall. Grow it in full sun and well-drained soil; plants reach 12 to 72 inches tall and 10 to 24 inches wide and are cold hardy in USDA zones 3 to 9.

title: Sea Holly
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Native opening photo of 'Sapphire Blue' sea holly blooming with spiky silver-blue flowers in a sunny garden.

title: Sea Holly
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Sea holly's sharply defined flower shape adds structure so softer flowers do not visually merge together. 'Big Blue' creates a dramatic blue accent among pink queen of the prairie and red bee balm.

title: Sea Holly
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Blue is a useful but uncommon flower color. 'Sapphire Blue' sea holly pops against gold Japanese spirea, while 'Big Blue' cools down red bee balm and pink queen of the prairie for a calmer view.

title: Sea Holly
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Silvery white Miss Willmott's ghost adds shimmer after sunset and is a strong moon-garden plant.

title: Sea Holly
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Rattlesnake master is a sea holly cousin native to eastern North America. Its 4- to 6-foot stems carry small globes above yucca-like foliage, and the flowers attract pollinators while leaves host black swallowtail larvae.

title: Sea Holly
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Grow sea holly in full sun and well-drained soil for healthy plants with many blooms. Too much shade produces fewer, longer, leggier stems; cool nights around 55 degrees F intensify blue color.

title: Sea Holly
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Sea holly thrives in most well-drained soils and prefers lean conditions, so it does not need regular feeding.

title: Sea Holly
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Potted nursery plants are the surest way to get a specific sea holly species or variety. Bare-root bags can be economical, but roots may arrive rotted; start viable roots in pots after frost danger passes.

title: Sea Holly
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Sea holly can be started from seed, but germination may be about 50 percent. Sow outdoors in early spring or fall up to two months before frost, or start indoors 6 to 8 weeks before the last frost. Seeds need light, so do not cover them.

title: Sea Holly
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Most sea hollies have taproots, making division difficult. Some types reseed, and plantlets at the base of mature plants can be sliced off with roots and leaves, then replanted at the same level.

title: Sea Holly
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Wear gloves when deadheading, dividing or spring-cleaning sea holly because dried leaves are even pricklier than fresh ones.

title: Sea Holly
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Cut sea holly blooms can last up to three weeks in a vase. To dry them, secure up to five stems with a rubber band and hang in a dry spot out of direct sunlight until ready for arrangements.

title: Sea Holly
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Native photo of dried sea holly stems hanging for dried flower arrangements.

title: Sea Holly
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Miss Willmott's ghost, Eryngium giganteum, grows 2 to 4 feet tall, up to 6 feet in ideal conditions, and 1 to 3 feet wide with 4-inch blooms; USDA zones 4 to 7.

title: Sea Holly
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: 'Big Blue', Eryngium x zabelii, grows 24 to 30 inches tall and wide with intense blue midborder flowers; USDA zones 5 to 9.

title: Sea Holly
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: 'Neptune's Gold', Eryngium x zabelii, grows 20 to 24 inches tall and 10 to 16 inches wide with lavender-blue flowers and chartreuse foliage; USDA zones 5 to 8.

title: Sea Holly
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: 'Blue Hobbit', Eryngium planum, grows 6 to 12 inches tall with many small spiny purple-blue flowers near the front of the border; USDA zones 4 to 8.

title: Sea Holly
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: 'Jade Frost', Eryngium planum, grows 18 to 30 inches tall and 12 to 18 inches wide with blue-green leaves edged cream and silvery blue flowers; USDA zones 5 to 8.

author: Sherri Ribbey
content: 'Blue Jackpot', Eryngium hybrid, grows 20 to 24 inches tall and 22 to 30 inches wide with strong blue color down the stem and wider bracts; USDA zones 4 to 8.

title: The Complete Package
author: Kristin Beane Sullivan
content: Variety makes the Gagnons' garden interesting. Different shapes, colors and textures provide something to enjoy no matter the season.

title: The Complete Package
author: Kristin Beane Sullivan
content: Native opening photo of Candy and Don Gagnon's award-winning garden with bold yellow flowers, layered plantings and a cottage structure.

title: The Complete Package
author: Kristin Beane Sullivan
content: Native full-page reader-garden photo of the Gagnons' layered garden border and path.

title: The Complete Package
author: Kristin Beane Sullivan
content: Maine gardeners Candy and Don Gagnon built a garden around trees, DIY projects and resourceful use of materials from their 2-acre property.

title: The Complete Package
author: Kristin Beane Sullivan
content: When the Gagnons built their current house, they cleared the property carefully and saved as many original oaks, maples and Canadian hemlocks as possible. Original and newly planted trees became the centerpiece of the garden.

title: The Complete Package
author: Kristin Beane Sullivan
content: The Gagnons added hardy magnolias such as 'Butterflies', 'Jane' and 'Leonard Messel', many dwarf conifers and several dogwoods, with at least one tree anchoring most garden beds.

title: The Complete Package
author: Kristin Beane Sullivan
content: Lawn paths wind through stone-bordered island beds. A crushed-granite maintenance path wide enough for a lawn tractor and cart encircles the property, which also has a cut-flower and vegetable bed and two ponds with waterfalls and streams.

title: The Complete Package
author: Kristin Beane Sullivan
content: Native garden photo of a Gagnon border with trees, perennials, annuals, tiger lilies and hostas for year-round appeal.

title: The Complete Package
author: Kristin Beane Sullivan
content: Native portrait photo of 2024 Reader Garden Award winners Candy and Don Gagnon.

title: The Complete Package
author: Kristin Beane Sullivan
content: Woody plants require vigilance. When a branch on the Gagnons' Swiss stone pine turned brown, they suspected pine borer and pruned until they found the larva and reached healthy wood.

title: The Complete Package
author: Kristin Beane Sullivan
content: Deer browse rhododendrons and other perimeter plants in winter, so the Gagnons watch year-round and install fencing cages around vulnerable plants.

title: The Complete Package
author: Kristin Beane Sullivan
content: Swiss stone pine, Pinus cembra, has soft slightly curly blue-green needles and green-purple cones; full sun; 30 to 40 feet tall and 15 to 25 feet wide; USDA zones 4 to 7.

title: The Complete Package
author: Kristin Beane Sullivan
content: Native tree or foliage photo of swiss stone pine in the Gagnon garden.

title: The Complete Package
author: Kristin Beane Sullivan
content: 'Autumn Moon' fullmoon maple, Acer shirasawanum, has chartreuse-orange new foliage, gold-orange summer foliage and vivid fall color; full sun to part shade; 8 to 15 feet tall and 6 to 15 feet wide; USDA zones 5 to 8.

title: The Complete Package
author: Kristin Beane Sullivan
content: Native tree or foliage photo of 'autumn moon' fullmoon maple in the Gagnon garden.

title: The Complete Package
author: Kristin Beane Sullivan
content: Golden Spirit smokebush, Cotinus coggygria, has chartreuse spring foliage, gold summer foliage, orange-red fall color and airy pink summer flowers; full to part sun; 8 to 15 feet tall and wide; USDA zones 4 to 8.

title: The Complete Package
author: Kristin Beane Sullivan
content: Native tree or foliage photo of golden spirit smokebush in the Gagnon garden.

title: The Complete Package
author: Kristin Beane Sullivan
content: Purple catalpa, Catalpa x erubescens 'Purpurea', has large purple new leaves that turn dark green and large late-spring flower panicles; full sun to part shade; 40 to 50 feet tall and wide; USDA zones 5 to 8.

title: The Complete Package
author: Kristin Beane Sullivan
content: Native tree or foliage photo of purple catalpa in the Gagnon garden.

title: The Complete Package
author: Kristin Beane Sullivan
content: The Gagnons fill the 2-acre garden economically by propagating plants they already grow. Purple coneflowers, gloriosa daisies and love-in-a-mist reseed into large sweeps of color.

title: The Complete Package
author: Kristin Beane Sullivan
content: Don moves volunteer seedlings to a nursery bed instead of discarding them. Visitors who admire a plant often leave with one or two starts, and new trees can be surrounded quickly with perennials from the nursery bed.

title: The Complete Package
author: Kristin Beane Sullivan
content: Twisty Baby black locust seedlings came true with the parent's contorted form, so the Gagnons saved and incorporated some into the garden.

title: The Complete Package
author: Kristin Beane Sullivan
content: Candy propagates intentionally from cuttings, including coleus and magnolias, and the couple has divided many perennials such as daylilies and ornamental grasses.

title: The Complete Package
author: Kristin Beane Sullivan
content: Native garden photo of a high table made from a dead peach-tree stump and a slice of tree trunk.

title: The Complete Package
author: Kristin Beane Sullivan
content: The Gagnons compost and reuse fieldstone found on the property for walls, pond and waterfall liners and island-bed edging. Don chooses flat stones along lawn edges so he can mow close and avoid extra trimming.

title: The Complete Package
author: Kristin Beane Sullivan
content: Old stone walls have been dismantled for new projects, including a new wall and gnome home with built-in winter storage for fairy-garden decor.

title: The Complete Package
author: Kristin Beane Sullivan
content: When trees must be removed, the Gagnons have the wood milled and save the lumber for future woodworking projects.

title: The Complete Package
author: Kristin Beane Sullivan
content: Candy makes colorful flower ornaments from household items such as fertilizer scoops, clothespins and hair dryer diffusers, gluing them to pine shapes and spray-painting in layers for dimension.

title: The Complete Package
author: Kristin Beane Sullivan
content: Native garden photo of Twisty Baby black locust with pronounced zig-zag new growth.

title: The Complete Package
author: Kristin Beane Sullivan
content: Native photo of the Gagnons' rebuilt stone wall and gnome home with storage.

title: The Complete Package
author: Kristin Beane Sullivan
content: Native photo of an upcycled garden flower ornament made from fertilizer scoops or similar household items.

title: The Complete Package
author: Kristin Beane Sullivan
content: The Gagnons overwinter tender lily of the Nile in pots in an insulated attached garage that stays above about 37 degrees F. Candy notes that lily of the Nile blooms better when root bound, so they divide only when necessary.

title: The Complete Package
author: Kristin Beane Sullivan
content: A spike plant from a summer container overwintered well in the garage and became the centerpiece of a later container grouping.

title: The Complete Package
author: Kristin Beane Sullivan
content: Candy stores elephant ear bulbs behind the basement stairs in a box of sawdust. In March she lays the bulbs on the sunroom floor and waits for sprouts before potting them.

title: The Complete Package
author: Kristin Beane Sullivan
content: Native photo of lily of the Nile and a spike plant overwintered in containers by the Gagnons.

title: The Complete Package
author: Kristin Beane Sullivan
content: Native plant photo of lily of the Nile bloom clusters in the Gagnon garden.

title: The Complete Package
author: Kristin Beane Sullivan
content: Candy starts many annuals from seed in spring, using sunroom trays and lighted shelves. When the house gets too full in April, she moves seedlings to an unheated greenhouse until outdoor planting is safe.

title: The Complete Package
author: Kristin Beane Sullivan
content: Candy gradually hardens off seedlings in shady spots for a few days before planting them, then babies them until they establish.

title: The Complete Package
author: Kristin Beane Sullivan
content: For petunias, Candy starts seed according to packet timing so plants do not become leggy and crowded indoors. She starts seed in straight vermiculite, then moves seedlings with four to six true leaves into potting mix and recycled pots.

title: The Complete Package
author: Kristin Beane Sullivan
content: After planting petunias outdoors, Candy feeds twice weekly with bloom-booster water-soluble fertilizer to keep them flowering.

title: The Complete Package
author: Kristin Beane Sullivan
content: During the growing season, Don and Candy end every early-morning walk with a pass through the garden, checking magnolia buds, pest-treated plants and dahlias that may need staking after wind.

title: The Complete Package
author: Kristin Beane Sullivan
content: The cut-flower bed at the back of the garden holds about 140 dahlias. Before planting tubers in spring, the Gagnons make one mini-tiller pass down each row to loosen soil in the mounds.

title: The Complete Package
author: Kristin Beane Sullivan
content: Landscape fabric between dahlia rows suppresses weeds year-round. A rebar stake with a label marks each tuber and provides support if plants need staking later.

title: The Complete Package
author: Kristin Beane Sullivan
content: Starting dahlia tubers early in pots did not make them bloom much earlier than tubers planted directly in the ground.

title: The Complete Package
author: Kristin Beane Sullivan
content: A drip irrigation line with an emitter at each dahlia plant delivers consistent moisture for the best blooms. The lines remain out year-round as long as they are drained before winter.

title: The Complete Package
author: Kristin Beane Sullivan
content: After frost kills dahlia foliage, the Gagnons dig tubers, wash off soil, dry them on the driveway, divide large clumps, label each one and store them in perforated plastic newspaper bags in boxes on garage shelves.

title: The Complete Package
author: Kristin Beane Sullivan
content: To discourage deer from dahlias, the Gagnons use a simple fence of two rows of rope strung a few feet above the ground.

title: The Sensory Garden
author: Marisa Reyes
content: A sensory garden offers experiences for all five senses: rustling grasses, colorful flowers, soft leaves, fragrant roses and fresh fruits, vegetables and herbs.

title: The Sensory Garden
author: Marisa Reyes
content: For sight, think about the first thing visible when entering the garden. Colorful blooms, a striking focal point, designed paths and layered borders can guide the gaze and reveal more interest as visitors move through.

title: The Sensory Garden
author: Marisa Reyes
content: A cohesive color palette can feel happy, tranquil or dramatic. Bright oranges and reds energize, soft blues and purples calm, and yellows can feel uplifting.

title: The Sensory Garden
author: Marisa Reyes

title: The Sensory Garden
author: Marisa Reyes
content: A front entry bed can set the stage for the whole garden. Lime-green foliage and white flowers draw the eye toward the porch while deep green boxwoods recede, and repeated rounded forms unify the border.

title: The Sensory Garden
author: Marisa Reyes
content: A specimen plant or feature placed at the end of a path or near a seating area creates a focal point. A panicle hydrangea standard can anchor a border and transition from low plants to taller trees.

title: The Sensory Garden
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Add surprise by tucking a whimsical fairy house between plants along a pathway.

title: The Sensory Garden
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Touch is often overlooked, but varied textures and tactile areas help visitors connect with the garden. Place touchable plants within reach along paths, patios and seating areas.

title: The Sensory Garden
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Smooth blue-green hosta leaves, feathery fern fronds, finely cut Japanese maple foliage, ground covers along path edges and rough or smooth bark all create tactile experiences.

title: The Sensory Garden
author: Marisa Reyes
content: A tactile zone for children can include a sandbox filled with pebbles, wood chips or sand so they can dig, touch, squish mud and explore.

title: The Sensory Garden
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Celosia, Celosia argentea cristata, is a annual with velvety, plush or papery flower heads in orange, red, purple, yellow or cream from summer to frost; 6 to 36 inches tall and 8 to 24 inches wide.

title: The Sensory Garden
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Lamb's ear, Stachys byzantina, is a perennial with extremely soft silver-gray velvety leaves and purple early-summer flowers; 9 to 18 inches tall and 12 to 18 inches wide; USDA zones 4 to 8.

title: The Sensory Garden
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Mexican bush sage, Salvia leucantha, is a tender perennial with velvety gray-green leaves and fuzzy purple-white flowers from late summer to frost; 24 to 40 inches tall and 28 to 36 inches wide; USDA zones 8 to 10.

title: The Sensory Garden
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Fragrance can evoke memories, relax the mind and invigorate the spirit. Place fragrant plants near paths, seating areas or windows so their scent can be enjoyed outdoors and indoors.

title: The Sensory Garden
author: Marisa Reyes
content: For multiseason fragrance, combine plants that bloom at different times, such as lilac in spring, honeysuckle in summer and autumn sage late in the season. Night-blooming common jasmine releases scent in cool night air.

title: The Sensory Garden
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Herbs add fragrance when touched and fresh flavor in the kitchen. Plant them near the patio or kitchen door, and use aromatic ground covers such as creeping thyme where they can be brushed or stepped on.

title: The Sensory Garden
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Common lilac, Syringa vulgaris, is a shrub with white, pink or purple sweet spring flower clusters with a hint of vanilla; 6 to 15 feet tall and 1 to 12 feet wide; USDA zones 3 to 8.

title: The Sensory Garden
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Gardenia, Gardenia jasminoides, is a evergreen with single or double white late-spring to early-summer flowers with a sweet floral citrus fragrance; 3 to 8 feet tall and 3 to 6 feet wide; USDA zones 7 to 11.

title: The Sensory Garden
author: Marisa Reyes
content: 'Leonard Messel' magnolia, Magnolia x loebneri, is a tree with white to purple-pink fragrant early-spring flowers with a hint of citrus; 10 to 20 feet tall and 10 to 18 feet wide; USDA zones 4 to 9.

title: The Sensory Garden
author: Marisa Reyes
content: A sensory garden should include culinary plants. Position a small kitchen garden near an outdoor dining area so fresh fruits, vegetables and herbs can be harvested at peak flavor.

title: The Sensory Garden
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Mix crops into front perennial beds or borders for easy harvest. Lettuce, raspberries, nasturtium flowers, strawberries, tomatoes, pole beans and cucumbers can bring taste into ornamental spaces.

title: The Sensory Garden
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Trellises and vertical gardens save space for climbing crops such as pole beans or cucumbers and can double as privacy screens.

title: The Sensory Garden
author: Marisa Reyes
content: To protect harvests from wildlife, plant crops closer to the house or cover ripening fruit with netting.

title: The Sensory Garden
author: Marisa Reyes
content: 'Patio Choice Yellow' cherry tomato, Solanum lycopersicum, is a annual determinate plant with round yellow summer fruit, 1 to 2 feet tall and wide, suitable for containers.

title: The Sensory Garden
author: Marisa Reyes
content: 'Seascape' strawberry, Fragaria x ananassa, is a perennial with white spring flowers and large red summer berries, strong disease resistance and evergreen foliage in warmer regions; 12 inches tall and 12 to 24 inches wide; USDA zones 4 to 9.

title: The Sensory Garden

title: The Sensory Garden
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Sound can come from rustling leaves, birdsong, bees, grasses moving in the breeze, flowing water, crunching gravel paths and wind chimes made of wood, metal or glass.

title: The Sensory Garden
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Invite birds with feeders, nesting boxes, berry-producing plants such as viburnum and downy serviceberry, and fresh seed or fruit when natural food sources are scarce.

title: The Sensory Garden
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Hedges and fences can reduce unwanted road or neighbor noise while improving privacy. Outdoor speakers that resemble rocks can blend into seating areas or path edges.

title: The Sensory Garden
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Honesty, Lunaria annua, is a perennial with coinlike dried seed pods that crackle in the breeze and purple spring flowers; 2 to 3 feet tall and 1 to 2 feet wide; USDA zones 5 to 9.

title: The Sensory Garden
author: Marisa Reyes

title: Backyard Getaway with Tropical Flair
author: Eric Flynn
content: A freestanding deck at the back of a small 25-foot-wide yard creates a destination while remaining close enough to the house for convenience.

title: Backyard Getaway with Tropical Flair
author: Eric Flynn
content: Straight lines in the bed, pond and path give this shady backyard a clean contemporary look. Tender red Abyssinian bananas add tropical punch, while most of the planting is hardy perennials and shrubs.

title: Backyard Getaway with Tropical Flair
author: Eric Flynn
content: Contrasting texture and foliage color keep the tropical-flair garden interesting from spring through fall, with at least one colorful flower in bloom each season.

title: Backyard Getaway with Tropical Flair
author: Eric Flynn
content: A small pond next to the deck is a hidden treasure, barely visible from the house but audible and reflective once visitors are on the deck.

title: Backyard Getaway with Tropical Flair
author: Eric Flynn
content: A close privacy fence works better than a distant one, and a slightly taller structure adds enclosure, looks good from the house and gives some shelter from the elements.

title: Backyard Getaway with Tropical Flair

title: Backyard Getaway with Tropical Flair
author: Eric Flynn
content: The flower show begins with rhododendrons in spring. In summer, smooth hydrangeas peak with hosta and ligularia flowers, while begonias bloom from planting until frost. Hydrangea blooms turn green and then papery brown by fall.

title: Backyard Getaway with Tropical Flair
author: Eric Flynn
content: Cut smooth hydrangea stems back to 1 to 2 feet tall every spring because this species blooms on new wood. More new growth means more flowers.

title: Backyard Getaway with Tropical Flair

content: In spring, cut or rake up dead foliage from hostas, ferns, ligularias and hakonechloas to make room for new growth.

title: Backyard Getaway with Tropical Flair
author: Eric Flynn
content: Plant begonias after nighttime frost danger passes. Wait until overnight temperatures are about 50 degrees F before moving red Abyssinian bananas and umbrella palm outdoors.

title: 5 Clever Ways to Use Frames in the Garden
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Old picture frames can be upcycled outdoors as living art, herb-drying racks, hanging-basket accents, tray birdfeeders and garden signs.

title: 5 Clever Ways to Use Frames in the Garden
author: Jennifer Howell
content: For living art, fasten chicken wire or hardware cloth to a shadowbox frame, or build a 2-inch-deep box behind a regular frame, fill it with potting mix and plant succulents through the grid. Grow flat for up to four weeks before hanging vertically.

title: 5 Clever Ways to Use Frames in the Garden
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Water a vertical frame planter by laying it flat to water and drain, then rehanging it.

title: 5 Clever Ways to Use Frames in the Garden
author: Jennifer Howell
content: To make an herb-drying rack, replace frame glass with hardware cloth. Use 1/2-inch grids for large-leaf herbs such as basil and sage, or 1/4-inch grids for oregano and thyme.

title: 5 Clever Ways to Use Frames in the Garden
author: Jennifer Howell
content: A multilevel herb-drying rack can be made with graduated frame sizes suspended by chain, leaving about 3 inches between layers so leaves can be spread and collected.

title: 5 Clever Ways to Use Frames in the Garden
author: Jennifer Howell
content: A sturdy frame such as an old window can suspend a hanging basket and highlight the planting. The frame must be strong enough for the basket weight and wide enough for an eye bolt.

title: 5 Clever Ways to Use Frames in the Garden
author: Jennifer Howell
content: For a lightweight decorative frame, install a turnbuckle so the hardware carries the basket weight instead of the frame itself.

title: 5 Clever Ways to Use Frames in the Garden
author: Jennifer Howell
content: An upcycled tray birdfeeder can be made by replacing frame glass with mesh or screen that drains. Window screen works for small birdseed, while tight mesh or perforated metal works for mealworms or larger seed.

author: Jennifer Howell

title: Q&A
content: Not all ornamental grasses are invasive, but some spread aggressively by seed or by roots and rhizomes. Problematic grasses include Amur silver grass, blue lyme grass, fountain grass, giant reed grass, Japanese blood grass, jubata grass, maiden grass and ravenna grass.

title: Q&A
content: A spore is the reproductive cell of nonflowering plants such as ferns, moss and fungi. It contains a nucleus but no embryo like a seed, yet can develop into a new plant.

title: Q&A
content: A moth orchid's oldest bottom leaf commonly turns yellow and withers as a new leaf forms at the plant center. Cut the yellow leaf off near the main stem; if more than one leaf yellows, overwatering may be the cause.

title: Q&A
content: Moth orchids are often grown in coarse potting mix so roots get air and do not rot. Water a 4-inch pot with the equivalent of three melted ice cubes at room temperature once a week.

content: Native photo of a moth orchid with a yellowing bottom leaf.

title: Q&A
content: A dwarf Alberta spruce can produce a vigorous shoot through genetic reversion to its original white spruce form. Prune the aggressive growth as close to the main trunk as possible and remove any resprouts.

title: Q&A
content: Leafy mistletoe mainly affects deciduous trees and rarely kills a healthy tree, while dwarf mistletoes are more aggressive, host-specific parasites of conifers and can kill stressed or unhealthy trees.

title: Q&A
content: Dwarf mistletoes spread by sticky seeds that explode from pods and shoot 10 to 20 feet to neighboring trees. Removing the infested branch or the entire tree is the only control.

title: Q&A
content: Wild parsnip, Pastinaca sativa, is a biennial with shiny yellow-green compound leaves and flat yellow umbels on 4- to 6-foot stalks. Above-ground parts produce toxic sap that can cause severe blistering phytophotodermatitis.

title: Q&A
content: Control wild parsnip with strong skin and eye protection. Cut rosettes 1 to 2 inches below the surface with a sharp spade, remove flowers before seed set and burn seed heads if seeds have formed.

title: Q&A
content: If skin is exposed to wild parsnip sap, protect it from sunlight immediately, wash with warm water and mild soap, stay out of sunlight for a couple of days and see a doctor if the rash is severe.

title: Timeless Shade Garden Beauty
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Cinnamon fern adds charm to shade gardens with spring fiddleheads, cinnamon-colored spore spikes and arching yellow-green fronds that reach 2 to 3 feet and mature gold and orange in fall.

title: Timeless Shade Garden Beauty
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Native to North and Central America, cinnamon fern gradually spreads into a lush green backdrop for shade borders, woodland gardens and pond or water-feature edges.

title: Timeless Shade Garden Beauty
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Grow cinnamon fern in part to full shade and rich, moist to wet soil. Start with nursery plants, amend planting soil with 1 to 2 inches of compost and keep soil consistently damp.

title: Timeless Shade Garden Beauty
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Divide cinnamon fern every three to four years in spring, especially when the cinnamon spikes become smaller and the center stops producing new growth.

title: Timeless Shade Garden Beauty
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Cinnamon fern needs no pruning. Remove dead or damaged leaves as needed, leave spent fronds for winter mulch and root protection, then clean up remaining material in spring.

title: Timeless Shade Garden Beauty
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Cinnamon fern, Osmundastrum cinnamomeum, is a perennial with arching yellow-green summer fronds that turn gold and orange in fall. Grow it in part to full shade and rich, moist to wet soil; plants reach 2 to 3 feet tall and wide and are cold hardy in USDA zones 3 to 9.

title: Timeless Shade Garden Beauty
author: Marisa Reyes
content: The Midsummer Flair shade combination pairs cinnamon fern with 'Blue Mouse Ears' hosta, 'All Gold' hakonechloa and 'Amethyst' astilbe for plumes, fine-textured fronds, golden movement and blue-green ground cover.

title: Put the Garden to Bed
content: Whether to cut back perennials in fall depends on reseeding, pests, winter interest and winter survival.

title: Put the Garden to Bed
content: Cut back or deadhead notorious reseeders such as black-eyed Susan, coneflower, hollyhock, sea oats and tickseed if you do not want unpredictable seedlings crowding the original plants.

title: Put the Garden to Bed
content: Cut pest- or disease-prone perennials such as bee balm, blackberry lily, garden phlox, iris and peony to the ground, then bury or remove the foliage because home compost piles may not kill disease organisms.

title: Put the Garden to Bed
content: Leave perennials such as epimedium, false indigo, hellebore, switchgrass and tall sedum standing for evergreen foliage, seedheads, branching structure, winter interest and bird food.

title: Put the Garden to Bed
content: Wait until spring to cut back plants such as burnet, butterfly bush, clematis, coral bells and milkweed because they look better after winter-dieback decisions or survive better if not cut in fall.

title: Put the Garden to Bed
content: Native bonus-article photo of yellow fall leaves or peony foliage used in fall cutback guidance.

title: Put the Garden to Bed
content: Recycle old plastic shower curtains as drop cloths in vehicles when hauling compost or mulch, or lay one on the ground while raking leaves and drag the debris to the compost pile.

title: Put the Garden to Bed
content: For one-person leaf bagging, loop a drawstring plastic bag over wheelbarrow handles so the bag stays open while both hands rake and scoop leaves.

title: Put the Garden to Bed
content: Use a small child's plastic garden rake to clean leaves from window wells because the head fits into corners and the handle reduces kneeling.

title: Put the Garden to Bed
content: Before leaves fall, spread black plastic bird netting over low evergreens such as 'Blue Rug' juniper and pin it with forked twigs. After trees are bare, drag off the netting and leaves together.

title: Put the Garden to Bed
content: Bundle torch lily foliage and tie it in place rather than cutting it back in fall. This keeps winter moisture out of the crown and reduces rot.

title: Put the Garden to Bed
content: Use a rigid garden or bow rake for spreading mulch and smoothing soil. Use a springy leaf rake of metal, plastic or bamboo for gathering leaves without tearing up grass.

title: Put the Garden to Bed
content: Native technique illustration showing fall raking tools, shower-curtain cleanup, leaf bagging, window-well rake, netting and tied torch lily foliage.

title: Put the Garden to Bed
content: Evergreen branches from pruning or a recycled Christmas tree make an airy winter blanket for perennials. Lay branches in a crisscross pattern and weave stems together so they do not blow away.

title: Put the Garden to Bed
content: Evergreen branches moderate soil temperature fluctuations, hold snow, keep leaves or other mulch from blowing away and do not pack down tightly enough to smother crowns.

title: Put the Garden to Bed
content: Use evergreen branches after the ground freezes, from late November to midwinter, then remove them when spring warms.

title: Put the Garden to Bed
content: Evergreen branches are useful over tap-rooted or shallow-rooted perennials that may heave, marginally hardy perennials, evergreen perennials such as heaths and heathers, mounded roses and snow-covered beds that need shade to keep snow insulating longer.

title: Put the Garden to Bed
content: Annuals can be composted in place by digging them up in fall, turning them under and chopping stems with a shovel. Leave the soil rough so it holds moisture rather than compacting it smooth.

title: Put the Garden to Bed
content: Do not compost annuals in place if they were diseased, harbored insects or may reseed problematically. Pull those plants and send them away with yard waste.

title: Put the Garden to Bed
content: Fall is a good time to remove weeds before they become a bigger spring problem. A weed is any plant growing where you do not want it.

title: Put the Garden to Bed
content: For mature weeds such as curly dock, use a shovel to pry the plant out and remove all roots. Wet soil makes roots easier to pull.

title: Put the Garden to Bed
content: For spreading or low-growing weeds, use a hoe nearly parallel to the soil to scrape them off. Chopping too deeply can bring more weed seeds to the surface.

title: Put the Garden to Bed
content: Scale insects are small sap-sucking pests with waxy armor that feed on many woody plants. In small numbers they weaken plants, and in large numbers they can kill them.

title: Put the Garden to Bed
content: Sooty mold on leaves may reveal scale infestations because the fungus grows on honeydew excreted by scale insects.

title: Put the Garden to Bed
content: For heavy scale infestations, prune affected branches, knock some insects off with a high-pressure jet of water, then spray horticultural oil until it drips from branches. A second spray in early spring before leaves emerge may be needed.

title: Put the Garden to Bed
content: Scale-susceptible woody plants include boxwood, camellia, dogwood, euonymus, hibiscus, holly, lilac, magnolia, mugo pine and viburnum.

title: Regional Tips
content: Early fall tasks include photographing successes and problem areas, planting cold-tolerant annuals, refreshing containers, buying and storing spring bulbs, planting bargain trees, shrubs and perennials, feeding the lawn, dividing late-spring and summer bloomers and treating insect problems.

title: Regional Tips
content: Midfall tasks include raking and composting leaves, cleaning dried debris, putting out bird feeders, planting and watering trees and shrubs, mowing one last time, bringing houseplants in before nights dip into the 50s, harvesting last produce, spreading compost and planting spring bulbs.

title: Regional Tips
content: Late-fall tasks include washing and storing containers, protecting trees and shrubs, sharpening and storing tools, mulching new or heaving-prone perennials, draining hoses, storing or heating birdbaths, using garden-friendly deicer and ordering plants for next year.

title: Regional Tips
content: Northwest gardeners can trap root weevils under rhododendrons, yews and hemlocks with folded burlap, then remove the hidden weevils before evening feeding. Sticky barriers and parasitic nematodes also help.

title: Regional Tips
content: Northwest gardeners should prepare for slugs as wet weather begins. Handpick small populations or use bait and traps for larger populations.

title: Regional Tips
content: Northwest gardeners can cover compost piles during rainy months with plastic or a tarp so piles stay moist but not too wet to heat and decompose.

title: Regional Tips
content: Northwest gardeners can overwinter tender fuchsias after a light frost by cutting plants to 6 to 8 inches and storing them cool and frost-free, watering every two or three weeks and bringing them into light in early February.

title: Regional Tips
content: Mountain gardeners should plant bulbs 2 to 3 inches deeper than in milder climates and mulch after the ground freezes so bulbs are not tricked into sprouting by warm winter sun.

title: Regional Tips
content: Mountain gardeners in wildfire-prone areas should clean up dry leaves and brush in fall and consider planting a green buffer around the house.

title: Regional Tips
content: Mountain gardeners can ripen fully formed green tomatoes off the vine by storing them in a shallow box with newspaper between rows at 55 to 70 degrees F.

title: Regional Tips
content: Mountain gardeners can set up rain barrels to collect roof runoff from melting snow and spring rain for later irrigation.

title: Regional Tips
content: Southwest gardeners should chill tulip and hyacinth bulbs in a paper sack in the refrigerator for 6 to 8 weeks before planting in late December or early January.

title: Regional Tips
content: Southwest gardeners can overseed Bermuda grass with annual ryegrass in midfall by mowing low, raking to expose soil, spreading ryegrass seed, watering and covering lightly with compost.

title: Regional Tips
content: Southwest gardeners should watch cool-season vegetables and flowers for aphids and spray with soapy water every few days until pests are gone.

title: Regional Tips
content: In hot, dry southwest areas, fall is the best time to plant smaller trees and shrubs so they establish before summer heat.

title: Regional Tips
content: Midwest gardeners should dig tender bulbs such as dahlia and canna after frost yellows foliage, dry good bulbs for 3 to 7 days and store them in ventilated containers where temperatures stay in the 50s.

title: Regional Tips
content: Midwest gardeners can prune out small fall webworm webs or knock webs from trees with a high-pressure sprayer. Most mature trees tolerate repeated infestations without permanent damage.

title: Regional Tips
content: Midwest gardeners can start compost in fall with grass clippings, chopped leaves and food scraps, then spread finished compost on beds and vegetable gardens to improve soil.

title: Regional Tips
content: Midwest gardeners can save seed from annuals such as zinnia, sunflower and marigold. Let blooms dry on the plant, crush dried flowers over white paper and store dry seed in a bag, envelope or jar for 3 to 4 years.

title: Regional Tips
content: Southeast gardeners can usually divide perennials into October if new divisions are mulched and kept moist.

title: Regional Tips
content: Southeast gardeners should tie loose climbing rose canes to trellises or arbors with strips of old cotton T-shirts so winter winds do not break them.

title: Regional Tips
content: Southeast gardeners can cut tired petunias back by one-third to one-half for better foliage and possibly a fresh flush of flowers; the same can help some perennials such as cranesbill and catmint.

title: Regional Tips
content: Southeast gardeners can use preemergent herbicide before planting cool-season annuals to reduce weed seed germination, following label directions.

title: Regional Tips
content: Northeast gardeners should clean and fill bird feeders in fall so nonmigratory birds find the food source before snow makes natural food scarce.

title: Regional Tips
content: Northeast gardeners should inspect houseplants for insects before bringing them indoors, checking leaf undersides, stem joints and the soil surface, then handpicking, spraying with soapy water or using insecticidal soap outside.

title: Regional Tips
content: Northeast gardeners can protect many plants from light frost with an old bed sheet or nonplastic cover; plastic can burn leaves where it touches.

title: In the Weeds
author: Jamie Seitz
content: Jamie loved gardening in flip-flops, but plantar fasciitis made unsupported footwear painful after garden work.

title: In the Weeds
author: Jamie Seitz
content: A chiropractor advised Jamie to stop wearing flip-flops, so she found sturdy outdoor hiking sandals that supported her feet without looking orthopedic.

title: In the Weeds
author: Jamie Seitz
content: After a productive spring day of moving patio furniture, buying mulch, cleaning the shed, tilling beds, cleaning leaves, mulching and power-washing cushions in old flip-flops, her feet hurt badly for the rest of the season.

title: In the Weeds
author: Jamie Seitz
content: The lesson from Jamie's flip-flop gardening fail is to wear supportive outdoor shoes or sandals so you can keep gardening for a long time.

title: Reader Tips
author: Dave Perry, MI
content: Dave Perry made a simple climbing-vine trellis by drilling long weather-proof screws near the top and bottom of a narrow porch support, stretching bungee cords tightly between them and winding black-eyed Susan vine, Thunbergia alata, around the cords.

title: Reader Tips
author: Dave Perry, MI
content: Miniature cable ties can secure vines to bungee-cord trellis lines while they are getting started. Bright orange cords can add color to the planting, or black and neutral cords can blend into the background.

title: Reader Tips
author: Sandra Toumbacaris, NY
content: Sandra Toumbacaris uses a long-handled garden rake as a measuring and planting tool in the vegetable garden. Marks every 6 to 12 inches on the handle help space rows, the handle presses a seed channel into the soil and the rake tines press and cover seeds with a light layer of soil.

title: Reader Tips
author: Kay Morris, SC
content: Kay Morris reuses cleaned zip-top plastic bags to cover seed-starting flats for extra moisture during germination. She cuts the bags halfway along the side seams, loosely secures them over the flats and removes them after seedlings emerge to avoid excess moisture and disease.

title: Reader Tips
author: Pat Paine, MO
content: Pat Paine keeps thrifted vintage tea kettles, coffee carafes and ice buckets filled with water near container plants so she can quickly water a droopy plant or dry pot without hauling a hose every time.

title: Reader Tips
author: Pat Paine, MO
content: Old silver-plated items, enamelware and hammered aluminum can hold water and add personality near containers, while lids help keep small critters out. Containers still need thorough watering with a hose or large watering can.

title: Reader Tips
author: Margie Sydney, CT
content: Margie Sydney protects ripening strawberries from birds by slipping reusable mesh produce bags over fruit clusters and gently securing the drawstring closure around the berries.

title: The Wild Side
content: Sleepy orange butterfly, Abaeis nicippe, is a small orange butterfly with thick brown wing margins and faint curving forewing marks that can look like closed eyes. Its 1 1/2- to 2 1/4-inch wings have yellow undersides with blurry brown and black markings, and the yellow deepens to rust in cooler months.

title: The Wild Side
content: Female sleepy orange butterflies lay slender oblong eggs on host plants in the pea family. Caterpillars are green with a slight blue cast, short fine white hairs and a creamy white side stripe; chrysalises have long pointed ends and may be green or dark brown.

title: The Wild Side
content: Sleepy orange butterflies occur in the southern half of the United States during summer and migrate farther south into Central America in winter. Caterpillars feed on Southern natives such as sensitive partridge pea, Chamaecrista nictitans, and wild senna, Senna hebecarpa, while adults nectar in open fields and along waterways and often gather minerals from wet soil and mud puddles.

title: Struggling With Stubborn Seeds? Try These Tips!
content: Some seeds do not sprout quickly or at all without specific light, darkness, temperature or pretreatment. Knowing each seed's needs before sowing can improve germination speed and success.

title: Struggling With Stubborn Seeds? Try These Tips!
content: Bells of Ireland, Moluccella laevis, is an annual that germinates in 14 to 28 days at 65 to 68 degrees F after chilling seed in the refrigerator for 1 to 2 weeks.

title: Struggling With Stubborn Seeds? Try These Tips!
content: Blue poppy, Meconopsis betonicifolia, is a perennial for USDA zones 3 to 8 that germinates in 21 to 35 days at 55 to 65 degrees F after chilling seed in the refrigerator for 3 weeks.

title: Struggling With Stubborn Seeds? Try These Tips!
content: Geum hybrids are perennials for USDA zones 4 to 9 that germinate in 21 to 30 days at 65 to 70 degrees F.

title: Struggling With Stubborn Seeds? Try These Tips!
content: Golden clematis, Clematis tangutica, is a perennial for USDA zones 3 to 9 that germinates in 21 to 35 days at 70 degrees F and may need a heat mat; chill seed in the refrigerator for 2 to 3 weeks.

title: Struggling With Stubborn Seeds? Try These Tips!
content: Passion flower, Passiflora caerulea, is a perennial for USDA zones 6 to 10 that germinates in 30 to 45 days at 75 to 80 degrees F and may need a heat mat; soak seed in water for 12 to 24 hours before sowing.

title: Struggling With Stubborn Seeds? Try These Tips!
content: Primula, Primula vulgaris, is a perennial for USDA zones 4 to 8 that germinates in 20 to 30 days at 50 to 60 degrees F.

title: Struggling With Stubborn Seeds? Try These Tips!
content: Stokes' aster, Stokesia laevis, is a perennial for USDA zones 4 to 9 that germinates in 25 to 30 days at 70 degrees F and may need a heat mat.

title: Struggling With Stubborn Seeds? Try These Tips!
content: Torch lily, Kniphofia species and hybrids, is a perennial for USDA zones 5 to 10 that germinates in 14 to 30 days at 70 to 75 degrees F and may need a heat mat.

title: Struggling With Stubborn Seeds? Try These Tips!
content: Turkish sage, Phlomis russeliana, is a perennial for USDA zones 5 to 9 that germinates in 40 to 60 days at 65 degrees F.

title: Struggling With Stubborn Seeds? Try These Tips!
content: Verbena hybrids are tender perennials for USDA zones 7 to 10 that germinate in 21 to 30 days at 75 degrees F and may need a heat mat; chill seed in the refrigerator for 1 week.

title: Struggling With Stubborn Seeds? Try These Tips!
content: Seeds that need light should be pressed lightly into seed-starting mix but not covered. Seeds that need darkness should be covered with mix and the flat should be covered with cardboard or plastic until germination.

title: The Romance of Spring
author: Jennifer Howell
content: With the arrival of spring, emerging perennials fill the garden with soft texture, fresh green leaves, early color and spring pollinators. Plants that return every year need only a little cleanup, and cool-loving annuals in pastel palettes can extend the relaxing mood before summer flowers arrive.

title: The Romance of Spring
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Delicate, airy flowers in soft blues, pinks and purples create a romantic spring feeling. The combinations use sweet colors and light textures to make cool spring days feel comfortable and inviting.

title: The Romance of Spring
author: Jennifer Howell
content: The Whispers of Blue design uses the soft blue hues of bugleweed and windflower for a cool, calming spring display. Windflower is a perennial rhizomatous tuber for USDA zones 7 to 10 that is planted in fall for spring bloom and retreats into dormancy as summer heat arrives.

title: The Romance of Spring
author: Jennifer Howell
content: When windflower foliage dies down, shade-loving summer annuals such as impatiens, wax begonias or browallia can be tucked among the bugleweed to provide extra color or continue the blue scheme.

title: The Romance of Spring
author: Jennifer Howell
content: As windflower fades, bugleweed spreads by runners to form a thick ground-hugging mat. Cut runners back to keep it in check, and after blooms fade, deadhead by hand or use a string trimmer or hedge shears to remove spent blossoms.

title: The Romance of Spring
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Windflower, Anemone coronaria 'Mr. Fokker', has violet-blue spring flowers above ferny foliage, grows in full sun to part shade, reaches 8 to 12 inches tall and wide and is cold hardy in USDA zones 7 to 10.

title: The Romance of Spring
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Windflower, Anemone coronaria 'Sylphide', has pink poppylike spring flowers above ferny foliage, grows in full sun to part shade, reaches 8 to 12 inches tall and wide and is cold hardy in USDA zones 7 to 10.

title: The Romance of Spring
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Bugleweed, Ajuga reptans 'Chocolate Chip', has short spikes of blue flowers above bronze-to-green foliage in mid- to late spring, grows in full sun to full shade, reaches 2 to 6 inches tall and 6 to 12 inches wide and is cold hardy in USDA zones 3 to 9.

title: The Romance of Spring
author: Jennifer Howell
content: In USDA zones 6 and colder, where windflower is not hardy, start the rhizomatous tubers indoors in late winter. Transplant them outdoors after frost danger passes for spring blooms, then lift the tubers in fall to overwinter or treat them as annuals.

title: The Romance of Spring
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Native garden-combination photo of a soft spring border with windflowers, bugleweed and pastel spring color.

title: The Romance of Spring
author: Jennifer Howell
content: The Dreamy Pastels combination fills the garden with weeks of color and needs only some deadheading to keep blooms going. Cool-loving pansies may falter in summer heat, so swap them for a sun-loving annual that matches the geraniums and fragrant alyssum.

title: The Romance of Spring
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Salvia, Salvia x sylvestris Blue Hill, has periwinkle-blue flower spikes above mounded foliage from late spring to midsummer, grows in full sun, reaches 18 to 24 inches tall and 12 to 18 inches wide and is cold hardy in USDA zones 4 to 9.

title: The Romance of Spring
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Zonal geranium, Pelargonium Rocky Mountain Lavender, has lavender-pink flower clusters from midspring to fall, grows in part to full shade, reaches 14 to 18 inches tall and 16 to 20 inches wide and is cold hardy in USDA zones 10 to 11.

title: The Romance of Spring
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Spring Matrix Blue Wing, Spring Matrix White Blotch and Mammoth Pink Berry pansies, Viola x wittrockiana, have bicolor flowers with facelike markings from early to late spring, grow in full sun to part shade, reach 6 to 8 inches tall and 8 to 10 inches wide and are cold hardy in USDA zones 6 to 10.

title: The Romance of Spring
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Sweet alyssum, Lobularia maritima, has fragrant white, purple, pink or peach flower clusters from midspring to frost, grows in full sun to part shade, reaches 3 to 9 inches tall and 6 to 14 inches wide and is cold hardy in USDA zones 9 to 11.

title: The Romance of Spring
author: Jennifer Howell
content: The Shady Serenity combination uses subtle pastels and variegated foliage for sparkle after spring bloom. Trim spent flowers so pulmonaria's speckled leaves show, and keep the grouping consistently moist through summer so the plants stay fresh.

title: The Romance of Spring
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Variegated Solomon's seal, Polygonatum odoratum var. pluriflorum 'Variegatum', has pendulous white spring flowers on long stems and variegated leaves, grows in part to full shade, reaches 2 to 3 feet tall and spreads, and is cold hardy in USDA zones 3 to 8.

title: The Romance of Spring
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Korean rock fern, Polystichum tsus-simense, has dark green shiny fronds that unfurl from fiddleheads in midspring, grows in part to full shade, reaches 12 to 15 inches tall and 6 to 18 inches wide and is cold hardy in USDA zones 6 to 9.

title: The Romance of Spring
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Pulmonaria hybrids have pink buds that open into blue flowers from mid- to late spring and fuzzy, often spotted leaves, grow in part to full shade, reach 6 to 18 inches tall and 12 to 18 inches wide and are cold hardy in USDA zones 3 to 9.
