title: Solve Garden Problems With Ground Covers
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Ground covers can replace struggling turfgrass in difficult sites and reduce water use, fertilizer and pesticide needs while supporting wildlife habitat when plants are matched to the right spot.

title: Solve Garden Problems With Ground Covers
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Kathy Jentz broadly defines a ground cover as any plant that densely covers soil, including annuals, perennials, vines, ornamental grasses and shrubs rather than only short evergreen plants.

title: Solve Garden Problems With Ground Covers
author: Marisa Reyes
content: On slopes and hillsides, ground covers can hold soil in place, prevent erosion and replace difficult mowing. Plants with strong fibrous roots, underground rhizomes or dense top growth are especially useful for stabilizing sloped soil.

title: Solve Garden Problems With Ground Covers
author: Marisa Reyes
content: While plants establish on a steep slope, biodegradable erosion-control fabric can hold roots and soil in place. Spread the fabric, secure it with landscape staples and cut a slit for each plant; mulch often washes downhill and may help less than expected.

title: Solve Garden Problems With Ground Covers
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Narrow strips, tight spaces and gaps between pavers are hard to mow, so low-growing, drought-tolerant ground covers that spread are ideal. For walkable areas, choose plants that tolerate some foot traffic.

title: Solve Garden Problems With Ground Covers
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Creeping juniper, Juniperus horizontalis, is useful on slopes; it is a shrub with green to blue-green scalelike foliage, grows in full sun, reaches 4 to 12 inches tall and 48 to 96 inches wide and is cold hardy in USDA zones 3 to 9.

title: Solve Garden Problems With Ground Covers
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Hakonechloa, Hakonechloa macra, helps cover slopes in shade; it has insignificant yellow-green flowers in late summer to fall and arching bright green leaves, grows in part to full shade, reaches 12 to 24 inches tall and wide and is cold hardy in USDA zones 5 to 9.

title: Solve Garden Problems With Ground Covers
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Pennsylvania sedge, Carex pensylvanica, stabilizes shaded slopes with spreading grasslike foliage. It has insignificant mid- to late-spring flowers, medium-green leaves, grows in full to part shade, reaches 6 to 10 inches tall and is cold hardy in USDA zones 3 to 8.

title: Solve Garden Problems With Ground Covers
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Winter jasmine, Jasminum nudiflorum, is a slope-covering shrub with nonfragrant bright yellow flowers in late winter before leaves emerge and green winter stems, grows in full sun to part shade, reaches 10 to 15 feet tall and 3 to 6 feet wide and is cold hardy in USDA zones 6 to 10.

title: Solve Garden Problems With Ground Covers
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Creeping Jenny, Lysimachia nummularia, can dress up areas mowers cannot reach. It has bright yellow summer flowers, round slightly ruffled green or gold leaves, grows in full sun to full shade, reaches 3 to 6 inches tall and 12 to 18 inches wide and is cold hardy in USDA zones 3 to 9.

title: Solve Garden Problems With Ground Covers
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Creeping thyme, Thymus serpyllum, is useful in tight spaces and between pavers. It has tiny white, red or pink summer-to-fall flowers, fragrant blue-green leaves, grows in full sun, reaches 2 to 5 inches tall and 6 to 12 inches wide and is cold hardy in USDA zones 4 to 9.

title: Solve Garden Problems With Ground Covers
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Dwarf mondo grass, Ophiopogon japonicus, tolerates some foot traffic in areas mowers cannot reach. It has small spikes of lilac summer flowers and dark green grasslike leaves, grows in part to full shade, reaches 9 to 12 inches tall and wide and is cold hardy in USDA zones 7 to 10.

title: Solve Garden Problems With Ground Covers
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Native garden photo of hakonechloa and epimedium covering a shaded slope beneath trees.

title: Solve Garden Problems With Ground Covers
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Native garden photo of dwarf mondo grass and creeping phlox filling tight spaces around pavers where a mower cannot reach.

title: Solve Garden Problems With Ground Covers
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Clay soil is dense, poorly draining and compacted, but deep-rooted plants such as black-eyed Susan and dwarf comfrey can break through compacted clay and create channels that improve aeration and water absorption.

title: Solve Garden Problems With Ground Covers
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Japanese painted ferns and autumn ferns thrive along paths in the moist conditions common in clay soil. Black-eyed Susan can act as a ground cover in masses because its clump-forming habit and persistent reseeding cover large areas.

title: Solve Garden Problems With Ground Covers
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Black-eyed Susan, Rudbeckia fulgida sullivantii, has golden-yellow daisylike flowers with black centers from summer to fall, grows in full sun to part shade, reaches 2 to 3 feet tall and 1 to 3 feet wide and is cold hardy in USDA zones 4 to 9.

title: Solve Garden Problems With Ground Covers
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Dwarf comfrey, Symphytum grandiflorum, has clusters of creamy yellow to white flowers from midspring to early summer and medium to dark green leaves, grows in full sun to part shade, reaches 12 to 18 inches tall and 18 to 24 inches wide and is cold hardy in USDA zones 5 to 8.

title: Solve Garden Problems With Ground Covers
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Japanese painted fern, Athyrium niponicum var. pictum, has soft gray-green fronds with dark maroon midribs, grows in part to full shade, reaches 12 to 18 inches tall and 18 to 24 inches wide and is cold hardy in USDA zones 3 to 8.

title: Solve Garden Problems With Ground Covers
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Bare shady areas often make turfgrass thin and weak. Allegheny spurge, variegated Solomon's seal and moss are practical alternatives, and ferns or hostas with shallow roots can redirect traffic away from exposed tree roots.

title: Solve Garden Problems With Ground Covers
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Native garden path photo showing autumn fern and Japanese painted fern thriving in moist clay-soil conditions.

title: Solve Garden Problems With Ground Covers
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Native plant portrait of black-eyed Susan flowers used as a massed clay-tolerant ground cover.

title: Solve Garden Problems With Ground Covers
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Allegheny spurge, Pachysandra procumbens, has spikes of tiny white spring flowers and whorls of dark green leaves, grows in part to full shade, reaches 6 to 10 inches tall and spreads, and is cold hardy in USDA zones 5 to 9.

title: Solve Garden Problems With Ground Covers
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Sweet woodruff, Galium odoratum, has small fragrant white spring flowers and dark green leaves in whorls, grows in part to full shade, reaches 6 to 12 inches tall and 12 to 15 inches wide and is cold hardy in USDA zones 4 to 8.

title: Solve Garden Problems With Ground Covers
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Variegated Solomon's seal, Polygonatum odoratum var. pluriflorum 'Variegatum', has white bell-shaped late-spring flowers and green-and-white variegated foliage, grows in part to full shade, reaches 24 to 30 inches tall and wide and is cold hardy in USDA zones 3 to 8.

title: Solve Garden Problems With Ground Covers
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Bugleweed, Ajuga reptans, suppresses weeds by filling in quickly and forming a dense mat. It has tiny blue-violet flower spikes in mid- to late spring, variable foliage colors, grows in full sun to part shade, reaches 4 to 10 inches tall and 10 to 24 inches wide and is cold hardy in USDA zones 3 to 9.

title: Solve Garden Problems With Ground Covers
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Creeping rosemary, Salvia rosmarinus, is a weed-suppressing shrub for sunny rose gardens and shrub borders. It has pale blue spring and summer flowers and fragrant needlelike leaves, grows in full sun, reaches 1 to 2 feet tall and 2 to 3 feet wide and is cold hardy in USDA zones 8 to 11.

title: Solve Garden Problems With Ground Covers
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Epimedium species and hybrids eventually create a dense weed-suppressing layer in shady bare spots under shrubs or trees. They have red, pink, yellow or white orchidlike spring flowers, heart-shaped green leaves, grow in part to full shade, reach 4 to 24 inches tall and spread, and are cold hardy in USDA zones 4 to 9.

title: Solve Garden Problems With Ground Covers
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Vigorous ground covers can be helpful in rose gardens or shrub borders but may overtake less-vigorous plants in a mixed perennial border. Choose problem-solving plants carefully so they do not become the new problem.

title: Solve Garden Problems With Ground Covers
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Ground covers can solve difficult landscape problems such as erosion, compacted clay, shade and weeds. Matching the plant to the situation creates a lush, low-maintenance landscape with year-round texture and interest.

title: Which Penstemon is Right for You?
content: Foxglove beardtongue, Penstemon digitalis, is native to most of the United States east of the Rocky Mountains and stands tall in the middle or back of the border. Its airy pastel blooms attract bees, hummingbirds and butterflies and make good cut flowers.

title: Which Penstemon is Right for You?
content: Foxglove beardtongue works best in informal cottage gardens, prairies, native gardens and rain gardens where it can reseed and mingle. It prefers average to dry soil, tolerates clay and handles fluctuating wet and dry cycles.

title: Which Penstemon is Right for You?
content: Grow foxglove beardtongue in full sun to part shade, with at least 6 hours of sun for the most blooms and the best burgundy or purple foliage color in dark-leaved cultivars. Avoid waterlogged soils, deadhead for tidiness and another bloom flush, divide in early spring and surface-sow seed in late fall because it needs cold moist conditions and light to germinate.

title: Which Penstemon is Right for You?
content: 'Dark Towers' foxglove beardtongue has pink late-spring to summer flowers above wine-red to purple foliage that keeps its color all summer, grows 18 to 36 inches tall and 12 to 24 inches wide and is cold hardy in USDA zones 3 to 8.

title: Which Penstemon is Right for You?
content: 'Pocahontas' foxglove beardtongue has lavender-pink summer blooms above dark burgundy leaves, grows 3 to 4 feet tall and 2 to 3 feet wide and is cold hardy in USDA zones 3 to 8.

title: Which Penstemon is Right for You?
content: Penstemons are often called beardtongues because each flower has a hairy stamen in the throat.

title: Which Penstemon is Right for You?
content: Pineleaf penstemon, Penstemon pinifolius, is native to dry regions of Arizona and New Mexico but can thrive with more regular moisture. It is long-lived, grows into a low woody shrub, attracts hummingbirds with warm tubular flowers and is usually deer resistant.

title: Which Penstemon is Right for You?
content: Pineleaf penstemon looks natural in rock gardens, on retaining-wall edges, at the front of mixed borders or as a foundation-planting specimen. Grow it in full sun and sharply drained sandy or gravelly soil, with space and air circulation to reduce fungal disease.

title: Which Penstemon is Right for You?
content: Use pea gravel or stone mulch around pineleaf penstemon instead of bark or compost to help prevent crown rot. The evergreen plant does not need spring trimming, but after flowering it can be sheared with hedge trimmers to encourage more blooms.

title: Which Penstemon is Right for You?
content: 'Luminous' pineleaf penstemon has bright red-orange flowers from late spring to early summer, grows 8 to 10 inches tall and 12 to 15 inches wide and is cold hardy in USDA zones 5 to 9.

title: Which Penstemon is Right for You?
content: 'Mersea Yellow' pineleaf penstemon has yellow mid- to late-summer flowers, grows 9 to 12 inches tall and 12 to 18 inches wide and is cold hardy in USDA zones 4 to 9. Seeds from yellow pineleaf penstemons may not produce yellow-flowering offspring.

title: 2025's Best New Plants!
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: New plant introductions for 2025 include shade epimediums, flower-covered agastaches, annual geraniums, heat-tolerant tuberous begonias, double mandevillas, multiseason foliage plants and improved classic garden plants.

title: 2025's Best New Plants!
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: 'Dream Catcher' epimedium, Epimedium hybrid, has rose-red sepals with large yellow wings in mid- to late spring above a foliage mound. It grows in part to full shade, reaches 18 to 24 inches tall and 24 to 36 inches wide, is cold hardy in USDA zones 5 to 8 and thrives in dry shade with little work; cut off dead foliage in late winter.

title: 2025's Best New Plants!

title: 2025's Best New Plants!
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: 'Rouge Harlequin' peony, Paeonia hybrid, has large 6-inch single pale-pink blooms brushed with fuchsia, strong stems, a large main flower and up to four side buds. It grows in full sun to part shade, reaches 3 feet tall and 4 feet wide and is cold hardy in USDA zones 2 to 8.

title: 2025's Best New Plants!

title: 2025's Best New Plants!

title: Dianthus
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Dianthus is loved for intricate fringed blooms and a sweet spicy fragrance reminiscent of cloves. Flowers come in pale pink, white, lavender, bold red, orange and bicolors, while grasslike green, blue-green or silvery leaves look good even when plants are not in bloom.

title: Dianthus
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Dianthus nectar-rich flowers attract hummingbirds, bees, butterflies and other pollinators while generally remaining unappealing to deer.

title: Dianthus
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Dianthus fits borders, ground covers and containers. Plants bloom best in cool spring weather, may taper off in summer heat and often bloom again in fall; many newer varieties bloom longer with regular deadheading.

title: Dianthus
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Cheddar pinks and carnations are hardy dianthus types known for neat foliage mounds and long-lasting fragrant blooms. They work well in beds, borders and small vases.

title: Dianthus
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Sweet William and China pinks are less-hardy dianthus types often grown as annuals in colder climates. Sweet William has tall upright stems and clusters of multicolored flowers; China pinks and hybrids are low-growing bedding and container plants with large long-lasting flowers.

title: Dianthus
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Dianthus species and hybrids can be perennial, with single or double often fragrant pink, white, lavender, red, orange or bicolored flowers in spring and fall, and some varieties blooming continuously. Grow in full sun and moist to dry well-draining or sandy soil; most have no serious pests, reach 3 to 24 inches tall and 8 to 24 inches wide and are cold hardy in USDA zones 3 to 9.

title: Dianthus
author: Marisa Reyes

title: Dianthus
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Shorter dianthus species such as Cheddar pinks, China pinks and many hybrids work well along the front of borders or edging walkways. 'Firewitch' Cheddar pinks grows 4 to 8 inches tall and 8 to 12 inches wide and tolerates heat reflected from stone paths.

title: Dianthus
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Some dianthus varieties reach about 24 inches tall and fit in the middle of a border. Sweet William provides magenta, pink and white blooms on longer stems that work in cut-flower gardens and arrangements for up to three weeks.

title: Dianthus
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Dianthus is heat- and drought-tolerant, making it a natural fit for rock gardens. 'Tiny Rubies' Cheddar pinks grows 2 to 4 inches tall and 8 to 12 inches wide, forming a low dense mat of flowers and foliage that spills over rocks.

title: Dianthus
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Grow dianthus in windowboxes or containers near seating areas to bring fragrance, color and texture up close. Taller sweet William varieties add height and drama, while mounding Cheddar pinks, China pinks or carnations can grow alone or with English lavender or snapdragons.

title: Dianthus
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Dianthus blooms best in full sun and rich, well-drained to sandy soil that is evenly moist but not soggy. Too much moisture can cause root rot, crown rot and fungal diseases; in hot climates, afternoon shade helps prevent wilted, discolored flowers and stunted growth.

title: Dianthus
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Apply slow-release granular fertilizer in spring as new dianthus growth begins, keeping fertilizer around the plant perimeter to avoid leaf and crown burn. Avoid overfertilizing because excess nitrogen encourages foliage at the expense of flowers.

title: Dianthus
author: Marisa Reyes
content: A layer of gravel or chicken grit works well as mulch for dianthus because it suppresses weeds while reducing root and crown rot risk. Bark mulch can be used in a 1- to 2-inch layer if it does not cover stems or crowns.

title: Dianthus
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Regular deadheading is key to a long dianthus bloom period and a fall rebloom. For single-flowering pinks with many blooms, wait until the flush fades and shear all stems back to the foliage mound with hedge shears or battery-powered grass shears.

title: Dianthus
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Double-flowering carnations and sweet Williams usually have fewer, larger blooms that can be deadheaded individually. Heat-tolerant hybrids such as the Capitan and Mountain Frost series should also be deadheaded individually so ongoing blooms are not removed.

title: Dianthus
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Useful dianthus deadheading tools include battery-powered grass shears for many small low-growing flowers, hedge shears for upright or mounded varieties with lots of blooms and long-nosed utility snips for precise pruning when only a few blooms need cutting.

title: Dianthus
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Divide dianthus in spring or early fall every three to four years or whenever the center opens up or flowering decreases. Water plants a day or two before digging, lift the foliage to locate the crown and loosen the soil around the clump with a hand trowel or soil knife.

title: Dianthus
author: Marisa Reyes
content: To divide dianthus, lift the whole clump with the rootball intact, use a sharp knife to cut through the central woody stem and separate sections, trim damaged roots and replant divisions in predug holes with crowns at soil level before watering in.

title: On Edge
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Garden edging defines where a garden starts and ends. It can give beds a finished look, deter lawn grasses, hold mulch, soil and gravel in place and separate paths from planting areas.

title: On Edge
author: Jennifer Howell
content: The best edging material depends on garden style, budget, construction ability, maintenance time and personal preference.

title: On Edge
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Tera Boeauf prefers a cut edge instead of installed edging because metal and plastic can hurt knees, feet and paws if stepped on, and a cut edge lets the garden shape change at any time. She cuts straight down 3 to 4 inches with a half-moon edger, leaving a vertical lawn-side edge and a shallow trench sloping into the bed.

title: On Edge
author: Jennifer Howell

title: On Edge
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Janie McCabe prefers steel edging because it can make sharp straight lines for formal beds or bend into flowing curves. She uses 4-inch-wide steel edging, 3/16 or 1/2 inch thick, in 10- or 16-foot lengths, anchored with steel stakes about every 6 feet and set 3 inches deep with the top inch exposed.

title: On Edge
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Lisa Bauer uses welded steel edging for a sharp durable look, especially in wet regions where wood will rot or may have chemicals if treated. Welded steel is installed by professionals, with angle-iron stakes welded on site, sometimes embedded in concrete and custom cut so there are no seams.

title: On Edge
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Keegan Lare likes natural stone edging for durability and because steel can heave during Midwestern winter freeze-thaw cycles. He recommends stones 6 to 8 inches tall and wide, set into a 2-inch-deep base of 3/8-inch aggregate just above ground level so the mower can run over the top.

title: One Garden, Two Worlds
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Tom and Courtenay Vanderbilt's North Carolina garden transitions from sunny, flower-filled front borders to a shady backyard hideaway.

title: One Garden, Two Worlds

title: One Garden, Two Worlds
author: Marisa Reyes
content: After foundation repairs required removing most original shrubs, Courtenay Vanderbilt started fresh in the garden. The house sits at the top of a steep slope, so a dry creek bed redirects water away from the foundation and a retaining wall levels the backyard and separates the garden from the ravine.

title: One Garden, Two Worlds
author: Marisa Reyes
content: The garden goal was a space with unique textures and colors plus evergreen shapes for winter interest and year-round privacy. In the front yard, common foxglove, peony and reseeding annuals provide spring bloom, then ornamental grasses and shrubs such as 'Adagio' maiden grass and 'Kaleidoscope' glossy abelia keep the bed interesting in summer.

title: One Garden, Two Worlds
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Courtenay started the side yard with about 200 plants divided from her previous garden, including hydrangeas, hostas, daylilies and irises. A mulch path runs through the bed from driveway to front door, passes beneath an arbor draped in 'Major Wheeler' honeysuckle and is defined by a 3-foot-tall white picket fence.

title: One Garden, Two Worlds
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Native garden photo of a lush green lawn and front garden bed with foxglove, 'Adagio' maiden grass and 'Kaleidoscope' glossy abelia.

title: One Garden, Two Worlds
author: Marisa Reyes
content: The Vanderbilt property sits on about 1/3 acre at the top of a slope, with the street 6 to 7 feet above the house. The garden includes front beds, a side yard, a dry creek bed, an attached deck, a freestanding deck, gate and arbor and a stone cascade point.

title: One Garden, Two Worlds
author: Marisa Reyes
content: A stone walkway off the mulch path leads to a seating area where Courtenay tries to relax, though sitting down often makes her notice another garden task.

title: One Garden, Two Worlds

title: One Garden, Two Worlds
author: Marisa Reyes
content: On one side of the front yard, conifers such as 'Fat Albert' Colorado blue spruce and 'Golden Mop' false cypress create privacy and curb appeal with varied foliage color and texture through every season.

title: One Garden, Two Worlds
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Candy Corn spirea and 'Moonshine' yarrow add changing color among the conifers and evergreens. Courtenay designs gradually by expanding beds whenever she has new plants to add, rather than beginning with a fixed plan.

title: One Garden, Two Worlds
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Native front-bed photo with Candy Corn spirea, 'Golden Mop' false cypress, 'Moonshine' yarrow and layered conifers.

title: One Garden, Two Worlds
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Breadseed poppies reseed freely in Courtenay's front beds and need only occasional thinning. Their dried seedpods can be spray-painted red, green and gold for holiday decor.

title: One Garden, Two Worlds
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Zinnias reseed with the breadseed poppies and are staked to keep them from sprawling onto the lawn. Other prolific reseeders in the beds include love-in-a-mist, verbena, celosia and snapdragons.

title: One Garden, Two Worlds
author: Marisa Reyes
content: The dry creek bed solved drainage by channeling water from neighboring yards and the house foundation toward the ravine. It is about 36 inches wide and 18 inches deep, with large stones along the edges and smaller fist-sized stones in the center to contain heavy rain runoff.

title: One Garden, Two Worlds
author: Marisa Reyes
content: The dry creek bed also became a garden feature, meandering between crape myrtle, Acadiana red holly and Chinese fringe tree. Irises, Indian pink, ornamental grasses and creeping juniper soften the stone edges and connect the front beds to the backyard garden.

title: One Garden, Two Worlds
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Courtenay protects deer-vulnerable plants such as impatiens with simple cages, especially while new plantings become established.

title: One Garden, Two Worlds
author: Marisa Reyes
content: A removable fishing-line deer door on the wooden arbor attaches to a hook and eye screw about 15 inches from the ground. When deer try to enter, the line touches their legs and confuses them, while the hook-and-eye setup keeps it from becoming a tripping hazard for people.

title: One Garden, Two Worlds
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Similar fishing-line deer doors protect side-yard and dry-creek-bed entry points, and repellents such as Bobbex and Deer Out add another layer of protection.

content: Native photo of a simple deer cage protecting impatiens or other vulnerable plants.

title: One Garden, Two Worlds
author: Marisa Reyes
content: A 3 1/2-foot-tall retaining wall at the property edge leveled the steep backyard and gave Courtenay about 12 feet of shaded garden to plant.

title: One Garden, Two Worlds
author: Marisa Reyes
content: The shady backyard beds rely on ferns, hostas, lobelia, foamflower and strawberry begonia, with dwarf mondo grass weaving between flagstones. The ferny foliage of Indigo Flair mahonia and 'Red Dragon' Japanese maple adds interest in the small space.

title: One Garden, Two Worlds
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Japanese maples are scattered throughout the garden. 'Red Dragon' and 'Bloodgood' grow in the ground, while others such as 'Sango-kaku' from the Georgia garden thrive in containers and add red or lime-green foliage contrast.

title: One Garden, Two Worlds
author: Marisa Reyes
content: For privacy, Courtenay and Tom built a 5 1/2-foot dark-brown wooden fence at the driveway end and an 8-foot arbor as a backyard entry point. The dark stain helps the fence blend into the landscape.

title: One Garden, Two Worlds
author: Marisa Reyes

title: One Garden, Two Worlds
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Tom and Courtenay built a 10-by-10-foot freestanding wooden deck that cantilevers about 3 feet over the retaining wall, creating a peaceful backyard sitting area.

title: One Garden, Two Worlds
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Tom built an upcycled glass-bottle screen by drilling bottle bottoms with a diamond bit, sliding the bottles onto rebar covered in rubber irrigation tubing and adding rubber disks and O-rings to protect the glass. Sunlight through the bottles creates a stained-glass effect.

title: One Garden, Two Worlds
author: Marisa Reyes
content: The garden balances sunny front beds filled with varied plants and a shady backyard rich with texture, creating year-round beauty and practical outdoor spaces.

title: What's Your Gardening Style?
author: Chloe Deike
content: Every garden has a theme because each gardener has a different reason for grabbing a trowel, whether the garden overflows with flowers, feeds the kitchen or focuses on foliage. The quiz groups preferences into four gardening styles while reminding readers that there are no rules.

title: What's Your Gardening Style?
author: Chloe Deike
content: The gardening-style quiz asks about how you celebrate milestones, shop for plants, grow vegetables, imagine a dream garden job, choose rewarding tasks, welcome garden visitors, enjoy the garden, started gardening, clean your house, value garden features and attend garden-related events. Tally A, B, C and D answers to find the closest style.

title: What's Your Gardening Style?
author: Chloe Deike
content: The Neighbor sees the garden as a way to foster relationships by supplying food, creating a place for kids to play or connecting with people and the past. This gardener often grows familiar plants year after year and treats gardening as a natural rhythm of life.

title: What's Your Gardening Style?
author: Chloe Deike
content: The Neighbor's garden has a cozy cottage feel with flowers tucked into every nook and cranny, often from plants passed down by family or shared by friends. Long-lived perennials that can be divided, shared or saved from seed suit this style, and packed beds help suppress weeds and reduce maintenance.

title: What's Your Gardening Style?
author: Chloe Deike
content: Native garden-style photo of a neighborly flower and vegetable garden with a chicken and generous plantings.

title: What's Your Gardening Style?
author: Chloe Deike
content: Love-lies-bleeding, Amaranthus caudatus, suits the Neighbor style with dramatic drooping magenta, green or pink flowers on annual plants 24 to 48 inches tall and 18 to 24 inches wide. Grow from seed in full sun and well-drained soil; leaves can be eaten like spinach and seeds as a grain.

title: What's Your Gardening Style?
author: Chloe Deike
content: Hollyhock, Alcea rosea, is a cottage-garden classic with soaring summer flower spikes in every shade but blue. It is biennial, reseeds readily, grows 3 to 8 feet tall and 1 to 3 feet wide in full sun and is cold hardy in USDA zones 2 to 10.

title: What's Your Gardening Style?
author: Chloe Deike
content: Balloon flower, Platycodon grandiflorus, has blue, white or pink starry flowers in full sun to part shade, grows 6 to 48 inches tall and 12 to 18 inches wide and adds long-lasting summer color in USDA zones 3 to 9.

title: What's Your Gardening Style?
author: Chloe Deike
content: Neighbor-style gardeners often pass extra produce and bouquets to neighbors, grow edible plants alongside flowers and make gardening an easy part of the daily routine.

title: What's Your Gardening Style?
author: Chloe Deike
content: The Naturalist gardens to care for the environment, use sustainable practices, avoid chemicals and enjoy plants that have purpose for personal well-being and community health.

title: What's Your Gardening Style?
author: Chloe Deike
content: A Naturalist's garden is manageable and productive, often converting lawn to native or drought-tolerant planting, using better lawn alternatives to reduce water use and growing organic food in raised beds.

title: What's Your Gardening Style?
author: Chloe Deike
content: Native garden-style photo of a naturalist garden with coneflowers and wildlife-friendly plantings.

title: What's Your Gardening Style?

content: Native photo of a praying mantis beneficial insect in the garden.

title: What's Your Gardening Style?
author: Chloe Deike
content: Red raspberry, Rubus idaeus, suits the Naturalist because it is native and edible. This shrub grows 3 to 5 feet tall and 2 to 3 feet wide, bears summer fruit from spring flowers, grows in full sun and is cold hardy in USDA zones 3 to 9.

title: What's Your Gardening Style?
author: Chloe Deike
content: Amsonia, Amsonia tabernaemontana, has sky-blue star-shaped early-summer flowers above glossy green leaves that turn yellow in fall. This perennial grows 2 to 3 feet tall and wide in full sun to part shade and is cold hardy in USDA zones 3 to 9.

title: What's Your Gardening Style?
author: Chloe Deike
content: Meadow blazing star, Liatris ligulistylis, has tall pink-purple summer flower spikes favored by pollinators. Plant in full sun to part shade; in rich soil it grows 3 to 5 feet tall and 1 to 2 feet wide and is cold hardy in USDA zones 3 to 8.

title: What's Your Gardening Style?
author: Chloe Deike
content: Naturalist-style gardeners often have bees, butterflies or caterpillars in every corner, use gravel pathways to help water absorption and reduce runoff and value plants that are functional as well as beautiful.

title: What's Your Gardening Style?
author: Chloe Deike
content: The Victorian sees the garden as a place of beauty, peace and relaxation, and enjoys the work of maintaining and improving it. Curb appeal, entertaining space, unusual plants and higher-maintenance specimens all matter to this style.

title: What's Your Gardening Style?
author: Chloe Deike
content: The Victorian garden is classic and romantic, with trimmed rolling lawns, designed beds and borders, pathways to intimate seating areas, ornate furniture, urns, birdbaths and flowers that are often ruffled, patterned or multicolored.

title: What's Your Gardening Style?
author: Chloe Deike
content: Native garden-style photo of a Victorian garden with paths, seating and romantic planted borders.

title: What's Your Gardening Style?
author: Chloe Deike
content: Climbing roses, Rosa species and hybrids, add height, color and fragrance to a Victorian garden. They can be solid or bicolored in nearly every color except blue, grow 6 to 30 feet tall in full sun and are cold hardy in USDA zones 3 to 11.

title: What's Your Gardening Style?
author: Chloe Deike
content: Gladiola, Gladiolus species and hybrids, is a timeless summer-blooming bulb in orange, yellow, pink, red, purple and patterned flowers. Plant corms in spring in full sun; plants grow 24 to 72 inches tall and 10 to 12 inches wide and are hardy in USDA zones 7 to 11, so dig and overwinter them where not hardy.

title: What's Your Gardening Style?
author: Chloe Deike
content: Angel's trumpet, Datura hybrids, has large white, pink, lavender or yellow flowers that show in moonlight. This tender perennial blooms from midsummer to frost, grows 2 to 4 feet tall and 3 to 6 feet wide and is cold hardy in USDA zones 9 to 10.

title: What's Your Gardening Style?
author: Chloe Deike
content: Victorian-style gardens may use well-trimmed hedges, durable furniture, glamorous materials, arbors and vines along paths and small water features with koi fish near seating areas.

title: What's Your Gardening Style?
author: Chloe Deike
content: The Plant Geek is captivated by plants, uses Latin names, loves plant history and growing information and may garden so much that it feels like a full-time job.

title: What's Your Gardening Style?
author: Chloe Deike
content: A Plant Geek's garden is marked by beds and borders packed with different varieties of the same plant, specialized tools for every task and containers of uncommon botanical treasures. Visitors are likely to get a plant lesson while walking through the garden.

title: What's Your Gardening Style?
author: Chloe Deike
content: Native garden-style photo of a plant-geek border packed with colorful unusual plants.

title: What's Your Gardening Style?
author: Chloe Deike
content: Vining monkshood, Aconitum episcopale, climbs when trained on a sturdy trellis and produces lavender-blue flowers from late summer to fall. This perennial grows 8 to 12 feet tall in moist soil and full sun to part shade and is cold hardy in USDA zones 5 to 9.

title: What's Your Gardening Style?
author: Chloe Deike
content: Roscoea, Roscoea purpurea f. alba, is a tuberous perennial with leaf sheaths topped by clusters of white and purple blooms that open in succession in summer. Grow in part sun to part shade and moist soil; it reaches 10 to 16 inches tall and 4 to 6 inches wide and is cold hardy in USDA zones 5 to 8.

title: What's Your Gardening Style?
author: Chloe Deike
content: Pitcher plant, Sarracenia species and hybrids, has modified leaves in shades of red, yellow, purple or green, grows 4 to 24 inches tall and 12 to 24 inches wide and does best in boggy soil in full sun to part shade. It is cold hardy in USDA zones 5 to 9.

title: What's Your Gardening Style?
author: Chloe Deike
content: Plant Geek-style gardeners tend to use advanced plant vocabulary, grow plants others consider difficult, know plant parentage and are recognized by garden-center employees.

title: Elevate an Evergreen Hedge
author: Chloe Deike
content: An evergreen hedge can become a formal-looking backdrop for a lower-maintenance garden when smaller evergreen hedges and symmetrical plantings add structure while plants are allowed to grow in their natural forms.

title: Elevate an Evergreen Hedge
author: Chloe Deike
content: Dark foliage can disappear in shadows without contrast, so a bright green hedge helps ninebark stand out and makes yellow peony flowers glow. Repeating purple and burgundy tones in hyacinths and front-of-border annuals ties the design together.

title: Elevate an Evergreen Hedge
author: Chloe Deike
content: Native illustration of an evergreen hedge design with ninebark, inkberry holly, candytuft, hyacinth, pansy, Itoh peony and daffodil.

title: Elevate an Evergreen Hedge
author: Chloe Deike
content: Small curving hedges create pockets of interest and hide fading spring bulb foliage. As daffodil leaves yellow, fold them toward the soil and secure them with plant stakes so they keep feeding bulbs while hidden by later peony foliage.

title: Elevate an Evergreen Hedge
author: Chloe Deike
content: A hedge's stiffness needs balancing with movement. Daffodils bob above inkberry holly in spring, Japanese anemone stems dance in fall and pansy petals ripple in wind, making the garden feel more alive.

title: Elevate an Evergreen Hedge
author: Chloe Deike
content: The design uses the power of thirds, with six ninebarks surrounding three peonies. Groups of three are pleasing in formal settings because they create centers and symmetry.

title: Elevate an Evergreen Hedge
author: Chloe Deike
content: Native continuation illustration of an evergreen hedge planting showing plant groupings and layered spring color.

title: Elevate an Evergreen Hedge
author: Chloe Deike
content: A tall hedge needs trimming at least once a year, and more often if kept at a set height. Leaving a couple feet between ninebark and the hedge provides access, and a powered hedge trimmer is a useful investment.

title: Elevate an Evergreen Hedge
author: Chloe Deike
content: Inkberry hollies in the design need little pruning if planted with enough space. If left untrimmed they may grow shaggy, which supports the casual look, and the same relaxed maintenance can apply to the short candytuft hedge.

title: Elevate an Evergreen Hedge
author: Chloe Deike
content: As hyacinth foliage fades, a replacement plant should be ready. Self-seeding love-in-a-mist can be sown among the hyacinth bulbs so seedlings emerge as bulb foliage declines and cover much of the dying foliage.

title: Elevate an Evergreen Hedge
author: Chloe Deike
content: Warm-weather annuals such as impatiens or zinnias can replace front-of-border pansies in summer, while Japanese anemones take over in late summer. Evergreen hedges keep winter structure, and peony foliage provides maroon late-season interest before it slumps and is cut back or left for spring cleanup.

title: Elevate an Evergreen Hedge
author: Chloe Deike
content: Native planting-plan diagram for an evergreen hedge border, including existing hedge, ninebarks, peonies, inkberry hollies, bulbs, pansies and love-in-a-mist.

title: Elevate an Evergreen Hedge
author: Chloe Deike
content: Little Devil ninebark, Physocarpus opulifolius, is a shrub with burgundy foliage and clusters of white late-spring flowers. Plant 6 in full sun; it grows 3 to 4 feet tall and wide and is cold hardy in USDA zones 3 to 7.

title: Elevate an Evergreen Hedge
author: Chloe Deike
content: 'Honorine Jobert' Japanese anemone, Anemone x hybrida, has medium white late-summer to fall flowers with ruffly yellow centers. Plant 15 in full sun to part shade; it grows 36 to 48 inches tall and 18 to 24 inches wide and is cold hardy in USDA zones 4 to 9.

title: Elevate an Evergreen Hedge
author: Chloe Deike
content: Candytuft, Iberis sempervirens, has small fragrant white flower clusters in midspring. Plant 20 in full sun; it grows 6 to 12 inches tall and 6 to 25 inches wide and is cold hardy in USDA zones 3 to 9.

title: Elevate an Evergreen Hedge
author: Chloe Deike
content: 'Bartzella' Itoh peony, Paeonia, has profuse yellow late-spring flowers. Plant 3 in full sun to part shade; it grows 30 to 36 inches tall and wide and is cold hardy in USDA zones 4 to 9.

title: Elevate an Evergreen Hedge
author: Chloe Deike
content: Squeeze Box inkberry holly, Ilex glabra, has dark evergreen foliage and a naturally pyramidal habit and can pollinate Gem Box to produce black berries. Plant 2 in full sun to part shade; it grows 4 to 6 feet tall and 2 to 3 feet wide and is cold hardy in USDA zones 5 to 9.

title: Elevate an Evergreen Hedge
author: Chloe Deike
content: Gem Box inkberry holly, Ilex glabra, has dark evergreen foliage with red spring tips and a naturally mounding habit. Plant 11 in full sun to part shade; it grows 2 to 3 feet tall and wide and is cold hardy in USDA zones 5 to 9.

title: Elevate an Evergreen Hedge
author: Chloe Deike
content: 'Mount Hood' daffodil, Narcissus, has 5-inch white midspring flowers with pale yellow throats. Plant 36 in full sun to part shade; it grows 16 to 18 inches tall and 6 to 8 inches wide and is cold hardy in USDA zones 4 to 8.

title: Elevate an Evergreen Hedge
author: Chloe Deike
content: 'Dark Dimension' hyacinth, Hyacinthus orientalis, has deep purple fragrant midspring flowers. Plant 36 in full sun to part shade; it grows 10 to 12 inches tall and 3 to 5 inches wide and is cold hardy in USDA zones 4 to 8.

title: Elevate an Evergreen Hedge
author: Chloe Deike
content: Nature Antique Shades pansy, Viola x wittrockiana, has lightly fragrant 2-inch flowers in cream, gold, peach and soft violet during cool weather. Plant 42 in full sun to part shade; it grows 6 to 10 inches tall and wide.

title: Elevate an Evergreen Hedge
author: Chloe Deike
content: 'Miss Jekyll Blue' love-in-a-mist, Nigella damascena, has soft blue late-spring and fall blooms followed by striped ornamental seedpods. Direct sow in spring in full sun to part shade; it grows 18 to 24 inches tall and 12 to 18 inches wide and reseeds.

title: Time to Crack Open a Good Book!
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Winter is a good time to read garden books that offer information or inspiration for next year's garden, including design, birdhouses, fragrant plants, edible or medicinal plants and container ideas.

title: Time to Crack Open a Good Book!
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Making Bird-Friendly Birdhouses by Melvin Toellner and Matthew Maguire explains how to attract 15 types of birds, from wrens to owls and ducks, by providing the right kind of birdhouse. It includes plans and step-by-step instructions for 13 birdboxes.

title: Time to Crack Open a Good Book!
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Beginner's Guide to Garden Planning and Design by Helen Yoest breaks garden design into manageable pieces, from design elements to practical techniques, and encourages readers to create a garden with confidence.

title: Time to Crack Open a Good Book!
author: Jennifer Howell
content: The Fragrant Flower Garden by Stefani Bittner and Alethea Harampolis profiles 55 fragrant plants and gives advice on growing, harvesting and using aromatic foliage and flowers in landscapes, arrangements, scented gifts and beauty products.

title: Time to Crack Open a Good Book!
author: Jennifer Howell
content: The 10-Minute Gardener by CaliKim offers vegetable-gardening time-saving tips divided into achievable tasks for gardeners who want more harvest without becoming overburdened.

title: Time to Crack Open a Good Book!
author: Jennifer Howell
content: A Year Full of Pots by Sarah Raven uses colorful photos and horticultural advice to inspire container gardens for every season, with design tips, month-by-month plant recommendations and care advice.

title: Time to Crack Open a Good Book!
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Medicinal Plants of North America by Jim Meuninck uses photographs and descriptions to identify plants with historical and modern medicinal uses and includes cautionary notes.

title: Time to Crack Open a Good Book!
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Edible Wild Plants by Todd Telander uses botanical illustrations and descriptions of 120 common edible plants, with notes on traditional consumption.

title: Time to Crack Open a Good Book!
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Pollinators of the American West by Denver Botanic Gardens and Butterfly Pavilion profiles more than 300 beneficial pollinating insects with photos and facts.

title: Time to Crack Open a Good Book!
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Wildflowers of North America by Damian Fagan organizes more than 500 wildflowers by flower color to help readers identify and learn about the plants.

title: Q&A
content: Divaricate describes woody or herbaceous plants that branch widely and spread out, often intersecting and knitting together to form a dense mat.

title: Q&A
content: Corrugated cardboard mulch can suppress weeds, hold soil moisture and cost little, but wet cardboard can block oxygen exchange, thick layers can kill beneficial organisms, some cardboard may add forever chemicals such as PFAS and it may attract termites.

title: Q&A
content: If using corrugated cardboard as mulch, use it only occasionally in a small area where vegetables are not growing, keep the layer thin, monitor moisture and remove it if it stays soggy so it can break down more easily.

title: Q&A
content: Tick bait boxes can reduce local tick populations by treating mice and other small rodents with the same tick-control material used for dogs, reducing ticks that feed on them and repelling new ticks without harming the animal.

title: Q&A
content: A homemade tick bait tube can be made with 0.5 percent permethrin, a spray bottle, toilet paper tube, cotton balls or dryer lint and rubber gloves. Spray but do not soak the nesting material, let it dry completely, stuff it into cardboard tubes and place tubes in spring and summer where rodents frequent, such as wood piles and garden sheds.

title: Q&A
content: Wet permethrin is toxic to humans, cats, bees and fish, so wear rubber gloves while spraying tick bait material and allow it to dry thoroughly before placing it outdoors. Replace or refill tubes every six to eight weeks for maximum control.

title: Q&A
content: A white granulated crust under hostas with brown leaf tips is likely salt or mineral buildup from fertilizer, hard water or water softened with salt. Excess salts prevent plants from taking up water and nutrients, can damage roots and may slow growth.

title: Q&A
content: To treat severe salt buildup, scrape off about an inch of encrusted soil and discard it somewhere plants are not cultivated, then soak the area to flush remaining minerals. Garden gypsum, or calcium sulfate, can help break down salts with less water; repeat soaking if residue remains after a few weeks.

title: Q&A
content: Brown spots on Italian parsley leaves are likely septoria leaf spot, Septoria petrosilini, a splashing-water disease that can overwinter in soil and infect seed. Prevent it with fresh seed each year, crop rotation every two to three years, morning watering at soil level, harvesting dry leaves and thinning plants for air circulation.

title: Q&A
content: Septoria-infected parsley leaves are usually harmful only to people who are immunocompromised or highly susceptible to molds, but they are unappetizing. Discard affected leaves in the trash, keep remaining plants dry and let clean foliage regenerate, or start a second crop in a new location or container if time allows.

title: Weed Watch
content: Stinging nettle, Urtica dioica, is a native perennial 1 to 7 feet tall with hollow hairs that inject histamines and other chemicals if touched, causing sharp itching pain and sometimes a mild rash for minutes to hours.

title: Weed Watch
content: Stinging nettle has sharply pointed coarsely serrated leaves 3 to 6 inches long and up to 1 1/2 inches wide, square stems and clusters of tiny green to creamy pink flowers in leaf axils from early to late summer. One large plant can produce more than 1,000 seeds that remain viable for 10 years, and rhizomatous roots spread up to 5 feet into colonies.

title: Weed Watch
content: Stinging nettle prefers moist soil in sun or shade but tolerates dry conditions and often appears in recently disturbed soil. Small plants can be pulled and larger plants dug, but wear sturdy gloves and cover arms and legs; herbicide can be used if the label matches the situation.

title: Front-of-the-Border Wow! Power
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: 'Ivory Queen' Turkestan onion, Allium karataviense, brings 3- to 6-inch globe-shaped white flowers to the front of a border, blooms for 2 to 3 weeks, tolerates drought and is usually left alone by deer and rabbits.

title: Front-of-the-Border Wow! Power
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Plant 'Ivory Queen' Turkestan onion bulbs in fall 3 to 5 inches deep in full sun and well-drained soil. In spring, 3- to 4-inch-wide leaves emerge followed by one bloom stem per bulb, and the dry seedheads can remain for late-summer interest before shattering.

title: Front-of-the-Border Wow! Power
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Water 'Ivory Queen' regularly while it blooms if weather is very dry, keeping soil moist but not soggy. Once foliage goes dormant, stop supplemental watering because the bulbs grow best dry during dormancy and may slowly form small colonies by offsets.

title: Front-of-the-Border Wow! Power
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: 'Ivory Queen' Turkestan onion works near the front of borders or in containers, and unlike many taller alliums its foliage does not look brown and scraggly while blooming. White blooms pair well with burgundy foliage or with soft casual colors.

title: Front-of-the-Border Wow! Power
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Beyond Blue blue fescue, Festuca glauca, has tan summer flowers and fine-textured blue foliage, grows in full sun to part shade, reaches 8 to 12 inches tall and 12 to 18 inches wide and is cold hardy in USDA zones 4 to 8.

title: Front-of-the-Border Wow! Power
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Tempo Rose geum, Geum, has rose-pink blooms from late spring to early summer, grows in full sun, reaches 8 to 10 inches tall, 21 inches in bloom and 10 to 12 inches wide and is cold hardy in USDA zones 4 to 9.

title: Front-of-the-Border Wow! Power
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: The cool casual front-border combination needs minimal care. Deadhead geum by removing spent stems, cut brown or damaged blue fescue leaves in early spring and let grass plus geum cover the dormant allium spot until frost.

title: In the Weeds
author: Jamie Seitz
content: A July tornado passed close to Jamie Seitz's neighborhood, damaging old trees and dropping large branches from a walnut tree and a neighbor's maple while leaving people safe and homes mostly intact.

author: Jamie Seitz
content: Jamie had nine dahlias nearly ready to bloom when branches and debris covered the shed and garden. The largest branch was nearly a foot in diameter and punched through a shed skylight while debris flattened the dahlia area.

title: In the Weeds

content: During cleanup, Jamie expected the dahlias to be broken, but each plant was battered yet salvageable. All nine dahlias survived, though each needed restaking.

title: In the Weeds

content: The backyard tornado reminded Jamie to be grateful: the trees lost branches but remained standing, the garden was messy but thrived afterward, and friends and neighbors with chainsaws helped with cleanup.

author: Ellen Wubbels, IA
content: A long-necked plastic funnel helps add potting mix beneath plant leaves without breaking delicate stems or getting poked by prickly plants. Ellen Wubbels uses a funnel with a 1/2-inch opening to direct soil exactly where it is needed.

title: Reader Tips
author: Patti Kitsch, PA
content: Broken terra-cotta pot shards make an attractive container top dressing. The porous pieces absorb excess water and dry quickly, help prevent moisture from lingering around leaves, insulate the soil and keep containers cooler in summer.

title: Reader Tips
author: Patti Kitsch, PA
content: To make terra-cotta shard mulch, put broken pots on a hard surface, wear safety glasses and use a ball-peen hammer to break them into roughly 1/2- to 1-inch pieces, then top dress container soil.

title: From the Wild Side: Rove Beetle
content: Rove beetles are beneficial predators found under logs, stones and mulch, where they hunt aphids and other insects. They prefer shady, damp and undisturbed garden areas.

title: From the Wild Side: Rove Beetle
content: More than 4,000 rove beetle species are native to North America. They have slender elongated bodies, exposed abdomens with five or six segments and short wing covers; the abdomen may curl upward like a scorpion, but rove beetles do not sting.

title: From the Wild Side: Rove Beetle
content: Rove beetles undergo complete metamorphosis. Females lay tiny white spherical or pear-shaped eggs in moist soil; wingless larvae are elongated flattened hunters that molt three or four times before pupating in soil or a silk casing.

title: From the Wild Side: Rove Beetle
content: In gardens, rove beetles eat mites, aphids, leafhoppers, mealybugs, thrips, insect eggs, nematodes, springtails and sometimes plant debris. The greenhouse rove beetle, Dalotia coriaria, is sold for biological pest control.

title: From the Wild Side: Rove Beetle
content: Encourage rove beetles by leaving moist sheltered habitat such as mulch, leaf litter, rocks and logs where they can hunt and overwinter.

title: Fast Garden Facts: Give Hungry Hummers a Helping Hand
content: Many hummingbirds migrate from Mexico and Central America to Canada, and spring feeders provide extra energy while they also feed on nectar and insects.

title: Fast Garden Facts: Give Hungry Hummers a Helping Hand
content: Use several small hummingbird feeders, space them 10 to 15 feet apart, hang them 4 to 5 feet high and place them in partial shade so nectar spoils less quickly.

title: Fast Garden Facts: Give Hungry Hummers a Helping Hand
content: Clean hummingbird feeders every 3 to 5 days with hot water and a bottle brush, and clean more often when temperatures rise above 90 degrees F.

title: Fast Garden Facts: Give Hungry Hummers a Helping Hand
content: Make hummingbird nectar by stirring 1 part white granulated sugar into 4 parts very hot or boiling water, cooling it before filling feeders and refrigerating leftovers for up to a week.

title: Fast Garden Facts: Give Hungry Hummers a Helping Hand
content: Help hummingbirds by providing perches such as shrubs, tall perennials or trellises, avoiding chemicals that reduce insects, adding a mister to a birdbath and growing nectar plants such as agastache, cardinal flower, columbine, cuphea, penstemon, rose of Sharon and salvia.

title: A Study in Texture
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Spring and early summer reveal plant habit, branch patterns and leaf shape. Large solid leaves command attention and make spaces feel smaller, fine foliage recedes and opens a space, and grassy or swordlike blades create vertical lines.

title: A Study in Texture
author: Jennifer Howell
content: A textured planting can hold attention even without flowers because contrasting leaf size, shape and habit add depth to the garden.

title: A Study in Texture
author: Jennifer Howell
content: In the Layered Landscape design by Joyce Householder, terracing slows runoff and erosion and improves the view of a full-sun perennial mix with strappy bearded iris, velvety Russian sage and solid false indigo.

title: A Study in Texture
author: Jennifer Howell
content: For the Layered Landscape planting, cut back salvia, spike speedwell, bearded penstemon and catmint after the first bloom flush for rebloom. Snip iris blossoms, let false indigo form black seed pods and cut most dead foliage in late fall or early spring.

title: A Study in Texture
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Salvia nemorosa 'Caradonna' adds texture to the Layered Landscape combination. Deep blue-violet flower spikes from early summer to fall above rough leaf mounds; full sun; 18 to 20 inches tall and 12 to 18 inches wide; USDA zones 4 to 9.

title: A Study in Texture
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Spike speedwell, Veronica 'Lavender Lightsaber' adds texture to the Layered Landscape combination. Lavender spikes from early to midsummer above medium-green clumps; full sun; 28 to 30 inches tall and 18 to 20 inches wide; USDA zones 4 to 8.

title: A Study in Texture
author: Jennifer Howell
content: False indigo, Baptisia 'Sparkling Sapphires' adds texture to the Layered Landscape combination. Violet-blue blooms from late spring to early summer with upright blue-green foliage; full sun to part shade; 30 to 36 inches tall and wide; USDA zones 4 to 9.

title: A Study in Texture
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Bearded penstemon, Penstemon barbatus 'Jingle Bells' adds texture to the Layered Landscape combination. Red-orange tubular flowers from late spring to early summer above basal foliage; full sun; 18 to 36 inches tall and 12 to 24 inches wide; USDA zones 4 to 9.

title: A Study in Texture
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Russian sage, Perovskia atriplicifolia adds texture to the Layered Landscape combination. Tiny lavender-blue flowers on silver fernlike stems from midsummer to late summer; full sun; 2 to 5 feet tall and 2 to 4 feet wide; USDA zones 5 to 9.

title: A Study in Texture
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Lanceleaf coreopsis, Coreopsis lanceolata adds texture to the Layered Landscape combination. Yellow daisies from late spring to early summer above narrow or lobed rosettes; full sun; 12 to 18 inches tall and 15 to 18 inches wide; USDA zones 4 to 9.

title: A Study in Texture
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Bearded iris, Iris 'Obsidian' adds texture to the Layered Landscape combination. Deep purple-black flowers from mid- to late spring above swordlike leaves; full sun to part shade; 30 to 33 inches tall and 18 to 24 inches wide; USDA zones 4 to 9.

title: A Study in Texture
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Catmint, Nepeta faassenii 'Cat's Meow' adds texture to the Layered Landscape combination. Blue-purple flowers from late spring to early summer on dusky-green mounds; full sun to part shade; 17 to 20 inches tall and 24 to 36 inches wide; USDA zones 4 to 9.

title: A Study in Texture
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Letting coreopsis, Russian sage and bearded penstemon reseed can introduce fresh variations and seedlings in unexpected spots, giving the planting a slightly different look each year.

title: A Study in Texture
author: Jennifer Howell
content: The Shady Mosaic design by Inta Krombolz uses little bloom color but creates variety through white-splashed Chinese fairy bells, chartreuse foliage, broad hosta leaves, fernlike dog fennel and fine-bladed grasses.

title: A Study in Texture
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Chinese fairy bells and Chinese wild ginger spread by rhizomes, while hakonechloa and Taiwan mondo grass expand in clumps. Let the carpet inhibit weeds and trim winter-damaged foliage to the ground in spring.

title: A Study in Texture
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Chinese fairy bells, Disporum cantoniense 'Moonlight' adds texture to the Shady Mosaic combination. White clusters from late spring to early summer above small variegated green leaves streaked with white and pink blush; part to full shade; 18 to 24 inches tall and wide; USDA zones 7 to 9.

title: A Study in Texture
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Hosta 'Brother Stefan' adds texture to the Shady Mosaic combination. White spikes from late spring to early summer above puckered green leaves with golden-yellow centers; part to full shade; 20 to 22 inches tall, 24 inches in bloom and 30 to 36 inches wide; USDA zones 3 to 8.

title: A Study in Texture
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Chinese wild ginger, Asarum splendens adds texture to the Shady Mosaic combination. Inconspicuous purple early-spring flowers hidden near the base of heart-shaped silver-splashed leaves; part to full shade; 6 to 9 inches tall and 9 to 12 inches wide; USDA zones 5 to 9.

title: A Study in Texture
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Hakonechloa macra 'All Gold' adds texture to the Shady Mosaic combination. Yellow-green midsummer flowers aging tan above bright chartreuse grassy foliage; part to full shade; 12 to 18 inches tall and wide; USDA zones 5 to 9.

title: A Study in Texture
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Dog fennel, Eupatorium capillifolium 'Elegant Feather' adds texture to the Shady Mosaic combination. Sterile insignificant white fall flowers atop feathery green foliage that turns red before frost; full sun to part shade; 3 to 6 feet tall and 1 to 3 feet wide; USDA zones 6 to 9.

title: A Study in Texture
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Taiwan mondo grass, Ophiopogon formosanus adds texture to the Shady Mosaic combination. White summer flowers followed by blue fruit over light green grassy foliage; part to full shade; 4 to 6 inches tall and 24 to 36 inches wide; USDA zones 7 to 9.

title: A Study in Texture
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Cut dog fennel back to a few inches when it gets leggy to encourage branching and a compact tuft.

title: A Study in Texture
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Small hostas can be featured in containers: 'Winsome' suits a tall slender container, while 'Frosted Mouse Ears' works in a low hypertufa container. Provide afternoon shade and moist soil.

title: A Study in Texture
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Hosta 'Lakeside Cupid's Cup' adds texture and variegation to the shade combination. Lavender trumpet flowers in midsummer above blue-green corrugated leaves with cream edges; part to full shade; 12 to 14 inches tall and 30 to 42 inches wide; USDA zones 3 to 9.

title: A Study in Texture
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Hosta 'Winsome' adds texture and variegation to the shade combination. Lavender trumpet flowers in summer above dark green leaves with white edges; part to full shade; 3 to 8 inches tall, 16 to 18 inches in bloom and 15 inches wide; USDA zones 3 to 9.

title: A Study in Texture
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Spigelia marilandica adds texture and variegation to the shade combination. Tubular red flowers with yellow interiors in early summer above glossy green leaves; part to full shade; 12 to 24 inches tall and 6 to 18 inches wide; USDA zones 5 to 9.

title: A Study in Texture
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Hosta 'Sum and Substance' adds texture and variegation to the shade combination. Lavender trumpet flowers in late summer above large corrugated chartreuse leaves; part to full shade; 2 to 3 feet tall, 4 feet in bloom and 3 to 5 feet wide; USDA zones 3 to 8.

title: A Study in Texture
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Weigela florida My Monet adds texture and variegation to the shade combination. Pink flowers from early to late spring on pink-tinged variegated leaves; full sun to part shade; 12 to 18 inches tall and 18 to 24 inches wide; USDA zones 4 to 6.

title: A Study in Texture
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Foamflower, Tiarella 'Starfish' adds texture and variegation to the shade combination. Pale pink late-spring flowers above green leaves with dark veining; part to full shade; 8 inches tall, 13 inches in flower and 13 inches wide; USDA zones 4 to 9.

title: A Study in Texture
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Hosta 'Frosted Mouse Ears' adds texture and variegation to the shade combination. Lavender early-summer flowers above rounded leaves with blue-green centers and white edges; part to full shade; 4 to 7 inches tall, 6 to 12 inches in bloom and 14 to 18 inches wide; USDA zones 3 to 8.

title: Which Shade Perennial is Right for You?
content: Hosta is a shade gardener's friend, with thousands of cultivars in many sizes, shapes and colors. Leaves can be accents or backdrops, and trumpet flowers feed hummingbirds; some blooms are fragrant.

title: Which Shade Perennial is Right for You?
content: Hostas grow best in full to part shade. Green and gold types tolerate more sun than blue hostas, but six or more hours of sun can crisp any hosta. Cut flower scapes below foliage after bloom.

title: Which Shade Perennial is Right for You?
content: Hosta flowers can be white, lavender or purple from late spring to fall, with stalks just above the foliage or up to 4 feet higher. Leaves may be green, blue, gold, variegated, smooth, glossy, matte, wavy, heavily veined or red-petioled.

title: Which Shade Perennial is Right for You?
content: The blue color on blue hostas is a waxy coating that can rub or burn off. Leaves may turn green when the coating is gone, but the plant is not harmed.

title: Which Shade Perennial is Right for You?
content: 'Blue Mouse Ears' hosta has a slow-spreading mounded habit, grows 4 to 6 inches tall and produces purple blooms in midsummer. It is bluest in full to part shade.

title: Which Shade Perennial is Right for You?
content: 'June' hosta has broad leaves with wide blue margins and chartreuse centers in spring, maturing to green. It grows 12 to 15 inches tall and 24 to 30 inches wide with purple midsummer blooms.

title: Which Shade Perennial is Right for You?
content: 'Empress Wu' hosta has huge dark green deeply veined leaves up to 18 inches wide, grows 4 to 5 feet tall and 6 to 8 feet wide, and has purple early- to midsummer flowers just above the foliage.

title: Which Shade Perennial is Right for You?

title: Which Shade Perennial is Right for You?
content: Brunnera spreads slowly by rhizomatous roots and can reseed, but cultivars do not come true from seed. Species brunnera has solid green leaves and spreads more vigorously, making it useful as a ground cover.
