title: Spring Ephemerals to Treasure in the Garden
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Spring ephemerals are often woodland natives that bloom before deciduous trees leaf out, set seed and complete their life cycles before a full leaf canopy shades the ground.

title: Spring Ephemerals to Treasure in the Garden
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Spring ephemeral flowers are fleeting but important: bees, beetles and ants rely on them for early food and pollinate them along the way.

title: Spring Ephemerals to Treasure in the Garden
author: Jennifer Howell
content: In the garden, spring ephemerals need little care after planting. Mix them with other perennials that cover fading foliage as ephemerals go dormant.

title: Spring Ephemerals to Treasure in the Garden
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Shooting star has nodding white, purple or pink flowers in midspring with petals swept backward and anthers forming a pointed tube. Native bees such as bumblebees vibrate the flowers to shake out pollen. Grow it in part shade and average to moist well-drained soil; plants reach 9 to 18 inches tall and 9 to 12 inches wide and are cold hardy in USDA zones 4 to 8.

title: Spring Ephemerals to Treasure in the Garden
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Shooting star is native to the eastern United States and thrives where soil is moist in spring but dry in summer dormancy. It suits the front of a border, a ground-cover bed, woodland gardens or meadow gardens and can be paired with slower perennials or grasses that fill space after it dies down.

title: Spring Ephemerals to Treasure in the Garden
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Shooting star spreads by seed but may take several years to reach blooming size. Divide in early fall by digging and splitting the crown, then replanting at the same depth. Cultivars include dark-pink 'Aphrodite' and tall magenta 'Goliath'.

title: Spring Ephemerals to Treasure in the Garden
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Plant portrait photo of shooting star, Dodecatheon meadia, with pale pink recurved flowers dangling above foliage.

title: Spring Ephemerals to Treasure in the Garden
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Dutchman's breeches has white to pink puffy flowers in early to midspring that look like upside-down pantaloons hanging above ferny blue-green leaves. Grow it in part to full shade and moist to wet soil; plants reach 6 to 12 inches tall and wide and are cold hardy in USDA zones 3 to 7.

title: Spring Ephemerals to Treasure in the Garden
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Dutchman's breeches is an eastern North American native that attracts bumblebees and other spring pollinators. It is deer and rabbit resistant, but the foliage is toxic if ingested and can irritate skin.

title: Spring Ephemerals to Treasure in the Garden
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Plant Dutchman's breeches in woodland shade beds with rich organic soil and shredded-leaf mulch. Water during dry spells, and divide crowns in early spring as leaves emerge or in late fall when dormant.

title: Spring Ephemerals to Treasure in the Garden
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Dutchman's breeches seeds are spread by ants, which eat the elaiosome attachment on the seed and then discard and effectively plant the seed in the garden.

title: Spring Ephemerals to Treasure in the Garden
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Plant portrait photo of Dutchman's breeches, Dicentra cucullaria, with white pantaloons-shaped flowers above ferny foliage.

title: Spring Ephemerals to Treasure in the Garden
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Mayapple is a common North American woodland wildflower that spreads by rhizomes into colonies. Each plant grows one long stem with one or two palmate umbrellalike leaves; plants with two leaves form a single waxy white flower where the leaves meet.

title: Spring Ephemerals to Treasure in the Garden
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Mayapple flowers feed early pollinators, and box turtles are fond of the fruit. The large lobed leaves bring tropical texture to woodland beds and naturalized gardens before plants go dormant.

title: Spring Ephemerals to Treasure in the Garden
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Mayapple prefers moist soil but tolerates dry soil under trees where roots compete for moisture. Leave fallen tree leaves as mulch to protect dormant rhizomes and build humusy soil.

title: Spring Ephemerals to Treasure in the Garden
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Divide mayapple in fall by digging the rhizome and cutting it into pieces, making sure each piece has several terminal buds. Grow in part to full shade and average to moist well-drained soil; plants reach 12 to 18 inches tall and 9 to 12 inches wide and are cold hardy in USDA zones 3 to 8.

title: Spring Ephemerals to Treasure in the Garden
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Plant photo of mayapple, Podophyllum peltatum, showing umbrella-like lobed leaves and a hidden waxy white flower.

title: Spring Ephemerals to Treasure in the Garden
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Bloodroot gets its common name from the red sap in its foliage and roots. In early spring, cigar-rolled leaves curl around emerging flower stalks, then open into large round lobed leaves; fragrant white flowers with yellow centers open by day and close at night.

title: Spring Ephemerals to Treasure in the Garden
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Bloodroot grows best in moist but not soggy soil in part to full shade. It suits rock gardens or beds near patios where its fragrance can be appreciated, and it works as early ground cover around later perennials and deciduous shrubs.

title: Spring Ephemerals to Treasure in the Garden
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Single-flowered bloodroot produces ant-dispersed seeds, but double-flowered sterile cultivars such as 'Multiplex' multiply only by division. Divide every three years after flowering and before summer dormancy; wear gloves because sap can irritate skin.

title: Spring Ephemerals to Treasure in the Garden
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Plant portrait photo of double-flowered 'Multiplex' bloodroot, Sanguinaria canadensis, with white blooms.

title: Spring Ephemerals to Treasure in the Garden
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Corydalis has delicate blue-green foliage that mounds into a spring ground cover beneath deciduous shrubs or among slow-to-emerge perennials. In midspring, plants produce bee-attracting tubular flowers in pink, red or purple.

title: Spring Ephemerals to Treasure in the Garden
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Corydalis likes cool moist conditions while growing but drier soil in summer dormancy so the underground corms do not rot. Let foliage dry, crumble it in place to compost and cut spent flowers if reseeding is unwanted.

title: Spring Ephemerals to Treasure in the Garden
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Rabbits like corydalis, so repellents or barriers may be needed. More vibrant cultivars include violet-purple 'Purple Bird', near-red 'George Baker', bright-pink 'Beth Evans' and white-with-violet 'Merlin'.

title: Spring Ephemerals to Treasure in the Garden
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Plant portrait photo of corydalis, Corydalis solida, with pink tubular flowers and delicate foliage.

title: Spring Ephemerals to Treasure in the Garden
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Yellow trout lily has downward-facing bright yellow flowers with recurved petals above two tongue-shaped mottled leaves. It is native to eastern North American woodlands and naturalizes in shady beds under deciduous trees.

title: Spring Ephemerals to Treasure in the Garden
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Plant yellow trout lily in part to full shade and moist acidic soil along ponds, streams or damp but not soggy sites. Plants grow 3 to 6 inches tall and wide and are cold hardy in USDA zones 3 to 8.

title: Spring Ephemerals to Treasure in the Garden
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Seed-grown trout lily may take up to five years to bloom, but corms spread by stolons and form colonies. Divide in fall when dormant, because plants dislike being moved.

title: Spring Ephemerals to Treasure in the Garden
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Yellow trout lily's brown-mottled leaves help camouflage it among fallen leaves. Mason bees and bumblebees pollinate the nectar-rich flowers, while ants distribute seeds. Young plants have one leaf; mature blooming plants have two.

title: Spring Ephemerals to Treasure in the Garden
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Plant portrait photo of yellow trout lily, Erythronium americanum, with nodding yellow flowers and mottled leaves.

title: Spring Ephemerals to Treasure in the Garden
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Large-flowered bellwort can be grown in loose clumps or massed in woodland borders. Plants produce long slender stems with minimal leaves and a single yellow twisted-petal flower that weighs each stem into a graceful arc.

title: Spring Ephemerals to Treasure in the Garden
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Large-flowered bellwort grows best under trees in dappled light shade and self-seeds into colonies. Move seedlings or divide mature plants in fall, and leave fallen leaves as moisture-conserving mulch.

title: Spring Ephemerals to Treasure in the Garden
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Plant portrait photo of large-flowered bellwort, Uvularia grandiflora, with dangling yellow twisted-petal flowers.

title: Spring Ephemerals to Treasure in the Garden
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Winter aconite is one of the earliest and hardiest spring ephemerals, with buttercup-yellow flowers that can bloom through snow. The flowers provide important nectar for early pollinators, followed by lobed leaves that store energy before midsummer dormancy.

title: Spring Ephemerals to Treasure in the Garden
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Winter aconite naturalizes in shady woodland areas or lawns and can form a yellow late-winter carpet. It prefers medium to dry, well-drained soil and competes well beneath deciduous trees while dormant in summer.

title: Spring Ephemerals to Treasure in the Garden
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Divide winter aconite before the leaves go dormant so the tubers are easy to find. After bloom, dig elongated tubers, break them into pieces and replant 1 to 2 inches deep.

title: Spring Ephemerals to Treasure in the Garden
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Plant portrait photo of winter aconite, Eranthis hyemalis, blooming yellow through early spring conditions.

title: Spring Ephemerals to Treasure in the Garden
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Red trillium emerges in late winter to early spring with three red to maroon petals and three red-tinged green sepals above a three-leaved bract. Its mildly fetid odor attracts fly, beetle and fungus-gnat pollinators.

title: Spring Ephemerals to Treasure in the Garden
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Grow red trillium where it receives spring sun and later shade as temperatures rise. It is long-lived but slow from seed, often taking five to nine years to bloom, so divide dormant rhizomes in fall and replant pieces 2 to 3 inches deep.

title: Spring Ephemerals to Treasure in the Garden
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Red trillium is native to North America, but habitat and pollinator loss have reduced wild populations. Buy from reputable nurseries and never collect trilliums from the woods.

title: Spring Ephemerals to Treasure in the Garden
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Plant portrait photo of red trillium, Trillium erectum, with maroon flower above a three-part bract.

title: Annual Geranium
content: Annual geraniums provide bold blooms and many have striking foliage with a zone or ring across the leaf. Some, including 'Vancouver Centennial', 'Mrs Pollock' and 'Wilhelm Langguth', are grown primarily as foliage plants.

title: Annual Geranium
content: Feature-opening photo of assorted annual geraniums with colorful blooms and variegated foliage.

title: Annual Geranium
content: Annual geranium, Pelargonium hybrids, is a tender perennial grown as an annual in most of North America. It blooms red, pink, orange, lavender, salmon or white from late spring to fall, grows in full sun to part shade and moist well-drained soil, and is hardy in USDA zones 10 to 13.

title: Annual Geranium
content: Photo of annual geranium varieties including Calliope Medium Salmon, Calliope Medium Violet, Dynamo Dark Salmon and variegated heirloom foliage types.

title: Annual Geranium
content: The most common annual geranium groups at garden centers are ivy geraniums, zonal geraniums and interspecific hybrids. Ivy geraniums have lobed ivylike leaves, single or double blooms and trailing habits for baskets or container edges.

title: Annual Geranium
content: Zonal geraniums grow upright with full dome-shaped blooms, and many have a dark zone on the leaf. They work well in containers and some also make good border companions.

title: Annual Geranium
content: Interspecific geraniums are crosses between zonal and ivy geraniums and are considered the most reliable for long-lasting bloom. Heat-resistant interspecifics keep flowering when summer temperatures slow other types.

title: Annual Geranium
content: Dynamo series Pelargonium hybrids are zonal geraniums with single or semi-double flowers in 15 colors, including bicolors. Plants have medium green foliage, are grown from cuttings and reach 12 to 14 inches tall and wide.

title: Annual Geranium
content: Big EEZE series Pelargonium hybrids are interspecific geraniums with large 4- to 5-inch blooms in 12 colors. Plants have solid dark green foliage, are grown from cuttings and reach 12 to 18 inches tall and 18 to 24 inches wide.

title: Annual Geranium
content: Rocky Mountain series Pelargonium hybrids are zonal geraniums with semi-double flowers in nine colors and light green foliage. Plants are grown from cuttings and reach 14 to 18 inches tall and 16 to 20 inches wide.

title: Annual Geranium
content: Pinto series Pelargonium hybrids are seed-grown zonal geraniums with single or semi-double flowers in 13 colors, including bicolors. Plants have dark green foliage with a red zone and reach 12 to 18 inches tall and 12 to 15 inches wide.

title: Annual Geranium
content: 'Mrs Pollock' Pelargonium hybrid is an heirloom zonal geranium known for tricolor foliage and a light flush of red-orange summer flowers. It is grown from cuttings and reaches 12 to 18 inches tall and wide.

title: Annual Geranium
content: Focus series Pelargonium peltatum are ivy geraniums with semidouble flowers in six colors, including bicolors. Plants have deep-green foliage and a neat trailing habit, are grown from cuttings and reach 8 to 10 inches tall and 12 to 14 inches wide.

title: Annual Geranium
content: Plant portrait photo of a pink Dynamo geranium flower cluster.

title: Annual Geranium
content: Collage of annual geranium series and cultivars, including Big EEZE, Pinto, Rocky Mountain, Focus and 'Mrs Pollock'.

title: Annual Geranium
content: Container photo of annual geraniums with ornamental grass and trailing plants in a wooden planter.

title: Annual Geranium
content: Cascade series Pelargonium hybrids are ivy geraniums with larger and more numerous single flowers than most ivy geraniums. Four colors are available; plants have solid green foliage, are grown from cuttings and reach 12 to 16 inches tall and 20 to 24 inches wide.

title: Annual Geranium
content: Calliope Medium series Pelargonium hybrids are interspecific geraniums with semidouble flowers in 16 colors, including bicolors. Foliage can be green with or without a zone; plants are grown from cuttings and reach 14 to 18 inches tall and 16 to 20 inches wide.

title: Annual Geranium
content: Precision series Pelargonium x peltatum are ivy geraniums with early-blooming semidouble flowers in 11 colors, including bicolors. Plants have solid green foliage, are grown from cuttings and reach 10 to 12 inches tall and 14 to 18 inches wide.

title: Annual Geranium
content: A geranium series is a group of plants with a common name, consistent size and bloom time, and multiple colors. The series is usually the first word in the plant name, followed by the color.

title: Annual Geranium
content: Regal geranium, Pelargonium x domesticum, extends the season into spring because it loves cool weather. Plants usually fade as temperatures rise, but the Candy Flowers series is more heat tolerant and blooms longer into summer; regals grow 10 to 20 inches tall and 12 to 20 inches wide.

title: Annual Geranium
content: Scented geraniums, Pelargonium species and hybrids, are grown for fragrant leaves that may smell like rose, lemon, orange, peppermint or pine. Flowers are small and unevenly produced, while leaves vary in shape, size and texture; plants range from 12 to 24 inches tall and wide.

title: Annual Geranium
content: Fairy cascades, Pelargonium ionidiflorum, brings color to dry summer gardens, roots along its stems and can make an excellent ground cover. Shear lightly if plants get leggy; it grows 12 to 18 inches tall.

title: Annual Geranium
content: Plant portrait photo of Candy Flowers Bright Red regal geranium.

title: Annual Geranium
content: Plant portrait photo of 'Lady Plymouth' scented geranium with variegated foliage.

title: Annual Geranium
content: Plant portrait photo of fairy cascades geranium with airy pink flowers.

title: Annual Geranium
content: Containers are a classic way to showcase geraniums. A single geranium in terra-cotta looks timeless and also suits the plant because porous terra-cotta lets soil dry slightly between waterings.

title: Annual Geranium
content: A modern take on the classic geranium-spike-vinca container can use 'Fireworks' fountain grass for height, yellow creeping zinnia and purple fanflower as trailers, and a mounded geranium as a colorful skirt for the grass.

title: Annual Geranium
content: Zonal and interspecific geraniums have many flower colors and tidy upright or mounding habits, making them easy to pair with other plants in borders or use in mass plantings.

title: Annual Geranium
content: Design photo of peachy pastel geranium blooms in a terra-cotta pot.

title: Annual Geranium
content: Design photo of a bright pink annual geranium container with fountain grass and trailing companions.

title: Annual Geranium
content: For full-looking border plantings, space geraniums their mature width apart on center so each plant touches its neighbor while the individual shapes remain visible.

title: Annual Geranium
content: Geraniums for borders need well-drained soil. Ball Floraplant trials found Galaxy, Dynamo, Fantasia and Solera series work well in both landscapes and containers.

title: Annual Geranium
content: Seed-grown geraniums in small pots or multipacks are economical for large borders or many containers. The plants and flowers are smaller than cutting-grown types, but close spacing can still create colorful impact.

title: Annual Geranium
content: Border photo of orange geraniums massed with 'Moonsong Deep Orange' African marigolds.

title: Annual Geranium
content: Annual geraniums grow best with 6 to 8 hours of sun and well-drained soil. Let soil or potting mix dry before watering again because too much moisture causes root rot.

title: Annual Geranium
content: A slow-release fertilizer at planting keeps geraniums healthy through the season. If yellow leaves appear, use a water-soluble flower fertilizer every two or three weeks to boost nutrition.

title: Annual Geranium
content: Geranium flower clusters are pseudoumbels, and individual blooms open and fade at different times. Remove spent individual flowers with a gentle tug, then snap or snip the entire stem at the widened node when most blooms in the cluster have faded.

title: Annual Geranium
content: Geraniums may yellow or flower poorly because of too much water, too little water or too little fertilizer. Many seed-grown and older varieties slow bloom production when temperatures reach 90 degrees F, while interspecific hybrids such as Calliope, Brocade and Big EEZE keep flowering in heat.

title: Annual Geranium
content: Step photo showing spent individual geranium blooms removed by hand.

title: Annual Geranium
content: Step photo showing how to snap off a spent geranium flower stem at the node.

title: Annual Geranium
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Gray mold, Botrytis species, can appear on geraniums after cool damp weather as soft brown spots on foliage or flowers that turn fuzzy gray and rot. Prevent it with mature spacing for airflow, watering at soil level and removing infected material or whole infected plants in the trash.

title: Annual Geranium
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: To overwinter geraniums bare-root, dig plants before a hard freeze, shake soil from roots and let plants dry for a couple of days in a sheltered spot. Store them in a paper sack or cardboard box at 50 to 60 degrees F.

title: Annual Geranium
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: In spring, remove overwintered geraniums from storage, strip dead foliage, cut stems back to green growth and repot.

title: Annual Geranium
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Pinto, Maverick and Bulls Eye geranium series are easy to find from online seed sources and economical for starting many plants. Sow seed in multipacks 13 to 15 weeks before flowers are wanted; move seedlings to larger containers when they have two true-leaf sets and plant outdoors when nights are about 50 degrees F.

title: Annual Geranium
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Disease photo showing gray mold on geranium foliage and flowers.

title: Viburnum
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Large garden photo of Chinese snowball viburnum grown as a tree-form specimen with rounded green-white blooms.

title: Viburnum
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Close-up photo of Chinese snowball viburnum flower clusters maturing from green to white.

title: Viburnum
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Viburnums can provide dramatic spring flower clusters, flat-topped blooms, colorful berries, fall foliage and structure as focal points or mixed-border anchors. Many are deer and rabbit resistant, drought tolerant and able to thrive near black walnut trees.

title: Viburnum
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Most viburnum species grow in full sun to part shade and moist well-drained soil. Regular pruning is usually unnecessary except to remove dead, damaged or weak stems.

title: Viburnum
author: Marisa Reyes
content: If a viburnum produces fewer flowers, thin older branches to improve airflow and light, encouraging healthy new growth and better flowering.

title: Viburnum
author: Marisa Reyes
content: For overgrown or declining viburnums, renewal prune by removing one-third of the oldest, thickest stems at ground level each year for three years.

title: Viburnum
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Prune spring-blooming viburnums such as doublefile, Japanese snowball and Chinese snowball immediately after bloom to preserve next year's buds. Rejuvenate summer and fall bloomers such as arrowwood and smooth viburnum in late winter or early spring.

title: Viburnum
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Chinese snowball has the largest snowball viburnum flower clusters, reaching up to 8 inches across. Sterile florets emerge lime green in spring and mature white; because flowers are sterile, plants do not reseed, produce fruit or carry fragrance.

title: Viburnum
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Chinese snowball has dark green summer foliage that turns red-purple in fall. Leaves resist bacterial leaf spot and powdery mildew and are more resistant to viburnum leaf beetles than many other species. It grows 6 to 20 feet tall and wide in full sun to part shade and USDA zones 6 to 9.

title: Viburnum
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Japanese snowball has 2- to 3-inch white sterile flower clusters in midspring to early summer that seem to float along the branches. Pleated dark green foliage turns burgundy and red-purple in fall, and flowers draw pollinators but do not produce berries.

title: Viburnum
author: Marisa Reyes
content: 'Popcorn' Japanese snowball grows 5 to 8 feet tall and 4 to 7 feet wide with rounded clusters that resemble popcorn and bloom earlier than many cultivars. 'Newport' is smaller at 4 to 5 feet tall and 5 to 6 feet wide.

title: Viburnum
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Landscape photo of 'Popcorn' Japanese snowball viburnum flowering above a formal boxwood hedge with peonies and alliums nearby.

title: Viburnum
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Doublefile viburnum has graceful tiered horizontal branches and flat-topped lacecap flowers that bloom about two weeks earlier than Japanese snowball, giving the garden a strong architectural element.

title: Viburnum
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Doublefile viburnum lacecaps have large sterile florets around tiny fertile flowers. Pollinated flowers develop red oval fruits that ripen black in late summer and fall, feeding birds; green foliage turns burgundy and bronze-purple in fall.

title: Viburnum
author: Marisa Reyes
content: 'Summer Snowflake' doublefile viburnum blooms repeatedly after its first late-spring flush and may flower sporadically through summer into early fall. 'Pink Beauty' has blooms that age to delicate pink. Check invasive-plant lists before planting the species.

title: Viburnum
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Landscape photo of doublefile viburnum with tiered horizontal branching and white lacecap flowers.

title: Viburnum
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Arrowwood viburnum is a vigorous cold-hardy North American native found in woodlands, wetlands and stream banks. It tolerates rich to poor soil, moist or dry conditions and occasional flooding; straight sturdy stems were once used to craft arrows.

title: Viburnum
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Arrowwood viburnum fits native plantings, hedges and wildlife gardens. Creamy white late-spring to early-summer flowers attract bees, hoverflies, butterflies, eastern tiger swallowtails and red admirals, and the plant hosts spring azure butterflies.

title: Viburnum
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Arrowwood viburnum fruits ripen blue-black in late summer and can be used for jams, jellies or syrups. Sparkler grows 10 to 15 feet tall with ruffled foliage; Blue Muffin grows 3 to 5 feet tall and wide with vibrant blue berries.

title: Viburnum
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Photo of arrowwood viburnum in bloom with white flower clusters and dense green foliage.

title: Viburnum
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Close-up photo of Blue Muffin arrowwood viburnum blue-black summer berries.

title: Viburnum
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Smooth viburnum is native to eastern and southern North America, often in woods, swamps and bogs. Fragrant creamy white late-spring to early-summer flowers attract sweat bees, eastern tiger swallowtail butterflies and monarchs.

title: Viburnum
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Smooth viburnum stands out for berries that ripen green, pink, blue and deep purple, creating late-summer color and food for cedar waxwings, robins and bluebirds. The tart berries are edible for jams, jellies and syrups.

title: Viburnum
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Smooth viburnum prefers moist to wet soil and tolerates some drought once established, making it a good rain-garden shrub. Brandywine grows 5 to 6 feet tall with pink and blue berries ripening simultaneously.

title: Viburnum
author: Marisa Reyes
content: For more berries on viburnum cultivars, plant at least one different cultivar of the same species that blooms at the same time within 50 feet. Sterile species such as Chinese and Japanese snowball will not produce fruit even with a partner.

title: Viburnum
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Landscape photo of smooth viburnum foliage and flowers in a moist garden setting.

title: Viburnum
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Close-up photo of Brandywine smooth viburnum fall berries in pink and blue tones.

title: Viburnum
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Koreanspice viburnum has a spicy clovelike spring fragrance. Pink buds open to creamy white ball-shaped clusters in early spring, small red berries mature black in late summer and dark green leaves may turn dull or attractive red in fall.

title: Viburnum
author: Marisa Reyes
content: 'Compactum' Koreanspice viburnum grows 3 to 4 feet tall and wide, while Spice Girl grows 6 to 7 feet tall and wide with many blooms and vivid fall color. Plant near patios and walkways to appreciate fragrance.

title: Viburnum
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Landscape photo of Spice Girl Koreanspice viburnum with spring flowers near a path.

title: Viburnum
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Close-up photo of Koreanspice viburnum pink buds and white fragrant flowers.

title: Viburnum
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Wayfaring tree tolerates dry conditions and tough low-maintenance sites. It produces slightly fragrant creamy white flat-topped late-spring flowers followed by fruits that shift from green to red and glossy black.

title: Viburnum
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Wayfaring tree has rough leathery dark green ovate leaves up to 5 inches long that turn yellow, orange and bronze in fall. 'Variegatum' has green leaves splashed with gold and grows a compact 8 to 10 feet tall and wide. Check invasive-plant lists before planting the species.

title: Viburnum
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Viburnum leaf beetles skeletonize leaves, with adults active from late spring through summer and larvae feeding heavily in early summer. Inspect leaves, handpick larvae or adults, prune and destroy egg-infested branches, apply horticultural oil or insecticidal soap to larvae and encourage ladybugs and lacewings.

title: Viburnum
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Crown borers are clearwing moth larvae that tunnel into viburnum shrub bases, causing wilting, dieback near the base, sawdust-like frass and small entry holes. Prune and dispose of affected branches, and treat soil with beneficial nematodes in late summer.

title: Viburnum
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Landscape photo of variegated wayfaring tree viburnum with gold-splashed foliage.

title: Viburnum
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Close-up photo of wayfaring tree viburnum red summer berries.

author: Marisa Reyes
content: Pest photo of viburnum leaf beetle larva skeletonizing viburnum foliage.

author: Marisa Reyes
content: Pest photo of adult viburnum leaf beetle.

author: Marisa Reyes

title: Powdery Mildew
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Powdery mildew is a common fungal disease that affects more than 10,000 plant species, including annuals, perennials, ornamental grasses, fruits and vegetables. It rarely kills plants but can weaken them, reduce vigor, diminish flowering and reduce yields.

title: Powdery Mildew
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Powdery mildew fungi create white or gray coating on leaves, stems, buds, flowers and fruit. Each species targets plants in one family or genus and cannot survive without that host, so powdery mildew on linden does not infect lilacs.

title: Powdery Mildew
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Powdery mildew often appears first on the upper leaf surface and may spread across the whole plant. Leaves can distort or turn purple or red, and severe infections cause yellowing, twisting, premature leaf drop, unopened buds and stunted fruit.

title: Powdery Mildew
author: Marisa Reyes
content: In cold weather, powdery mildew survives as hardened chasmothecia on infected leaves, stems, plant debris or dormant buds. These structures protect sexual spores through freezing temperatures; in mild climates, asexual conidia may also survive in plant crevices or debris.

title: Powdery Mildew
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Disease photo of powdery mildew coating garden phlox foliage.

title: Powdery Mildew
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Close-up photo of chasmothecia on the underside of an infected leaf.

title: Powdery Mildew
author: Marisa Reyes
content: When temperatures rise above 50 degrees F and humidity reaches 85 percent or higher, chasmothecia release ascospores that land on susceptible hosts, germinate and form powdery hyphal colonies on leaf surfaces.

title: Powdery Mildew
author: Marisa Reyes
content: In summer, powdery mildew colonies release conidia from conidiophores. Under ideal conditions of 70 to 80 degrees F, nighttime humidity above 85 percent and daytime humidity below 50 percent, conidia can mature in 48 hours and spread infection rapidly.

title: Powdery Mildew
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Manage powdery mildew by replacing chronically infected plants with resistant varieties or nonsusceptible alternatives, especially with garden phlox or bee balm.

title: Powdery Mildew
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Remove fallen leaves and diseased plant debris in the trash rather than compost so powdery mildew spores and chasmothecia do not overwinter and reinfect plants.

title: Powdery Mildew
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Improve airflow to manage powdery mildew by thinning dense foliage, spacing plants properly and pruning crowded growth, especially in shady or humid plantings.

title: Powdery Mildew
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Fungicides can prevent new powdery mildew infections but cannot cure already infected leaves. Apply before symptoms appear and cover all plant surfaces, especially undersides; natural options include sulfur, potassium bicarbonate and horticultural oils.

title: The Big Haul
author: Jennifer Howell
content: A wheelbarrow or cart makes gardening easier when moving bags of soil, mulch, debris and heavy garden materials. The best choice depends on load type, terrain, storage space and whether you need to push, pull or dump.

title: The Big Haul
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Air-filled wheels are easier to push and pull and navigate rough terrain, but they can go flat. Solid rubber tires do not deflate, but they travel bumpier over rough or soft ground.

title: The Big Haul
author: Jennifer Howell
content: A wheelbarrow uses two lever handles plus a pivoting wheel and axle so one person can lift, move and dump heavier loads. It is pushed rather than pulled, dumps in several directions and maneuvers well in tight spaces and slopes.

title: The Big Haul
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Wheelbarrows excel at moving loose materials such as mulch, soil, debris and rock. Sloped sides make bags easy to load and unload; collapsible canvas models suit light jobs, metal models move rock and concrete, and resin models weigh less for most garden jobs.

title: The Big Haul
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Product photo of a red wheelbarrow with a tray attachment for carrying garden tools.

title: The Big Haul
author: Jennifer Howell
content: A garden cart is built like a wagon with straight sides, a flat bottom and four big tires, making it easy to pull through rough backyards. It needs more turning space and can roll away on slopes.

title: The Big Haul
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Garden carts are best for moving pots and trays of plants that need to stay upright, and they can also work as mobile potting benches or work stations. Useful features include dump boxes, metal mesh sides, removable sides and flatbed conversion.

title: The Big Haul
author: Jennifer Howell
content: A two-wheeled dump cart adds stability to the wheelbarrow shape so loads are easier to balance, though it only dumps forward and needs room for both wheels along paths or between plants.

title: The Big Haul
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Two-wheeled dump carts are good for weeds, leaves, branches and garden debris that can be tipped into a compost pile. Variations include collapsible or removable sides, dolly conversion arms, battery-assisted self-propelled movement and garden-tractor hitches.

title: The Big Haul
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Kids' toys can be upcycled for hauling garden materials: a baby pool can slide loose mulch, soil and debris across the yard, a saucer sled may already have a rope handle, and a little red wagon can move tools, plants, pots and bagged soil.

title: The Big Haul
author: Jennifer Howell
content: A convertible dolly can move bags of potting mix, fertilizer, potted trees, transplant boxes and loose mulch by switching between upright platform, flatbed and wheelbarrow-style positions.

title: The Big Haul
author: Jennifer Howell
content: A woven poly or canvas tarp can haul large loads of garden debris to the compost pile. Poly tarps slide well over grass or pavement, and tarp handles or rope loops in grommets make pulling easier.

title: The Big Haul
author: Jennifer Howell
content: A small-barreled two-wheeled cart is lightweight, easy to maneuver in tight spaces and useful for small jobs such as moving a bag of potting mix, a potted shrub or a coiled garden hose.

title: The Big Haul
author: Jennifer Howell
content: For deadheading and trimming, a 5-gallon bucket, garden trug or collapsible nylon garden bag can hold clippings while staying small enough to set between plants. Collapsible bags store flat and can ride in the car for garden-center trips.

title: The Big Haul
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Harvest aprons and forage bags leave both hands free for picking fruit, vegetables or flowers. A garden hod is a shallow handled basket that can carry tools, produce or long-stemmed flowers, and mesh versions make rinsing harvests easy.

title: The Big Haul
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Plant caddies roll heavy containers around patios or into winter storage. For frequently moving heavy pots across the yard, a two-wheeled dolly or a container-specific hand truck with a larger curved platform is easier.

title: Drought-Tolerant Beauty
content: Prairie grasses, native perennials and other drought-tolerant plants that tolerate hot, dry summers can fill resilient borders in tough sites.

title: Drought-Tolerant Beauty
content: Full-page garden photo of a drought-tolerant border filled with prairie grasses, shrubs and native perennials.

title: Drought-Tolerant Beauty
content: Opening photo of a drought-tolerant California garden with a path, grasses and layered shrubs.

title: Drought-Tolerant Beauty
content: Garden designer Rebecca Sweet started her Granite Bay, California, garden from scratch on a 1-acre property, using the space to test resilient plants and design combinations in her zone 9 garden.

title: Drought-Tolerant Beauty
content: Rebecca began with the large berm next to the driveway because it was well defined and frequently viewed. The 6-foot-tall southwest-facing berm is in full sun with reflected heat, months without rain and summer temperatures that regularly reach 110 degrees F.

title: Drought-Tolerant Beauty
content: 'Long John' grevillea and 'Wynyabbie Highlight' westringia provide screening, summer flowers and foliage on the hot berm, while low-growing 'Mt. Tamboritha' grevillea softens the curb line.

title: Drought-Tolerant Beauty
content: Rebecca found that 'Aphrodite' sweetshrub and oakleaf hydrangea tolerated drought better than expected. An oakleaf hydrangea even thrived for months before she realized its drip irrigation had not been connected.

title: Drought-Tolerant Beauty
content: Illustrated site plan showing the house, driveway, berm, rain garden, backyard turnaround and pool on a sloped 1-acre property.

title: Drought-Tolerant Beauty
content: On an established berm, extensive plant roots and carefully placed stones help prevent erosion, while the stones add color, shape and texture to the border.

title: Drought-Tolerant Beauty
content: A driveway border can greet visitors with spring bulbs followed by 'Long John' grevillea, summer Stoke's aster and tall sedum, year-round westringia bloom and fragrant variegated 'Meerlo' lavender foliage.

title: Drought-Tolerant Beauty
content: Driveway berm photo with 'Long John' grevillea, 'Wynyabbie Highlight' westringia, 'Meerlo' lavender, Stoke's aster and tall sedum.

title: Drought-Tolerant Beauty
content: When mature oak trees are lost, Rebecca uses Japanese maples to fill empty spots because they grow in full sun to part shade and many have beautiful fall color. For screening, she chooses evergreens such as knife-leaf acacia and horned spurge.

title: Drought-Tolerant Beauty
content: A slightly wetter strip at the front of Rebecca's sloped yard supports plants that tolerate drought but need more moisture than plants near the house, including Little Lime panicle hydrangea, Arkansas amsonia and New Zealand sedge.

title: Drought-Tolerant Beauty
content: To keep many experimental plantings cohesive, Rebecca repeats yellow and cream flowers and foliage through the borders. A shared color palette can unify different plant species, while repeating a favorite plant adds even more continuity.

title: Drought-Tolerant Beauty
content: Front-yard photo of Little Lime panicle hydrangea, Arkansas amsonia and New Zealand sedge in a lower-moisture strip.

title: Drought-Tolerant Beauty
content: Blanket flower, Gaillardia x grandiflora, has yellow and red daisylike summer blooms, attracts butterflies and grows 1 to 3 feet tall and 1 to 2 feet wide in USDA zones 3 to 10.

title: Drought-Tolerant Beauty
content: Drumstick flower, Craspedia globosa, has floating yellow globe-shaped blooms from summer to frost, grows 24 to 30 inches tall and 12 to 24 inches wide and is cold hardy in USDA zones 7 to 10.

title: Drought-Tolerant Beauty
content: Jerusalem sage, Phlomis fruticosa, has bright yellow blooms at each leaf joint from late spring to summer and soft felty foliage; it grows 2 to 6 feet tall and 2 to 5 feet wide in USDA zones 7 to 10.

title: Drought-Tolerant Beauty
content: 'Peaches and Cream' grevillea has spidery pale yellow to peachy pink blooms off and on all year, is a hummingbird favorite and grows 6 to 8 feet tall and 8 to 12 feet wide in USDA zones 9 to 11.

title: Drought-Tolerant Beauty
content: 'Wynyabbie Highlight' westringia has small lavender flowers all year and variegated green-and-cream evergreen foliage that complements canary-yellow flowers; it grows 3 to 4 feet tall and wide in USDA zones 9 to 10.

title: Drought-Tolerant Beauty
content: Garden photo showing yellow flowers and foliage repeated through a drought-tolerant border.

title: Drought-Tolerant Beauty
content: Large garden photo of a layered waterwise front-yard planting with shrubs, grasses and trees.

title: Drought-Tolerant Beauty
content: The driveway turnaround has become a favorite sitting spot because layers of trees, shrubs and perennials dampen street sound, provide privacy and glow with Japanese maple color in fall.

title: Drought-Tolerant Beauty
content: Rebecca expanded a low spot in a border into a rain garden that catches water from the driveway during winter downpours so runoff does not flood the neighbor's yard or rush into the street.

title: Drought-Tolerant Beauty
content: Driveway turnaround photo with multiseason view of trees, shrubs and perennials around a rain-garden border.

title: Drought-Tolerant Beauty
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: In the backyard, Rebecca and Tom removed thousands of cobblestone pavers by hand, hauling what Tom estimated as 5 to 6 tons in 5-gallon buckets before replacing them with smoother mortared stone and steps.

title: Drought-Tolerant Beauty
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Large boulders in the patio area looked oversized until Rebecca softened them with plantings. Crimson Sunset maple, Lime Tight mat rush and 'Silver Mound' artemisia stair-step from the stones to the patio and help screen the pool pump house.

title: Drought-Tolerant Beauty
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Around an old oak tree near the house, Rebecca replaced irrigated lawn with dry-loving succulents because turf irrigation can harm oak trees.

title: Drought-Tolerant Beauty
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Large backyard containers filled with drought-tolerant bulbs, perennials and small shrubs are connected to drip irrigation, while smaller pots of succulents and cacti stay near the house for hand watering and afternoon shade.

title: Drought-Tolerant Beauty
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Backyard makeover photo showing a shed, stone path and drought-tolerant plantings around a patio area.

title: Drought-Tolerant Beauty
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Water succulents and cacti about every 10 days even in summer; too much water causes rot.

title: Drought-Tolerant Beauty
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Feed container succulents every six weeks with all-purpose water-soluble plant food at half strength.

title: Drought-Tolerant Beauty
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Use a fast-draining potting mix labeled for cactus and repot every few years to refresh the mix.

title: Drought-Tolerant Beauty
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: If succulents get leggy, pinch stems back by 1/4 to 2/3 depending on the plant, then let cut pieces harden for a few days before planting them.

title: Drought-Tolerant Beauty
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Clean cacti with long tweezers, wear thick leather gloves and wrap a narrow piece of cardboard around prickly plants when repotting.

title: Create a Backyard Rain Garden
content: A rain garden directs excess water into a designed planting that can help keep basements dry and improve local water quality by slowing runoff and filtering impurities through plant roots.

title: Create a Backyard Rain Garden
content: A dry creek bed can direct downspout water into a wide basin that temporarily captures runoff, preventing water from rushing to storm drains with contaminants.

title: Create a Backyard Rain Garden
content: The sample rain garden is a 9-by-12-foot bed about 10 feet from the foundation and 5 feet from the property line, designed to harvest roof runoff from one downspout.

title: Create a Backyard Rain Garden
content: A dry creek bed can be a shallow trench lined with pond liner and river rock, or it can be replaced by a long downspout buried several inches beneath the soil and hidden from view.

title: Create a Backyard Rain Garden
author: Chloe Deike
content: Illustration of a backyard rain garden catching roof runoff through a dry creek bed from a downspout.

title: Create a Backyard Rain Garden
content: Mix plants with shallow roots, such as sedges, and plants with wide deep roots, such as Virginia sweetspire, to create a dense root layer that improves drainage and filters impurities.

title: Create a Backyard Rain Garden
content: An 8-inch-deep oval depression can look obvious in the middle of a bed, so grow taller plants in the basin center to create a mounded shape that blends into the rest of the border.

title: Create a Backyard Rain Garden
content: Rain-garden plants must handle both high moisture and dry spells. Water regularly during the first year so plants develop the strong root systems they need.

title: Create a Backyard Rain Garden
author: Chloe Deike
content: Detail illustration of a rain-garden basin with mixed root depths and taller center plantings.

title: Create a Backyard Rain Garden
author: Chloe Deike
content: Before digging a rain garden, learn the soil type and drainage rate. Loamy, humus-rich soil absorbs water well, while dense clay can prevent quick drainage.

title: Create a Backyard Rain Garden
author: Chloe Deike
content: To percolation-test a rain-garden site, dig a 6-inch-wide and 6-inch-deep hole, saturate the soil, fill the hole with water and check it after 24 hours. If water remains, the site may not drain fast enough because standing water should not linger longer than 24 hours.

title: Create a Backyard Rain Garden
author: Chloe Deike
content: The rain-garden basin should slope steeply at the edges and remain flat in the center to maximize water-absorbing surface area. Plant perennials and shrubs upright and perpendicular to the soil line.

title: Create a Backyard Rain Garden
author: Chloe Deike
content: Use slender-leaved or draping plants such as sedge and white bouquet tansy along basin edges to blur harsh lines. Mulch to reduce weeding, avoid chemical fertilizers and trim dry perennial foliage in late fall or early spring if a tidy look is preferred.

title: Create a Backyard Rain Garden
author: Chloe Deike
content: Illustrated rain-garden planting plan showing a 6- to 8-inch-deep basin and plant placement.

title: Create a Backyard Rain Garden
author: Chloe Deike
content: Palm sedge, Carex muskingumensis, has slender draping leaves, grows in full sun to part shade, reaches 2 to 3 feet tall and wide, is cold hardy in USDA zones 4 to 9 and is used here at 38 plants.

title: Create a Backyard Rain Garden
author: Chloe Deike
content: Wild bergamot, Monarda fistulosa, has light lavender-pink midsummer flowers, grows in full sun to part shade, reaches 2 to 5 feet tall and 2 to 3 feet wide, is cold hardy in USDA zones 3 to 8 and is used here at 14 plants.

title: Create a Backyard Rain Garden
author: Chloe Deike
content: White bouquet tansy, Tanacetum niveum, has white daisylike flowers from early summer through fall, grows in full sun to part shade, reaches 18 to 30 inches tall and 18 to 24 inches wide, is cold hardy in USDA zones 4 to 10 and is used here at 5 plants.

title: Create a Backyard Rain Garden
author: Chloe Deike
content: Red chokeberry, Aronia arbutifolia 'Brilliantissima', has small white late-spring flowers, red late-summer berries and orange-red fall foliage, grows in full sun to part shade, reaches 6 to 8 feet tall and 3 to 4 feet wide, is cold hardy in USDA zones 4 to 9 and is used here at 2 shrubs.

title: Create a Backyard Rain Garden
author: Chloe Deike
content: Virginia sweetspire, Itea virginica Fizzy Mizzy, has fragrant white bloom spikes in early summer, grows in full sun to full shade, reaches 2 to 3 feet tall and wide, is cold hardy in USDA zones 5 to 9 and is used here at 5 shrubs.

title: Create a Backyard Rain Garden
author: Chloe Deike
content: False indigo, Baptisia australis, has purple two-lipped flower spikes in early summer and black seedpods later, grows in full sun to part shade, reaches 3 to 4 feet tall and wide, is cold hardy in USDA zones 3 to 9 and is used here at 2 plants.

title: Create a Backyard Rain Garden
author: Chloe Deike
content: Pale purple coneflower, Echinacea pallida, has drooping pale purple petals from mid- to late summer, grows in full sun to part shade, reaches 24 to 36 inches tall and 12 to 18 inches wide, is cold hardy in USDA zones 3 to 10 and is used here at 7 plants.

title: Create a Backyard Rain Garden
author: Chloe Deike
content: Switchgrass, Panicum virgatum 'Niagara Falls', has blue-green foliage and light yellow blooms from late summer to fall, grows in full sun, reaches 3 to 4 feet tall and wide, is cold hardy in USDA zones 4 to 9 and is used here at 5 plants.

title: Create a Backyard Rain Garden
author: Chloe Deike
content: Cardinal flower, Lobelia cardinalis, has vivid red late-summer flower racemes, grows in full sun to part shade, reaches 2 to 4 feet tall and 1 to 2 feet wide, is cold hardy in USDA zones 3 to 9 and is used here at 5 plants.

title: Create a Backyard Rain Garden
author: Chloe Deike
content: Blue flag iris, Iris versicolor 'Purple Flame', has light purple early-summer flowers and deep indigo emerging foliage, grows in full sun to part shade, reaches 24 to 36 inches tall and 18 to 24 inches wide, is cold hardy in USDA zones 3 to 9 and is used here at 10 plants.

title: 8 Solutions for Spring Garden Problems
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Spring garden problems are easier to manage when predicted early. Preventive steps can save time, labor and frustration later in the season.

title: 8 Solutions for Spring Garden Problems
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Wet spring soil can compact if you step into perennial beds or till vegetable beds too soon. Squeeze a handful of soil into a ball and toss it gently; if it crumbles, it is dry enough to work, and if you must enter wet beds, lay down a board to spread your weight.

title: 8 Solutions for Spring Garden Problems
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Seeds planted outdoors in soil that is too cold may fail to germinate or rot. Use a soil thermometer 1 to 3 inches deep for three mornings to average the temperature; cold-tolerant crops can go in at 45 degrees F, while corn and beans need at least 65 degrees F.

title: 8 Solutions for Spring Garden Problems
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Photo of a gardener testing wet spring soil by squeezing it into a ball.

title: 8 Solutions for Spring Garden Problems
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Photo of a soil thermometer used to check spring soil temperature before sowing seeds.

title: 8 Solutions for Spring Garden Problems
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Tangled hoses, drippy connectors and clogged emitters waste spring setup time. Label hose ends, irrigation lines, couplers and emitters with tags or tape and permanent marker, test the system before it is needed and keep spare repair parts on hand.

title: 8 Solutions for Spring Garden Problems
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Twisted carrots, small onions and tiny radishes often result from overcrowded seedlings. Thin plants when they have one or two sets of leaves to the spacing listed on seed packets, or use biodegradable seed tapes; containers and raised beds need 12 to 15 inches of soil for most vegetables.

title: 8 Solutions for Spring Garden Problems
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Sharp digging and cutting tools make spring chores less painful because sharp tools require less effort and cause fewer sore joints and muscles.

title: 8 Solutions for Spring Garden Problems
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Photo of labeled irrigation lines and connectors for spring setup.

title: 8 Solutions for Spring Garden Problems
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Photo of radishes or root crops that need thinning to prevent crowding.

title: 8 Solutions for Spring Garden Problems
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Daffodils, hyacinths and other spring bulbs may produce fewer and smaller flowers when crowded. Photograph or tag their locations for fall division, or dig and transplant in late spring as foliage collapses and yellows or browns.

title: 8 Solutions for Spring Garden Problems
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Woody herbs such as rosemary, sage and thyme become lanky if not pruned. Harvest regularly and cut back by one-third in early spring as new leaves emerge, but avoid cutting into old woody stems because they will not sprout new leaves there.

title: 8 Solutions for Spring Garden Problems
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Protect fresh spring growth and new transplants from rabbits and deer with chicken wire, wicker, metal fencing or row cover fabric. Use barriers sized for mature plants if browsing is persistent, and apply repellents early and after rain.

author: Jennifer Howell
content: Photo of a bulb marker or spring bulb foliage used to locate bulbs before division.

title: 8 Solutions for Spring Garden Problems
author: Jennifer Howell

title: 8 Solutions for Spring Garden Problems
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Ground covers can look stringy, tangled and debris-filled in spring. Mow or shear plants such as mondo grass, periwinkle and plumbago close to ground level before bloom, then rake clippings to compost or let small clippings self-compost.

title: 8 Solutions for Spring Garden Problems
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Do not fertilize every spring out of habit. A soil test can show which nutrients the garden actually needs, if any.

title: Q&A
content: Hilum is the spot on a seed where it was attached to the parent plant, similar to a belly button. It is hard to see on tiny seeds but easy to find on large seeds such as beans, and it is where water is first absorbed to stimulate germination.

title: Q&A
content: Active robin nests should not be moved because the federal Migratory Bird Treaty Act of 1918 protects active nests of native North American species, including robins. After fledglings leave, remove the nest and block the spot with screen or wood.

title: Q&A
content: Invasive introduced birds such as house sparrows and European starlings are not protected the same way as native robins, so their nests can be moved at any time.

title: Q&A
content: A weeping pussy willow, Salix caprea, is grafted and usually will not grow much taller than its trunk height. The top graft produces horizontal branches that drape to the ground, so prune occasionally for shape.

title: Q&A
content: Prune weeping pussy willow in spring as new growth starts and the form is visible. Remove branches sprouting below the graft, suckers at ground level, and some main branches back to the trunk if the head becomes too dense.

title: Q&A
content: Rooting hormones contain auxins such as indole-3-butyric acid, or IBA, that stimulate root development. Powder, liquid and gel forms may also include synthetic compounds such as naphthalene acetic acid to reduce rotting.

title: Q&A
content: Rooting hormones speed root formation on cuttings, but they are not useful when rooting cuttings in water because the hormones wash off.

title: Q&A
content: Lilac buds that fail to open and dieback can be caused by root rot in heavy oxygen-poor soil, verticillium wilt or lilac borers. Improve soil oxygen for root rot, prune and sterilize between cuts for verticillium, and cut out borer-infested branches showing round holes, sap or sawdust.

title: Weed Watch: Bedstraw
content: Bedstraw, Galium aparine, is a gangly annual with square stems and leaves covered in tiny hooklike hairs. Its weak stems wind through neighboring plants, and six to eight narrow pointed leaves form whorls around each stem.

title: Weed Watch: Bedstraw
content: Bedstraw may sprout in fall or early spring depending on location. Tiny pale green or white flowers form at stem tips, then produce hook-covered round seeds; one plant can produce more than 400 seeds that hitchhike on clothing, fur and animals.

title: Weed Watch: Bedstraw
content: Bedstraw is native to much of the Northern Hemisphere, including all of the United States. It prefers part to full shade but tolerates full sun with enough moisture and is often found in cultivated gardens rather than lawns.

title: Weed Watch: Bedstraw
content: To remove bedstraw, hoe young plants instead of pulling because stems break away from the root. Foliar herbicides are not recommended where bedstraw is woven into other plants, but preemergent herbicides can reduce germination in some cases.

title: A Dew-Dappled Delight
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Lady's mantle, Alchemilla mollis, is a perennial with soft scalloped light-green leaves that hold beads of dew and delicate star-shaped chartreuse flower clusters in late spring to early summer.

title: A Dew-Dappled Delight
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Lady's mantle grows in full sun to part shade and moist well-drained soil, reaches 10 to 18 inches tall and 18 to 30 inches wide, has no serious pests and is cold hardy in USDA zones 4 to 8.

title: A Dew-Dappled Delight
author: Marisa Reyes
content: In warmer regions, lady's mantle grows best with afternoon shade so leaves and flowers do not scorch in intense sun. It softens path edges, works as a ground cover, frames taller perennials and fits formal borders or cottage gardens.

title: A Dew-Dappled Delight
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Lady's mantle contrasts with finer foliage and its chartreuse flowers blend with many color palettes. The blooms can be used in fresh or dried arrangements.

title: A Dew-Dappled Delight
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Maintain lady's mantle by removing spent flowers to prevent self-seeding and encourage a light late-summer rebloom. Water during dry spells for lush foliage and divide every few years to refresh vigor and prevent overcrowding.

title: A Dew-Dappled Delight
author: Marisa Reyes
content: A fragrant summer border can pair lady's mantle with English shrub rose 'The Ancient Mariner' and salvia 'Violet Riot' so violet-blue spires contrast with chartreuse flower clouds and deep-pink fragrant rose blooms.

title: A Dew-Dappled Delight
author: Marisa Reyes
content: English shrub rose Rosa 'The Ancient Mariner' has fragrant pink blooms with lighter edges and golden-yellow stamens in early to late summer, grows in full sun, reaches 4 feet tall and wide and is cold hardy in USDA zones 4 to 11.

title: A Dew-Dappled Delight
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Salvia nemorosa 'Violet Riot' has violet-blue flowers with deep purple calyxes from late spring into early summer, grows in full sun, reaches 22 to 24 inches tall and 20 to 24 inches wide and is cold hardy in USDA zones 3 to 8.

title: The Wild Side: Common Green Lacewing
content: Common green lacewings, Chrysoperla spp., have slender pale green bodies, long antennae and transparent wings with a lacy network of veins. Their larvae, called aphid lions, are brown or gray hunters with curved mouth pincers.

title: The Wild Side: Common Green Lacewing
content: Common green lacewings are found across North America in gardens, meadows and woodlands from spring through fall. Adults rest in shade during the day and become active in the evening.

title: The Wild Side: Common Green Lacewing
content: Green lacewing females lay oval eggs on slender stalks attached to leaves, and the larvae grow quickly before spinning a silken cocoon. Several generations can be produced in a growing season.

title: The Wild Side: Common Green Lacewing
content: Adult lacewings feed on nectar, pollen and honeydew; attract them with nectar-rich blooms such as sweet alyssum and goldenrod. The red-lipped green lacewing, Chrysoperla rufilabris, is sold for biological pest control.

title: Fast Garden Facts: Plan a Garden with Nonstop Color
content: For a flowery garden from early summer to late fall, combine perennials with different bloom times. Choose plants from each part of the bloom-season chart to keep color moving through the border.

title: Fast Garden Facts: Plan a Garden with Nonstop Color
content: Early-summer perennial choices in the nonstop-color chart include peony, Paeonia hybrids, zones 3 to 8; Siberian iris, Iris sibirica, zones 3 to 9; cheddar pink, Dianthus gratianopolitanus, zones 4 to 8; penstemon, Penstemon digitalis, zones 3 to 8; astrantia, Astrantia major, zones 4 to 7; and catmint, Nepeta x faassenii, zones 3 to 8.

title: Fast Garden Facts: Plan a Garden with Nonstop Color
content: Midsummer perennial choices in the nonstop-color chart include yarrow, Achillea millefolium, zones 3 to 10; speedwell, Veronica spicata, zones 3 to 8; daylily, Hemerocallis spp. and hybrids, zones 3 to 11; coneflower, Echinacea spp. and hybrids, zones 3 to 9; Joe Pye weed, Eutrochium spp. and hybrids, zones 4 to 8; black-eyed Susan, Rudbeckia fulgida, zones 3 to 9; and garden phlox, Phlox paniculata, zones 4 to 8.

title: Fast Garden Facts: Plan a Garden with Nonstop Color
content: Late-summer and fall perennial choices in the nonstop-color chart include turtlehead, Chelone lyonii, zones 3 to 9; tall sedum, Hylotelephium hybrids, zones 3 to 10; New England aster, Symphyotrichum novae-angliae, zones 3 to 8; garden mums, Chrysanthemum hybrids, zones 4 to 9; and rough-stemmed goldenrod, Solidago rugosa, zones 4 to 9.

title: Fast Garden Facts: Plan a Garden with Nonstop Color
content: Siberian iris has an upright habit that adds height and contrast to borders; fragrant cheddar pink makes a good cut flower; and catmint can be sheared by a third after its first flush for reliable rebloom.

title: Fast Garden Facts: Plan a Garden with Nonstop Color
content: Coneflower blooms for weeks and its seedheads look good too. Tall sedum blooms dry in place and persist through winter, and garden mums are more likely to return every year if planted in spring.

title: No-Fail Combos: Add Energy to Your Summer Garden
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Feeling unmotivated in summer's heat? A vivid, dynamic garden can recharge the mood: boisterous vibrant hues add stimulation, vertical plant habits uplift, and bold defined blooms command attention in high-visibility places such as entries.

title: No-Fail Combos: Add Energy to Your Summer Garden
author: Jennifer Howell
content: In the Elevate the Mood design, spiky ligularia and astilbe flowers pull the eye into and upward through the garden, while vertical lines contrast with large hosta leaves and mounded sedum.

title: No-Fail Combos: Add Energy to Your Summer Garden
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Deadhead ligularia when blooms are spent. Astilbe flowers can fade to brown and stay on the plant as a warm complement to sedum later in summer and fall, and mulch helps keep ligularia and astilbe moist so foliage does not crisp.

title: No-Fail Combos: Add Energy to Your Summer Garden
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Ligularia 'Bottle Rocket' is a perennial with yellow flower spikes in midsummer on mounded foliage; grow it in part to full shade, 28 to 34 inches tall and 24 to 30 inches wide, in USDA zones 4 to 9.

title: No-Fail Combos: Add Energy to Your Summer Garden
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Garden phlox, Phlox paniculata, has lavender to purple flower clusters from early to late summer; grow it in full sun to part shade, 12 to 48 inches tall and 12 to 36 inches wide, in USDA zones 3 to 9.

title: No-Fail Combos: Add Energy to Your Summer Garden
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Tall sedum 'Autumn Joy' has rose-pink late-summer flower clusters that age red-brown in fall above succulent foliage; grow it in full sun, 18 to 24 inches tall and wide, in USDA zones 3 to 9.

title: No-Fail Combos: Add Energy to Your Summer Garden
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Hosta hybrids have white, purple or lavender flowers in midsummer; grow them in part sun to full shade, 4 to 72 inches tall and 6 to 72 inches wide, in USDA zones 3 to 9.

title: No-Fail Combos: Add Energy to Your Summer Garden
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Astilbe x arendsii 'Amethyst' has lavender flower spires in early to midsummer above fernlike foliage; grow it in part to full shade, 12 to 24 inches tall, up to 36 inches in bloom and 18 to 24 inches wide, in USDA zones 4 to 8.

title: No-Fail Combos: Add Energy to Your Summer Garden
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Unify a planting by repeating a color, such as the lavender of this astilbe and garden phlox.

title: No-Fail Combos: Add Energy to Your Summer Garden
author: Jennifer Howell
content: In the Go Big and Bold design, large flowers command attention even at a distance. Panicle hydrangea flowers start white, age deep red-pink, dry and persist into winter; remove them in early spring with light pruning.

title: No-Fail Combos: Add Energy to Your Summer Garden
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Hardy hibiscus flowers last only a day, so snap withered blooms off to keep foliage clean. Leave hollow stems standing for winter insect nesting, and leave false sunflower seedheads for birds.

title: No-Fail Combos: Add Energy to Your Summer Garden
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Fire Light panicle hydrangea, Hydrangea paniculata, is a shrub with white conical flower clusters that age pomegranate from summer to fall; grow it in full sun to part shade, 6 to 8 feet tall and wide, in USDA zones 3 to 9.

title: No-Fail Combos: Add Energy to Your Summer Garden
author: Jennifer Howell
content: 'Midnight Marvel' hardy hibiscus has scarlet-red 9-inch blooms from midsummer to fall on wine-purple foliage; grow it in full sun, 3 to 4 feet tall and wide, in USDA zones 4 to 9.

title: No-Fail Combos: Add Energy to Your Summer Garden
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Tuscan Gold false sunflower, Heliopsis helianthoides, has bright yellow daisylike flowers from summer to fall on a coarse mound; grow it in full sun to part shade, 24 to 32 inches tall and 20 to 24 inches wide, in USDA zones 4 to 9.

title: No-Fail Combos: Add Energy to Your Summer Garden
author: Jennifer Howell
content: In the Warm Welcome design, red and orange tuberous begonias and coleus energize shade, blue hosta gives the eye a resting point, and chartreuse creeping Jenny plus ostrich fern weave continuity through the planting.

title: No-Fail Combos: Add Energy to Your Summer Garden
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Cut hosta and ostrich fern to the ground in early spring, and plant tender coleus and begonias after all danger of frost has passed. Creeping Jenny can be aggressive, so annual sweet potato vine can provide a similar chartreuse effect with less spread.

title: No-Fail Combos: Add Energy to Your Summer Garden
author: Jennifer Howell
content: 'Halcyon' hosta has lavender late-summer spikes above blue-green leaves; grow it in part to full shade, 18 to 24 inches tall, 28 inches in bloom and 30 to 36 inches wide, in USDA zones 3 to 9.

title: No-Fail Combos: Add Energy to Your Summer Garden
author: Jennifer Howell
content: 'Goldilocks' creeping Jenny has inconspicuous yellow summer flowers on chartreuse vining foliage; grow it in full sun to full shade, 3 to 6 inches tall and 12 to 18 inches wide, in USDA zones 3 to 9.

title: No-Fail Combos: Add Energy to Your Summer Garden
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Sedona Sunset coleus is a tender perennial with blue-purple late-summer to fall flower spikes on copper-orange foliage; grow it in full sun to part shade, 24 to 40 inches tall and 18 to 36 inches wide, in USDA zones 10 to 11.

title: No-Fail Combos: Add Energy to Your Summer Garden
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Ostrich fern, Matteuccia struthiopteris, has vase-shaped light-green fronds; grow it in part to full shade, 3 to 6 feet tall and 5 to 8 feet wide, in USDA zones 3 to 7.

title: No-Fail Combos: Add Energy to Your Summer Garden
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Nonstop tuberous begonia has red, orange or bicolor summer flowers; grow it in part to full shade, 8 to 12 inches tall and 12 to 14 inches wide, in USDA zones 9 to 10.

title: Top Picks: Dark, Dramatic Plants for a Midnight Garden
author: Marisa Reyes
content: A midnight garden, or gothic garden, embraces moody plant colors rather than bright ones. No flower is truly black, but deep blooms and foliage shift with the light, looking darker in shade and more burgundy or purple in sun.

title: Top Picks: Dark, Dramatic Plants for a Midnight Garden
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Dark plants need shadowy allies to shine. Silvery foliage such as 'Jack Frost' brunnera and lamb's ear gives sharp contrast, lush green ferns and hostas add depth, and white or pale flowers brighten the space and draw the eye.

title: Top Picks: Dark, Dramatic Plants for a Midnight Garden
author: Marisa Reyes
content: A midnight garden is about atmosphere, not only nighttime. Soft lighting along paths or beside inky foliage can highlight dark textures, while reflective gazing balls or mirrors catch ambient light.

title: Top Picks: Dark, Dramatic Plants for a Midnight Garden
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Japanese cobra lily, Arisaema sikokianum, emerges in early spring with an unusual hooded bloom above silver-splashed five-lobed leaves. The 8-inch spathe is purple, green and white striped outside and pure white inside, with a snowy spadix at the center.

title: Top Picks: Dark, Dramatic Plants for a Midnight Garden
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Japanese cobra lily thrives in moist, humusy soil near ponds, streams or shaded beds where conditions stay damp. Grow it in part to full shade, moist well-drained soil, 18 to 24 inches tall and wide, in USDA zones 5 to 8.

title: Top Picks: Dark, Dramatic Plants for a Midnight Garden
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Japanese cobra lily mimics the scent of mushrooms to lure fungus gnats into its spathe long enough for pollination. The white spadix holds the plant's true flowers, while the striped spathe acts like a protective hood.

title: Top Picks: Dark, Dramatic Plants for a Midnight Garden

title: Top Picks: Dark, Dramatic Plants for a Midnight Garden
author: Marisa Reyes
content: 'Green Wizard' coneflower, Rudbeckia occidentalis, skips bright petals and instead forms green sepals around a nearly black cone. The 6- to 9-inch cones last after the tiny yellow flowers fade and feed birds if left standing.

title: Top Picks: Dark, Dramatic Plants for a Midnight Garden
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Grow 'Green Wizard' coneflower in full sun and average well-drained soil; plants reach 36 to 60 inches tall and 18 to 24 inches wide in USDA zones 3 to 9. Deadhead for more blooms and to prevent self-seeding.

title: Top Picks: Dark, Dramatic Plants for a Midnight Garden
author: Marisa Reyes
content: 'Black Swan' poppy, Papaver somniferum, has deep burgundy, almost black, fully double 5-inch flowers with ruffled, featherlike petals. The self-seeding annual also produces interesting seedpods and tiny black seeds for baking.

title: Top Picks: Dark, Dramatic Plants for a Midnight Garden
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Direct-sow 'Black Swan' poppy four weeks before the last spring frost or in late fall. Grow it in full sun to part shade and average or moist well-drained soil; plants reach 24 to 36 inches tall and 10 to 12 inches wide.

title: Top Picks: Dark, Dramatic Plants for a Midnight Garden
author: Marisa Reyes
content: 'Nightrider' Asiatic lily, Lilium asiatica, has deep burgundy trumpet blooms that look violet-black in full sun and almost inky black in light shade. Each stem carries three to five lightly fragrant flowers that attract pollinators.

title: Top Picks: Dark, Dramatic Plants for a Midnight Garden
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Plant 'Nightrider' lily bulbs three times their height in rich, well-drained soil. Let foliage die back before cutting yellow or brown stems, and divide crowded bulbs if blooming slows. Plants reach 3 to 4 feet tall and 1 to 2 feet wide in USDA zones 3 to 8.

title: Top Picks: Dark, Dramatic Plants for a Midnight Garden
author: Marisa Reyes

title: Top Picks: Dark, Dramatic Plants for a Midnight Garden
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Black bat flower, Tacca chantrieri, has dark bracts up to a foot wide, whiskerlike filaments and maroon-black flowers set against pleated lance-shaped leaves. It brings a tropical understory look to shaded containers.

title: Top Picks: Dark, Dramatic Plants for a Midnight Garden
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Grow black bat flower as a container annual or houseplant in warm humid conditions, part to full shade and average or moist well-drained soil. It reaches 2 to 3 feet tall and 1 to 2 feet wide and is hardy only in USDA zones 10 to 11.

title: Top Picks: Dark, Dramatic Plants for a Midnight Garden
author: Marisa Reyes
content: 'Black Barlow' columbine, Aquilegia vulgaris var. stellata, has fully double, pom-pom-like near-black plum blooms on slender stems above soft green lacy foliage. It suits borders, woodland edges and cut-flower gardens.

title: Top Picks: Dark, Dramatic Plants for a Midnight Garden
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Grow 'Black Barlow' columbine in full sun to part shade and average or moist well-drained soil. It attracts hummingbirds and pollinators, self-seeds and reaches 24 to 30 inches tall and 14 to 16 inches wide in USDA zones 3 to 9.

title: Top Picks: Dark, Dramatic Plants for a Midnight Garden
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Photo of black bat flower with dark batlike bracts, maroon-black flowers and long whiskerlike filaments.

title: Top Picks: Dark, Dramatic Plants for a Midnight Garden
author: Marisa Reyes

title: Top Picks: Dark, Dramatic Plants for a Midnight Garden
author: Marisa Reyes
content: 'Black Sprite' perennial bachelor's button, Centaurea montana, has deep burgundy to nearly black feathery thistlelike blooms that attract bees and butterflies and work as cut or dried flowers.

title: Top Picks: Dark, Dramatic Plants for a Midnight Garden
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Grow 'Black Sprite' in full sun and average or moist well-drained soil, 12 to 24 inches tall and 20 to 24 inches wide, in USDA zones 3 to 9. Deadhead regularly, cut back after the first flush and watch for self-seeding.

title: Top Picks: Dark, Dramatic Plants for a Midnight Garden
author: Marisa Reyes
content: 'Black Gamecock' Louisiana iris has satiny near-black standards and falls with rusty-orange signals, and it tolerates damp borders, rain gardens, pond edges, clay soil and even standing water up to 6 inches deep.

title: Top Picks: Dark, Dramatic Plants for a Midnight Garden
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Grow 'Black Gamecock' Louisiana iris in full sun to part shade and moist to wet well-drained soil. Divide clumps every few years; plants reach 2 to 3 feet tall and wide in USDA zones 4 to 9.

title: Top Picks: Dark, Dramatic Plants for a Midnight Garden

title: Top Picks: Dark, Dramatic Plants for a Midnight Garden
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Persian lily, Fritillaria persica, sends up tall spikes of dusky plum to near-black bell-shaped flowers with silvery-green lance foliage. It fits rock, gravel and Mediterranean-style gardens with dry drainage.

title: Top Picks: Dark, Dramatic Plants for a Midnight Garden
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Plant Persian lily bulbs in early fall about 6 inches deep in full sun to part shade and average or moist well-drained soil. Avoid wet heavy soil; plants reach 12 to 36 inches tall and 12 to 18 inches wide in USDA zones 4 to 8.

title: Top Picks: Dark, Dramatic Plants for a Midnight Garden

content: Plant portrait photo of Persian lily with tall spikes of dusky plum bell-shaped flowers.

title: Top Picks: Dark, Dramatic Plants for a Midnight Garden
author: Marisa Reyes
content: 'Edge of Night' calla lily, Zantedeschia hybrid, has burgundy-black trumpet blooms with curled edges and deep green lance-shaped leaves flecked silver-white. It is also sold as 'Black Star'.

title: Top Picks: Dark, Dramatic Plants for a Midnight Garden
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Grow 'Edge of Night' calla lily in full sun to part shade and moist well-drained soil. Plant rhizomes 3 to 4 inches deep with growing tips up, remove fading stems at the base, and lift/store rhizomes in zones 7 and colder.

title: Top Picks: Dark, Dramatic Plants for a Midnight Garden
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Plant portrait photo of 'Edge of Night' calla lily with dark trumpet blooms and spotted foliage.

title: Top Picks: Dark, Dramatic Plants for a Midnight Garden
author: Marisa Reyes
content: 'Dark Side of the Moon' astilbe emerges yellow with a dark margin, deepens to chocolate brown and carries rosy-purple midsummer flower spikes. Stronger sun intensifies the foliage color.

title: Top Picks: Dark, Dramatic Plants for a Midnight Garden
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Grow 'Dark Side of the Moon' astilbe in full sun to part shade and average or moist well-drained soil. Keep moisture consistent, deadhead for tidiness or leave dried seedheads, and divide clumps every few years.

title: Torch Lily
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Torch lilies, Kniphofia spp. and hybrids, are native to South Africa and thrive in hot sunny borders. Sturdy flower stems can reach 6 feet, and hybrids range from classic red, orange and yellow bicolors to softer solids.

title: Torch Lily
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Torch lily foliage can be deciduous or evergreen, and most bloom from early to late summer. 'Coral' can bloom in late spring, while 'Yellow Cheer' and 'Alcazar' can flower from late summer into late fall until hard frost.

title: Torch Lily
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Torch lily flower racemes are dramatic, often 4 to 7 inches long, so one plant can highlight a seating area and several can lead the eye along a path. Pair torch lilies with contrasting flower shapes such as nodding Virginia sweetspire blooms.

title: Torch Lily
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Torch lily tubular flowers are nectar-rich and attract hummingbirds as well as heavier birds including orioles, grosbeaks, cedar waxwings and goldfinches. Flowers open from the bottom up and the lower blooms can stay colorful for weeks.

title: Torch Lily
