title: Torch Lily
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Torch lilies can set a bold mood through flower shape and color. Orange and yellow blooms against a cobalt-blue wall create strong complementary contrast, while a white variety such as 'Ice Queen' gives a calmer effect.

title: Torch Lily
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Torch lily sizes vary widely. Kniphofia linearifolia can send 6-foot stems above 3- to 5-foot foliage, 'Lady Luck' reaches about 5 1/2 feet in bloom, while smaller 'Mango Popsicle' and Poco Orange stay under 2 feet and rebloom from summer to frost.

title: Torch Lily
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Grow torch lily in full sun for dense foliage, strong stems and flowers. It tolerates sandy-loam soil and salt spray, but good drainage is essential because cold wet winters, dense soil and heavy mulch on the crown can cause rot.

title: Torch Lily
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Feed torch lily with slow-release fertilizer in spring or a layer of compost. Use 2 to 3 inches of mulch for moisture and temperature moderation, but keep mulch 6 to 12 inches away from the crown.

title: Torch Lily
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Torch lily is heat and drought tolerant once established, but watering during dry spells improves flowering. Deadhead after most individual flowers have fizzled by cutting the stem down toward the crown.

title: Torch Lily
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Leave torch lily foliage in place through winter to protect the crown. In spring, cut back deciduous or semi-evergreen foliage to 3 to 4 inches above the crown.

title: Torch Lily
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Divide torch lily only when you want to spread or share plants. In spring before new foliage expands, dig the dense root ball, pull or cut it apart with forks or a spade, replant divisions at the same depth and water well.

title: Torch Lily
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Torch lilies may reseed, but hybrid seedlings will not come true. Start seeds indoors 6 to 8 weeks before the last frost at 70 to 75 degrees F; germination usually takes 10 to 20 days.

title: Torch Lily
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Torch lily, Kniphofia spp. and hybrids, is a perennial with yellow, red, orange, peach, yellow-green or bicolor spikes from late spring to fall. Grow it in full sun and well-drained soil; plants range from 12 to 72 inches tall and 14 to 60 inches wide in USDA zones 5 to 9.

title: Troubleshoot Your Tomatoes
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Tomatoes are rewarding but frustrating when spots, splits, curled leaves, pests, diseases, nutrient problems or weather issues threaten the crop. Diagnosing the symptom helps gardeners respond and still get a harvest.

title: Troubleshoot Your Tomatoes
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Catfacing produces puckered, misshapen or scarred tomato fruit, often with a rough sunken blossom end. It happens when flowers fail or fuse, often after nights below 50 degrees F following transplanting, high nitrogen, aggressive pruning or thrips.

title: Troubleshoot Your Tomatoes
author: Marisa Reyes
content: To reduce catfacing, plant tomatoes after nights stay above 55 degrees F, use row covers or black plastic for warmth, remove deformed flowers or fruit early, avoid excess nitrogen and prune lightly. Heirloom tomatoes are more prone, but affected fruit is edible after trimming tough parts.

title: Troubleshoot Your Tomatoes
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Close-up tomato photo showing pest or disease damage on green fruit for the tomato troubleshooting opener.

title: Troubleshoot Your Tomatoes
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Close-up flower photo showing a tomato bloom related to fruit-set problems.

title: Troubleshoot Your Tomatoes
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Anthracnose fruit rot causes dark, sunken, watery blemishes on ripe tomatoes in warm, humid conditions. Spores spread by splashing water, ripe and overripe fruit are most vulnerable, and fruit near the ground is at highest risk.

title: Troubleshoot Your Tomatoes
author: Marisa Reyes
content: To manage anthracnose fruit rot, harvest ripe fruit promptly, avoid overhead watering, mulch to reduce splashing, remove infected fruit, clean debris, rotate crops and avoid saving seed from infected fruit.

title: Troubleshoot Your Tomatoes
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Septoria leaf spot causes tan-gray circular spots with yellow halos, starting on lower tomato leaves. Leaves yellow and drop, baring the plant and reducing production, while the fungus spreads upward in warm humid weather.

title: Troubleshoot Your Tomatoes
author: Marisa Reyes
content: To manage Septoria leaf spot, improve airflow with spacing, staking or caging, water at the base, prune lower leaves, mulch, remove infected leaves when first noticed, clean debris and rotate crops.

title: Troubleshoot Your Tomatoes
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Photo of a tomato with catfacing, showing a puckered scarred blossom end.

title: Troubleshoot Your Tomatoes
author: Marisa Reyes

title: Troubleshoot Your Tomatoes
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Blossom end rot causes a mushy, sunken, water-soaked spot on the bottom of tomato fruit that darkens and turns leathery. It is a calcium problem caused by the plant's inability to absorb calcium, often after inconsistent watering, dry periods, high nitrogen, root damage or fertilizer burn.

title: Troubleshoot Your Tomatoes
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Prevent blossom end rot by watering deeply whenever soil is dry, mulching, avoiding high-nitrogen fertilizer, planting carefully to protect roots and using soaker or drip irrigation for steady moisture.

title: Troubleshoot Your Tomatoes
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Tomato leaf curling shows up as leaves that roll, twist or crinkle, especially on lower older leaves. It is usually stress rather than disease, often caused by heat above 90 degrees F, a quick shift from spring to hot dry weather or inconsistent watering.

title: Troubleshoot Your Tomatoes
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Reduce tomato leaf curling by watering consistently, using mulch, choosing less-prone varieties such as 'Solar Flare' and 'Florida 91' and providing temporary shade when temperatures stay above 90 degrees F.

title: Troubleshoot Your Tomatoes
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Photo of blossom end rot on a tomato, with a dark sunken lesion at the fruit bottom.

title: Troubleshoot Your Tomatoes
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Photo of tomato leaves curling from heat or moisture stress.

title: Troubleshoot Your Tomatoes
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Tomato fruit cracking happens when fruit absorbs water faster than the skin can stretch, especially after rain follows a dry spell or irrigation is inconsistent. Thin-skinned and large tomatoes are more prone, and rapid temperature swings or intense sun can weaken skin.

title: Troubleshoot Your Tomatoes
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Prevent fruit cracking by giving tomatoes steady deep water, mulching, harvesting nearly ripe fruit before heavy rain and choosing crack- or split-resistant hybrids. Fruit with healed cracks and no mold can still be eaten.

title: Troubleshoot Your Tomatoes
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Tobacco hornworms are large green caterpillars with white diagonal stripes and a curved red horn. They blend into tomato plants, feed on nightshade crops at night, strip leaves and chew fruit.

title: Troubleshoot Your Tomatoes
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Control tobacco hornworms by handpicking them into soapy water, encouraging parasitic wasps and birds, or using Bt, which targets caterpillars without harming most beneficial insects.

title: Troubleshoot Your Tomatoes
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Colorado potato beetles have 3/8-inch adult bodies with black stripes on yellow-orange wing covers, and fat red-orange larvae with dark spots. They skeletonize nightshade leaves on tomatoes, eggplants, peppers and potatoes.

title: Troubleshoot Your Tomatoes
author: Marisa Reyes
content: Control Colorado potato beetles by handpicking adults and larvae into soapy water, using floating row covers to prevent egg laying and applying neem or spinosad only if damage becomes severe.

title: Finding Joy in the Garden
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Joyce and Dave Ludlow's Iowa zone 5 garden is designed for long-lasting interest and manageable maintenance, with plants chosen so the garden can remain joyful rather than overwhelming.

title: Finding Joy in the Garden
author: Jennifer Howell
content: A retaining wall around the front porch created a spacious 30-foot curving bed with curb appeal while keeping the street view open. The 12-inch ledge is wide enough for sitting and kneeling during maintenance.

title: Finding Joy in the Garden
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Joyce removed roses that drew chronic Japanese beetles and replaced them with panicle hydrangeas, birchleaf spirea and naturally globe-shaped barberry that needs only light spring trimming.

title: Finding Joy in the Garden
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Joyce uses drought-tolerant annuals such as Meteor Shower verbena, Skyscraper Pink salvia, Senorita Rosalita spider flower and Sweet Caroline Sweetheart Lime sweet potato vine for long-lasting color with less watering.

title: Finding Joy in the Garden
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Planting annuals tightly between perennials helps deter weeds and reduces mulch. Repeating favorite plants throughout the front and back garden creates continuity.

title: Finding Joy in the Garden
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Lamb's ear is one of Joyce's favorite ground covers because it fills fast, smothers weeds, needs only a spring cutback and is easy to divide and spread.

title: Finding Joy in the Garden

content: Joyce's cool palette of pink, lavender, silver, white and chartreuse blends with the neutral house color and cools the feeling of a full-sun garden.

author: Jennifer Howell
content: The backyard slope was leveled with truckloads of soil, and a landscaper designed a 13-foot circular patio and hardscaping. Joyce prefers the open circle to the firepit that was originally planned because it feels calm and centered.

author: Jennifer Howell
content: A 2-foot tumbled concrete block wall encloses the circular patio. Bobo panicle hydrangeas and 'Autumn Frost' hostas fill the 3-foot planting space between wall and patio more reliably than bigleaf hydrangeas in zone 5.

title: Finding Joy in the Garden

content: 'Helen von Stein' lamb's ear, also sold as 'Big Ears', has large silver fuzzy leaves and few flowers; grow it in full sun, 8 to 12 inches tall and 12 to 18 inches wide, in USDA zones 4 to 9.

title: Finding Joy in the Garden
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Glow Girl spirea has white spring flower clusters over chartreuse foliage; grow it in full sun to part shade, 3 to 4 feet tall and wide, in USDA zones 4 to 8.

title: Finding Joy in the Garden

title: Finding Joy in the Garden
author: Jennifer Howell

title: Finding Joy in the Garden
author: Jennifer Howell
content: 'Green Velvet' boxwood has insignificant creamy green spring flowers and evergreen foliage; grow it in full sun to part shade, 2 to 4 feet tall and wide, in USDA zones 5 to 9.

title: Finding Joy in the Garden
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Invincibelle Limetta smooth hydrangea has lime-green-white summer flowers that age darker green by fall; grow it in full sun to part shade, 3 to 4 feet tall and wide, in USDA zones 3 to 8.

title: Finding Joy in the Garden

content: 'Curly Fries' hosta has lavender midsummer spikes and narrow ripple-edged leaves; grow it in part to full shade, 6 to 10 inches tall, 16 inches in bloom and 16 to 20 inches wide, in USDA zones 3 to 9.

content: Joyce prunes 'Royal Purple' smokebush after early-summer bloom by cutting the shrub back, deadheading smoky pink blooms and removing one-third of the stems to encourage glowing red new growth.

title: Create a Tropical Look Anywhere
author: Sherri Ribbey

title: Create a Tropical Look Anywhere
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: A tropical look can be created outside the back door with dense borders full of large plants, colorful foliage and bold flowers that bring drama and an exotic flair to almost any spot.

title: Create a Tropical Look Anywhere
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: To imitate a tropical rainforest, use a few big plants with big leaves. Tasmanian tree fern has dramatic 3- to 6-foot-long leaves but is hardy only in zones 9 to 11, so cold-climate gardeners can use elephant ear, canna or banana plants as annuals or overwintered specimens.

title: Create a Tropical Look Anywhere
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Tender tropicals need plenty of water and fertilizer to reach maximum size and impact and often need greenhouse overwintering. Cold-hardy large-foliage perennials such as ornamental rhubarb, hosta and ligularia can create a similar effect.

title: Create a Tropical Look Anywhere
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Garden photo showing red Abyssinian banana and large-leaf tropical-style plants in a dense border.

title: Create a Tropical Look Anywhere
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: A tropical planting feels dense and layered, like a canopy of trees with vines and a tapestry of different plants. Tight spacing lets plants weave together, screen views and muffle sound.

title: Create a Tropical Look Anywhere
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: A bright color palette of magenta, purple and coral pink near a patio creates an energetic tropical mood, while soft yellow, white and peachy orange can make the same dense design feel more relaxing.

title: Create a Tropical Look Anywhere
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Containers can create a tropical theme where space is small or soil is difficult. Group pots of various sizes to imitate dense layered planting, and include vines or trailing plants such as tradescantia for abundance.

title: Create a Tropical Look Anywhere
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Long-blooming annuals such as New Guinea impatiens bring color in limited space, while variegated tradescantia and dracaena can do double duty as houseplants indoors over winter.

author: Sherri Ribbey
content: A water feature can echo the moist air, sudden rain and dripping leaves of a tropical rainforest. Flowing water and pond reflections bring calm, while concrete pillars and a pond surrounded by rodgersia and hostas create a jungle-ruin feeling.

title: Create a Tropical Look Anywhere
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Even without room for a large pond, a recirculating fountain around a path bend or on a tabletop can add calm and serenity to a small tropical-inspired garden.

title: Create a Tropical Look Anywhere
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Crocosmia, Crocosmia spp. and hybrids, is a bulb with bright red, orange or yellow tubular flowers from midsummer to fall; grow it in full sun to part shade, 12 to 48 inches tall and 6 to 18 inches wide, in USDA zones 5 to 9.

title: Create a Tropical Look Anywhere
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Foxtail lily, Eremurus spp. and hybrids, is a bulb with large dramatic spikes in yellow, pink, white, orange or brown from late spring to early summer; grow it in full sun to part shade, 36 to 72 inches tall and 18 to 24 inches wide, in USDA zones 5 to 9.

title: Create a Tropical Look Anywhere
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Golden bamboo, Phyllostachys aurea, has enormous light-green canes that turn bright golden yellow in sun; grow it in full sun to part shade, 10 to 30 feet tall and spreading, in USDA zones 6 to 10, with root control because it can be aggressive.

title: Create a Tropical Look Anywhere
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Hardy hibiscus, Hibiscus moscheutos, has red, pink, white, lavender or pale yellow blooms up to 12 inches across from midsummer to fall; grow it in full sun to part shade, 2 to 12 feet tall and 2 to 6 feet wide, in USDA zones 4 to 10.

title: Create a Tropical Look Anywhere
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Ligularia, Ligularia spp. and hybrids, has bold yellow or golden-orange spikes or daisylike summer blooms and jagged leaves; grow it in part to full shade, 1 to 6 feet tall and 1 to 4 feet wide, in USDA zones 3 to 9.

title: Create a Tropical Look Anywhere
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Oyama magnolia, Magnolia sieboldii, is a shrub with fragrant 4-inch white blooms and crimson stamens from spring to summer; grow it in full sun to part shade, 10 to 15 feet tall and wide, in USDA zones 6 to 8.

title: Create a Tropical Look Anywhere
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Pitcher plant, Sarracenia spp., has red, yellow or pink umbrella-like spring flowers and upright pitchers in red, yellow, purple, burgundy or green; grow it in full sun, 4 to 24 inches tall and 12 to 24 inches wide, in USDA zones 5 to 9.

title: Create a Tropical Look Anywhere

title: A Drought-Tolerant Gathering Spot
author: Chloe Deike
content: A hot, dry full-sun corner with drought-prone soil can become a pleasant place to connect and relax with thoughtful design and plucky plants rather than a sparse desertlike patch.

title: A Drought-Tolerant Gathering Spot
author: Chloe Deike
content: The drought-tolerant design uses a minimal shade structure, durable comfortable seating, cool-toned plants, long bloom and plant movement to create a calm gathering spot that works as cold as USDA zone 4.

title: A Drought-Tolerant Gathering Spot
author: Chloe Deike
content: Solar-powered cafe lights fastened to the shade structure extend the gathering spot into evening, and a hidden weathertight storage container behind a privacy panel keeps cushions dry and protected from fading when not in use.

title: A Drought-Tolerant Gathering Spot
author: Chloe Deike

title: A Drought-Tolerant Gathering Spot
author: Chloe Deike
content: Drought-tolerant does not have to mean sparse. Beds that wrap around the patio create enclosure, while low-growing snow-in-summer creeps between stepping stones so the space feels full of plants.

title: A Drought-Tolerant Gathering Spot
author: Chloe Deike
content: Plant heights stay low enough to let airflow reach the sectional, while ornamental grasses sway in wind and Cupid's dart, sea holly and tickseed bob with a breeze.

title: A Drought-Tolerant Gathering Spot

content: Full-page illustration of the drought-tolerant gathering spot showing wrapped beds, stepping stones, privacy panel and low airy plantings.

title: A Drought-Tolerant Gathering Spot
author: Chloe Deike
content: During the first year, drought-tolerant plants still need deep, occasional soakings so roots grow downward. Water early in the morning with a slow steady stream so moisture soaks in rather than evaporating or running off.

title: A Drought-Tolerant Gathering Spot
author: Chloe Deike
content: Snow-in-summer should be cut back after its first bloom to keep a tidy look and prevent aggressive reseeding, and it can be trimmed where it creeps between flagstone cracks.

title: A Drought-Tolerant Gathering Spot
author: Chloe Deike
content: Poppy mallow has a taproot that helps it withstand dry periods but makes division and transplanting difficult. It can sprawl at least 2 feet wide, reblooms off and on after early summer and can be trimmed back if it creeps out of bounds.

title: A Drought-Tolerant Gathering Spot
author: Chloe Deike
content: Fountain grass foliage turns golden in fall and can be cut back in early spring. Cupid's dart benefits from a thick layer of late-fall mulch and is short-lived, so leaving seedheads lets it reseed and replace older plants.

author: Chloe Deike
content: Rocky Mountain juniper 'Blue Arrow', Juniperus scopulorum, is an icy blue slender evergreen tree for full sun, 12 to 15 feet tall and 1 to 2 feet wide, hardy in USDA zones 4 to 9; plant 3.

title: A Drought-Tolerant Gathering Spot
author: Chloe Deike
content: Catmint 'Purrsian Blue', Nepeta x faassenii, has dense periwinkle-purple flower racemes from early summer into fall; grow it in full sun, 12 to 18 inches tall and 18 to 30 inches wide, in USDA zones 3 to 8; plant 9.

title: A Drought-Tolerant Gathering Spot
author: Chloe Deike
content: Threadleaf coreopsis Creme Caramel has buttery peachy-pink flowers from early summer to early fall; grow it in full sun to part shade, 12 to 18 inches tall and 18 to 24 inches wide, in USDA zones 5 to 9; plant 12.

title: A Drought-Tolerant Gathering Spot
author: Chloe Deike
content: Globe thistle 'Veitch's Blue', Echinops ritro, has steel-blue spiky globe flowers from midsummer to fall; grow it in full sun, 24 to 36 inches tall and 18 to 24 inches wide, in USDA zones 3 to 9; plant 3.

title: A Drought-Tolerant Gathering Spot
author: Chloe Deike
content: Snow-in-summer, Cerastium tomentosum, has white flowers in early summer and spreading silver foliage; grow it in full sun, 6 to 12 inches tall, in USDA zones 3 to 7; plant 24.

title: A Drought-Tolerant Gathering Spot
author: Chloe Deike
content: Fountain grass 'Red Head', Pennisetum alopecuroides, has smoky purple plumes up to 10 inches long from midsummer to fall; grow it in full sun to part shade, 3 to 4 feet tall and 2 to 3 feet wide, in USDA zones 5 to 9; plant 2.

title: A Drought-Tolerant Gathering Spot
author: Chloe Deike
content: Poppy mallow, Callirhoe involucrata, has cerise to purple-red flowers off and on from spring through fall; grow it in full sun to part shade, 6 to 12 inches tall and 24 to 30 inches wide, in USDA zones 4 to 9; plant 5.

title: A Drought-Tolerant Gathering Spot
author: Chloe Deike
content: Tall sedum 'Night Embers', Hylotelephium, has mauve flower clusters with burgundy stems in late summer and fall and deep purple foliage; grow it in full sun, 24 to 26 inches tall and wide, in USDA zones 3 to 9; plant 3.

title: A Drought-Tolerant Gathering Spot
author: Chloe Deike
content: Cupid's dart, Catananche caerulea, has lavender-blue daisylike flowers on long bare stems above slender basal foliage from midsummer to fall; grow it in full sun, 12 to 24 inches tall and 10 to 12 inches wide, in USDA zones 4 to 7; plant 9.

title: 5 Tips for Your Summer To-Do List
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Summer in the garden is not just about watering. Pinching, trimming, shading, delaying bolting and managing weeds can keep flowers and vegetables healthier through the season.

title: 5 Tips for Your Summer To-Do List
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Petunias grow and bloom vigorously when first planted, but summer heat can make stems stretch and flowering taper off as faded blossoms produce seed.

title: 5 Tips for Your Summer To-Do List
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Once petunias slow and get leggy, trim up to one-third of the stem length just above a leaf node. Pinching removes spent blooms, prevents seed energy loss, encourages new buds and forces side shoots for fuller plants.

title: 5 Tips for Your Summer To-Do List
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Pinching a couple of petunia branches on each plant every week keeps fresh growth and more flowers coming, and scissors or garden snips can replace finger-pinching if sticky stems are unpleasant.

title: 5 Tips for Your Summer To-Do List
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Technique photo showing fingers pinching a petunia stem just above a leaf node.

title: 5 Tips for Your Summer To-Do List
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Fall-blooming asters can get tall and flop. Trim them before midsummer by pinching just a few leaves or cutting one-third to one-half of each stem so plants become fuller, bushier and less likely to flop.

title: 5 Tips for Your Summer To-Do List
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Cut aster stems at different heights, shorter in front and gradually taller in back or in a mounded shape, so more flowers are visible when they bloom in fall.

title: 5 Tips for Your Summer To-Do List
author: Jennifer Howell
content: When temperatures stay above 90 degrees F for more than a few days, temporary shade over tomatoes and peppers can prevent wilt, scorched leaves and fruit sunscald while cooling soil and conserving moisture.

title: 5 Tips for Your Summer To-Do List
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Shade cloth, row cover, lattice, an umbrella or a patio shade sail can protect vegetables from the hottest sun. Place the cover at least 2 to 3 feet above the top leaves and position it where the whole plant is shaded at midday.

title: 5 Tips for Your Summer To-Do List
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Avoid transplanting in summer because plants struggle to establish in high temperatures and are difficult to keep hydrated; spring and fall are better transplanting seasons.

title: 5 Tips for Your Summer To-Do List
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Cool-season vegetables bolt when high temperatures, long summer days and dry conditions push plants into flowering and seed production. Spinach and lettuce become bitter, while kohlrabi and radishes can develop pithy woody roots.

title: 5 Tips for Your Summer To-Do List
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Delay bolting by choosing bolt-resistant varieties, watering regularly, mulching to keep roots cool and moist, shading plants as temperatures rise and pinching off forming flowers to gain a couple more weeks of harvest.

title: 5 Tips for Your Summer To-Do List
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Peas, beans and zucchini do not bolt, but they can stop producing if fruit stays on the plant and ripens, so keep harvesting.

title: 5 Tips for Your Summer To-Do List
author: Jennifer Howell

title: 5 Tips for Your Summer To-Do List
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Annual weeds such as crabgrass, lambsquarters and ragweed compete for water and nutrients. Removing them before they set seed can reduce future weed problems.

title: 5 Tips for Your Summer To-Do List
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Small weeds are easiest to pull when soil is moist, but mature weeds in dry hard soil can be cut at or just below ground level to avoid disturbing soil, losing moisture and bringing buried weed seeds to the surface.

title: 5 Tips for Your Summer To-Do List
author: Jennifer Howell
content: If cut annual weeds are not diseased and have no seedheads, the chop-and-drop method leaves the tops as mulch to cool soil, conserve moisture and compost in place.

title: 5 Tips for Your Summer To-Do List
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Before leaving container plants for a week or two, water pots thoroughly, move them to a shady wind-protected spot, cover potting mix with 1 to 2 inches of mulch, use an inverted water bottle, set up timed drip irrigation or fill self-watering reservoirs.

title: 5 Tips for Your Summer To-Do List
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Mowing the lawn higher shades the soil, inhibits weeds and helps conserve moisture.

title: Q&A
content: Entomophilous plants are pollinated primarily by insects such as bees and wasps, rather than by wind, water, animals or birds.

title: Q&A
content: For ceramic garden containers, good drainage requires at least one unobstructed hole in the bottom. Gravel or pot shards in the base do not improve drainage and can keep the wettest soil closer to roots, increasing the risk of rot.

title: Q&A
content: If a smooth flat-bottomed container seals to the ground, raise it slightly on blocks or pot feet so water can drain away.

title: Q&A
content: A general water-soluble fertilizer for containers should have roughly a 3-1-2 NPK ratio, with nitrogen highest but not overpowering, and should include micronutrients.

title: Q&A
content: Container plants benefit from a steady nutrient supply. Apply a weak dilution frequently instead of one strong dose, which can burn roots or be flushed away and wasted.

title: Q&A
content: To remove little black beetles from raspberries after harvest, soak the fruit for 10 to 20 minutes in 1 part table salt to 9 parts cold water so insects float to the surface, then rinse again in cold clean water.

title: Q&A
content: Illustration showing a container drainage question, including a pot and bowl graphic for Q&A.

title: Q&A
content: Bald-faced hornets kill other insects for food and pollinate as they eat sap, nectar and rotting fruit, but they can be aggressive toward humans and sting repeatedly with painful stings.

title: Q&A
content: If a bald-faced hornet nest must be removed, work early in the morning or at night, wear protective clothing with cuffs and collar taped shut, use a labeled wasp and hornet aerosol from a safe distance, respray only after checking activity every 24 hours, and consider hiring a professional.

title: Q&A
content: Bald-faced hornets, Dolichovespula maculata, are up to 1 1/2 inches long with a smooth hairless chubby red-brown body and black-and-white rings. Their large spherical nests hang from tree branches and have one opening at the bottom.

title: Q&A
content: Northern paper wasps, Polistes spp., are 1/3 to 1 inch long with smooth slender hairless black bodies and yellow-and-black rings. They usually attack only when provoked and build open comb nests of chewed wood fiber and saliva in protected places such as eaves.

title: Weed Watch: Beggartick
content: Beggartick, Bidens frondosa, is a native reseeding annual with 3/4-inch yellow-orange flower heads from midsummer into fall. The colorful heads have no petals.

title: Weed Watch: Beggartick
content: Beggartick grows 1 to 3 feet tall on erect branched stems. Its compound leaves have three to five sharply toothed leaflets, each 2 to 4 inches long, with soft fine hairs on the undersides.

title: Weed Watch: Beggartick
content: After beggartick flowers fade, the round heads split open and reveal 1/4-inch seeds with two barbed hooks that grab fabric and fur. Birds and small mammals also eat and spread the seeds.

title: Weed Watch: Beggartick
content: Beggartick prefers full sun and moist soil but tolerates part shade and well-drained sites across most of North America, often in disturbed flower beds and vegetable gardens.

title: Weed Watch: Beggartick
content: Control beggartick by pulling or hoeing the shallow lightly branched taproot before seed forms. Herbicides are rarely necessary, though pre-emergents can help in heavy infestations.

title: Dainty Blooms for Hot Spots
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Safari Sky South African phlox, Jamesbrittenia hybrid, is a heat-tolerant container annual that resembles bacopa but handles hot spots better and blooms from spring until frost.

title: Dainty Blooms for Hot Spots
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Safari Sky flowers have lilac-purple petals with a white throat and gold-to-orange eye. As blossoms age, they fade to pink-tinged white, giving the plant more depth of color, and flowers drop without deadheading.

title: Dainty Blooms for Hot Spots
author: Jennifer Howell
content: South African phlox needs good drainage, extra water during the hottest part of summer and fertilizer at planting plus a midsummer top-dressing or regular water-soluble feed during the growing season.

title: Dainty Blooms for Hot Spots
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Safari Sky grows low and mounded, trailing enough to drape over a hanging basket or container. It also works in the ground cascading from a retaining wall or edging a border, and stringy growth can be cut back by a third.

title: Dainty Blooms for Hot Spots
author: Jennifer Howell
content: Safari Sky South African phlox is an annual with lilac-purple flowers with white throats and gold eyes from spring until frost. Grow it in full sun to part shade and moist well-drained soil; plants reach 6 to 12 inches tall and 12 to 24 inches wide and are hardy in USDA zones 10 to 11.

title: Dainty Blooms for Hot Spots
author: Jennifer Howell
content: The Patio Perfection container uses heat-tolerant plants that can handle a missed day or two of watering. Deadhead the salvia to keep blooms coming, and move little bluestem from the container into the garden at the end of the season.

title: In the Weeds: Terrified of Topping Flowers
author: Jamie Seitz
content: As a first-time dahlia farmer, Jamie Seitz found it terrifying to snip off the center bloom, or top, young dahlia plants after carefully checking tubers, planting them and waiting for shoots.

title: In the Weeds: Terrified of Topping Flowers
author: Jamie Seitz
content: Jamie Seitz's dahlia mentor told her to top teenage dahlia plants when they were about a foot tall and had at least four sets of leaves so they would grow fuller and produce more blooms.

title: In the Weeds: Terrified of Topping Flowers
author: Jamie Seitz
content: After watching many videos for reassurance, Jamie topped all but two dahlias. Later in the season, the topped plants were more robust, bushier and bloom-filled, while the two skipped plants were weaker.

title: In the Weeds: Terrified of Topping Flowers
author: Jamie Seitz
content: The dahlia-topping experience taught Jamie Seitz to trust experienced gardeners even when a recommended cut feels risky; topping a healthy dahlia can produce more branching and more blooms.

title: from the editor
author: Kristin Beane Sullivan
content: Weeks can go by in summer and it seems I barely see my garden. Sometimes I pause just long enough to water thirsty containers or pull a gigantic weed camouflaged in the middle of the baptisia plant. Honestly, I'm not sure if I saw most of my daylilies this year. Was I away? Was it too hot to go outside when they were blooming? I don't remember. I blinked and summer is nearly over. But once fall arrives, I'll be back to daily wanderings, stopping to count the different insects buzzing around the asters and admiring the way the light glows through the switchgrass seedheads. I want to soak it all in because it'll be over soon. If you find yourself anxiously checking the long-range forecast, hoping you don't see frost coming, I'm right there with you. I never want autumn to end.

title: from the editor
author: Kristin Beane Sullivan
content: Working on this fall issue reminded me of all there still is to look forward to this year: Seedheads (and the birds they feed), better weather for planting, cool-season color combinations, and bouquets of mums. Last year at this time, Sherri toured Lisa Graff's gorgeous Portland, Oregon, garden (that's a shot of them talking about Lisa's dahlias above). Check out our feature story about the visit on page 62, where you'll see Lisa's favorite long-blooming perennials and how she designed her garden to enhance beautiful borrowed views. We hope that you enjoy reading this autumn issue as much as we did developing it for you.

title: Reader Tips
content: Audri collects seeds each fall to share or donate, but she needed a way to keep them fresh and dry. Her method? Saving the small food-grade silica gel packets that come in prescription and overthe-counter medicines! By adding a packet to her stored seeds, she prevents moisture buildup and ensures better germination for next season's planting. - Audri Goronson, CO

title: Reader Tips
content: Garden mums not blooming? Leilah Khaled, OK In mid-October Leilah was puzzled when her friends were posting photos of their flower-covered garden mums ( Chrysanthemum hybrids) while hers were still just mounds of green foliage. It occurred to her that leaving the lamp on above the mums all night might be the culprit. Leilah's instinct was correct. Garden mums are photoperiodic and don't set buds until the days get shorter and the nights longer. Once she removed the light bulb, the plants started forming buds within the week, and by November she had loads of beautiful blooms.

title: Reader Tips
content: Save room for veggies Rosalind Malin, OR Every fall, Rosalind plants garlic bulbs in her vegetable bed for harvest the following summer. She also likes to add peppers and eggplants to that same bed in spring. To save room for the other vegetables and prevent damage to the garlic bulbs, she "plants" empty 4-inch nursery pots at the same time the garlic goes in, then uses that space for the eggplants and peppers in spring. Filling the pots with compost or soil helps prevent a misstep if she's working in that garden later.

title: Reader Tips
content: Upcycled garden caddy Ellen Miller, IN When Ellen's husband could no longer use his walker, she decided to put it to work in the garden. Now, whenever she needs them, they're easy to find-no more hunting for missing gloves!

title: Fast Garden Facts: Match the Shovel to the Job
content: If you've been using the same shovel for all your gardening jobs, you may be working harder than you need to. A tool tailored to the task of moving compost, planting or edging can tackle the job more efficiently and be easier on your back. Let us help you match the tool to the task.

title: Fast Garden Facts: Match the Shovel to the Job
content: Look for a single-forged and tempered steel shovel blade. Stamped metal is more likely to bend. Examine the spot where the blade joins the handle on the back of the shovel. A closed socket is better than an open one, which tends to break or bend more easily. For shovels with a steel blade, go with 12-, 14- or 16-gauge steel. Lower numbers mean thicker steel, which is less likely to bend or break.

title: Fast Garden Facts: Match the Shovel to the Job
content: A scoop has a large head - usually twice the size of a round-point shovel - and a flat edge. It's often made of plastic or aluminum to make it easier to lift. The depth of the dish and ribbing patterns may vary, but all do the same job.

title: Fast Garden Facts: Match the Shovel to the Job
content: The 14- to 16-inch-long blade on this shovel is great for digging deep. With its narrow footprint, the drainage spade fits easily in a crowded border when you need to do some transplanting. The only caveat is there's not a lot of room to step on the tread for added pressure.

title: Fast Garden Facts: Match the Shovel to the Job
content: A garden spade is almost flat with a sharp, straight edge that slices through soil.

title: Fast Garden Facts: Match the Shovel to the Job
content: A garden spade is useful for straight edges along garden beds or paths, cutting through sod or digging a straight row for planting vegetables.

title: Fast Garden Facts: Match the Shovel to the Job
content: The round-point shovel's angled sides and pointed tip breaks ground easily, and the wide rolled tread at the top makes it comfortable to add more pressure with your foot.

title: Fast Garden Facts: Match the Shovel to the Job
content: The head of a floral shovel is half to two-thirds the size of a standard round-point, but it's a bit more curved, so it still holds plenty of soil.

title: Fast Garden Facts: Match the Shovel to the Job
content: Floral shovels are lightweight and easy to handle. They're great for digging in small spaces or crowded borders and planting small perennials when a trowel is too small but a round-pointed shovel is too big.

title: Fast Garden Facts: Match the Shovel to the Job
content: A round-point shovel is especially handy when you want to start a new bed or add a few plants to the border. While the head's shallow bowl holds a load without spilling, that curved shape isn't the best choice for edging or digging holes with perfectly straight sides.

title: The Wild Side: Hosting Butterflies on the Doorstep
content: Butterfly gardens provide nectar plants for the adults, and host plants for the caterpillars. Here a pipevine swallowtail is feeding on ironweed nectar.

title: The Wild Side: Hosting Butterflies on the Doorstep
content: Walking out the door one September morning, I saw a tiny black blip at my feet. It was the final molt of a pipevine swallowtail caterpillar, the old, squashed skin (and face!) that drops when a butterfly caterpillar becomes a chrysalis. So, I looked up. And there was the chrysalis, fresh and glistening, hanging from a brick above my head.

title: The Wild Side: Hosting Butterflies on the Doorstep
content: But the best part was when I made my kid look at the black blip, and then he too looked up to find the butterfly-in-progress who dropped it. He knew.

title: The Wild Side: Hosting Butterflies on the Doorstep
content: The little wad of caterpillar skin tells a big story: the story of a native plant and animal interaction, and of the astonishing specificity of a larval host plant. Here, the plant is wooly pipevine, and the larva is the caterpillar of a pipevine swallowtail butterfly ( Battus philenor ). Pipevines are the only plants a pipevine swallowtail will lay eggs on because that's what her caterpillars can eat. The plant and animal evolved together in the habitat native to this place, Nashville, Tennessee.

title: The Wild Side: Hosting Butterflies on the Doorstep
content: This is why I grow plants that make new butterflies. And why my boy and I knew what the blip was.

title: The Wild Side: Hosting Butterflies on the Doorstep
content: Wooly pipevine can grow 20 to 30 feet tall and has unique yellowgreen and purple flowers tucked mostly beneath large heartshaped leaves in late spring to early summer.

title: The Wild Side: Hosting Butterflies on the Doorstep
content: Photo of a pipevine swallowtail butterfly feeding on ironweed nectar in a butterfly garden.

title: The Wild Side: Hosting Butterflies on the Doorstep
content: Close-up photo of a pipevine swallowtail chrysalis or molt on a nearby surface.

title: The Wild Side: Hosting Butterflies on the Doorstep
content: A butterfly host plant at the door means we get to see, just by taking a step outside, every stage of a butterfly life cycle. It's an ideal show-and-tell for what a host plant does.

title: The Wild Side: Hosting Butterflies on the Doorstep
content: We can watch as a fluttering pipevine swallowtail mom extrudes one tiny orange egg at a time, her abdomen curved to aim at a leaf just so. We can see the hatchlings emerge, watch them eat their own eggshell, and then start eating the leaf. When they get bigger, we can even hear them munch! With a host plant, leaf damage is a good thing.

title: The Wild Side: Hosting Butterflies on the Doorstep
content: Best of all, we get to see a caterpillar become a chrysalis, and a chrysalis become a butterfly. When I showed my mom the pipevine action, she freaked. I'd been talking about host plants for years, but she'd never witnessed proof. "You should tell people," she yelled, "people who want to make butterflies! They can just plant this vine!"

title: The Wild Side: Hosting Butterflies on the Doorstep
content: Every butterfly species needs particular food plants for the larval stage, as do 90 percent of all insects that eat plants. They are specialists. Monarch butterflies are a famous example; they cannot reproduce without milkweeds. But all specialists have adapted to digest particular chemicals in certain plant families, genera or species. This is why every butterfly garden needs not just nectar plants for adults, but also caterpillar host plants for babies.

title: The Wild Side: Hosting Butterflies on the Doorstep
content: For example, one of the easiest species to "make" at home is black swallowtail ( Papilio polyxene s). Its range is huge, and the caterpillars eat plants in the carrot family-also huge- which includes not only the gorgeous native perennial golden Alexander, but related, nonnative herbs, such as parsley, fennel and dill.

title: The Wild Side: Hosting Butterflies on the Doorstep
content: Other easy show-and-tell species are Gulf fritillary and variegated fritillary butterflies, which use passion flowers native to your area.

title: The Wild Side: Hosting Butterflies on the Doorstep
content: Pipevine swallowtail caterpillars hatch and eat in a group, which makes them easy to find and watch. They become more solitary as they grow older.

title: The Wild Side: Hosting Butterflies on the Doorstep
content: Joanna, author of This Is How a Robin Drinks: Essays on Urban Nature, knows that trees and shrubs can make butterflies too, but they aren't as convenient for show-and-tells that freak people out. Follow her blog at sidewalknature.com.

title: The Wild Side: Hosting Butterflies on the Doorstep
content: If a swallowtail caterpillar becomes a chrysalis late in fall, it will overwinter and emerge in spring. Larvae leave their host plants when it is time to pupate, so a camouflaged chrysalis may be on a random stem, porch brick or down in the leaves.

title: No-Fail Combos: Summer's Last Hurrah
author: Stephanie Polsley Bruner
content: The growing season may be winding down, but there's plenty of time for your garden to show off! Choosing the right combination of plants can keep it looking good until cold weather finally arrives. While there are plenty of flowers that still look great, don't forget about foliage texture and color, as well as structural elements such as tree limbs and trunks. All these items together create a gorgeous fall garden.

title: No-Fail Combos: Summer's Last Hurrah
author: Stephanie Polsley Bruner
content: Let's take a look at three plant combinations that can brighten your garden in late summer and fall.

title: No-Fail Combos: Summer's Last Hurrah
author: Stephanie Polsley Bruner
content: Let your garden shine with this combination of bright annuals. With their slender stems weaving together and the butterflies they'll attract, these plants will make your garden feel like a summery meadow right up until frost.

title: No-Fail Combos: Summer's Last Hurrah
author: Stephanie Polsley Bruner
content: Annuals don't get much easier than these three. They all like a sunny spot with well-drained soil, but they don't need any special care or fertilizer to strut their stuff. You could sow the seeds directly in the ground after the last frost in spring, but these three beauties are also easy to find as small plants in spring. If you want to keep globe amaranth plants a little bushier, pinch them back by about half in early summer. Verbena and celosia often reseed, so you can enjoy them next year too.

title: No-Fail Combos: Summer's Last Hurrah
author: Stephanie Polsley Bruner
content: A Verbena Verbena bonariensis Tender perennial; rose-violet flowers from early summer to frost; full sun; 24 to 48 in. tall, 18 to 24 in. wide; cold hardy in USDA zones 7 to 11 (grown as an annual in colder zones) B Celosia Celosia argentea var. cristata 'Cramer's Rose'

title: No-Fail Combos: Summer's Last Hurrah
author: Stephanie Polsley Bruner
content: Celosia 'Cramer's Rose' is an annual with bright pink crested flowers from midsummer to frost; full sun; 30 to 48 inches tall and 9 to 12 inches wide.

title: No-Fail Combos: Summer's Last Hurrah
author: Stephanie Polsley Bruner
content: QIS Orange globe amaranth, Gomphrena globosa, is an annual with papery orange blooms from spring to frost; full sun; 22 to 26 inches tall and 8 to 10 inches wide.

title: No-Fail Combos: Summer's Last Hurrah
author: Stephanie Polsley Bruner
content: Garden photo of jewel-bright annuals including verbena, celosia and globe amaranth for late summer and fall color.

title: No-Fail Combos: Summer's Last Hurrah
author: Stephanie Polsley Bruner
content: You can dry both celosia and globe amaranth to enjoy indoors for months. Cut the flowers, strip off the leaves, gather a few stems together and hang them upside down in a warm, dark, dry place for a few weeks or more.

title: No-Fail Combos: Summer's Last Hurrah
author: Stephanie Polsley Bruner
content: Celosia flowers may shed many tiny black seeds as they dry, so hang them over a box or newspaper to make cleanup easy.

title: No-Fail Combos: Summer's Last Hurrah
author: Stephanie Polsley Bruner
content: Full-page garden photo of rosy annuals, celosia and globe amaranth with a good-to-know note about drying flowers.

title: No-Fail Combos: Summer's Last Hurrah
author: Stephanie Polsley Bruner
content: Late summer and early fall may be hot, but this combination will look cool! The star of the show is the lungwort, whose leaves emerge spotted in spring but turn shining silver-white as the summer progresses. The fine-textured, arching stems of the bush clover create a striking contrast with the lungwort, while the bush clover's profusion of purple flowers keep the interest alive until frost. Feathery juniper branches also provide some contrast, and those evergreen needles will step into their own, adding structure to the garden as cold weather creeps in.

title: No-Fail Combos: Summer's Last Hurrah
author: Stephanie Polsley Bruner
content: Pulmonaria does best if it has some shade in the heat of the day, especially in gardens farther south. This perennial also likes a little more moisture than the juniper and the bush clover, so make sure you give it attention if the weather is dry.

title: No-Fail Combos: Summer's Last Hurrah
author: Stephanie Polsley Bruner
content: Bush clover blooms on new growth, so cut this shrub back hard, even all the way to the ground, in late winter or early spring. You'll end up with a lush, full plant later in the summer. Be aware that it can reseed and stems may root where they touch the ground, so keep an eye out for plants popping up in the wrong spot.

title: No-Fail Combos: Summer's Last Hurrah
author: Stephanie Polsley Bruner
content: A Bush clover Lespedeza thunbergii 'Gibraltar' Shrub; rosy purple flowers from late summer to fall; full sun to part shade; 4 to 5 ft. tall, 4 to 10 ft. wide; cold hardy in USDA zones 4 to 9

title: No-Fail Combos: Summer's Last Hurrah
author: Stephanie Polsley Bruner
content: B Lungwort Pulmonaria 'Diana Clare' Perennial; blue and purple flowers in early to midspring; part to full shade; 8 to 12 in. tall, 12 to 18 in. wide; cold hardy in USDA zones 3 to 9

title: No-Fail Combos: Summer's Last Hurrah
author: Stephanie Polsley Bruner
content: C Juniper Juniperus chinensis 'Nick's Compact' Shrub; evergreen needles may have slight blue cast; full sun; 2 to 4 ft. tall, 3 to 6 ft. wide; cold hardy in USDA zones 4 to 9

title: No-Fail Combos: Summer's Last Hurrah
author: Stephanie Polsley Bruner
content: Garden photo of the Cool and Lush combination with silver lungwort, bush clover and juniper.

title: No-Fail Combos: Summer's Last Hurrah
author: Stephanie Polsley Bruner
content: Who says you need flowers to create a striking garden? This little corner lights up with colorful foliage. When you work with a lot of fine-textured plants like the golden hakonechloa, front and center here, be sure to plant them in groups instead of in ones and twos. They'll make a bolder statement and help anchor the rest of the planting.

title: No-Fail Combos: Summer's Last Hurrah
author: Stephanie Polsley Bruner
content: Besides their beauty, these plants are pretty low-maintenance. Hakonechloa and ferns prefer cool, moist conditions, but both are fairly drought tolerant once they're established. Even if you live where they're evergreen, trim back ragged foliage as needed on all of them in late winter or early spring to promote fresh new growth.

title: No-Fail Combos: Summer's Last Hurrah
author: Stephanie Polsley Bruner
content: A Daisy bush Brachyglottis greyi Shrub; yellow blooms in summer, evergreen gray foliage; full sun; 4 to 5 ft. tall, 5 to 6 ft. wide; cold hardy in USDA zones 8 to 10 B Hakonechloa Hakonechloa macra 'Aureola'

title: No-Fail Combos: Summer's Last Hurrah
author: Stephanie Polsley Bruner
content: Hakonechloa 'Aureola' has airy yellow-green midsummer flower panicles and green-and-gold variegated foliage that may be evergreen in milder climates; part to full shade; 1 to 2 feet tall and wide; USDA zones 5 to 9.

title: No-Fail Combos: Summer's Last Hurrah
author: Stephanie Polsley Bruner
content: Western sword fern, Polystichum munitum, has long upright fronds that are semievergreen in warmer zones; part to full shade; 2 to 5 feet tall and wide; USDA zones 4 to 9.

title: No-Fail Combos: Summer's Last Hurrah
author: Stephanie Polsley Bruner
content: Sedum 'Angelina' has small clusters of yellow midsummer flowers and chartreuse foliage that can take on an orange tinge in fall; full sun to part shade; 4 to 6 inches tall and 12 to 24 inches wide; USDA zones 5 to 9.

title: A Foundation Garden with Nonstop Curb Appeal
content: Opening photo of a colorful raised foundation planter with fall containers, shrubs and annuals against a brick house.

title: A Foundation Garden with Nonstop Curb Appeal
content: When Ryan McEnaney moved into his Minnesota home a few years ago, the narrow border where a foundation planting used to be was completely empty. As the marketing and communications manager for Bailey Nurseries, he didn't want to live in a home with no garden, so he designed this unique planter box that's raised bed, windowbox and foundation planting all in one. Filled with annuals, perennials and shrubs, it provides bright flowers and foliage from spring to frost. Greenery, colorful stems and seasonal decor keep it looking great through winter. Neighbors and passersby are fascinated by the ever-changing scene-in fact they'll often stop by with questions or compliments when Ryan is working in the front yard. Let's take a look at how he built the planter box and came up with this head-turning design.

title: A Foundation Garden with Nonstop Curb Appeal
content: Before With no plants in the spot where a foundation planting used to be, Ryan came up with a simple and creative plan to quickly brighten up the north-facing front yard.

title: A Foundation Garden with Nonstop Curb Appeal
content: Before-and-after style image of the empty foundation area and the new raised planter with ornamental grass.

title: A Foundation Garden with Nonstop Curb Appeal
content: Ryan custom built this planter with pressure-treated dimensional lumber from the local home improvement store. The sidewalk angles toward the front door, leaving an irregular space between it and the house. So he planned accordingly, making the 24-foot-long planter 4 feet wide at the driveway and 2 feet wide close to the front door. This left space between the planter and the sidewalk for a few annuals and perennials to soften the wall of the planter.

title: A Foundation Garden with Nonstop Curb Appeal
content: The planter boxes vary in height from 1 to 31/2 feet tall, which gives small starter plants added punch right away. To leave the windows unobstructed, Ryan grows compact shrubs, such as Summer Crush bigleaf hydrangea and Lucky Devil ninebark, and keeps others shorter than 4 feet tall with pruning. Eventually a few of the original shrubs grew too big, so Ryan moved them to the border in the backyard and replaced them.

title: A Foundation Garden with Nonstop Curb Appeal
content: To build a large planter box like this, start with a 2x4 lumber frame for the base. Position it so you can leave 6 to 8 inches between the house and planter to allow air to circulate and prevent moisture from damaging the home's siding. Leave the bottom open so deep-rooted plants can reach into the soil beneath. Then attach a series of box frames of different heights down the length of the base.

title: A Foundation Garden with Nonstop Curb Appeal
content: Add 1x4 siding to the planter box frame, leaving 1/2 inch between the slats, and back the planter with solid plywood. Ryan chose to finish his planter with a brown stain that coordinates with the brick siding and ensures the plants take center stage.

title: A Foundation Garden with Nonstop Curb Appeal
content: Photo of a raised planter box filled with magenta flowers, shrubs and trailing annuals along the house foundation.

title: A Foundation Garden with Nonstop Curb Appeal
content: Raised bed DIY photo sequence showing the foundation planter frame, slatted siding and finished box.

title: A Foundation Garden with Nonstop Curb Appeal
content: Fantastic curb appeal Ryan wanted colors that would pop against the siding, especially during the shady parts of the day, and raspberry pink Summer Crush bigleaf hydrangea does just that. And the contrast between the chartreuse- and burgundy-leafed plants grabs attention even from the street.

title: A Foundation Garden with Nonstop Curb Appeal
content: To keep potting medium from falling out between the boards, Ryan recommends stapling landscape fabric to the interior front and sides. He filled the bed with potting mix, but raised bed mix is another good option. Water the bed thoroughly once it's full to help the mix settle, then top off with more mix and begin planting. Note that you may need to add mix every year if it continues to settle.

title: A Foundation Garden with Nonstop Curb Appeal
content: Start by auditioning shrubs to see which foliage colors and plant shapes look good in which spot and to make sure you don't have too much of the same thing in one area. This ensures that the "bones" of the planting stay interesting all year. Find more about which plants Ryan used and how he put them all together on the next page.

title: A Foundation Garden with Nonstop Curb Appeal
content: Garden photo of the raised foundation planter with hydrangeas, ninebark, sumac and colorful annuals for curb appeal.

title: A Foundation Garden with Nonstop Curb Appeal
content: Backbone shrubs Just like an in-ground foundation planting, shrubs are the backbone of this planter. Upright panicle hydrangea and bright yellow Tiger Eyes cutleaf staghorn sumac provide punctuation between repeated soft mounds of bigleaf hydrangea. Ryan positioned the taller sumac on the wall between the windows to fill the empty space with color.

title: A Foundation Garden with Nonstop Curb Appeal
content: Foundation plantings need to look good all year, and this group doesn't disappoint. In spring, fresh new foliage is accented by tulips and daffodils tucked near the front of the planter. Ryan adds new ones annually to ensure a colorful display. The foliage fills in and flowers really take off in summer. Low-growing China asters rebloom with deadheading, while Bloomstruck bigleaf hydrangea's blue to purple blooms and Pop Star's lacecap flowers last for weeks before aging to tan. Mums, coral bells and Eclipse bigleaf hydrangea at right provide a rich fall color palette that really turns heads. Once a hard frost kicks off the winter season, evergreen shrubs and dried hydrangea blooms take center stage and are supplemented with evergreen branches, birch logs and colorful dogwood stems.

title: A Foundation Garden with Nonstop Curb Appeal
content: Photo of the front foundation planter showing backbone shrubs and annual color near the garage.

title: A Foundation Garden with Nonstop Curb Appeal
content: Inset photo of yellow false sunflower or similar bright annual/perennial in the foundation planter.

title: A Foundation Garden with Nonstop Curb Appeal
content: Terrifi c trailers Annuals are a great way to boost color and bridge the gaps between bloom times. Ryan used a lot of them early on to fill the space between smaller perennials and shrubs. As those plant have matured, there's less room for annuals. But there's always room for a few trailers. Just like in a windowbox, you can tuck them near the front so they flow over and soften the edge. The first year, Ryan planted the vigorous sweet potato vines on the previous page - one plant can take up a lot of space and put on a big show. However, as the shrubs and perennials grew larger, smaller trailers, such as English ivy and licorice plant, were easier to work into the design.

title: Better Raised Beds
author: Marisa Reyes and Kristin Beane Sullivan
content: The first time that New Jersey's Resh Gala tried to grow tomatoes, she didn't get a single edible fruit, thanks to blossom end rot and other struggles. But she was determined to learn from her failure. The next year, she had more encouraging results in her small raised bed and decided to keep growing. Since then, she's learned that not everything will be perfect: Whether it's a new pest infestation, bad weather or something else, every year is different. But when one crop struggles, another one usually thrives. This determination to keep trying new things and continue gardening through diffi culties lead to Resh being named 2020 Gardener of the Year by Burpee Home Gardens. Now she's launched a business, Hundred Tomatoes LLC, to help other aspiring gardeners achieve their hoped-for harvests, and written the book Vegetable Gardening Made Easy.

title: Better Raised Beds
author: Marisa Reyes and Kristin Beane Sullivan
content: Her specialty is intensively planting herbs, flowers and vegetables together in raised beds that are both visually striking and productive.

title: Better Raised Beds
author: Marisa Reyes and Kristin Beane Sullivan
content: Resh says, "Most home gardeners seek a beautiful garden that takes minimal time and effort to thrive." That's why she recommends polyculture gardening-growing several types of plants together in the same space. It's a very different look than the traditional rowed-out vegetable garden. This planting style mimics nature, reducing pest problems while attracting pollinators and benefi cial insects in a healthy backyard ecosystem. Learn some of her favorite plant combinations in "Companion Planting" at right.

title: Better Raised Beds
author: Marisa Reyes and Kristin Beane Sullivan
content: Resh designs gardens with a layered approach: Tall and climbing plants grow vertically on trellises placed at the center or back of raised beds, while medium-height plants fill the middle and shorter or trailing varieties spill over the edges and corners. This arrangement not only creates visual depth but also makes everything easy to reach. Growing vertically frees up valuable space for additional crops, and the shorter plants act as living mulch, suppressing weeds and helping retain moisture.

title: Better Raised Beds
author: Marisa Reyes and Kristin Beane Sullivan
content: For example, a bed might have creeping rosemary, strawberries, lettuce or even pansies at the corners and edges; peppers, bush beans or zinnias in the middle; and tomatoes, pole beans or cucumbers in the middle or back. And size isn't the only consideration. She looks for texture contrasts and color combinations as well.

title: Better Raised Beds
author: Marisa Reyes and Kristin Beane Sullivan
content: One thing to keep in mind when planting intensively is that a packed bed requires frequent pruning. For example, when the lower foliage of greens, tomatoes and some flowers, such as nasturtium and pot marigold, doesn't get as much sunlight in tight spaces, it can turn yellow or brown. You'll want to clean this out at least once a week. And you can add airflow and prevent disease with preemptive pruning on indeterminate tomatoes: When a plant is 18 inches tall, remove the lower third of its foliage.

title: Better Raised Beds
author: Marisa Reyes and Kristin Beane Sullivan
content: Photo of Resh Gala in an intensively planted raised-bed vegetable garden.

title: Better Raised Beds
author: Marisa Reyes and Kristin Beane Sullivan
content: Resh says, "Polyculture confuses pests. I think of it as natural pest control for the garden." Some plants repel insects and others act as trap crops, luring the pests away from susceptible plants. She often plants a border of herbs around her raised beds, using it as the first line of defense against insects.

title: Better Raised Beds
author: Marisa Reyes and Kristin Beane Sullivan
content: For example, the chives in this photo help repel pests from the strawberries and lettuce.

title: Better Raised Beds
author: Marisa Reyes and Kristin Beane Sullivan
content: The annual flower pot marigold acts as a trap crop because It attracts aphids, which remain on the sticky calendula foliage and leave peppers and tomatoes alone. Once you notice several insects trapped in the plant, it's time to pull and dispose of it.

title: Better Raised Beds
author: Marisa Reyes and Kristin Beane Sullivan
content: Raised beds are easy to maintain because clearly defined edges help manage the garden layout and reduce weed creep. They also make watering, harvesting and rotating crops easier to plan and execute, and they can be built high enough to reduce back and knee strain.

title: Better Raised Beds
author: Marisa Reyes and Kristin Beane Sullivan
content: Raised beds make the most of small or awkward areas-tuck them into tight corners, patios, or even rooftops. They're completely customizable.

title: Better Raised Beds
author: Marisa Reyes and Kristin Beane Sullivan
content: Once a bed is established, compost is the secret sauce for healthy plants. Resh makes her own in a compost tumbler with kitchen scraps and pine pellets, and every fall she top-dresses beds with 3 to 4 inches of compost. When plants are starting to produce and set fruit, she sidedresses with more. If you don't have access to this much compost, she recommends feeding your garden earthworm castings or compost purchased in bulk.

title: Better Raised Beds
author: Marisa Reyes and Kristin Beane Sullivan
content: For raised bed planting medium, fill the bottom 75% with 30% topsoil, 30% compost, 10% vermiculite for water retention and 5% perlite for drainage; fill the top 25% with a high-quality raised bed mix.

title: Better Raised Beds
author: Marisa Reyes and Kristin Beane Sullivan
content: For a 4x8x1-foot raised bed with 32 cubic feet of material, use 8 cubic feet of raised bed mix, 9.6 cubic feet of topsoil, 9.6 cubic feet of compost, 3.2 cubic feet of vermiculite and 1.6 cubic feet of perlite.

title: Better Raised Beds
author: Marisa Reyes and Kristin Beane Sullivan
content: For several beds, it may be most cost-effective to order in bulk, measured in cubic yards. Divide cubic feet by 27 to determine cubic yards. Staple 1/4-in. hardware cloth to bottom.

title: Better Raised Beds
author: Marisa Reyes and Kristin Beane Sullivan
content: Raised beds allow gardeners to control soil quality from the start. Instead of spending years trying to transform poor ground soil, a raised bed can be filled with a plant-ready mix so crops can grow well even where native soil is nutrient-poor, too dry, soggy or heavy clay.

title: Better Raised Beds
author: Marisa Reyes and Kristin Beane Sullivan
content: Arches are useful for vining beans, gourds, melons, squash and even cherry tomatoes. You may need to secure heavy fruit with netting or old stockings to keep them from breaking off. Resh likes to extend an arch between two beds.

title: Better Raised Beds
author: Marisa Reyes and Kristin Beane Sullivan
content: Obelisks are perfect for plants whose foliage needs to be corralled, such as sweet peas, tomatoes, bush cucumbers, peas and even pole beans.

title: Better Raised Beds
author: Marisa Reyes and Kristin Beane Sullivan
content: Fence panels let you harvest beans, cucumbers and peas from both sides of these, and they're easy to make with a cattle panel and wooden posts.

title: Better Raised Beds
author: Marisa Reyes and Kristin Beane Sullivan
content: For teepees, tie four garden stakes together with twine to create an easy structure for pole beans or peas. If plants need a little help climbing, make layers by wrapping twine at different heights.

title: Better Raised Beds
author: Marisa Reyes and Kristin Beane Sullivan
content: Traditional tomato cages are too small for tomatoes, but they work well to corral medium-sized bushy plants, such as eggplants and peppers.

title: Better Raised Beds
author: Marisa Reyes and Kristin Beane Sullivan
content: Resh builds each bed with 2x6 untreated red cedar or Douglas fir boards and attaches a 4-inch-wide trim piece to the top edge of every bed. This makes it comfortable to rest a basket or sit on.

title: Better Raised Beds
author: Marisa Reyes and Kristin Beane Sullivan
content: She recommends a height of 12 to 24 inches. The taller a bed, the less bending you'll have to do to take care of it, but taller beds also require more amendments and soil, increasing the cost up front. Resh suggests beds no larger than 4x8 feet for structural integrity and ease of access.

title: Better Raised Beds
author: Marisa Reyes and Kristin Beane Sullivan
content: If deer and rabbit damage is a concern, these 24-inch-tall hinged chicken wire cages will keep them out. Ready to work in the garden? Unhook, slide a barrel bolt open and flip the side down.

title: Better Raised Beds
author: Marisa Reyes and Kristin Beane Sullivan
content: To keep digging pests out, Resh staples 1/4 -inch hardware cloth to the bottom of each bed. Line the inside with landscape fabric or cardboard before filling with soil to help the wood last longer.

title: Better Raised Beds
author: Marisa Reyes and Kristin Beane Sullivan
content: Install 1/2-inch drip irrigation tubing with emitters spaced 6 inches apart to provide even coverage for both large and small plants in a garden with several beds, where watering becomes more of a chore.

title: Which Daisy Is Right for You?
content: Cape daisies, Osteospermum hybrids, are colorful cool-season annuals also known as African daisies. They add zing to spring or fall bedding and are especially useful in containers, where they can bloom for months.

title: Which Daisy Is Right for You?
content: Plant Cape daisies as soon as they are available in spring or fall. They prefer temperatures between 55 and 75 degrees F, full to part sun, moist well-drained soil and dry foliage to reduce fungal problems.

title: Which Daisy Is Right for You?
content: Feed Cape daisies with a 10-10-10 fertilizer about once a month and deadhead to keep them blooming. If plants look tattered by midsummer, cut them back to healthy foliage and wait for them to rebound in fall.

title: Which Daisy Is Right for You?
content: Cape daisies bloom in shades of pink, orange, purple, yellow, white and bronze, often with purple centers, and make good cut flowers. Mounded plants grow 8 to 20 inches tall and wide, with semigloss medium-green toothed leaves.

title: Which Daisy Is Right for You?
content: Cape daisy cultivars include Akila Purple, with vibrant purple flowers and lots of branching at 10 to 14 inches tall and 14 to 20 inches wide; the Zion series with showy shaded colors at 16 to 20 inches tall and 16 to 24 inches wide; and Bright Lights Double Moonglow, a pale semidouble selection 8 to 12 inches tall and wide.

title: Which Daisy Is Right for You?
content: Shasta daisies, Leucanthemum x superbum, are classic summer perennials, usually white with yellow centers, with newer cultivars offering yellow blooms or fluffy double flowers.

title: Which Daisy Is Right for You?
content: Shasta daisies are stars in perennial beds and cottage gardens. Their flat open flowers attract butterflies, the neat clumps are easy to grow around other perennials and the crisp white flowers combine well with many colors.

title: Which Daisy Is Right for You?
content: Grow Shasta daisies in full sun, with a little afternoon shade tolerated, and well-drained soil. They peak in early to midsummer, often continue lightly until fall, and benefit from deadheading and division every two or three years.

title: Which Daisy Is Right for You?
content: Shasta daisy cultivars include 'Banana Cream II' with soft yellow flowers for two or three months at 20 to 24 inches tall, 'Belgian Lace' with light yellow buds opening to frilly 3 1/2-inch white flowers at 9 to 12 inches tall, and compact 'Snowcap' with single white flowers at 12 to 15 inches tall and wide.
