title: Top Picks: Perennials with Interesting Seedheads
author: Nancy J. Ondra
content: Shorter days and cooler temperatures mean the growing season is drawing to a close. But once frosts and freezes have called a halt to flowers and foliage, long-lasting perennial seedheads continue the show well into the winter months.

title: Top Picks: Perennials with Interesting Seedheads
author: Nancy J. Ondra
content: Sure, the color palette is more muted, but that makes the lingering shapes and forms all the more interesting. They also have a wonderful way of changing with the weather. If you're an early riser, you may get to enjoy your seedheads transformed by feathery white hoarfrost before it melts in the sun. Freezing rain turns them into fabulous ice sculptures, and a dusting of snow makes for magical effects as the seedheads catch the drifting flakes.

title: Top Picks: Perennials with Interesting Seedheads
author: Nancy J. Ondra
content: All this beauty has a practical benefit too: Seedheads supply welcome winter food for birds, and their stems provide shelter for tiny creatures.

title: Top Picks: Perennials with Interesting Seedheads
author: Nancy J. Ondra
content: There are dozens of delightful perennials to choose from. Start with border classics like bee balms ( Monarda spp.) and coneflowers ( Echinacea spp.), then look to some lesser-known options, like these 10 North American natives with marvelous multiseason features.

title: Top Picks: Perennials with Interesting Seedheads
author: Nancy J. Ondra
content: Veronicastrum virginicum Though this dependable and distinctive perennial can be a bit sprawling for the first year or two, Culver's root has a strongly upright form once established, further strengthened by the spiky flower heads that form at the stem tips over whorls of rich green foliage. Its branching heads are lined with hundreds of tiny blooms that provide a wealth of pollen and nectar for a wide variety of interesting insects starting in early to midsummer. Once the flowers finish, the plant's elegant form remains as the seeds ripen in fall, drying and darkening as the season winds down and standing tall through much or all of the winter.

title: Top Picks: Perennials with Interesting Seedheads
author: Nancy J. Ondra
content: The fine-textured seedheads of this eastern U.S. native show off well against a solid background, such as a wall or fence. For a magical combination that will look good from summer to spring, pair it with the bobbles of bee balm ( Monarda didyma ), the branching heads of a Joe-Pye weed ( Eutrochium spp.) or the airy panicles of a tall, warm-season grass, such as switchgrass ( Panicum virgatum ), all of which look lovely when fresh in bloom and dried in place for winter interest.

title: Top Picks: Perennials with Interesting Seedheads
author: Nancy J. Ondra
content: Culver's root, Veronicastrum virginicum is a perennial with Spiky heads of white (or pale pink to lavender) flowers in summer; dark, branching seedheads in fall and winter Light Full sun to part shade Soil Average to wet Size 4 to 6 ft. tall, 2 to 4 ft. wide Cold hardy USDA Zones 3 to 8

title: Top Picks: Perennials with Interesting Seedheads
author: Nancy J. Ondra
content: Showy seedheads are terrific for outdoor holiday decorating. After pulling out annuals, fill pots, planters and windowboxes with evergreen boughs, berried branches and seedheads; for the best holiday display, collect seedheads in midfall once they are fully dry but before birds eat the seeds, then store them somewhere dry and protected from mice.

title: Top Picks: Perennials with Interesting Seedheads
author: Nancy J. Ondra
content: Photo of Culver's root seedheads and flower spikes standing in an autumn garden.

title: Top Picks: Perennials with Interesting Seedheads
author: Nancy J. Ondra
content: Carolina lupine Thermopsis villosa Spectacular in bloom and splendid in seed, Carolina lupine is guaranteed to please for months on end. Its unbranched stems shoot up from the ground in midspring, reaching their full height by late spring to early summer. The sturdy stems are clad in three-parted, grayish green leaves, then topped with spikelike bloom clusters for several weeks. When you take a close look at the sunny yellow flowers, you can easily see that this pretty perennial is in the same family as peas and beans. It's related to true lupines, too, but this southeastern U.S. native is much more tolerant of heat and humidity.

title: Top Picks: Perennials with Interesting Seedheads
author: Nancy J. Ondra
content: After they're pollinated, the flowers are replaced by silvery green seedpods that darken to gray-brown by late summer. The chunky pods stand all through the winter, visible even above deep snow, until you cut them down in spring. Carolina lupine can be a little slow to settle into the garden, but as the years go by, it forms a broad clump that makes an outstanding vertical accent for the back of a border or the middle of an island bed.

title: Top Picks: Perennials with Interesting Seedheads
author: Nancy J. Ondra
content: Carolina lupine, Thermopsis villosa is a perennial with Racemes of bright yellow flowers in late spring to early summer; showy seedheads in fall and winter Light Full sun to part shade Soil Average, well-drained Size 3 to 5 ft. tall, 2 to 3 ft. wide Cold hardy USDA Zones 4 to 9

title: Top Picks: Perennials with Interesting Seedheads
author: Nancy J. Ondra
content: Photo of Carolina lupine with flowers and developing seedpods.

title: Top Picks: Perennials with Interesting Seedheads
author: Nancy J. Ondra
content: Prairie dropseed Sporobolus heterolepis Whether you're a longtime fan of ornamental grasses or new to their charm, prairie dropseed is an excellent addition to your garden plant palette. It starts out as tight, bright green tufts in spring, maturing into mounds of fine-textured foliage by early to midsummer; then slender flowering stems shoot upward from the crown as late summer approaches. The flowers themselves are tiny, but the airy, finely branched panicles create a shimmering, graceful haze that's a charming contrast to the many bold, daisy-form flowers peaking this time of year. Prairie dropseed also offers an unusual feature for a grass: a noticeable fragrance in bloom! (It reminds some people of buttered popcorn and others of cilantro.) The flowers develop into beadlike seeds in fall, often causing the stems to arch elegantly under their weight.

title: Top Picks: Perennials with Interesting Seedheads
author: Nancy J. Ondra
content: The seeds have a wonderful way of catching moisture, transforming fall mist and drizzle into diamond drops. Winter birds and other wildlife eventually feed on the seeds, but the remaining stems and foliage stay in place, turning showy gold to orange in fall, bleaching to tan for winter, and lasting until the growing season begins again. Native to much of North America, this superb grass looks delicate but is as tough as nails, tolerating both heat and drought.

title: Top Picks: Perennials with Interesting Seedheads
author: Nancy J. Ondra
content: Prairie dropseed, Sporobolus heterolepis is a perennial with Fragrant flowers in late summer; bright leaf color in fall; airy seedheads and persistent foliage in fall and winter Light Full sun Soil Average, well-drained to dry Size 2 to 3 ft. tall and wide Cold hardy USDA Zones 3 to 8

title: Top Picks: Perennials with Interesting Seedheads
author: Nancy J. Ondra
content: Photo of prairie dropseed grass with airy seedheads and golden fall color.

title: Top Picks: Perennials with Interesting Seedheads
author: Nancy J. Ondra
content: Spike blazing star Liatris spicata Blazing stars are indeed garden stars, both during the growing season and well beyond. This species is particularly striking, with its tightly packed, pink-purple (or sometimes white) blooms lining the upper third to half of each stem and slender, bright green leaves along the lower part. The flowers at the tip open first, usually in midsummer, then proceed down the spike. The spikes are fabulous in fresh arrangements, but if you want to use them that way, grow extra plants in a separate cutting area so you don't lose the blooms and seedheads in your borders. As the plants of this eastern U.S. native mature over the years, they produce more and more stems per clump, making an even better display if you leave them undisturbed.

title: Top Picks: Perennials with Interesting Seedheads
author: Nancy J. Ondra
content: During the bloom season, the flowers attract butterflies as well as a wide range of benefi cial insects; once the seeds develop, birds swoop in to feed on them. When the seeds are gone, the spikes aren't as fluffy, but the remaining spiky skeleton is still an outstanding contrast to the many other rounded or clustered seedhead forms in the winter garden.

title: Top Picks: Perennials with Interesting Seedheads
author: Nancy J. Ondra
content: Spike blazing star, Liatris spicata is a perennial with Feathery pink-purple or white flower spikes in summer; fluffy seedheads in fall to winter Light Full sun Soil Average to moist Size 18 to 48 in. tall, 12 to 24 in. wide Cold hardy USDA Zones 3 to 8

title: Top Picks: Perennials with Interesting Seedheads
author: Nancy J. Ondra
content: Photo of spike blazing star seedheads and purple flower spikes.

title: Top Picks: Perennials with Interesting Seedheads
author: Nancy J. Ondra
content: Photo of white seedheads or frost-coated perennial seedheads in winter interest.

title: Top Picks: Perennials with Interesting Seedheads
author: Nancy J. Ondra
content: Eryngium yuccifolium Almost otherworldly in form, rattlesnake master is practically a must-have if you appreciate intriguing seedheads. It starts the growing season by sending up clumps of spiky, gray-green leaves. Later its stout stems are topped by branching clusters tipped with dense globes of greenish white blooms. A single plant makes an eyecatching accent; in masses, it's an amazing sight! The summer flowers give way to dark brown seedheads in fall. Deer and rabbits usually leave the plants alone, but various pollinators feed on the flowers, and wild birds appreciate the seeds as winter food. Even after the seeds are gone, the dried stems and branching heads stand through the winter months to provide visual interest until you remove them in spring.

title: Top Picks: Perennials with Interesting Seedheads
author: Nancy J. Ondra
content: Rattlesnake master is native to the central and eastern United States and grows well elsewhere too, adapting to a range of soil conditions. Just keep in mind that it may sprawl in good garden soil; in dryish, infertile conditions, the stems tend to stay upright without support.

title: Top Picks: Perennials with Interesting Seedheads
author: Nancy J. Ondra
content: Rattlesnake master, Eryngium yuccifolium is a perennial with Showy green-white flowers in mid- to late summer; dramatic seedheads in fall and winter Light Full sun Soil Average, well-drained Size 2 to 5 ft. tall, 2 to 3 ft. wide Cold hardy USDA Zones 3 to 8

title: Top Picks: Perennials with Interesting Seedheads
author: Nancy J. Ondra
content: Photo of rattlesnake master dried globe seedheads on strong stems.

title: Top Picks: Perennials with Interesting Seedheads
author: Nancy J. Ondra
content: Showy goldenrod Solidago speciosa Thank goodness goldenrods are no longer shunned by gardeners in the mistaken belief that they are the cause of fall allergies. Like its close relatives, showy goldenrod offers the classic yellow flowers in late summer to early fall, gracing beds and borders with large bloom clusters atop upright, green or red-tinged stems. It's invaluable as a source of pollen and nectar for insects and butterflies during its flowering period; then, the fluffy seedheads supply an abundance of food for wild birds. Even after the seeds are gone, the sturdy, cylindrical to cone-shaped structure holds up beautifully through much of the winter, providing a contrasting form to other persistent stems and seedheads. The fact that deer tend to leave it alone is a nice bonus.

title: Top Picks: Perennials with Interesting Seedheads
author: Nancy J. Ondra
content: Native to much of the central and eastern United States, showy goldenrod tends to form distinct clumps or small patches rather than spreading rampantly, which makes it one of the best goldenrods for bright color and showy seedheads in a garden setting.

title: Top Picks: Perennials with Interesting Seedheads
author: Nancy J. Ondra
content: Showy goldenrod, Solidago speciosa is a perennial with Yellow flowers in late summer to early fall; red fall foliage color; fluffy seed plumes in fall and winter Light Full sun to part shade Soil Average, well-drained to dry Size 2 to 3 ft. tall and wide Cold hardy USDA Zones 3 to 8

title: Top Picks: Perennials with Interesting Seedheads
author: Nancy J. Ondra
content: Photo of showy goldenrod flowers and fluffy seed plumes for fall and winter.

title: Top Picks: Perennials with Interesting Seedheads
author: Nancy J. Ondra
content: Wild quinine Parthenium integrifolium Also known as American feverfew, this long-lived eastern U.S. native deserves more attention for its easy-care nature and superb ornamental features. Wild quinine starts the growing season as a rosette of broad, rough-surfaced, aromatic leaves, then sends up sturdy, upright, top-branching bloom stems. Flowering from late spring or early summer to late summer or early fall, the closely packed, white blooms of this aster relative have a prominent center with just a few tiny ray flowers (petals). They're well supplied with pollen and nectar, making them a magnet for bees, beetles, flies and other pollinators. The summer blooms are also outstanding as cut flowers, but be sure to leave some of the stems in place so the seedheads can mature.

title: Top Picks: Perennials with Interesting Seedheads
author: Nancy J. Ondra
content: As they dry in fall, they'll turn shades of gray and then dark brown, standing strong long after birds and winter weather have taken the seeds. Add the ability to adapt to a range of sites and soils, the fact that wild quinine is rarely bothered by pests or diseases, and even deer resistance, and you have a perennial that will delight you months on end with minimal effort.

title: Top Picks: Perennials with Interesting Seedheads
author: Nancy J. Ondra
content: Wild quinine, Parthenium integrifolium is a perennial with White flowers in late spring to late summer; flat-topped seedheads in fall and winter Light Full sun to part shade Soil Average, well-drained Size 2 to 4 ft. tall, 1 to 2 ft. wide Cold hardy USDA Zones 4 to 8

title: Top Picks: Perennials with Interesting Seedheads
author: Nancy J. Ondra
content: When seedheads stand through fall and winter, When you leave seedheads standing in your garden for fall and winter, you may find seedlings in spring and summer. It's not so much of an issue in a closely planted border, where the established perennials will fill out quickly and smother most of the germinating seeds. But if you have areas of bare soil you keep for annuals or tropicals, you may well discover a bounty of baby perennials popping up when it comes time to plant there. Fortunately, they're easy to pull out when they are small. Don't want them to go to waste? Dig them out with a trowel and move them, or pot them and share with friends. If you'd prefer to discourage them from sprouting, cover open areas of bare soil with a 1- to 2-inch-thick layer of mulch in early spring.

title: Top Picks: Perennials with Interesting Seedheads
author: Nancy J. Ondra

title: Top Picks: Perennials with Interesting Seedheads
author: Nancy J. Ondra
content: Eutrochium maculatum If you appreciate perennials that do double duty in the garden, making a great show and supporting wildlife as well, spotted Joe-Pye weed is defi nitely worth a look. Its stout, purplish red or purple-spotted stems carry whorls of rich green leaves, then branch at the tips to develop broad clusters of densely packed, rosy pink blooms in mid- to late summer, much to the delight of bees and butterflies. Later on, the fragrant flowers of this eastern U.S. native give way to fluffy-tufted seeds that cling into late fall or early winter. Once birds have feasted on the seeds and the wind has blown away the rest, the domed structure remains for several more months, creating intriguing garden sculptures when topped with snow.

title: Top Picks: Perennials with Interesting Seedheads
author: Nancy J. Ondra
content: Spotted Joe-Pye weed can easily reach head height by bloom time, but there are compact species and selections that can give you a similar look and seedhead effect at a scale better suited to a small garden, such as 'Baby Joe' coastal Joe-Pye weed ( Eutrochium dubium ), which only reaches 3 to 4 feet tall.

title: Top Picks: Perennials with Interesting Seedheads
author: Nancy J. Ondra
content: Spotted Joe-Pye weed, Eutrochium maculatum is a perennial with Domed clusters of pink flowers in summer to fall; fluffy seedheads in fall to winter Light Full sun Soil Average to wet Size 3 to 7 ft. tall, 2 to 4 ft. wide Cold hardy USDA Zones 3 to 9

title: Garden Mums
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Opening photo of fall garden mums in a container with red celosia and ornamental grass.

title: Garden Mums
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Garden mums are perennials with white, yellow, orange, peach, red, purple or pink blooms from late summer to late fall. They grow in full sun and well-drained soil, have no serious pest problems, reach 12 to 60 inches tall and 15 to 48 inches wide, and are hardy in USDA zones 3 to 9.

title: Garden Mums
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Sometimes by fall, borders are starting to get that "I just can't go on" look. Thank goodness for garden mums! These tried-and-true perennials keep patios, pots and borders colorful for up to eight weeks, from late summer to late fall, without serious pest or disease problems.

title: Garden Mums
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: The big garden mums that you see at practically every store in town this time of year are full-grown and ready to pop in the ground or containers. Often called "cushion" mums, most of these types have been treated with growth regulators and pruned multiple times to form classic 12- to 24-inch flower-covered mounds like 'Autumn Fire' at left. Those in a series, such as Chelsey, Paradiso or Cosmic, are the same size but have different bloom colors. Even if plants are cold hardy in your zone, they probably won't make it through winter if they're put in the ground during fall, because the roots won't have time to get established.

title: Garden Mums
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Smaller florist mums sold as gifts also make great seasonal tabletop accents or container companions and are usually grown as annuals. Spring-planted mums bought as potted plants or rooted cuttings that you buy in spring may be small, but they grow quickly and are much more likely to survive winter than the fall-planted ones. Usually springplanted mums are more upright with a looser habit and grow around 2 to 3 feet tall. But the Mammoth series can reach 4 feet tall and wide with single, semidouble or quilled blooms. Even better, this series is extra cold hardy, surviving winter in zones 3 to 9 (most "hardy" garden mums survive winters in zones 5 or 6 to 9).

title: Garden Mums
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: As the local cut flower movement has grown, heirloom garden mums have seen a resurgence in popularity. They produce fancy blooms in a wide range of shapes, sizes and colors and make beautiful fall bouquets. Note that some are only hardy to zone 7, but many gardeners plant them in spring and grow them as annuals or overwinter cuttings.

title: Garden Mums
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Multitalented mums include 'Autumn Fire', which leans politely over the edge of this path but won't get lanky or in the way. Pint-sized Gigi Gold adds bright color to the container.

title: Garden Mums
author: Sherri Ribbey

title: Garden Mums
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Muted red mum flowers help tone down bright orange pumpkins, giving this grouping a formal feel that fits in with the brick entry.

title: Garden Mums
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: While the colorful foliage in this pot provides interest through the growing season, popping in this florist mum is an easy way to add a splash of seasonal color.

title: Garden Mums
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: When you have containers to fill at the end of the season, fall-planted mums are perfect for the job. Their mounded, flower-covered habit provides a wealth of late-season color.

title: Garden Mums
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Because garden mums, especially the cushion types, are pinched into such neat and tidy forms, they lend themselves to formal designs. The fall grouping in photo 2 builds on the elegant feel of the brick to create eye-catching curb appeal. These longlasting bloom-covered mounds attract attention to the front door for weeks.

title: Garden Mums
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Mums make such a dramatic impact in fall, they inspired the annual Longwood Gardens Chrysanthemum Festival (longwoodgardens. org). This October event stars mums from Longwood's extensive collection and research program displayed in every way you can imagine: Some trained into works of art; others allowed to grow naturally. It's a sight to behold.

title: Garden Mums
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Fall mums are a great way to rescue an otherwise lovely container that's lost a plant to summer's heat or just needs a seasonal touch. If the open spot is small, a florist mum, such as the one in photo 3, makes a polite companion.

title: Garden Mums
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: To get the longest season of bloom, look for fall mums with buds that are just starting to show color so they open once you get the plants home-there won't be time for a rebloom.

title: Garden Mums
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: The absolute easiest way to use cushion mums in containers is to buy one at the garden center, slip the nursery pot into a decorative pot and place it where you want some added color. Bright yellow, rusty orange or red is probably the most common palette that you'll find. But with all the falling leaves in warm tones, maybe you'd prefer pastels in pink, white or lavender to create a softer, laid-back vibe like the seating area in photo 4.

title: Garden Mums

title: Garden Mums
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: When you allow mums to grow into their natural form in the garden, the result is usually a taller plant with a looser habit. They look lovely in a perennial border.

title: Garden Mums
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Mums spend the first part of the growing season as a leafy backdrop for showy annuals and perennials. Then as summer days wind down, garden mums burst into bloom. 'Five Alarm Red' and the smaller white variety at the garden's edge in photo 5 give this border a colorful boost and extend the garden's season of interest. Faded smooth hydrangea and spirea flowers add to the display, but you could grow dahlias and canna nearby if you wanted a bolder color combo.

title: Garden Mums
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: 'Sheffi eld Pink' in photo 6 is beloved for its abundance of pink flowers with a sunny yellow center. And while the National Chrysanthemum Society (mums.org) lists 13 different shapes for showing, single blooms like this one, with easy access to the tiny true flowers in the center disc, are a boon to late-season pollinators.

title: Garden Mums
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Heirloom garden mums are often grown in rows in dedicated cut flower gardens, but they look good in the border too. Grow them front to midborder, where it's easy to reach in and snip a few of those unique blooms that can last for up to two weeks in a vase.

title: Garden Mums
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: On the other hand, the fall-planted mums can also add a pop of color in the late-season garden. Pick up a few at the garden center to replace bedding annuals that are looking tired, and swap them in for a quick fall makeover. Without the ones in photo 7, the moody 'Wentworth' American cranberrybush foliage and shorter fall days could cause this short path to the patio to feel a bit dark. But the cheery yellow mum tempered by its more subdued companions in bronze and red provides a welcoming glow.

title: Garden Mums
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Garden mums have been hybridized for hundreds of years, starting in Asia, moving to Europe and then on to North America. The ones for sale now are complex hybrids, mostly the progeny of two species from China and Japan, Chrysanthemum indicum and C. x morifolium. The selection at right is just the tip of the iceberg but gives you an idea of the range of flower shapes and colors that are the result.

title: Garden Mums
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Like many plants with a long history of hybridization, garden mums have peaked and waned in popularity over the years, but now they're seeing a resurgence. Fortunately, when general interest declined, passionate gardeners and small specialty nurseries took on the task of preserving these beauties for the future.

title: Garden Mums
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: For example, Steve and Mandy O'Shea, owners of 3 Porch Farm, take advantage of big mum festivals like Longwood's to connect with other enthusiasts who trade and buy cuttings. Thanks to these connections, Steve and Mandy started their own nursery and kept varieties going that might otherwise have been lost.

title: Garden Mums
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Cynthia Stringham was hooked when she was introduced to a collection of Lehmann Gardens' cold hardy mums several years ago. Now she preserves and sells these beauties, some dating from the 1930s, through her own business, Heritage Mums. Cynthia stresses the importance of checking the bloom time for each mum when you shop. Early varieties are best if you live in zone 5 and colder. They start flowering in late summer and finish up by early October. Later varieties are better suited for mild winter areas with longer growing seasons-some don't start showing color until November.

title: Garden Mums
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Spring-planted garden mums grow best in full sun and well-drained soil. Afternoon shade is acceptable, but it may make the habit looser. Because mums are photoperiodic, outdoor lights that come on every evening can prevent them from setting flower buds.

title: Garden Mums
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: For strong garden mum stems with lots of flowers, apply a balanced granular fertilizer in spring when new growth appears and again when buds form. Mums usually do not need deadheading because they bloom late, and seedlings from reseeded varieties will not come true.

title: Garden Mums
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Garden mums can grow from small spring cuttings into large clumps with woody dead centers. Divide plants every few years in spring to reinvigorate them so they look and bloom better.

title: Garden Mums
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: To divide garden mums in spring, dig the entire plant with a fork or spade, shake off excess soil, split the clump into smaller sections, cut away the woody crown, choose vigorous outer pieces with big stems and plenty of roots, then replant divisions a couple of inches apart with the foliage-root junction covered by soil and water regularly until new growth appears.

title: Garden Mums
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Pinch garden mum stem tips a couple of times by midsummer to encourage a fuller, bushier plant with more flowering stems. Start when plants are 6 to 8 inches tall, pinch again when new growth is 3 to 6 inches long, and stop by early to mid-July so buds have time to form; skipping pinching makes taller, earlier plants, while pinching too late can delay bloom past frost.

title: Garden Mums
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Technique photo sequence showing garden mum division and replanting in spring.

title: Garden Mums
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: To start garden mum cuttings, cut 2- to 3-inch pieces in spring, remove the lower foliage so at least two leaves remain at the top, stick them into moistened potting mix and keep them in shade with the mix moist but not soggy. Roots should form in a week or two, and the cuttings can move into more sun and be transplanted into the garden by about six weeks.

title: Garden Mums
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Tender heirloom mums can be overwintered indoors. After a hard freeze kills the foliage, cut stems back to 3 or 4 inches, dig the plant, repot it in potting mix and keep it in a greenhouse, garage or basement that stays above freezing; water occasionally so it does not desiccate, and take new cuttings after spring growth begins.

title: Garden Mums
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Hardy spring-planted garden mums can get extra winter protection if dead stems are left in place over winter and the crown is covered with 2 to 4 inches of organic mulch such as straw to keep soil temperatures even and protect roots.

title: Garden Mums
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Garden mums bloom for a long time in cool weather and often shine through a light frost. For cut flowers, cover plants with a sheet or towel when frost is predicted to prevent damage.

title: Root Wash for a Better Start
content: Root washing is an alternative planting method for container-grown trees and shrubs. Instead of leaving the root ball mostly undisturbed, the gardener removes potting mix, exposes the root structure and redirects roots before planting so they can establish more naturally in garden soil.

title: Root Wash for a Better Start
content: Potting mix benefits container-grown plants because roots can push through it freely, it drains quickly and its light weight makes transport easier. But it is very different from garden soil, and by the time a tree or shrub is purchased, repeated repotting may have produced a dense, spiraling, pot-bound root mass that needs to be trained to spread horizontally into the garden.

title: Root Wash for a Better Start
content: A root-strangled tree may show slow growth, stunted foliage and branch dieback. Root washing and retraining spiraling roots at planting time can prevent a root from eventually girdling the tree.

title: Root Wash for a Better Start
content: When a plant slips out of its container and the roots hold the pot's shape, the roots should be loosened before planting.

title: Root Wash for a Better Start
content: Opening photo of a panicle hydrangea being root washed in a blue tub before planting.

title: Root Wash for a Better Start
content: Shake off the potting mix Thump or shake the root ball until you've loosened as much of the potting medium as possible. Rolling and pressing on the cylinder can help.

title: Root Wash for a Better Start
content: You'll likely start to reveal smaller, hairlike roots as well as thicker, anchoring roots.

title: Root Wash for a Better Start
content: To help correct pot-bound roots and reduce the chance that they could eventually strangle a plant, the conventional wisdom is to gently loosen the spiraling roots with your fingers or even slice into the root mass in a couple places to redirect them. But that does nothing to unseen interior roots that could be strangling a tree or shrub. Nor does it encourage them to spread from their "comfortable" potting mix into denser garden soil.

title: Root Wash for a Better Start
content: Root washing is a planting method for trees and shrubs. I prefer to remove as much potting mix as possible so I can see and redirect the roots as necessary. Here's how I do it: First, know that fall and early spring are the best times to plant trees and shrubs because temperatures are generally milder and there's usually more precipitation to help plants settle in than in the summer.

title: Root Wash for a Better Start
content: Start by slipping the root mass out of the pot. Gently thump it to get as much of the potting mix off as you can (photo 2). Next, place the root ball in a tub of water. Let it soak until it all begins to loosen. Slosh the roots in the water, using your fingers to pull the roots apart and dislodge potting mix. This may take several periods of soaking and sloshing (photo 3).

title: Root Wash for a Better Start
content: Be gentle, as some plants, like this panicle hydrangea, have rather brittle roots. Break too many off, and the plant could have a harder time establishing.

title: Root Wash for a Better Start
content: Soak and slosh As you slosh the roots in water, work your fingers into the center of the root ball. You may find a layer of heavier clay soil toward the middle. The roots here are likely the most densely bound up. Try to work them loose too.

title: Root Wash for a Better Start
content: Technique photo showing the bottom inch of a root ball being sliced off before root washing.

title: Root Wash for a Better Start
content: Technique photo showing potting mix loosened from shrub roots in a tub of water.

title: Root Wash for a Better Start
content: Close-up photo of exposed roots after washing away potting medium.

title: Root Wash for a Better Start
content: Prune out wrong-way roots This root had developed a bend that directed it back toward the center of the plant. Because it's so brittle, it couldn't be redirected so needed to be cut off.

title: Root Wash for a Better Start
content: Note the planting depth On trees, look for the root flare to determine planting depth. On shrubs, note the original soil line in the container and maintain that.

title: Root Wash for a Better Start
content: Now examine the exposed roots. Your goal is to direct them to grow away from the center, out into the garden, so they won't girdle, or strangle, the main stems or trunk. If the roots are well spaced and not spiraling, you can move directly to planting. But if you find problem roots that you can't straighten, cut them off to redirect the growth (photo 4). Look for roots that made right turns when they reached the pot wall and started to grow back into the root ball, and cut them off where they bend.

title: Root Wash for a Better Start
content: When setting a tree or shrub in the hole, it's always better to plant high rather than too deep. Look for the original soil line (photo 5) and replant at that depth. To prevent losing the soil line while sloshing the plant in water, consider marking it with a permanent marker before you begin. Then set the root ball in a wide, but not necessarily deep, hole (photo 6). You may need a helper to hold the top of the plant so you can spread the roots and adjust the depth as you backfill the hole (photo 7).

title: Root Wash for a Better Start
content: Because there is no longer a heavy root mass, you might want to lightly stake a tall plant to keep it stable until it's established. And keep the area moist, not soaking wet (photo 8). Once all of the roots have been exposed, they will be more vulnerable to drying out than if they were left in their original potting mix. A couple inches of organic mulch spread around the root zone, but a couple inches away from the trunk or main stem can help. And you may need to check the soil (and possibly water) every day through the first growing season.

title: Root Wash for a Better Start
content: Check with your garden center before root washing. Check with your garden center. Because root-washed plants require extra care in the short term to get well established, some nurseries will not guarantee those that have been planted using this method. But if watered carefully, your new trees and shrubs should quickly anchor themselves, leaving no reason to utilize a nursery's guarantee.

title: Root Wash for a Better Start
content: Jim has employed this method of planting trees and shrubs for many years. It takes a little more time and energy up front, but he's found it well worth the effort in the long run.

title: Root Wash for a Better Start
content: Technique photo showing a gardener gently teasing and redirecting roots after root washing.

title: Root Wash for a Better Start
content: Technique photo showing pruners trimming circling or damaged roots.

title: Root Wash for a Better Start
content: Once the potting mix is removed, it's likely you'll need a hole that's more shallow than the original pot.

title: Root Wash for a Better Start
content: Make a wide hole Once the roots are washed off and spread out, you may need to dig the hole wider. Take the time to do this so they won't be encouraged to start circling again.

title: Root Wash for a Better Start
content: Prepare to plant Set the plant in the hole and backfill around the roots. I like to fill partway, water the soil to settle it around the roots, then add more soil.

title: Root Wash for a Better Start
content: If a perennial is especially root-bound, this technique also works. But in most cases, it shouldn't be necessary.

title: Root Wash for a Better Start
content: Settle the shrub in Firm up the soil around the plant, ensuring that the crown or root flare isn't below soil level. Then water again to settle the soil, and remove air pockets around the roots. You may need to top with more soil once you've watered.

title: A View for Every Season
content: It's all about the view This amazing panorama that includes Mount St. Helens isn't the only attraction in Lisa Graff's backyard. Take a seat on the patio or in the gazebo to enjoy the ever-changing borders, listen to the bubbling fountain or gaze at the pond and watch the wildlife that comes and goes.

title: A View for Every Season
content: Photo of a gazebo and water feature in Lisa Graff's garden with golden fall foliage.

title: A View for Every Season
content: Terracing the slope near the patio using dry-stacked stone walls provided level areas that are easier to plant and maintain.

title: A View for Every Season
content: Considering herself an English garden groupie, Lisa Graff has visited the United Kingdom several times to see gardens and take design classes. So when she and her husband, Brad, built their home in the hills around USDA zone 8 Portland, Oregon, 15 years ago, it was a given that she'd include design elements from her favorite English gardens: a beautiful borrowed view, curved pathways, a water feature, borders packed with flowers and the dry-stacked stone walls in photo 2. And her passion for flowering plants inspired her to start her business, Lux Perennials Nursery.

title: A View for Every Season
content: Keeping the flowery beds to the edges of the backyard also preserves the mountain view for maximum appreciation. By choosing similar color palettes in shades of pink, purple and orange, the borders have a cohesive look even though they're on opposite sides of the yard.

title: A View for Every Season
content: An English garden wouldn't be complete without a few boxwoods, and Lisa has several small hedges that supply structure and color all year. She achieved a similar effect along the path in photo 4 using 'Purple Dome' New England aster. This densely growing hybrid works well as a substitute hedge because it stays upright.

title: A View for Every Season
content: To frame the view of Mount St. Helens, Lisa Graff centered a fountain and rill on the house so water flows down the slope and leads the eye toward the mountain. Gardeners without a mountain vista can borrow a view of a nearby flowering tree, stately evergreen, park or greenbelt by selectively pruning hedges, keeping a fence lower in one spot, or using colorful containers to direct attention outward.

title: A View for Every Season
content: Garden photo of colorful containers and stone steps in a coordinated seasonal entrance.

title: A View for Every Season
content: A tidy concrete border helps the rill fit into the contemporary home and patio's style.

title: A View for Every Season
content: At the bottom of the slope is a gazebo near the pond. It's one of Lisa's favorite places to sit, even on a rainy day. She can read a book or enjoy the peaceful scene of the pond and wild wooded area just beyond. The subtle colors and natural features contrast with the borders packed with colorful blooms behind her.

title: A View for Every Season
content: Create a colorful hedge This row of neatly mounded 'Purple Dome' New England asters supplies a leafy green edge for the path in summer and by fall is covered in blooms that late-season pollinators can enjoy too.

title: A View for Every Season

title: A View for Every Season

title: A View for Every Season

title: A View for Every Season
content: Dahlias are a staple in Lisa's fall borders, and though they're cold hardy in her zone 8 garden, she used to lose them regularly to rot because of the dense clay soil. After talking with nursery professionals that specialize in dahlias, she discovered this method that helps them survive: At planting time in spring dig a wide hole 6 to 7 inches deep. Mix equal parts native soil, compost and clean quarter-ten gravel (gravel with no sand in it) in a wheelbarrow. Partially refill the hole so the tuber sits 4 to 5 inches deep, and refill with more of the mixture. Add a 3-inch layer of gravel mulch to keep crowns from getting too wet.

title: A View for Every Season
content: Photo of a red dahlia bloom with a note about sturdy support.

title: A View for Every Season
content: The wisteria-draped pergola creates an eye-catching entry for one of the borders, especially in spring. Walking the path underneath this huge vine creates anticipation as more of the planting is revealed.

title: A View for Every Season
content: The backyard was full of clay soil when they moved in, so Lisa needed to do something if she wanted to grow all the plants on her wish list. Amending it with compost at the beginning and topping it off every two to three years has improved the texture, and the plants are thriving.

title: A View for Every Season
content: Easy-to-find long-blooming plants, such as hardy geranium, Jupiter's beard, geum, catmint and sage, make up most of the plantings. Unusual specimens, such as the ornamental rhubarb that's blooming in photo 5, punctuate the more common finds. Once the spikes fade, the plants' enormous leaves take center stage. In other parts of the garden, Jerusalem sage, tall Peruvian lilies and 'Red Feathers' echium grab attention.

title: A View for Every Season
content: Throughout the garden, different types of hydrangeas-bigleaf, smooth, oakleaf and panicle-provide large, beautiful flowers from June to October.

title: A View for Every Season
content: Foliage plays an important role at every level of this garden. Lisa loves how burgundy-leaved plants, such as 'Royal Purple' smokebush and Wine and Roses and Spilled Wine weigela, help all the hot pink and orange flowers really pop.

title: A View for Every Season
content: Lisa Graff plans for a succession of blooms so the garden has color from April to November. In one border, geum and Jupiter's beard provide bright orange and deep pink flowers early, Rozanne hardy geranium blooms for up to five months through late fall, and towering dahlias and panicle hydrangeas take over by late summer.

title: A View for Every Season
content: Japanese maples add both foliage color and distinctive growth habits to Lisa Graff's garden. 'Twombley's Red Sentinel' grows in a narrow column 10 to 12 feet tall and 3 to 5 feet wide, 'Inaba Shidare' has a weeping form with delicate red leaves and reaches 6 to 8 feet after 10 years, and 'Sango-kaku' coral bark maple has coral-pink stems after its lacy yellow leaves drop in late fall.

title: A View for Every Season
content: Garden photo of a long-lasting border with shrubs, paths and late-season color.

title: A View for Every Season
content: Rejuvenate plants for long-lasting appeal Most of the Rozanne geraniums stay flowery and compact without any help. But if yours get leggy with fewer blooms, cut them back by a third for another colorful show by fall.

title: A View for Every Season
content: Besides colorful foliage, 'Sango-kaku' Japanese maple (also called coral bark maple) sports coral-pink stems that are most prominent once its lacy yellow leaves drop in late fall.

title: A View for Every Season
content: Seeds and berries add to the seasonal interest and support wildlife too. For example, rugosa roses offer months of color, first with pink flowers in spring and summer, then with the large red to purple hips in photo 7 in fall and winter.

title: A View for Every Season
content: Hip, hip, hooray Rose hips are red and ripe in fall but age to deep purple or black by winter - if they last that long. Lisa finds that the birds eat them up before the season ends. You can eat them too if you like the tangy sweet flavor. Fresh rose hips are high in vitamin C and antioxidants and can also be used to make jam or jelly.

title: A View for Every Season
content: Full-page garden photo with pergola, paths and vibrant late-season border planting.

title: A View for Every Season
content: Tree challenges There are lots of trees in this part of the yard, but Lisa works around and with them. She does find that in some spots, competition from roots means a new plant needs more watering. If it's wilting too often, she moves that plant and looks for one that's more drought tolerant.

title: A View for Every Season

title: A View for Every Season
content: In the front yard Lisa added borders several years ago so she could experiment with different plant combinations. She's come up with a formula to ensure each border has plenty of variety and interest but is still harmonious. Here's a look at her design technique.

title: A View for Every Season
content: Starting with flower shape, Lisa looks for a few plants with big round blooms, such as peony, allium or hydrangea, to create a pool of color in the border.

title: A View for Every Season
content: Combine the round flowers with spire-shaped blooms like the anise hyssop and salvia at left, to create a visual tension that's always interesting.

title: A View for Every Season
content: Groups of the same plant boost the impact in a border and ensure it's cohesive. Plus it can make some flowers, such as this slender persicaria, easier to see than if there were just one or two.

title: A View for Every Season
content: Tall garden photo of a mixed border with blue-green foliage and warm flower color.

title: A View for Every Season
content: warm up a cool season Lisa loves the changing blooms of 'Pinky Winky' panicle hydrangea that start out white and end the season this dusky shade of pink. 'Dragonberry' dahlia picks up the pink tones of the hydrangea blooms for a warm contrast that's cooled off by the purple geranium below.

title: A View for Every Season
content: show off dahlias Combining strong colors and bold textures is a sure way Lisa has found to get head-turning combos. Castor bean's large burgundy palmshaped leaves stand out among the surrounding green foliage and make the beautiful coral blooms of 'Intrigue' dahlia really pop. For dahlias, her husband, Brad, welds circular plant supports-sold at their nursery and used in their own garden-to keep the heavy blooms upright.

title: Repetition, Repetition, Repetition
author: Lisa Nunamaker
content: Repeat, repeat, repeat. As a landscape architect and teacher of garden design, this simple advice is something I often share with new designers. In outdoor spaces, it can be tempting to add a variety of elements, but repetition is what brings a design together. Using the same shapes, colors and materials helps create a sense of unity and adds rhythm and visual interest. The result is a space that's not only more visually appealing but also easier to understand and navigate. You can see this principle at work in the garden at left. Here, repeated ornamental grasses, allium blooms and rusty orbs create rhythm and unity while adding just enough variety to keep the look lively and engaging.

title: Repetition, Repetition, Repetition
author: Lisa Nunamaker
content: As in other design disciplines, repetition in a landscape brings structure to creativity. When elements are echoed, they turn a scattered collection into a cohesive, intentional and welcoming environment.

title: Repetition, Repetition, Repetition
author: Lisa Nunamaker
content: Follow along and I'll show you some practical ways to incorporate this powerful tool into your garden.

title: Repetition, Repetition, Repetition
author: Lisa Nunamaker
content: Consider using rounded or columnar plants but varying their sizes throughout your garden. The variation in photo 3 creates a flowing rhythm, where the echoing of form remains constant, but the change in scale introduces movement and interest. Similarly, you could use a single style of obelisk, but place them at varying heights in different areas of the garden.

title: Repetition, Repetition, Repetition
author: Lisa Nunamaker
content: Repetition also doesn't have to be rigid or overly symmetrical. In fact, varying the spacing of repeated elements can create a dynamic rhythm that keeps the eye engaged. Yes, you can plant in straight lines, but also try arranging plants or features in staggered, irregular or wavelike patterns. This approach is more organic and less predictable.

title: Repetition, Repetition, Repetition
author: Lisa Nunamaker
content: Groupings or drifts of the same plant type help guide the eye through a space. By strategically repeating key plants across different areas of the garden, you establish a sense of continuity and rhythm.

title: Repetition, Repetition, Repetition
author: Lisa Nunamaker
content: Though repetition is a key tool in garden design, too much of the same thing can make a space feel flat or predictable. Maintain consistency while introducing subtle variations so the space keeps unity without feeling dull.

title: Repetition, Repetition, Repetition
author: Lisa Nunamaker
content: The container garden in photo 2 highlights the use of repetition in its simplest form. But this doesn't have to mean uniformity in size or shape. By repeating a plant or element in different scales (small, medium and large) you can create a dynamic, visually engaging rhythm that still maintains a sense of unity. This adds depth and dimension.

title: Repetition, Repetition, Repetition
author: Lisa Nunamaker
content: Groupings of upright evergreens in this black planter create a calm, unified rhythm, perfect in a formal garden.

title: Repetition, Repetition, Repetition
author: Lisa Nunamaker
content: For a more organic approach to repetition, plant ornamental grasses in flowing curved lines that mimic wind or water rather than in a straight row. When repeating plant groupings, vary the numbers by using threes, fives and sevens instead of duplicating one group size throughout; this keeps the design lively while preserving continuity.

title: Repetition, Repetition, Repetition
author: Lisa Nunamaker
content: While repetition creates a strong backbone in the garden, seasonal change is what keeps it alive and evolving. One way to balance both is by repeating structural, year-round elements, like evergreen shrubs, ornamental grasses or hedging, then layering in seasonal performers that shift throughout the year.

title: Repetition, Repetition, Repetition
author: Lisa Nunamaker
content: For example, a row of multiple evergreen shrubs like the one in photo 4 can anchor a border year-round, while spring bulbs emerge in between for a burst of early color, followed by summer perennials and late-season grasses or seedheads. Though the underlying structure stays the same, the look changes with each season. This strategy not only enhances visual interest but also supports pollinators and local wildlife throughout the year.

title: Repetition, Repetition, Repetition
author: Lisa Nunamaker
content: A limited color palette can help unify diverse areas of a garden, making them feel like parts of a whole rather than isolated zones. Color repetition also sets a mood. For instance, the cool blues in the garden in photos 5 and 6 create a calm, serene feel, while warm reds and oranges would bring energy and vibrancy.

title: Repetition, Repetition, Repetition
author: Lisa Nunamaker
content: Using slightly different shades or tones within the same color family often creates a richer, more dynamic effect. For example, a purple-themed garden could combine soft lavender, smoky mauve, vibrant violet and deep plum tones. These subtle shifts in hue add depth and variety, while still tying the planting scheme together.

title: Repetition, Repetition, Repetition
author: Lisa Nunamaker
content: The repetition doesn't have to be all in one medium to be effective. Use similar color tones through flowers, foliage, containers, and painted garden accents to reinforce a theme while giving the eye small surprises to discover. It's one of my favorite ways to create interest without sacrificing unity. It works on a large scale, throughout an entire garden, as you can see in photos 5 and 6, or even in a container grouping, as in photo 7.

title: Repetition, Repetition, Repetition
author: Lisa Nunamaker
content: Using the same materials across features like paving, walls, furniture, containers, pergolas and fences can create a seamless flow throughout the landscape. For example, repeating a specific type of stone or wood in both pathways and patio areas helps visually link different zones, even if their functions vary. In the garden in photo 8, this approach is carried from the patio to the bench. Even smaller elements, such as matching hardware finishes on gates and furniture, or consistently styled planters, can unify.

title: Repetition, Repetition, Repetition
author: Lisa Nunamaker
content: Even if you repeat a material, don't be afraid to change up the pattern to introduce subtle contrast from one area to the next.

title: Repetition, Repetition, Repetition
author: Lisa Nunamaker
content: Red brick could be laid in a basket-weave pattern for a patio, adding visual texture and complexity, while appearing in a simple running bond along garden paths for a cleaner, more directional look. The material ties the spaces together, but the shift in pattern keeps the design from feeling static or overly uniform. This approach works equally well with wood decking or flagstone, and is especially useful when transitioning between areas that are used differently within a garden.

title: Repetition, Repetition, Repetition
author: Lisa Nunamaker
content: Repetition often works best when paired with small changes. By keeping one element consistent while varying another, you maintain a sense of unity while adding layers of interest. This approach is especially useful in smaller gardens, where too much variety can feel chaotic, but too much sameness can feel dull.

title: Repetition, Repetition, Repetition
author: Lisa Nunamaker
content: For example, use the same style of planter throughout your garden, but fill each one with different plant combinations suited to their location; sun-loving plants in one, shade-tolerant varieties in another. Or swap this idea by using different planters but filling them all with the same plant.

title: Repetition, Repetition, Repetition
author: Lisa Nunamaker
content: Repeating curves, circles, rectangles or organic lines creates rhythm and reinforces style in patio edges, paths and beds. Straight lines tend to feel formal and curves feel relaxed, but a repeated geometry can organize informal plantings too; Lisa Nunamaker's garden uses a series of rectangles, while a pollinator theme garden repeats hexagon shapes in paths, raised beds and a patterned wall.

title: Repetition, Repetition, Repetition
author: Lisa Nunamaker
content: Repetition is one of the simplest and most powerful tools in a garden designer's tool kit. Whether it's used with plants, colors, materials or shapes, this principle brings order, beauty and a sense of flow to outdoor spaces. Just remember: Consistency creates harmony, and subtle variation keeps it interesting. So the next time you're designing or refreshing your garden, pause and ask-what could I repeat? You might be surprised how quickly your space begins to come together with clarity and purpose.

title: A Cozy Fall Garden Nook
content: Whether you have an empty garden bed or an eclectic collection of gardening odds and ends, one thing about the side of the garage is that it makes a great hiding place. Here's a plan for turning that space into a shady and private hideaway-a spot to lounge as the heat of summer drifts into the crispness of fall.

title: A Cozy Fall Garden Nook
content: This small-space garden doesn't cover a lot of ground, but it still contains a variety of growing conditions. Even though it's mostly a shade garden, sunny pockets here and there require some sun-loving plants too. It's a delicate, but interesting, balance to strike. Groups of ground cover sedum stretch across the sunniest spots in the front of the border, nearly reaching clumps of hostas and other classic shade perennials that thrive in the partly shaded spots along the garage and under the tree.

title: A Cozy Fall Garden Nook
content: Instead of making the classic straight border along the side of the garage, fan it out to make a right angle with the front corner of the garage and the back fence. Connect these two points with a wide curving edge. Then make the back corner of the garage the center point, and build the layers out from there so all of the plants are visible.

title: A Cozy Fall Garden Nook
content: Why not create a reading spot? Stash a weatherproof storage box in the side table and keep a pair of reading glasses and a book or your latest knitting project inside.

Clusters of spring bulbs could easily be worked into this garden if you want more early spring blooms, but the foliage alone will put on quite a show. Every shade garden needs some bright yellow foliage, in my opinion. The hostas and oakleaf hydrangea brighten the darkest corners of the garden throughout the growing season.

title: A Cozy Fall Garden Nook
content: By summer, flushes of flowers start to emerge among the corydalis, creeping sedum, oakleaf hydrangea, spireas and geraniums. After the first bloom, deadhead the spireas and geraniums to encourage a second flush of flowers. If the oakleaf hydrangea sprawls beyond its space, you can trim back wayward branches, but because the shrub blooms on old wood,

title: A Cozy Fall Garden Nook
content: prune immediately after flowers fade so new branches have time to set buds for next year. Sometimes corydalis needs to be cut back in the heat of the summer if the foliage starts to wane. But it will bounce back in time for a good fall show. Let the perennials remain in the garden as deep into the fall as you'd like and watch them all turn a shade of red, copper or gold. Even the solomon's seal brightens to a rich yellow with showy round blue berries. Wait to start garden cleanup until late winter or early spring. Then cut back any remaining foliage and trim back the spirea, because it blooms on new wood. Spread a thin layer of compost across the soil to give plants a boost for the season ahead. Though this garden needs your care to produce the best show of flowers, you can always depend on the foliage to flush with stunning color every fall.

title: Q&A
content: Thigmotropism is a plant's ability to respond to touch, such as a vine detecting and wrapping stems around a support or a Venus flytrap quickly closing when an insect touches the pads.

title: Q&A
content: Gypsum, or calcium sulfate, can help loosen heavy clay, but gardeners should test soil before spreading it because gypsum can throw nutrients and soil properties out of balance. For most gardeners, adding compost every year is a better way to improve soil texture without damaging nutrient balance.

title: Q&A
content: Iris borer control starts with understanding the life cycle. Female moths lay eggs on iris foliage in late summer to early fall, eggs overwinter on leaves, caterpillars hatch in spring, damage leaves, enter rhizomes by summer and create bacterial soft rot before pupating in soil.

title: Q&A
content: To break the iris borer cycle, trim iris leaves just above the rhizome after a hard frost, remove surrounding debris, press rhizomes to find soft damaged parts and throw infected debris in the trash.

title: Q&A
content: If cleanup is not enough for iris borers, spray an insecticide containing acephate, spinosad or permethrin when leaves are about 5 inches tall, or apply beneficial nematodes as borer eggs hatch when leaves are fully grown but before flowers open; keep the area moist and repeat nematodes about a week later.

title: Q&A
content: For daffodils that form larger clumps, shop for Narcissus cultivars described as naturalizing or good multipliers, buy the largest bulbs available, and plant them in full sun to light shade with good drainage.

title: Q&A
content: Before planting daffodils, add a low-nitrogen bulb fertilizer such as 4-10-10 or 3-6-6 under the bulbs. As foliage emerges each year, work fertilizer into the top 3 to 5 inches without damaging leaves and water it in.

title: Q&A
content: After daffodil blooms fade, let the foliage mature and die back naturally to feed the bulb. Daffodils prefer dry soil during summer dormancy, so avoid watering that area.

title: Q&A
content: Daffodil cultivars useful for naturalizing include 'Carlton', 'February Gold', 'Flower Record', 'Ice Follies', 'Minnow' and 'Tete-a-Tete'. All daffodil bulbs produce side bulbs as they establish, but some cultivars produce them faster.

title: Q&A
content: A spray of 1 part cow's milk to 2 parts water can help prevent powdery mildew and blackspot on roses, but it cannot cure already infected foliage. Spray leaf tops and bottoms to the dripping point once a week during the growing season.

title: Q&A
content: Milk spray may help because milk contains nitrogen and lactoferrin, which is believed to reduce fungal growth. It can also repel aphids, which spread plant diseases such as blackspot and powdery mildew.

title: Weed Watch: Giant Foxtail
content: Giant foxtail, Setaria faberi, is a fast-growing annual grass with bristly late-summer seedheads up to 7 inches long and 3/4-inch-wide leaf blades with dense short hairs. It grows 2 to 4 feet tall or more and can crowd desirable plants.

title: Weed Watch: Giant Foxtail
content: Giant foxtail was introduced from Asia and now occurs in nearly all 50 states, especially the eastern half of North America. It prefers full sun to light shade, and birds and rodents spread its seeds.

title: Weed Watch: Giant Foxtail
content: Control giant foxtail by hoeing or pulling its shallow roots before seed set; one plant can produce more than 1,000 seeds. Repeated mowing and spring preemergent herbicide can help, while nonselective herbicides are a last resort for large colonies.

content: 'Ha Ha Tonka' little bluestem, Schizachyrium scoparium, is a tough prairie-style grass for hot, dry spots. Its soft blue-green leaves are covered in tiny hairs that catch the light, while purple-brown seedheads fade to fluffy white and last into winter.

title: One Tough Native Plant: Ha Ha Tonka Little Bluestem
author: Stephanie Polsley Bruner
content: 'Ha Ha Tonka' little bluestem works in wild or prairie-style plantings, reaches about 2 feet tall in foliage and about 4 feet in bloom, and fits the middle of a border where airy stems reveal taller plants behind it.

title: One Tough Native Plant: Ha Ha Tonka Little Bluestem
author: Stephanie Polsley Bruner
content: Grow 'Ha Ha Tonka' little bluestem in full sun so it keeps stiff upright clumps. Water during the first summer, then expect drought tolerance with little special care; cut stems to 2 or 3 inches in early spring and divide every three to five years.

title: One Tough Native Plant: Ha Ha Tonka Little Bluestem

title: The Best Bulb-Planting Techniques
content: Let's face it-gardening requires a certain amount of planning ahead. Take bulbs, for example. Those classic spring bulbs we all love, like tulips, daffodils and hyacinths, need to be planted in the fall in much of North America. Finally, after a winter's worth of anticipation, up they come to welcome spring. Worth the wait, isn't it? But what do you need to do to get bulbs off to a good start?

title: The Best Bulb-Planting Techniques
content: Look for large, firm bulbs that feel heavy for their size. Soft or shriveled ones won't make it. However, a little bit of blue-gray mold won't hurt anything if it wipes off easily.

title: The Best Bulb-Planting Techniques
content: With tulips and other true bulbs, it's easy to tell. But with some plants that grow from corms, tubers, tuberous roots and rhizomes, it's a little trickier. Look for dried, stringy roots, fleshy finger roots or a ring of fat dots that will indicate the bottom of the bulb. On top, you may see tiny irregularly placed "eyes" or buds. But don't worry too much if you can't tell which way it goes-the bulb will figure it out eventually!

title: The Best Bulb-Planting Techniques
content: Nothing boosts your spirits in early spring like the first bulb foliage poking through the ground. But the honeymoon's over when the flowers are done and the foliage starts to fade. You can, however, disguise the ratty-looking leaves until they're completely yellow and it's OK to snip them back. David Jones from South Carolina always combines ornamental grasses with his spring-blooming bulbs. When the bulbs first emerge, the grasses are still dormant. But after the bulbs bloom, the grasses' foliage is large enough to help hide the yellowing leaves.

title: The Best Bulb-Planting Techniques

title: The Best Bulb-Planting Techniques
content: Most bulbs have a thin, dry tunic that helps them retain moisture. If it's still attached, smooth and glossy, the bulb is probably in good shape. But it's fine even if the tunic is missing, as long as the bulb isn't shriveled or soft.

title: The Best Bulb-Planting Techniques
content: Photo of a gloved hand planting mixed spring bulbs in soil.

title: The Best Bulb-Planting Techniques
content: Bulbs like plenty of sun when they're blooming, although it's OK if the area is shaded when they're dormant. Most also like well-drained soil.

title: The Best Bulb-Planting Techniques
content: The rule of thumb is to plant a bulb three times as deep as its height if you want it to come back year after year. After you plant, spread a 1/2- to 1-inch layer of grit over the top of the hole to prevent squirrels from digging up your hard work.

title: The Best Bulb-Planting Techniques
content: In cold zones, you'll plant spring-blooming bulbs in fall. Wait until after the first hard frost, but before the ground freezes. Once the soil has frozen, add 3 to 4 inches of mulch. (Your goal is to keep the soil at a constant temperature, not to keep it "warm.") Bulbs need several weeks of cold to start to grow, so in warmer climates, you may have to buy spring bulbs prechilled, plant them in late winter and just treat them as spring annuals.

title: The Best Bulb-Planting Techniques
content: Frustratingly, squirrels love going after the bulbs in fall, when they're freshly planted and the soil is still loose. Luckily, there are easy things you can do to protect your spring bloomers from becoming dinner this season.

title: The Best Bulb-Planting Techniques
content: The best way is to prevent the squirrels from reaching them. Plant up a bed, then lay down a sheet of chicken wire over it. Stake it in place along the edges with small loops of wire, and let it sit all winter. Squirrels won't be able to dig through the small holes, and if you pull it up in early spring, it won't interfere with the new bulbs' foliage. Or, if you're just planting a few bulbs here and there, create "sleeves" for them by cutting out the bottom of old nursery pots. Plant the pots, then put the bulbs inside them, fill with soil and cover with chicken wire. This way, squirrels won't be able to reach the bulbs from any direction.

title: The Best Bulb-Planting Techniques
content: Using the right tool makes a big difference when planting. Take your soil structure, bulb size and how many you have to plant into consideration before you start.

title: The Best Bulb-Planting Techniques
content: Simply tighten this attachment into your drill and you can dig a lot of holes without much effort. Augers work well in lawns and even tough garden soil (but stay away from tree roots and hard-packed clay). Just make sure you're using a 12-in. or shorter length auger (this one is 7 in.), and remember to wear eye protection. The longer ones are more likely to bend when the going gets tough. However, the longshafted augers are more comfortable to work with (you don't have to lean over as much), and they're fine if you're working in prepared soil.

title: The Best Bulb-Planting Techniques
content: A traditional bulb planter is handy because it digs the right size hole and gives you planting depth at a glance. The long-handled version at right is easy on your back and knees. Step on it to plunge the digging end into the soil, then squeeze the handle to release the "core" of soil. Wear sturdy shoes so you don't bruise the bottom of your foot. It works best in prepared soil and pretty well in turf because you can put your body weight into digging. But don't use it in heavy clay. It would smooth and compress the sides of the hole, making future root growth more diffi cult.

title: The Best Bulb-Planting Techniques
content: For minor bulbs like grape hyacinth, crocus and snowdrops, you don't need a big planting hole. In soft, prepared soil or containers, as you can see, a dibble works perfectly: Slip it into the soil to the depth you want, rock it back to open a hole, drop in the bulb, slide the blade out and close the hole up again. If your soil is a little heavier, or if you're starting a patch of naturalized crocus in your lawn, try the soil knife instead. It works just like the dibble does, but it's a little sharper and has a longer blade, which makes it easier to open a hole in less "fluff y" soil.

title: The Best Bulb-Planting Techniques
content: The trick to adding to your garden every year is keeping the look and color scheme cohesive - and not digging into a clump of dormant bulbs! Pamela Ritz plants something new in her Indiana garden every year, so she marks the placement and hue of each spring-blooming bulb with a color-coded rock painted to match the flower. title: In the Weeds: Debugging Outdoor Plants
author: Jamie Seitz
content: After a long, luxurious summer season on the patio, the saddest day in a house plant's life is when it is dragged back indoors before the first frost. I imagine it's similar to how I feel when forced to return from vacation. All I want to do is lounge under a beach umbrella and live my best life, like the indirect sun-loving monstera that I am, when all that's waiting at home for me is laundry and dinner chores. (And my kids, of course.)

title: In the Weeds: Debugging Outdoor Plants
author: Jamie Seitz
content: I'm empathetic to each house plant's inevitable winter depression. After all, even the sunniest spot in your home is still substantially darker than the shadiest spot outdoors. So, when they wilt in spirit, I wilt. I understand that when their soil dries out more quickly, it's because the furnace is on. (The amount of lotion I use in winter is embarrassing.) But I have less compassion when it comes to one thing: the bugs.

title: In the Weeds: Debugging Outdoor Plants
author: Jamie Seitz
content: Although I know in my heart that insects are a part of nature and life, I despise the creepy-crawly pests that come in each fall.

title: In the Weeds: Debugging Outdoor Plants
author: Jamie Seitz
content: Every summer, I promise myself I will be proactive about debugging the house plants. But the first frost almost always sneaks up on me, and I call my entire family to line up like a fire brigade to help me get the plants indoors before they die.

title: In the Weeds: Debugging Outdoor Plants
author: Jamie Seitz
content: But last fall, I was on it. First, I filled a large tub with 9 parts water and 1 part gentle dish soap. Then I dunked each plant in the tub one by one, soaking the entire pot and as many of the leaves as would fit. After all the plants had been dunked, I sprayed them well with water, carefully rinsing the leaves' undersides to remove any excess soap or well-hidden critters. Later, after they had dried, I sprayed each house plant down with neem oil before bringing them into the sunroom to acclimate. What a responsible plant owner I am!

title: In the Weeds: Debugging Outdoor Plants
author: Jamie Seitz
content: I'll be honest: With the ridiculous number of house plants I have, this process took a bit of time. But I had far fewer insects making a break for it in my house than in years past, and every plant was happy to get a good soak and bath after a long summer outside. Maybe next year I'll invite some friends and make a party out of it. Who wants to join me?

title: In the Weeds: Debugging Outdoor Plants
author: Jamie Seitz
content: One of Jamie's biggest flexes is that her two adult children have become proud plant parents. Nothing is more satisfying than chatting about propagation stations and hitting up a new plant store with your kids while visiting them.

title: Reader Tips
author: Tingshu Hu, MA
content: Tingshu Hu grows pennywort, Hydrocotyle umbellata, as an indoor water garden in glasses, vases and bowls without drainage holes. A layer of clay pebbles holds stems upright, and care is simply adding water up to the pebbles every week or so; the transparent glass makes moisture levels easy to check.

title: Reader Tips
author: Kay Delano, TX
content: Kay Delano protects heat-stressed hostas in North Texas by shading them from harsh afternoon sun with umbrellas. She pounds a 2-foot-long metal stake into the soil and secures each umbrella handle to the stake with duct tape.

title: Reader Tips
author: JoAnne Rando-Moon, UT
content: JoAnne Rando-Moon supports delicate stems by cutting the bottom off a clear disposable plastic cup, slitting the side, slipping it around the stem and taping the cut sides together. The clear collar can support a house plant, newly planted perennial or cutting while it grows.

title: Reader Tips
author: Lori Rebenitsch, SD
content: When strawberries in raised deck planters developed sunburn, Lori Rebenitsch moved the plants into 12 1/2-inch square containers and slid them under the raised planters. The plants stayed warm but out of direct sun and produced well.

title: The Wild Side: Winter Happy Hour for the Birds
author: Joanna Brichetto
content: Cedar waxwings are named for the Eastern red cedar fruit they rely upon, and for the red tips on secondary wing feathers.

title: The Wild Side: Winter Happy Hour for the Birds
author: Joanna Brichetto
content: Photo of cedar waxwings perched in winter branches, paired with the Wild Side story about fruiting native plants that feed birds.

title: The Wild Side: Winter Happy Hour for the Birds
author: Joanna Brichetto
content: A t daybreak, there are hundreds of robins above the sidewalks: robins coming to town, leaving town, staying, and all of them are eating hackberry fruit. Gobbling, gorging on hackberries. This is a bumper year and birds know. Robin throats are busy with cheers and chirrs and yeeps and cucks, and there are cedar waxwings, too, whistling way up where the sun touches the tops of trees. I doubt birds can sound happier.

title: The Wild Side: Winter Happy Hour for the Birds
author: Joanna Brichetto
content: Every winter morning starts with a happy hour. Not just for me-happy to be out of bed and onto the sidewalk-but for the birds. After a long, cold and hungry night, they are ready for a breakfast buffet.

title: The Wild Side: Winter Happy Hour for the Birds
author: Joanna Brichetto
content: Here in my Nashville neighborhood, breakfast for robins is heavy on the hackberry but also Eastern red cedar, American holly, winterberry, a few spicebush and sumac, and today I found some withered pokeweed on the interstate bridge. There is mistletoe in the American elms, Virginia creeper in the trash alley, coralberry in a neighbor's yard and the black chokeberry I planted in mine.

title: The Wild Side: Winter Happy Hour for the Birds
author: Joanna Brichetto
content: Robins and cedar waxwings don't eat seeds, nor do Eastern bluebirds, hermit thrushes and other birds that need fruit and insects even in winter. They get what they need from native plant drupes and berries, and from all sorts of small creatures hosted in stem, leaf, bud, bark or gall. Winter hummingbirds pluck spiders from dead frostweed. Golden-crowned kinglets glean prey from pine needles. Robins head-butt raked leaves to find snack after snack of overwintering insects, worms and other little invertebrates.

title: The Wild Side: Winter Happy Hour for the Birds
author: Joanna Brichetto
content: Watching birds gives me joy, but helping birds makes me happy. What's the difference? Here's the quote from Annie Dillard that convinced me: "Dedicate [donate, give all] your life to something larger than yourself and pleasure-to the largest thing you can... Happiness lies this way, and it beats pleasure hollow."

title: The Wild Side: Winter Happy Hour for the Birds
author: Joanna Brichetto
content: At home, our hackberry tree and three bird baths give robins a mini happy hour every morning. Birds gobble fruit, then grab a drink and a wash. Overhead, they carol - cheerily, cheery-up! - but on the ground, they squawk and call and sometimes fight. It is fascinating to see two robins face off at a bath: sidestepping, sizing up, then darting with open beaks like double daggers. And then a blue jay swoops from nowhere, and all the robins disappear, poof!

title: The Wild Side: Winter Happy Hour for the Birds
author: Joanna Brichetto
content: The baths are just plastic saucers in the driveway: another small effort that pays off big. As the sun comes up, I wait for a lull in traffic noise, then raise the kettle high to let warm water fall and splash. Birds can't resist the sound of water. If the saucers freeze, I bring a refill, then watch steam rise as birds descend. What joy to see dozens of cedar waxwings appear at once, like magic, and crowd the rims of the saucers - a solid circle of birds on each - while they drink and drink, heads rising and dipping in sudden silence: no more high, sighing whistles until they flit back up to the trees, to the fruit, to the sunshine, happy.

title: The Wild Side: Winter Happy Hour for the Birds
author: Joanna Brichetto
content: My own "largest thing" is native habitat: to learn about it and to make more where I can. Too many sidewalks take me past silent, manicured turf and the usual exotic "foundation" shrubs that aren't foundational to our local food web. I've learned that even the smallest effort can make big changes, and that what's good for birds is good for all of us: the right food, clean water, enough space, a place to raise young. If birds ain't happy, nobody's happy.

title: Fast Garden Facts: Anatomy of a Winter Porch Pot
content: If you are going to leave a pot out all winter with potting mix inside, use container materials that can withstand freezing temperatures, such as plastic, wood, fiberglass or metal.
