title: Fast Garden Facts: Anatomy of a Winter Porch Pot
content: Arrange a porch pot much like a floral bouquet. Start by poking evergreen branches into the potting mix to form the greenery base. Add twigs or logs for height. Create a focal point with a cluster of accents to draw your eye, then fill in gaps with colorful elements to unify the arrangement. Water it all in so the potting mix freezes the stems into place.

title: Fast Garden Facts: Anatomy of a Winter Porch Pot
content: If the potting mix is packed with roots - or frozen - use a large drill bit to bore holes for branches. Pouring hot water over frozen mix will also soften it, but be careful if your container is ceramic - a quick temperature change could crack the pot. A heating pad, electric blanket or even a blow-dryer also works to thaw the potting mix.

title: No-Fail Combos: Grow Where You're Planted
author: Stephanie Polsley Bruner
content: Many plants work across different North American regions, but gardeners may need to adapt. Tender perennials may be treated as annuals or grown in movable containers in cold climates, while warm-climate gardens may need more shade and water because plants bloom earlier and face more heat.

title: No-Fail Combos: Grow Where You're Planted
author: Stephanie Polsley Bruner
content: The Foliage for the Win shady-bed combination uses bronze sweet potato vine, variegated sedge, ostrich fern and sulfur-yellow snapdragons. In Maine, sweet potato vine is grown as an annual, while in frost-free climates it can be perennial; in zones 7 and warmer, give the fern, sedge and snapdragons part to full shade and steady water through summer heat.

title: No-Fail Combos: Grow Where You're Planted
author: Stephanie Polsley Bruner
content: Sweet potato vine, Ipomoea batatas, is a tender perennial with green, bronze, burgundy or nearly black foliage; full sun to part shade; 6 to 16 inches tall and 18 to 72 inches wide; hardy in USDA zones 8 to 11.

title: No-Fail Combos: Grow Where You're Planted
author: Stephanie Polsley Bruner
content: Variegated sedge, Carex 'Ice Dance', is a perennial with insignificant cream flowers and dark green foliage with bright white variegation; part to full shade; 12 to 16 inches tall and 12 to 24 inches wide; hardy in USDA zones 5 to 9.

title: No-Fail Combos: Grow Where You're Planted
author: Stephanie Polsley Bruner
content: Ostrich fern, Matteuccia struthiopteris, is a perennial with midgreen foliage; full sun to part shade; 3 to 6 feet tall and 5 to 8 feet wide; hardy in USDA zones 3 to 7.

title: No-Fail Combos: Grow Where You're Planted
author: Stephanie Polsley Bruner
content: Snapshot Yellow snapdragon, Antirrhinum majus, is a tender perennial with sulfur-yellow flowers from spring to early summer and again from early fall to frost; full sun to part shade; 6 to 10 inches tall and 10 to 12 inches wide; hardy in USDA zones 7 to 10.

title: No-Fail Combos: Grow Where You're Planted
author: Stephanie Polsley Bruner
content: Shade combination photo with bronze sweet potato vine, variegated sedge, ostrich fern and yellow snapdragons.

title: No-Fail Combos: Grow Where You're Planted
author: Stephanie Polsley Bruner
content: The Blazing Colors combination pairs cardinal flower and globe amaranth for bold flower-shape contrast and intense mid- to late-summer color in gardens with cold winters and hot, humid summers.

title: No-Fail Combos: Grow Where You're Planted
author: Stephanie Polsley Bruner
content: Globe amaranth blooms best in full sun, while lobelia usually prefers part shade but tolerates full sun with adequate water. In dry climates, site lobelia where supplemental water is easy. Hummingbirds visit lobelia, and gomphrena can be pinched when plants are about 6 inches tall to encourage branching and more blooms for fresh or dried flowers.

title: No-Fail Combos: Grow Where You're Planted
author: Stephanie Polsley Bruner
content: Starship Scarlet cardinal flower, Lobelia x speciosa, is a perennial with scarlet flowers on dark stems from midsummer to fall and bronze-green foliage; full sun to part shade; 20 to 24 inches tall and 8 to 12 inches wide; hardy in USDA zones 6 to 10.

title: No-Fail Combos: Grow Where You're Planted
author: Stephanie Polsley Bruner
content: Ping Pong Purple globe amaranth, Gomphrena globosa, is an annual with papery purple flowers from midsummer to frost; full sun; 16 to 20 inches tall and 8 to 10 inches wide.

title: No-Fail Combos: Grow Where You're Planted
author: Stephanie Polsley Bruner

title: No-Fail Combos: Grow Where You're Planted
author: Stephanie Polsley Bruner
content: The Cool Shades for a Sunny Spot combination pairs variegated sweet iris with Tiny Rubies dianthus. The iris foliage stays interesting after bloom, while the dianthus forms a dark green, spiky, semi-evergreen mat with pink flowers.

title: No-Fail Combos: Grow Where You're Planted
author: Stephanie Polsley Bruner
content: Variegated sweet iris and dianthus both prefer well-drained soil and full sun to part shade. Dianthus appreciates midday shade in warmer zones because foliage may die back if it gets too hot and dry.

title: No-Fail Combos: Grow Where You're Planted
author: Stephanie Polsley Bruner
content: Variegated sweet iris, Iris pallida 'Variegata', is a perennial with fragrant lavender flowers in late spring to early summer and green-and-white variegated foliage; full sun to part shade; 2 to 3 feet tall and 1 to 2 feet wide; hardy in USDA zones 4 to 9.

title: No-Fail Combos: Grow Where You're Planted
author: Stephanie Polsley Bruner
content: Tiny Rubies dianthus, Dianthus gratianopolitanus, is a perennial with fragrant double pink flowers in mid- to late spring; full sun; 4 to 5 inches tall and 6 to 12 inches wide; hardy in USDA zones 3 to 10.

title: Which Annual Is Right for You?
content: Impatiens, Impatiens walleriana, are shade annual favorites with long bloom, wide color range and undemanding habits. They work in the ground or containers, line walkways, encircle trees and fill space quickly when kept well shaded and watered.

title: Which Annual Is Right for You?
content: Impatiens bloom best with a couple of hours of morning sun but wilt if they get too hot. They need about 2 inches of water per week, more in containers, plus slow-release fertilizer at planting or water-soluble fertilizer every two to four weeks. Cut leggy plants back by about a third in midsummer.

title: Which Annual Is Right for You?
content: Impatiens blooms come in white, pink, magenta, red, orange, coral and lavender, with some double and picotee varieties. Plants have tender mid-green oval to elliptic leaves and mounded habits, usually 6 to 20 inches tall and wide.

title: Which Annual Is Right for You?
content: Impatiens cultivars include Beacon Orange, often sold in flats with good downy mildew resistance at 12 to 14 inches tall and wide; Rockapulco Appleblossom, a heat- and humidity-tolerant double impatiens 10 to 20 inches tall and 12 to 24 inches wide; and Musica Bicolor Dark Red, a double two-tone selection 10 to 15 inches tall and 15 to 20 inches wide.

title: Which Annual Is Right for You?
content: Browallia, Browallia spp. and hybrids, brings rich blue, purple or white star-shaped flowers to shade. It grows well in containers or in the ground, but because it is often sold in larger pots, it may be best reserved for containers near a deck or patio where hummingbirds can visit.

title: Which Annual Is Right for You?
content: Browallia blooms well in hot weather if kept shaded. It tolerates some morning sun, but too much sun scorches leaves. Feed with a balanced 10-10-10 fertilizer every three to four weeks in summer, keep moisture consistent and provide good drainage.

title: Which Annual Is Right for You?
content: Browallia is a tropical perennial hardy in USDA zones 9 to 11 but usually treated as an annual. It has dark green, slightly glossy oval-to-elliptic leaves, upright clumps 12 to 24 inches tall and wide, and star-shaped flowers with tubular throats.

title: Which Annual Is Right for You?
content: Browallia cultivars include Endless Illumination, with dark blue flowers that do not need deadheading; Endless Flirtation, with white flowers; and Blue Lady, with violet-blue flowers with white centers and a looser habit. title: Transform Your Garden with Stone
author: Marcia Westcott Peck
content: Transform Your Garden With Stone My "stone age" began in my childhood, when my dad would take our family on hikes to the creek behind our house. Each of us five kids "got" to pick out a flat cobblestone and carry it back home (with some complaining, of course). By the end of summer, we had a beautiful cobblestone path leading to our front door.

title: Transform Your Garden with Stone
author: Marcia Westcott Peck
content: They say childhood memories are strong and stay with you. That must be true, because in our garden, my husband Dennis and I have created cobble paths much like the one I helped make with my dad all those summers ago. My father is no longer with us, but his memory lives on.

title: Transform Your Garden with Stone
author: Marcia Westcott Peck
content: What you might not know-even if you read the column Dennis and I wrote for The Oregonian's Homes & Gardens section for a decade- is that stones play a huge role in our landscape. From stone paths to the front door to the mosaic paths, from crushed-rock patios to a fire pit with rock work reflecting the night sky and even the stone designs topping off containers, virtually every stone was handpicked at our local rock yard.

title: Transform Your Garden with Stone
author: Marcia Westcott Peck
content: Throughout our garden we have developed many stories and memories of our own. For example, our daughter, who never showed any interest in gardening when she was young, is now an avid gardener who grew 49 varieties of tomatoes from seeds last summer. Our son was married in our garden, and our beloved pets are buried under the cobblestones.

title: Transform Your Garden with Stone
author: Marcia Westcott Peck
content: Even though these projects have been a lot of work, I wouldn't change a thing. I'll show some of the hows and whys on the following pages, and I hope that you can be inspired by these creations, whether you have room for a mosaic patio or just enough space for a small pot topped with stone.

title: Transform Your Garden with Stone
author: Marcia Westcott Peck
content: When I first started experimenting with stone mosaics more than 30 years ago, I started with wet concrete. This was like playing a game of Whac-A-Mole, because as I pushed one stone down, another would pop up. Then I tried dry concrete, which was a game changer. If it was dry outside, I could even take a few days to create a mosaic. Over time, I learned to cut and carve stone with my tile saw and angle grinder, though you can make beautiful stone mosaics without doing that. The large 4-foot-diameter mosaic at left took about 12 hours to make. That's a big investment of time and effort, and it's a dusty job. But, like childbirth, you'll fall in love with the end result, forget the labor and have the mosaic for a lifetime.

title: Transform Your Garden with Stone
author: Marcia Westcott Peck
content: Be sure the area for your mosaic is level, then dig a hole 4 to 5 inches deep and 3 to 4 inches wider than the ultimate size of your design. Extra room on the outside will help support the mosaic as you're working on it. Don't worry about getting the shape just right-you'll cut the final shape later.

title: Transform Your Garden with Stone
author: Marcia Westcott Peck
content: The mosaic will have two layers: a bottom layer of all-purpose concrete, which has rock in it and allows it to expand and contract with temperature and moisture changes; and a top layer of mortar, which has a smooth finish. The illustration below right shows how it all goes together.

title: Transform Your Garden with Stone
author: Marcia Westcott Peck
content: Work when temperatures won't drop below 40 degrees F for an extended period, as concrete loses half its strength if it freezes within the first 48 hours after pouring.

title: Transform Your Garden with Stone
author: Marcia Westcott Peck
content: Put on a dust mask and gloves, then pour the bag of dry concrete into the hole. You will be surprised by how many bags you will use.

title: Transform Your Garden with Stone
author: Marcia Westcott Peck
content: This 4-foot-wide circular mosaic is part of a 60-foot-long path that took 3 years of off-and-on work to create.

title: Transform Your Garden with Stone
author: Marcia Westcott Peck
content: Materials for a dry stone mosaic include Quikrete all-purpose concrete (about 280 pounds for a 32-inch-diameter circular mosaic), Quikrete mortar (about 30 pounds), stone or tile for the design, and 1/4-inch crushed rock (about 25 pounds).

title: Transform Your Garden with Stone
author: Marcia Westcott Peck
content: Tools for a dry stone mosaic include a rubber mallet, dust mask, disposable gloves, shovel, concrete trowel, plastic sheeting, and optionally an angle grinder or tile saw.

title: Transform Your Garden with Stone
author: Marcia Westcott Peck
content: Technique image for making a dry stone mosaic, showing a circular stone design and dry concrete or mortar base materials.

title: Transform Your Garden with Stone
author: Marcia Westcott Peck
content: Level the dry concrete with a concrete trowel, then add about an inch of dry mortar on top. The concrete and mortar at the center of the mosaic should be slightly higher (1/2 to 1 inch) than the edges, which should be level with the ground to ensure water runs off and does not pool.

title: Transform Your Garden with Stone
author: Marcia Westcott Peck
content: Now you're ready to make your mosaic. Slowly and gently add rocks to the dry concrete-I lightly tap them about half way into the dry concrete with a rubber mallet. They may be tightly packed or have space between each stone. The nice thing about working with dry concrete is you can take your time and move stones around, then use a fine brush to remove any concrete covering them. I used to think I needed to finish a project in one day: I'd make 3- to 4-foot-diameter mosaics and be up until 1:00 a.m. with floodlights and a tile saw. Now, I take a couple of days to finish and just cover it overnight with plastic, putting up a barricade of outdoor chairs so no critters can step on it. I learned the importance of that when I woke up one morning and found our dog, Roxanne, had left paw prints across my mosaic.

title: Transform Your Garden with Stone
author: Marcia Westcott Peck
content: Luckily, the concrete was dry enough and she was so small that there was no structural damage.

title: Transform Your Garden with Stone
author: Marcia Westcott Peck
content: I work with all kinds of stone and tile. If you live where winter temperatures get below 0 degrees F, avoid limestone, slate and other porous rock that is susceptible to the freeze-thaw cycle. Granite and quartzite are more cold-weather resistant.

title: Transform Your Garden with Stone
author: Marcia Westcott Peck
content: Finally, it's time to add water. Use the mist nozzle setting on your hose and slowly-and I can't stress the word "slowly" enough-mist the mosaic, never letting the water pool up and run off, which would mar the surface and weaken the mosaic. Instead, let the mortar and concrete act as a sponge. If you add too much water, the mixture loses strength, and if you under-water, it will wind up crumbly. Better

title: Transform Your Garden with Stone
author: Marcia Westcott Peck
content: to underthan overwater, though. A 30-inchdiameter mosaic can take 30 to 45 minutes of off-and-on misting. Now let the concrete slightly set for 30 to 60 minutes. If it's hot and in direct sun it will set faster than if it's in the shade.

title: Transform Your Garden with Stone
author: Marcia Westcott Peck
content: Next, carve the outer edge of the concrete into the shape of your design. I test to see if it's ready by carving a bit off the outer edge with a small concrete trowel. If the concrete is slightly hard, holds together and isn't crumbly or soft, I begin at the outer edge, taking a bit off at a time, and slowly work toward the design. Leave an inch or so of concrete border to help hold the stones in place. If the border chips a little, I patch it with mortar.

title: Transform Your Garden with Stone
author: Marcia Westcott Peck
content: The next day, water the mosaic gently in the space left after removing part of the border. This allows water to really soak in and ensure all the concrete gets wet.

title: Transform Your Garden with Stone
author: Marcia Westcott Peck
content: Keep your mosaic protected and stay off it for about five days to let it cure. Then take down the barricade and clean up any concrete you carved away. Backfill around the mosaic to the existing grade with 1/4-inch crushed rock for drainage.

title: Transform Your Garden with Stone
author: Marcia Westcott Peck
content: After the mosaic cures for about a month, I apply Miracle Sealants 511 Impregnator Sealer.

title: Transform Your Garden with Stone
author: Marcia Westcott Peck
content: When we dug out and leveled the area for our crushed rock dining patio, we needed some transitions from the higher area to the new patio below. I created the cobblestone wall above and the concrete and mosaic steps at left for easy access to the rest of the yard. The whole area came together as we incorporated the pots into the wall along with the planting bed above. We entertain a lot, and it's so magical to be in that space surrounded by the garden.

title: Transform Your Garden with Stone
author: Marcia Westcott Peck
content: We framed out the steps with 2x4s and mixed our own concrete, adding rock chips and carved stone on the surface of the treads.

title: Transform Your Garden with Stone
author: Marcia Westcott Peck
content: For the 18-inch-high wall, I dug a trench 6 inches deep and 12 inches wide for the footing, added 3 inches of 3/4-inch crushed rock to the bottom and placed the bottom row of 4- to 6-inch somewhat flat cobbles. Step each row back in a running bond pattern for stability. Leave 6 to 8 inches directly behind the wall and backfill it with 3/4-inch clean crushed rock as you stack the cobbles to hold the rocks in place. This crushed rock relieves hydraulic pressure and helps with drainage.

title: Transform Your Garden with Stone
author: Marcia Westcott Peck
content: As much as I love, love, love the wonderland of the rainy Pacific Northwest, which is where I have lived and gardened for the past 30-plus years, I am pulled at times to my roots in Southern California. Into our exuberant yard, we've tucked a 40-square-foot xeric rock garden next to our driveway.

title: Transform Your Garden with Stone
author: Marcia Westcott Peck
content: Into that area we mixed enough local crushed basalt, sand and compost in with our native clay soil to let it drain well and keep it from turning into adobe brick. The rock garden is on a natural slope, which we bermed for even better drainage. I've found that most of the rock garden plants don't die from the rain and cold but rather from poor drainage. Occasionally, when we have a real doozy of an ice storm, I cover our agave with blankets or plastic.

title: Transform Your Garden with Stone
author: Marcia Westcott Peck
content: I treat the rock garden as if it's a living art installation, moving, pinching and propagating succulents, cacti and xeric plants. And, of course, arranging rocks. That 40 square feet is constantly changing, and I hope it does for many years to come. Someone told me once that

title: Transform Your Garden with Stone
author: Marcia Westcott Peck
content: After years of making concrete mosaic stepping stones, I had buckets of leftover rocks and tiles. I started experimenting with placing them, sans concrete, in patterns in my potted plants. It takes minutes to do instead of the hours my concrete and stone creations take.

title: Transform Your Garden with Stone
author: Marcia Westcott Peck
content: If you don't have leftovers, buy bags of stones or handpick interesting flat rocks from the rock yard or craft store. I use both cut and natural stone to create designs like the container above. I buy travertine and slate floor tile from big-box stores, cut them into squares and rectangles with my tile saw and incorporate them into my designs. Just place them on top of the soil around your potted plant in patterns. It's that easy!

title: Epimedium
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: This tough shade perennial provides year-round, deer-resistant beauty where few others thrive.

title: Epimedium
author: Sherri Ribbey

title: Epimedium
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: When other perennials haven't shown the slightest intention of emerging or are just peeking through the soil in spring, epimedium is up and at 'em. Its dainty starburst blooms create a cloud of color that draws you out to the garden even on chilly days. Once the flowers are done, there's often a second flush of colorful spring leaves as plants begin to form a tidy mound of foliage for summer. Many varieties end the season with a brilliant fall show, and some are evergreen in mild winter areas. Easy to grow, deer resistant and drought tolerant once established, this underappreciated shade perennial has so much to offer!

title: Epimedium
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: More than 50 species of epimedium (also called barrenwort) thrive in the woodlands and shaded rocky areas of Asia, Europe and North Africa. Most gardeners grow hybrids or the easy-to-find species available at nurseries- there are lots to choose from. Karen Perkins, retired owner of Garden Vision Epimediums (epimediums.com), has cultivated this shadeloving perennial for decades. She says, "I love epimediums for their unique and delicate beauty, toughness and versatility. They're easy to grow, so they work not only for beginning gardeners but also for collectors of the weird and wonderful." Though no longer selling plants, Karen maintains her website to share all the information on different varieties and growing tips that she's compiled over the years.

title: Epimedium
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Epimedium is most known for its spidery blooms with long nectar-filled spurs like those of 'Pierre's Purple'. There are also flowers with short spurs and large sepals, such as 'Sulphureum', and a few, such as bell-shaped 'Lemon Zest', with almost no spurs at all. Flower colors include raspberry pink, pale yellow, deep purple with white spur tips, and solid white.

title: Epimedium
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Epimedium is a perennial with pink, white, yellow, red, burgundy, orange or lavender starburst-shaped blooms in early spring. Grow it in part to full shade and moist, well-drained soil; it has no serious pests, reaches 6 to 24 inches tall and 6 to 36 inches wide, and is hardy in USDA zones 4 to 9.

title: Epimedium
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: The photo of 'Pierre's Purple' at left shows what epimedium looks like in spring, with small leaflets accompanying the flowers. Larger mature leaves are starting to fill in from the crown. By summer, spring coloration fades and plants form a mound of pest- and disease-resistant foliage that doesn't require pruning to maintain a neat appearance throughout the growing season. Deciduous 'Pierre's Purple' will lose its foliage after the first hard frost, but semi-evergreen types will stay colorful into early winter and evergreen ones keep going into spring.

title: Epimedium
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: 'Pierre's Purple' thrives in this garden filled with lots of tree roots and visiting deer. Plants grow 9 to 18 inches tall and wide, with wine purple flowers.

title: Epimedium

title: Epimedium
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Cooler spring temperatures trigger burgundy, purple, red or bronze foliage colors on some varieties. Out-of-the-ordinary 'Bandit' has a thin purple edge, and 'Domino' in photo 2 has splashes of burgundy. As the foliage matures, the markings fade and leaves turn green.

title: Epimedium
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: While E. rubrum in photo 3 has the classic flush of red in spring, its green summer foliage also transforms into the colorful show you see in photo 4. It's a great companion for garden mums before the leaves die back after frost. Another deciduous type, 'Red Queen', has red-orange fall foliage. Evergreen 'Thunderbolt' turns purple-black with green veins and remains vibrant through winter. Snow cover and mild winters will protect the foliage in colder USDA zones 5 and 6. If they get winter burn, you can always cut stems back earlier than you usually would and the plants will be fine.

title: Epimedium
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Shade gardens can feel a little monotonous if there's not much variety, but epimedium's multiseason performance changes all that. In spring, wiry stems begin to unfurl into whimsical epimedium blooms, along with small, often colorful new leaves that brighten up the almost empty border. Flowers bloom just once, and Karen says that they'll last for up to two weeks if the weather stays cool. Blooms range in size from 1/4 to 2 inches in diameter, so you'll need a good-sized clump to see them from a distance. Its early bloom time bridges the gap between late winter's crocus and hellebores to later spring's bleeding heart and columbine. Individual stems form loose racemes that have just a few blooms to as many as 30, as with 'Pink Champagne'.

title: Epimedium
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: One of the great things about epimedium is that you can plant it and not worry about it. The flowers and foliage will provide subtle but reliable points of interest in shade all year.

title: Epimedium
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Epimedium has either a clump-forming or spreading habit. Some can thrive under a big, shallow-rooted tree, such as a Norway maple, and make a lush ground cover. If you're looking for the kind of coverage you see in photo 5, Karen recommends 'Sulphureum', 'Frohnleiten' or 'Thunderbolt'. They spread by runners about 4 to 8 inches per year, eventually growing into broad pools of colorful flowers and foliage. Clump-forming types grow a bit wider than they are tall, forming a dense mound that ranges in size from 10 to 18 inches wide.

title: Epimedium
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: The tapestry of foliage in photo 6 is just as vibrant and interesting as one filled with flowers. In summer, the showy hosta and bright 'Variegatum' bishop's weed strut their stuff while epimedium takes on a supporting role. It's a low-key companion that won't elbow other plants out of the border, but you can count on it to grab the limelight in other seasons. Heart-shaped leaves are most common and echo the shape of the hosta foliage, creating a laid-back mood for this shady border. For a little more drama, try lance-shaped evergreen varieties with toothed or spiny edges.

title: Epimedium
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Though not as widely known as shade classics such as hosta and impatiens, epimedium deserves more attention. It's tougher than those charming little blooms might suggest and has a range of interesting flower and foliage colors, sizes and shapes. Although with new varieties coming to the market every year, there's likely to be a wider selection than ever at your local garden center, you'll still find even more options through mail-order nurseries.

title: Epimedium
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Older varieties and species tend to have small blooms that sit below the leaves, where they're harder to see. In recent years plant breeders have been working to develop eye-catching colors and larger, longer-lasting blooms that sit high above the foliage. Check out the gallery at right for a selection of epimediums that will look great in your shade garden.

title: Epimedium
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Cut back old foliage before the delicate flower stems emerge and you can shear at ground level. But if stems are starting to poke through, as they are here, grab handfuls of the dry stems and cut a few inches above the ground with pruners so you don't accidentally cut off the blooms.

title: Epimedium
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: There's no real need to fertilize epimedium growing in organic rich soil. In fact, Karen warns that chemical fertilizers easily burn the foliage -she's seen growers lose whole crops after a chemical feed. In less-than-ideal growing conditions, an annual application of organic mulch will gradually break down, feeding both the soil and the plants. The only other thing this tough little plant needs to keep it looking good is an early spring cleanup. See how to do this in photo 7.

title: Epimedium
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: The ideal spot for epimedium is under the high canopy of a mature tree or at the edge of a border that gets morning sun or dappled shade. It thrives in well-drained soil with lots of organic matter and a pH that is more alkaline than acid, though some species and hybrids tolerate acid soil. Avoid full sun, which can scorch the foliage, and wet soil, which can cause the crown to rot. Because epimedium is slow to take off, do not pair it with quick-growing ground covers that can crowd it out.

title: Epimedium
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Photo showing how to cut back old epimedium foliage above emerging spring growth without damaging flower stems.

title: Epimedium
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Close-up epimedium cleanup photo showing new spring growth among last year's stems.

title: Epimedium
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Many other shade plants struggle in dry shade, but epimedium tolerates it quite well. It may take a bit longer to reach mature size or be a little less flowery there. Water regularly for the first year or so to get new plants off to a good start; afterward, plants only need a thorough soaking during long dry spells. Species from Europe and the Mediterranean, such as E. alpinum, E. pinnatum and their progeny, tend to be more drought tolerant than those from Asia.

title: Epimedium
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Dense roots can be hard to divide with your hands and hard to see unless you spray the soil off of the clump with the hose.

title: Epimedium
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Spreading rhizomes like this evergreen species are easy to divide - even when the plant is still in the ground. Just use a spade to slice through the soil and rhizomes.

title: Epimedium
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Epimediums vary in how densely their rhizomes pack together. This one's slightly elongated rhizomes make division a little easier.

title: Epimedium
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Spring is the best time to divide, while new growth is just emerging. That way you won't break the brittle stems. You can also divide in fall right up until the first frost, and divisions will still have a chance to root in before the soil freezes. Division isn't necessary to keep epimedium vigorous, but it's an easy way to get more of your favorite variety to spread around the garden or share with friends.

title: Epimedium
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Epimedium can reseed but not vigorously, and because plants are slow growing you have plenty of time to notice seedlings and then decide whether you want to pull or keep them. It takes three to four years before blooming starts, and there's no guarantee that it will look like the parent plant.

title: Epimedium
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Karen Perkins notes that epimedium rhizomes vary widely by species and variety. Clump-forming types grow very slowly and can form a dense woody knot that may need a pruning saw to separate. Other clump-formers have distinct rhizomes that are not elongated enough to spread much, so they can be sliced through or pulled apart to divide.

title: Epimedium
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Spreading rhizomes have a looser structure, so it's easy to dig up a part of the plant. Then use pruners to cut off a few new divisions. Even small pieces, like the ones in photo 10, will grow fine. Karen suggests removing a third of the foliage to help prevent too much water loss through transpiration when you're dividing in late summer or fall.

title: Epimedium
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Replant new divisions at the same depth they were growing, water them well and you'll have more epimedium flowering in your garden the following spring!

title: Regional Pest Roundup
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: We asked four experts which pests we should be watching for next year. Here's what they told us.

title: Regional Pest Roundup
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Stepping into the garden and discovering that the plants you've lovingly nurtured are now looking ragged, or even stripped bare, is incredibly frustrating. Voracious insect pests can quickly unravel your hard work and shatter your garden dreams. Finding the culprit is the first step to getting your garden back on track. While many pests are widespread, I talked with experts from various regions to find out which ones were causing the most trouble in their areas and what you can do about them. One thing they all agreed on: Tackling pest problems with integrated pest management (IPM) is easier on the environment and helps prevent pesticide resistance.

title: Regional Pest Roundup
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: This decision-making approach for pest control starts with low-environmental-impact strategies first, then steps up the strength of the response if necessary. For example, when you notice damage, use an insect identification app or check your county extension resources to pinpoint the culprit. Then decide how much damage you can tolerate. If you're willing to wait it out, many pest problems fizzle as the moisture or temperatures change, and most plants will bounce back with new growth in just a few weeks.

title: Regional Pest Roundup
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: If you find that a problem returns every year, the next level of prevention could include cultural practices, such as growing resistant varieties, rotating crops or using row cover or landscape fabric to prevent pests from laying eggs. If all else fails, the final step might be a targeted chemical control, whether it's organic or synthetic. The idea is to be strategic and only do the minimum necessary to deal with the most damaging pests in your garden.

title: Regional Pest Roundup
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Sherri has been battling Japanese beetles in her Midwest garden for years - they're especially fond of the rose of Sharon and roses. Handpicking them and dropping them in soapy water helps.

title: Regional Pest Roundup
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Pacific Northwest Mountain ranges create diverse growing environments here, with one side having fertile soil and regular winter rainfall, while the other is dry and arid.

title: Regional Pest Roundup
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: These red-brown ⅝-inch-long insects with long or short cerci (the pincerlike appendage in back) are most active in spring through fall and have one or two generations per year.

title: Regional Pest Roundup
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Slender green-bronze ⅜-inch-long flathead beetles are most active in early summer and produce one generation of 3/4- to 1-inch-long cream larvae per year.

title: Regional Pest Roundup
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Shiny green and bronze, this 1/3- to 1/2-inch-long beetle is most active in early to midsummer and produces one generation of C-shaped ⅛-inchlong white grubs per year.

title: Regional Pest Roundup
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: What it eats Though earwigs eat aphids and other insects, they also feed on seedlings, flowers, foliage, soft fruit and vegetables. Fast moving with a big tail-end pincer, this insect also has the startle factor when it darts out from under foliage or a container. Damage Earwigs are most active at night, chewing holes in fruit, flowers and leaves. This voracious pest can decimate entire plants or a row of seedlings in a single feeding, then hides during the day. IPM tips Professor Sanchez finds this homemade trap helpful in reducing earwig damage: She fills an empty 16-ounce plastic container about a third full with vegetable oil, adds a little soy sauce and cuts a few 1/2 -inch holes in the lid before putting it back on the container. Then she digs a hole and positions the container flush with the ground. The soy sauce lures earwigs into the trap, where the oil smothers them.

title: Regional Pest Roundup
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: What it eats This beetle is a serious problem in the Pacific Northwest, killing birch ( Betula spp. and hybrids) trees of all kinds, especially white-barked types. River birch ( Betula nigra ) seems to be somewhat resistant. Damage Sparse yellow foliage and twig dieback in the upper crown are an early clue that bronze birch borer larvae are burrowing through a tree and disrupting its nutrient flow. The decline can be reversed if you catch it early, but if more than 50 percent of the crown is damaged, it likely can't be saved. Look for small ⅛- to 1/4 -inch D-shaped exit holes in the bark where adults have emerged or zigzag lines on the bark. IPM tips Drought stress makes birch trees especially vulnerable.

title: Regional Pest Roundup
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Keep them growing strong by choosing a planting spot on the north or east side of the house, where it's cooler, watering during dry spells and providing a 2- to 3-inch layer of organic mulch.

title: Regional Pest Roundup
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: What it eats Japanese beetles have become common in the Eastern United States and Midwest but are only now making their way into the Pacific Northwest. It eats hundreds of different plants, but rose ( Rosa spp. and hybrids), canna ( Canna spp. and hybrids) and hibiscus ( Hibiscus spp. and hybrids) are some favorites. Damage Metallic-looking adults feed on the flowers and upper surfaces of leaves and skeletonize them. Flower petals have holes or are completely consumed. While the damage looks bad, it doesn't usually kill the plant. Larvae nibble on turfgrass roots below ground, which causes brown patches in the lawn. IPM tips Protect small plants with row cover from June to September when adults are active. You can also pick and drop adults into a bucket of soapy water. Avoid pheromone traps - they attract even more beetles.

title: Regional Pest Roundup
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: To create a less hospitable environment for egg laying and young larvae, don't water your lawn in mid- to late summer.

title: Regional Pest Roundup
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Even with hot, humid summers and winter temperatures that get below 0 degrees F, there are lots of pests to battle in Midwest gardens.

title: Regional Pest Roundup
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: These 1/2-inch-long yellow-green caterpillars with an orange head do all the damage and are active from spring to early summer. The adult looks like a fly but is actually a wasp.

title: Regional Pest Roundup
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: These tiny arachnids measure 1/50 of an inch long and range in color from rusty green to brown, yellow, red or orange with two black spots on their backs. They are most active from spring through summer and produce multiple generations per year.

title: Regional Pest Roundup
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: The 1-inch-long adults have brown forewings with black spots and black, white and scarlet hind wings. They're active from spring through fall and produce one generation of black to red nymphs per year.

title: Regional Pest Roundup
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: What it eats This pest eats all kinds of roses ( Rosa spp. and hybrids), but it is especially attracted to ramblers. Damage The caterpillar chews and scrapes the upper surface of leaves, creating a windowpane effect. Damage is mostly cosmetic and may diminish flowering, but it won't kill the rose. Professor Broderick noticed that populations were high in recent years but finds that they tend to peak and wane over time. IPM tips Handpick caterpillars early in the season or spray them off with a strong stream of water. Beetles, birds, parasitic wasps and small mammals will feed on the roseslug sawfly. Insecticidal soap can help but must come into contact with the larvae to work. Spray both the upper and lower leaf surfaces in early morning or early evening, when cooler temperatures keep the soap from drying too quickly, so more larvae are affected.

title: Regional Pest Roundup
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: What it eats First spotted in Pennsylvania in 2014, this colorful, invasive plant hopper is slowly spreading to other states. It feeds on more than 100 plant species, such as grape vines ( Vitis spp.), hops ( Humulus lupulus ), maple ( Acer spp. and hybrids) and fruit trees, along with a host of ornamental garden plants. Damage Both nymphs and adults use piercing mouthparts to feed, which results in oozing sap, wilting, leaf curling and dieback. They also produce honeydew, which smells bad as it ferments and attracts wasps, ants and bees. The damage doesn't usually kill plants but causes stress that allows other pests or diseases to move in. IPM tips Remove the weedy tree of heaven ( Ailanthus altissima ), as it is a favorite host plant. In fall, look for and remove the distinctive 1-inchlong egg masses, which look like smeared mud on tree trunks.

title: Regional Pest Roundup
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: What it eats Two-spotted spider mites are a problem for more than 200 plant species. Damage Adults and nymphs (juveniles that look like the adults but are smaller) use piercing mouthparts to feed on the undersides of leaves, which causes a stippled or mottled look. As populations rise, plants look bronzed or bleached, leaves and flowers become distorted and these spider relatives produce webbing often found on the undersides of the leaves. They thrive in dry growing conditions and temperatures above 90 degrees F. Healthy plants can withstand some mites, but stressed ones may succumb. IPM tips To prevent infestations, use mulch, choose drought-tolerant plants and don't fertilize during a drought. Spraying with water can help dislodge two-spotted spider mites from foliage.

title: Regional Pest Roundup
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: The long growing season in the Southeast means lots of flowers and a plentiful harvest - unless pests take over.

title: Regional Pest Roundup
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Eggs laid by the 1-inch brown Brazilian skipper butterfly hatch and grow into this 2-inch-long translucent green caterpillar with an orange head. Both are active in summer, and there are two generations per year.

title: Regional Pest Roundup
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Dark red females grow ⅞ of an inch long and are covered with a white feltlike covering. Active in spring through summer, they produce two to four generations of pink nymphs per year.

title: Regional Pest Roundup
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: The tiny ⅛-inch pale green cotton jassid has one dark spot on the back of each wing and moves diagonally, instead of straight ahead like most other insects. It's active in summer, and each year it can produce up to 11 generations of pale green wingless nymphs that look similar to the adults.

title: Regional Pest Roundup
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: What it eats Crape myrtle ( Lagerstroemia indica ) is by far the most common host for this invasive pest. Occasionally you'll find it on beautyberry ( Callicarpa americana ), St. John's wort ( Hypericum spp. and hybrids) and boxwood ( Buxus hybrids). Damage Females and nymphs feed on the sap of small branches, twigs of trees and shrubs, and cluster around pruning cuts, causing poor growth, fewer flowers and leaf drop. Stem dieback can occur when populations are high. Bees and wasps are attracted to the scale's honeydew, which can also cause sooty mold to develop. IPM tips Because of its covering, crape myrtle bark scale is a challenge to treat. This is still a relatively new pest, but researchers have found lady beetle larvae to be especially effective predators.

title: Regional Pest Roundup
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: What it eats Cannas ( Canna spp. and hybrids) are by far the favorite plant of this butterfly's pesky larvae. It will occasionally feed on Indian arrowroot ( Maranta arundinacea ). Damage The caterpillar secures part of the canna leaf around itself with a silk strand for protection while feeding. Generally, it stays on the same leaf, eating and molting before metamorphosing into a butterfly. Severe infestations can defoliate plants. IPM tips Handpick and squish the larvae to kill them. If you've had problems in the past, avoid growing red-leafed canna varieties and those with red or orange flowers. For large populations, spray Bt ( Bacillus thuringiensis ). The caterpillars have to ingest this for it to be effective, so apply liberally to thoroughly coat the leaf.

title: Regional Pest Roundup
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: What it eats Cotton jassid was first identified in Florida in 2024 and moved into Georgia and North Carolina in 2025. Cotton is a top choice for this invasive pest, but so is sunflower ( Helianthus spp. and hybrids), tropical hibiscus ( Hibiscus rosa-sinensis ), okra and eggplant. Damage You're likely to see the damage before noticing the insect, so if your plants have yellowing foliage that eventually turns redbrown, check the undersides of the leaves, especially around the third to fifth leaves from the terminal (the leaf at the end of the stem), for insects. Both nymphs and adults feed on sap. IPM tips Researchers are still looking for solutions. Spiders, lady beetles, ants and green lacewings are possible predators. If you find cotton jassid in your garden, contact your local extension agency.

title: Regional Pest Roundup
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Snow-covered winters and warm, humid summers create the ideal growing conditions for plants and pests.

title: Regional Pest Roundup
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: This 1/3-inch-long green-yellow plant bug has four black strips and is most active in late spring to early summer. The nymphs are bright red to orange with black spots on the abdomen.

title: Regional Pest Roundup
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: You're more likely to see the "bags," or cases, than the gray caterpillars with dark splotches inside them. The bags start small and get larger as the caterpillar grows and adds more foliage pieces. Bagworms are active in spring through summer, producing one generation per year.

title: Regional Pest Roundup
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: The small gray 1/8-inch-long flies have a yellow head and produce two generations of cream 5/16-inchlong larvae each year. They're most active in spring and fall.

title: Regional Pest Roundup
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Favorite plant The four-lined plant bug is a pest of more than 250 plant species but seems especially fond of plants in the mint family. Damage Both adults and nymphs use piercing mouthparts to feed on foliage. This causes black or brown spots that are often confused with fungal disease. In small numbers, four-lined plant bug feeding only makes the plants look bad. But with a big population, entire leaves can curl up and fall off. New growth may be deformed. IPM tips Insecticidal soap can get rid of nymphs. Handpick the larger adults. Dr. Legrand recommends holding a container of soapy water under infested foliage and tapping the plant so these fastmoving insects fall in and drown. Look closely at leaf stems for 2- to 3-inch-long scarring where females have made small slits to lay eggs. Remove these leaves and put them in the trash to prevent the next generation from developing.

title: Regional Pest Roundup
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Favorite plant Ornamental allium ( Allium spp. and hybrids), chives, garlic and leeks are beginning to be attacked by this new invasive pest in Northeast gardens. Damage In spring and fall, females lay eggs on the tips of allium leaves. The spring larvae tunnel through the leaves and leaf sheaths, causing disfigured foliage and creating openings for fungi and bacteria. In fall the larvae overwinter. IPM tips Insect netting or row cover can help prevent adults from laying eggs in spring. Keep an eye out for rows of white spots (the injury caused by egg laying) descending from leaf tips near the ends of the leaves, and remove any that you find. Rotate crops and clean up the garden in fall so larvae don't have a place to overwinter.

title: Regional Pest Roundup
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Favorite plant Bagworms are attracted to a wide range of conifers, including arborvitae ( Thuja occidentalis ), juniper ( Juniperus spp. and hybrids) and spruce ( Picea abies ). They'll also feed on deciduous trees, such as sycamore ( Platanus occidentalis ), honey locust ( Gleditsia triacanthos f. inermis ) and linden ( Tilia spp.). Damage Bagworm larvae eat the needles and foliage of their host tree. Though the damage is light at first, as the larvae grow they cause serious defoliation, which can be especially hard on evergreens. IPM tips Keep an eye out for the distinctive bags the larvae create from silk and bits of foliage from the host plant. Pull or cut them off and send them away in the trash. For larger trees or infestations, spray Bt when young bagworms emerge in late spring to early summer.

title: Regional Pest Roundup
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: A 2005 study at the University of Illinois found that bagworm-infested shrubs surrounded by flowering plants had 71 percent higher rates of parasitism on the bagworms than shrubs that didn't have flowers nearby. And while it's true that you can buy some predatory insect species, growing flowers whose pollen and nectar feed beneficial insects, such as lady beetles, hoverflies or predatory wasps, is a more reliable (and easier!) way to bring them in. For example, if your peonies attract adult tiphia wasps, they'll lay eggs on nearby adult Japanese and Oriental beetles. And the larvae of hoverflies and lady beetles are voracious predators of aphids, plant hoppers, caterpillars and other pests. Follow these tips and grow the plants at right to make your garden more attractive to beneficial insects.

title: Regional Pest Roundup
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Dill Anethum graveolens Tender perennial; airy yellow flowers on top of long stems from summer to early fall; full sun; 3 to 5 ft. tall, 2 to 3 ft. wide; cold hardy in USDA zones 7 to 11 Attractive to lady beetles, lacewings, ichneumon wasp

title: Regional Pest Roundup
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Goldenrod Solidago spp. and hybrids Perennial; plumes, spikes or long arching stems covered in small individual flowers from late summer to fall; full sun to part shade; 1 to 6 ft. tall, 2 to 3 ft. wide; cold hardy in USDA zones 3 to 9 Attractive to hoverflies, leatherwing soldier beetle

title: Regional Pest Roundup
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Peony Paeonia hybrids Perennial; single or double pink, white, purple, yellow or red blooms in early to late spring; full sun; 2 to 4 ft. tall and wide; cold hardy in USDA zones 3 to 8 Attractive to tiphia wasps

title: Regional Pest Roundup
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Pot marigold Calendula officinalis Annual; daisy-shaped blooms in golden yellow, orange, pink, peach, cream or bronze from late spring to frost; full sun to part shade; 12 to 24 in. tall, 12 to 18 in. wide Attractive to lady beetles, hoverflies

title: Regional Pest Roundup
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Grow long-blooming plants. That way there are always flowers for insects to feed on. While it's often the larvae that feed on pests, adults can have a short lifespan and need food at just the right time to feed, reproduce and lay eggs.

title: Regional Pest Roundup
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Insects need water too. Add a few stones to a birdbath so insects have shallow areas where they can safely access moisture.

title: Regional Pest Roundup
author: Sherri Ribbey
content: Flower shape makes a difference. Many beneficial insect adults feed on nectar and pollen but have small mouthparts. Make it easy for them to access by growing umbelshaped and daisy-shaped blooms.

content: Queen Anne's lace Daucus carota Biennial; white blooms in summer; full sun to part shade; 36 to 48 in. tall, 6 to 12 in. wide; cold hardy in USDA zones 3 to 11 Attractive to hoverflies, lacewings, lady beetles

title: The Giving Garden
author: Kristin Beane Sullivan
content: Walk through Sue and Bob Olson's Mankato, Minnesota, garden, and you'll find just as many stories as you'll find plants. Connections to other people are the heart of this 1/2-acre garden. For example, Sue says, "My brother built this shed for me about 15 years ago. I love it because it's his handiwork." Nearly every plant and ornament here carries a memory or a tie to a friend, family member or experience. This is why we chose the Olsons as our Annual Reader Garden Award grand prize winners. Congratulations to this creative gardening couple! Now let's take a tour and hear their stories.

title: The Giving Garden
author: Kristin Beane Sullivan
content: Reader Garden Award photo of the Olson backyard filled with mature perennial beds, annual color and garden paths.

title: The Giving Garden
author: Kristin Beane Sullivan
content: When Sue and Bob moved to Mankato and purchased this zone 5 property 26 years ago, the backyard was all lawn except for a perennial-filled island bed in need of renovation. Sue had grown up in a family of gardeners and always kept a garden as an adult. So she knew that it was better to watch the existing beds for a season to get to know the property before she started executing all of her backyard dreams.

title: The Giving Garden
author: Kristin Beane Sullivan
content: When they did dig into the perennial bed project, they found Siberian iris, garden phlox, daylilies, purple coneflowers and many other Midwestern stalwarts. Sue says, "I kept as much as I could but cleaned that bed up and spread the plants around."

title: The Giving Garden
author: Kristin Beane Sullivan
content: They raised their children in this house and now welcome grandchildren to visit. Once she had more time to garden, Sue really ramped up the outdoor projects, and every spring she and Bob seem to add another element to the backyard. (The latest project is a series of raised beds filled with cut flowers at the back of the garden.) You can see in the overhead view at right that the plantings extend around the backyard's

Over time, the couple has learned how to protect plantings from deer that live in the wooded area at the back of the property and how to keep a garden colorful from spring through fall.

title: The Giving Garden

content: Late-season enjoyment The wood fireplace gets the most use in the fall as the weather cools down and the mosquitos are less active.

title: The Giving Garden
author: Kristin Beane Sullivan
content: In warmer weather, they enjoy eating alfresco on the lower patio, which has two dining sets that accommodate their growing family. Up a few steps, visitors can retire to a comfortable lounge area complete with the wood-burning fireplace in photo 3, perfect for cool evenings in spring and fall.

title: The Giving Garden
author: Kristin Beane Sullivan
content: As all gardens do, this one has evolved. In the early years here, the couple dined on an upperlevel deck and had a hot tub on the nearby patio. Over time, habits and space usage changed. When entertaining became a bigger priority, they removed the hot tub, renovated that patio and added the fireplace. Then Sue and Bob built a second patio large enough to comfortably accommodate a group.

title: The Giving Garden
author: Kristin Beane Sullivan
content: Of course the Olsons enjoy entertaining in their backyard, but this isn't the only way they create memories and connect with people in the garden. Experiences with friends and family have contributed to the garden's décor and design as well.

title: The Giving Garden

content: A resting spot near the vegetable garden Because they don't have enough indoor storage space for it, Sue bought a furniture cover for the church pew, "cinches it tight and says a prayer" over winter.

title: The Giving Garden
author: Kristin Beane Sullivan
content: Beds and borders throughout this backyard are filled with reminders of loved ones and different experiences. CONNECTIONS TO THE PAST Several years ago Bob drove three hours with his car's hatchback open to bring home the pew in photo 4 from his childhood church. (On this trip he learned that if he turned the music volume high enough, he could drown out the dinging trunk alarm!) Sue painted a favorite quote on it and sealed it with Gronomics Cedar Garden Bed Oil to protect it.

title: The Giving Garden
author: Kristin Beane Sullivan
content: She says, "We used to carry every ornament and pot indoors every fall. But we got to the point that we couldn't do that anymore." She felt emboldened to leave glazed containers outdoors when she saw that a nearby nursery left their stock out in winter. Now the couple empties the pots, turns them upside down and leaves them where they stand. Sue says that they haven't lost one to winter damage yet.

title: The Giving Garden
author: Kristin Beane Sullivan
content: The colorful mosaic in photo 5 is made on window frames that Sue saved from Bob's grandmother's house. She has a few of these "stained glass" windows positioned throughout the garden and plans to store them indoors in winter.

title: The Giving Garden
author: Kristin Beane Sullivan
content: When they establish a new garden bed, the couple often adds meaningful mementos. For example, Bob finally talked Sue into purchasing a football-shaped stepping stone a few years ago with the agreement that he would maintain the part of the garden where it was displayed. He leaned into his love for the Minnesota Vikings NFL team, and planted a Velvet Viking Japanese maple among purple and gold plants, including the annual angelonias planted in a "V" shape in photo 6.

title: The Giving Garden
author: Kristin Beane Sullivan
content: Ten years ago, Sue was diagnosed with breast cancer in April. She says, "I knew what I was faced with, but I didn't want to let my gardens go. So I threw myself into the yard that spring." As she was working the night before treatments began, a butterfly landed on her again and again. She says, "In that moment, I knew everything would be OK." She later added some butterfly ornaments (you can see one of them in photo 7) in the area where she was working to remind her of the peace the butterfly brought her that day.

title: The Giving Garden
author: Kristin Beane Sullivan
content: And when Sue's dad passed away, they planted the river birch in photo 8 in his memory and added owl statuary beneath it. Sue says, "We always said Dad was the wise owl of the family."

title: The Giving Garden

title: The Giving Garden
author: Kristin Beane Sullivan
content: Gardening is a family pastime. In fact, many members of Sue's extended family grow pieces of the same bearded iris, peony and clematis passed down from her great-grandparents' garden. And her dad "kept gardening until he absolutely couldn't do it anymore. Then he loved to come here and give me ideas."

title: The Giving Garden
author: Kristin Beane Sullivan
content: Receiving and sharing divisions has been a key part of the garden's success. Filling these large beds wouldn't have happened as quickly without pass-along plants from other gardeners. Not only is this a budget-friendly way to acquire plants, it's also a good way to find those that you know will thrive. If they're already doing well in a neighbor's garden, you know they'll survive your particular climate's challenges. (Just do a bit of research before accepting divisions. Sometimes well-meaning friends share plants that are a little too aggressive!) Friends have passed along speedwell, more bearded iris, tall sedum and garden mums. They even have a division of the old-fashioned bleeding heart that Bob's mother received from a friend when he was born.

title: The Giving Garden
author: Kristin Beane Sullivan
content: Every spring, Bob and Sue grab their spades and look for perennials that are spreading too far or are overcrowded and need rejuvenation. Some go into new beds on their own property, but they plant the rest into recycled nursery pots in preparation for a giveaway. At this annual spring event, they set 250 or more potted plants onto the driveway and put out a call to gardeners in their neighborhood and in local social media groups, offering free plants.

title: The Giving Garden
author: Kristin Beane Sullivan
content: Sue says, "We love the idea of our passion being shared and nurtured, and we hope that some of it will be paid forward." It's a fun way to connect with old friends and make new ones (and a good way to recycle those ubiquitous plastic nursery pots, which often make their way back to the Olsons to be refilled another year!).

title: The Giving Garden
author: Kristin Beane Sullivan
content: To keep track of plants for herself and visitors in this ever-expanding garden, Sue inserts the tags you see in photo 10 near most perennials. She writes the plant name on the front of the tag and important details, such as its size, who gave it to her and the year it was last divided, on the back with a paint pen.

title: The Giving Garden
author: Kristin Beane Sullivan
content: Because the view of the backyard is so prominent from inside the house, it's important that it has year-round interest. Sue has achieved this by mixing hardscaping, ornaments and a variety of different types of plants. You can see the effect in photo 11.

title: The Giving Garden
author: Kristin Beane Sullivan
content: In many gardens, even with careful planning, there are lulls between bloom times throughout the growing season. But not here. Sue says, "I'm always paying attention to where I need more color. Will this spot need more purple when this plant fades? Do I need more yellow here?"

title: The Giving Garden
author: Kristin Beane Sullivan
content: The flower show begins with daffodils, grape hyacinths, peonies and Siberian irises in spring, and ends with garden mums and New England asters in late fall.

title: The Giving Garden
author: Kristin Beane Sullivan
content: Ribbons and splashes of annual begonias knit the Olson garden together. Sue likes Dragon Wing and Big series begonias, especially bronze-leaved varieties, and tries new varieties each year. She plants them in containers and clusters along border edges, pinches young plants to encourage branching, and roots cuttings directly in garden gaps so the plants fill in by late summer.

title: The Giving Garden
author: Kristin Beane Sullivan
content: Before the first frost, she cuts some plants back, pots them up and sets the pots on a shelf in the basement with no lights. They lie dormant until late winter, when she starts to water regularly. Sue says, "You'd swear that they're deader than dead, but they come back every year."

title: The Giving Garden
author: Kristin Beane Sullivan
content: Come spring, she begins taking cuttings again so she has plenty of little begonias to jump-start the year.

title: The Giving Garden
author: Kristin Beane Sullivan
content: Raised beds and extra fencing keep rabbits out. A layer of low fencing helps prevent rabbits from squeezing beneath the 6-foot-tall deer fence.

title: The Giving Garden
author: Kristin Beane Sullivan
content: A few years ago, Sue and Bob installed a 6-foot-tall aluminum fence around the backyard perimeter to keep deer out, but they still struggled with rabbits. Over the years, they sprayed vulnerable plants with Liquid Fence Deer and Rabbit Repellent in spring and caged shrubs in winter, but as the garden grew those extra chores became too tedious to manage.

title: The Giving Garden
author: Kristin Beane Sullivan
content: Eventually they discovered that planting vegetables and cut flowers in 17- to 32-inch-tall Vego Metal Raised Garden Beds made them diffi cult for bunnies to access. This year, Bob purchased 700 feet of 2-foot-high fencing and used plastic ties to secure it to the bottom of the fence, extending to soil level. So far it's kept rabbits from entering the garden. He knows that he'll have to patrol regularly to check for vulnerable spots and secure loose areas in the fence.

title: The Giving Garden
author: Kristin Beane Sullivan
content: Since only the backyard is fenced, Sue and Bob still spray and cage unprotected front-yard plants. Sue acknowledges that rabbits are frustrating but cute, and she has a large tongue-in-cheek collection of rabbit ornaments scattered through the beds; 'count the bunnies' is a game to play with grandchildren.

title: The Giving Garden
author: Kristin Beane Sullivan
content: A fresh layer of mulch every spring keeps weeding and watering chores manageable.

title: Pretty Permaculture
author: Chloe Deike
content: After some home construction, Joseph and Shalyn Donofro's zone 5 backyard was left with low-quality, compacted soil and not much of anything else. They envision a beautiful space that supports their young family's healthy lifestyle goals, teaches responsibility to their children and enables them to spend quality time outdoors together. They want the cottage garden aesthetic, as well as the benefits of basic permaculture practices, which encourage sustainability and enrich the well-being of both the garden and the gardeners.

title: Pretty Permaculture
author: Chloe Deike
content: Improving the depleted soil is priority number one. Some plants, such as the red clover used as a ground cover in several spots, have nitrogen-fixing abilities and add nutrients to the soil over time. Raised beds filled with quality soil provide an immediate solution. As the garden evolves, they'll be able to feed the soil with compost made on their own property.

title: Pretty Permaculture
author: Chloe Deike
content: A potting shed greenhouse brings that classic cottage garden feel, adds much-needed storage, extends the growing season and increases the garden's yield. Gutters and a rain barrel collect the rainwater, make it easy to access for use in the garden and keep the water bill down. And a small gravel patio makes a great spot for soaking up some vitamin D.

title: Pretty Permaculture
author: Chloe Deike
content: Enjoy these ideas for a design that's as practical as it is pleasing to the eye, then turn the page to learn how to make it work for you.

title: Pretty Permaculture
author: Chloe Deike
content: In permaculture landscapes, plant guilds are groups with mutual benefits and multiple functions. For example, one of the guilds in this garden includes chives, yarrow and red clover, which benefits the fruiting shrubs nearby. Chives are not just edible but have a strong aroma that keeps some pests at bay. The yarrow attracts pollinators and beneficial insects. This nonaggressive red clover adds nitrogen to the soil and acts as a living mulch. Under the apple trees, a guild of red clover and yellow archangel does the same.

title: Pretty Permaculture
author: Chloe Deike
content: Design Challenge rendering of a pretty permaculture backyard with raised beds, paths, ground covers, fruiting shrubs and a potting shed greenhouse.

title: Pretty Permaculture
author: Chloe Deike
content: Trim back bridal wreath spirea after it blooms - and use the branches elsewhere. Weave them together to make wattle fencing for the raised beds. Lay them as mulch around the base of the apple trees, or dry them and use as fire kindling.

title: Pretty Permaculture
author: Chloe Deike
content: Permaculture gardens can sometimes tend toward unruly looking. Here, a low, casual hedge brings definition and tidiness. If budget is a concern, plant a third of the shrubs each year until the hedge is complete.

title: Pretty Permaculture
author: Chloe Deike
content: Discreet pathways along the length of the property are wide enough to maneuver a wheelbarrow to the apple trees and compost bins. Use fine-textured shredded mulch, which knits together and stays in place well (and is soft enough for bare feet!), to cover these paths.

title: Pretty Permaculture
author: Chloe Deike
content: Full-page permaculture design illustration showing wattle fencing, berry hedges, mulch paths and productive backyard garden zones.

title: Pretty Permaculture
author: Chloe Deike
content: Approaching a garden with a permaculture mindset recognizes that things are always changing. Lumber and logs may not have the permanence of stone, but that is the purpose: they decompose and add back to the environment. The pathway is made from untreated 4x4s; as the lumber decomposes, larger pieces can be composted and replaced.

title: Pretty Permaculture
author: Chloe Deike
content: Ground covers in a new permaculture backyard will spread, but mulch around them for the first year or two while they get established. Save money on large quantities by taking divisions from friends, ordering flats of plugs from a local nursery, or planting sparsely and letting plants fill in. Red clover can be direct-sown in spring after the soil warms, then covered with a light layer of soil.

title: Pretty Permaculture
author: Chloe Deike
content: Plant scarlet runner bean seeds directly in the soil, or start indoors a few weeks before frost. At the end of the season, let bean shells dry and harden to save for the next year.

title: Pretty Permaculture
author: Chloe Deike
content: While you likely won't need to do much pruning to the fruiting shrubs, both can be cut back in late winter or early spring before buds emerge. Remove old branches to encourage greater production.

title: Pretty Permaculture
author: Chloe Deike
content: Over time, as the soil improves, feel free to swap some of the ground covers with a variety of plants. And be sure to thank your past self for working to create a fertile and growing environment!

title: Q&A
content: To attract toads, provide damp shade and water. A shallow saucer or pond gives toads a place to absorb moisture, while a cracked terra-cotta pot can become a toad house that helps them stay moist and hide from predators.

title: Q&A
content: Toads eat slugs, caterpillars, grasshoppers, beetles and many other insects, with one toad able to eat thousands in a month. Limit pesticide use so their food supply is not reduced and chemicals are not absorbed through their permeable skin.

title: Q&A
content: In northern climates, toads hibernate as temperatures drop by burrowing under damp leaves and garden debris. Leave some leaf litter in fall, build a woodpile or lay a few old boards on the ground to create hiding places.

title: Q&A
content: Peace lily flowers may turn brown before opening if temperature, light, humidity, water quality or fertilizer are wrong. Keep plants around 70 to 75 degrees F, away from drafts, in bright indirect east or north light, and increase humidity with a pebble tray or misting with distilled or rainwater.

title: Q&A
content: Peace lilies can react poorly to tap-water chemicals, so use rainwater, distilled water, filtered water or tap water left overnight before watering. Feed with a half-strength water-soluble fertilizer each time you water, and flush the pot with clear water if salts build up on the potting mix.

title: Q&A
content: Pruning cuts on trees usually heal best unsealed. Petroleum-based pruning sealers can damage the cambium, prevent callousing, block oxygen and trap moisture, encouraging bacteria and fungus that eventually rot heartwood and weaken the tree.

title: Q&A
content: Seeds advertised as vividly colored hostas are misleading because bright blue, vivid red and rich purple hosta cultivars do not exist. Buy hostas from reputable local or online sources that stand behind their plants.

title: Q&A
content: Colorful hosta options are real, but subtler than doctored seed ads. Red hosta leaves are still elusive, though cultivars such as 'Island Breeze', 'Cherry Berry' and 'Red Dragon' have red or burgundy petioles or leaf stems; blue hostas such as 'Halcyon', 'Blue Mouse Ears' and 'Blue Angel' are shade tolerant, and gold hostas such as 'Coast to Coast', 'Lemontini' and 'Lipstick Blonde' shine best with some sun.

title: Weed Watch: Motherwort
content: Motherwort, Leonurus cardiaca, is a perennial in the mint family that grows 2 to 5 feet tall with stiff upright square stems. From midsummer to late summer it produces tightly packed fuzzy light pink to lavender flowers along the stems.

title: Weed Watch: Motherwort
content: Motherwort leaves can be up to 4 inches long with five lobes and prominent veins. Crushed leaves and stems release a pungent odor; after flowers fade, spiky calyxes dry into brown spines that remain along the stems much of the winter. Pollinators visit the flowers, but animals rarely eat the plant because of the scent and spiny seedheads.

title: Weed Watch: Motherwort
content: Motherwort is native to Asia and was imported as a medicinal herb. It spreads by seed and rhizomes across much of North America, tolerates dry conditions and full sun, but prefers moist soil in part shade.

title: Weed Watch: Motherwort
content: Control motherwort by pulling young plants or digging older specimens with their shallow, fibrous roots and small surface rhizomes. Frequent mowing reduces seed production but may not stop rhizomes; herbicide is an option if necessary.

title: Q&A
content: Thigmotropism is the growth or movement of plant parts in response to physical contact. For example, when a vine touches a support, hormones cause one side of a stem or tendril to grow faster and direct a permanent wrapping action.

title: Q&A
content: A Venus flytrap uses a different mechanism called a thigmonastic response. The trap closes when an insect triggers it, but it can reopen and reverse the action to catch more food.

title: One Tough Native Plant: Light Up the Shade
author: Stephanie Polsley Bruner
content: Carolina pink, Spigelia marilandica, is a striking southeastern U.S. native for shade gardens and is becoming more common as a garden plant even though it is increasingly rare in the wild.

title: One Tough Native Plant: Light Up the Shade
author: Stephanie Polsley Bruner
content: Carolina pink reaches 12 to 24 inches tall and fits the middle of a shade border. It has red trumpet-shaped flowers with yellow centers, bold clean foliage that gives structure when plants are not blooming, and early-summer flowers that coincide with ruby-throated hummingbird arrivals.

title: One Tough Native Plant: Light Up the Shade
author: Stephanie Polsley Bruner
content: Carolina pink prefers moist, rich soil with plenty of organic matter and part shade. It tolerates more sun when it has more moisture. Deadheading or cutting plants back by about a third after the first flush can encourage some later rebloom.

title: One Tough Native Plant: Light Up the Shade
author: Stephanie Polsley Bruner
content: Carolina pink has tubular red flowers with yellow interiors in early to midsummer; part to full shade; moist, rich soil but tolerates wet soil; no serious pests; 12 to 24 inches tall and 12 to 18 inches wide; hardy in USDA zones 5 to 9.

title: One Tough Native Plant: Light Up the Shade
author: Stephanie Polsley Bruner
content: Compact Carolina pink cultivars include 'Ragin' Cajun', 'Little Redhead' and 'Apple Slices'.

title: One Tough Native Plant: Light Up the Shade
author: Stephanie Polsley Bruner
content: The Light Up the Shade combination pairs Carolina pink with cardinal flower 'Vulcan Red' and hosta 'Fire Island' near a deck or patio to draw hummingbirds. Spigelia blooms in early to midsummer with some flowers lasting until fall, lobelia adds mid- to late-summer red flowers, and the chartreuse hosta leaves glow all summer.

title: One Tough Native Plant: Light Up the Shade
author: Stephanie Polsley Bruner
content: Cardinal flower 'Vulcan Red', Lobelia x speciosa, is a perennial with bright red blooms on dark foliage in mid- to late summer; full sun to part shade; 24 to 32 inches tall and 10 to 14 inches wide; hardy in USDA zones 6 to 10.

title: One Tough Native Plant: Light Up the Shade
author: Stephanie Polsley Bruner
content: Hosta 'Fire Island' has burgundy red stems and lavender midsummer flowers; part shade to full shade; 14 inches tall and 18 inches wide; hardy in USDA zones 3 to 8.
