title: 3 Small-Space Gardens
content: Here are three 14x14-foot patio plans, each with its own distinct flavor, because a small space doesn't have to limit your style.

title: 3 Small-Space Gardens
content: Plant a short layer of plants in front of the larger vegetables to keep both accessible for harvest. Swap out edible nasturtiums for greens, cabbage or more herbs if desired.

title: 3 Small-Space Gardens
content: Use a decorative obelisk instead of a standard tomato cage to keep the space looking refined.

title: 3 Small-Space Gardens
content: Who says small spaces can't still produce a large amount of flowers and food? If you're a sucker for big blooms and homegrown edibles, here's everything you need to know.

title: 3 Small-Space Gardens
content: Plant this garden outside your kitchen door to easily access the veggies when prepping dinner, and you don't have to go far to enjoy a meal.

title: 3 Small-Space Gardens
content: One secret to getting the most produce in a small space is to add pollinator plants. Here, garden phlox brings in the butterflies and bees, ensuring a bumper crop of vegetables. And you can't beat the coziness of being surrounded by plants on almost all sides. 'Shockwave' phlox is also a long bloomer and has variegated foliage for even more interest. The hybrid foxglove lives and flowers longer than most other varieties. The shape of the patio allows for a little more growing space for edibles but still leaves enough room to walk around the table.

title: 3 Small-Space Gardens
content: Some vegetables are grown in containers because there isn't enough in-ground space available. In this garden, containers are placed in the border. The pots add height and keep the plants a manageable size. 'Astia' bush zucchini has lovely foliage that looks good in a container, but compact eggplant and okra make pretty plants too.

title: 3 Small-Space Gardens
content: Design plan illustration for a 14-by-14-foot cottage-style small-space garden with vegetables, flowers, containers and seating.

title: 3 Small-Space Gardens
content: Garden phlox 'Shockwave', Phlox paniculata, is a perennial with lavender-pink summer flowers and vibrant green-and-gold variegated foliage. Grow it in full sun to part shade; it reaches 12 to 18 inches tall and wide and is hardy in cold zones 4 to 8. Number to plant: 9.

title: 3 Small-Space Gardens
content: Foxglove Illumination Raspberry, Digitalis, is a tender perennial with multiple spikes of fuchsia-pink flowers with apricot throats that bloom on the same plant all summer. Grow it in full sun to part shade; it reaches 18 to 24 inches tall and wide and is hardy in cold zones 8 to 10. Number to plant: 6.

title: 3 Small-Space Gardens
content: Tomato 'Garden Gem', Solanum lycopersicum, is an annual bush tomato with snack-sized red fruit that matures early and produces prolifically on smaller plants. Grow it in full sun; it reaches 30 to 42 inches tall and 12 to 20 inches wide. Number to plant: 2.

title: 3 Small-Space Gardens
content: Nasturtium 'Aloha Mix', Tropaeolum majus, is an annual mix with apricot, cream, soft yellow and rose flowers from late spring until frost. The flowers are edible. Grow it in full sun; plants reach 10 to 12 inches tall and 12 to 15 inches wide. Number to plant: 12.

title: 3 Small-Space Gardens
content: Bush zucchini 'Astia', Cucurbita pepo, is an annual with yellow flowers that produce green fruit on bushlike plants with large white-mottled leaves. Grow it in full sun; plants reach 12 to 15 inches tall and 30 to 36 inches wide. Number to plant: 2.

title: 3 Small-Space Gardens
content: Mandevilla vines climb structures pretty easily, but you can also attach a small trellis or piece of lattice to the fence to help them climb.

title: 3 Small-Space Gardens
content: A lightweight aluminum bench is easy to move out of the way when you need to access the plants for maintenance.

title: 3 Small-Space Gardens
content: Adding privacy can be a challenge for a small space. Tall, solid fences can make an area feel congested and limit your plants to only those that can handle deep shade. But a fence also gives the opportunity for a total transformation - in this case, into a tropical oasis. Choose fencing that has room between each slat to let in a little more sun and promote airflow.

title: 3 Small-Space Gardens
content: In winter, bring these containers indoors, where the plants can be kept until the next growing season.

title: 3 Small-Space Gardens
content: Foliage-focused plants, like the banana and coleus, bring the tropical flair and provide long-lasting color. But the big banana leaves are also important for softening the corner to make it feel less like you're sitting in a box. Plus, it leads your eye up toward the sky and beyond the fence. On the opposite side, a mandevilla vine softens the sharp edges. A vigorous blooming vine like this is a great space-saving hack because it grows upward and not outward. The ligularia and fern are hardy perennials that keep this garden looking good all season long.

title: 3 Small-Space Gardens
content: Cozy white furniture with black metal accents sits atop a simple paver patio for a contemporary feel. A sectional can host a gathering of friends or give you space to lounge on your own. Black metal containers create a cohesive look.

title: 3 Small-Space Gardens
content: Design plan illustration for a tropical small-space garden with privacy fencing, mandevilla, banana, coleus, fern, ligularia and seating.

title: 3 Small-Space Gardens
content: Mandevilla 'Alice Du Pont', Mandevilla x amabilis, is a tender vine with large hot pink flowers in clusters from summer to fall. Cut it back and bring it indoors in winter. Grow it in full sun to part shade; it reaches 3 to 20 feet tall with a spreading habit and is hardy in cold zones 10 to 11. Number to plant: 1.

title: 3 Small-Space Gardens
content: Christmas fern, Polystichum acrostichoides, is a perennial with lacy green foliage that stays evergreen even in colder zones. Grow it in part to full shade; it reaches 1 to 2 feet tall and wide and is hardy in cold zones 3 to 9. Number to plant: 4.

title: 3 Small-Space Gardens
content: Coleus 'Superfine Rainbow Color Pride', Coleus scutellarioides, is a tender perennial with green, pink and purple mottled leaves. Pinch back flowers as they appear. Grow it in part to full shade; it reaches 12 to 15 inches tall and wide and is hardy in cold zones 10 to 11. Number to plant: 6.

title: 3 Small-Space Gardens
content: Ligularia 'Bottle Rocket' is a perennial with tall yellow flower spikes in summer above large dark green, deeply veined leaves. Grow it in part to full shade; it reaches 28 to 34 inches tall and 24 to 38 inches wide and is hardy in cold zones 4 to 9. Number to plant: 2.

title: 3 Small-Space Gardens
content: Red Abyssinian banana, Ensete maurelii, is a tender perennial with large green leaves that have a burgundy tint and burgundy stems, plus insignificant late-summer flowers. Grow it in full sun to part shade; it reaches 5 to 20 feet tall and 6 to 8 feet wide and is hardy in cold zones 9 to 11. Number to plant: 1.

title: 3 Small-Space Gardens
content: Cut back the perennials in fall after they die back, and add a fresh layer of mulch to keep the space looking tidy through winter and spring.

title: 3 Small-Space Gardens
content: You don't need to prune often to keep the loose topiary shape after the Seville orange is established; just trim off new growth.

title: 3 Small-Space Gardens
content: Add even more color by painting the furniture or putting an outdoor area rug underneath.

title: 3 Small-Space Gardens
content: Put the containers on saucers with wheels so they can be moved when you need to maintain the plants in the bed behind them.

title: 3 Small-Space Gardens
content: Less can be more, especially when creating a small, formal garden to sit and converse with company. Low-maintenance plants with compact and controlled habits keep the space looking tidy and well-kept at all times.

title: 3 Small-Space Gardens
content: When working with a limited plant palette, it's important to go for long-blooming choices that have multiseason interest. It's more obvious when something in a small space isn't looking its best. Compact 'Jelly Belly' blueberries start the show in spring with white blossoms, indigo blue berries in summer and deep red fall foliage. With more compact cultivars of shrubs available, there are many options for growing your old favorites without using all the real estate. 'Little Quick Fire' hydrangea is smaller than most panicle hydrangeas, but still big enough to garner attention. Its creamy flowers slowly turn dark pink and can be cut, or left for winter interest. Its size makes a nice backdrop for a bistro set and provides a touch of privacy.

title: 3 Small-Space Gardens
content: Traditional iron furniture and fencing build on the stylish theme. Symmetry is important to creating a formal atmosphere. That's why the left side mirrors the right. And topiaries always lend a polished look. The edible bitter orange tastes best as a marmalade - include it on a cheese plate for guests!

title: 3 Small-Space Gardens
content: Design plan illustration for a formal small-space garden with hydrangeas, speedwell, blueberry, Seville orange topiary, containers and bistro seating.

title: 3 Small-Space Gardens
content: Speedwell 'Pink Marshmallow', Veronica spicata, is a perennial with spires of light pink buds that become dark pink flowers in summer. Grow it in full sun to part shade; it reaches 12 to 18 inches tall and 18 to 24 inches wide and is hardy in cold zones 4 to 8. Number to plant: 20.

title: 3 Small-Space Gardens
content: Little Quick Fire panicle hydrangea, Hydrangea paniculata, is a shrub with white flowers in early summer that bloom before other hydrangeas and fade to pink by fall. Grow it in full sun to part shade; it reaches 3 to 5 feet tall and wide and is hardy in cold zones 3 to 8. Number to plant: 1.

title: 3 Small-Space Gardens
content: Seville orange, Citrus x aurantium, is a tree with white flowers in early spring that lead to orange fruit. It can be kept to a manageable size in a container and overwintered indoors. Grow it in full sun; it reaches 13 to 26 feet tall and 8 to 13 feet wide and is hardy in cold zones 9 to 11. Number to plant: 2.

title: 3 Small-Space Gardens
content: Perennial geranium 'Rozanne' has violet-blue flowers from late spring to fall. Grow it in full sun to part shade; it reaches 12 to 20 inches tall and 12 to 24 inches wide and is hardy in cold zones 4 to 8. Number to plant: 10.

title: 3 Small-Space Gardens
content: Blueberry Jelly Bean, Vaccinium corymbosum, is a compact shrub with white spring flowers, blue summer berries and yellow-red fall foliage. Grow it in full sun to part shade; it reaches 1 to 2 feet tall and wide and is hardy in cold zones 4 to 8. Number to plant: 6.

title: Seasonal Guide: Winter Garden Tasks
content: Winter is a great time to do some much-needed cleaning in and around your garden. As the days slowly begin to get longer, take advantage of those extra few minutes of daylight to get outside and work, but there's also plenty to do indoors!

title: Seasonal Guide: Winter Garden Tasks
content: Late winter is an ideal time to prune most roses, while the plants are dormant. Perfect timing really depends on the type of roses you're growing and your hardiness zone, so do your homework if you're not sure. Once-blooming roses should be pruned after they bloom in the spring, for instance. Repeat-blooming roses (many hybrid teas and floribundas) bloom on new growth in that season. Prune these in late winter while they're still dormant, or just before they break dormancy.

title: Seasonal Guide: Winter Garden Tasks
content: More than 100 bird species supplement their natural diets with foods offered at feeders. They often rely most heavily on feeders in winter, when food is scarce. Selecting a specific feeder design and a variety of foods can set the table for a greater diversity of birds. Providing more than one feeder will prevent crowding at your backyard buffet. Keep birds coming back with three essential ingredients: the right mix of quality seed and other foods, a source of fresh water for drinking and bathing, and trees and plants that can offer shelter.

title: Seasonal Guide: Winter Garden Tasks
content: Starting plants from seeds indoors can be an enjoyable project for any gardener. It's a relatively inexpensive way to grow a wide variety of plants. Many garden favorites are found in a greater assortment of colors, sizes and growth habits as seeds, rather than as plants. Look on the seed packet to find the number of weeks you're supposed to start seeds indoors before the average last frost date. Count backward from that frost date: It's usually six to eight weeks.

title: Seasonal Guide: Winter Garden Tasks
content: The last thing you want to do in the spring is waste your time (and money) shopping for new tools. Take a few minutes to properly clean and store them. Use soap and water to remove residual dirt and dried-on materials from garden tool surfaces. Scrape off stubborn clumps with a putty knife or a wire brush. The steel brushes made for cleaning grills work great for this because they usually have bristles on one side and a scraping tool on the other.

title: Seasonal Guide: Winter Garden Tasks
content: Cold winter days are the perfect opportunity for planning your garden for the following year. Sit back with a glass of wine and enjoy plotting the year to come. Look at gardening books, magazines and seed catalogs for inspiration. Always remember to be realistic about the size of your garden and the time you have available. Sketch out your garden plan to visualize the entire space. It doesn't have to be as elaborate as the one shown here; it can be as simple as drawing circles on paper to represent garden elements.

title: Seasonal Guide: Winter Garden Tasks
content: Now is the time to walk around your garden and see where you can add plants for winter interest. Choosing plants that will look good during the colder months is often a matter of thinking about bark, berries and shapes. Many plants, such as Japanese maple ( Acer palmatum ), have unusual colors of bark. Other trees, like the Kousa dogwood ( Cornus kousa ), have interesting fruits or seeds that form during the fall and winter. Deciduous vines like wisteria can form strange, twisting branches that look like surreal sculptures in the winter. Even dried seedheads, like the clematis shown here, offer their own appeal. Use your imagination and you're bound to create a beautiful winter landscape.

title: Seasonal Guide: Winter Garden Tasks
content: One of the best ways to escape the season's chill is to visit one of the many winter flower shows being held across the country. These are fantastic places to gather ideas, meet fellow gardeners and learn what is new. Just remember to wear a good pair of walking shoes because you will want to see everything and there will be a lot of ground to cover. Bring a tote bag or backpack, a small camera, a pen and a notepad. Be sure to write down the names of any plants that catch your eye.

title: Seasonal Guide: Winter Garden Tasks
content: Forcing bulbs indoors lets you enjoy the colors and fragrance of spring when it's still months away. The key to success is planning ahead. There are two types of bulbs for forcing: those you need to chill and those you don't. Amaryllis ( Hippeastrum spp. and hybrids) and paperwhites ( Narcissus papyraceus ) don't require chilling and can be grown in a pot filled with soil or in a shallow bowl filled with pebbles and water. Daffodils ( Narcissus spp. and hybrids), hyacinths ( Hyacinthus orientalis ) and crocus ( Crocus spp. and hybrids), however, require a chilling period before they'll bloom, usually 8 to 12 weeks. Chill these in the crisper drawer of your refrigerator.

title: Seasonal Guide: Winter Garden Tasks
content: Winter is a great time to repot house plants. A sign that it's time to repot is if you see roots on the surface of your container or roots growing out of the drainage holes at the bottom. Slow growth can also be a sign that your plants have become root-bound. Check to see if the roots are coiling around the inside of the pot; if so, it is time to repot. Many indoor plants like to be repotted prior to a new growing season.

title: Know Your Zone
content: The USDA Plant Hardiness Zone Map has long been the authority to help gardeners pick plants that will survive through the winter. It designates zones based on average annual minimum temperatures throughout the United States. A plant's cold-hardiness zone rating indicates where it's likely to survive the winter.

title: In the Weeds: Lettuce Might Be Magical
author: Jamie Seitz
content: Leaf lettuce grows so quickly after cutting that it can feel magical. For gardeners who eat a lot of salad, homegrown leaf lettuce reduces produce costs, tastes better and builds confidence because seedlings appear quickly after winter.

title: In the Weeds: Lettuce Might Be Magical
author: Jamie Seitz
content: Cut-and-come-again lettuce can be harvested for dinner without cutting the whole plant at once. After a harvest, the leaves grow back fast enough that another cutting may be ready almost immediately.

title: In the Weeds: Lettuce Might Be Magical
author: Jamie Seitz
content: The magic of leaf lettuce fades when harvests become overwhelming. When hot temperatures arrive, letting lettuce go to seed ends the nonstop salad cycle until fall planting brings the excitement back again.
